stem: A 45-year-old man attends the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 4week history of profuse watery diarrhoea. He has been experiencing intermittent cramping abdominal pain and episodes of nausea, but he denies vomiting. His appetite is reduced and he is now feeling extremely fatigued. There is no history of recent travel or a change in diet. He denies any past medical history or regular medications. On examination, his temperature is 36.1 °C. He appears pale and cachectic, but he is not jaundiced. His heart rate is 102 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 99/69 mmHg. He has generalised abdominal tenderness but no guarding or palpable masses. There are needle track marks visible in his left antecubital fossa. Modiﬁed Ziehl–Neelsen stain – positive What is the most likely causative organism for this patient’s presentation?
explanation:
D Cryptosporidium hominis This patient has a prolonged diarrhoeal illness. His examination ﬁndings, including needle track marks, pallor and cachexia, suggest an underlying diagnosis of human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV). C. hominis is a parasitic organism that is a common cause of diarrhoea in immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV. The most common symptoms are watery diarrhoea and cramping abdominal pain. However, in more severe disease, the parasite can cause complications such as pancreaticobiliary infection, including pancreatitis or cholecystitis. The positive modiﬁed Ziehl–Neelsen stain should help conﬁrm the diagnosis. Treatment of cryptosporidiosis includes treatment of the parasitic infection, but also the immunodeﬁciency with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). A Giardia duodenalis G. duodenalis is an intestinal parasite that causes a diarrhoeal illness spread via the faecal–oral route, following exposure to contaminated food, water or faeces. It causes a more prolonged illness lasting up to six weeks in duration. Other features of the illness include abdominal bloating, ﬂatulence or malabsorption. The presentation is similar to the case described in the question. However, the addition of needle track marks suggests that this man is an intravenous drug user. Combined with his pale and cachectic appearance, the question hints towards an underlying diagnosis of human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV). C. hominis is a common cause of diarrhoea in individuals with HIV and is the most likely causative organism in this patient. B Shigella dysenteriae S. dysenteriae is a Gram-negative bacillus that causes shigellosis or bacillary dysentery characterised by bloody diarrhoea and passing mucus per rectum. In immunocompromised patients, it can cause systemic upset and complications include haemolytic uraemic syndrome. This presentation is not reﬂected in the question, making it less likely to be the correct answer.

C Entamoeba histolytica E. histolytica is a protozoan responsible for the disease amoebiasis. It is common in South and Central America, South East Asia and West Africa. The majority of infections are asymptomatic. However, in some patients, amoebiasis can lead to dysentery or invasive disease, including amoebic liver abscess formation. This patient has neither features of dysentery nor a history of recent travel, making his diagnosis less likely to be amoebiasis. E Escherichia coli E. coli is a Gram-negative bacillus that can cause acute gastroenteritis and is the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea. It typically causes profuse watery diarrhoea with abdominal pain and nausea. The illness is usually self-limiting and a 4-week history of diarrhoea should raise suspicion of an alternative diagnosis.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents complaining of a 4-week history of joint pain since returning from his holiday in Spain with a group of male friends. He has noticed stiffness and pain in his ﬁngers and hands, and pain in his lower back. A couple of weeks previously he had also noticed stinging when passing urine, although this has now improved a lot. His mother has commented on how red his eyes look. He has no past medical history but is concerned as his uncle has ankylosing spondylitis. On examination, there is no swelling of the joints of the hand but there is some clear discomfort on movement. Flexion and extension of the spine is also limited by pain and there is tenderness over the sacroiliac joint. There are no skin rashes but he his eyes are shown below. Which test will be most useful in making the diagnosis?
explanation: D Urethral swab for microscopy The symptoms (arthralgia, urethritis and conjunctivitis) are classical of sexually acquired reactive arthritis (SARA) with symptoms developing within 30 days of unprotected sexual intercourse and a mean lag of 14 days between the symptoms of urethritis and the joint symptoms. If the patient is found to have >5 polymorphonuclear cells/high-powered ﬁeld then that will give the diagnosis. Associated conjunctivitis is a common association, more rarely, iritis can occur. A Urinalysis This would be the correct answer if urinary tract infection was the right diagnosis. However, this is very unlikely given the patient is a young man, and also would not explain joint pain and conjunctivitis. B Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) typing This option suggests a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis. Ankylosing spondylitis is a possibility but should not cause dysuria. However, even if typing reveals human leukocyte antigen (HLA)B27, that will in no way prove ankylosing spondylitis as imaging of the sacroiliac joints and a close history would be far more helpful in establishing that diagnosis. C Rheumatoid factor It would be helpful in establishing a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. While rheumatoid arthritis can cause joint pain and eye symptoms, the absence of any joint swelling, erythema or tenderness on examination, as well as stiffness in the history, makes this unlikely. His demographics and the presence of dysuria further make this an unlikely diagnosis. E X-ray of the sacroiliac joint This would be the most appropriate investigation to establish ankylosing spondylitis and would have been the correct answer if the history did not have dysuria and there was stiffness of his back.

stem: A 32-year-old man is readmitted to the hospital some 14 days after his renal transplant. He has begun feeling very unwell with ﬂu-like symptoms, a headache and sore throat. He has been checking his temperature at home and is now spiking fevers of 38.5 °C. On examination, he looks poorly, with pyrexia of 38.2 °C in the Emergency room and evidence of pharyngitis. On reviewing his notes, you see that he was CMV-, Hep B- and Hep C- negative before his transplant. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 235 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 49 mm/hour < 10 mm/hour Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
explanation:
A Intravenous (iv) ganciclovir

The most likely diagnosis here is one of CMV infection post-renal transplant, for which IV ganciclovir is the default treatment choice. It is very likely that the kidney has come from a CMV-positive donor. Symptoms of CMV infection post-transplant can appear any time from 6-60 days after surgery and are characterised by pyrexia, ﬂu-like symptoms or an infectious mononucleosis-type picture as seen here. Indeed, transplant surgeons now consider the option of prophylactic ganciclovir in patients who are CMV- but their transplanted kidney comes from a CMV+ donor. The concern is that active CMV infection is associated with accelerated failure of the transplanted kidney. D iv benzylpenicillin and gentamycin This would be a reasonable option for the treatment of bacterial endocarditis. B iv Foscarnet Ganciclovir is preferred to foscarnet as a treatment option because of adverse events associated with foscarnet therapy, including marrow suppression. C iv Vancomcin and teicoplanin This would be an option for bacterial sepsis as a result of the transplant. The modest increase in ESR and normal white blood count make a viral infection more likely. E iv aciclovir Although acyclovir was previously used for CMV prophylaxis, valgancyclovir is now preferred.

stem: A 32-year-old man, whose main hobby is ﬁshing in local freshwater lakes, comes to the Emergency Room feeling extremely unwell. Over the past few days, he has suffered from a ﬂu-like illness but, during the past 24 h, has deteriorated further with a cough productive of blood-stained sputum, a severe headache, fevers and jaundice. On examination, he is pyrexial (37.9 °C). His BP is 100/60 mmHg, his pulse is 95 bpm and regular. He has a non-speciﬁc skin rash and tenderness in the right upper quadrant on abdominal examination. Investigations: Hb 111 g/l WCC 13.2 × 109/l PLT 95 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l Creatinine 201 μmol/l CK 980 U/l ALT 152 U/l Bilirubin 280 μmol/l Given the likeliest diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy for him?
explanation: E Benzylpenicillin This man has symptoms consistent with severe leptospirosis, or Weil’s disease. It is likely he acquired it through exposure to rats’ urine associated with his ﬁshing trips. Erythromycin and doxycycline may be considered in patients who are unsuitable for penicillin therapy, or in those with very mild symptoms of infection, but IV penicillin is the primary treatment for severe disease. The peak in incidence of cases of leptospirosis appears to be in the late summer/early autumn in temperate climates, where it may be that moist, humid conditions allow the bacteria to persist for longer. C Erythromycin Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic with activity against Grampositive and atypical organisms. This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of leptospirosis, and although erythromycin has some activity, there is a better option available. A Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotic with a wide spectrum of activity against Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria. The patient’s presentation is suggestive of leptospirosis, and so ciproﬂoxacin would not be an effective treatment. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. B Doxycycline Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with activity against Grampositive and atypical organisms. The patient’s presentation is consistent with severe leptospirosis, and although doxycycline is the treatment of choice for milder forms of the disease, this patient warrants admission and parenteral therapy. D Chloramphenicol Chloramphenicol is a long-established antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity against Gram-positive, - negative and atypical organisms. Its use has been limited due to severe potential adverse effects. The presentation described is highly suspicious for leptospirosis, and thus chloramphenicol is not an appropriate treatment for this condition.

stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department complaining of a severe sore throat. He was brought to the Emergency Department having returned from a holiday in the Caribbean. He has a temperature of 38.2 oC, his pulse is 58 beats per minute (bpm) and regular, and his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg. Examination of the pharynx is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his infection?
explanation:
A Corynebacterium diphtheriae (C diphtheriae) The clues to this patient suffering from diphtheria include the fact that he has recently returned from the Caribbean, and that he has the typical adherent grey/white membrane associated with pharyngitis seen in the condition. Sporadic outbreaks are still seen around the world, although it is extremely rare. The most recent occurred in Haiti in 2019. This patient’s relatively low pulse rate may be as a result of myocarditis related to diphtheria toxin. Diphtheria antitoxin combined with erythromycin is the preferred intervention.

E Streptococcus pyogenes (S pyogenes) S pyogenes is a common cause of pharyngitis. It is usually sensitive to penicillin and presents with erythema where there is often adherent pus over the tonsillar bed. It does not present with the grey-white pseudomembrane seen here. B Haemophilus inﬂuenzae (H inﬂuenzae) The main concern with respect to H inﬂuenzae infection is acute epiglottitis which is seen in children. It is not associated with the grey/white adherent membrane seen here. Vaccination against H inﬂuenzae type B has signiﬁcantly reduced the incidence of acute epiglottitis. Ceftriaxone, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and azithromycin are all potential treatment options. C Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P aeruginosa) Pseudomonas pharyngitis is more rarely reported. It is usually associated with erythema, but frank pus is unusual, and a membrane is not seen. Antibiotic therapy is chosen according to sensitivities, but for example, it may include ciproﬂoxacin, gentamycin or piperacillin, and tazobactam. D Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus) S aureus is recognised as a cause of recurrent tonsillitis. Patients with staphylococcal tonsillitis have erythema on examination and often frank pus, although the grey-white membrane seen here is absent. Most staphylococcal isolates seen in tonsillitis are resistant to penicillin.

stem: A 21-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of malaise and arthralgia, and a non-itchy red rash all over his body, particularly his lower legs. Two days before he presented, his right knee became increasingly red, swollen and painful with extreme limitation of movement. He had no other past medical history. On examination he had a temperature of 38.5 °C, and pulse rate was 105 bpm. He had an erythematous maculopapular rash formed of small (< 5 mm) lesions in the distribution mentioned above. His right knee was swollen, erythematous and exquisitely painful with a large effusion. On examination of the other joints, there was some evidence of tenosynovitis at the wrists. His right knee joint was aspirated and a turbid yellow ﬂuid was removed. What is most likely to be seen on microscopy?
explanation:
A High numbers of neutrophils This patient clearly has a septic arthritis of the right knee. The history is classic for gonococcal septic arthritis, with malaise caused by disseminated gonococcal infection and a triad of tenosynovitis, arthritis and dermatitis. This is followed by a localised phase where the arthritis can either resolve spontaneously (as in 40–60% of cases) or develop into a septic arthritis. However, organisms are seen in the joint aspirate in less than 25% of cases: it is far more common simply to ﬁnd turbid ﬂuid and a large number of neutrophils. The aspirate and blood should be cultured. Clearly, intravenous antibiotics are needed for this degree of sepsis and joint involvement. There is signiﬁcant resistance of gonorrhoea to penicillin and ciproﬂoxacin, and therefore ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice. Examination of the joint and wash-out under anaesthetic is also indicated. D Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals Acute gout can cause a hot, swollen joint and fever; however, given this patient’s age and lack of comorbidities, gout is an unlikely diagnosis. Furthermore, gout does not explain the prodromal rash, or the tenosynovitis evident in the patient’s wrists. Instead, this is a classical history for gonococcal septic arthritis. There is a bacteraemic phase with a triad of arthritis, tenosynovitis and dermatitis. This is followed by a localised phase where the patient can develop a septic arthritis, as seen here. Organisms are only seen in 25% of joint aspirates in gonococcal septic arthritis, and therefore the most likely ﬁnding in the aspirate is high numbers of neutrophils. B Gram-negative diplococcic You may have identiﬁed that this patient has a history consistent with gonococcal septic arthritis: however, organisms are seen in joint aspirates in less than 25% of cases and it is far more likely that the aspirate will be turbid and reveal neutrophils alone. The malaise and triad of tenosynovitis, arthritis and dermatitis (as seen in this patient) is caused by a bacteraemic phase. There is then a localised phase where either the arthritis resolves spontaneously or patients develop a septic arthritis, as seen here. C Gram-positive cocci This patient has a septic arthritis, and his prodrome of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and arthritis is typical of disseminated gonococcal infection, with a bacteraemic and then a localised phase. Gonococcus is a Gram- negative diplococcus; however, organisms are only seen on microscopy of joint aspirates in 25% of cases. It is far more

common for the aspirate to simply show high numbers of neutrophils. E Positively birefringent rhomboidal-shaped crystals Pseudo-gout can cause a hot and swollen joint, and sometimes a fever. However, given this patient’s age and lack of comorbidities, it is an unlikely diagnosis and the patient should be assumed to have septic arthritis until proven otherwise. In fact, this patient’s history is classic for gonococcal arthritis: a bacteraemic phase with a triad of arthritis, tenosynovitis and dermatitis, and then a localised phase in which patients can develop a septic arthritis. Organisms are seen in the joint aspirate in only 25% of cases, and therefore the most likely ﬁnding on microscopy is high numbers of neutrophils.

stem: A 70-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of severe, watery diarrhoea. He was originally from Namibia, but had not left the UK for 45 years. He had had a similar episode of diarrhoea 15 years ago, but was otherwise well. He admits to losing around 10 kg in weight over the past year. On examination, he was afebrile, and he appeared thin. There was non-speciﬁc abdominal tenderness. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 192 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 159 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Eosinophils 0.7 × 109/l 0.04–0.4 × 109/l Which of the following is the most likely cause for his symptoms?
explanation:
D Strongyloides stercoralis This patient’s presentation with non-bloody, watery diarrhoea and no signiﬁcant systemic upset would be typical, especially when combined with a chronic disease course (suggested by the previous episode of diarrhoea and the weight loss) and a mild eosinophilia. Strongyloidiosis is endemic to Namibia and chronic infection can last for many years with only the mildest of symptoms. It can be diagnosed through microscopic examination of the stool for larvae. Despite only minor symptoms, all strongyloidiosis should be treated in order to avoid a hyper-infection syndrome: treatment is with ivermectin for two days. A Campylobacter jejuni Campylobacter is the most common cause of infectious gastroenteritis in the UK, typically transmitted through food. It classically causes a short-lived severe bloody diarrhoea accompanied by signiﬁcant systemic upset, with high fevers. This patient does not have bloody diarrhoea and appears generally well. Furthermore, this patient has an eosinophilia, which would not be consistent with Campylobacter. Instead, the eosinophilia, lack of systemic upset and the patient’s Namibian background would suggest a parasite – speciﬁcally, Strongyloides spp. This parasite is endemic in Namibia and in its chronic form can cause non-speciﬁc abdominal pain and profuse diarrhoea after many years without symptoms, as seen here. B Cryptosporidium spp. Cryptosporidium spp. are parasites causing diarrhoea that typically affect young children and the immunocompromised. Typically the diarrhoea is green, offensive smelling and watery. Patients generally have mild malaise and a low-grade fever; high fevers are not seen in cryptosporidiosis. If this was an acute presentation of cryptosporidiosis, you would not expect to see weight loss. This patient is afebrile and systemically well. He has a background of a previous episode of diarrhoea and is thin, suggesting a long-term cause of malabsorption that could not be explained by a single episode of cryptosporidiosis. Instead, given this patient’s presentation, history and Namibian background, infection with Strongyloides spp. is the most likely cause. Strongyloidosis is endemic in Namibia. This would also explain the patient’s eosinophilia. C Escherichia coli E. coli is the most common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller and a common cause of infectious diarrhoea in the UK, especially in young children. E. coli would not explain the eosinophilia seen in this patient, and also could not explain his chronic weight loss. These features point towards a parasitic intestinal infection, causing a low-grade inﬂammatory response and

prolonged malabsorption. In this case, with the patient’s presentation and Namibian background, Strongyloides spp. is the most likely cause. This parasitic infection is endemic in Namibia and chronic infection can persist for many years with the most minor of symptoms. E Vibrio parahaemolyticus This is a bacterial cause of infectious gastroenteritis, causing severe watery diarrhoea. It is typically contracted through eating raw or undercooked seafood. Although this patient has severe watery diarrhoea, he also has weight loss and has had a previous similar episode, which suggests a chronic disease course with malabsorption. More importantly, he has an eosinophilia which cannot be explained by a bacterial gastroenteritis. This, combined with his Namibian background, makes Strongyloides stercoralis the most likely cause of his symptoms. This is a parasitic intestinal infection endemic to Namibia, which can cause a chronic disease with episodes of mild abdominal pain and severe watery diarrhoea, and malabsorption leading to weight loss.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presented with a 9-day history of lower abdominal pain which worsened during intercourse. She also reported two episodes of post-coital per vaginam bleeding. Her sexual history included unprotected intercourse with two male partners in the preceding 2 weeks. On examination, she was pyrexial at 37.6 °C, and there was bilateral pain on bimanual palpation. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 126 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC Cervical smear 9.5 × 109/l Neutrophils + 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Chlamydia Chlamydia is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the UK, with a prevalence of around 8% in the under 20s and 5% in those aged 20–24. This patient’s symptoms of bilateral pelvic pain and intermittent fever, and deep dyspareunia, are suggestive of pelvic inﬂammatory disease, of which chlamydia is the most common cause. The neutrophils on microscopy without any visible

bacterial is typical of chlamydia: however, the preferred method of diagnosis now is nucleic acid ampliﬁcation testing (NAAT) from a high vulvo-vaginal swab, rather than endocervical swabs. Men can be tested via ﬁrst-catch urine samples or urethral swabs. First-line antibiotics would be either doxycycline or a single dose of azithromycin, and contact tracing should be undertaken. D Gonorrhoea Gonorrhoea can be asymptomatic, or cause pelvic pain as seen here. However, classically it presents with mucopurulent discharge. Furthermore, you would expect to see Gram-negative diplococci on microscopy, not simply neutrophils as seen in this case. This patient’s symptoms, signs and investigations are consistent with pelvic inﬂammatory disease, the most common cause of which is chlamydia. A Bacterial vaginosis Bacterial vaginosis does not cause dyspareunia, pelvic pain or fever. Instead, patients typically complain of a change in vaginal discharge: an increased amount of thin, whitish malodourous discharge. A cervical smear would typically show ‘clue cells’ – these are vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria. Instead, this patient’s dyspareunia, pelvic pain and intermittent fever, combined with a history of unprotected sex, are more suggestive of chlamydia, causing pelvic inﬂammatory disease. B Candidiasis Candidiasis, or thrush, causes soreness, itching, erythema and a thick, white, curd-like discharge: none of these symptoms are described here. Vaginal thrush does not cause deep dyspareunia (though if severe, it may cause superﬁcial dyspareunia), pelvic pain or intermittent fever. Microscopy would not show polymorphs, as in this case. Instead, this patient’s symptoms and investigations are more consistent with a diagnosis of pelvic inﬂammatory disease caused by chlamydia. E Trichomonas Trichomonas is a very common sexually transmitted infection, typically causing cervicitis and increased frothy, yellow malodorous discharge. It can cause lower abdominal pain but would be unlikely to cause sustained pain, fevers or dyspareunia. This patient’s symptoms are more in keeping with pelvic inﬂammatory disease caused by chlamydia.

stem: A 51-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1week history of intermittent fever and ﬂu- like symptoms. He complains of general malaise and myalgia. There is no past medical history of note and he has otherwise been well, having recently returned from a hiking trip. He has no allergies. On examination, he appears lethargic. He has a tachycardia of 102 bpm and blood pressure of 123/81 mmHg. The remainder of his observations are within the normal range. On his left lower leg, there is a target-shaped lesion. There is no evidence of crusting or bleeding and the rest of his skin and mucosa are spared. He is given a prescription for an antimicrobial. What is the mechanism of action of his antimicrobial prescription?
explanation: C Inhibits 30S subunit of ribosomes This patient has Lyme disease, an illness spread by tick bites. A recent hiking trip gives a hint to the likely diagnosis, along with the target-shaped lesion on his leg. The treatment of choice is doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic that works by binding to the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Aminoglycosides also have a similar mechanism of action. E Inhibits deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) synthesis This patient has Lyme disease, for which the treatment is with doxycycline, which works by blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit. Quinolones, such as ciproﬂoxacin work by inhibiting DNA synthesis. They bind to the enzyme DNA gyrase and, therefore, inhibit the replication of bacterial DNA. A Damages bacterial DNA Metronidazole is an antibiotic with a good afﬁnity against anaerobic organisms. It works by damaging bacterial DNA through the production of toxic metabolites. It is not used in the treatment of Lyme disease. B Disrupts cell membrane function Penicillin antibiotics work by disrupting cell membrane function by binding to and inhibiting, proteins in the bacterial cell wall. They are not used in the ﬁrst-line treatment for Lyme disease. D Inhibits 50S subunit of ribosomes This patient has Lyme disease, for which the treatment is with doxycycline that works by blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit. Macrolides, such as erythromycin and different classes of antibiotics, including clindamycin and linezolid, work in a similar way to tetracyclines. However, rather than blocking the 30S ribosomal subunit, they block the 50S subunit.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe pain in his left lower leg that began 24 hours ago. The pain has rapidly worsened, out of proportion to the physical ﬁndings, and he now has swelling and erythema extending from the knee to the ankle. He has a history of type II diabetes and hypertension. On examination, the leg is swollen with erythematous, tender skin and patches of discoloration, but there are no clear signs of ﬂuctuance or abscess formation. His temperature is 39°C his BP is 90/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 110 bpm. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 129 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 25 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l CRP 250 mg/l < 5 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 129 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Creatine kinase (CK) 820 U/l 30–200 U/l What is the most appropriate next step in investigating this patient’s condition?
options: Doppler ultrasound of the affected leg
explanation:
C Surgical exploration Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement to halt the spread of infection. Prompt surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic, as it allows direct visualisation of tissue necrosis and removal of infected tissue. D MRI of the affected leg MRI can show soft tissue involvement and may aid in diagnosis when the clinical presentation is uncertain. However, MRI may delay deﬁnitive treatment, and in cases with high clinical suspicion, immediate surgical exploration is preferred. A Urgent tissue biopsy While a tissue biopsy can conﬁrm the diagnosis microscopically, surgical exploration is prioritised to establish the diagnosis and to allow for immediate debridement, which is lifesaving in necrotising fasciitis.

B Blood cultures Blood cultures are indicated in patients with suspected severe infections, especially in the presence of systemic signs such as hypotension and fever. However, they are not diagnostic for necrotising fasciitis, which requires urgent exploration and debridement. Blood cultures are often taken alongside immediate surgical intervention. E Doppler ultrasound of the affected leg Doppler ultrasound may be useful in evaluating vascular compromise, but is not diagnostic for necrotising fasciitis and is not indicated in this emergency. Rapid surgical intervention is necessary to prevent mortality.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a 1-day history of dark urine, 3-day history of headache, fever, feeling generally unwell and a 5-day history of diarrhoea and vomiting. He is a medical student who returned from an elective in East Africa one day ago. He had unprotected sexual intercourse with two fellow students while abroad, and just before returning to the United Kingdom, he did some freshwater swimming in Lake Malawi. He took doxycycline as malarial prophylaxis throughout the trip and had continued to do so since his return. He has no other complaints. On examination, he has rigors, mild jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. He had tachycardia of 100 bpm and a temperature of 38.1 °C. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation: A Artesunate This patient has a malarial infection due to poor absorption of doxycycline, following a bout of diarrhoea and vomiting. His presentation with signs of possible blackwater fever ( jaundice) is concerning and therefore, he needs aggressive treatment with intravenous artesunate and admission to the Intensive Care Unit. D Praziquantel Praziquantel is a treatment for Schistosoma haematobium, which is a ﬂuke infection causing itchy rash, eosinophilia and Katayama fever 4–8 weeks post-exposure. Although this can be the result of swimming in freshwater, the patient’s signs and symptoms do not suggest this. B Benzylpenicillin Benzylpenicillin would be a treatment option for syphilis, which is not the diagnosis of this patient. C Malarone Malarone is a treatment for uncomplicated malarial infection. The jaundice found on examination and the presence of dark urine is suspicious of blackwater fever (intravascular haemolysis due to malarial infection), and therefore, treatment for uncomplicated infection is not appropriate. E Stop doxycycline Doxycycline is unlikely to be a cause of this patient’s presentation. The most common side effects are oesophagitis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and photosensitivity. Although the patient has had diarrhoea and vomiting (which may have been due to doxycycline or ingestion of pathogen during freshwater swimming), it is likely that this resulted in inadequate cover from doxycycline allowing malarial infection to occur.

stem: A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of facial weakness. He also reported a 1-month history of joint pain and stiffness, particularly affecting his elbows and knees. Three months previously, he had had a ﬂu- like illness with a red rash, fever and malaise. In the preceding 6 months he had travelled to Kenya and Massachusetts, USA for cross-country running competitions. On examination, he was afebrile, and there were no skin rashes. He had bilateral lower motor neurone facial nerve palsies. There was no evidence of active synovitis in his joints though his elbows appeared stiff and painful. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Lyme disease Lyme disease is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted through tick bites. This patient has travelled to Massachusetts, an area known to harbour Lyme disease, and has been running in the countryside and therefore could have been bitten by a tick. The description of a rash consistent with erythema migrans, malaise and joint pain is classical. Weeks or months later the arthritis and neurological complications develop. Diagnosis is via serology for antibodies to B. burgdorferi. Treatment should be with 2–3 weeks of oral doxycycline. E Secondary syphilis Although syphilis can cause a rash and cranial nerve palsies, it would be extremely uncommon for it to cause bilateral facial palsies. It would also not explain the arthritis experienced by this patient. A much better explanation would be Lyme disease, contracted from a tick bite whilst running in Massachusetts. The rash could have been erythema migrans, and Lyme would also explain the myalgia, fever, malaise and arthritis. It is a known cause of bilateral facial palsies. A Cerebral toxoplasmosis There is no suggestion that this patient is immunocompromised, and therefore cerebral toxoplasmosis is extremely unlikely. Furthermore, cerebral toxoplasmosis would not explain his history of rash, malaise and joint pain. This presentation is more typical of Lyme disease, to which the patient was presumably exposed whilst in the countryside of Massachusetts, via a tick bite. This would explain the rash (erythema migrans), general malaise, joint pains and bilateral facial palsies. B Leprosy It would be very unusual for leprosy to cause facial nerve palsies without any sensory involvement, which is not reported in this case. Given the patient’s travel history and history of a rash, myalgia, malaise and joint pain, a diagnosis of Lyme disease is more likely. He is likely to have contracted this after a tick bite whilst running in Massachusetts. D Reactive arthritis Although this patient has arthritis and ﬂu-like symptoms, he does

not have urethritis or conjunctivitis/uveitis. Reactive arthritis would also not explain the rash, or his bilateral facial palsies. Bilateral lower motor neurone facial palsies are extremely uncommon. This patient’s constellation of symptoms and signs would be better explained by Lyme disease, caused by a tick bite. He may have contracted it whilst running in Massachusetts. The rash would be erythema migrans, and Lyme disease would explain his malaise, arthritis and bilateral facial palsies.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is admitted with a febrile illness of one week’s duration. She was prescribed amoxicillin for cough and right-sided pleuritic pain but had not completed the course. One day ago, she developed a severe headache and became more confused. She was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus some ten years ago and is managed with metformin and sitagliptin. On examination there is obvious herpes labialis, her BP is 100/80 mmHg and pulse is 88 and regular. She is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.8 °C. Her GCS is 13 and there is obvious neck stiffness and meningism. Fundi are not seen. Auscultation reveals basal crackles at the right lung base. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 120 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 15 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 8 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l ALT 44 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Urine glucose ++, no ketones What is the most likely cause of the lung ﬁndings here?
explanation:
C Streptococcus pneumoniae This lady has a febrile illness with signs of consolidation of the right base of the lung with leucocytosis, suggestive of a communityacquired pneumonia, the most common of which is S. pneumoniae. She has developed signs of bacterial meningitis and her level of consciousness has deteriorated. Herpes labialis is also commonly associated with S. pneumoniae infection. CT scanning should be carried out to exclude signs of raised intracerebral pressure, and to assess the risks of lumbar puncture to conﬁrm the diagnosis of S.

pneumoniae meningitis and rule out potential herpes encephalitis. A Cryptococcus Cryptococcus is a cause of meningitis in patients who are immunocompromised. B Listeria monocytogenes Listeria is a cause of meningitis, primarily in pregnant women and the elderly. D Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus pneumonia is usually seen in association with inﬂuenza infection. E Mycoplasma pneumoniae Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a rarer cause of community-acquired pneumonia, and is often associated with much more marked changes on CXR than would be expected given the examination ﬁndings.

stem: A 27-year-old teacher presents to the Respiratory Clinic following abnormal screening results found during a work up for immunotherapy for multiple sclerosis. The health provider asks him about contacts, and the patient mentions his girlfriend, a teacher, with whom he split up three months earlier. He is reviewed in the clinic, looks well, is apyrexial and has no symptoms of infection. His blood results are described below. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 209 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l ESR 8.0 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1sthour Quantiferon test + HIV test - His CXR is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage the patient?
options: Rifampicin and isoniazid for three months
explanation: B Rifampicin and isoniazid for three months This patient has latent tuberculosis as exempliﬁed by the positive quantiferon test against a background of deﬁnite TB exposure, with no signs of pulmonary TB and a normal chest X-ray. Dual therapy is recommended for three months, or isoniazid alone can be given for six months. C Repeat CXR in four weeks The diagnosis of latent TB can already be made, so there is no need to repeat a chest ﬁlm at this point. A Full anti-tuberculous therapy This would be considered for a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis. D Recheck Quantiferon The quantiferon gold test has a sensitivity of 92% and a speciﬁcity of >99%. It is highly unlikely therefore that this patient's result is a false negative. E Rifampicin for one month Only isoniazid should be considered as monotherapy treatment for latent TB.

stem: An 18-year-old Russian foreign exchange student presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of sore throat and bloodstained nasal discharge. He feels lethargic and complains of intermittent fevers and myalgia. He has otherwise been well and there is no past medical history of note. On examination, he has a temperature of 39.2 °C. His heart rate is 119 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 102/55 mmHg. He is saturating at 94% on room air, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min. On auscultation, his chest is clear, with normal heart sounds. Ear, nose and throat examination shows a thin grey membrane over his tonsils and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely complication associated with this patient’s diagnosis?
explanation:
A Myocarditis This patient has diphtheria caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive rod. It is more common in

Eastern Europe and symptoms include a watery nasal discharge that turns purulent and bloodstained. A sore throat with cervical lymphadenopathy and a classical grey membrane over the tonsils leads to the diagnosis. The diphtheria toxin can damage cardiac muscle, causing cardiac complications. They initially arise within the ﬁrst 10–14 days of the illness and include tachycardia, heart block and myocarditis. Myocarditis is a potentially fatal complication of diphtheria. It is, in fact, the most important cause of mortality in patients with diphtheria. In a study by Meera et al., all deaths except one was attributed to myocarditis. Myocarditis has been reported in 19–68% of cases with diphtheria. However, a signiﬁcant proportion of these individuals will just present with ECG changes without any symptoms of failure or shock. Besides sinus tachycardia and bradycardia, atrioventricular blocks, bundle branch blocks (BBB), ST-T changes, T wave inversion and ventricular/atrial ectopics are seen in varying frequencies in patients with myocarditis. E Encephalopathy Neurological symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy can be seen following infection with C. diphtheriae. However, encephalopathy is not a frequently seen complication. A Pancreatitis This patient has diphtheria. The disease has several complications, including peripheral neuropathy, renal impairment and myocarditis. However, pancreatitis is not a complication of diphtheria and is incorrect. B Peritonsillar abscess A peritonsillar abscess usually arises following acute tonsillitis. Common causative organisms include Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. The clinical history of a sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy may suggest a diagnosis of tonsillitis. However, the bloodstained nasal discharge and grey tonsillar pseudomembrane should point towards diphtheria. A peritonsillar abscess is not a complication of diphtheria, making it incorrect. C Pneumonia Pneumonia is a complication occasionally seen following streptococcal and staphylococcal throat infections such as tonsillitis. However, it is not commonly seen following infection with C. diphtheriae.

stem: A 20-year-old woman attends the Genitourinary Clinic with a 6-day history of vulval itching. She denies fever or lower urinary tract symptoms and there is no history of vaginal discharge. She had unprotected sex with a new partner two weeks ago. There is no past medical history of note. She is ten weeks pregnant and other than regular folic acid, she takes no other medication. She has no allergies. On examination, she has a temperature of 36.3 °C; her heart rate is 75 bpm and her blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. There are multiple ﬂesh-coloured papules around the vulva, with the largest measuring 5 mm in diameter. Some of the papules have an irregular border with evidence of mild bleeding. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
E Cryotherapy This woman has a diagnosis of anogenital warts secondary to human papillomavirus (HPV). The virus is spread via skin-to-skin contact and results in the appearance of itchy, ﬂesh-coloured papules which have a tendency to bleed. Treatment is not always indicated. However, it is important to minimise the number of lesions in pregnancy to prevent neonatal exposure to HPV. Cryotherapy is a treatment for anogenital warts. It often needs to be repeated every 1– 3 weeks until the warts resolve. Cryotherapy tends to be reserved for a small number of warts with a small volume in size. In pregnancy, cryotherapy is the recommended choice of treatment, as per British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) guidelines. A Oral aciclovir Oral aciclovir is an antiviral medication used in the treatment of the herpes virus. Herpes simplex virus (predominantly type II) causes genital ulcers – a very painful and itchy eruption of vesicles and

ulcers with associated surrounding erythema. Dysuria is a common symptom with genital herpes and as the disease progresses, tender lymphadenopathy can appear. This scenario describes a young woman with ﬂeshy protuberances, rather than painful vesicles, making genital warts the most likely diagnosis. B Topical clotrimazole Topical clotrimazole is a treatment of Candida albicans, otherwise known as thrush. Thrush presents with severe itch and a thick, white, curd-like discharge. Dysuria is also common, as is the eruption of dermatitis over the surrounding vulva. C Topical podophyllotoxin Topical podophyllotoxin is the ﬁrst-line treatment for anogenital warts. However, podophyllotoxin is teratogenic, making it unsuitable to be prescribed during pregnancy. D Topical imiquimod Topical imiquimod, along with topical podophyllotoxin, is one of the recommended treatments for human papillomavirus (HPV). Usually, topical podophyllotoxin is used initially. There are little data to support the safety of imiquimod to treat anogenital warts in pregnancy. Therefore, the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) guidelines currently recommend that the treatment of anogenital warts in pregnant patients should be with cryotherapy.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with rapidly worsening infection of his left lower limb. He is obese and has poor mobility, and says the infection began with only a small area of erythema around 24 hours earlier. Since that time, the area of erythema has extended signiﬁcantly, with large areas of necrotic tissue and the skin is boggy to touch. He is requiring large amounts of morphine for pain relief.
explanation: E M protein The diagnosis here with rapidly progressive cellulitis and large areas of necrotic tissue is consistent with a diagnosis of necrotising fasciitis. Group A streptococci are well recognised as a cause of type II necrotising fasciitis, and M proteins are a key virulence factor in the development of the disease, particularly the 1 and 3 subtypes. As well as extensive surgical debridement, a typical empirical antibiotic regimen includes piperacillin- tazobactam combined with vancomycin. D Enterotoxin-A Enterotoxin A is a leading cause of staphylococcal food poisoning. This is seen as a result of ingesting dairy products which have been kept at room temperature for a signiﬁcant period of time. It leads to profuse vomiting, and symptoms settle spontaneously after a few hours. A Alpha toxin Alpha toxin is a key virulence factor in Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene. It is not linked to the progression of necrotising fasciitis, which is often related to Streptococcus group A infection. It is thought that alpha toxin in the context of gas gangrene drives inﬂammation and oedema and accelerates tissue necrosis. Type III necrotizing fasciitis is usually caused by Clostridium perfringens. When type III necrotizing fasciitis occurs spontaneously, C septicum is more likely to be the etiologic agent; these cases usually occur in association with colon cancer or leukemia. B Cereulide Cereulide is the toxin which causes vomiting in Bacillus cereus (B cereus) food poisoning. It does not have a role in pathogenesis of necrotising fasciitis. B cereus food poisoning is most often related to under-cooked rice, symptoms of food poisoning occur 4-6 hours after ingestion, and usually resolve within 24 hours. C Choleragen Choleragen is the enterotoxin produced by cholera, which drives the profuse watery diarrhoea seen with Vibrio cholerae infection. It leads to constant overstimulation of chloride, water, sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate into the lumen of the small intestine.

stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of general malaise, fever up to 38.5oC and night sweats. For the past 2 days he has had painful mouth ulcers. He returned to the UK 3 weeks previously from Nigeria, where he had been living for several months. On direct questioning, he reported having unprotected sexual intercourse with two local women over the past two months. On examination he had widespread lymphadenopathy. There was no rash. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 142 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 1.9 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 190 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l HIV antibodies - Blood cultures No growth in 48 h from 2 samples Thick and thin blood ﬁlm Negative in 2 samples Chest X-ray Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A HIV infection This patient has a prolonged fever, night sweats and widespread lymphadenopathy after unprotected sex; the most likely diagnosis is HIV. HIV antibody can be negative during seroconversion; a p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR test would be a much better diagnostic test for this patient. A Dengue fever Typically dengue causes headache and fever in the returning traveller, and sometimes haemorrhagic rashes. However, it is unusual for dengue to cause night sweats, and very unusual for it to cause illness more than 2 weeks after returning from an endemic area. You might expect a higher fever than 38.5°C if this were

dengue. This patient’s symptoms and signs are better explained by HIV seroconversion; this would explain the lymphadenopathy and night sweats. HIV antibody can be negative in seroconversion: p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR would be a better test for this patient. B Falciparum malaria This patient has returned from a malaria-endemic area and does have a fever, but he has had two negative blood ﬁlms for malaria which makes this diagnosis less likely. Malaria does not explain his widespread lymphadenopathy or mouth ulcers. A much more likely diagnosis is HIV seroconversion. HIV antibody can be negative in seroconversion; a much better test would be either p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR. D Lyme disease Lyme disease is not endemic in Nigeria. Widespread lymphadenopathy is uncommon in Lyme disease, and this patient does not have any rash. A much better explanation for his symptoms and signs is HIV seroconversion, especially given that he has recently had unprotected sex. HIV antibody can be negative in seroconversion; a much better test would be p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR. E Typhoid infection Typhoid results in prolonged high fever in the returning traveller and is caused by Salmonella infection. Classically patients have headache, constipation, high fever and a salmon-pink maculopapular rash. Typhoid would not explain this patient’s widespread lymphadenopathy or mouth ulcers. You might expect a higher fever than 38.5°C if this were typhoid. This patient’s presentation is much better explained by HIV seroconversion. HIV antibody can be negative during seroconversion; a much better test would be p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR.

stem: An 18-year-old student is referred by her general practitioner to the Emergency Department, suffering from pharyngitis, shortness of breath with wheeze and a morbilliform skin rash. Examination reveals generalised lymphadenopathy; wheeze in the lower zones is conﬁrmed, and some skeletal muscle tenderness to palpation is noted. Investigations reveal a slightly elevated white blood cell count, with normal urea and electrolytes. The presence of cold agglutinins is noted.
explanation:
A Clarithromycin The answer is Clarithromycin (Option A). This patient has Mycoplasma pneumonia, which is primarily said to affect school-aged children and young adults. Symptoms include non-exudative pharyngitis, bullous myringitis, skin rashes and wheeze on respiratory examination. Other symptoms and signs may include muscle tenderness, nerve palsies, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and conjunctivitis. Hints as to the diagnosis come from the fact that the chest X-ray, showing extensive left lower lobe pneumonia, appears much worse than the clinical ﬁndings and that cold agglutinins are positive. For patients with microbiologically conﬁrmed M. pneumoniae pneumonia, ﬁrst-line treatment options include macrolides (eg, azithromycin), tetracyclines (eg, doxycycline), and respiratory ﬂuoroquinolones (eg, levoﬂoxacin or moxiﬂoxacin). Mycoplasma pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams due to its lack of a cell wall. Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is managed empirically generally, based on severity and suspicion of the cause, before an organism can be cultured. Mild and previously untreated CAP is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus inﬂuenzae,

and typical treatment could be oral amoxicillin. Moderate CAP is caused by the above organisms, as well as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and can be managed with oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin. Severe CAP should usually be treated in higher care areas with broad-spectrum antibiotics such as intravenous co-amoxiclav and oral clarithromycin. Clarithromycin has very good oral bioavailability and causes thrombophlebitis if given intravenously and therefore should be given orally, even in severe infections. Atypical CAP can be caused by Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydophilaspecies and Pneumocystis jiroveci. Local guidelines may differ in the progression of antimicrobial choices, due to differences in the prevalence of different infectious organisms. Also, if culture results become available, then these should be used to guide further antibiotic choice. C Amoxicillin Amoxicillin (Option C) is incorrect. Amoxicillin may be given to this patient with CAP, depending on the severity, as described above. It provides good antimicrobial effect against the main Gram-positive pathogens. B Penicillin V Penicillin V (Option B) is incorrect. Penicillin V is more commonly used for oral infections, including tonsillitis, otitis media, erysipelas and cellulitis. It can also be used prophylactically in the prevention of recurrence of rheumatic fever, prevention of secondary group A streptococcal infection and prevention in asplenism and sickle-cell disease. D Co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav (Option D) is incorrect. Co-amoxiclav may be given to this patient with CAP, depending on the severity, as described above. It provides good antimicrobial effect against the main Gram-positive pathogens. Co-amoxiclav is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. Clavulanic acid prevents the breakdown of amoxicillin in some resistant organisms. E Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin (Option E) is incorrect. Ciproﬂoxacin provides good antimicrobial activity against Pseudomonas species – important pathogens in exacerbations of bronchiectasis and in the immunosuppressed patient – but has little value in treating chest infections without evidence of an underlying chronic lung disease such as bronchiectasis or a previous Pseudomonas infection. Quinolone treatment is also no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but signiﬁcant risk of debilitating adverse effects.

stem: A 33-year-old man returned 2 weeks ago from an 8-month business trip with colleagues to Peru. He noticed a few papules on his trunk and legs. One of these has changed, as shown below. He feels well in himself and denies fever, diarrhoea or headaches. He does remember having a ﬂu-like illness while he was in Peru. Routine bloods, including full blood count and white cell differential, are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Cutaneous leishmaniasis The image shows a superﬁcial ulcer which, in combination with the history of travel and ﬂu-like illness is most likely due to cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL). The incubation time is 7 days to several months. In cutaneous larva migrans, worm-like lesions have an incubation period 1–4 days and are found mainly after holidays to Caribbean beaches. Treatment of CL is determined by species type and by the potential to develop into mucosal disease. C Tick typhus eschar The eschar of tick typhus is a papule, which evolves to a black scab. This condition is also found in southern Africa, and has an incubation period of fewer than 7 days. B Cutaneous larva migrans Cutaneous larva migrans occurs as a result of hookworm infection caused by walking barefoot. The trails caused by the larvae are usually seen on the feet and ankles. D Dengue fever Dengue fever occurs in tropical countries, with an incubation period of under two weeks and is associated with systemic features and a

morbilliform rash. E Cutaneous tuberculosis Cutaneous lesions are relatively uncommon in TB infection, occurring in only 1-2% of infected patients. The clinical ﬁndings vary: inﬂammatory papules, verrucous plaques, suppurative nodules, chronic ulcers or other lesions may be seen. Superﬁcial ulcers on the trunk are not a usual manifestation of TB.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He complains of a rash on the left upper chest and has trouble with extensive papillary warts. He admits to weight loss of 2 stone over the course of the past year. He admits to having had a number of sexual partners and has regularly had unprotected sex. On examination, he has erythematous blistering rash in a dermatomal distribution, extensive papillary warts and other lesions, pictured below. He is emaciated and there is evidence of cervical lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
A HIV infection With this picture of weight loss, extensive papillary warts, the pictured pink macular lesions which may be Kaposi’s sarcoma and herpes zoster infection, conﬁrmatory HIV antibody testing is recommended, and measurement of CD4+ lymphocyte levels is useful in assessing risk of opportunistic infections. The overlying picture is that of several opportunistic infections without a known cause. Aciclovir is the treatment of choice for herpes zoster infection, and a number of topical treatments for viral warts are available. Retinoid gels may be of value in the management of Kaposi’s sarcoma. C Hodgkin’s lymphoma Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a malignant disease of lymphatic system with multinucleated giant (Reed–Sternberg) cells. Presentation usually occurs in early adulthood, and again is insidious with asymptomatic lymph node enlargement, weight loss, night sweats and unexplained fever. Some patients have chest symptoms and alcohol-induced pain. This patient does not have night sweats or fever, and Hodgkin’s lymphoma would not explain the presence of multiple opportunistic infections. B Chronic myeloid leukaemia Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder affecting one or all cell lines. Progression is characterised into a chronic phase, an accelerated phase, and ﬁnally blast crisis. Most patients present in the chronic phase with insidious symptoms of

fatigue, weight loss and night sweats. Examination can reveal features of cell line disruption such as anaemia and bruising, but while lymphoadenopathy can occur it is not a major feature. It is not associated with immunodeﬁciency and would therefore not explain this patient’s infections, and the age of presentation of CML is usually around 65 years old. D Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia Acute lymphoblastic lymphoma (ALL) is incorrect. ALL is a malignant transformation of lymphoid progenitor cells which replace normal bone marrow and blasts, eventually spilling into circulation. It is primarily a childhood disease, mostly occurring before the age of 6 years. It is associated with fatigue and malaise leading to bone marrow failure, and can cause bone pain, recurrent and severe infections and unexplained fevers, among other symptoms. This diagnosis could explain the immunosuppression in this patient, as well as lymphadenopathy and weight loss; however, the age of the patient, as well as the absence of features of other cell line disruption, make this diagnosis less likely. E Herpes zoster infection Herpes zoster is an opportunistic infection in this patient, and while it is most likely present, it would not explain his general symptoms.

stem: A 32-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of severe, worsening headache, vomiting and double vision. He was HIVpositive and had refused antiretroviral treatment or prophylactic medications. He has a CD4 count of 120 × 106/l (normal range 300– 1400). On examination, his temperature was 37.5°C. There was a rightsided facial nerve palsy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values CD4+ 120 × 106/l 430 - 1690 × 106/l CT head Two large ring-enhancing lesions, with midline shift Based on the likeliest diagnosis, what treatment should be started?
options: Sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine, plus folinic acid
explanation:
E Sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine, plus folinic acid This patient has untreated HIV and, as such, is extremely vulnerable to opportunistic infection. One such infection is toxoplasmosis, which can infect the CNS causing focal neurology due to mass

lesions, visible on imaging as ring-enhancing lesions. Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection contracted from infected raw meat or from handling cat faeces or soil contaminated with cat faeces. First-line therapy is with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid. The patient should also probably receive dexamethasone given the presence of midline shift. C Ceftazidime Because this patient has untreated HIV, he is severely immunocompromised and vulnerable to opportunistic infection. In this case he has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis: focal neurology with signs of raised intracranial pressure, and ring-enhancing lesions on brain imaging. As toxoplasmosis is caused by a parasite, antibiotics such as ceftazidime will not be an effective treatment. The correct therapy would be sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid. A Aciclovir This patient has untreated HIV and is severely immunocompromised. As a result he has contracted cerebral toxoplasmosis, as evidenced by the focal neurological signs and ring-enhancing lesions on CT head. An antiviral such as aciclovir will not treat cerebral toxoplasmosis, as this is caused by a parasite. The correct treatment is sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid. B Amphotericin This patient has untreated HIV, and consequently he is severely immunocompromised. This renders him vulnerable to opportunistic infection: in this case, he has contracted cerebral toxoplasmosis. This causes focal neurological signs and is visible as ringenhancing lesions on CT or MRI head. An antifungal such as amphotericin will not treat toxoplasmosis, as this is caused by a parasite. The correct therapy would be sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid. D Chemotherapy This patient has untreated HIV; although HIV, and especially poorly controlled disease, is associated with malignancy (particularly with primary CNS lymphoma), the presentation and appearance of this patient’s central nervous system lesions are not quite consistent with cerebral malignancy. The time course is quite rapid for metastases in the brain, and he does not have any other symptoms of primary malignancy elsewhere in the body. Ringenhancing lesions would be an atypical appearance for primary CNS lymphoma. It is much more likely that this patient, in his immunocompromised state, has contracted cerebral toxoplasmosis. This should be treated with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with folinic acid.

stem: A 33-year-old man is rushed into the Emergency Department by his wife. He complains of generalised weakness and blurred vision. Other than a short-lived episode of diarrhoea and vomiting two days ago, he has been well recently, with no past medical history. His observations are recorded as being within normal limits. On examination, he has bilateral third and sixth cranial nerve palsies and failure of pupil accommodation. He has dry mucous membranes and impaired swallowing. There is ﬂaccid paralysis of his upper limbs, with normal power and reﬂexes in his lower limbs. Sensation is spared throughout. What is the most likely causative organism responsible for this patient’s symptoms?
explanation:
C Clostridium botulinum This patient has botulism, a bacterial infection caused by C. botulinum. It is a common environmental organism that is often contracted from contaminated canned or bottled food. The symptoms of the disease often begin with blurred vision and occasionally diarrhoea and vomiting can be seen. They later manifest as a profound neuromuscular blockade with a classical symmetrical descending pattern of paralysis. Often cranial nerves are affected ﬁrst, with bilateral cranial nerve palsies being common. This is followed by upper limb and lastly lower-limb paralysis. Death can occur from paralysis of respiratory muscles.

E Clostridium tetani Tetanus is a bacterial illness caused by C. tetani. It is found in soil and enters the body through a contaminated wound or through a break in the skin, including from intravenous drug use. After an incubation period of between a few days to several weeks, symptoms of the disease will manifest, typically starting with general malaise and progressing to muscular spasms such as lockjaw. In more severe disease, muscular spasms can be painful and affect different organ systems. Respiration can be impaired from laryngospasm and oesophageal and urethral spasm can cause dysphagia and urinary retention, respectively. This is in contrast to the question given where the patient is suffering from paralysis rather than muscular spasm, hinting towards an alternative diagnosis of botulism. A Campylobacter jejuni Very rarely, following infection with C. jejuni, a neurological condition known as Guillain–Barré syndrome can develop. However, Guillain–Barré syndrome classically causes an ascending pattern of paralysis, rather than descending paralysis, which is seen in this question. B Clostridium perfringes C. perfringes is a common cause of gastroenteritis and is also the most common bacterial cause of gas gangrene. While this patient exhibits symptoms of vomiting and diarrhoea, C. perfringes would not explain his neurological symptoms, making it incorrect. D Clostridium difﬁcile C. difﬁcile is a severe and highly contagious gastrointestinal illness. While this patient does exhibit symptoms of vomiting and diarrhoea, C. difﬁcile would not explain his neurological symptoms, making it incorrect.

stem: A 29-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of abdominal pains and bloody diarrhoea. He had returned from Uganda one week ago. During his 4 weeks stay in Uganda, he was asymptomatic. On examination, his temperature was 37.5°C. His abdomen was generally tender to touch but no masses could be felt, and he had active bowel sounds. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 330 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 8.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Amoebic dysentery Amoebic dysentery is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, which is most often acquired in the tropics. The organism invades the mucosa of the colon, creating shallow ulcers with undermined edges. Although infection may be asymptomatic, the symptoms can include fever, chills, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. The stool may contain blood and/or mucus. The organism may rarely invade the liver to form an abscess, and other complications include inﬂammation of the intestine or rarely perforation. Diagnosis is usually made by microscopic examination of the patient’s stool for the organism’s trophozoites and/or cysts, and PCR stool testing. C Ischaemic colitis Ischaemic colitis causes severe abdominal pain, which this patient does not complain of. You might expect him to be more unwell, possibly in shock, if he had signiﬁcant ischaemic colitis. The patient does not appear to have any risk factors for ischaemic colitis: he is young, without vascular disease or atrial ﬁbrillation. This patient’s travel history and presentation are more consistent with amoebic dysentery. B Campylobacter enterocolitis Although Campylobacter is the most common cause of bloody diarrhoea in the UK, it typically causes high fever and constitutional upset. This patient is quite well and has only a low-grade fever. This, combined with his travel history, makes amoebic dysentery much more likely. D Giardasis Although a common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller, giardiasis does not cause bloody diarrhoea, as seen here. Instead it causes steatorrhoea, belching and ﬂatulence, and sometimes nausea. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with amoebic dysentery. E Pseudomembranous colitis Pseudomembranous colitis is caused by Clostridium difﬁcile overgrowth, and is associated with institutionalisation or the use of antibiotics, neither of which are the case for this patient. C. difﬁcile causes an offensive diarrhoea, but not a bloody diarrhoea. This patient’s travel history and presentation are more consistent with amoebic dysentery.

stem: A 30-year-old Ugandan woman presented to the genito-urinary medicine (GUM) clinic for a sexual health screen on her GP's advice. She has been with the same partner for 8 years and has not had other sexual partners in that time frame. Before coming to the UK 10 years ago, she had previously been a sex worker in Africa. She is asymptomatic and consents to tests for chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV and syphilis. Her syphilis serology is as follows: TPHA +ve RPR -ve She has never heard of syphilis and does not think she has been tested before. She does not recall ever having had symptoms of genital ulceration or rash. Which one of the following statements is most correct regarding this patient?
options: She does not require any treatment for syphilis
She needs an urgent lumbar puncture
explanation:
C This is late latent syphilis Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete, which spreads as a sexually transmitted infection to form a hard ulcer, termed chancre in primary syphilis. In a time from six weeks to six months secondary syphilis can occur. This can cause malaise, fever, tonsillitis and a rash with ﬂat papules as well as other complications. Tertiary syphilis, or latent syphilis, occurs two years following infection with granuloma formation. T. pallidum heamagglutination assay (TPHA), is a Treponema-speciﬁc test which stays positive following infection permanently, while rapid plasma reagin (RPR) is a cardiolipin antibody test which, whilst non-speciﬁc, becomes negative following successful treatment. Late latent syphilis is no longer infectious, and the diagnosis is supported by the fact that RPR has become negative although TPHA is positive.

D This is neurosyphilis Neurosyphilis is associated with both positive RPR and positive TPHA. Neurosyphilis can cause cranial nerve palsy, dementia, psychosis, ataxia and tabes dorsalis. Currently there are no features of neurosyphilis, but leaving her untreated risks progression of her disease. A She does not require any treatment for syphilis As she has never been treated for syphilis, she needs to be treated now and the treatment of choice is three doses of IM benzathine penicillin. Left untreated she is at risk of signiﬁcant long term complications of syphilis infection. B This is early latent syphilis Early latent syphilis can only be diagnosed if there had been a deﬁnitive negative result within the last two years. Given she has only been tested once this cannot form the basis of a diagnosis. E She needs an urgent lumbar puncture hili

The absence of any features of neurosyphilis makes this unnecessary, and a negative RPR also excludes

stem: A 24-year-old man returned from a 3-week holiday in India 10 days ago. He presents with a 48-h history of fever, generalised myalgia, headache, dry cough and diarrhoea. On examination, he is pyrexial and has hepatosplenomegaly but no other signiﬁcant ﬁndings. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 102 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets (PLT) 160 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l WCC 3.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0× 109/l ALT 140 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT) 140 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 290 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 20 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 28 g/l 35–55 g/l
explanation:
D Salmonella typhi Salmonella typhi is the causative organism of typhoid fever. Typhoid fever is seen in travellers returning from countries in the developing world. The presence of Gram-negative rods on the microscopy image conﬁrms the underlying cause. The incubation period is 1–3 weeks. The illness is characterised by fever, myalgia and headache. Diarrhoea or constipation can occur. Rose spots are characteristic ﬁndings, usually on the trunk: they are faint, salmoncoloured, maculopapular, blanching lesions. It is often difﬁcult to differentiate typhoid from malaria clinically. Blood cultures are the diagnostic method of choice. S. typhi appears as a Gram-negative bacillus on Gram ﬁlm. Serology (the Widal test) is not performed routinely in the UK. Ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice due to problems with ﬂuoroquinolone resistance. C Coxiella burnetii C. burnetii is the cause for Q fever, a zoonosis acquired from farm animals. The organism is a Gram-negative coccobacillus. Symptoms of Q fever can be variable in onset, presenting with myalgia, headache and dry cough, and can occur with hepatitis and hepatomegaly. However, it would not explain splenomegaly and there is no history of exposure to farm animals. A Legionella pneumophila L. pneumophila is the causative organism of Legionnaire’s disease (LD). LD is an atypical pneumonia which is difﬁcult to distinguish from typical pneumonia clinically. It is heavily related to foreign travel as the organism is prevalent in stagnant water and usually contracted via poorly regulated air conditioning units. LD presents after 2–10 days with headache and myalgia followed by fever, rigors and cough. A third of patients have gastrointestinal symptoms. While L. pneumophila is a Gram-negative rod and the patient has possible symptoms, this diagnosis would not explain the noted hepatosplenomegaly. B Salmonella enteritis S. enteritis is a cause of gastroenteritis. Following an incubation of 6–72 hours, the patient experiences fever, diarrhoea (which can be

bloody) and abdominal cramps usually lasting 4–7 days before recovery. This diagnosis would not explain the headache, cough or oraganomegaly. S. enteritis is a Gram-negative rod. D Leptospira interrogans L. interrogans is a spirochaete causing leptospirosis which is spread from rat urine into aquatic areas and then contact with abraded skin or mucosa leads to infection. Water activities increase risk. Following an incubation of 1–3 weeks, there is an abrupt onset of fever, headache, myalgia, dry cough and lethargy. This phase may resolve without treatment but can lead to an immune phase with jaundice, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, rash, meningitis and organ failure. It would explain the high LFTs and low haemoglobin, and would also explain hepatomegaly but not splenomegaly.

stem: A 38-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of a ﬁrm, painless ulcer on the glans penis. He had recently returned from a 3month trip to Thailand, China, Hong Kong and Australia. He was otherwise well. Examination revealed an ulcer as described by the patient, with no associated lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Syphilis Painless ulcers, developing 10–90 days after exposure, are typical of syphilis. However, it is worth noting that syphilitic ulcers can be painful and herpetic ulcers can be painless, and therefore this ulcer should be swabbed, and bloods should be taken for an immunoassay to conﬁrm the diagnosis. This patient has presented with primary syphilis; secondary syphilis, which can develop roughly 6 weeks after the skin lesions have appeared, typically consists of constitutional ﬂu-like symptoms and a non-pruritic rash which classically affects the face, palms and soles. This patient should be treated with benzathine penicillin as a single intramuscular dose. Oral azithromycin as a single dose is an acceptable second-line treatment. Fifty per cent of patients with primary syphilis will develop the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction after treatment: ﬂu-like symptoms and rigors which typically self-resolve within 24 h. D Non-gonococcal urethritis Non-speciﬁc urethritis does not cause genital ulceration, but instead presents with dysuria. Commonly it is caused by chlamydia, though it can be caused by other bacteria or viruses. This patient’s presentation with a painless ulcer is more consistent with syphilis: to conﬁrm the diagnosis the ulcer should be swabbed and bloods should be taken, but he should be treated for syphilis. A Chancroid Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a Gramnegative bacterium, Haemophilus ducreyi. It does cause penile ulceration, but you would expect the ulcer to be painful and to have associated lymphadenopathy. There is also typically a purulent exudate. The ulcer described in this patient is much more consistent with a diagnosis of syphilis: classically syphilitic ulcers are shallow

and painless. They may or may not be associated with lymphadenopathy. These ulcers should be swabbed, as it is unreliable to make a clinical diagnosis in cases of penile ulcer. However, the patient should be treated for syphilis. B Genital herpes Herpetic genital ulcers are typically painful, may be associated with a prodromal mild, ﬂu-like illness and may have associated lymphadenopathy. This painless ulcer is more consistent with syphilis. The ulcer should still be swabbed, and blood should be taken, in order to make a formal diagnosis: clinical diagnosis is unreliable in cases of genital ulcers. However, this patient should be treated for syphilis. C Gonorrhoea Gonorrhoea can occasionally cause penile ulcers, but this is a very uncommon presentation. Typically gonorrhoea is either asymptomatic or presents with urethritis (dysuria) and/or purulent penile discharge. This patient’s symptoms and signs are more consistent with syphilis, which typically causes painless ulceration. Making a clinical diagnosis in penile ulceration is difﬁcult, and therefore these ulcers should be swabbed and blood tests should be taken, but this patient should be treated for syphilis.

stem: A 72-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of vague tingling over the upper right side of his face. On waking up that morning, a vesicular rash had developed over his upper right face, including the tip of his nose, and he noticed that his right eye was watering. He had a history of lichen planus, and for the past 3 years, he had used topical tacrolimus to treat it. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
E Urgent ophthalmology opinion This patient has herpes zoster ophthalmicus; he had a prodrome of tingling in a dermatomal distribution and subsequently developed a vesicular rash. However, the key point in this case is that he has signs of impending corneal involvement – the rash involves the tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) and he has watering of the eye. Hutchinson’s sign occurs as the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve innervates the cornea and the lateral dorsum of the nose and tip. You would start oral high-dose aciclovir immediately, but it is

vital to refer him urgently to ophthalmology for assessment the same day, as herpes zoster ophthalmicus can be sight- threatening. D Stop tacrolimus ointment This patient has been using tacrolimus ointment for several years, and therefore this is unlikely to be a reaction to the drug. Furthermore, vesicular drug rashes are unusual.
