This rash is typical of herpes zoster (dermatomal, vesicular and with preceding tingling in the affected area), and in this case there are symptoms and signs to suggest corneal involvement (the rash affects the tip of the nose and there is eye watering). This case should be referred urgently to ophthalmology, as herpes zoster ophthalmicus can be sightthreatening. You would also immediately start high-dose oral aciclovir. A Prescribe artiﬁcial tear solution This patient has a vesicular rash involving his upper face and the tip of his nose; this is consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. The watering of his eye and the involvement of the tip of the nose are suggestive of corneal involvement. It is important to urgently refer this patient to ophthalmology, as herpes zoster can be sightthreatening. You would start high-dose oral aciclovir immediately. Artiﬁcial tear solution may reduce this patient’s symptoms, but it will not treat the underlying condition and therefore does not address the risk of sight impairment. B Start chloramphenicol eye drops Chloramphenicol eye drops are an antibiotic eye drop used for bacterial conjunctivitis. This patient has a rash consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus; it is vesicular and dermatomal. Consequently, antibiotic eye drops have no role in the management of this viral infection. The watering of his eye and the involvement of the tip of the nose are suggestive of corneal involvement. You must urgently refer this patient to ophthalmology for assessment to reduce the risk of visual impairment. You should also start high-dose oral aciclovir immediately. C Start topical aciclovir This patient’s rash is vesicular and dermatomal, and is therefore consistent with herpes zoster. Although aciclovir is the correct therapy for this condition, the patient has symptoms and signs that suggest corneal involvement (the rash affects the tip of the nose and there is eye watering). This means that high-dose oral aciclovir should be given, not topical aciclovir. You also must refer this patient urgently to ophthalmology for assessment, as ophthalmic herpes zoster can be sight-threatening.

stem: A 28-year-old man presented with a 6-month history increasing fatigue and lethargy, muscle pains and headache, accompanied by symptoms of indigestion. He had lost 4 kg in weight over the preceding 4 months. He was a voluntary aid worker and had been living in Chile for the past 5 years. Past history of note included a pulmonary embolus, for which he was taking warfarin. His ECG is shown below. Investigations: Barium swallow Dilated oesophagus Oesophageal manometry Increased pressure Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Chagas’ disease Chagas’ disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is caused by infection with Trypanosoma cruzi, carried by the kissing bug. Initial infection typically causes no or non-speciﬁc symptoms, but chronic infection leads to gastrointestinal and cardiac complications, such as conduction defects (hence the right bundle branch block on this patient’s ECG) and mega-oesophagus, as seen here. It also increases the tendency for thromboembolic disease, which may explain why he has developed a pulmonary embolism. Chagas’ disease can be diagnosed via PCR. Until recently no speciﬁc treatments were advocated for Chagas’ disease, and it had signiﬁcant morbidity and mortality. However, more recently it has been shown that nifurtimox may clear parasites in 50–60% of patients, though it has signiﬁcant side effects. D Oesophageal achalasia Although oesophageal achalasia could explain the ﬁndings on barium swallow and oesophageal manometry, it does not explain why this patient has conduction abnormalities on his ECG, or his other symptoms of fatigue, headache and myalgia. The combination of his travel history, conduction abnormalities, mega-oesophagus and history of thrombosis would ﬁt with Chagas’ disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, carried by the kissing bug. B Fasciolosis

Fasciola are liver ﬂukes, and cause an acute condition with fever, urticaria, anaemia, jaundice and abdominal pain, progressing to chronic inﬂammation and obstruction of the bile ducts and gall bladder. This patient does not have hepatic symptoms or signs; instead his symptoms and signs are more consistent with Chagas’ disease, caused by chronic infection with Trypanosoma cruzi. The dilated oesophagus is typical, and the disease also classically affects the heart, causing conduction problems as seen here. C Myasthenia gravis Myasthenia gravis causes difﬁculty with swallowing due to failure of coordinated peristalsis and muscular fatigue; however, it does not cause a dilated oesophagus on barium swallow. This patient’s travel history, combined with the dilated oesophagus and conduction abnormalities on his ECG, are more suggestive of Chagas’ disease, caused by chronic infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and spread by the kissing bug. E Sleeping sickness Sleeping sickness, or African trypanosomiasis, causes an acute ﬂulike illness with headache and myalgia, facial swelling and urticaria, and may develop into late-stage illness with a progressive meningoencephalitis. It does not cause mega-oesophagus, conduction abnormalities or and thromboembolism. This patient’s symptoms, signs and travel history are more consistent with Chagas’ disease, or American trypanosomiasis, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and carried by the kissing bug.

stem: A 31-year-old male is admitted with behavioural changes. One month before admission, he was on holiday in North Tanzania. He was exposed to multiple bites from insects and he developed an erythematous swelling on his left ankle. He then developed intermittent fever, myalgia and headache and was given quinine by a local doctor, with little effect. Over the last week, he has been sleeping most of the day and been up all night and has developed episodes of mania with rapid bursts of speech, followed by generalised apathy. He also complains of generalised headache with no blurred vision or change with posture, sneezing or coughing. He smokes 20 cigarettes/day and drinks alcohol at weekends, he has tried cannabis in the past and admits to occasional crack use, but his partner is not sure whether he has taken any recently. On examination, he is agitated but afebrile. His pulse is 120/min and blood pressure 102/65 mmHg. His chest is clear and abdomen soft although there is generalised tenderness. On examination of his peripheral nerves there is a ﬁne tremor in his upper limbs and increased tone throughout. He has generalised decreased power but reﬂexes are normal. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema. Investigation Result Normal values WCC 9.8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Hb 95 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 82.1 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ Platelets (PLT) 67 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Total protein 84 g/l 60 - 83 g/l Albumin 29 g/l 35 - 55 g/l ALT 35 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 68 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Bilirubin 9 µmol/l 1 - 22µmol/l Chest X-ray normal ECG sinus tachycardia Thick and thin ﬁlms for malaria parasites negative Which investigation would be most appropriate as the next step, given the suspected diagnosis?
options: Urgent computerised tomography (CT) of the brain
explanation:
A Urgent computerised tomography (CT) of the brain This patient has Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (East African or Rhodesian African trypanosomiasis) infection. A number of tourists to game parks in northern Tanzania recently acquired East African trypanosomiasis, which is transmitted through the bite of the tsetse ﬂy. This illness manifests as an erythematous swelling or chancre at the site of the ﬂy bite 5–15 days later, fever, headache and myalgia, before it progresses to meningoencephalitis. The second phase often occurs after a few weeks or a month in East African trypanosomiasis, but can take longer than one year in the West African disease. It is manifested by persistent headaches, daytime somnolence followed by night-time insomnia and behavioural changes, mood swings and, in some patients, depression. In late disease the patient becomes comatose (i.e. sleeping sickness) and it can be fatal. A computerised tomography (CT) of the head is required in order for a LP (lumbar puncture) to be performed. CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain in late disease reveal cerebral oedema and white matter enhancement. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) investigations should always be performed in patients with parasitaemia or lymphadenopathy. The double centrifugation technique is the most sensitive method to detect trypanosomes. Other CSF ﬁndings include a high WCC, elevated IgM and elevated protein levels. The treatment of choice is suramin in stage 1 (chancre/fever/myalgia) disease and melarsoprol in stage 2 (central nervous system (CNS)/meningoencephalitic) stage. B Blood culture During the acute phase of the disease, trypanosomes are often detectable on smears of peripheral blood, but blood cultures would not be able to demonstrate any parasites. C Psychiatry consultation

There is plenty of evidence for organic disease such as low platelet count, high white cell count and abnormalities on physical examination that would require a physical cause to be sought before seeking a psychiatric explanation. D Serology There is no current serological test for East African trypanosomiasis, but there is serological testing for T. gambiense, which occurs in West and Central Africa. There is also serological testing for T. cruzi, American trypanosomiasis. E Serum electrophoresis There is unlikely to be monoclonal expansion, this is unlikely to be a helpful investigation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Gynaecologist with complaints of bilateral lower abdominal pain and a thick, yellowish vaginal discharge that has a foul odour for the past week. She reports unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. Her menstrual cycles are regular and her last menstrual period was ﬁve days ago. Physical examination revealed bilateral lower abdominal tenderness and cervical motion tenderness on bimanual vaginal examination. Her blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 96 bpm and temperature 37.8 °C. Which of the following is the best line of management in this patient?
options: Intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous doxycycline for 14 days
Intramuscular ceftriaxone single dose, oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
Oral oﬂoxacin with oral metronidazole for 14 days
explanation: B Intramuscular ceftriaxone single dose, oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days Ceftriaxone provides microbiological cover for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and doxycycline is combined with this to prevent/slow down the development of resistance to ceftriaxone by N. gonorrhoeae. Metronidazole is included to improve coverage of anaerobic bacteria. D Oral moxiﬂoxacin for 14 days Oral moxiﬂoxacin alone is not recommended for treatment of PID. A Intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous doxycycline for 14 days Inpatient admission and treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and doxycycline has been recommended in patients with severe pelvic inﬂammatory disease (PID) (fever > 38 °C), hypotension, features of tubo-ovarian abscess, pelvic peritonitis or lack of response to oral therapy. Since these features are not present in this patient, outpatient treatment is appropriate. C Oral oﬂoxacin with oral metronidazole for 14 days Oral oﬂoxacin, in combination with metronidazole, is only a secondline therapy in the treatment of PID. E Oral azithromycin single dose Combination drug therapy, rather than monotherapy with azithromycin, is the preferred treatment for PID.

stem: A 28-year-old immigrant is transferred to the hospital from the local Detention Centre. He complained to the medical staff there of a cough and weight loss. Sputum testing and a chest X-ray have conﬁrmed tuberculosis (TB) with multidrug resistance (MDR). Which of the following is the most appropriate step with respect to protecting from spread of infection?
options: Negative pressure room and personal protective equipment
Single room no personal protective equipment needed
Single room and personal respiratory protection
Ward nursing and surgical mask for patient
explanation: A Negative pressure room and personal protective equipment Guidance on MDR TB is clear that patients should be isolated in a negative pressure room, and those treating the patient should utilise full personal protective equipment. These measures should be continued until a two- week period has passed and some clinical improvement in the patient’s condition has been observed. E Ward nursing and surgical mask for patient Even a patient without MDR TB should not be nursed on an open ward because of the risk of infection spread between patients or between the patient and nursing staff. A Single room no personal protective equipment needed This patient has active MDR TB and must be placed under maximal protective measures to reduce spread of infection. B Single room and surgical mask Patients in the ﬁrst few days of treatment for non-MDR TB are asked to wear a surgical mask whenever they are outside their room (eg to undergo radiological investigations). C Single room and personal respiratory protection A negative pressure environment is also required to reduce accidental spread of TB bacteria outside the room.

stem: A 26-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department from the airport, having just returned on a ﬂight from Bangladesh. Around 1 h before landing he collapsed after severe vomiting and diarrhoea on the plane. His travelling partner reports that he became ill one day before leaving Bangladesh, with high-volume, painless, watery diarrhoea. Blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg and his pulse is 100/min and regular. Dark-ﬁeld microscopy of a fresh stool specimen reveals Gramnegative bacilli. Given the likeliest diagnosis, which one of the following antibiotic choices would be most appropriate in the treatment of this patient?
explanation:
A Erythromycin This patient has cholera, a comma-shaped Gram-negative bacillus. It causes clinical disease by releasing an enterotoxin that affects the small bowel, leading to secretion of huge amounts of ﬂuid and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Diagnosis is via dark-ground microscopy of a fresh stool specimen. While rehydration is the primary therapy for cholera, use of antibiotics is proven to shorten the duration and severity of the illness. Antibiotic choices may include quinolones such as ciproﬂoxacin, tetracyclines, erythromycin and co-trimoxazole, but there are problems with resistance to tetracyclines emerging in patients from the Indian subcontinent in particular. Quinolone treatment is also no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but signiﬁcant risk of debilitating adverse effects. For these reasons, erythromycin is the most appropriate answer in this scenario. With appropriate rehydration and antibiotic therapy where required, patients usually show signs of recovery over a few days. C Amoxicillin Amoxicillin is a good antimicrobial choice for chest infections and can be useful in the treatment of urine and skin infections, but is of limited used in gastrointestinal problems. B Metronidazole Metronidazole would be a good antibiotic choice if anaerobes such as Gardnerella, Entamoeba, Giardia or Clostridium were suspected. This might be suspected with bloody diarrhoea or, for C. difﬁcile, recent antibiotic use. D Co-trimoxazole Co-trimoxazole is not widely used now due to associated risks of blood dyscrasias. It is still primarily utilised for the treatment and prophylaxis of pneumocystis pneumonia.

E Penicillin V Penicillin V is more commonly used for pharyngeal infections than gastrointestinal infections.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the clinic with symptoms of indigestion and heart burn that have worsened over the past 18 months. She is most concerned as her uncle died of oesophageal carcinoma. You arrange an upper GI endoscopy on the routine list. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 175 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Endoscopy Helicobacter gastritis She is treated with eradication therapy, which is thought to be successful. How would you advise her with respect to the future risk of cancers / re-treatment of her helicobacter?
options: Her future risk of oesophageal carcinoma is likely to be increased
She can be reassured that she no longer has a clinically signiﬁcant increased risk of gastric cancer
She is at increased risk of gastric lymphoma
She should be re-treated with eradication therapy every 3 years
Consumption of 5 units of alcohol per week will signiﬁcantly increase her risk of stomach cancer
explanation:
B She can be reassured that she no longer has a clinically signiﬁcant increased risk of gastric cancer Eradication of H.pylori can prevent the progression to atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia (a premalignant condition). Even in patients with established intestinal metaplasia, eradication of H.pylori in patients has been shown to prevent the progression to gastric cancer. For more information see “Management of Helicobacter pylori – the Maastricht IV/Florence consensus report”. Gut. 2012. D She should be re-treated with eradication therapy every 3 years Recurrence of infection in developed countries is rare. H.pylori breath or stool testing should be performed where recurrence is

suspected; there is no evidence to support empirical regular eradication. A Her future risk of oesophageal carcinoma is likely to be increased Eradication of H.pylori has no effect on symptoms of gastrooesophageal reﬂux disease or its sequelae, in particular the development of Barrett’s or oesophageal carcinoma. C She is at increased risk of gastric lymphoma Eradication of H.pylori is the ﬁrst line treatment of low grade gastric marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, curing 60-80% of cases. E Consumption of 5 units of alcohol per week will signiﬁcantly increase her risk of stomach cancer Alcohol is one of the environmental factors that has been shown to signiﬁcantly increase the risk of gastric cancer. However, 5 units (40g of alcohol) has not been shown to be statistically signiﬁcant in increasing this risk.

stem: A 31-year-old man presents to the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic, requesting post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) following a high-risk encounter. Under which of the following circumstances would PEP be recommended?
options: Following a bite which punctured the skin, but not deep tissue, from a person with human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) and a detectable viral load
A woman having receptive unprotected anal sex with a HIV positive man, who takes anti-viral therapy, and has a viral load of between 140-180 copies/ml one day ago
A woman performing fellatio with an HIV-positive man without ejaculation one day ago
A man having insertive anal sex with a woman from the UK one day ago
A woman receiving unprotected insertive anal sex from a man who has sex with men with an unknown HIV status
explanation:
E A woman receiving unprotected insertive anal sex from a man who has sex with men with an unknown HIV status Within the United Kingdom men who have sex with men are currently deemed to be high risk for transmission of human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), where the HIV status is unknown or known to be positive. In cases of unprotected receptive anal intercourse, but not vaginal intercourse, and an unknown HIV status, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended. The risk of transmission in vaginal or insertive anal intercourse is felt to be lower, and PEP is not required. Ideally, according to guidelines, PEP should be started within 72 hours of exposure. A Following a bite which punctured the skin, but not deep tissue, from a person with human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) and a detectable viral load Generally, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is not recommended following a bite as the risk of transmission is likely to be negligible unless the following three criteria are all met: 1. The person who performed the bites' saliva is visibly

contaminated with blood 2. There is a known HIV viral load of over 1000 copies/ml 3. The bite has caused deep tissue injuries These criteria are fortunately rarely met. B A woman having receptive unprotected anal sex with a HIV positive man, who takes anti-viral therapy, and has a viral load of between 140-180 copies/ml one day ago Typically, PEP is not required if the if the HIV-positive partner is adherent to antiviral therapy and has sustained undetectable viral load (less than 200 copies/ml). C A woman performing fellatio with an HIV-positive man without ejaculation one day ago The rate of transmission is considered to be low risk, even if ejaculation occurred. D A man having insertive anal sex with a woman from the UK one day ago While the behaviour is considered to be high risk for HIV transmission, a woman from the UK is considered to be in the lowprevalence group and therefore, no PEP should be recommended.

stem: A 33-year-old white man was admitted with a 1-week history of rash, pyrexia, generalised weakness and decreased urine output. On examination, he was obese, with a temperature of 38.5 °C, BP 156/70 mmHg. He had nail-fold vasculitic skin lesions. On auscultation, he had a soft systolic murmur. Abdominal examination was limited given his size, but unremarkable. Initial investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 90 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 18.5 × 109/ 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 16.4 × 109/ 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/ Platelets (PLT) 80 × 109/ 150 - 400 × 109/l Creatinine (Cr) 336 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urine microscopy Red cell casts Hepatitis B negative Hepatitis C negative ANCA/GBM negative Cryoglobulins positive ASOT negative Protein electrophoresis negative Ultrasound renal scan of the abdomen showed an 11-cm spleen. Renal biopsy was not performed, as it was not technically possible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Infective endocarditis The history and investigations are consistent with infective endocarditis. One third of patients with bacterial endocarditis develop AKI. The glomerulonephritis is associated with deposition of immune complexes containing bacterial antigens in glomeruli. Cryoglobulins (polyclonal or type III) are present in 50% of subjects. A Microscopic polyangiitis Microscopic polyangiitis may present with nail-fold vasculitic lesions but these patients are commonly ANCA- positive. C Acute pyelonephritis The heart murmur, negative urinary sediment and positive cryoglobulins make this unlikely. D HIV-associated nephropathy There is no weight loss or lymphopenia. HIVAN occurs almost exclusively in black patients, and they tend to be normotensive.

E Renal tuberculosis Renal TB is associated with an insidious onset of renal impairment with asymptomatic urinary abnormalities such as persistent sterile pyuria. It may or may not be associated with extrarenal systemic manifestations.

stem: A 42-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. He complains of multiple joint pains, including in his hands, feet, wrists, elbows, and knees. He is unable to bend down, which is making it very difﬁcult to continue his job as an electrician. He tells you he was unwell about ten days earlier with a diarrhoeal illness after eating under-cooked chicken. He has knee effusions more marked on the left than the right. An image of his knees is shown below: Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 137 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) Sodium (Na+) 243 × 109/l 144 mmol/l 150 - 400 × 109/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 118 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 78 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely cause of his arthritis?
explanation:
C Reactive arthritis This man’s recent bout of diarrhoea is most likely related to Campylobacter infection. The rate of reactive arthritis is low at approximately 2.5%, although the prevalence of joint symptoms

may be higher, in up to 13 percent of cases. The likelihood of developing reactive arthritis appears to be unrelated to the severity of diarrheal illness. Reactive arthritis is seen more commonly among patients with the HLA-B27 phenotype. Most cases regress spontaneously within six months of onset, and non-steroidal antiinﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are effective in managing symptoms. A Gout Gout is usually characterised by mono-arthritis with redness, swelling, and limitation of movement. It does not ﬁt with the picture seen here with multiple joint pains. NSAIDs, colchicine, or prednisolone are all potential interventions for the treatment of acute gout. Over the longer-term precipitant drugs should be withdrawn if possible, and allopurinol instituted. A Pyrophosphate arthropathy Pyrophosphate arthropathy, like gout, is usually characterised by mono-arthritis during an acute episode, most frequently the knee. Knee aspiration with microscopy and crystal examination can help conﬁrm the diagnosis. Crystals have a rhomboid shape and weak positive birefringence on polarised light microscopy. D Rheumatoid arthritis The proximity of this patient’s symptoms to the diarrhoeal illness ﬁts better with an episode of reactive arthritis rather than acute onset of rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with positive rheumatoid factor antibodies and/or positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (antiCCP) antibodies. E Septic arthritis Septic arthritis tends to affect a single joint only unless it has occurred via haematogenous spread in a condition such as gonococcal infection. In the event that septic arthritis is suspected, joint aspiration for microscopy and culture is the most important investigation. In most cases of septic arthritis, the white cell count exceeds 50 000 cells per µl.

stem: A 68-year-old man presented to clinic with a 3-week history of fever, malaise and a dry cough. He was a dairy farmer who specialised in unpasteurised milk and cheeses. He had no other medical conditions and was otherwise well. On examination his temperature was 38.4oC. There was an ejection systolic murmur and hepatomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values Bilirubin 27 µmol/L 1.7 - 20.5 µmol/L ALT 89 u/l 7 - 55 u/l AST 67 u/l 10 - 40 u/l Blood cultures Negative in serial samples separated by time and site Trans-oesophageal echocardiogram Vegetations visible on the aortic valve What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Coxiella endocarditis Coxiella infection is widespread in domestic and farm animals. It usually spreads between animals by ticks, which act as reservoirs of infection. Infection may be also be spread via unpasteurised milk. It causes fever and malaise, which may progress to pneumonia, hepatitis or. in rare cases, to culture-negative endocarditis, as seen here. Coxiella is usually diagnosed via complement ﬁxation. B Fungal endocarditis Fungal endocarditis is a cause of culture-negative endocarditis, but it is extremely uncommon, especially in immunocompetent individuals. In most cases it is associated with cardiac surgery or healthcare settings. This patient is more likely to have Coxiella endocarditis; Coxiella is common in domestic and farm animals and causes a culture-negative endocarditis as seen in this case. C Libman–Sacks endocarditis Libman–Sacks endocarditis is a non-infective vegetative endocarditis seen in systemic lupus erythematosus. Therefore although it is a cause of culture-negative endocarditis, it is an unlikely diagnosis in this case as the patient has no history of, or symptoms and signs suggestive of, systemic lupus erythematosus. This patient is most likely to have Coxiella endocarditis as a result of contact with livestock; Coxiella causes a culture-negative endocarditis. D Staphylococcal endocarditis It would be unusual not to identify Staphylococcus spp. in serial blood cultures in a patient with vegetative endocarditis, but this patient has culture-negative endocarditis. Coxiella causes a culturenegative endocarditis, and is common amongst farm livestock; this is the most likely diagnosis. E Streptococcal endocarditis If a patient had vegetative streptococcal endocarditis, it would be unusual for serial blood cultures to be negative. Instead, it is more likely that this patient has Coxiella endocarditis, which is also consistent with his prodromal illness. Coxiella is a common infection in livestock and can be carried by ticks.

stem: A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of general malaise, lethargy and difﬁculty swallowing with some occasional regurgitation of undigested food. He had been living in Bolivia for 6 years as a relief worker. On examination, his blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, his pulse was 95 bpm and his jugular venous pulse was elevated. He had bilateral basal inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest, and bilateral pitting leg oedema. Barium swallow revealed a dilated oesophagus. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
E Trypanosoma cruzi This parasite is spread via the faeces of the reduviid bug, which is left on the skin after the bug feeds and can enter the bloodstream after scratching or rubbing the skin in response to the insect bite. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas’ disease. The acute phase of Chagas’ disease manifests as constitutional symptoms and facial or generalised oedema, and there may be diarrhoea and vomiting, or ECG changes. This is followed by a latent phase and then a chronic phase; this patient has presented in the chronic phase with megaoesophagus, which is characteristic of Chagas’ disease. Patients may also have megacolon, congestive heart failure and arrhythmias. Diagnosis is by serology, and the patient should have an ECG and echocardiogram to check for cardiac complications. Patients in the chronic phase can be treated with nitroheterocycles if they have been infected for less than 10 years, as in this case. B Entamoeba histolytica Entamoeba histolytica is very common in South America where it causes amoebic dysentery, and can also affect the liver. It does not cause mega-oesophagus, as seen in this patient. This patient’s travel history, combined with his signs and symptoms, would be consistent with a diagnosis of Chagas’ disease, which is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi infection. A Borrelia burgdorferi Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative bacterium of Lyme disease. It is not found in tropical climates, and therefore is unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s symptoms. Furthermore, Lyme disease has a variety of stages and manifestations, but it does not cause megaoesophagus, as seen in this patient. Instead, this patient’s travel history and presentation is more consistent with Chagas’ disease, which is caused by infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by the faeces of the kissing bug, left on the skin after the insect has fed.

C Leishmania donovani This organism causes visceral leishmaniasis and is found in India and Africa, but it is not native to South America. Furthermore, visceral leishmaniasis has a variety of manifestations but would be unlikely to cause mega-oesophagus, as seen in this patient. This patient’s presentation is consistent with Chagas’ disease, which is caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, spread by the faeces of the kissing bug which is left on the skin after feeding. D Rickettsia rickettsi This organism causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and is endemic in the USA and parts of South America. It is a tick-borne illness, and has a variety of manifestations but classically causes a petechial rash, beginning on the feet and hands. It does not cause megaoesophagus, as seen here. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with Chagas’ disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. This causes mega-oesophagus and constitutional symptoms. The parasite is spread by the faeces of the kissing bug, left on the skin after feeding.

stem: A 24-year-old man who has recently returned from India presents with bloody diarrhoea and mucus. More recently, he has also developed some abdominal pain and vomiting which has increased over the past few days. His blood pressure 95/70 mmHg and his pulse is 100 bpm and regular. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 112 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 16.3 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 756 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Urea 11.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l ESR 56 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 2.7 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 72 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Discharge with advice on rehydration and outpatient appointment
explanation:
D IV Fluid and electrolyte replacement The two most likely diagnoses are infective diarrhoea and ulcerative

colitis. The clinical history and laboratory results would be consistent with both. However, given his recent history of abdominal pain and vomiting, the most important diagnosis to exclude is toxic megacolon. He therefore requires ﬂuid and electrolyte replacement, and an abdominal X-ray. B Discharge with advice on rehydration and outpatient appointment The extent of his abnormalities of biochemistry, especially hypokalaemia, indicates that he has had severe diarrhoea from his infection and needs inpatient electrolyte correction and ﬂuid support. A Oral metronidazole Antibiotics are seldom needed for gastroenteritis. If the patient is systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or elderly. Metronidazole would be a useful treatment for protozoal gastrointestinal infection. C IV ceftriaxone As above, antibiotics are not indicated for this patient. Ceftriaxone is a broad-spectrum antibiotic commonly used for meningitis and can be used for typhoid and paratyphoid fever. E Oral ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin can be used for when Salmonella, Shigella or Campylobacter infection is conﬁrmed as the speciﬁc cause of gastroenteritis, however quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but signiﬁcant risk of debilitating adverse effects.

stem: A 40-year-old Asian man is referred to the Neurology Clinic with a 9-month history of distal sensory loss and weakness. There is no history of headache or visual change and his coordination remains intact. He denies any constitutional symptoms or recent infective illnesses. He has a past medical history of diet-controlled type II diabetes and hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 5 mg once daily. On examination, he is systemically well with normal observations. He has visible wasting in the intrinsic muscles of his right foot, with a Medical Research Council (MRC) power of 4/5 for ankle dorsiﬂexion. There is associated loss of temperature and light touch sensation down the posterolateral aspect of his right leg. The remainder of his neurological examination shows no further motor deﬁcits and his cranial nerves are intact. He has multiple hypopigmented patches over the extensor surfaces of his arms and legs, with associated sensory loss for all but deep pressure stimuli. What is the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation: B Skin-slit smear This patient has leprosy. Leprosy is a granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae which affects the peripheral nerves and skin. Initial symptoms include numbness, typically with loss of temperature followed by light touch, pain and ﬁnally deep pressure. Cutaneous lesions follow later in the disease and appear as hypopigmented patches of skin with associated sensory loss. The investigation of choice is a skin-slit smear; a slit is made over a lesion of skin which is then smeared onto a glass slide. It is examined for acid-fast bacilli under microscopy. If detected, the treatment of choice is with dapsone, rifampicin and clofazimine. D Viral DNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR) This patient has leprosy, a granulomatous disease caused by M. leprae. It is detected by examining for the presence of acid-fast bacilli under microscopy. Skin biopsy and M. leprae DNA PCR are alternative methods that can be used to diagnose the disease. However, a viral DNA PCR would not diagnose leprosy, given the disease is caused by a bacterial infection. A Nerve conduction studies Nerve conduction studies can be useful to investigate the cause of a peripheral neuropathy and help determine if there is an underlying demyelinating or axonal cause. However, nerve conduction studies do not have a role in diagnosing leprosy. C Lumbar puncture A lumbar puncture would be indicated if there were reason to expect that an underlying neurological illness was responsible for this patient’s symptoms, including multiple sclerosis or a central nervous system (CNS) infection. However, it is not needed to make a diagnosis of leprosy. E Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain An MRI would be indicated if there were reason to expect that an underlying central neurological illness was responsible for this patient’s symptoms, including multiple sclerosis or a neurodegenerative condition. However, it is not needed to make a diagnosis of leprosy.

stem: A 23-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with severe vomiting, which began some 90 minutes after eating rice-based takeaway food that he had the night before. He complains of abdominal cramps, retrosternal pain, and has vomited ten times. He has struggled to keep water down. There is no diarrhoea. His blood pressure (BP) is 100/70 mmHg; his pulse is 98 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is a postural drop of 15 mmHg on standing. He is tender in the epigastrium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Bacillus cereus (B cereus) food poisoning B cereus is widespread in the environment and commonly found in the soil. It is resistant to heat and desiccation and can grow if food is stored under favourable conditions, (temperature 8-55 oC), and has a pH > 4.8. It is commonly found in rice preparations and can present with either diarrhoeal or vomiting forms – although not with both. The vomiting form occurs due to ingestion of cereulide (a recognised emetic), while the diarrhoeal form occurs due to enterotoxin released in the small bowel. Most people recover without treatment within 24 hours. E Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus) food poisoning Staphylococcus food poisoning occurs most commonly when patients ingest bacteria from dairy products (eg fresh cream cakes) which have been left out at room temperature for a considerable period of time. It is the result of staphylococcal enterotoxin ingestion. The onset of vomiting symptoms begins 2 to 8 hours later. Symptoms rapidly resolve after a few hours. B Norovirus infection Norovirus infection leads to gastroenteritis with symptoms of nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. It tends to occur in outbreaks during autumn and winter, and symptoms settle without intervention in the majority of patients over a 24 to 48-hour period. Patients may excrete virus up to 48 hours after the cessation of diarrhoea, and so should not return to environments in which they will come into contact with others during this time. C Rotavirus infection Rotavirus is a common cause of outbreaks of diarrhoea and vomiting, particularly in children. Severe vomiting and diarrhoea are seen, and symptoms may last between 3 and 8 days in total. Outbreaks may also be seen in elderly care homes. Supportive therapy with oral rehydration/intravenous (IV) ﬂuid replacement may be required. The patients age, presentation and symptom timeline do not support this diagnosis. D Salmonella typhi (S typhi) food poisoning In salmonella infection, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps are a prominent feature, and are often accompanied by fever. Nausea and vomiting may also be seen. The diarrhoea may also be bloody. The

illness usually lasts for between 4–7 days and is self-limiting. Antibiotics are not recommended for salmonella infection; they are only used in those with severe comorbidities and where there are features of signiﬁcant infection with, for example, pre-renal disease.

stem: A 63-year-old Sri Lankan man presented with a 4-week history of cough, intermittent fever, night sweats and malaise. Six weeks previously, he had travelled to Sri Lanka for 2 months to visit his family. He denied haemoptysis or any contacts with tuberculosis. On examination, his temperature was 38.3 °C and pulse rate was 94 bpm. There was reduced chest expansion on the right, and the right base was dull to percussion, with bronchial breathing above. There was 2-cm, tender hepatomegaly, with an irregular border. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Bilirubin 29 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 27 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 146 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Blood cultures No growth Sputum cultures No growth CT chest, abdomen, pelvis Multi-loculated, right-sided pleural effusion, 10 × 6 cm hepatic collection Pleural biopsy No acid-fast bacilli The pleural effusion was drained. Which is the best choice of further treatment?
explanation:
C Co-amoxiclav, clarithromycin and metronidazole This patient has signs and symptoms suggestive of amoebiasis. Entamoeba histolytica is common in South and South East Asia, and hepatic amoebiasis typically causes constitutional symptoms, as seen here. There is usually tender hepatomegaly and pleural effusions. Empyemas are a common complication. It is common for liver function tests to be normal, or there may be an obstructive picture with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin levels (mildly raised here, but the alanine aminotransferase level is normal). The patient should be treated with metronidazole, and this can be given as a monotherapy. However, until the diagnosis is conﬁrmed by serology or aspirate polymerase chain reaction (PCR), it would be appropriate to prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy by adding co-

amoxiclav and clarithromycin. D Peginterferon alpha Peginterferon alpha is the ﬁrst-line therapy for patients with hepatitis B. Although hepatitis B is endemic in large parts of Asia, its prevalence is low in Sri Lanka. Hepatitis B could certainly present with constitutional symptoms. However, it is highly unlikely that the patient would have a normal alanine aminotransferase level in the context of untreated hepatitis B infection. Hepatitis B increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma but would not cause a collection in the liver, and it does not explain the unilateral pleural effusion. This patient’s presentation is much better explained by an amoebic liver abscess with associated empyema and should be treated with metronidazole (though additional broad-spectrum antibiotics should be continued until the diagnosis is conﬁrmed). A Co-amoxiclav This patient has recently returned from Sri Lanka with constitutional symptoms and a swinging fever. He has a collection in the liver and an associated pleural effusion; together with his symptoms, this is suggestive of amoebiasis, and therefore metronidazole should be added to his treatment. It would be appropriate to continue broadspectrum antibiotics alongside this (ideally co-amoxiclav and a macrolide), until the diagnosis of amoebiasis is conﬁrmed, at which point these can be stopped and metronidazole can be continued as a monotherapy. B Co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin This is appropriate therapy for an atypical pneumonia. However, this patient has recently returned from Sri Lanka with constitutional symptoms and a swinging fever. He has a collection in the liver and an associated pleural effusion; together with his symptoms, this is suggestive of amoebiasis, and therefore metronidazole should be added to his treatment. It would be appropriate to prescribe coamoxiclav and clarithromycin, in addition to metronidazole, until the diagnosis of amoebiasis is conﬁrmed, at which point metronidazole can be continued as monotherapy. E Rifampicin, isoniazid and ethambutol These are treatments for tuberculosis. This patient’s malaise and night sweats could be explained by tuberculosis, but tuberculosis does not normally cause a swinging fever (this is more associated with abscesses). Tuberculosis can seed into the liver, but it is uncommon. You would also expect to see acid-fast bacilli on pleural biopsy if this were tuberculosis. A more likely explanation for this patient’s symptoms and investigation ﬁndings would be amoebiasis, which is common in Sri Lanka. Amoebiasis explains the liver abscess, and pleural effusions are a common complication. The correct treatment would be metronidazole (though it is reasonable to continue additional broad-spectrum antibiotics until the diagnosis is conﬁrmed).

stem: A 25-year-old man was referred with a four-day history of gradualonset headache, abdominal pain, constipation and high fevers. He had returned from a holiday in Thailand 10 days previously. He had not gone swimming in any freshwater while he was away. He had sexual intercourse and used barrier methods. On examination, his temperature is 39.7 °C, pulse 76 bpm and regular and blood pressure 98/60 mmHg. He appeared ﬂushed and lethargic. There was no rash, or axillary or neck lymphadenopathy. His abdomen was mildly tender in the left iliac fossa. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 107 g/l 115 - 165 g/l MCV 83.2 ﬂ 80 - 96 ﬂ WCC 6.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 83 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Bilirubin 34 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l ALT 154 u/l 5 - 35 u/l ALP 221 u/l 45 - 105 u/l g-glutamyl transferase 264 u/l 4 - 35 u/l CRP 298 μg/l < 10 μg/l Sodium (Na) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.9 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 64 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Typhoid fever This is an uncommon bacterial infection (Salmonella typhii) and typically causes high fevers, abdominal pain, constipation and headache, as seen in this patient. Classically, patients demonstrate Faget’s sign – a relative bradycardia. Note that despite a temperature of 39.7 °C, this patient has a pulse of 76 bpm, perhaps lower than expected, given the high temperature. Treatment is with ceftriaxone or azithromycin in milder cases. B Human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) Although this patient did have sexual intercourse during his trip, he used barrier protection, which dramatically reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections. HIV seroconversion can cause malaise, low-grade fever, diarrhoea and rash; however, instead this patient has constipation and a high fever, which would not be typically for seroconversion. This patient’s symptoms and signs would be more consistent with typhoid fever. A Escherichia coli gastroenteritis

E. coli is the most common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller; however, instead, this patient has constipation. This is not a feature of E. coli infection. Although E. coli can cause diarrhoea, leading to dehydration and subsequently headache, you would not expect headache to be an early symptom. It is uncommon for E. coli gastroenteritis to cause such a high fever and high CRP. Instead, this patient’s symptoms and signs would be more consistent with typhoid fever. C Inﬂuenza The patient does not complain of any coryzal symptoms, and abdominal pain would be atypical for inﬂuenza infection. As inﬂuenza is a viral infection, you would not expect such a high CRP, as seen in this case, unless there was a secondary pneumonia (of which there is no suggestion in the clinical stem). A high CRP such as this is typical of typhoid fever. D Schistosomiasis Schistosomiasis is a ﬂatworm, or ﬂuke, and is typically contracted by swimming in fresh water; this patient has not swum in any lakes or rivers and therefore is unlikely to be exposed to the organism. Schistosoma mekongi is the most common species found in Thailand, and it usually causes intestinal disease, leading to abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea; this patient has constipation. It would not usually cause a headache. Instead this patient’s symptoms and signs would be more consistent with typhoid fever.

stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted to the Respiratory Ward following a 10-day history of high fevers, myalgia and nausea and vomiting. Over the last four days, he has deteriorated with worsening shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. He has a background of alcohol dependence and hypercholesterolaemia and regularly takes atorvastatin 20 mg once daily, vitamin B complex two tablets daily and thiamine 100 mg daily. On examination, he has a temperature of 39.2 °C. His heart rate is 126 bpm and regular and his BP is 155/93 mmHg. He has coarse crackles at the left base of his lungs and is saturating at 94% on 6 litres of oxygen by Venturi mask. His heart sounds are normal, and his abdomen is soft, with no palpable masses. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 136 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 17.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 15.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.7 × 109/l 0.8–5.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 365 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 146 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 11.3 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 141 µm/l 50–120 µm/l EGFR 60+ CRP 194 mg/l < 10 mg/l Chest X-ray: left mid-zone consolidation What is the most likely causative organism for this presentation?
explanation:
B Staphylococcus aureus This patient has staphylococcal pneumonia. Clues to the diagnosis are the onset of his pneumonia following a period of ﬂu-like symptoms and lymphopenia on the blood results. The most likely cause of pneumonia after infection with the inﬂuenza virus is S. aureus. A Chlamydia psittaci C. psittaci, an obligate intracellular bacterium can rersult in pneumonia (psittacosis) in approximately 1% of all cases. Most cases occur following contact with birds (turkeys, chickens, cockatiels and various migratory birds) with an incubation period between 5-14 days. Extra pulmonary symptoms are common, such as headache, pharyngitis and diarrhoea. Given the preceding ﬂu like illness, lack of contact with birds and a lack of extra pulmonary features described, C. psittaci is less likely here. B Klebsiella pneumoniae K. pneumoniae is a Gram-negative rod that causes pneumonia more commonly in those with a history of diabetes, alcohol excess, poor dental hygiene and other co-morbidities. It is associated with serious complications, including the development of lung abscesses and is associated with high mortality. While this patient has a background of alcohol dependence, the preceding ﬂu-like symptoms and lymphopenia suggest an underlying viral illness, making S. aureus the most likely answer. C Legionella pneumophila Legionnaires’ disease is an atypical pneumonia commonly spread via a contaminated water supply. Not only does a patient present with pneumonia, but extrapulmonary symptoms are also seen, including hyponatraemia, deranged liver function tests and neurological symptoms, including confusion and ataxia. These are not seen in this patient’s presentation. D Mycoplasma pneumoniae M. pneumoniae is another cause of an atypical pneumonia. Flu-like symptoms are seen in Mycoplasma pneumonia, similarly to this patient’s case presentation. However, Mycoplasma pneumonia can also cause extrapulmonary symptoms such as haemolytic anaemia and erythema multiforme, which are not seen here making it less

likely.

stem: A 27-year-old man with a history of human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV), who is poorly compliant with his medication, comes to the Emergency Department. He has been feeling increasingly unwell over the past two to three weeks with fever, shortness of breath, weight loss and diarrhoea up to ﬁve times a day. Examination reveals a temperature of 37.9 °C, a pulse of 90 bpm and regular and a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. There is generalised lymphadenopathy, and his body mass index is 21 kg/m2. There is tender hepatosplenomegaly. Bilateral basal crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 91 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 98 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CD4 count 4/mm3 500–1500 mm3 Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 185 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 38 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 182 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Mycobacterium avium infection The constellation of symptoms, including respiratory symptoms, weight loss, diarrhoea, generalised lymphadenopathy and abnormal liver function tests, ﬁt best with a diagnosis of Mycobacterium avium (MAI). Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is now available as an option for conﬁrming the underlying diagnosis. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) should be recommenced, assuming the patient has not been compliant with his medication. Triple therapy with a macrolide, ethambutol and rifabutin is the optimal choice for management of the underlying MAI. D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma This is an important differential in a patient who has a low CD4 count. It would be important to send this patient for computed tomography (CT) of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis to exclude this as a diagnosis. A Cryptococcosis Cryptococcosis is often associated with central nervous system (CNS) infection in HIV and is more rarely associated with diarrhoea, compared to the other options given. Treatment is with intravenous ﬂuconazole. B Cryptosporidium infection Cryptosporidium is associated with more profuse watery diarrhoea than that reported here and an increased risk for gall bladder infection. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed using acid staining testing. Treatment is usually supportive, but in patients with HIV, it is imperative that they maintain good compliance with their antiretroviral therapy. Nitazoxanide can be used if persistent and severe. E Pneumocystis jirovecii infection Pneumocystis is not usually associated with diarrhoea. It is more readily associated with signiﬁcant breathlessness on exertion, weight loss and night sweats. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by identiﬁcation of the organism by sputum staining or PCR. A presumptive diagnosis or ‘treat as’ can be made with a typical history and chest X-ray ﬁndings and elevated serum levels of beta-D-glucan. Treatment is with co-trimoxazole.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with malaise, fatigue, and night sweats. She denies any past medical history but admits to drinking excessively and having no ﬁxed abode. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.7 °C and tiny black streaks on her nails. A small cutaneous lesion, consisting of a central red mark with surrounding erythema, is seen in the cubital fossa. What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
explanation: B Infective endocarditis Infective endocarditis is a well known association in patients who inject heroin as in this case. Common symptoms include: fever, malaise, heart murmurs, and septic emboli (splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions). E Meningococcal sepsis Meningococcal sepsis causes generic signs of infection (fever, malaise, haemodynamic instability) in addition to focal signs depending on the organ that has been affected (i.e. photosensitivity in meningitis or cough in pneumonia). A Cerebral vasculitis Cerebral vasculitis leads to a wide range of symptoms, such as headaches, skin rashes, tiredness, joint pains, weakness, and alterations in behaviour. In addition, in 10% it can lead to intracranial haemorrhage. C Toxic shock syndrome Toxic shock syndrome is a potentially fatal illness caused by bacterial toxins. Patients are pyrexic with signs of haemodynamic compromise (tachypnoea, hypotension, and tachycardia). D Heroin overdose The skin lesions represent needle marks from intravenous (iv) injections (track marks) that indicate intravenous drug use. However, the patient doesn’t have any more signs of opiate overdose such as miosis or drowsiness. Non-fatal overdose is common among heroin injectors and is strongly related to the misuse of multiple other substances such as methadone, benzodiazepines, and alcohol.

stem: A 42-year-old farmer is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. She is very worried about him, as he has been unable to leave the house and get to work because of a fever and feeling completely washed out. He has been working particularly hard as they have some concerns about ﬁnance. They tell you that he was clearing some drainage ditches on the edge of one of his ﬁelds a week. On examination, he is pyrexial 38.2 °C and looks jaundiced. There is a bandage on his right leg from where he cut himself on some brambles. He has abdominal tenderness, particularly over his liver. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 114 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 56 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 6.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 235 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l ALT 320 U/l 25–55 U/l Bilirubin 290 μmol/l 1.7–20.5 μmol/l Creatinine kinase (CK) 780 U/l 22–198 U/l Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for him?
explanation: C Benzylpenicillin This unfortunate man has the severe form of leptospirosis known as Weil’s disease, spread via rats’ urine. It is likely that the cut on his leg, and wading through his drainage ditches, provided the route for infection. Infection leads to thrombocytopenia, jaundice with only a modest rise in transaminases, kidney disease and increased CK. Benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are drugs of choice for severe infection, with doxycycline a possible alternative in patients who are penicillin allergic. Thankfully most patients with leptospirosis suffer from a relatively mild infection and recover. Mortality from Weil’s disease is particularly high, however, in patients who are elderly or in those with pre-existing pathology. D Fresh frozen plasma Fresh frozen plasma may be used to correct speciﬁc clotting factor deﬁciencies or to reverse the effect of warfarin (although its use is superseded by prothrombin complex concentrate). This patient’s presentation is suggestive of leptospirosis and therefore targeted antimicrobial therapy is the treatment of choice. A N-acetylcysteine N-acetylcysteine is the treatment of choice for signiﬁcant paracetamol overdose. This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of leptospirosis, and as we are not given any suggestion of paracetamol exposure, targeted antimicrobial treatment is the treatment of choice. B Erythromycin Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic with activity against Grampositive and atypical organisms. This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of leptospirosis, and although erythromycin has some activity there is a better option available. E Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotic with a wide spectrum of activity against Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria. Because the patient’s presentation is suggestive of leptospirosis, ciproﬂoxacin would not be an effective treatment. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever there is an effective alternative available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) is reviewed in clinic six weeks after starting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). She had been feeling clinically well prior to starting therapy, but over the past fortnight has been feeling increasingly tired and weak. She is also complaining of exertional dyspnoea. She denies fever, chest pain or cough. She has no other previous medical history of note and is taking tenofovir, emtricitabine and elvitegravir/cobicistat, along with co-trimoxazole for prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Investigations reveal the following: Test Pre-treatment After six weeks Normal Value Hb 132 g/l 86 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 95 ﬂ 102 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ CD4 count 500–1500 Haptoglobin 830 mg/l 850 mg/l 410–1650 mg/l What is the most likely cause for the anaemia?
options: Bone marrow inﬁltration by Mycobacterium aviumintracellulare (MAI)
explanation:
D Red cell hypoplasia The anaemia associated with emtricitabine therapy is due to red cell hypoplasia or aplasia. This is seen more rarely than with zidovudine and lamivudine and more frequently in children than in adults. Bone marrow examination may demonstrate pure red cell aplasia, erythroid maturation arrest, erythroid hypoplasia, and megaloblastic erythropoiesis. Erythropoietin levels are normal or increased. A Bone marrow inﬁltration by Mycobacterium aviumintracellulare (MAI) Given this patient has commenced treatment and has seen an improvement in their CD4 count, inﬁltration by MAI is unlikely versus other causes of anaemia. B Haemolytic anaemia with anti-erythrocyte antibodies Overt haemolysis is rarely seen in the context of HIV infection, and is likely to be less common once HAART is initiated. C Folic acid deﬁciency Folate deﬁciency is usually only seen with co-trimoxazole therapy when it is given concurrently with other anti- folate drugs such as methotrexate. E Erythropoietin suppression

Levels of erythropoietin are usually increased in patients with red cell hypoplasia.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Gynaecologist with complaints of a thin, greyish-white vaginal discharge with a foul odour for the past ﬁve days. She notices it to be more prominent after sexual intercourse. She has multiple sexual partners and says she has been having unprotected sexual intercourse for the past few months.
explanation:
E Oral metronidazole This patient is suffering from bacterial vaginosis, which occurs due to a shift of the local microbiota away from Lactobacillus and increased growth of bacterial species such as Gardnerella, Prevotella, Bacteroides, etc. The picture shows the presence of a clue cell (vaginal epithelial cell studded with coccobacilli) in the bottom left corner and two other normal epithelial cells. Amsel criteria include: homogenous, thin, greyish-white discharge, vaginal pH > 4.5, positive whiff amine test and clue cells on saline wet mount. The treatment of choice is oral metronidazole for seven days. Alternatively, clindamycin intravaginally as a cream for seven days may also be used in the management of these patients. A Intramuscular ceftriaxone Intramuscular ceftriaxone is used in the management of pelvic inﬂammatory disease in combination with other agents. This patient has bacterial vaginosis and oral metronidazole is the treatment of choice.

B Intravaginal clotrimazole Intravaginal clotrimazole can be used for the treatment of Candida infections, which usually present with a thick, creamy white vaginal discharge, which is not the case in this patient. C Oral doxycycline Oral doxycycline is used for the treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis infection in non-pregnant women. This patient has bacterial vaginosis, and not an infection with C. trachomatis. D Oral ﬂuconazole Oral ﬂuconazole can be used for the treatment of Candida infections, which usually presents with a thick, creamy white vaginal discharge, which is not the case in this patient.

stem: A 36-year-old farmer was referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 1-month history of ﬂu-like symptoms and nausea and vomiting. He is frequently feeling bloated with intermittent abdominal pain and has lost his appetite, having lost 3 kg in weight over the last month. He has no past medical history and no known drug allergies. On examination, he appears lethargic and slightly jaundiced. He has a temperature of 37.8 °C. His heart rate is 97 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 118/77 mmHg. On auscultation, his chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. He is saturating well on room air, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. His abdomen is distended and there is right upper quadrant tenderness. Bowel sounds are present.
explanation: B Albendazole This patient has hydatid liver disease, a helminthic disease caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. It is a zoonotic illness found throughout the world and is more common in those who handle animals. Contact with contaminated faeces carrying the eggs of the tapeworm infects the host where the eggs later hatch and migrate to the liver, lungs, brain or other organs, forming a hydatid cyst. The disease has an insidious onset and often symptoms arise after cyst formation. The liver is the most commonly affected organ, and symptoms and signs include abdominal pain, jaundice and hepatomegaly. A CT abdomen classically shows a parent cyst with numerous daughter cysts. Treatment is with albendazole. C Ivermectin Ivermectin is used to treat parasitic infections, including Strongyloides. However, it is not indicated for the treatment of hydatid disease. A Broad-spectrum antibiotics This would be true if the patient was suffering from a pyogenic liver abscess. Most are secondary to an ongoing intra-abdominal infection and they are more common in the immunocompromised. Symptoms are more acute in onset and include a swinging fever, nausea and vomiting, night sweats and right upper quadrant tenderness. They often have a polymicrobial origin, needing broad-spectrum antibiotic cover and surgical drainage. B Metronidazole Metronidazole is the treatment of choice for amoebic liver abscess. Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan responsible for the disease amoebiasis. It is common in South and Central America, South East Asia and West Africa. The majority of infections are asymptomatic. However, in some patients, amoebiasis can lead to dysentery or invasive disease, including amoebic liver abscess formation. Abscesses in amoebiasis tend to be singular. C Liver transplantation Liver transplantation is a treatment option for hydatid liver disease that fails to respond to initial therapy, including pharmacological therapy and surgical removal of cysts. It is not a ﬁrst-line treatment and albendazole should be trialled ﬁrst.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to Accident and Emergency Department. He is known to be HIV positive. His last outpatient appointment was several months ago and at that time his CD4 cell count was 210 × 106/l. He did not attend his most recent scheduled appointment. He is on no regular medication and has no other medical problems. He presents with a 3-week history of increasing shortness of breath and dry cough. On examination: T38.5, RR30/min, Sats 89% on air, heart rate 110 bpm. His chest is clear to auscultation. A chest X-ray reveals diffusely increased shadowing bilaterally. Arterial blood gas on air reveals a pa(O2) 8.8 kPa, pa(CO2) 3.5 kPa, bicarbonate 22 mmol/l, Sats 88%. His chest X-ray shown below.
explanation:
C Co-trimoxazole IV and methylprednisolone IV The chest x-ray reveals diffusely increased shadowing bilaterally.The diagnosis is Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP) pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii (previously called carinii). BHIVA guidelines recommend addition of methylprednisolone to IV co-trimoxazole when pa(O2) <9.3 kPa (or <70 mmHg) or SpO2 <92%, as this is an indicator of severe disease. The BHIVA guidelines have provided criteria for further clariﬁcation of severity of PCP. This would be the correct answer if the patient did not have hypoxia as steroids are needed to acutely help relieve breathlessness. In mild disease oral treatment can be considered. B Co-trimoxazole IV and antiretroviral therapy Antiretroviral treatment will be needed and should be offered soon after treatment for the PCP is commenced.

E Low molecular weight heparin PEs occur with a much higher incidence within the HIV-positive population and should always be considered in the differential diagnosis. However, in view of the high fever and chest X-ray changes, this is less likely.

stem: A 33-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of skin lesions. The lesions had increased in number and size over preceding months. He did not have any medical conditions or take any medications. On examination, he had a number of purple-red scaly patches, predominantly on both lower limbs. He also had oral candidiasis and widespread low-volume lymphadenopathy. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.9 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 x 109/l What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation:
B HIV testing This rash is consistent with Kaposi’s sarcoma, an AIDS-deﬁning illness: in the context of oral candidiasis (in the absence of a background of inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression), lymphopenia and widespread lymphadenopathy, this is highly suggestive of undiagnosed HIV infection. D Lymph node biopsy This patient has Kaposi’s sarcoma, and combined with his oral candidiasis without a background of inhaled steroids, this is strongly suggestive of underlying immunosuppression, particularly of HIV. HIV would explain his lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia, and hence the most appropriate next investigation would be an HIV test. A HHV-6 testing Human herpes virus 6 causes roseola infantum, and can also reactivate in the immunosuppressed or transplant recipient, causing bone marrow suppression or pneumonitis. This patient has a lymphopenia, widespread lymphadenopathy and oral candidiasis without any background of inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression. In the context of his rash, which would be consistent with

Kaposi’s sarcoma, this patient is likely to have undiagnosed HIV infection, not HHV-6, and so he should be tested for HIV positivity. Human herpes virus 8 (HHV-8) is the herpesvirus associated with Kaposi’s sarcoma. C HPV testing Human papilloma virus causes warts, and is associated with various malignancies including cervical carcinoma. This patient has a rash consistent with Kaposi’s sarcoma, which is not associated with HPV infection. Kaposi’s sarcoma is an AIDS-deﬁning illness, and this patient should be tested for HIV, especially given that he has widespread lymphadenopathy, a lymphopenia and oral candidiasis without any history of inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression. E Skin prick allergy testing This patient’s rash is not consistent with allergy; the description is suggestive of Kaposi’s sarcoma. He has no history of allergy symptoms (itch, wheeze, swelling), but instead has oral candidiasis which cannot be explained by inhaled steroids or other immunosuppression. When combined with his widespread lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia, this patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of undiagnosed HIV, and he should be HIV tested.

stem: A 32-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 2week history of general malaise, fever and myalgia after returning from a backpacking holiday in Brazil. He also complains of occasional nausea and vomiting. He has no past medical history and has otherwise been ﬁt and well. On examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.1 °C. His heart rate is 106 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 121/75 mmHg. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. His abdomen is soft, with a palpable 2-cm liver edge. There are prominent palpable cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph nodes. He has signiﬁcant unilateral conjunctivitis and periorbital oedema affecting his left eye. His visual acuity remains intact. Electrocardiogram (ECG): sinus tachycardia, PR interval 210 ms. Which of the following vectors has a role in transmission of the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
E Triatomine bugs This patient has Chagas’ disease, a parasitic disease spread by triatomine or ‘kissing’ bugs. The disease is prevalent in Latin America and consists of an initial acute phase and a chronic phase. In the earlier stages of the disease, symptoms include generalised malaise, fever, headaches and myalgia, along with anorexia, nausea and vomiting. Generalised lymphadenopathy is common. Unilateral conjunctivitis and periorbital cellulitis (known as Romaña’s sign) is seen in up to 50% of cases and represents the point of transmission of infection. In others, if the infection is transmitted through a bite in the skin, a chagoma (an indurated, oedematous skin lesion) may be seen. ECG ﬁndings include sinus tachycardia and a prolonged PR interval. Treatment in the acute phase includes bed rest and expert consultation regarding the prescription of antiparasitic agents such as benznidazole. D Ticks Ticks are well known to spread Lyme disease, a bacterial infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. They are not involved in the transmission of Chagas’ disease. A Aedes mosquito The Aedes mosquito is responsible for the transmission of dengue fever. Although there is an overlap of symptoms with Chagas’ disease, dengue fever tends to have a shorter duration of illness and does not cause unilateral eye signs. B Anopheles mosquito The Anopheles mosquito is the vector for malaria. There are multiple subtypes, of which malaria falciparum is the most common. The disease is generally transmitted in Africa, South East Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Western Paciﬁc. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgia, headache and nausea and vomiting.

Hepatosplenomegaly may appear. C Sandﬂy Sandﬂies spread the parasitic disease leishmaniasis. There are different species of Leishmania that are responsible for different manifestations of the disease, with cutaneous leishmaniasis being the most common. Initially, a small red papule appears at the site of the sandﬂy bite which gradually enlarges to up to 2 cm in diameter. It later ulcerates in the centre before spontaneously resolving. The time to resolution varies between two months and one year.

stem: A 27-year-old man attends clinic with a 3-day history of painful and itchy penile ulcers. He also had flu-like symptoms over the preceding week, dysuria and a white urethral discharge. Ten days ago, he had unprotected penetrative anal intercourse with a casual partner. On examination, there were three shallow, tender, sloughing ulcers under the foreskin, as well as generalised erythema of the surrounding skin. Urine dipstick was normal. Investigations: Urethral swab microscopy Pus cells ++ Which investigation is most likely to provide the diagnosis?
options: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for herpes simplex
explanation:
D Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for herpes simplex This is a typical presentation of herpes simplex with multiple painful ulcers following unprotected sex. The prodromal flu-like symptoms are also a classic feature, though not all patients will experience a prodrome. PCR is the most sensitive test for herpes simplex. In clinical practice, this patient would also be tested for syphilis, as co-infection can occur and sometimes it is difficult to differentiate the two conditions clinically; typically, however, syphilitic ulcers are single and painless; hence, herpes simplex is a more likely diagnosis here. E Syphilis serology Syphilis is a reasonable differential diagnosis for this patient’s

presentation; however, syphilitic ulcers are typically single and painless. This patient’s multiple painful ulcers are more typical of herpes simplex, for which the most sensitive diagnostic test is PCR. In clinical practice, it can be difficult to differentiate the two conditions, and therefore you would likely test for both. A Culture for herpes simplex The most likely diagnosis here is herpes simplex (given that the ulcers are painful and multiple) , but polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is more sensitive than culture in diagnosing herpes simplex, and therefore is the correct answer here. However, it is important to note that, in clinical practice, it is difficult to tell syphilis and herpes apart from the history and clinical examination alone, and you would test for both at the same time. B Culture for Treponema pallidum T. pallidum is syphilis; this patient has multiple painful ulcers, whereas syphilitic ulcers are typically single and painless. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with herpes simplex, for which PCR is the most sensitive test. However, it is important to note that, in clinical practice, it is difﬁcult to tell syphilis and herpes apart from the history and clinical examination alone, and you would test for both at the same time. C Human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) serology Rashes can be a presenting feature of HIV seroconversion, but HIV does not typically cause painful penile ulcers. This presentation is more consistent with herpes simplex (multiple painful ulcers), for which the most sensitive test is PCR; PCR for herpes simplex is the correct answer here. In clinical practice, this patient would be screened for HIV (though it is likely too early at this point, and the patient would need to be screened after 3 months to rule out HIV infection), chlamydia, syphilis and herpes simplex.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has attended the GU Clinic for multiple (>7) episodes of painful genital ulceration in the last year. One such episode two years before caused acute urinary retention, and was treated with IV aciclovir. According to the case notes from that admission, at that time she was noted to have ‘multiple small ulcers affecting the labial and vulval area with erythema of the surrounding skin, and marked tender inguinal lymphadenopathy’. However, on examination today at the Outpatient Clinic she has no ulcers. What treatment should you offer her?
explanation: B 1 year aciclovir This patient has frequently recurring herpes simplex virus (HSV) episodes. Usually if a patient has more than six episodes yearly they are offered prophylactic treatment, which consists of 1 year oral aciclovir (400 mg BD) with the aim of suppressing the HSV. E 3 months’ ganciclovir Ganciclovir is not usually used for HSV infections but can be used for cytomegalovirus (CMV). A 5 days’ aciclovir This would be the correct option for treating acute HSV sores but none are present at this time. C 3 months’ valaciclovir Valaciclovir is a pro-drug of aciclovir and has the advantage of needing to be taken only twice daily. This would be a treatment option, but it is generally not offered as it is considerably more expensive. D 5 days’ valaciclovir This would be an option for treating an acute course of HSV sores.

stem: A 23-year-old man attends because of a painful mouth. He has a past history of asthma for which he takes a ﬂuticasone/salmeterol combination inhaler This was recently changed from using a beclomethasone inhaler alone. On examination, he looks well but has evidence of extensive oral candidiasis. Which is the most likely cause?
explanation:
A Steroid-related candida infection Given the history of use of inhaled corticosteroids for asthma, this is the most likely cause of this man’s candida infection. Steroids cause immunosuppression by glucocorticoid action, and inhaled steroids can lead to localised immunosuppression and opportunistic infection with poor inhaler technique. Patients should be advised on

good inhaler technique, with the use of a spacer device when they are prescribed a metered dose inhaler for steroid delivery, rinsing of the mouth with water after use of the inhaler or teeth cleaning, and adequate oral hygiene when taking their night-time dose. E Hodgkin’s lymphoma Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a malignant disease of lymphatic system with multinucleated giant (Reed–Sternberg) cells.
