Presentation usually occurs in early adulthood, and again is insidious with asymptomatic lymph node enlargement, weight loss, night sweats and unexplained fever. Some patients have chest symptoms and alcohol-induced pain. B HIV infection HIV with a low CD4+ count could be an explanation for oral candidiasis, but in the absence of any mentioned risk factors and without evidence of systemic features and other opportunistic disease this is a less likely diagnosis. C Chronic myeloid leukaemia Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder affecting one or all cell lines. Progression is characterised into a chronic phase, an accelerated phase and ﬁnally blast crisis. Most patients present in the chronic phase with insidious symptoms of fatigue, weight loss and night sweats. Examination can reveal features of cell line disruption such as anaemia and bruising, but while lymphadenopathy can occur it is not a major feature. It is not associated with immunodeﬁciency and would therefore not explain this patient’s oral candidiasis, and the age of presentation of CML is usually around 65 years old. D Chronic lymphoblastic leukaemia Chronic lymphoblastic leukaemia (CLL) is a malignant monoclonal expansion of B lymphocytes. CLL occurs at a median age of 72 years and presents insidiously with susceptibility of infection, symmetrically enlarged lymph nodes, abdominal pain from splenomegaly, bleeding from thrombocytopenia and fatigue from anaemia. Signs include lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. The absence of systemic features and organomegaly makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends the hepatology clinic for review. She is 14 weeks’ pregnant and was found to have abnormal hepatitis serology at her booking visit. She has no past medical history of note, although admits to intermittent IV drug abuse during her teenage years. On examination, her blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, with pulse 65/min and regular. Her BMI is 22 and there are no signs of chronic liver disease. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 125 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l ALT 32 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALP 182 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Hep B surface antibody Positive Hep B core antibody Positive Hep Be antigen Negative Hep Bs antigen Negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Cleared hepatitis B The presence of core and surface antibodies, in the absence of Hep B antigen, suggests that this patient has now cleared hepatitis B infection. It is likely she was exposed as a result of previous IV drug abuse. The elevated alkaline phosphatase will be related to the pregnancy rather than to underlying liver disease. B Chronic hepatitis B The absence of hepatitis B antigens and normal liver function tests makes this unlikely. A Autoimmune hepatitis Autoimmune hepatitis is an idiopathic cause of hepatitis and cirrhosis. There is association with autoimmune diseases and with anti-smooth muscle (ASMA) and anti-LKM-1 antibodies, as well as ASMA. Presentation is variable and can range from asymptomatic to fulminant, with associated features of liver disease on examination. This patient’s liver function tests are normal for her, given that the ALP is likely raised from pregnancy. D Non-A non-B hepatitis Hepatitis C is another viral infection transmitted via blood and is relatively common in IV drug users. D Vaccination for hepatitis B Vaccination for hepatitis B is associated with the presence of surface antibodies but not core antibodies.

stem: A 32-year-old man, who spent 3 months on a school building project in Nepal, visits the clinic for review. He suffered a severe episode of diarrhoea with associated blood while in the country, and now complains of intermittent sweats and pain in his right lower chest. On examination, his temperature is 37.7 °C, and he has hepatic tenderness. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 102 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 145 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 45 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 72 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 342 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Computed tomography (CT) thorax and upper abdomen Single homogenous abscess in the right liver lobe, measuring 5 cm in diameter You ask for an opinion from an interventional radiologist. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical treatment for him?
explanation:
A Metronidazole This patient has a history suggestive of amoebic liver abscess. The initial illness was colitis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. This invasive amoeba travels via the portal circulation to the liver. Diagnosis can be made based on imaging and positive serology. Unlike bacterial abscess management, this condition does not require drainage. Metronidazole is the treatment of choice for liver trophozoites, followed by a luminal amoebacide such as paramomycin. C Chloroquine Chloroquine is an antimalarial drug used in the treatment of nonfalciparum malaria. Its use in malaria prophylaxis and the treatment of falciparum malaria has ceased due to widespread resistance. Chloroquine can be used second line to treat amoebic liver abscess (as suggested in this case), but there is a better option.

A Doxycycline Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity. It is used to treat Gram-positive and atypical bacterial infections, as well as malaria . The case described is highly suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess, and therefore doxycycline would not be appropriate treatment for this. D Cefotaxime Cefotaxime is a third-generation cephalosporin with a broad spectrum of activity against both Gram-positive and -negative bacteria. The history and ﬁndings in this case are more suggestive of an amoebic liver abscess than a pyogenic abscess. In practice it would be appropriate to cover for both pyogenic infection and amoeba until the diagnosis is serologically conﬁrmed. E Quinine Quinine is an antimalarial drug used in the treatment of falciparum malaria, though its use has been superseded by artesunate/artermisinine combination therapy where available. It is not a treatment for amoebic infection.

stem: A 40-year-old builder presents with a 5-hour history of increasingly severe headaches and myalgia. Two weeks ago, he was seen in the Emergency Department following a fall from the scaffolding of a building on which he was working. At that time, he had a skull Xray that was reported as being normal. As he had no speciﬁc symptoms or signs at that time, he was not admitted. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks 21 units of alcohol a week. He has no other past medical history. On examination, he looks unwell. He is wearing his sunglasses. His temperature is 38 °C. His blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, oxygen saturation (Sp(02)) is 98% on air. He appears to have mild neck stiffness on examination. He is orientated in time, place and person but seems alternately sleepy and slightly aggressive towards staff. GCS is graded as 14/15 by the examining doctor. Blood cultures have been taken and a CT and lumbar puncture are arranged. Which other step should be taken in the immediate management of this patient?
explanation:
A IV ceftriaxone

This patient has a history of a head injury and presents with what sounds like meningitis. In this particular case the fact that the patient has sustained a head injury means that CT is mandatory. That the previous skull X-ray was reported as normal is not 100% reliable as some fractures may be missed, particularly those of the temporal bones. In general, CSF examination allowing conﬁrmation of the diagnosis and identiﬁcation of the organism is preferable prior to starting antibiotics. In most cases it is preferable to perform CT ﬁrst, and this is absolutely required in the context of reduced conscious level, history of head injury or presence of focal neurological signs. However, in a very unwell patient with a typical clinical picture of bacterial meningitis, for whom waiting for such investigations would risk undue delay in starting treatment, antibiotics may be commenced simply after blood cultures and CT/LP performed afterwards. Starting antibiotics, however, usually alters the CSF obtained and the likelihood of identifying an organism becomes less the longer the delay after the ﬁrst dose of antibiotics. Starting IV dexamethasone at the same time as, or just prior to, antibiotics and continued until S. pneumoniae is ruled out as the causative organism is now recommended. D Antituberculous therapy TB can cause meningitis which can be identiﬁed from CSF results. However, this patient has no described exposure to anyone with TB nor is there any mention of travel to TB endemic countries. Also, the acute onset makes this less likely. B IV tazocin Penetration of beta lactam agents across the blood-brain barrier is poor. Although it is recognised that the inﬂammation involved in meningitis may well improve this penetration the ﬁrst line therapy remains ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. C IV mannitol It is a treatment option for cerebral oedema. However, the high temperature suggests an infective aetiology to this patient’s confusion. E IV aciclovir Aciclovir is treatment for viral meningitis and encephalitis. Viral infection is possible but would be unrelated to trauma, making a bacterial infection more likely.

stem: A 28-year-old nurse who was working in the Gastroenterology department presented to the Emergency Room one hour after receiving a needlestick injury whilst at work. Her needlestick injury had been received from a hepatitis C-positive patient, who was taking ribavirin and pegylated alpha interferon. At the time of the needlestick injury nurse had been wearing gloves and had punctured the pad of her left index ﬁnger. She had washed the wound with running water afterwards. Donor virology investigations: Hepatitis C RNA Low levels detected HBsAg - Anti-HBc - Anti-HBs - HIV RNA PCR - What should be the next step?
options: Take blood from the nurse for virology
explanation:
E Take blood from the nurse for virology It is important to take baseline samples from the nurse to determine whether she was a carrier or was infected with a blood-borne virus before her exposure to this patient (as this would have different implications for treatment). If these are negative, her blood will continue to be monitored to check whether she has contracted hepatitis C from this patient. If she has, treatment for the virus will begin at that point. Post-exposure prophylaxis is not recommended for hepatitis C. C Reassure and discharge home Although it is not appropriate to give this nurse post-exposure prophylaxis (this is not recommended for hepatitis C), it is important to take the nurse’s blood for virology. This is to check whether, at baseline, she was a carrier or was infected with a blood-borne virus (i.e. before her exposure to this patient). Her virology will then be monitored to determine whether she has contracted hepatitis C from this patient. A Arrange hepatitis B vaccination This nurse is likely to have already had the hepatitis B vaccination, as this is a requirement for healthcare workers. Furthermore, vaccinating the patient against hepatitis B will not inﬂuence her risk of contracting hepatitis C from the donor patient. The most important step is to take virology bloods from the nurse. These bloods are used to tell whether the nurse is already a carrier or infected with a blood-borne virus, before her exposure to the patient. Her virology bloods will then be monitored to decide whether she has contracted hepatitis C from the patient. B Give anti-hepatitis C immunoglobulin This is not a treatment option for hepatitis C, and there is no evidence that it is effective as a vaccine or post- exposure prophylaxis. Furthermore, at this stage, it is unclear whether the nurse has contracted hepatitis C from the patient. Guidance is that treatment for hepatitis C should not be started unless the patient has contracted the condition, i.e. post-exposure prophylaxis therapies are

not recommended. The most important action here is to take the nurse’s blood for virology; this acts as a baseline to decide whether she was already a carrier or infected with a blood-borne virus before her exposure to the patient. Her virology will then be monitored to decide whether she has contracted hepatitis C from the patient. D Start post-exposure prophylaxis Post-exposure prophylaxis has not been shown to be effective in the prevention of contracting hepatitis C, and therefore is not recommended. Instead, the nurse’s blood should be taken for virology; this is in order to have a baseline sample to check whether she was carrying or was infected with a blood-borne virus before her exposure to this patient. Her blood will then be monitored to determine whether she has contracted hepatitis C from this patient.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2 hour history of sudden loss of vision in his left eye. He had a past history of hypertension but was otherwise well. A sexual history reveals that he had has unprotected intercourse with multiple partners over the preceding 2 years. He had not been screened for sexually transmitted infections for 5 years. The fundoscopic appearance of his eye is shown below.
explanation:
C Ganciclovir There is evidence of haemorrhages and exudates. This patient is

likely to have HIV (the diagnosis would need to be conﬁrmed with laboratory testing) and consequent cytomegalovirus retinitis, an AIDs-deﬁning illness. It is the most common cause of eye disease and blindness in HIV patients. CMV retinitis is a slowly progressive disorder; visual loss may occur suddenly as a result of haemorrhage or retinal detachment, or more slowly due to progressive involvement of the macula and optic nerve. He would need treatment with intravenous ganciclovir. E Warfarin You may have considered central retinal vein occlusion as a differential diagnosis in this patient, but central retinal vein occlusion would not explain why the patient had exudates on fundoscopy. In addition, warfarin and other anticoagulants are not recommended as treatment for central retinal vein occlusion, as they can cause complications such as vitreous haemorrhage. Instead, this patient probably has cytomegalovirus retinitis as a result of untreated HIV infection, for which the most appropriate treatment is intravenous ganciclovir. A Aciclovir This patient likely has a diagnosis of HIV (this would need to be conﬁrmed with full laboratory testing) and has had a sudden loss of vision. Combined with the fundoscopy ﬁndings, his presentation is suggestive of cytomegalovirus retinitis. Aciclovir is simply not potent enough to treat this; ganciclovir is the appropriate choice and is administered intravenously. B Aspirin You may have thought that this patient had a central retinal vein occlusion; however, this would not explain the exudates seen on fundoscopy. Furthermore, aspirin is not an appropriate treatment for retinal vein occlusion. In combination with the positive HIV test, this patient is more likely to have cytomegalovirus retinitis, for which the appropriate treatment is intravenous ganciclovir. D Low-molecular weight heparin You may have thought that this patient had central retinal vein occlusion; however, central retinal vein occlusion does not explain why he has exudates on fundoscopy. Furthermore, heparin and other anticoagulants are not appropriate therapy for central retinal vein occlusion due to the risk of haemorrhagic complications in the eye. This patient is more likely to have cytomegalovirus retinitis as a result of untreated HIV, and he should be treated with intravenous ganciclovir.

stem: A 49-year-old veterinarian is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 2-month history of general malaise and weight loss. He describes initially having ﬂu-like symptoms with intermittent fevers and headaches before the onset of severe lethargy and loss of appetite. He is usually well with a past medical history of mild asthma only. His regular medications include salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers. There are no allergies. On examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.1 °C. His heart rate is 117 bpm and his blood pressure is 109/68 mmHg. His capillary reﬁll time is < 2 seconds. He has a dry cough, but his chest is clear, with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute and saturations of 94% on room air. There is a pansystolic murmur radiating towards the apex and the apex beat is palpable in the ﬁfth intercostal space in the mid-axillary line. His abdomen is soft, with no palpable masses. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 14.2 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Neutrophils 10.1 × 10 /l 2.5–7.5 × 10 /l Lymphocytes 3.4 × 10 /l 0.8–5.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 338 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.3 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 125 µm/l 50–120 µm/l Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 60+ ESR 62 mm/hour < 15 mm/hour Chest X-ray: clear lung fields with no evidence of focal consolidation or effusion Blood cultures: negative What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
B Coxiella burnetii This patient has infective endocarditis. The history of general malaise and ﬂu-like symptoms, together with fever and a new murmur, is suggestive of the diagnosis. This patient’s pansystolic murmur points towards mitral regurgitation, with the mitral valve being the most commonly affected valve in infective endocarditis. Blood cultures form part of the modiﬁed Duke criteria needed to conﬁrm the diagnosis. C. burnetii causes blood culture-negative endocarditis. It is a zoonotic disease and those at higher risk of infection include those who work with animals such as farmers and veterinarians. Treatment is with a course of doxycycline. A Brucella melitensis Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease secondary to close contact with infected animals or from ingestion of unpasteurised milk or undercooked meat. Those who work with livestock have an

increased risk of the disease. However, it is a very rare, albeit fatal, cause of infective endocarditis. C Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis. It is particularly more common in patients with a history of intravenous drug use. However, it typically produces positive blood cultures. D Streptococcus bovis S. bovis is a rare cause of infective endocarditis. It is most commonly associated with colorectal cancer. E Streptococcus viridans S. viridans is a common cause of subacute infective endocarditis. It forms part of the normal ﬂora of the mouth, therefore increasing the risk of infection following a dental procedure. However, like S. aureus, it generally causes a positive culture.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department some 18 h after eating tinned salmon. She complains of nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, diplopia and an extreme thirst that is unquenchable. Over the few hours in the Observation Ward, she develops worsening double vision and ptosis. Mini-mental State Examination is normal. She has complex restriction with eye movements, with restriction of abduction and adduction bilaterally. She is also dysarthric. Although progressive incoordination and diminished reﬂexes are noted, there is no sensory loss. Her blood pressure is 110/72 mmHg, with a pulse of 85/min and temperature is 37.2 °C. Which one of the following interventions would be most appropriate given this clinical picture?
explanation:
A Urgent review by Intensivist This clinical picture is highly suggestive of botulism, infection having occurred due to defective canning of the ﬁsh. Sporadic outbreaks of the disease, although rare, do still occur. Laboratory tests and imaging studies are not generally helpful in the diagnosis of the condition. The neurotoxin produced leads to CNS and autonomic nervous system paralysis, and later respiratory muscle weakness and hypoventilation can occur. For this reason the patient should be managed in an ITU setting. Supportive therapy with

intubation and ventilation, respiratory physiotherapy, nasogastric tube placement and catheterisation is the treatment of choice for severe disease. Recovery occurs on average between 30 and 100 days after infection; severe cases may require ventilation for many months. E Computed tomography (CT) of the brain The likely clinical diagnosis is botulism, and a CT brain is likely to delay reaching deﬁnitive airway management before respiratory paralysis occurs. B IV immunoglobulin IV immunoglobulin in the form of botulinum antitoxin can be useful, but only if given very early in presentation and in those who have ingested toxin but are as yet asymptomatic. This patient has presented with severe symptoms following several hours of illness, and it is too late to be of value. C IV Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is not useful for botulism, which is the most likely clinical diagnosis. D IV Metronidazole The antibiotics which can potentially be used in botulism against Clostridium botulinum include benzylpenicillin and metronidazole. However, whilst metronidazole can be used as treatment, the most important management is to stabilise the patient’s airway as the paralysis can lead to respiratory arrest and she may need ventilation.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presented with a 12-hour history of fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and severe myalgia. Three days ago, she had completed a 3-day course of oral trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. She took the oral contraceptive pill, and her last menstrual period had ended the previous day. On examination, her temperature was 39.5 °C, heart rate 130 bpm and BP 72/40 mmHg. There was no nuchal rigidity or photophobia. There was a diffuse macular erythrodermic rash on the trunk and lower limbs, and marked tenderness of the thigh muscles. She had diffuse abdominal tenderness. Neurological examination was normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Blood cultures No growth in two samples after 48 hours Urine cultures No growth What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Toxic shock syndrome This is a typical presentation of toxic shock syndrome, in this case, most probably caused by a retained tampon. The patient is in shock, with a high fever, myalgia and erythroderma. The profound hypotension is due to direct inhibition of myocardial contractility by the exotoxin. It is common for blood cultures to be negative in toxic shock syndrome; high vaginal swabs may be positive for Staphylococcus. A Bacterial meningitis The patient does not have any signs of meningism, does not complain of headache, and meningitis could not explain this rash. Instead, this patient’s presentation is more suggestive of toxic shock syndrome, caused by a retained tampon, leading to release of staphylococcal exotoxin (TSST-1). This would explain the high fever, myalgia and rash in the presence of sterile blood and urine cultures. B Gastroenteritis This patient is in shock, with a high fever, myalgia and a rash; this picture does not ﬁt with gastroenteritis. This would be more typical for toxic shock syndrome caused by TSST-1, as a result of a retained tampon. C Renal abscess You might expect speciﬁc ﬂank tenderness, and a ballotable kidney, if there was a renal abscess. Instead, this patient has diffuse abdominal tenderness, erythroderma, high fever and myalgia. This is more ﬁtting with toxic shock syndrome, caused by the release of TSST-1 as a result of a retained tampon. E Ulcerative colitis This patient does have diarrhoea, but otherwise her presentation is not typical for a ﬂare of ulcerative colitis; it cannot explain the erythroderma or myalgia. This presentation of shock (with profound hypotension), erythroderma, myalgia and high fever is typical of toxic shock syndrome caused by the release of TSST-1. In this case, it is likely related to a retained tampon.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2week history of general malaise, anorexia and fever. He has lost 6 kg in weight. He had a sore throat a week before and his General Practitioner had told him that it was a viral infection. On examination, he has a temperature of 37.6 °C and three splinter haemorrhages on his right index ﬁnger. On cardiac auscultation, he has a pansystolic murmur, loudest at the apex and radiating to the axilla. Blood cultures are taken from three peripheral sites which grow Staphylococcus aureus and the patient is started on intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrates a 0.5 × 0.9 cm vegetation attached to the posterior surface of the mitral valve. Which of the following is the most likely complication of this condition in this patient?
explanation:
A Embolic stroke Infective endocarditis results from microbial infection of the endothelial surface of the heart. Blood cultures are positive in > 95% of cases of infective endocarditis. Three sets of cultures should be taken with 10 ml of blood in each bottle. These should be incubated for up to three weeks to grow fastidious organisms. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is speciﬁc in 91–98% of cases at detecting vegetations, although the sensitivity is only 45–60%. Suboptimal views are seen with prosthetic valves and transoesophageal echocardiography should be undertaken if vegetations are not seen on TTE. There are several complications associated with infective endocarditis, including acute heart failure, systemic embolisation (including stroke), acute kidney injury, valvular dehiscence (most commonly in the presence of a prosthetic valve), splenic abscess and mycotic aneurysms. Systemic embolisation occurs in 22–50% of patients with infective endocarditis and the risk increases if the vegetation is > 10 mm in size. Other risk factors include S. aureus infection, intravenous drug use and mitral valve vegetation. Up to 65% of emboli involve the central nervous system. Other affected areas are the lungs, spleen and joints. C Splenic abscess Splenic abscess is a rare complication of infective endocarditis. It occurs due to bacterial seeding or direct embolism to the splenic arteries. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are the best diagnostic tools. Splenectomy is often the treatment of choice in patients who are amenable to surgery. B Mitral valve abscess Mitral valve abscess occurs in around 15% of patients with mitral valve involvement. It typically affects the annular portions of the valve, involving the posterior leaﬂet, mitral annulus and underlying myocardium. If surgical intervention is required for mitral valve abscess, this typically involves valve replacement and the use of a

bovine patch to reconstruct the posterior annulus. This complication occurs less frequently than embolic stroke, making this complication unlikely. D Valvular dehiscence Valvular dehiscence occurs most commonly in patients with prosthetic valve involvement, particularly with S. aureus infection. As such, S. aureus infection is an indication for surgery if it has invaded a prosthetic valve. However, as this patient has a native valve, this is unlikely to be a complication in this patient. E Valvular ﬁstula Valvular ﬁstulation is most common in S. aureus infection in a prosthetic valve, making this complication unlikely as this patient has a native valve.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an 8-day history of progressive breathlessness that is worse on exertion, fevers and dry cough. He has a past medical history of HIV infection, for which he is partially compliant with his antiretroviral therapy. His temperature is 38.5 °C, heart rate 100 bpm and BP 120/75 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. On examination, scattered crackles are heard on auscultation of both lung ﬁelds. His cardiovascular and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value CD4 count 80 cells/mm3 500–1500 cells/mm3 HIV viral load 90 000 copies/ml < 75 copies/ml What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation:
A Co-trimoxazole This patient has a likely diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), given the history of fever, dry cough and progressive shortness of breath against a background of uncon-

trolled HIV. Immunocompromised patients are at higher risk of developing the condition, including HIV patients who are noncompliant with antiretroviral therapy. Co-trimoxazole is the preferred treatment for PCP in HIV-infected individuals. B Empirical treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics Empirical treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics is not appropriate for the management of PCP, as PCP is caused by a fungal pathogen and requires speciﬁc antimicrobial treatment. Clinically broad-spectrum antibiotics may be started alongside cotrimoxazole while tests are performed to conﬁrm a diagnosis of PCP. However, the presentation here, along with the duration of symptoms, make PCP a more likely diagnosis than a bacterial pneumonia. Therefore, co-trimoxazole is the most appropriate initial management. C Pentamidine IV pentamidine may be used as an alternative treatment for PCP in patients who are intolerant of, or allergic to, co-trimoxazole. However, it is not the preferred ﬁrst-line therapy due to its higher risk of adverse effects and lower efﬁcacy. D Recommence antiretroviral therapy It is very important to ensure that this patient is compliant with his antiretroviral therapy, and reinitiation of antiretroviral therapy is an essential component of long-term management for this patient. However, it should not be used alone, as this patient also has a likely diagnosis of PCP. Initial management should be treatment with antimicrobial agents targeting the causative pathogen (eg cotrimoxazole). E Sputum cultures for tuberculosis While tests should be performed to conﬁrm the underlying cause for this patient's presentation, the most likely infection is PCP. Therefore, appropriate antimicrobial therapy with co-trimoxazole should be initiated as the initial management. While patients who are immunocompromised are at higher risk of infections such as tuberculosis, the rapid onset of symptoms make this diagnosis unlikely in this case.

stem: A 24-year-old man attends the Sexually Transmitted Diseases Clinic after a recent trip to visit his grandparents in Barbados. He admits to having had unprotected sex during his 2-week holiday. On examination, he has an extremely painful, deep ulcer with soft, ragged margins on the coronal sulcus of his penis. He has painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which one of the following treatments would be the most appropriate choice in this case?
explanation: B Azithromycin This clinical picture is suggestive of chancroid infection, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Chancroid is endemic in parts of the Caribbean basin, Africa and south-west Asia and is commoner in non-white, uncircumcised populations. Patients may present with single or multiple genital ulcers, and painful lymphadenopathy occurs in 30–60% of patients. Gram-staining of ulcer exudates may demonstrate a ‘school of ﬁsh’ collection of short, thick Gramnegative rods. Deﬁnitive diagnosis is based on culture using enriched chocolate agar. Patients should be screened for other sexually transmitted diseases to rule out co-infection with other organisms. Suitable antibiotic treatments for H. ducreyi include macrolides and quinolones. D Aciclovir This is another antiviral treatment option for herpes simplex and, as described above, this is not the most likely diagnosis. A Metronidazole Metronidazole could have been used for a painful oral ulcer associated with gingivitis or with bacterial vaginosis. It can also be used for some protozoal infections, but this patient is unlikely to have any of the above. C Valiciclovir This is an antiviral option for herpes simplex infection. Herpes causes painful genital ulcers following sexual transmission, but the ragged margin and inguinal lymphadenopathy make chancroid a more likely diagnosis. E Oxytetracycline This is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that can be used for treatment for Chlamydia. The presentation of genital ulceration makes Chlamydia an unlikely cause, and therefore oxytetracycline an inappropriate treatment. Chlamydia normally presents in men with dysuria or discharge.

stem: A 28-year-old man presented with warts around the anal margin and on the shaft and subpreputial space on the penis. He was distressed by their appearance. Examination conﬁrmed the presence of multiple soft, nonkeratinised papillomas. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: E Podophyllotoxin ointment This patient is distressed by the genital warts, and therefore it is appropriate to treat him. First-line therapy for non-keratinised warts is podophyllotoxin ointment, applied directly to the warts twice a day for three days. This is followed by four rest days, and can be repeated weekly until the lesions resolve. If this is ineffective, cryotherapy is an appropriate second line treatment. A Aciclovir ointment Although genital warts are caused by a virus (human papilloma virus), antiviral therapies are ineffective, especially if given topically. Instead, topical podophyllotoxin can be applied directly to the warts by the patient. If the warts are particularly refractory, cryotherapy can be used. B Cryotherapy Cryotherapy can be used to treat genital warts, but it is usually reserved for extensive or refractory cases. First- line treatment would be podophyllotoxin ointment. The patient should also be advised to use condoms, or if the warts are not covered by a condom, refrain from sexual activity until the lesions have resolved. C No treatment This patient is distressed by the warts and therefore should have treatment to remove them. It can be acceptable not to treat warts, as up to one third will regress spontaneously within 6 months. If warts are treated, ﬁrst-line treatment for nonkeratinised warts is podophyllotoxin ointment, administered by the patient. D Oral doxycycline This patient has genital warts, caused by the human papilloma virus. An antibiotic will be ineffective against genital warts. The most appropriate treatment in this case would be podophyllotoxin ointment, applied by the patient.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the Sexual Health Clinic with a papular rash over her lower abdomen, inner thighs, and genital area. She denies unprotected sexual intercourse but admits to sharing sportswear and a towel at a hockey match a few weeks earlier.
explanation:
E Molluscum contagiosum virus-1 (MCV1) The umbilicated rash seen here is consistent with molluscum contagiosum, caused in the majority of cases by MCV1. MCV2 is seen more frequently in patients with immunocompromise who have molluscum infection. It is likely that the sharing of a towel and sports clothing is responsible for the infection seen here. Most cases of molluscum resolve spontaneously over a period of up to 18 months. A Cochrane review has revealed little evidence to support the use of agents such as imiquimod or benzoyl peroxide in healthy individuals. Cryotherapy and podophyllotoxin have some evidence of effectiveness. D Human papilloma virus-18 (HPV18) HPV18 is a human papillomavirus which is strongly implicated in the development of cervical carcinoma. HPV16 and HPV18 are responsible for 70% or more of cases of cervical cancer and precancerous cervical lesions. Vaccination with one of the two available HPV vaccines protects against serotypes 6,11,16 and 18. A Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV1) HSV1 is the oral herpes simplex virus and is responsible for the development of cold sores. Infection may also transfer to the genitalia in patients who have active infection and engage in oral sexual intercourse with a partner. Topical acyclovir is the usual ﬁrst-line intervention.

B Human herpes virus-4 (HHV4) HHV4 is the Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever, where pharyngitis is the most frequent presentation. Individuals also often have evidence of viral hepatitis. Patients may complain of left upper- quadrant pain related to splenic oedema. They should be advised to avoid contact sports because of the risk of splenic rupture. C Human herpes virus-6 (HHV6) HHV6 is the cause of roseola infantum, also known as exanthem subitum, in children. It is readily passed between children in the group childcare setting and is therefore rarely seen in adults. Reactivation is seen in patients post-transplantation.

stem: A 34-year-old man presented with intermittent sore throat, fever, joint pain and general malaise for 3 months. He also complained of decreasing exercise tolerance. Over the past 6 weeks, he had developed raised, red, tender lesions on his shins. He was diagnosed with human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) 8 years ago but had had a number of problems with medications because of their side-effects. Investigation Result Normal values WCC 4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 0.2 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Haemoglobin 131 g/l 130 - 180 g/l Platelets 120 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l CD4+ count 100 × 106/l 430 - 1690 × 106/l Chest X-ray Two cavitating lesions in the right lung ﬁeld Which organism is the most likely culprit?
explanation:
A Histoplasma capsulatum This patient has a low CD4+ count, but importantly he is also neutropenic. Any neutropenic patient is at signiﬁcant risk of opportunistic infections, including fungal infections such as Histoplasma capsulatum. In this case, the patient has a cavitating pneumonia; the only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia are Staphylococcus aureus and H. capsulatum. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, not as an indolent course as

seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis; it is associated with erythema nodosum, as seen in this patient. Other infectious causes of erythema nodosum which can affect the respiratory system are Streptococcus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis and blastomycosis. D Pneumocystis jiroveci Although Pneumocystis jiroveci is an important cause of pneumonia in the immunocompromised, and particularly HIV-positive patients with low CD4+ counts, it causes an indolent, dry cough, with bilateral inﬁltrates on chest X-ray. It does not cause cavitating lung lesions. The only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia are S. aureus and H. capsulatum. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, as not an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis; it is associated with erythema nodosum, as seen in this patient. A Legionella species This patient is immunocompromised with neutropenia and a low CD4+ count; this makes him vulnerable to any infection, including Legionella species. However, Legionella species do not cause cavitating pneumonia, as seen here; typically, they cause consolidation. S. aureus and H. capsulatum are the only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, not as an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis. B Mycoplasma pneumoniae This patient is immunocompromised with neutropenia and a low CD4+ count, which makes him vulnerable to any infection, including Mycoplasma. Furthermore, Mycoplasma does cause subacute illness, with prominent malaise, headache and dry cough, and can be associated with erythema nodosum, as described in this patient. However, Mycoplasma does not typically cause cavitating pneumonia, as seen in this patient; the only two organisms in this list that cause cavitating pneumonia are S. aureus and H. capsulatum. Typically, S. aureus cavitating pneumonia would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, not as an indolent course as seen in this patient. Therefore, H. capsulatum is the most likely diagnosis; it is associated with erythema nodosum, as seen in this patient. E Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus does cause cavitating pneumonia, as seen on this patient’s chest X-ray, but it would present as an acute, severe pneumonia, typically following a viral infection. This patient has a subacute course of illness. Any immunocompromised patient is vulnerable to fungal infection; this patient not only has a low CD4+ count but is also neutropenic. H. capsulatum is a fungal infection that can cause cavitating lung lesions and is the correct answer in this case.

stem: A 19-year-old student who has been travelling in Thailand presents for review after commencing with symptoms of severe inﬂuenza in the last 36 hours. He has made a point of visiting street markets and staying in small local Thai hostels during his visit. You understand that a father and son who work in the poultry market near to where he has been staying recently died of H5N1 inﬂuenza. Both were treated with oseltamivir. On examination, his blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, pulse is 100 bpmn. He is pyrexial at 38.5 °C. He has severe shortness of breath and there are scattered crackles throughout both lung ﬁelds. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 295 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CXR Patchy consolidation through both lung ﬁelds Which of the following represents the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
B Inhaled zanamivir Zanamavir is a neuraminidase inhibitor shown to reduce the associated morbidity in severe inﬂuenza. It can be delivered by inhalation or intravenously. In this case the patient is at high risk of avian inﬂuenza (H5N1) and we have been told that two other patients died despite treatment with oseltamivir. There is less known resistance to zanamavir and therefore this should be the treatment of choice. C Oral amantadine Amantadine is a drug used both as an antiviral and for the treatment of Parkinson’s disease. Its use against inﬂuenza has been superceded by the neuraminidase inhibitors in recent years due to concerns regarding resistance and efﬁcacy. Additionally inﬂuenza B is intrinsically resistant to amantadine. A IV Cefotaxime Cefotaxime is a broad spectrum third- generation cephalosporin with activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Although in this scenario it would be prudent to cover for potential bacterial pneumonia, this patient is at very high risk of

avian inﬂuenza and the blood picture would be more typical of a viral infection; therefore the deﬁnitive treatment of choice should be an antiviral with activity against inﬂuenza. D Oral co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin-based antibiotic which is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulinic acid; it has a broad-spectrum of activity against Gram-negative, Gram-positive and anaerobic bacteria. In this case the history is suggestive of a viral rather than a bacterial infection and therefore the deﬁnitive treatment would be an antiviral. B Oral oseltamivir Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor shown to reduce the morbidity associated with severe inﬂuenza. However there is recognised resistance to oseltamivir and we are told that two patients have died despite its use. Zanamivir would therefore be a more appropriate choice as resistance is less likely.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of fever, chills and headache. Her symptoms started shortly after returning from a trip to Ghana to see her family. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history and takes no regular medication. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 100 g/l 120–160 g/l WCC 12.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 90 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 150 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Thick blood ﬁlm Parasite level 4% Thin blood ﬁlm Malaria falciparum species What is the recommended management for this patient?
explanation:
A Artesunate This patient has a signiﬁcant malarial infection, particularly given the raised parasite level (more than 2%). Other signs of severe infection include anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. The most appropriate management is parenteral artesunate, which is typically given IV. It should be continued until the parasite level drops to less than 1%, at which point the patient can be stepped down to PO treatment. C Chloroquine monotherapy Chloroquine is a commonly used antimalarial drug, provided that there is unlikely to be chloroquine resistance. However, it is not given to patients with symptoms of severe malarial infection, as seen in this patient’s presentation. B Atovaquone–proguanil combination therapy Atovaquone-proguanil is an artemisinin-based combination therapy that is recommended for the treatment of falciparum malaria. However, these drugs are usually indicated following initial treatment with artesunate and when the patient's drug regimen can be changed to PO medication. It is effective against chloroquineresistant strains. D Doxycycline monotherapy Doxycycline can be used as both prophylaxis and treatment for malaria. However, it is not indicated in patients with severe malaria. Rather, IV drugs, such as artesunate, are recommended. E Quinine plus clindamycin combination therapy Quinine plus clindamycin combination therapy is an alternative

treatment option for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. It can be considered for this patient as a PO switch after completion of IV artesunate. However, it is not indicated in the initial management, given the patient's presentation with severe disease.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Unit with groin pain that has come on over the past few hours, which is severe in intensity and leaves him unable to walk. He denies dysuria, haematuria or penile discharge. There is no history of trauma. On examination, he has a fever of 38.3 °C, with severe tenderness on palpation of the left testis, which is also warm and swollen. A ﬁrm, tender mass is noted at the posterior aspect of the testes. The cremasteric reﬂex is present. There is a change in the pain noticed when the scrotum is elevated. Urine dipstick showed leukocytes. Radionucleotide scan shows increased blood ﬂow to the left testicle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Epididymitis This is a case of acute epididymitis, which is commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The increased blood ﬂow is secondary to the inﬂammation process. E Testicular torsion In testicular torsion, the pain is usually worse with elevation of scrotum, and the cremasteric reﬂex is usually absent. It would also not explain the leukocytes in the urine dip or the increased rather than decreased blood ﬂow. Colour ﬂow Doppler, in the hands of a skilled scanning technician, will demonstrate reduced blood ﬂow in testicular torsion, and may be more available than radionucleotide scanning in the acute setting. A Mumps orchitis Mumps orchitis can occur 4 or 5 days following parotitis but does not occur in vaccinated patients. B Testicular malignancy It would not explain the acute onset, high temperature, leukocytes in the urine or tenderness. D Urinary tract infection This would present with dysuria and not with testicular tenderness.

stem: A 45-year-old man is seen in the Ambulatory Care Clinic with a 6month history of general malaise and intermittent fevers. He complains of recurrent respiratory tract infections and has recently been treated for oral candida. He has a past medical history of hypertension which is treated with ramipril 5 mg once daily.
explanation: A Bone marrow suppression Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). A common side-effect of all NRTIs is bone marrow suppression, causing anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia. D Renal calculi Renal calculi are a side-effect seen in patients taking HAART. However, it is a side-effect of the protease inhibitor indinavir due to its poor solubility and renal excretion, rather than a side-effect of NRTIs. B Peripheral neuropathy Peripheral neuropathy is a very rare side-effect of lamivudine. Paraesthesiae is another very rare side-effect of lamivudine. C Pancreatitis Pancreatitis is a side-effect of NRTIs but is much rarer than bone marrow suppression. E Insulin resistance Insulin resistance is not very common side-effect of protease inhibitors and NRTI.

stem: A 32-year-old, HIV-positive man is brought to the Emergency Department by his partner, who has noticed increasing confusion over the past four weeks. The patient has been non-compliant with his antiretroviral therapy and has not attended outpatient clinic for over six months. The patient denies any headache or neurological symptoms but scores 0/10 on the Mental Test Score. Neurological examination reveals some past pointing and dysdiadochokinesis on the left but nil else. The patient is afebrile. Computed tomography (CT) of the head with contrast demonstrates no focal lesions. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) results reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Protein 0.8 g/l < 0.45 g/l Glucose (plasma) Cryptococcal antigen (CRAG) 4.8 (5.2) mmol/l Negative 2.5–3.9 mmol/l WCC 2 cell/mm3 < 5/mm3 Red blood cells (RBC) 4 cell/mm3 < 5/mm3 Microscopy No organisms seen Which treatment is most likely to improve the symptoms?
explanation:
B Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) The most likely diagnosis is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is a unique demyelinating disease which usually occurs in a person with abnormal immune responses resulting from serious disease, treatment with cytotoxic drugs or irradiation, or long-term immunosuppression. The pathology of PML is distinctive and consists of multiple foci of demyelination of varying size from pinpoint lesions to areas of several centimetres. The lesions may occur anywhere but are usually in the cerebral hemispheres, less often in the cerebellum and brainstem and rarely in the spinal cord. Typically, PML evolves gradually, with impairment of mental function and disturbance of speech and vision. Movement may also be affected. The disease then progresses rapidly and the patient is severely disabled, eventually becoming demented, blind and paralysed, and ﬁnally there is coma and death. Almost any neurological sign can be part of the clinical spectrum, motor sensory or cerebellar signs depending on the white matter areas affected. Often nothing is seen on CT, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a much more useful modality in this condition. PML generally occurs only at low CD4 counts and there is no speciﬁc therapy. PCR for JC virus, a polyomavirus and the causative organism, should be performed. Commencing HAART can improve symptoms in some patients, although some can deteriorate. It is

inevitably progressive. Another possibility is HIV-associated encephalopathy, where the HIV virus itself is responsible for the pathology. HAART is also the treatment of choice for this. The clinical details do not suggest neurological toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV) or cryptococcal meningitis, so the other answers are incorrect. E High-dose ﬂuconazole This is an alternative to amphotericin B in cryptococcal infection in HIV-positive individuals. Cryptococcal infection usually presents with high fever and headache, and patients may also have evidence of raised intracranial pressure. The negative antigen testing makes this a less likely diagnosis. A Sulphadiazine and pyrimethamine This is the treatment for toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasma gondii is a common cause of cerebral abcesses in patients with a low CD4 count. The presentation is with focal neurological signs, confusion and evidence of raised intracranial pressure. Imaging in these patients shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions which can be associated with mass effect. The absence of major neurological signs and headache makes this diagnosis less likely, as does the normal CT scan. C IV ganciclovir It is the ﬁrst-line treatment for CMV infection. CMV infection in the HIV immunocompromised brain normally presents with worsening confusion and mental withdrawal. On examination there can be cranial nerve palsy and nystagmus. CT ﬁndings in these patients can demonstrate diffuse white matter hypodensities with ependymal enhancement, ventricular enlargement, meningeal enhancement and focal or ring-enhancing lesions. The absence of any relevant examination ﬁndings and the absence of CT ﬁndings makes this an incorrect answer. D IV aciclovir It is not used against any causes of confusion in HIV-positive individuals. It would be an appropriate treatment against herpes simplex virus (HSV)-associated encephalitis, for example.

stem: A 29-year-old intravenous (IV) drug abuser is admitted with lethargy, night sweats, and a new systolic murmur noted by the doctor at the Drug Rehabilitation Clinic. Examination reveals a temperature of 38.0 oC; blood pressure is 105/82 mmHg. His pulse is 85 beats per minute (bpm) and regular, and there is a pansystolic murmur. There is wheeze on auscultation of the chest. His body mass index is 21 kg/m2. You note multiple marks consistent with selfinjection of heroin. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 97 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.9 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 103 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 139 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 241 mg/l < 10 mg/l Transthoracic echocardiogram Mitral regurgitation with valve vegitations Blood cultures Bacillus cereus identiﬁed What is the most appropriate antibiotic intervention?
explanation:
E Vancomycin Glycopeptides, such as vancomycin, are highly effective in the treatment of invasive Bacillus cereus (B cereus) infection, with little or no evidence of resistance to their use. Out of the options given, this makes intravenous (IV) vancomycin the most appropriate intervention. B cereus rarely causes serious infections but is a rare cause of both native and prosthetic valve endocarditis. In this scenario, vancomycin is the best option, but it would also depend on drug susceptibilities and response to treatment. D Penicillin G Most B. cereus isolates produce beta-lactamases and are resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins. For this reason, penicillins and cephalosporins should not be used for empiric treatment of Bacillus spp infection. A Ampicillin Ampicillin is the intervention of choice for listeria infection. For listeria meningitis it is given in combination with gentamicin. Meropenem and linezolid are potential alternatives for the treatment of listeria meningitis. B Ceftriaxone B cereus isolates have signiﬁcant levels of resistance to cephalosporins which precludes their use as a ﬁrst-line agent here. Vancomycin is preferred where signiﬁcant resistance is yet to be identiﬁed. C Ciproﬂoxacin Although quinolone resistance is not as prevalent as resistance to

cephalosporins among B cereus isolates, around 10% of patients in one case series were found to have an intermediate or quinoloneresistant strain of the bacterium.

stem: A 31-year-old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant attends the Emergency Department. She is very worried as her 3-year-old son has been sent home from nursery with ‘slapped cheek’ disease. Which of the following is the most likely complication associated with fetal slapped cheek infection?
explanation:
B Hydrops fetalis Slapped cheek disease is caused by parvovirus B19 infection. It is known to cause fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis in 1–3% (2nd trimester), and intrauterine fetal death. Infections peak in spring and autumn. Incubation period is usually around 12–14 days, meaning that this lady is likely to have been already exposed via contact with her son. In total, B19 infection may account for up to 20% of nonimmune cases of hydrops. Autopsy studies indicate that highest viral concentrations are found in bone marrow and myocardium. Infection can be conﬁrmed either with IgM serology or PCR where it is available. IV immunoglobulin may be of value in some patients. E Congenital blindness This can be caused by several pathologies, including antenatal rubella, antenatal varicella and antenatal cytomegalovirus. Other diseases can cause other eye problems which can lead to blindness if not treated. A Congenital deafness This could be caused by antenatal rubella. Rubella is a viral infection causing a pink rash and lymphadenopathy behind the ears. Infection in the ﬁrst 11 weeks of pregnancy can cause fetal rubella syndrome

if the mother is not vaccinated. Fetal rubella syndrome causes deafness, cataracts, learning disability, growth restriction and heart defects. Diagnosis during pregnancy is via serology. Other causes include antenatal cytomegalovirus. C Fetal clotting disorder This could be caused be antenatal toxoplasmosis through cat exposure. Systemic neonatal infection can include thrombocytopenic pupura, hepatosplenomegaly, pneumonia, rash and jaundice. There can also be signiﬁcant neurological disease. D Fetal polycythaemia This can be caused by increased fetal erythropoiesis related to hypoxia which can be secondary due to placental insufﬁciency, endocrine disorders, delayed cord clamping, twin–twin transfusion and intrapartum asphyxia.

stem: A 20-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe sore throat. He arrived a few days earlier from Central America to visit a relative. He is extremely lethargic, with a fever, and is ﬁnding it increasingly difﬁcult to swallow. His temperature is 38.1 oC, his blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, and his pulse is 72 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Investigation reveals a grey pseudomembrane forming on the posterior pharynx. Which of the following is the most important initial investigation for this patient?
options: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for anthrax spores
PCR for diphtheria toxin A subunit
explanation:
E PCR for diphtheria toxin A subunit This patient has diphtheria, with the typical grey/white pseudomembrane forming on the posterior pharynx. It is important to conﬁrm the diagnosis as rapidly as possible, with PCR for the A-subunit of diphtheria toxin proving an early pointer to the diagnosis. This should be followed by formal culture and Elek testing. Treatment is with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics, usually erythromycin. A Crystal Vibrio Cholera (VC) testing Crystal VC testing is a rapid stool dipstick test for cholera that can provide rapid diagnosis for individuals out in the ﬁeld who suspect an outbreak of cholera. Where a positive result is found, conﬁrmation is recommended with formal stool culture. B Elek testing

This is an in-vitro test of virulence performed on specimens of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, the cause of diphtheria. It is used to test for toxigenicity of strains of the bacterium. PCR is preferred to conﬁrm the diagnosis of toxin-producing diphtheria infection because of the speed in conﬁrming the diagnosis and potential for then isolating the patient. C Monospot testing Monospot testing is used to conﬁrm the diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis. Although infectious mononucleosis does present with pharyngitis, the membrane formation here is a much stronger pointer towards diphtheria as the underlying diagnosis. D Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for anthrax spores Anthrax infection does cause respiratory tract symptoms, but it does not cause the pharyngitis with membrane formation seen here. Respiratory anthrax infection is extremely rare, and outside use as a bioweapon it is seen in individuals who work in poorly regulated abattoirs or in tanneries in the developing world. It is diagnosed by PCR.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is treated with doxycycline for an exacerbation. Which of the following represents the mode of action of doxycycline?
options: Inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30s ribosomal subunit
Inhibits protein synthesis by blocking the action of peptidyltransferase
Inhibits bacterial DNA synthesis by inhibiting bacterial dihydrofolate reductase
Inhibit bacterial DNA replication by inhibiting the action of bacterial DNA gyrase
Inhibits bacterial wall synthesis by stopping the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links
explanation:
A Inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30s ribosomal subunit Tetracyclines inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30s ribosomal subunit. This prevents the binding of transfer RNA to messenger RNA at the ribosomal subunit. Amino acids then cannot be added to polypeptide chains, and new proteins cannot be made. The class are bacteriostatic and have a wide range of activity against gram-positive, gram-negative bacteria, and Plasmodium falciparum. E Inhibits bacterial wall synthesis by stopping the

formation of peptidoglycan cross-links Penicillin inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking in bacterial cell walls. By doing this they block bacterial cell division. There is also synergy with aminoglycosides, with penicillin destroying the integrity of bacterial cell walls and facilitating their entry to interfere with protein synthesis. B Inhibits protein synthesis by blocking the action of peptidyltransferase Macrolides such as clarithromycin inhibit the action of bacterial peptidyltransferase, preventing the enzyme from adding the growing peptide attached to tRNA to the next amino acid. They also inhibit ribosomal translocation. They are mainly used to treat grampositive infections and a limited range of gram-negative infections such as Bordetella pertussis and Haemophilus inﬂuenzae. C Inhibits bacterial DNA synthesis by inhibiting bacterial dihydrofolate reductase Trimethoprim is an inhibitor of bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. It is primarily used in the treatment of urinary tract infection. Because it may reduce folic acid levels, its use is not recommended in early pregnancy. By inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, it blocks the production of bacterial DNA. D Inhibit bacterial DNA replication by inhibiting the action of bacterial DNA gyrase Quinolones interfere with DNA replication, and they do this by blocking the action of DNA gyrase. They also interfere with the topoisomerase IV enzyme, another enzyme involved in DNA replication. Quinolones have fallen out of favour because of associations with adverse events, including tendon rupture, joint pains, and neuropathies.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of blurred vision and a 3- hour history of increasing shortness of breath. She was a user of intravenous heroin and had previously been admitted with groin abscesses. On examination, her temperature was 36.7 °C, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and saturations 95% on air. There was no rash or neck stiffness. Her chest was clear. She had dysarthria and an ataxic gait. Her pupils were normal in diameter but were ﬁxed and did not accommodate. There was bilateral ptosis and facial weakness. Investigations: Chest X-ray Normal Blood gas Result Normal values pH 7.21 7.35 - 7.45 p(O2) 8.7 kPa 11.3 - 12.6 kPa p(CO2) 6.0 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa HCO3 20 mmol/l 21 - 29 mmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Botulism This is a rare condition, but the patient’s presentation is typical. This patient is an intravenous drug user, which is the most common route of exposure to botulinum toxin. Initially (within 1–8 days of contact with the toxin), the patient develops bilateral cranial nerve signs; here the patient has developed the typical blurred vision resulting from diplopia, and slurred speech from bulbar involvement. She has no impairment of consciousness, and the pupils are ﬁxed but of normal diameter – again, this is a classical presentation of botulism. The patient is afebrile – fever is unusual in botulism. Her type I respiratory failure is due to paralysis of the respiratory muscles; she is likely to progress to type II respiratory failure rapidly without appropriate treatment. D Meningococcal sepsis Although a raised respiratory rate is common in sepsis, meningococcal sepsis without pulmonary disease (her chest X-ray is normal) cannot explain the type I respiratory failure seen in her blood gas. If this were meningococcal meningitis, you would expect the patient to report a headache or you would expect to ﬁnd fever, photophobia or neck stiffness on examination. None of these features are present. Cerebellar and bulbar signs (as seen here) have been reported in meningococcal meningitis, but it is an extremely uncommon presentation. Therefore, although the patient has neurological signs, these are unlikely to be explained by meningococcal meningitis. In fact, bilateral involvement of multiple cranial nerves and ﬁxed pupils are typical of botulism; botulism can also explain her rapid-onset respiratory failure caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles (hence type I respiratory failure on the blood gas). A Heroin overdose Patients with a heroin overdose would not present with blurred vision and shortness of breath; instead patients are usually brought to the Emergency Department with severely impaired conscious-

ness. In milder cases, patients have drowsiness, nausea and vomiting and constipation. You would also expect the patient to have pinpoint pupils in opiate overdose, which are not seen here. Finally, opiates are respiratory depressants and therefore in overdose can cause hypoxaemia (as in this patient’s case), but through a reduced respiratory rate; here the patient’s respiratory rate is raised. This patient’s presentation is classic of botulism. B Guillain–Barré syndrome Typically, Guillain–Barré syndrome presents with ascending weakness and sensory disturbance (ie beginning in the legs and progressing towards the arms and ﬁnally the face). It does not cause a truly ataxic gait, and ocular involvement is exceedingly uncommon. Therefore, although Guillain–Barré syndrome could explain her respiratory failure, it would not explain her presentation with blurred vision without any leg weakness or sensory disturbance. It also could not explain her ﬁxed pupils. Instead, this constellation of symptoms and signs is typical of botulism. E Myasthenia gravis There are many features of this patient’s presentation that are compatible with myasthenia gravis, speciﬁcally diplopia, ptosis and facial weakness and respiratory failure due to neuromuscular weakness. However, there are two features that are not compatible: ﬁxed pupils and ataxia. These are not features of myasthenia gravis, and therefore an alternative diagnosis should be sought. In this case, the constellation of symptoms is typical of botulism.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of fatigue, intermittent low-grade fever, night sweats and weight loss. He has a history of a prosthetic aortic valve replacement ﬁve years ago. On examination, he is afebrile, with no peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. Blood cultures are persistently negative, and ECHO reveals vegetations on the prosthetic aortic valve. Laboratory investigations show elevated inﬂammatory marker levels and mild normocytic anaemia. Which test is most appropriate to conﬁrm a diagnosis of Coxiella burnetii endocarditis?
options: Serological testing for phase I and II antibodies
Repeat blood cultures by using specialised media
explanation: B Serological testing for phase I and II antibodies This is the gold standard for diagnosing C. burnetii endocarditis. High titres of phase I immunoglobulin G antibodies (more than 1 : 800) are diagnostic in the appropriate clinical context. C. burnetii is an obligate intracellular pathogen that cannot be routinely cultured, making serological tests essential for diagnosis. E Histopathology of the valve tissue Valve histopathology may demonstrate inﬂammatory changes consistent with infective endocarditis, but it is invasive and not typically used for primary diagnosis. PCR or immunohistochemistry on excised valve tissue could conﬁrm the organism if surgery is performed. A 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing This method can detect bacterial DNA and identify uncommon pathogens, but it is typically used in culture- negative endocarditis when a speciﬁc organism is not suspected. Serology remains more accessible and speciﬁc for C. burnetii. C PCR on blood samples PCR may detect C. burnetii DNA and can be useful in acute infections, but it is less sensitive for chronic infections such as endocarditis. PCR is usually complementary to serology. D Repeat blood cultures by using specialised media C. burnetii does not grow in standard or specialised blood culture media, and repeated cultures would not yield results.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with bloody diarrhoea and lower abdominal cramps. She works as a volunteer at the local petting farm. Apparently three other workers from the same farm have presented with symptoms over the past week. She is otherwise well with a history of asthma, for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, a temperature of 37.8 °C and a pulse of 88 bpm and regular. There is dull left-sided abdominal pain on palpation. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 119 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 123 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Prothrombin time (PT) 17.2 s 10.6–14.9 s APTT 33 s 20–41 s Stool sample: E. coli 0157 Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: E Supportive therapy only The majority of patients with E. coli 157 infection recover spontaneously within one to two weeks. Recently, application of a monoclonal antibody that speciﬁcally binds to C5, eculizumab, became available to treat patients with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, replacing plasma exchange or infusion as primary therapy. B Naproxen Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may actually exacerbate renal impairment in patients with HUS and should be avoided here. Should pain relief be required, then paracetamol is a more appropriate option. A Ciproﬂoxacin Evidence from case series suggests that use of antibiotics may increase the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome, and so they are avoided in the majority of cases. C Prednisolone Small case series suggest a potential positive impact for immune intervention in HUS, including with prednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin, although the evidence is not strong enough to recommend routine use of prednisolone here. D Probiotic supplements The main evidence for beneﬁt of probiotic supplements comes from treatment of Clostridium difﬁcile where they may reduce the risks of infection in the elderly population.

stem: A 42-year-old woman who has received a renal transplant for chronic renal failure related to type 1 diabetes comes to the Emergency Department with a dry cough and increasing shortness of breath. This has now limited her exercise tolerance to approximately 50 m before she gets short of breath. She is taking multiple immunosuppressive agents and received her transplant approximately eight weeks ago. She says the cough and shortness of breath began some ﬁve days earlier. She has a temperature of 38.2 °C; her blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg, and pulse 82 bpm and regular. Her renal transplant scar looks well healed. There are scattered crackles and wheezes heard across both lung ﬁelds on auscultation. Her oxygen saturation measured on pulse oximetry is 94% at rest and drops to 91%, as you ask her to walk back and forth ten times across the consulting room. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 142 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 189 mg/l 0–10 mg/l LDH 672 u/l 100–190 IU/l CXR: Perihilar ﬂuffy opacities. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
C IV Co-trimoxazole The underlying diagnosis is P. jirovecii (PCJ) pneumonia, to which this patient has increased susceptibility because of her immunosuppression. Out of the options given, co-trimoxazole is more effective than pentamidine, although it is not always tolerated. Duration is usually from 14 to 21 days. Prognosis is poor, and in patients without an underlying human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) infection, mortality may be 30% or higher. B IV Co-amoxiclav This would be an appropriate intervention for a community-acquired pneumonia. However, the X-ray ﬁndings, history of immunosuppression and low ambulatory oxygen saturations suggest a diagnosis of P. jirovecii pneumonia. A Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone Ceftriaxone would be potential choices for treating bacterial community-acquired pneumonia. However, the X- ray ﬁndings, history of immunosuppression and low ambulatory oxygen saturations suggest a diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii

pneumonia. D IV Pentamidine This is used as prophylaxis against PCJ infection in patients undergoing stem cell transplantation. It is not commonly used as treatment due to the risk for toxicity. E Nebulised Pentamidine Nebulised pentamidine does offer some beneﬁt in the treatment of PCJ pneumonia, but it is less effective than iv co-trimoxazole. It should be considered for use if iv co-trimoxazole is not tolerated. It should be noted that it is highly teratogenic, so it should be administered in a well-ventilated room away from staff members who are of childbearing age.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department after returning from a backpacking trip around South America. She has a 2-day history of abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. There is a small amount of fresh blood mixed in with her vomit. Her symptoms have followed from a 4-day period of intermittent fevers, myalgia and headaches. Prior to this, she has been well, with no other past medical history. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8 °C. Her heart rate is 113 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 117/65 mmHg. She has a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, with saturations of 95% on room air. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. She has generalised abdominal tenderness and voluntary guarding in the epigastrium. Bowel sounds are present. There is a widespread maculopapular rash over her face, trunk and limbs. Examination of the ear, nose and throat system was unremarkable, other than some mild gum irritation and bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Dengue fever This patient has dengue fever. It is spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito and is common in many areas of the world, including Asia and South America. The presence of fever, headache, myalgia and a maculopapular rash early on in the illness is common, along with facial ﬂushing. In some, the disease can progress to a viral haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome in severe cases. Treatment is mostly supportive with intravenous ﬂuids and

transfusion as required. E Typhoid fever Typhoid fever is a bacterial illness secondary to Salmonella typhi. It is an enteric fever with symptoms comprising abdominal pain and distension, along with either constipation or diarrhoea. Characteristic features that point to a diagnosis of typhoid fever include pale pink macules, otherwise known as rose spots on the trunk of infected patients. It does not explain this patient’s symptoms, making it an incorrect answer. Yellow fever Yellow fever is a viral haemorrhagic illness spread by the Aedes mosquito. It presents as a mild ﬂu-like illness followed by a brief remission period before the onset of haematemesis, jaundice and oliguria. It is common in Central and South America, as well as Africa. The presenting symptoms in the question are milder than those of yellow fever, with no mention of jaundice or oliguria and only a small amount of fresh blood mixed in with the patient’s vomitus. While yellow fever should still be considered as a differential diagnosis, alternative diagnoses should also be considered. The presence of a maculopapular rash, for example, hints towards the diagnosis of dengue fever, the correct answer in this case. B Zika virus Zika virus is spread by the A. aegypti mosquito. It is common in Africa, the Americas, Asia and the Paciﬁc. It is a short-lived illness with symptoms including fever, rash, arthralgia and conjunctivitis. Haemorrhagic symptoms are not seen in the Zika virus, making it a less likely diagnosis. D Malaria Malaria is a parasitic disease spread by the Anopheles mosquito. There are multiple subtypes, of which malaria falciparum is the most common. The disease is generally transmitted in Africa, South East Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean and Western Paciﬁc countries. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgia, headache and nausea and vomiting. Hepatosplenomegaly may appear. Complications of malaria include cerebral malaria and blackwater fever which is an intravascular haemolysis causing acute kidney injury and jaundice. This patient has travelled back from South America, where malaria is less prevalent. The maculopapular rash and minor bleeding also suggest an alternative diagnosis.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department following a seizure witnessed by her daughter. The daughter reports that her mother is normally ﬁt and well but the latter has been complaining of headaches recently. The patient is on no known medications and is a non-smoker. She has recently returned from a trip to China. Physical examination ﬁndings are normal, although the patient is in a post-ictal state. An urgent computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is arranged, which shows a periventricular cystic lesion in the parietal lobe, with surrounding oedema. The Radiologist says that the appearance is compatible with neurocysticercosis. Which of the following investigations would be most speciﬁc for neurocysticercosis?
options: Fundoscopic examination to directly visualise subretinal parasites
Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detection of cysticercal antigens
Resolution of intracranial cystic lesions after therapy with albendazole
Serum anticysticercal antibodies demonstrated by immunoblot assay
Single stool examination for ova and parasites of Taenia solium
explanation:
A Fundoscopic examination to directly visualise subretinal parasites The pork tapeworm (T. solium) is the causative organism in cysticercosis, which can affect either the intestine, causing an intestinal tapeworm infection, or the central nervous system, causing neurocysticercosis. The infection is acquired through ingestion of undercooked pork containing cysticerci of T. solium. It is important to elicit a history of exposure to an area where the parasite is endemic.
