Since signs and symptoms can be non- speciﬁc, certain criteria are required to diagnose the infection. Diagnosis can be difﬁcult as radiological signs and immunological tests are often non-speciﬁc. However, direct visualisation of parasites has a very high diagnostic yield and is considered an absolute criterion. The mainstay of treatment is symptomatic relief, eg anticonvulsants for seizures, and corticosteroids for cerebral oedema. Antiparasitic drugs (albendazole) are used if viable cysticerci are suspected and they should be given under expert supervision. E Single stool examination for ova and parasites of Taenia solium It is worth noting that since the eggs are shed intermittently, a single stool examination looking for ova and parasites may not be enough to identify the tapeworm carriers. While a positive result would be very speciﬁc, the sensitivity of the test is low. B Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detection of cysticercal antigens This is because while neurocysticercosis often involves high parasite counts within the ventricles and basal cisterns, there is not always evidence of antibodies within the cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF). If positive, it is considered a major, rather than an absolute, criterion. The CSF could also show an elevated eosinophil count

and the presence of parasite antigens. C Resolution of intracranial cystic lesions after therapy with albendazole Albendazole is not always necessary for lesion resolution, as has been documented in many cases. D Serum anticysticercal antibodies demonstrated by immunoblot assay Antibody studies are frustratingly non-speciﬁc for neurocysticercosis. Antibody results are still considered a major criterion, although not as speciﬁc as direct parasite visualisation.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the clinic with headache, neck stiffness, malaise and photophobia which has been worsening over the past few days. He came to the UK 2 years ago and since then has been at university. Over the past few months, his partner tells you that he has lost weight and seems to suffer from night sweats. On examination, he is pyrexial 37.8 °C, has neck stiffness and photophobia. There is axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. He appears to have isolated 6th nerve palsy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 120 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lumbar puncture Turbid appearance, 22 cm water opening pressure, elevated CSF protein, lymphocytes ++, neutrophils + India ink test Positive Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Cryptococcal meningitis Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast (fungus) which can cause a meningitis in the immunocompromised. The India ink test is used to

diagnose cryptococcal meningitis, and the raised opening pressure, turbid appearance to the CSF, raised protein and mixed lymphocytic/neutrophil picture are relatively typical of the diagnosis. From his history there is a strong suspicion that he may be HIV positive, accounting for the underlying cryptococcal infection. Management of the condition involves the use of amphotericin B, which is typically given as IV combination therapy with ﬂucytosine for a period of 2 weeks. Raised CSF opening pressure is associated with a poor prognosis in this condition. D Meningococcal meningitis Meningococcal meningitis is the most common bacterial meningitis in the UK and is caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Presentation is with acute-onset fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting. Prompt treatment with IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) is essential as the disease is rapidly fatal. CSF typically shows a neutrophilia, low glucose, raised protein and Gram-negative diplococci on the Gram stain. A Herpes simplex encephalitis Herpes simplex encephalitis is most commonly caused by HSV-1. Presentation is typically with fever and altered mentation, there may also be a recent history of cold sores. Onset is typical over a few hours to days and immunocompetent patients may be affected. In this case the tempo of presentation, as well as the CSF ﬁnding, excludes herpes simplex encephalitis. B Cytomegalovirus (CMV) meningoencephalitis CMV meningoencephalitis is rare but possible in the immunocompetent host. In the immunocompromised (eg HIV positive, transplant recipient) the risk is increased. Presentation would typically be with acute-onset fever, meningism and altered mentation. In this case the tempo of presentation, as well as the CSF ﬁndings, exclude CMV meningoencephalitis. E Tuberculous meningitis Tuberculous meningitis may result from primary infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis or reactivation of latent infection. It is more common in the immunocompromised. Presentation is often subacute with fever, neck stiffness, headache and altered mentation. Typical MRI changes are of a basal meningitis. CSF ﬁndings are typically a lymphocytosis with low glucose and raised protein. In this case we are told that the India ink stain is positive which points to an alternative explanation for the patient’s symptoms.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 6-week history of lower abdominal pain. This had not limited her activities, but the pain was persistent and on occasion she had felt feverish. She did not have dysuria or an abnormal discharge. She had had multiple urinary tract infections in her twenties. On examination, the temperature was 37.3 °C. There was mild lower abdominal tenderness, and bowel sounds were present and normal. Urine dipstick was normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 132 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 255 × 109/l 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 72 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 4.9 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l CRP 45 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
explanation:
A Chlamydial infection This is a classic description of pelvic inﬂammatory disease. This patient complains of subacute or long-term pelvic pain; patients may also experience mucopurulent discharge, dyspareunia or abnormal vaginal bleeding. The ‘urinary tract infections’ this patient reports may have included sexually transmitted chlamydial infections causing dysuria. Typically, patients have lower abdominal pain on examination and may have cervical motion or adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination. Fever and raised inﬂammatory markers are common ﬁndings. As this patient is clinically stable, oral treatment, as opposed to admission for intravenous treatment, is appropriate. Current British Association for Sexual Health and HIV guidelines recommend a combination of oral doxycycline plus oral metronidazole plus IM ceftriaxone. D Renal stones You would expect a patient with renal stones to complain of severe, colicky unilateral loin-to-groin pain, which is not what this patient describes; instead, she has persistent bilateral pelvic pain. Although a low-grade fever (as seen here) is common with renal stones, you might expect to see some blood in the urine dipstick; instead, this patient’s urine dipstick is normal. This patient’s presentation is classic for pelvic inﬂammatory disease – long-standing, non-speciﬁc bilateral pelvic pain with intermittent fevers and mildly raised inﬂammatory markers. The background of recurrent dysuria suggests there may have been a previous sexually transmitted infection. The most common cause of pelvic inﬂammatory disease

in the UK is chlamydial infection, and therefore this is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms. B Gonococcal sepsis This patient is not septic; although she has raised inﬂammatory markers, she is not systemically unwell. If this were acute gonococcal infection, you would expect purulent vaginal discharge, which this patient does not have. This patient has pelvic inﬂammatory disease – long-standing non-speciﬁc pelvic pain with mildly raised inﬂammatory markers on a background of recurrent episodes of dysuria. Pelvic inﬂammatory disease can be caused by gonococcal infection; however, Chlamydia is the most common cause in the United Kingdom and therefore is the most likely cause in this case. C Pyelonephritis If this were pyelonephritis, you would expect a history of dysuria and a positive urine dipstick; you would also expect the patient to be more systemically unwell with a higher temperature. This patient has pelvic inﬂammatory disease, with long-standing nonspeciﬁc pelvic pain and mildly raised inﬂammatory markers on a background of recurrent episodes of dysuria. The most common cause of pelvic inﬂammatory disease in the UK is Chlamydia, and therefore this is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms. E Urinary tract infection You would not expect such a long history for a patient with a urinary tract infection. If this were a urinary tract infection, you would expect the patient to complain of dysuria and the urine dipstick to be positive. Instead, this patient has a history typical of pelvic inﬂammatory disease – subacute non-speciﬁc bilateral pelvic pain, with intermittent fevers and mildly raised inﬂammatory markers. The background of recurrent dysuria may, in fact, have included sexually transmitted infections, not simply urinary tract infections. The most common cause of pelvic inﬂammatory disease in the UK is chlamydial infection; therefore, this is the correct answer.

stem: A 32-year-old man returns from a trip across the Mediterranean, North and sub-Saharan Africa. He reports feeling generally unwell for the past few days with a fever. On examination, you notice a tick bite eschar and a surrounding rash on the left mid-thigh. Which is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
C Rickettsia conorii This patient has infection with R. conorii, the hallmark of which is the tick bite eschar. Common presenting features include fever, rash, malaise, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and joint and muscle pain. Diagnosis is usually made on clinical history and serological testing. The most appropriate choice for antibiotic therapy is doxycycline. Other choices include ciproﬂoxacin and levoﬂoxacin, however these should be avoided wherever possible, as ﬂuoroquinolone use is associated with an increased risk of severe potentially irreversible side effects such as peripheral neuropathy and tendonitis. Although fatalities can occur due to infection, they are rare. Complications may include neuropathy, Guillain– Barré syndrome, acute kidney disease, hepatomegaly and thrombocytopenia. E Orientia tsutsugamushi This organism is most common in South East Asia and is therefore unlikely. It presents with eschar, hepatomegaly, cough and lymphoadenopathy. A Rhiphicephalus sanguineus The vector for infection with R. conorii is commonly R. sanguineus or dog tick and is not an infectious organism of humans. B Rickettsia rickettsii This is the pathogen which causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF). RMSF is endemic throughout the Americas and following one to two weeks after a tick bite there is general malaise, fever and a rash. The rash starts as a centripetal macular rash progressing to a petechial rash by day six. The absence of such a rash makes this diagnosis unlikely, and RMSF usually has a target rash around the bite lesion rather than an eschar. D Rickettsia prowzekii Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, which is transmitted by the body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis).This causes headaches, fever, muscle and joint pain as well as

nausea and vomiting, with a discrete rash six days after onset. The absence of this constellation makes this diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends the Genito-urinary Medicine (GUM) Clinic. She is concerned about vaginal discharge with an unpleasant smell. She has noticed these symptoms for the past 3 weeks and has been washing her genitals regularly with soap and shower gel. She sometimes puts Dettol in her bath. She is married and has had no other sexual partners for 5 years. On examination, she has a normal vulva, vagina and cervix. There is a thin, white discharge with a ﬁshy smell. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Bacterial vaginosis Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is caused by replacement of the usual vaginal lactobacilli with anaerobic bacteria, genital mycoplasmas and others. Douching, washing with scented soaps and gels have been implicated and the patient should be advised to stop these practices. Treatment is with metronidazole. BV is not sexually transmitted. BV is the commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age. It is twice as common as vaginal candidiasis. The prevalence of BV has varied from 5% in asymptomatic college students, 12% in pregnant women and 30% in women undergoing termination of pregnancy. E HIV +ve This is very unlikely given the lack of exposure and HIV does not cause vaginal discharge. A Candida Candida causes a severe itch and white lumpy discharge, which would commonly be seen on examination. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is the second most common cause of vaginitis and vaginal discharge after BV: the lifetime incidence of vulvovaginal candidiasis is estimated at 50–75%. The prevalence of vulvovaginal candidiasis is not known, but the disease is diagnosed in 5–15% of women who attend sexually transmitted disease and family planning clinics C Trichomonas Trichomonas gives an itch, offensive green discharge and is sexually transmitted. In 1997, GUM clinics in the UK reported over 5600

cases of trichomoniasis in women and 250 cases in men. D Chlamydia Women present with dysuria, abdominal pain, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and vaginal discharge. Men can have urethritis with dysuria and discharge and sometimes epididymo-orchitis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department after being found collapsed at home by her partner. She is two weeks postpartum and had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. There is no past medical history of note and her only regular medication includes vitamin supplements. On examination, she is drowsy and disoriented with a GCS of 13. Her temperature is 39.5 °C with a heart rate of 140 bpm and a BP of 88/45 mmHg. Her mucous membranes and skin are diffusely erythematous with desquamation. Investigation Results Normal value Hb 118 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 28.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 290 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 145 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 12.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 180 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 229 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Toxic shock syndrome This patient has a diagnosis of toxic shock syndrome (TSS), given the features of acute systemic upset with fever, hypotension and a desquamating erythematous rash. TSS is an exotoxin-mediated illness secondary to bacterial infection with Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and group A streptococcal species such as Streptococcus pyogenes. On the ﬁrst presentation, the signs and symptoms of TSS may generally be nonspeciﬁc, with signs of systemic upset and no clear source. However, if left untreated, the TSS can cause multiorgan failure and death. TSS secondary to group A streptococcus is most commonly associated with an infected cutaneous site (eg necrotising fasciitis). In contrast, TSS secondary to staphylococcus is associated with

prolonged tampon use and postpartum infections. The recent history of a vaginal delivery points toward S. aureus as the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation. Treatment of TSS involves early broadspectrum antibiotic treatment, intravenous ﬂuid resuscitation and likely admission to the Intensive Care Unit. D Stevens-Johnson syndrome Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a severe skin reaction associated with skin and mucocutaneous sheet loss. It is usually secondary to medication use, including anticonvulsants, antibiotics and non-steroidal anti- inﬂammatory drugs. Although this patient has evidence of desquamation, the only medication use given is vitamin supplements that are unlikely to cause SJS. A Amniotic ﬂuid embolus Amniotic ﬂuid embolism is a very important differential diagnosis to consider, given that this patient has recently given birth. It can also give rise to the presentation of collapse, tachycardia and hypotension. However, it is not associated with an erythematous desquamating rash, making this diagnosis less likely. B Erythroderma Erythroderma is a rare dermatological condition characterised by diffuse reddening of the skin, usually secondary to an underlying skin disease (eg eczema), although up to 30% of cases are idiopathic. However, the presence of systemic upset in a postpartum woman with signiﬁcantly elevated inﬂammatory markers and evidence of an acute kidney injury is more suggestive of a more serious underlying condition. C Gram-negative septic shock Gram-negative septic shock is a reasonable differential diagnosis given the systemic features of sepsis. However, it is uncommon for Gram-negative organisms to give rise to a desquamating rash, as seen in this patient. The diffuse erythematous skin involvement is the key distinguishing factor that points toward toxic shock syndrome (TSS) as the likely diagnosis.

stem: A schoolgirl returns from trip to France with 4-day history of headache, vomiting and fever. On examination, she is alert with neck stiffness and no focal neurology signs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain demonstrates no obvious lesions. Investigations of cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Opening pressure 24 cm water (5–18cm) 6–20 cmH O Protein 0.8 g/l < 0.45 g/l WCC 110/mm (99% lymphocytes) < 5/mm Glucose 3.2 mmol/l (serum glucose 4.0 mmol/l) 2.5–3.9 mmol/l (two-thirds plasma value) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Viral meningitis A clinical meningitis with an elevated CSF pressure, slightly elevated protein and lymphocytosis is likely to be of viral aetiology, particularly in young previously ﬁt individual. E TB meningitis TB meningitis would result in lymphocytes in the CSF, but it is unlikely given the lack of immunosuppression and travel to a TBprevalent country. It is also less likely given the absence of meningeal enhancement on the MRI and the short presentation. B Cryptococcal meningitis Cryptococcal and mycoplasma meningitis both give rise to lymphocytic CSF but the cell counts are usually lower (<80/ml) and the glucose reduced. Also, cryptococcal infection is signiﬁcantly associated with severe T- dysfunction such as immunosuppression from HIV or iatrogenic immunosuppression following organ transplant. The normal MRI also makes this a less likely diagnosis. C Pneumococcal meningitis This diagnosis is associated with polymorphic cells in the CSF and relatively low glucose, with severe systemic upset and a shorter presentation. D Meningococcal meningitis This diagnosis is associated with polymorphic cells in the CSF and relatively low glucose, with severe systemic upset and a shorter presentation.

stem: A 38-year-old HIV-positive patient presents to the clinic complaining of increasing shortness of breath, dry cough and wheezing. On examination, you can hear a left-sided monophonic wheeze. You notice several lesions on his exposed skin, including on his nose, as below. He is a lifelong non-smoker. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 103 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 130 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CD4 count 92 cells/mm3 500–1500 cells/mm3 Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CXR Limited left lower zone collapse Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Endobronchial Kaposi’s sarcoma This patient has violaceous plaques on his nose characteristic of Kaposi’s sarcoma.Pulmonary Kaposi’s sarcoma is found in between 6% and 30% of patients with HIV, and is the most common tumour seen. In patients who have cutaneous Kaposi’s, up to 75% have demonstrable pulmonary tumours on endobronchial biopsy. Unfortunately use of HAART does not signiﬁcantly appear to affect the prognosis in patients with pulmonary Kaposi’s, with a mean prognosis of only 1.6 years from the point of diagnosis. D Bacterial pneumonia Bacterial pneumonia typically presents with a history of fevers and a

productive cough. Blood tests would classically show a neutrophilia. However in practice it may be difﬁcult to exclude infection in this case and further imaging and possible bronchoscopy would be indicated. A Bronchial carcinoma Bronchial carcinoma would be on the differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with these symptoms and lobar collapse. However we are told he is a non-smoker and in the context of his profound immunosuppression and cutaneous Kaposi’s, an alternative diagnosis is more probable. B Bronchial carcinoid Carcinoid is a paraneoplastic syndrome characterised by facial ﬂushing, diarrhoea and bronchial constriction. Pulmonary carcinoid syndrome occurs when the primary neuroendocrine tumour occurs in the lung. In our patient with profound immunosuppression and cutaneous Kaposi’s, an alternative diagnosis is more likely. E Tuberculosis Pulmonary tuberculosis most commonly causes upper-lobe consolidation and cavitation. Presentation would be with fever, a productive cough and weight loss. However clinically it may be difﬁcult to exclude tuberculosis in this case and further investigation such as a bronchoscopy would be indicated.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department for review. He returned from a holiday in Spain a few days ago, during which he had unprotected sexual intercourse with a number of women. He had an onset of multiple vesicles which has now formed into multiple ulcers and he has developed burning and tingling over his penis. On examination he is pyrexial 37.8Â°C, his BP is 115/85 mmHg; pulse is 72/min and regular. There are multiple small, shallow, painful ulcers over the glans penis and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. The ulcers are swabbed and he is referred to the GUM clinic. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
C Oral Aciclovir The answer is Oral Aciclovir - Standard treatment for genital herpes is oral Aciclovir, administered

at a dose of 200 mg ﬁve times daily OR 400 mg three times daily for ﬁve days. A more prolonged course of aciclovir may be required in patients who have a history of HIV. Anti-viral therapy reduces the severity and duration of herpes episodes, but does not impact on the overall course of the disease. Chancroid is a differential diagnosis of genital herpes, but this usually presents with a single deep purulent ulcer, although in less common cases multiple can be present. Lymphadenopathy occurs usually 1 week after the onset of the initial ulcer in such cases. E Topical Aciclovir Topical Aciclovir, is incorrect because it is ineffective for the treatment of primary genital herpes versus oral options. A IM Penicillin IM Penicillin, is incorrect because 2.4 mega units of Penicillin IM is the standard treatment for syphilis, not for Herpes Simplex. B Oral Azithromycin Oral Azithromycin, is incorrect because Azithromycin is an alternative therapy for primary syphilis. D Oral Famciclovir Oral Famciclovir is incorrect, it is an option for recurrent herpes, but is not usually considered as an initial therapy.

stem: A 26-year-old man with HIV infection presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 2-week history of general malaise, nausea and abdominal pain. He is generally eating less than usual but is opening his bowels and passing urine normally. He is known to have gallstones. On examination, he appears cachectic and has a temperature of 38.2 °C, with a heart rate of 90 bpm and a BP of 110/63 mmHg. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant but no guarding or palpable organomegaly. Bowel sounds are present. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 120 g/l 135 – 175 g/l White blood count (WCC) 4.0 × 109/l 4.0 – 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 151 × 109/l 150 – 400 × 109/l INR 1.0 < 1.1 Bilirubin 20 µmol/l 1.71 – 20.5 µmol/l ALT 37 U/l 4 – 36 U/l ALP 380 U/l 44 – 147 U/l Gamma GT (GGT) 189 U/l 9 - 48 U/l Albumin 35 g/l 35 - 55 g/l CD4 count 185 cells/mm3 500–1500 cells/mm3 What is the most appropriate step for a deﬁnitive diagnosis?
explanation:
D Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography Biliary involvement in HIV infection is commonly known as acquired immune deﬁciency syndrome (AIDS) cholangiopathy and is a syndrome of biliary obstruction resulting from infection-related strictures of the biliary tract. There is a spectrum of involvement, including acute acalculous cholecystitis, papillary stenosis and sclerosing cholangitis. Cholangiopathy is mostly associated with Cryptosporidium parvum, but other pathogens have also been identiﬁed, including cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Microsporidium. The deﬁnitive diagnosis of cholangiopathy is made by direct visualisation by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), which can reveal several patterns of biliary abnormality; the combination of papillary stenosis and sclerosing cholangitis is the most unique to AIDS cholangiopathy. Also, ERCP allows both conﬁrmation of the diagnosis and the performance of therapeutic procedures, if indicated. Biliary brushings and biopsy, biliary aspiration and small bowel biopsy can also be performed to aid in diagnosis, including detection of the aetiologic agent using appropriate stains. However, other studies (particularly ultrasound and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) can be helpful in early evaluation and in selecting patients for ERCP. Symptomatic patients with papillary stenosis have responded symptomatically to endoscopic sphincterotomy. Antibiotics have not been shown to be useful. Some clinicians use ursodeoxycholic acid in patients with intrahepatic disease, with an observed improvement in liver enzymes. A Blood culture Although this patient has a fever, there are no other markers of sepsis and cultures are therefore unlikely to contribute to making a diagnosis. Imaging of the biliary tree is required to explore this patient’s symptoms and pattern of liver enzyme derangement. B CT abdomen CT is more useful than ultrasound in identifying intrahepatic strictures and can be effective in identifying intrahepatic masses, abdominal adenopathy and pancreatic disease in jaundiced patients. However, CT is inferior to ERCP in its ability to display the necessarily precise biliary anatomical details for the deﬁnitive diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy. C Liver biopsy Liver biopsy has little value in the diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy. Diagnosis is informed by imaging of the biliary tree.

E Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography This is a cost-effective and sensitive initial screening investigation. However, ERCP is considered the deﬁnitive modality, given the patient is known to have gallstones, as it carries further diagnostic and therapeutic options. MRCP pre ERCP in patients at high risk of choledocholithiasis is known to result in poorer outcomes than moving straight to ERCP.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a 1-week history of headache and 2-day history of confusion. Three days ago, he had returned from a 6-month trip to rural Kenya. On examination, his temperature was 39 °C, his blood pressure 125/85 mmHg and his pulse 88 beats per minute (bpm) and regulation. Saturation on air is normal. A physical examination of all systems is unremarkable except for bilateral upgoing plantars. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 100 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White cellcount (WCC) 9 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 3.1 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 110 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Glucose 4.0 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Thick and thin blood ﬁlm No malarial parasites in one sample CXR Normal Computed Tomography (CT) head Normal Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) WCC 3/µlProtein 0.5 g/dl Glucose 3.8 mmol/l 0.15 - 0.45 g/dl protein3.3 - 4.4 mmol/l glucose Which drug is most appropriate in his immediate management?
explanation:
C Intravenous quinine This patient’s travel history, anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia and lower limit of blood, and their symptoms, ﬁt with malaria. Typically, three ﬁlms are required to rule out malaria, this patient had just one negative ﬁlm.

Intravenous quinine or artesunate would be the most appropriate treatment. C Intravenous methylprednisolone There is debate over the use of steroids in bacterial meningitis, and even in malaria. Steroids would certainly not be the one most appropriate medication in this case. Although steroids can be useful in reducing cerebral oedema, their administration can also suppress host immune response and therefore risk overwhelming sepsis. In this case, the most likely diagnosis is malaria, given the patient’s travel history, mild anaemia, thrombocytopenia and mild hypoglycaemia. Blood ﬁlms can be negative, and three or more negative ﬁlms would be required before a diagnosis of malaria could be excluded. The most appropriate treatment would therefore be intravenous quinine. A Intravenous aciclovir Intravenous aciclovir is used in the treatment of herpes simplex encephalitis. Although this patient could have herpes simplex encephalitis, it is not the most likely diagnosis in this case. The travel history, combined with anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia and mild hypoglycaemia, is suggestive of malaria, which is the most likely diagnosis here. If there is a strong clinical suspicion of malaria, blood ﬁlms should be repeated; three or more negative blood ﬁlms are needed to completely rule out malaria. Therefore the most appropriate treatment is intravenous quinine, to treat malaria. B Intravenous cefotaxime Intravenous cefotaxime would be an appropriate treatment for bacterial meningitis; however, this patient does not have any signs of meningism. Given his travel history, anaemia, mild hypoglycaemia and mild thrombocytopenia, malaria would be a much more likely explanation. Films can be false negatives, and three or more negative ﬁlms are required to rule out a diagnosis of malaria. To treat malaria, intravenous quinine would be the most appropriate option. E Oral antiretroviral therapy Oral antiretroviral therapy would be a treatment for HIV; this patient does not have a history, examination or investigations consistent with HIV. The most likely diagnosis in this case is malaria; it ﬁts with his travel history, and would explain his anaemia, mild thrombocytopenia and hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 26-year-old who is taking long-term oral prednisolone (10 mg/day) therapy comes to the Emergency Department because he is worried, as his brother has been admitted to the hospital with acute chicken pox infection and he had seen him two days earlier. He is certain that he has never suffered from chicken pox. What is the most appropriate course of action?
explanation:
A Check varicella antibody status Steroid use within 3 months of chicken pox exposure increases the risk of severe infection in patients who are non-immune. Guidance supports the use of varicella zoster virus (VZV) immunoglobulin within 3 days of exposure if possible, and not later than 10 days after exposure. Given that IV immunoglobulin is not without risk,

antibody status should of course be assessed ﬁrst. Conﬁrmed chicken pox infection should be managed aggressively with anti-viral therapy, and specialist opinion from an infectious disease consultant is advised. Complications of infection in this population include pneumonitis, hepatitis, encephalitis and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). D Observe for signs of infection This patient has had a signiﬁcant chicken pox exposure and is known to be immunosuppressed, and as such is at risk of severe disease. In this setting, if he has no immunity to varicella it would be necessary to give varicella immunoglobulin. A Start prophylactic acyclovir This patient has had a signiﬁcant chicken pox exposure and is immunocompromised. It is important to determine immune status to plan further management. All cases should be discussed with an infectious diseases specialist. There is no role for prophylactic acyclovir in this setting. B Start prophylactic valacyclovir This patient has had a signiﬁcant chicken pox exposure and is immunocompromised. It is important to determine immune status to plan further management. All cases should be discussed with an infectious diseases specialist. There is no role for prophylactic valacyclovir in this setting. E Give varicella immunoglobulin This patient has had a signiﬁcant chicken pox exposure and is known to be immunosuppressed, and as such is at risk of severe disease. However, giving varicella immunoglobulin is not without risk and is unnecessary if he is already immune (either through previous exposure or vaccination). There is sufﬁcient time to test varicella antibody status, and therefore this should be done prior to giving immunoglobulin.

stem: A 44-year-old woman attends the Respiratory Clinic with a 5-week history of a dry cough. She had a mild sore throat and fever initially but says this has now resolved. Her cough is worse in the evenings and is triggered by cold air. She has mild chest pain on repeated bouts of coughing, but she denies shortness of breath and is still able to carry out normal daily activities. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, her temperature is 36.3 °C. Her heart rate is 74 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 121/79 mmHg. Her capillary reﬁll time is < 2 seconds. She has a clear chest, with no audible crackles or wheeze and good air entry bilaterally. Heart sounds are normal and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Ear, nose and throat examination shows a mildly erythematous throat and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. She has bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhages. What is the most likely causative organism responsible for this patient’s diagnosis?
explanation: A Bordetella pertussis This patient has whooping cough caused by the Gram-negative bacteria B. pertussis. A prolonged history of a dry cough that is triggered by cold air and that is worse in the evenings is a symptom of the illness. A mild fever and sore throat may be seen initially. Classically, the increased pressure from prolonged coughing can cause subconjunctival haemorrhages. E Streptococcus pneumoniae S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. However, symptoms of pneumonia typically include fever, shortness of breath and productive cough of purulent sputum. Secondly, the symptoms usually have a shorter duration, making it less likely to be the correct diagnosis. B Group A Streptococcus Group A Streptococcus is a common cause of sore throat and tonsillitis. On examination, classical ﬁndings are an erythematous throat with inﬂamed tonsils. Palpable cervical lymphadenopathy is also seen. As these are not the symptoms and signs present in this patient, group A Streptococcus is an incorrect answer. C Mycobacterium tuberculosis M. tuberculosis is the organism responsible for the respiratory illness tuberculosis. Symptoms of tuberculosis have a more insidious onset, with constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fever and night sweats also being common. This is not present in this patient, making it an incorrect answer. D Parainﬂuenza virus Parainﬂuenza virus is the cause of croup or laryngotracheobronchitis. It is characterised by the classical barking cough, which is often at its worst at night. The virus is typically seen in younger children and its duration is not typically much longer than one week.

stem: A 35-year-old man from Nigeria presents to the Emergency Department with fevers, night sweats and 10 kg weight loss over the past 2 months. There is no cough or shortness of breath. He says that he was diagnosed HIV positive 6 months previously in Africa but does not know any further details. On examination, he is febrile at 38 °C and cachectic. He has a 4 cm lymph node in his left axilla, and his chest is clear. On examination, he has 2 cm hepatomegaly. Chest X-ray is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 86 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 2.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 311 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Urea and electrolytes (U&Es) Within normal range ALP 330 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 75 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 9 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 25 g/l 35–55 g/l LDH 1500 U/l 100–190 IU/l An ultrasound of the liver reveals diffuse hepatomegaly with no duct dilatation. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: C Lymph node biopsy This is a young, HIV-positive patient with fevers, night sweats, weight loss and enlarged .The most likely diagnoses are tuberculosis and lymphoma; histoplasmosis and atypical mycobacteria are also a possibility. A tissue sample is needed to differentiate between these diagnoses and a lymph node biopsy is the least invasive method of obtain histology. Further microscopy and staining will be able to provide a deﬁnitive diagnosis. A Sputum culture There are two main differential diagnoses: tuberculosis and lymphoma. Sputum culture is unlikely to show any bacilli as the patient is not coughing, and even if they were the sensitivity would be low. B Bone marrow trephine This is a very invasive investigation to obtain a tissue sample and would be a secondary investigation following established diagnosis of lymphoma. D CT of the abdomen A computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen will add little; a tissue sample is needed to look for lymphoma, granulomas or acidfast bacilli. E Liver biopsy The patient does have hepatomegaly, but investigating for underlying causes would be more appropriate.

stem: A 25-year-old man who is known to be an IV heroin abuser presents to the Emergency Department by ambulance with severe muscle spasms and abdominal pain. He admits that he has had increasing problems sourcing both clean needles and sites to inject himself over the past few weeks. On examination there is an injecting abscess in the right groin. There is bilateral increased tone and hyperreﬂexia. He suffers from muscle spasms when you test reﬂexes in the arms, and has a tense, rigid abdomen. You ask him to swallow a glass of water and he begins to choke. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 189 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 205 mg/l 0–10 mg/l ALT 85 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline Phosphatase 185 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 22 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
C IM Anti-tetanus immunoglobulin The answer is IM Anti-tetanus immunoglobulin - The increased tone and muscle spasms seen here, coupled with the history of IV drug abuse suggests injection related tetanus. The signs of infection with raised white count and CRP ﬁt with this picture. The abnormal LFTs may be related to viral hepatitis. There is signiﬁcant risk of this patient deteriorating very rapidly, requiring intubation and ventilation as a prophylactic measure in many cases. A Debridement of groin abscess Debridement of groin abscess, id incorrect, it is appropriate but not until anti-tetanus immunoglobulin has been administered, because of the risks of increasing the load of tetanus toxin in the peripheral circulation.

B IV immunoglobulin IV immunoglobulin, in incorrect, it is an appropriate intervention for Guillain Barré (GBS), associated with ﬂaccid paralysis not seen here. D IV Methylprednisolone IV Methylprednisolone, is incorrect given the underlying probable tetanus infection. In addition, corticosteroids are ineffective in managing GBS. E IV Metronidazole IV Metronidazole, in incorrect, it may reduce the duration of tetanus symptoms, although it is additive to use of tetanus immunoglobulin and debridement of any abscess.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic complaining of dysuria for the past week. He is systemically well. In his sexual history, he has had unprotected sexual intercourse with three partners in the past 6 months. The patient is allergic to tetracycline based antibiotics. On examination, there is no penile discharge, testicular masses or tenderness. The abdomen is soft and non- tender. Urethral swab reveals 33 neutrophils per high-power ﬁeld, no organisms are seen. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
D Azithromycin The patient has non-speciﬁc or non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) as there were no gonococci seen on microscopy but presence of neutrophils on the penile swab. NGU is caused by chlamydia in 60% of cases. It can be caused by other bacteria such as Ureaplasma urealyticum and Mycoplasma genitalium. These organisms are rarely detected but are well covered by azithromycin and doxycycline which are both commonly used for NGU: doxycycline b.d is recommended as ﬁrst-line treatment by the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH), with ﬁrst alternative being Azithromycin and less commonly used alternative treatments include oﬂoxacin.

E Metronidazole This is the correct treatment for bacterial vaginosis. A No treatment needed The patient most likely has a signiﬁcant infection as is evidenced by the neutrophils on the penile swab and will need treatment. If the swab is negative then no treatment should be offered. B Nitrofurantoin This would be a possible treatment for urinary tract infection but this is unlikely to be the correct diagnosis as dysuria is a common presentation for NGU as well as UTI, especially in a male patient with a history of unprotected sexual encounters. C Ceftriaxone This would be the treatment for gonorrhoea. For this diagnosis microscopy would reveal Gram-negative diploccoci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

stem: A 46-year-old intravenous drug user comes to the Accident and Emergency Unit with a purplish rash on his arms and feet. He states that the rash has been present for nearly 2 weeks and is progressively worsening. It is not pruritic or painful. On examination, he is not in any acute distress. There is mild jaundice present. Heart and lung examination is within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows right upper quadrant tenderness with liver edge palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin. Skin examination reveals palpable purpura on both arms and his left foot. His right lower limb shows some erythematous nodules as well as livedo reticularis. CNS examination shows decreased strength in plantar ﬂexion as well as decreased sensation of the left foot. Some laboratory results are shown below: Investigation Result HIV test Negative Hepatitis B surface antigen Positive Urine microscopy reveals the following: Investigation Result Red blood cells (RBCs) +++ Protein ++ White blood cells (WBCs) Negativ What is the most likely cause of his rash?
options: Impaired coagulation secondary to liver cirrhosis
explanation: C Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) The ﬁndings such as erythematous nodules, livedo reticularis, mononeuritis multiplex and kidney involvement are all suggestive of PAN, which also occurs in patients with hepatitis B. The presence of hepatitis B surface antigen demonstrates hepatitis B infection. E Impaired coagulation secondary to liver cirrhosis The absence of features of chronic liver disease makes this an unlikely diagnosis and it also would not explain neurological features. A Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura This diagnosis most often presents with bruising, petechiae and epistaxis and is usually seen in children. It would not explain the proteinuria as well. B Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP) The purpuric rash of Henoch–Schönlein is usually present in lower extremities and buttocks. Renal involvement can be seen in HSP, but not the signs of mononeuritis multiplex. D Kaposi’s sarcoma This diagnosis is extremely unlikely without HIV and would not explain the neurological features.

stem: A 32-year-old patient presented with a 2-day history of progressive deterioration in his visual acuity and loss of colour vision. He had no ocular pain. Six weeks previously, he was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and HIV. He was taking quadruple antituberculous therapy and antiretroviral therapy. On examination, bilateral fundoscopy was unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values CD4 count at diagnosis 146 × 106/l 430 - 1690 × 106/l CD4 count at presentation 302 × 106/l 430 - 1690 × 106/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Ethambutol toxicity This patient will be receiving ethambutol as standard ﬁrst-line treatment for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect of this medication. It should be stopped immediately, and the patient should be referred to ophthalmology as an emergency. It is common for fundoscopy to be normal in the early stages of neuropathy. D Rifampicin toxicity This patient will probably be taking rifampicin for tuberculosis, but his signs and symptoms are consistent with an optic neuropathy, which is not a side effect of rifampicin (major side effects of rifampicin are turning secretions orange and acting as an enzyme inducer). Instead ethambutol is the likely culprit: he will be taking this as part of ﬁrst-line therapy for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect. A Cytomegalovirus retinitis Although this can present with loss of visual acuity, it would be unusual for it to affect colour vision so early in its presentation. Furthermore, you might expect to see signs of retinal inﬂammation on fundoscopy, which is normal here. Lastly, this patient’s CD4 count is improving and he is on effective retroviral treatment, and therefore opportunistic infection with cytomegalovirus is less likely. Instead, this patient’s symptoms are much more likely to be caused by optic nerve toxicity, a known side effect of ethambutol: ethambutol is standard ﬁrst- line therapy for tuberculosis. C Retinal vein thrombosis This typically presents with unilateral blurred vision, but loss of colour vision would be unusual: this implies optic nerve pathology. Furthermore, if this were retinal vein occlusion, you would expect to see signs on fundoscopy, which is normal here. Instead, this patient is likely to be suffering from ethambutol toxicity. Ethambutol is standard ﬁrst-line therapy for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect. E Toxoplasmosis Ocular toxoplasmosis typically presents as a blurring of the vision; however, it would be unusual for it to cause loss of colour vision as this implies involvement of the optic nerve. Furthermore, you might expect to see retinal scarring if this were toxoplasmosis. This patient may be immunosuppressed, but not signiﬁcantly so: his CD4 count has improved and he is on effective antiretroviral medication. Instead, this patient’s optic neuropathy is much more likely to be caused by ethambutol toxicity. He will be taking ethambutol as a ﬁrst-line therapy for tuberculosis, and optic neuropathy is a known side effect.

stem: A 24-year-old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant is admitted to the Emergency Department with ﬂu-like symptoms, diarrhoea and an increasingly severe headache over the last 48 hours. Apparently she has been careful with her diet but attended a wedding where a number of canapés were served approximately four days earlier. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, she is pyrexial at 38.2 °C; blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg, and pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft, although there is some left-sided abdominal tenderness. She is drowsy with clear signs of meningism, although there is no focal neurological deﬁcit. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 12.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 145 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Glucose 6.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) glucose 2.9 mmol/l 2.5–3.9 mmol/l (two-thirds plasma value) CSF protein 1.8 g/l < 0.45 g/l CSF: Gram positive bacilli, mixed neutrophils and lymphocytes seen. Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: A Amoxicillin Gram-positive bacilli associated with symptoms of meningism in a pregnant woman are suggestive of Listeria infection. It is likely that infection occurred at the wedding party and is consistent with the incubation period for Listeria which may be anything from three to 70 days in duration. The drug of choice is amoxicillin, which is used in combination with gentamicin, except in pregnant women where it is used as monotherapy. In those who are penicillinallergic, erythromycin is the drug of choice. At least three weeks of therapy are usually indicated for meningitis. C Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin, like all quinolones, is contraindicated in pregnancy. Resistance to quinolones is increasing, with the large plasmid pLM80 thought to be responsible for conferring more rapid emergence of resistant strains. B Cefuroxime Unfortunately Listeria are naturally resistant to a range of modern cephalosporins, including cefuroxime. This is therefore an inappropriate option. D Co-trimoxazole Co-trimoxazole may be effective in some strains of Listeria, but minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing suggests that it is at least four times less effective than amoxicillin/ampicillin at treating the infection. E Erythromycin Erythromycin is the intervention of choice in patients who are allergic to penicillin. There is no documented penicillin allergy here.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a history of intravenous (IV) drug use is admitted feeling generally unwell. She has a fever, arthralgia and a rash, and has been deteriorating with increasing tiredness over the past six weeks. She admits to having run out of injection sites and is currently using areas around her groin and in her feet. Her blood pressure (BP) is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular, her temperature is 37.8 °C. On examination, she has a soft systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Values Electrocardiogram Sinus tachycardia Hb 102 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.2 × 109/l 4.0 – 11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 474 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 15.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urine microscopy Red cell casts ESR 32 mm/h 1- 20 mm/h C-reactive protein 64 mg/l < 10 mg/l Complement C3 20 mg/dl 65 - 190 mg/dl Complement C4 3 mg/dl 15 - 50 mg/dl Renal biopsy Focal segmental proliferative glomerulonephritis Which one of the following is an appropriate next investigation?
options: Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax and abdomen
explanation:
E Serial blood cultures This patient has hypocomplementaemia and glomerulonephritis with features in the history and examination suggesting infective endocarditis as the aetiology. The blood results suggest an underlying infection with the raised white cell count and C-reactive protein. The ESR, an indicator for inﬂammation, is also raised. Serial blood cultures from different sites and an echocardiogram are the next investigations of choice. She should be managed with intravenous (iv) ﬂucloxacillin and gentamicin and there is no need to wait for investigations before commencing therapy. B Anticardiolipin antibodies Anticardiolipin antibodies are antibodies often directed against

cardiolipin and found in syphilis, antiphospholipid syndrome, livedoid vasculitis, Behçet syndrome, idiopathic spontaneous abortion and SLE. This patient does not have systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) given the clinical scenario and anti-double- stranded DNA antibody (anti-dsDNA) is negative. A Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies The anti-double-stranded DNA antibody (anti-dsDNA) is a speciﬁc type of ANA antibody found in about 30% of people with systemic lupus. Less than 1% of healthy individuals have this antibody, making it helpful in conﬁrming a diagnosis of systemic lupus. SLE is associated with complement activation, and the low complement levels would ﬁt with the diagnosis, although bacterial endocarditis should be ruled out ﬁrst. C Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax and abdomen A CT may identify any malignancy or abnormal masses but it is not useful in infective endocarditis. D Rheumatoid factor Rheumatoid factor is the autoantibody that was ﬁrst found in rheumatoid arthritis. It is deﬁned as an antibody against the Fc portion of IgG and different rheumatoid factors can recognise different parts of the IgG-Fc. Although it is found in rheumatoid arthritis, it is not present in every patient. This test would not be useful in infective endocarditis.

stem: A 27-year-old man presented to clinic for review. He had been diagnosed with HIV 2 weeks previously and was due to be started on antiretroviral therapy at this clinic visit. He complained of some fatigue and severe headache. He had no past medical history. On examination he had a low-grade fever at 37.7°C. He had some purpuric lesions on his lower limbs. The remainder of the examination was normal. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 95 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 3.0 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 11 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l What is the most important test to do next?
explanation:
D Renal function This patient’s anaemia and thrombocytopenia could be caused by thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which is associated with HIV. However, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is also associated with HIV: this tends to improve either over time or with treatment of the HIV. In contrast, TTP requires immediate management and can be life-threatening. In order to decide whether this is HIV-associated ITP or TTP, evidence of clinical features of TTP must be sought: there is a pentad of associated features. This pentad includes thrombocytopenia, fever, neurological symptoms, haemolytic anaemia and renal impairment. Thus renal function would be the most appropriate test in this case. If this were TTP, treatment would be by plasmapheresis and steroids. E Ultrasound abdomen This patient has an anaemia and thrombocytopenia; an ultrasound of the abdomen will not help to diagnose the cause or decide management. The concern is whether this could be HIV-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). TTP is characterised by a pentad of fever, haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms and renal impairment: hence renal function would be the most appropriate test in this case. A Bone marrow aspiration A bone marrow aspirate can sometimes be appropriate in the context of pancytopenia; however, this patient has a normal white cell count and therefore is not pancytopenic. This patient is anaemic, but also severely thrombocytopenic in the context of a new diagnosis of HIV. HIV can be associated with both thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP): ITP typically improves as the disease progresses and with treatment, whereas TTP needs speciﬁc intervention. TTP is characterised by a pentad of fever, thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms, haemolytic anaemia and reduced renal function: therefore the most appropriate investigation would be renal function. B CD4 count The CD4 count can be useful as a marker of the level of disease control in HIV, but the problem here is that the patient has an anaemia and thrombocytopenia: the CD4 count will not help to determine the cause or management of this. In fact, HIV can be associated with both thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). TTP is a serious condition requiring immediate treatment, whereas the ITP associated with HIV tends to improve with treatment of HIV. TTP is associated with a pentad of symptoms which includes impaired renal function: hence renal function would be the most appropriate investigation in this case. C Liver function This patient has an anaemia and thrombocytopenia: liver function tests cannot aid in diagnosing the cause or deciding management.

HIV is associated with both thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Whilst TTP requires immediate deﬁnitive management, ITP in HIV tends to improve over time and with treatment of the HIV. To distinguish between the two, one must look for evidence of clinical features of TTP. One of these is renal impairment, and hence renal function would be the most appropriate investigation in this case.

stem: A 19-year-old Thai woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of malaise and shortness of breath. On examination, she has multiple enlarged cervical and axillary nodes and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 61 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 3.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.9 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 31 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Urea and electrolytes (U&Es) NAD ALP 205 IU/l 30–130 IU/l AST 80 IU/l 10–40 IU/l Bilirubin 6 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 21 g/l 35–55 g/l She is admitted and transfused three units of blood. As part of her investigation, an HIV test is done, which is positive. After the transfusion, her breathlessness is much improved and she remains stable. A bone marrow trephine and lymph node biopsy are requested. On the ward round, she mentions in passing that the vision in her right eye has been steadily deteriorating for the past 3 weeks. You perform dilated fundoscopy. Whilst the left fundus shows just exudates the below changes are found on the right. What is the best treatment for this patient?
explanation: C IV ganciclovir The optic disc appears swollen with evidence of exudates and haemorrhages covering the macula. The cause of these changes and of her impaired vision is cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. CMV retinitis is a common cause of blurred vision in immunodeﬁciency which can lead to blindness. It can be asymptomatic as well. Fundoscopy can show haemorrhagic necrosis, granular lesions or frosted branch angiitis around retinal vessels. B IV foscarnet IV foscarnet is incorrect. Either IV ganciclovir or foscarnet could be used and although trial evidence suggests marginally more rapid clearance with foscarnet versus ganciclovir, ganciclovir is still preferred under UK Guidelines as the ﬁrst treatment of choice. Foscarnet is generally the second-line therapy of choice in patients who fail to gain an adequate response to ganciclovir. A IV aciclovir IV aciclovir is incorrect. Aciclovir would not be effective against CMV but could be used against herpes simplex virus infection. D IV cidofovir IV cidofovir is incorrect. Cidofovir can be used if both ganciclovir and foscarnet are contraindicated or there is a failure to respond to one of these therapies. It is, however, the drug of choice for varicella zoster retinitis. There are very limited data comparing cidofovir with ganciclovir and foscarnet, but ganciclovir efﬁcacy is well established. Cidofovir may have a greater role in future treatment as it can be dosed less frequently with its longer half-life. E IV ribavirin IV ribavirin is incorrect. Ribavirin is an antiviral agent used to treat respiratory syncytial virus, hepatitis C virus and viral haemorrhagic fever.

stem: A 21-year-old man is brought in with fever, rash and headache. He returned from a riding trip to Utah one week ago and admits that he had probably been bitten by many different bugs when he was out there, despite using repellent. He noticed feeling hot and cold the day before leaving Utah, but put it down to a ﬂu-like illness as he had a headache, rhinorrhoea, dry cough and intermittent severe muscle pain in his lower back and legs. His fever and headache had, however, persisted and he was now concerned as he had developed a rash on his wrists and ankles which had now started to spread up his body. On examination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38.1 °C and appears slightly agitated. He has a maculopapular eruption over his arms and legs, including a rash over the palms of his hands and soles of his feet. His pulse is 60/min and heart sounds are normal. His chest is clear but he is tender in the right upper quadrant. There is no meningism and neurology is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 75 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 131 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 34 g/l 35–55 g/l Urea 5.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l ALT 101 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 34 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l CXR Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Rocky Mountain spotted fever This is a tick-borne disease caused by the organism Rickettsia rickettsii. RMSF can be lethal. Physicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for RMSF in patients who are febrile, as it is essentially a clinical diagnosis. Key aspects include history of potential tick exposure, travel to an endemic area and presentation in the spring or autumn. Patients with unexplained febrile illness, even if they have no history of a tick bite or travel to an endemic area but have rash and myalgia, should be suspected to have RMSF. Rash is a major diagnostic sign. The maculopapular rash usually appears 2–6 days after the onset of fever and progresses through stages and distribution that are never pathognomonic. The rash begins as a maculopapular eruption on the wrists and ankles, and spreads centripetally to involve the trunk and extremities. The rash involves the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Later in the illness, the

rash becomes petechial in 50% of patients. For adults, the preferred drug of choice is doxycycline. Chloramphenicol is an alternative. A Dengue fever Dengue is caused by an arbovirus transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. The incubation period is one to two weeks and the typical symptoms are fever, frontal headache, musculoskeletal pains and a widespread maculopapular rash. Laboratory ﬁndings commonly show a rising haematocrit, falling platelets and transamenitis. The clue here is the travel; cases of dengue arising in the United States are sporadic and usually associated with travel to Central and South America. An outbreak has been seen in Florida, but to date dengue is not endemic in northern Texas. B Ehrlichiosis Ehrlichiosis is an uncommon tick-borne infection caused by obligate intracellular bacteria of the genera Anaplasma and Ehrlichia. Incubation is one to two weeks and the most common symptoms are fever, headache, fatigue and myalgia. A rash may be present but is uncommon. Ehrlichiosis is clinically difﬁcult to differentiate from other febrile illnesses such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, but is much less common in the states to the Western side of the US and therefore is not the most likely diagnosis. C Lyme disease Lyme disease is an infectious illness caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi. It is transmitted through tick bites. It initially presents with a slowly expanding skin lesion around the tick bite, erythema migrans, malaise and joint aches. If not treated, neurological, cardiac and joint involvement can occur. The rash described is not consistent with acute Lyme disease. E Syphilis Syphilis is an infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, and it is most commonly acquired through sexual intercourse. Primary syphilis presents as a local painless ulcer (chancre) at the inoculation site. Secondary syphilis occurs weeks to months after the primary chancre and is typiﬁed by a widespread rash, fever, lethargy and lymphadenopathy. You might expect a question to describe risk factors for syphilis and an antecedent chancre, but in practice it may be prudent to check syphilis serology in this patient.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with an infected human bite on her left arm. She says that she was involved in a ﬁght three days ago while drunk. On examination, there is a bite affecting the left upper arm which is discharging pus, and there is a 3 cm radius of erythema around the wound. She is pyrexial (37.8 °C). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 13.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for antibiotic therapy?
explanation: C Co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav is the antibiotic therapy of choice for human bite wounds. It is crucial that beta-lactamase- producing Staphylococci are covered, and clavulanic acid makes sure of this. A standard course is the 625 mg TDS dose for a period of 5–7 days. It is also crucially important to make sure that the patient is covered for tetanus infection. Commonly isolated organisms include Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Haemophilus, Bacteroides and Eikenella corrodens. E Metronidazole Metronidazole alone does not provide adequate coverage, and should be used in combination with either a tetracycline or clarithromycin. A Amoxicillin Amoxicillin fails to cover against beta-lactamase-producing organisms and therefore cannot be used here. B Pencillin V Penicillin V only covers a limited range of mouth commensals, and doesn’t have activity against a range of anaerobes that may cause signiﬁcant wound infection. D Oxytetracycline Tetracyclines may be used as a treatment for human bites, but only in combination with metronidazole. Metronidazole and doxycycline, or metronidazole and clarithromycin, may be reasonable alternatives in penicillin-allergic patients.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department by her carers after becoming drowsy and less responsive over the past 24 hours. On waking, she complains of a headache and refuses to open her eyes. Her past medical history includes type II diabetes and severe osteoarthritis that has left her wheelchair-bound. On examination, her blood pressure is 124/77 mmHg, she has a heart rate of 95 bpm and her temperature is 38.5 °C. She is neglecting her left side, with a 3/5 power weakness. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 18.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 120 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lumbar puncture Gram-positive rods, low cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) glucose Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
B Listeria monocytogenes L. monocytogenes is a motile, non-spore-forming Gram-positive bacillus. A central nervous system (CNS) infection can manifest as meningitis and meningoencephalitis or even with symptoms of hemiparesis, mimicking a stroke. Amoxicillin is the treatment of choice for Listeria CNS infection. It is worth noting that cephalosporins, such as ceftriaxone, commonly used empirically to treat meningitis have no activity against Listeria. Therefore, if the diagnosis is suspected (eg in the elderly), amoxicillin should be included in the treatment regime. C Neisseria meningitidis N. meningitidis (meningococcus) is a Gram-negative diplococcus which is one of the most common causes of bacterial meningitis in the United Kingdom. Symptoms are typically fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting, with or without a nonblanching rash. Treatment is with intravenous ceftriaxone. In this case, the risk factors, presentation and CSF ﬁndings point to an alternative diagnosis. A Klebsiella pneumoniae

Klebsiella is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria. It is a commensal of the human gut and most commonly causes intra-abdominal or urinary tract infections. A CNS infection is very uncommon outside of neonates and neurosurgery patients. D Pseudomonas aeruginosa P. aeruginosa is a Gram-negative bacterium that is intrinsically quite antibiotic-resistant. A CNS infection is very uncommon. E Streptococcus pneumoniae S. pneumoniae is another very common cause of meningitis in the United Kingdom. However, this bacterium is a Gram-positive diplococcus, making it an unlikely organism for this patient.

stem: A 39-year-old sheep farmer presents to the Emergency Department with jaundice, fevers and right upper quadrant pain, which has developed over the past 24 hours. He also has diarrhoea and feels that he is passing much smaller amounts of dark urine compared to his normal toilet habits. He tells you that he has been clearing dead wood out of some ﬂooded hedges over the past few days. Examination reveals a temperature of 38.9 °C and his blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg; pulse is 95 bpm. He is jaundiced. Abdominal palpation reveals marked right upper quadrant tenderness. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 91 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 95 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 201 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l INR 1.8 < 1.1 Glucose 5.1 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l ALT 450 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 320 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 88 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Urine Blood ++, Protein ++ Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
explanation: A Intravenous (IV) benzylpenicillin The diagnosis here is that of leptospirosis, as evidenced by the patient’s occupation presumably putting him at risk of infection from animal urine, fever, jaundice and renal impairment (Weil’s disease). Amoxicillin, doxycycline and macrolides are appropriate treatments for mild to moderate leptospirosis; however, the patient is clinically on the severe end of the condition and therefore IV antibiotics are the appropriate choice. Other supportive measures should be considered, including correction of clotting abnormalities. The role of steroids has not been fully established in leptospirosis; however, they may reduce the risk of vasculitic complications such as pulmonary haemorrhage and acute renal failure. B IV ciproﬂoxacin Although this patient is on the severe end of the condition and requires IV antibiotics, IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are the appropriate ﬁrst choices for severe leptospirosis treatment. Another supportive measure should be to consider including correction of clotting abnormalities. The role of steroids has not been fully established in leptospirosis; however, they may reduce the risk of vasculitic complications like pulmonary haemorrhage and acute renal failure. C Oral amoxicillin This patient is on the severe end of the spectrum of leptospirosis and therefore requires intravenous antibiotics. IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are ﬁrst choice for treatment. Mild to moderate forms of the condition can be treated with oral amoxicillin or doxycycline. A Oral clarithromycin Oral Clarithromycin is the incorrect answer. Macrolides, such as clarithromycin or azithromycin, can be used in mild to moderate disease. This patient has severe disease and should be treated with IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins. B Oral doxycycline Although doxycycline is sensitive to leptospirosis, it is only indicated in mild to moderate forms of the infection. This patient is systemically unwell with features of sepsis and therefore requires IV antibiotics. IV benzylpenicillin or IV cephalosporins are ﬁrst choice for treatment.

stem: A 40-year-old man presented to clinic with a 2-week history of fever, myalgia and lethargy. He also complained of mouth ulcers. Two months ago he had visited friends and relatives in South Africa. He had no medical conditions. He admits to unprotected sexual intercourse during his holiday. He has no medical conditions. On examination, his temperature was 37.6ºC. He had cervical lymphadenopathy but no hepatosplenomegaly. There were aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 136 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.2 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.9 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 96 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Bilirubin 26 mmol/l 1.7 - 20.5 mmol/l ALT 72 u/l 7 - 55 u/l Blood ﬁlm Atypical reactive lymphocytes HIV antibodies - What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D HIV infection This patient has recently returned from travelling in an area with a high HIV prevalence, and has a ﬂu-like illness with lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes on a blood ﬁlm, a mild transaminitis and fever. HIV antibodies can be negative if the patient is currently seroconverting; a better diagnostic test would be either HIV RNA PCR or p24 antigen. C Hepatitis C Hepatitis C may cause malaise, fever and liver dysfunction. However, liver function tests would likely be more markedly abnormal in symptomatic hepatitis C, and hepatitis C would not explain the lymphadenopathy or atypical lymphocytes seen in this patient. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion. HIV antibodies can be negative during seroconversion, and therefore a better diagnostic test would be either p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR. A Cytomegalovirus infection In the immunocompetent, cytomegalovirus infection is typically asymptomatic or may cause a mild, ﬂu-like illness. In the immunosuppressed, cytomegalovirus can cause pneumonia, retinitis or, most commonly, diarrhoea or colitis. This patient’s fever, lymphadenopathy and liver dysfunction are best explained by HIV seroconversion. HIV antibodies may be negative during seroconversion: a p24 antigen test or HIV RNA PCR would be better suited to diagnosis. B Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B could cause malaise and liver dysfunction, but you might expect liver function tests to be more markedly abnormal if this were hepatitis B. Furthermore, hepatitis B would not explain the lymphadenopathy or atypical lymphocytes seen here. This patient’s presentation would ﬁt with HIV seroconversion; HIV antibodies may be negative during seroconversion. A better diagnostic test would be either a p24 antigen test or HIV RNA PCR. E Malaria Malaria is an important cause of fever in the returning traveller and should always be a differential diagnosis; however, malaria does not explain the lymphadenopathy or atypical lymphocytes seen in this case. This picture of malaise, a relative lymphopenia, transaminitis and lymphadenopathy is more suggestive of HIV. As the patient is seroconverting, HIV antibodies can be negative. A better test would have been either p24 antigen or HIV RNA PCR.

stem: A 19-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 10-day history of fevers. He had returned from a 1-month holiday in Peru 1 week previously. Before travelling to Peru, he had received hepatitis A and typhoid vaccinations. He took malaria prophylaxis regularly while on holiday but had stopped it 5 days before returning, as he lost his tablets. On examination, his temperature was 39 °C, with a pulse of 56 bpm. His chest is shown below and there was also cervical lymphadenopathy. Urine dipstick was positive for leukocytes. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 124 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 340 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l CRP 440 mg/l < 10 mg/l Creatinine (Cr) 97 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Urea 6.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Blood cultures Gram-negative rods in two out of three bottles Thin malaria ﬁlms Three separate samples are negative CXR Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Salmonella typhi infection A high fever in a returning traveller should prompt you to think of two conditions: malaria and typhoid. S. typhi causes typhoid fever, which is a major differential diagnosis in a returning traveller with high fever. Typically, S. typhi has an incubation period of 10–14 days, followed by a prodrome of ﬂu-like symptoms. In the ﬁrst week, patients have a high fever, with a relative bradycardia (as seen here). Next, they develop small salmon-pink maculopapules, termed rose spots, as here. In conjunction with these changes lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly occur. Following this, complications may develop (pneumonia, endocarditis, haemolytic anaemia, meningitis, acute cholecystitis, osteomyelitis). Although the patient had been vaccinated, vaccines are unfortunately only between 30% and 70% effective. Empirical treatment of hospitalised patients is with ceftriaxone. Relapse is common, and the organism can persist in the gall bladder. A Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection In immunocompetent individuals, CMV infection is usually asymptomatic. It can cause a ﬂu-like illness, which may be complicated by Guillain–Barré syndrome or Bell’s palsy. By the age of 60, around 80% of patients have been exposed to CMV, and it can be problematic if a patient later becomes immunosuppressed, for example, after transplantation or in human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV)-infected patients. In such patients, it can cause colitis, severe retinitis, oesophagitis and central nervous

system (CNS) disease. Treatment would be with ganciclovir. As this patient is not immunocompromised, the presentation does not ﬁt with CMV, since it does not cause prolonged fevers or rashes in the immunocompetent. B Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection Primary EBV causes glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) in around 50% of infected illness. This primary infection does cause a maculopapular rash (though not typically a salmon-pink rash), but it would be unusual for EBV infection to cause such a high fever, as seen in this patient. The positive blood cultures also count against EBV infection being the diagnosis. EBV is associated with Burkitt’s lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and oral hair leukoplakia. C Plasmodium falciparum malaria Malaria is among the top important differential diagnoses in the returning traveller with prolonged fever; however, this patient has had three negative ﬁlms, which rules out malaria. The incubation period of malaria does vary between species but tends to be at least 12 days, which would make it highly unlikely, given her prophylaxis covered this period. E Schistosomiasis Schistosomiasis is a trematode infection, particularly associated with freshwater lakes in Africa and the Middle East. Acute infection is usually with cercarial dermatitis (swimmer’s itch), which causes a self-limiting, itchy papular rash within 24 hours of exposure. Katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis) is less common and develops 4–8 weeks post-exposure and presents with fever, urticaria, eosinophilia and wheeze. This patient’s presentation does not ﬁt with the incubation period of swimmer’s itch and does not have the features of acute schistosomiasis. Treatment of acute schistosomiasis would be with praziquantel and steroids.
