stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the GP some 6 weeks after returning from a holiday to Thailand with a maculopapular rash. He denies sexual intercourse during the course of his holiday. During his holiday, he went trekking through the jungle. The only thing he remembers is a very odd single lesion that looked like a large, warty lump on his arm which formed during his holiday and then healed up. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 120 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 234 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l P24 Negative TPHA Positive Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Yaws infection Yaws is endemic in tropical areas of America, Asia, Africa and Oceania and is caused by Treponema pertenue. Early lesions may almost look papillomatous, and as well as direct skin to skin contact, the organism may be carried by biting insects. The TPHA is positive for both yaws and syphilis. Penicillin is the drug of choice for treatment. D Tungiasis Tungiasis is a skin condition caused by Tunga penetrans, also called sand ﬂea. It is endemic in Africa, India, and South and Central America. It causes a black dot at the site of infection with a swollen red lesions surrounded by a white halo. It is very painful and itchy. It is always associated with desquamation. The absence of this and the fact that the patient has not travelled to an endemic area makes this diagnosis unlikely. A HIV infection This patient does not have any direct history of possible exposure nor does he have any evidence of multiple opportunistic infection. The negative P24 test excludes HIV infection as well. B Syphillis infection The warty lesion described does not correspond to a syphilitic lesion. There is also no history corresponding to primary syphilis with nonpainful ulcerating genital or anal lesions. The TPHA is positive in any Treponema species, meaning that it lacks speciﬁcity for syphilis. In addition, TPHA remains positive for life following infection at any point. E Leishmaniasis Leishmania are protozoa spread by sandﬂies in Africa, Asia, India, Middle East, the Mediterranean and Latin America causing

granulomata. Cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions develop at the site of the bite starting as an itchy papule which crusts to form an ulcer healing over 2-15 months. Visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, has an incubation period of months to years. It spreads to the lymphatic system and multiply in macrophages, presenting with dry, warty, hyperpigmented lesiosn whilst the patient complains of fever, burning feet, arthralgia, cough, epistaxis. Splenomegaly occurs in 96% and hepatomegaly in 63%. Diagnosis with microscopy of lymph nodes, spleen or bone marrow, or antibody detection. Treatment is with amphotericin. This patient does have a warty lesions but the fact that it healed rather than forming an ulcer makes cutaneous leishmanisasis unlikely and the absence of systemic features makes visceral leishmaniasis unlikely as well.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the Sexual Health Clinic for review. She is ﬁve months’ pregnant and has had dysuria and vague lower abdominal pain for the past few days. There has been a recent split with her partner after he admitted to an affair. On examination, her temperature is 37.8 °C, her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg, and her abdomen is consistent with a 20-week pregnancy. Chlamydia testing is positive and urine growth is negative for pathogens known to cause urinary tract infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
B Azithromycin PO Azithromycin has the twin advantages of being a safe option in pregnancy and being a single 1 g dose. It is recommended as the pragmatic option in pregnancy for chlamydia by the SIGN guidelines. Latency and reactivation are rarely seen in pregnancy; therefore, a test of cure is usual, some six weeks after azithromycin treatment. D Doxycycline PO While a 7-day course of doxycycline would be a reasonable ﬁrstline option in uncomplicated chlamydia infection, this patient is pregnant. It is therefore contraindicated due to the risk of suppression of fetal bone growth and teeth staining. A Amoxicillin PO While amoxycillin is safe in pregnancy and is a recommended

treatment when given for seven days, it has the potential to induce latency and re-emergence of infection. Therefore, azithromycin is the ﬁrst-line agent here. C Benzylpenicillin IM Benzylpenicillin IM would be a treatment of syphilis, which is not suggested by the presenting symptoms, rather than chlamydia. E Oﬂoxacin PO Oﬂoxacin is a second-line option in chlamydia infection. While it is not strictly contraindicated in pregnancy, like doxycycline, it should be avoided due to the risk of arthropathy in animal models. As there is a ﬁrst-line agent, azithromycin, which is able to be given here, oﬂoxacin is not indicated.

stem: A 23-year-old Burmese man presents to Gastroenterology Clinic. He has lived in the UK for 8 months and works in a nightclub. He is complaining of severe persistent diarrhoea for the past month, ever since he took a trip back home to Burma where his family live in a small village. He has lost 15 kg; he denies fever or night sweats. The diarrhoea is watery with no blood or mucus. There is some associated abdominal discomfort and he feels nauseated but has not vomited. He has noticed a rash over his trunk which seems to be more obvious at some times more than others. On examination, he is slim but looks well, pulse 90 bpm; BP 135/72 mmHg; afebrile. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no organomegaly; the rest of the clinical examination is unremarkable. The GP has performed some tests: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 75 fl 80 - 100 fl WCC 6.5 × 10 /l 4.0 - 11.0 × 10 /l Eosinophils 2.5 × 10 /l 0.04 - 0.4 × 10 /l Lymphocytes 1.0 × 10 /l 1.5 - 4.0 × 10 /l Neutrophils 2.6 × 10 /l 1.5 - 7.0 × 10 /l For renal function: Investigation Result Normal values Sodium (Na ) 134 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.1 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l For liver function: Investigation Result Normal values Bilirubin 22 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l ALT 32 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 101 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Albumin 30 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Amylase 95 u/l 23 - 85 u/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 35 mg/l < 10 mg/l Stool microscopy & culture – No growth. The GP had previously prescribed a week’s course of ciproﬂoxacin which has made very little difference to the patient’s symptoms. On further testing, he is found to be both HIV positive and have positive serology for strongyloides. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for strongyloides?
explanation:
C Ivermectin Strongyloides is a nematode endemic in the sub-tropics. Transmission occurs via direct skin exposure followed by cutaneous larva currens seen as migrating urticarial on the legs and trunk. It can cause enteritis, malabsorption and pneumonitis. In the wake of the

nematodes, bacteria infection can follow, which can cause septicaemia and meningitis. Treatment is usually with ivermectin for 48 hours. A Mebendazole Mebendazole would be the correct threadworm or whipworm but these infections do not cause this level of infection. B Albendazole This antiprotozoal can be considered in patients with AIDS and strongyloides hyperinfestation. Whilst there is positive HIV serology, there is no CD4 count or AIDS-deﬁning illnesses at this point and therefore there is no clear diagnosis of AIDS. It is the standard second line agent in the UK. D Thiabendazole Thiabendazole is an older anthelminthic therapy. Side effects have limited its use, although a topical suspension of thiabendazole can be used for cutaneous larva migrans. D IV gentamicin This treatment is not used in the treatment of nematodes and is more suited to bacterial infections.

stem: A 26-year-old woman, who is 4 weeks post-partum, comes to the Emergency Department. She had an uneventful pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery requiring episiotomy. She presents now feeling extremely ill, with a purpuric rash and a fever. On examination, she has a pyrexia of 38.5 °C, a BP of 95/60 mmHg, and a pulse of 105 bpm regular. She has lower abdominal tenderness on palpation and you notice erythema around her episiotomy site. She is wearing a pad and you notice some foul-smelling, blood stained, yellow discharge on the pad. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 111 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 13.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 132 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
explanation: A High vaginal swab The patient likely has endometritis. Symptoms of endometritis include fever, foul smelling vaginal discharge, and erythema or discharge around a wound site if present. A late presentation is not unusual, given that patients may assume their feeling unwell is just a slow recovery from labour. Studies suggest that empirical treatment covering penicillin resistant anaerobes appears most effective at treating endometritis. According to Cochrane reviews, a regime containing gentamicin and clindamycin appears to be the most efﬁcient combination. Unfortunately over the longer term, adhesions and scarring post infection may lead to problems with future fertility. A high vaginal swab would be particularly useful on this occasion in targeting appropriate antibiotic therapy. D Urine culture This is unlikely to be a urine infection as there is a clear gynaecological source of infection and urine testing may be misleading as samples can easily be contaminated. A Ultrasound scan abdomen Whilst an ultrasound may be helpful, it is not the most important investigation in the acute setting. If the patient does not improve with treatment or there are concerns about abscess formation or deeper infection, then an ultrasound can be helpful. B Blood cultures Whilst blood cultures should be taken as the patient is septic, they are not the most important investigation as blood cultures are unlikely have as high a diagnostic sensitivity as direct swabbing. E Wound swab The site of episiotomy is likely to be contaminated with dermal ﬂora and therefore may not be as useful as a high vaginal swab.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the Dermatologist with complaints of a rash over his face, neck and upper back for the past three weeks. He also complains of intense pruritus, further adding that he is unable to sleep at night because of the pruritus. There is a history of intravenous (IV) drug abuse. On examination, his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 74 bpm. He appears emaciated and there are multiple needletrack marks present near the cubital fossa. There are multiple papulopustular lesions present over the face, neck and upper back. Oral examination reveals the presence of a whitish membrane suggestive of oral candidiasis. Which of the following will cause regression of this patient’s skin lesions?
explanation: A Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) This patient’s rash is typical of eosinophilic folliculitis. In this patient with multiple risk factors for human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) infection, the diagnosis is eosinophilic folliculitis secondary to HIV infection. It occurs in patients with a CD4 cell count < 250/mm3. With highly active antiretroviral therapy, the lesions resolve when CD4 cell counts improve to > 250/mm3. E Topical retinoid and oral doxycycline This would be appropriate in a patient with acne, which is a differential diagnosis for eosinophilic folliculitis due to the similar distribution of skin lesions. However, the presence of intense pruritus and the absence of comedones are features that differentiate eosinophilic folliculitis from acne vulgaris. A Indomethacin Idiopathic eosinophilic folliculitis (Ofuji’s disease) usually responds to indomethacin. However, in this patient, HIV infection is likely. B Oral ﬂuconazole Oral ﬂuconazole may be helpful in the management of oral candidiasis which occurs commonly in patients with HIV infection. However, it will not cause regression of the skin lesions. C Permethrin cream Permethrin cream may be used in the treatment of scabies which involves the interdigital regions. It is not recommended for the treatment of eosinophilic folliculitis.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with diarrhoea, which also contains blood and pus. He admits to unprotected anal sex some 2–3 weeks earlier. On examination, he is apyrexial, and there are no abnormal ﬁndings apart from tenderness on rectal examination. Investigations: Hb 131 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l PLT 210 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 130 µmol/l Which of the following is the most important next step?
explanation: C Nucleic acid ampliﬁcation test (NAAT) swab The suspicion here is that this patient has developed rectal gonococcus infection due to his unprotected anal sex. The investigation of choice when collecting rectal specimens is a NAAT swab, which is useful if gonococcus or chlamydia is suspected. Prior to treatment he should be screened for other sexually transmitted infections including HIV, and if he knows the partner with whom he had anal intercourse, that individual should also be screened. A Rectal biopsy This patient presents with a short history of bloody diarrhoea. Given his risk factors, it is likely that a less invasive test will yield the diagnosis. Of course should his symptoms persist without explanation, a rectal biopsy may be warranted at a later stage. B Colonoscopy This patient presents with a short history of bloody diarrhoea. Given his risk factors, it is likely that a less invasive test will yield the diagnosis. Of course should his symptoms persist without explanation, a colonoscopy may be warranted at a later stage. D Stool culture The patient presents with a short history of diarrhoea with blood. Given his risk factors, there is a high suspicion of gonococcal proctitis. Gonococcus is notoriously difﬁcult to culture in the laboratory, requiring speciﬁc set-up, and therefore would not be identiﬁed on standard culture. E Trial of antibiotics In this patient it would not be appropriate to give empirical antibiotics, as treatment choices are dependent on the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 36-year-old man with known HIV is admitted with increasing shortness of breath. He is on antiretroviral medications. On examination, he has raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), bilateral lower limb oedema and crackles on both bases. BP is 105/60 mmHg, pulse 95/min. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 114 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 156 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CD4 count 235 cells/mm3 500–1500 cells/mm3 ECHO Severe dilated cardiomyopathy Ejection fraction 24% His chest X-ray is shown below What is the most likely cause of his problem?
explanation:
D Zidovudine Zidovudine (AZT) is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor and was the ﬁrst drug licensed for treatment of HIV. It has signiﬁcant mitochondrial toxicity and is known to be associated with dilated

cardiomyopathy. The CXR shows evidence of left ventricular overload with pleural effusions, bilateral interstitial changes and prominent upper lobe diversion. In patients such as this, myocardial biopsy usually reveals mitochondria full of myelin, a sign of mitochondrial dysfunction. Withdrawal of zidovudine and substitution with an agent associated with less mitochondrial toxicity, coupled with appropriate treatment for heart failure with diuretics and ACE inhibition, usually resolves the problem, although HIV itself is decreasingly recognised as a cause of cardiomyopathy. E Ritonavir Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor now used at low dose in combination with other protease inhibitors to boost their potency. Serious side effects include hepatitis, pancreatitis and arrhythmia. Its use is not associated with myocarditis. A Cytomegalovirus Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a member of the herpes virus family (HHV 5). It typically causes a glandular fever syndrome, but presentation is varied and in the immunocompromised host disease can be severe. CMV can cause a cardiomyopathy, but this is rare and an alternative explanation is more probable in our patient. B Toxoplasmosis Toxoplasmosis is caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. Acute infection may result in a ﬂu-like illness, but is more commonly asymptomatic. In the immunocompromised it may cause an encephalitis. The presentation described does not ﬁt with toxoplasmosis. C Inﬂuenza Inﬂuenza is a virus responsible for ﬂu. Infection is characterised by upper respiratory symptoms, as well as fever and muscle aches. Myocarditis is a possible but uncommon sequalae of inﬂuenza infection. In the patient described above, an alternative diagnosis is more likely.

stem: A 44-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of watery diarrhoea. He had returned from France the previous day. On examination his temperature was 37.3°C, blood pressure 134/76 mmHg and pulse rate 88 bpm. His abdomen was soft, with epigastric tenderness. He did not have any rashes. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 142 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 11.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 108 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 9.1 mmol/l (2.5– 7.0) 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 9.0 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALT 27 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 72 u/l 30 - 150 u/l GGT 31 u/l < 50 u/l What is the most likely cause of his diarrhoea?
explanation:
B Escherichia coli This is by far the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea and typically causes a watery diarrhoea that is self-limiting, with little systemic upset, as seen here. C Giardiasis Giardia is a parasite and is a very common cause of diarrhoea in the returning traveller. However, it typically causes steatorrhoea, not watery diarrhoea, and it also causes belching and ﬂatulence, which are not reported here. The most common cause of watery diarrhoea in the returning traveller is E. coli, which is the answer in this case. A Amoebiasis Amoebiasis typically causes dysentery, not watery diarrhoea (although in early amoebiasis, diarrhoea may be watery. Amoebiasis can cause liver dysfunction and abscesses, but this patient has normal liver enzymes. However, most importantly, amoebiasis is very uncommon. E. coli is the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea, and therefore is the correct answer here. D Salmonella typhi Salmonella typhi causes bloody diarrhoea, which is not seen in this case, and it is the organism responsible for typhoid fever. Patients with typhoid fever have very high fevers, headache and often constipation. They are systemically unwell and may have a salmonpink maculopapular rash. These features are not present in this patient, who is much more likely to have E. coli, the most common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea.

E Shigella spp. Shigella spp. typically cause a bloody diarrhoea, rather than the watery diarrhoea that this patient reports. Furthermore, E. coli is the most common cause of diarrhoea in returning travellers, and therefore this is the correct answer in this case.

stem: An HIV-positive man has a CD4 count of 220 × 106/l. He is generally asymptomatic but has noticed white patches in his mouth. They are quite unsightly and he is keen for treatment. On examination, you observe irregular white patches, with a corrugated appearance along the side of his tongue. On probing with a swab, they cannot be dislodged. What is the best way to eradicate these patches?
explanation:
C Antiretroviral therapy The diagnosis is oral hairy leukoplakia, which is an AIDs-deﬁning illness but can occur in other cases or immunosuppression. The clinical picture is described above and it is often mistaken for oral candida, the only difference being that plaques of leucoplakia cannot be dislodged. The condition is caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and it only needs to be treated if it is causing symptoms such as pain or dysphagia. The best treatment is to commence antiretroviral therapy, as the CD4 count rises, it will resolve. Other treatment options are high- dose aciclovir (3 g/day) and it may respond to other antivirals. Surgery is also an option. E Improve oral hygiene This would be the correct treatment for gingivitis. Gingivitis is inﬂammation of the gum and usually presents with gums that bleed easily. A Oral ﬂuconazole It would be a treatment option if the history and examination suggested oral candida. The clinical picture would be very similar except that oral candida can be rubbed off while leukoplakia cannot. B Nystatin lozenges This is another treatment option for oral candida, which is not the most likely diagnosis.

D Aciclovir 200 mg 5× daily This would be the correct treatment for herpes simplex viral sores. Oral lesions can appear as ulcers ﬁlled with yellow slough or cold sores. These are typically painful as well. As the clinical description does not match, this is not the right treatment option.

stem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She complains of paroxysms of coughing that are so severe that she is exhausted afterwards and sometimes vomits as a reaction to the coughing. She has little contact with medical facilities and spends most of her time helping look after younger siblings. Her symptoms have been continuing for around the past four weeks, and right at the beginning of her illness, around six weeks ago, she had what she thought was a heavy cold. Physical examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 123 g/l 115 - 160 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 274 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 37 mg/l < 10 mg/l What would be the most useful test to perform for this patient?
explanation:
E Serology testing Key features which drive us towards a diagnosis of Whooping Cough related to Bordetella pertussis (B pertussis) infection include: the typical history of cold symptoms which last for approximately two weeks followed by paroxysms of coughing, she is also less likely to have engaged with vaccination services. Given her age and stage of infection, serology is the most appropriate next step in conﬁrming the likely diagnosis. At this stage of her disease antibiotics have no value in shortening the duration of symptoms. Her coughing symptoms will improve over the course of a few weeks. D Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) There is no indication for PCR testing here. PCR testing is used to

test for B pertussis infection in severely ill, hospitalised infants. A nasopharyngeal swab would be used to collect material for PCR testing in these cases. A Induced sputum culture Induced sputum culture is primarily used in the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis, where patients struggle to produce sputum themselves. The patient inhales hypertonic saline which liqueﬁes secretions and promotes coughing so a specimen can be collected. The symptoms here are much more consistent with a diagnosis of B pertussis (Whooping Cough), which at this stage in an adult is best conﬁrmed by serology testing. B Nasopharyngeal swab culture Nasopharyngeal swab testing is most sensitive for the diagnosis of Whooping Cough when performed in the ﬁrst two weeks of symptoms. It is also more sensitive for detecting infection in younger individuals. In this patient (who is 18 years old) serology testing is likely to be most useful. C Oral ﬂuid testing Oral ﬂuid testing is recommended in people aged 5-16 who have had a cough with features of whooping cough for more than two weeks. They should not have received a vaccine in the preceding year. This test for anti- pertussis toxin immunoglobulin G (IgG) is conducted when a blood sample cannot be collected. In adults, serological testing via a blood test would be more appropriate.

stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the Respiratory Ward with a 1week history of persistent fever, dry cough and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a past medical history of acute myeloid leukaemia, for which he is currently receiving chemotherapy. His temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate 110 bpm and BP 120/65 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 93% on room air.
options: CT-guided needle aspiration for tissue biopsy
explanation:
D Serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen

This patient has a likely diagnosis of aspergillosis, given the history of fever, pleuritic chest pain and dry cough in an immunocompromised patient. The CT ﬁndings of bilateral inﬁltrates and a pulmonary nodule, with a positive halo sign, are also indicative of the condition. Serum galactomannan antigen testing is a noninvasive diagnostic test with high sensitivity and speciﬁcity for invasive aspergillosis, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Therefore, it is the most appropriate investigation to consider in the next step of the management of this patient. E Sputum smear Although a sputum smear can be used in the diagnosis of aspergillosis, with a positive sample showing hyphae, sputum production is uncommon with the condition, making it a less useful investigation than serum galactomannan antigen testing. A Bronchoalveolar lavage for fungal cultures A bronchoscopy can be performed with BAL for respiratory ﬂuid, which can be used for fungal testing. In patients with aspergillosis, the BAL ﬂuid may be positive for hyphae. However, the yield of BAL ﬂuid is low, and the procedure itself is invasive and carries risks, particularly in more unwell patients. B CT-guided needle aspiration for tissue biopsy The most deﬁnitive investigation is tissue biopsy. However, this procedure is invasive and carries risks such as bleeding and postprocedure pneumothorax. Instead, alternative investigations, such as serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen testing, which are noninvasive should be utilised. A PCR for Aspergillus DNA PCR testing of respiratory specimens for Aspergillus DNA may be used as an adjunctive diagnostic test. However, it is not the primary diagnostic test for invasive aspergillosis.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is seen in the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic with a 1-week history of lower abdominal pain and deep dyspareunia. She denies lower urinary tract symptoms but has noticed an occasional creamy vaginal discharge. There is no past medical history of note. She had the Mirena® coil intrauterine system (IUS) inserted three months ago and takes no regular medications. She has no allergies. On examination, her temperature is 37.8 °C. Her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 131/83 mmHg. Chest sounds are clear, with saturations of 98% on room air and heart sounds are normal. She has lower abdominal tenderness and is guarding in the left iliac fossa. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Bimanual examination elicits bilateral adnexal tenderness. Swabs are taken. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 134 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 16.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 12.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 3.4 × 109/l 0.8–5.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 233 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.2 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 115 µm/l 50–120 µm/l EGFR 60+ CRP 299 mg/l < 10 mg/l (HCG) 3 mIU/ml < 5 mIU/ml Progesterone 5 ng/ml 5–20 ng/ml Urinalysis: +++ leucocytes What is the most likely causative organism contributing to this patient’s diagnosis?
explanation:
B Chlamydia trachomatis This patient has pelvic inﬂammatory disease. The symptoms of deep dyspareunia, along with her lower abdominal and adnexal tenderness, point towards the diagnosis. C. trachomatis is the most common cause of pelvic inﬂammatory disease and is responsible for up to 35% of cases. A Chlamydia psittaci C. psittaci causes a type of respiratory pneumonia called psittacosis. It is an organism that infects birds and is, therefore, more common in those who keep birds as pets. However, it is not a cause of pelvic inﬂammatory disease. C Neisseria gonorrhoeae N. gonorrhoeae is a causative organism of pelvic inﬂammatory disease. However, it is less common than C. trachomatis, making it an incorrect answer. D Escherichia coli E. coli is a common cause of upper and lower urinary tract infections. Raised inﬂammatory markers, lower abdominal tenderness and leucocytes in the urine can raise suspicion of the diagnosis. However, it does not explain this patient's vaginal discharge or adnexal tenderness. E Mycoplasma genitalium M. genitalium is a causative organism of pelvic inﬂammatory disease. However, it is less common than C. trachomatis, making it an

incorrect answer.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fevers, myalgia and a sore throat. She also complains of nausea and reduced oral intake. Her 2-year-old daughter has been off sick from nursery with similar symptoms. There is no past medical history and she only takes over-thecounter vitamin supplementation. She has no allergies. On examination, she is febrile with a temperature of 40.2 °C. Her heart rate is 131 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 101/65 mmHg. She is coryzal with a dry cough. Chest sounds are clear, with no audible crackles or wheeze and her saturations are 99% on room air. She has a red throat and palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of her ear, nose and throat examination is unremarkable. Throat swab: inﬂuenza A positive She is discharged home with advice to take regular analgesia and encourage ﬂuid intake. An outpatient prescription of oseltamivir is given. What is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir?
explanation: A Neuraminidase inhibitor Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor. Neuraminidase inhibitors block the action of the neuraminidase enzyme, an enzyme found on the surface of the inﬂuenza virus, which enables movement of the virus into and out of host cells. D Integrase inhibitor Integrase inhibitors are designed to inhibit the action of the enzyme integrase; a viral enzyme used to incorporate the genome of the virus into the host cell’s DNA. It is an important step in the viral replication process and preventing this step helps to reduce further spread of the virus. One example of an integrase inhibitor includes raltegravir, an inhibitor of HIV integrase. A Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), such as efavirenz, are used in the treatment of human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) and are one of the components of highly active antiretroviral treatment (HAART). They are non-competitive inhibitors of the reverse transcriptase enzyme, therefore stopping viral deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) synthesis. B Protease inhibitor Protease inhibitors are used in the treatment of HIV. An example is ritonavir. Protease inhibitors work by inhibiting the protease enzyme, which prevents the virus from packaging and releasing new virions. E Nucleoside analogue Nucleoside analogues incorporate into viral DNA or ribonucleic acid (RNA), causing chain termination. One example is ribavirin, used in the treatment of chronic hepatitis C infection in adults or of life-threatening respiratory syncytial virus infection in children.

stem: A 27-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe shortness of breath, and lethargy such that he is only able to walk a few yards. He admits feeling generally unwell with fevers, weight loss and a dry cough over the past few months. He is a former IV drug abuser who moved to the UK from southern Italy a few years earlier. Examination reveals blood pressure of 105/80 mmHg, with pulse is 86/min and regular. He looks pale. There is generalised lymphadenopathy and his BMI is 20. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 76 g/l (reticulocyte count not elevated) 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 197 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l ESR 65 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Bone marrow aspirate Pure red cell aplasia Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Parvovirus infection The general deterioration over the past few months, coupled with a previous history of intravenous drug abuse, raises the possibility of underlying HIV. Parvovirus B19-related red cell aplasia is associated with HIV infection and accounts for the picture seen here: anaemia without reticulocytosis and red cell aplasia on bone marrow aspiration. B19 DNA can be identiﬁed by PCR to conﬁrm the underlying cause. IV immunoglobulin is the intervention of choice. D Myeloﬁbrosis Myeloﬁbrosis is clonal haemopoietic stem cell proliferation with histological evidence on bone marrow biopsy. Presentation is variable and can be with features of changes in haemaglobin, white cell counts or platelet numbers, as well as constitutional symptoms and massive splenomegaly. This is unlikely based on the absence of clinical ﬁndings, and peripheral blood ﬁlm should show leukoerythoblastosis with teardrop poikilocytosis and there may be megakaryocyte fragments. Bone marrow aspiration is usually dry and biopsy is needed. A Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is destruction of red blood cells through an antibody-mediated process. There are multiple causes split into three categories: warm antibody types (e.g. SLE, Evans syndrome, CLL), cold antibody type (viral infection, Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection) or drug related. The history may that of anaemia with the suggestion of an underlying cause, and there may also be evidence of increased bilirubin such as gallstones or jaundice. The lack of evidence of raised bilirubin does not exclude autoimmune haemolytic anaemia in this patient, but the evidence of aplasia of red blood cells does, as does the normal reticulocyte count, of which the latter should be raised during haemolysis. B Cytomegalovirus infection Cytomegalovirus is a common herpesvirus which can cause gastrointestinal disease, pneumonia, retinitis and encephalitis during immunosuppression. In the immunosuppressed patient complications include haemolytic anaemia via an antibody-mediated process. As with the above explanation, the absence of a raised reticulocyte count and the presence of aplasia make this a less likely diagnosis. C Myelodysplasia Myelodysplasias are haematopoietic disorders characterised by dysplastic changes in cell linages of the bone marrow. The marrow itself becomes hyper- or hypocellular due to clonal proliferation of abnormal cells leading to peripheral blood cytopenias. This usually occurs in the elderly, but can be due to previous chemotherapy, environmental toxins or some rare disorders. The absence of such risk factors makes this a very unlikely diagnosis, and the bone marrow results exclude this diagnosis.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the general practitioner (GP). He is from Southern India and is visiting the UK to see his son. His family has brought him to the doctor as he is unable to extend his wrist and has clawing of his ﬁngers. On examination, there is a dry scaling rash above the elbow on the affected side. The skin rash itself is painless and non-itchy, and there is evidence of sensory loss distal to the lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
D Tuberculoid leprosy This man comes from a region where leprosy infection is endemic

and this clinical picture is highly suggestive of a tuberculoid leprosy picture. Serological testing can be employed to conﬁrm the diagnosis and a number of PCR-based techniques are growing in popularity. Nerve conduction studies may show segmental slowing at the site of nerve entrapment. Skin biopsy may also be useful in conﬁrming the diagnosis. Combination treatment with dapsone and rifampicin is usually employed for 6 months for paucibacillary leprosy; in the UK a 2-year course is recommended for multibacillary disease. While further nerve damage may be arrested by treatment, recovery of nerve function already lost is very unlikely. Clinical leprosy lies between two extremes: tuberculoid (TT) and lepromatous (LL). Between the two ends of the spectrum lies a broad group designated as borderline, and subclassiﬁed as borderline tuberculoid (BT), midborderline (BB) and borderline lepromatous (BL). The disease does not remain static but evolves spontaneously or in response to therapy. Transition toward the TT pole is referred to as upgrading (and may lead to a reversal or type I reaction) and transition toward the LL pole as downgrading (leading to type II reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum [ENL]). The reactions reﬂect abrupt changes in the host–parasite immunological balance and are associated with acute clinical exacerbations. E Syphillis infection While secondary syphilis can have a painless and asymptomatic limb rash, and tertiary syphilis can be associated with focal neurological lesions, the absence of any other features makes this an unlikely diagnosis. Primary syphilis causes a single painless ulcer at the site of infection with lymphoadenopathy. Secondary syphilis can occur 6 weeks later in 25% of untreated patients; it features a polymorphic rash of the palms and soles, but other organs can be affected. Over time, tertiary syphilis can develop with neurological syphilis and cardiovascular syphilis. A Herpes zoster infection Herpes zoster virus causes varicella (chickenpox) in childhood and shingles during immunosuppression or old age. Shingles is characterised ﬁrst by a pre-eruptive phase causing burning, itching or paraesthesia in one dermatome, leading to an eruptive phase with erythematous swollen plaques with clusters of small vesicles which are limited by dermatomal distribution. The absence of pain and the presence of weakness make this diagnosis unlikely. B Rickettsial infection Rickettsia organisms are Gram-negative coccobacilli which are obligate intracellular parasites found primarily in rats and mice. They cause several diseases, including typhus which is characterised by fever, myalgia, headache and diarrhoea with a rash on the chest which can spread to the extremities. The absence of systemic features and rash on the chest make this diagnosis far less likely, and it would not explain the neurological features. C Lepromatous leprosy This form of leprosy is systemic with symmetrical distribution and associated symptoms and signs. It is far more severe with reddish or hypopigmented patches with reduced sensation. There is also ocular involvement and systemic disease affecting the respiratory tract,

kidneys and lymph nodes.

stem: A 21-year-old woman was brought by ambulance after as a ‘red alert’. Her brother accompanied her and reported that she was very lethargic the previous evening and had complained of a sore throat and muscle aches. The following morning, he subsequently found her vomiting and complaining of a headache. On examination, her blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, temperature 38.7 °C and pulse rate 110 bpm. There was a purpuric skin rash and evidence of subconjunctival haemorrhage. With the thigh ﬂexed at the hip and the knee at 90 degrees, the patient found further extension of the leg painful. Investigation Result Normal values WCC 14.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 11.4 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l APTT 51 s 25 - 35 s Urea 10.1 mmol/l (2.5–7.0) 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 148 mmol/l (60–110 50 - 120 µmol/l Random plasma glucose 4.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
A Ceftriaxone The answer is Ceftriaxone (Option A). This patient has signs, including a positive Kernig’s sign, and symptoms consistent with meningitis, probably meningococcal meningitis, given the evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. The most appropriate treatment is intravenous ceftriaxone, which should be given immediately. This patient will need to be transferred to intensive care. A computerised tomography (CT) scan is required before progressing to lumbar puncture, to rule out cerebral oedema and therefore the risk of coning on lumbar puncture. Cerebral herniation occurs in about 5% of patients with acute bacterial meningitis, accounting for about 30% of mortality. Bacterial meningitis would give a typically turbid or purulent cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF), 200–300 polymorphs/mm3, 0.5– 2.0 g/l of protein and CSF glucose levels of < 50% of the blood value. It is important to treat contacts of patients with meningococcal disease with prophylaxis against infection with oral ciproﬂoxacin. A

single dose of ceftriaxone is appropriate for prophylaxis in pregnant women. B Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin (Option B) is incorrect. This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with bacterial meningitis, likely meningococcal. She is extremely unwell, with signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation. The appropriate antibiotic here is intravenous ceftriaxone. Ciproﬂoxacin is not a ﬁrstline agent for bacterial meningitis, though oral ciproﬂoxacin may be used for prophylaxis for exposed contacts. C Glucose Glucose (Option C) is incorrect. This patient is not signiﬁcantly hypoglycaemic and therefore does not require glucose replacement. The hypoglycaemia is likely to be a feature of sepsis, rather than a cause of her current symptoms. Hypoglycaemia as an underlying problem should be considered in patients with a low glucose on hypoglycaemic agents, who can present with reduced consciousness, hunger, irritability or confusion. In such cases, oral glucose treatment, intramuscular glucagon and intravenous dextrose can be used. Had the hypoglycaemia been more severe, then correction would have been warranted, but the highest priority should be ceftriaxone to treat the underlying cause. D Hydrocortisone Hydrocortisone (Option D) is incorrect. This patient has bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal, and will require transfer to intensive care. Steroids have been shown to reduce the risk of hearing loss in bacterial meningitis, but there is no evidence that they reduce overall mortality. If steroids were given, dexamethasone would be the agent used, rather than hydrocortisone. Hydrocortisone would have been the correct answer to the management of an Addisonian crisis, which can present with vomiting and hypotension, but the fever, rash and headache make that a less likely diagnosis. E Naloxone Naloxone (Option E) is incorrect. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist, used in overdose situations. There is no evidence that this patient has overdosed on opioids; instead, she has a purpuric rash, neurological signs and fever. This should be treated as bacterial meningitis, until proven otherwise. Evidence of an opiate overdose would be a low respiratory rate, pinpoint pupils and evidence of intravenous drug abuse such as track-marks.

stem: A 25-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant presents to the Emergency Department. She returned ten days ago from a visit to Bangladesh for a family funeral. She has been feeling unwell with nausea, ﬂu-like symptoms and diarrhoea over the past few days and has become jaundiced. On examination, her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, temperature 37.8 °C and pulse 95 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination reveals a uterus consistent with her stage of pregnancy and she is tender in the right upper quadrant. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 105 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 209 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 108 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 2015 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 30 g/l 35–55 g/l ALP 321 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 122 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l INR 1.2 1.1 She has been vaccinated against hepatitis A and B Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Hepatitis E Given the acute nature of this patient’s symptoms, coupled with a lack of exposure to potential viruses borne by blood/other body ﬂuids, hepatitis E is the most likely underlying diagnosis. It is spread by the faecal/oral route and genotypes 3 and 4, in particular, are responsible for disease in humans. While mortality is 1–4% when the general population is considered, it may be as high as 20% in pregnant women. Treatment is supportive and immunoglobulin ineffective, and no vaccine exists. C Hepatitis D Hepatitis D infection always coexists with hepatitis B. As this patient has no history of contact with bodily ﬂuids or contaminated blood products and she has been vaccinated against hepatitis B, there is no chance of her having hepatitis D. A Epstein Barr virus Epstein–Barr virus is associated with pharyngitis, which is not seen here. It can cause abnormal liver function tests. However, the large increase in ALT that is present in this case is not classically seen with Epstein–Barr virus infection. B Hepatitis C

There is no history of contact with bodily ﬂuids or contaminated blood products in this case, which makes this diagnosis unlikely. E Typhoid fever Typhoid fever is associated with intermittent diarrhoea, followed by headaches, high fever, a non-productive cough and eventually a tendency to constipation. Mild elevations in liver function tests can be seen, and not the very large rise in transaminases seen here.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. Her brother tells you that she has been having fevers, tiredness, a sore throat and lower body muscle ache for a week, but in the last three days has felt better. She has a regular boyfriend and only drinks at the weekends. He tells you that two weeks ago they were out clubbing and she was so drunk she fell in the city river when two of her friends had to jump in and get her out. She was seen in hospital after this and was given the all-clear. On examination, she exhibits meningism and photophobia. She is jaundiced and is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.7 °C. She has no rash but has bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhage and has pharyngeal injection and enlarged tonsillar lymph nodes. Her heart rate is 120/min, blood pressure 90/62 mmHg. She has hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal examination. Computerised tomography (CT) of the head is normal. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) results reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value WCC 42/mm3 (PMN leucocytes 36) < 5/mm3 Protein 0.54 g/l < 0.45 g/l Glucose 3.8mml/l 2.5–3.9 mmol/l Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Urea 16.3 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 215 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 198 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 168 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 98 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Glucose 5.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l WCC 20.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Urine dipstick shows protein 3+, blood 3+. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Leptospirosis Leptospirosis is caused by pathogenic spiral bacteria belonging to the genus Leptospira. The disease is more prevalent in tropical climates and those with a heavy rainfall. In the developed world it has become associated with recreational watersports and those exposed to raw sewage. The disease incubates for 7–12 days and many patients never present with clinical features. The ﬁrst phase is known as the septicaemic or leptospiraemic phase, as the bacteria can be cultured in the blood and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF). In this phase, patients often have ﬂulike symptoms. The patient usually then feels better for three days before developing the immune or leptospiruric stage because circulating antibodies may be detected or the organism may be isolated from urine. However, it may not be cultured from blood or CSF. In this phase, patients often present with aseptic meningitis, haemorrhagic shock or kidney disease. Treatment includes supportive management. Doxycycline and penicillin are both reasonable choices for antimicrobial therapy. A Meningococcal septicaemia Meningococcal septicaemia is an infection caused by the Gramnegative coccus Neisseria meningitides. Patients present with sepsis and typically a non-blanching petechial rash. Meningitis can occur, but typical CSF ﬁndings would be of a much higher white cell count (>100/microlitre) with neutrophil predominance, and a reduced glucose (<0.5 × serum level). A Mollaret’s meningitis This is a recurrent benign meningitis, most commonly associated with HSV-2. Patients present with recurrent episodes of meningism lasting several days which are then self-resolving. CSF analysis shows a lymphocytic CSF as seen in the question, but the rest of the clinical history is not consistent. B Streptococcal meningitis This is meningitis caused by the Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, a commensal of the human oropharynx. Presentation is usually with a rapid-onset meningism and sepsis. Typical CSF ﬁndings would be of a much higher white cell count (>100/µl) with neutrophil predominance, and a reduced glucose (<0.5 × serum level). E Meliodosis Meliodosis is an infection caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei. Most patients have subclinical disease, but infection can present with pneumonia, skin abscess formation and sepsis. While sporadic cases have been reported worldwide, the disease is endemic to South and South East Asia.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of fever, pain and swelling over bilateral knees, wrist and hands for the past ﬁve days. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and her heart rate is 94 bpm. There is a generalised purplish rash noted. She has swelling and tenderness on palpation of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, but no deformities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Parvovirus B19 infection Acute infection with parvovirus B19 in young women more often causes acute symmetric polyarticular arthritis than infection in men or children. Polyarticular arthritis often involves the hands and joints of the lower limbs. It is usually associated with a vasculitic rash in up to 18% of cases. In immunocompetent adults with no haemoglobinopathies or primary red cell disorders, there is only mild anaemia that is self-limiting. The disease is usually self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals and resolves with symptomatic management. D Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis presents with joint pain for at least six weeks, unlike this patient who has an acute presentation and no deformities. A Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with features of asthma, mononeuritis multiplex and renal involvement, which are not present in this patient. Other features include arthritis and arthralgia, as well as peripheral eosinophilia. C Polyarteritis nodosa Polyarteritis nodosa may present with a rash and arthralgia. However, it is necrotising vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries, resulting in glomerulonephritis, stroke, bowel ischaemia, etc. These features are not present in this patient. E Systemic lupus erythematosus Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause polyarticular symmetrical arthritis but the distribution and description of this patients rash make this a less likely diagnosis. Common skin involvement in SLE involves rash over the malar distribution (termed a 'butterﬂy rash') and less commonly, inﬂammatory discoid lesions.

stem: A 32-year-old man presented with extensive burns over the forearms after attending a blaze as part of his work as a ﬁreﬁghter. Three days later the burns on his forearms deteriorated. On examination, his temperature was 38.1 °C. The burns had developed a violaceous/black discolouration, bullae and sweetsmelling green pus. Wound culture and microscopy revealed Gram-positive rods. The wounds were surgically debrided. What is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
explanation:
A Benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin This patient has signs consistent with gas gangrene, which is caused by Clostridium perfringens. This is further supported by microscopy, as Cl. perfringens is a Gram-positive rod. Benzylpenicillin has good activity against Cl. perfringens and should be used in combination with clindamycin. E Vancomycin Vancomycin gives excellent coverage of Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negative cocci. It is often used in addition to other antibiotics in the treatment of resistant Gram-positive cocci – for example, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. This patient, however, has a super-infection with Gram-positive rods. Having presented with sweet-smelling pus and multiple bullae, this is consistent with gas gangrene, caused by Clostridium perfringens. Vancomycin is not bactericidal for Cl. perfringens, and therefore would not be an appropriate choice here. A better choice would be benzylpenicillin, which can be used alone or with clindamycin. B Chloramphenicol The sweet-smelling pus and multiple bullae seen in this patient are suggestive of superinfection with Clostridium perfringens, which causes gas gangrene. Cl. perfringens is a Gram-positive rod, as seen on microscopy here. Chloramphenicol covers some Gram-positive rods, including Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) and Listeria monocytogenes, but it does not give adequate coverage of Cl. perfringens to treat this infection. A better choice would be benzylpenicillin, which is either used alone or in combination with clindamycin. C Flucloxacillin Flucloxacillin is a good empirical choice for the treatment of cellulitis as it gives excellent coverage of Staphylococcus, a common cause of cellulitis and wound super-infection. However,

microscopy has revealed Gram-positive rods in this patient (Staphylococcus would appear as Gram-positive cocci). This, combined with the sweet-smelling pus and multiple bullae, is suggestive of gas gangrene, caused by Clostridium perfringens. This organism is not covered by ﬂucloxacillin. A more appropriate antibiotic would be benzylpenicillin, which is either used alone or with clindamycin. A Gentamicin Gentamicin provides excellent cover for Gram-negative organisms, and can work synergistically to treat some Gram-positive infections. This patient has an infection with a Gram-positive rod: combined with his presentation (sweet-smelling pus, multiple bullae), this is suggestive of gas gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens. Gentamicin would not cover Cl. perfringens. A better choice would be benzylpenicillin, either alone or in combination with clindamycin.

stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department with worsening vision affecting her left eye. She says she woke that morning with progressively worsening visual acuity and can now only detect light and dark on the left-hand side. There is a crusted papular lesion on the dorsum of her left hand, which she says was caused by a scratch from some kittens at a local farm a few days earlier. Left axillary lymphadenopathy is also observed. Fundoscopy of the left retina reveals cotton wool spots and haemorrhages. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg. What is the most likely cause of her visual loss?
explanation:
A Bartonella henselae (B henselae) neuroretinitis This patient has cat scratch disease (CSD), related to B henselae infection which is often carried by young cats, and cats that live a less domesticated existence (such as those on a farm). Around 1-2% of patients with cat scratch disease develop neuroretinitis, which is characterised by a rapid deterioration in visual acuity. Retinal ﬁndings may include haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and evidence of deep retinal scarring/inﬂammation. Most patients have a good chance of recovery from CSD related neuroretinitis, although some have residual loss of colour vision and diminished contrast sensitivity. Azithromycin is the intervention of choice for CSD.

D Central retinal artery occlusion Central retinal artery occlusion is associated with retinal pallor and a “cherry red” spot because the macula receives its blood supply from the posterior ciliary arteries. Retinal artery occlusion is also not associated with Bartonella infection. B Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis CMV retinitis has a similar appearance to that seen here, with cotton wool spots and haemorrhages, although it is more likely to be seen in patients with immunosuppressive disorders. The other symptoms seen here, including evidence of a cat scratch and lymphadenopathy, are more consistent with Bartonella infection. C Hypertensive retinopathy Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy is associated with multiple ﬂameshaped haemorrhages. The rapid deterioration seen here in visual acuity would, however, be unexpected in hypertensive retinopathy. The other features of cat scratch disease also do not ﬁt with hypertensive retinopathy as the cause of visual acuity loss. E Central retinal vein occlusion Central retinal vein occlusion is associated with multiple ﬂameshaped haemorrhages on fundoscopy. It occurs more commonly in patients with thrombophilic disorders such as anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, protein C, protein S deﬁciency, and antithrombin III deﬁciency. It is not associated with Bartonella infection.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department, complaining of pain when passing urine over the past few days. In addition, she has ﬂitting arthritis affecting the small joints of her hands and feet and a generalised maculopapular rash. In particular, her left knee is causing considerable pain. On examination, you notice that there is a medium-sized effusion; the joint is hot, and ﬂexion is limited by pain. On further questioning, she admits to having unprotected sexual intercourse with two different partners during a recent holiday to Spain. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 12.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Knee aspirate: Gram-negative intracellular cocci. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: B Ceftriaxone and azithromycin The patient is suffering from gonococcal arthritis. Gonococcus remains sensitive to ceftriaxone. As such, it is the intervention of choice here. Intravenous (iv) therapy should be continued preferably for up to 48 hours post- initial improvement, after which treatment with an oral cephalosporin should be continued for at least a week. Chlamydia trachomatis is a frequent copathogen with N. gonorrhoeae and should be empirically treated with azithromycin if not speciﬁcally excluded with microbiologic testing. A Benzylpenicillin Benzylpenicillin is not routinely used in the treatment of gonococcal infection. C Ciproﬂoxacin Signiﬁcant resistance to quinolones exists, and they are therefore no longer recommended for the treatment of gonorrhoea. D Doxycycline Increasing resistance to tetracyclines has been found in Gonococcus infection, which precludes the use of doxycycline here. E Erythromycin Macrolides are generally used as second-line therapy in the treatment of gonococcal arthritis where patients cannot tolerate a cephalosporin.

stem: A 54-year-old sheep farmer comes to the Hepatology Clinic complaining of dull right upper quadrant pain and intermittent shortness of breath which has steadily worsened over the past 3-6 months. He has no past medical history of note, takes no regular medication, and is usually well. On examination, his blood pressure is 125/82 mmHg, with pulse 67/min and regular. Breath sounds are slightly reduced at the right lung base on auscultation. Abdomen is soft, and he is mildly tender in the right upper quadrant with two ﬁnger-breadth hepatomegaly. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 110 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 9.9 x 109/l (elevated eosinophils) 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 212 x 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l ESR 45 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h CRP 82 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l AST 192 u/l 10 - 40 u/l ALP 245 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Bilirubin 23 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l USS liver Multiple cysts in the right lobe of the liver with internal septae His chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
explanation:
D ELISA testing for Echinococcus This man’s profession, coupled with steadily worsening symptoms, elevated ESR, eosinophilia, abnormal LFTs, multiple cysts and a right pleural effusion, suggests liver hydatid disease. Serological testing is most likely to be positive (90%+ in most series) for patients with liver cysts, and this, therefore, represents the most appropriate next step in the diagnosis. B CT guided cyst aspiration CT-guided aspiration without drug cover runs the risk of anaphylaxis

or seeding of Echinococcus along the track. A Albendazole trial of therapy Intervention depends on the size of the cyst. Smaller cysts responding well to medical therapy alone, although larger cysts usually require albendazole combined with surgical excision. It is important, of course, to conﬁrm the diagnosis ﬁrst. C CT guided pleural ﬂuid aspiration The pleural ﬂuid may be reactive or due to seeding of Echinococcus because of cyst rupture. Aspiration may risk further spreading, and other measures to conﬁrm the diagnosis should be attempted ﬁrst. E Surgical cyst excision Surgical cyst excision was formerly the only treatment for Echinococcus but is now considered an intervention either in combination with drug therapy or after a period of drug therapy, rather than as a diagnostic tool. 70501

stem: A 23-year-old medical student has returned from a six-week holiday travelling in Kenya. Prior to leaving he took all the relevant immunisations and was taking malaria prophylaxis up until the day he returned. Over the last 12 days, he has since been experiencing intermittent fevers and rigors. For the last two days he has also been complaining of drenching night sweats and vomiting. On examination, he appears drowsy but orientated. There is no lymphadenopathy or rash. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable. Abdominal examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Thin malaria ﬁlm Negative Blood cultures No growth in 24 hours Hb 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 100 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 129 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Glucose 3.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Urea 15.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 118 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Plasmodium falciparum Plasmodium falciparum malaria is the most likely diagnosis, (given the geographical distribution of falciparum and the fact he has symptoms of cerebral disease). It is important to remember that serial ﬁlms are required to exclude the diagnosis. Prophylaxis does not give full protection and in addition this patient stopped taking his prophylactic treatment too early, whatever his treatment regime (Atovaquone/proguanil combination should be continued seven days after return, other drugs such as meﬂoquine for 4 weeks after return). The incubation period is 1–2 weeks. Patients often give a history of prodromal symptoms of headache, myalgia and anorexia. Signs include anaemia, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly but without lymphadenopathy. Complications include cerebral malaria, which has a mortality of 20%. Hypoglycaemia occurs in patients who are taking quinine but also is a poor prognostic indicator. Acute kidney disease and pulmonary oedema are other less common complications. C Plasmodium malariae This is a cause of malaria but is less likely than falciparum because the patient took prophylaxis against malaria and resistance rates are low in malariae. Also, falciparum is far more likely to cause cerebral symptoms than malariae. A Typhoid fever Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella subspecies following typically 10-20 days. It causes a high fever, dry cough, malaise, abdominal pain following by green diarrhoea and hepatosplenomegaly and in the ﬁnal stages can causes complications in multiple organs. There can be associated bradycardia as well. Diagnosis is by culture and treatment is usually with azithromycin but if severe then IV ceftriaxone. Typhoid fever is associated with neurological features including headache and confusion, accompanied by vague abdominal symptoms including constipation. Whilst typhoid fever is a good differential for fever and hepatosplenomegaly in the returning traveller, the absence of rash, lymphopenia and diarrhoea makes this a less likely diagnosis and therefore an incorrect choice. D Paratyphoid fever Paratyphoid fever is very similar to typhoid fever except being caused by S. paratyphi. The absence of a rash, lymphopenia and diarrhoea makes this diagnosis unlikely as well. E Dengue fever Dengue fever is endemic in tropical South-East Asia, and outbreaks have also occurred in the tropical regions of Australia. The illness is a haemorrhagic fever, carried by the Aedes mosquito and is caused by the Dengue virus. It is characterised by fever, severe headache and facial ﬂushing. Dengue fever usually presents with a morbilliform rash in the trunk area and widespread lymphadenopathy, coupled with severe muscle pains. In the early stages there is a lymphocytosis, with later lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and bleeding. On examination there may be hepatosplenomegaly.

Treatment is supportive. The absence of myalgic features, headache and a rash makes this a less likely diagnosis, and the duration of fever for two weeks is long for dengue and makes it less likely.

stem: An elderly woman is admitted to the Care Of The Elderly Ward. She presented with mild confusion and a fever. She has a past medical history of diverticular disease, for which she has been most recently admitted two years ago. Otherwise, she is in good health. In Accident and Emergency, urinalysis reveals nitrites in the urine and treatment with co-amoxiclav is commenced. The next day, urine culture conﬁrms an E. coli urinary tract infection (UTI). She continues the treatment for a further three days. Both the fever and confusion resolve and she is able to mobilise around the ward. On the fourth day of her admission, she develops some diarrhoea. She has ﬁve episodes of watery diarrhoea. That evening she develops a fever of 38 °C. She is seen by the on-call SHO who examines her and arranges for routine blood tests, blood cultures and stool culture. You arrive back on the ward the next morning to ﬁnd the patient very unwell. She is tachycardic, pulse 120 bpm; BP 120/65 mmHg; temperature 38 °C. The nurses report several more episodes of profuse, green, watery diarrhoea overnight. On examination, the patient has a diffusely tender abdomen with active bowel sounds. There is no evidence of peritonism. Chest and cardiovascular examination are unremarkable. You obtain IV access and commence IV ﬂuids. Blood tests from last night are as follows: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 161 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 32 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 220 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Urea 9.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Bilirubin 18 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l ALT 47 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 87 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Albumin 28 g/l 35 - 55 g/l You stop the co-amoxiclav. Of the following, which is the most urgent next step?
options: Send stool for C. difﬁcile toxin a
Send stool for C. difﬁcile toxin b
explanation: D Commence oral vancomycin Clinically there is ample evidence that this is Clostridium difﬁcile infection. This patient is clearly extremely unwell, and the most important steps are to stop the co-amoxiclav which will have been the main precipitant of the C. difﬁcile infection in the ﬁrst place and to commence the appropriate treatment, which is oral vancomycin. B Send stool for C. difﬁcile toxin b Whilst testing for toxins is the correct way to diagnose C. difﬁcile infection, it is not the most urgent action as this patient needs treatment prior to conﬁrmation of the likely diagnosis. A Send stool for C. difﬁcile toxin a Whilst testing for toxins is the correct way to diagnose C. difﬁcile infection, it is not the most urgent action as this patient needs treatment prior to conﬁrmation of the likely diagnosis. C Commence oral ciproﬂoxacin This would be a very dangerous option as ciproﬂoxacin can precipitate C. difﬁcile infection and worsen current infection E Abdominal X- ray Both AXR and CT would be useful if there was evidence of peritonitis or obstruction. A possible complication with C. difﬁcile is toxic megacolon which can be seen with abdominal X-ray if suspected. The presence of bowel sounds and absence of signs of peritonism makes this a less urgent.

stem: A 34-year-old man presented to clinic with an 18-month history of an intensely pruritic rash. He was diagnosed with HIV infection 6 years ago and is currently not taking antiretroviral therapy or other medications. On examination there are many excoriated papules and pustules on the chest, back and extensor surfaces of the arms. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values CD4+ count 270 × 106/l 430 - 1690 × 106/l Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Eosinophilic folliculitis This is a relatively common dermatological manifestation of HIV, and this patient has a classic history and signs of the condition. It typically occurs in patients with CD4+ counts less than 300, as seen here, and improves when antiretroviral therapy is started. Other agents that can be used are topical steroids or antihistamines. It can also occur in the absence of HIV infection, and can be associated with malignancy. E Urticaria Urticaria manifests as wheals and large, raised lesions that are migratory. It does not cause papules and pustules, and although itchy is not intensely itchy as described here. This patient is more likely to have eosinophilic folliculitis, which is associated with HIV infection, particularly in patients with CD4+ counts less than 300, as seen here. A Acne rosacea Acne rosacea causes predominantly ﬂushing or redness of the face. It can cause papules, but it would be very unusual for acne rosacea to be intensely itchy, and it does not have any particular association with HIV infection. This patient has typical eosinophilic folliculitis, which is associated with HIV infection. As described here, it manifests as intensely itchy papules over the face, trunk and limbs. It typically occurs in patients with CD4+ counts less than 300, as seen here. B Acne vulgaris This patient has eosinophilic folliculitis, which can look similar to acne vulgaris; however, acne vulgaris is not intensely itchy and does not have any speciﬁc association with HIV. This is a typical description of eosinophilic folliculitis, which typically occurs in patients with a CD4+ count of less than 300, as in this case. D Seborrhoeic dermatitis Seborrhoeic dermatitis can be itchy but is usually not intensely itchy, as seen here. It is ﬂaky and scaly, not papular and pustular as seen here. This patient’s history and signs are most consistent with eosinophilic folliculitis, which is associated with HIV infection (especially where the CD4+ count is less than 300).

stem: A 28-year-old illegal immigrant who has been started on HAART for HIV some 7 weeks ago, presents to the Emergency Department for review. Over the past few days he has suffered increasing tiredness with a cough and night sweats, and has felt off his food. On examination his temperature is 37.5°C, pulse is 78/min and regular, and his BP is 110/80 mmHg. There is generalised lymphadenopathy, wheeze on auscultation of the chest, and vague tenderness in the right upper quadrant on palpation of the abdomen. Investigations; Hb 94 g/l WCC 4.3 x109/l PLT 95 x109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 95 micromol/l ALT 85 U/l ALP 185 U/l CXR Mediastinal lymphadenopathy Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Mycobacterium avium intracellulare The answer is Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI) - The time period post starting HAART is highly suggestive of immune reconstitution syndrome (IRS), of which MAI is a manifestation. The generalised lymphadenopathy, coupled with a cough, night sweats and abnormal LFTs are typical of the condition. Triple anti-mycobacterial therapy is recommended, and HAART may be continued in the majority of cases. A CMV infection CMV infection is incorrect, is usually associated with uveitis when it occurs in association with IRS. It is not therefore the most likely diagnosis here. B Cryptosporidiosis Cryptosporidiosis is incorrect, is predominantly associated with GI symptoms including diarrhoea, which does not signiﬁcantly feature here. D Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis is incorrect Whilst sarcoidosis is associated with a dry cough, night sweats and lymphadenopathy, and is reported in association with IRS, the pancytopaenia seen here would be unusual. E Toxoplasmosis Toxoplasmosis is incorrect, is primarily associated with CNS infection / encephalitis, of which there are no features in the scenario described here.

stem: A 28-year-old woman attended clinic. She was planning to move to South America and was 12 weeks’ pregnant. She wanted to review her vaccination status prior to travelling. Which one of the following vaccines is considered safe in pregnancy?
explanation:
C Tetanus Tetanus is a toxoid-based vaccine and therefore is considered safe in pregnancy. All the other examples are live attenuated vaccines, and therefore should not be given in pregnancy due to the potential risk of fetal infection. Other examples of vaccines considered safe in pregnancy are whooping cough, hepatitis B and inﬂuenza. E Yellow fever The yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine, and therefore there is a theoretical risk of fetal infection if it is given in pregnancy. However, occasionally if the mother must travel to a yellow feverendemic area, vaccination will be considered on a risk–beneﬁt basis. Only toxoid-based or killed vaccines are considered safe in pregnancy: some examples include tetanus, hepatitis B and inﬂuenza. A BCG The BCG vaccination affords some protection against tuberculosis infection. However, it is a live attenuated vaccine, and as such is not recommended in pregnancy as there is a theoretical risk of infection of the fetus. Only toxoid-based or killed vaccines are considered safe in pregnancy if the risk of infection outweighs the risk of vaccination: common examples are inﬂuenza, hepatitis B, whooping cough and tetanus. B Rubella Women who are planning to conceive are advised to have the rubella vaccine (as part of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine – MMR) at least a month before conceiving. It is a live attenuated vaccine, and therefore should not be administered in pregnancy due to a theoretical risk that the fetus could become infected. Only killed or toxoid-based vaccines are considered safe in pregnancy, though it is always important to weigh the risks and beneﬁts of any medication in pregnancy. Examples of safe vaccines include inﬂuenza, hepatitis B, whooping cough and tetanus. D Varicella zoster

The varicella vaccine is a live, attenuated vaccine and therefore should not be given in pregnancy due to the theoretical risk that the fetus could be infected. Only vaccines based on toxoids or killed vaccines are considered safe in pregnancy: examples include tetanus, whooping cough, hepatitis B and inﬂuenza.

stem: A 35-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of pus and blood mixed in his stool with severe rectal pain, especially on defaecation. He was HIV positive and was on antiretroviral therapy. He had several episodes of unprotected receptive anal sex with new partners in the preceding 6 months. On examination his temperature was 37.8 °C, and pulse rate was 95 beats/min. The abdomen was soft with some mild lower abdominal discomfort. Per rectal examination was very painful and revealed some blood mixed in with stool. There were large, tender inguinal lymph nodes. Proctoscopy was attempted but was too painful. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values CD4+ 410 × 106/l 430 - 1690 × 106/l HIV viral load Undetectable (lower detection limit 40 copies/ml) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Lymphogranuloma venereum This is a sexually transmitted disease caused by Chlamydia. Lymphogranuloma venereum has increased in incidence in developed countries with the major risk factors being men who have sex with men and HIV co- infection. This patient has a background of multiple episodes of unprotected receptive anal sex, and is therefore at risk of sexually transmitted rectal disease. The large-volume, tender lymph nodes are typical of lymphogranuloma venereum, and tenesmus and pain on defaecation with bloody or mucopurulent discharge are also typical features. Diagnosis is via nucleic acid ampliﬁcation testing (NAAT) on swabs, or by PCR. Treatment is with 21 days of oral doxycycline. E Visceral Kaposi’s sarcoma Visceral Kaposi’s sarcoma can affect the rectum, in which case it presents with rectal pain and bleeding. However, it would be extremely uncommon for Kaposi’s sarcoma to present without any

skin involvement at all, and therefore it is not the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms, especially as his HIV is well controlled and he is on antiretroviral therapy. The combination of rectal pain, bleeding, tenesmus and bloody discharge with large lymph nodes is much more typical for lymphogranuloma venereum, a sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia. A Campylobacter gastroenteritis Campylobacter does cause bloody diarrhoea, but it would typically have a shorter clinical course and would not cause rectal ulceration (leading to the pain on defaecation reported here). It would also be unusual to ﬁnd large- volume, tender lymphadenopathy in Campylobacter gastroenteritis. This presentation is more typical of lymphogranuloma venereum, a sexually transmitted disease caused by Chlamydia. It is particularly common amongst men who have sex with men, and can present with rectal ulceration, tenesmus and bloody discharge, as seen here. B Cytomegalovirus colitis This can occur as an opportunistic infection in HIV, and is an AIDsdeﬁning illness. However, this patient has a good CD4 count and undetectable viral load. He is on antiretroviral therapy, and therefore there is no reason why he should develop an opportunistic infection such as this. Instead, given his history of unprotected receptive anal sex, large-volume tender lymphadenopathy and rectal pain, this is more likely to be lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by Chlamydia.
