D Rectal gonorrhoea Rectal gonorrhoea can cause some discomfort and mucopurulent discharge, but would be unlikely to cause frank pain or rectal bleeding. Although there may be associated lymphadenopathy, it would be unlikely to cause buboes as described here. This presentation is more consistent with lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by Chlamydia.

stem: A 33-year-old woman who has completed her family comes to the Sexually Transmitted Diseases Clinic complaining of a grey-white ﬁshy smelling vaginal discharge. She is married with one regular partner, has completed her family, and had an intra-uterine contraceptive device inserted some 10 weeks earlier. She tells you that she is washing herself 3-4 times per day, but the problem has not improved. Examination reveals a grey-white malodourous vaginal discharge. Microscopy reveals the presence of clue cells. Which one of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
E Oral metronidazole This patient’s symptoms, coupled with the presence of clue cells on

microscopy, are consistent with a diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis. Oral metronidazole at a standard dose can be given for 5–7 days, one 2 g dose can be given stat, or metronidazole vaginal gel can also be used. Clindamycin or tinidazole are alternatives to metronidazole. B Oral clarithromycin Macrolides are ineffective in clearing Gardnerella. A Oral cephalexin Cephalosporins are not as effective as metronidazole in clearance of Gardnerella, although some limited data do suggest they clear the bacteria. C Oral coamoxiclav Co-amoxiclav is ineffective in this setting and may increase the risk of Candida infection. D Oral doxycycline Doxycycline is a ﬁrst-line therapy for treatment of chlamydia, not for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis.

stem: A 46-year-old Bangladeshi chef was admitted with a 3-month history of night sweats, weight loss and malaise. Examination in the clinic reveals a BP of 154/88 mmHg, with pulse 80 bpm and regular. Auscultation of the chest appears normal apart from occasional wheezes, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Abdominal examination is normal. He has been checking his temperature at home and produces a diary to conﬁrm swinging fevers up to 39.0°C over the last 2 weeks. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 205 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 104 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 7.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l CRP 72 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sputum microscopy No evidence of AAFB Abdominal CT scan Bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands Sputum Gene Xpert TB Not detected His chest X-ray is shown below: By Mikael Häggström [CC0], from Wikimedia Commons Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
B Groccott-stained adrenal biopsy The differential diagnosis for a pyrexia of unknown origin and bilateral adrenal swelling would be lymphoma, tuberculosis or histoplasmosis. Tuberculosis is unlikely in view of the normal chest X-ray and negative sputum microscopy and Gene Xpert. Lymphoma is unlikely as the white count is normal. Histoplasmosis, which is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic soil fungus, should therefore be excluded. A slowly progressing chronic form occurs in those who are ﬁt and immunocompetent. Those who are weak, very young, very old or immunocompromised tend to acquire a disseminated infection. Acute infection causes malaise, fevers, anorexia and headache. It can cause a TB-like illness with dyspnoea, cough and haemoptysis, or can simply cause bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Disseminated infection causes bilateral adrenal enlargement in 79% of cases. It can result in adrenal insufﬁciency. Diagnosis made by adrenal biopsy or ﬁne needle aspirate (FNA). The Groccott stain identiﬁes the organism. Treatment is with

itraconazole. A Mantoux test The Mantoux test is used as a screening test for exposure to tuberculosis, a positive test being declared according to the degree of induration identiﬁed after the skin is inoculated with tuberculin protein. C Bone marrow trephine Bone marrow involvement is seen in chronic disseminated histoplasmosis, although in this case adrenal biopsy is more likely to demonstrate infection. D 17-Hydroxyprogesterone Elevated levels of 17-hydroxyprogesterone are seen in patients with congenital adrenal hyperplasia as a result of 21-hydroxylase deﬁciency. E Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test Dexamethasone suppression testing is utilised in the investigation of hypercortisolism, which doesn’t ﬁt with the biochemical investigations seen here.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea, which has been bloodstained for the past 12 hours. He remembers eating under-cooked chicken. An electron microscope image of the bacteria which caused his infection is shown below: What is the likely cause of this patient’s gastroenteritis?
explanation:
B Campylobacter jejuni (C jejuni) The electron micrograph here shows they typical spiral-shaped bacteria of C jejuni. Infection with campylobacter leads to abdominal cramps and diarrhoea, which can become bloody around 24 hours after the onset of symptoms. The majority of patients only require supportive therapy. Antibiotics are only considered in patients with marked symptoms and/or signiﬁcant comorbidities. E Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus) S aureus gastroenteritis occurs most commonly after exposure to undercooked meat or poultry and also dairy products which have been incorrectly stored. Vomiting typically occurs abruptly 2 to 8 hours after ingestion of the contaminated food and settles spontaneously. Outbreaks are most commonly seen at summer parties where desserts are left in a warm environment for some

hours. A Bacillus cereus (B cereus) B cereus gastroenteritis exists in two forms – one which causes severe vomiting, and the other which causes severe diarrhoea. It is a gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium. Symptoms begin between 6 and 15 hours after eating contaminated food and generally resolve within 24 hours. Diarrhoeal symptoms are thought to stem from three toxins, haemolysin BL (Hbl), non-haemolytic enterotoxin (The), and cytotoxin K (CytK). Cereulide is the emetic toxin which is found in the vomiting forms of B cereus. C Escherichia coli (E coli) E coli is a cause of gastroenteritis, but it does not ﬁt with the electron micrograph seen here. E coli are gram- negative rod-shaped bacteria and they do not carry the characteristic corkscrew shape of campylobacter which is seen here. E coli are a common cause of traveller’s diarrhoea, where individuals who visit a new country for holidays complain of gastrointestinal upset which they put down to a change in climate. D Salmonella typhi (S typhi) Salmonella infection can cause similar symptoms to campylobacter, although it is the electron micrograph picture here which drives us towards campylobacter as the correct answer. Salmonella exists as rod-shaped bacteria, not the corkscrew shape seen here.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a history of fatigue, abdominal cramps, ﬂatulence and diarrhoea. Her symptoms have been present for around ten weeks. She reports abdominal bloating which coincides with the diarrhoea and, more recently, her stools have become difﬁcult to ﬂush. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history and is only taking over-thecounter vitamin tablets. She works at a dog daycare centre and smokes ten cigarettes per day. On examination, she appears well, although it is noticed that her clothes are loose-ﬁtting. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Observations reveal a heart rate of 80 bpm, blood pressure of 100/65 mmHg and temperature of 37.4 °C. She denies any signiﬁcant rectal bleeding but has occasionally noticed ﬂecks of blood in the stool. Blood tests reveal no abnormalities and a stool culture sent by her GP is negative . What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: C Giardiasis This patient has Giardia infection. She presents with typical symptoms, similar in nature to irritable bowel syndrome such as cramps, intermittent constipation and diarrhoea and ﬂatulence. The key to diagnosis here is her profession as she may have picked up the protozoal infection from clearing up dog faeces. Stool cultures and antigen tests are often negative in Giardia, and multiple test samples may be required to conﬁrm the diagnosis. It is likely that due to the prolonged nature of symptoms, she has begun to experience some malabsorption. Treatment is with a 1-week course of metronidazole or single-dose tinidazole. E Laxative abuse This patient presents with a short history of diarrhoea associated with ﬂatulence and abdominal cramps associated with recent travel. Laxative abuse could be suspected, but as it often coincides with an eating disorder, patients are likely to hide their symptoms and not present them to medical professionals. Laxative abuse is commonly associated with electrolyte abnormalities which may or may not progress to cause cardiovascular complications. There is nothing in this patient’s history to suggest this. Her profession, which may have introduced an infection, and relatively symptom course makes laxative abuse less likely. A Campylobacter jejuni Campylobacter infection is the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the United Kingdom. It usually has a 2 to 4-day incubation period and causes diarrhoea and vomiting which is usually selflimiting. Given this patient’s prolonged symptom course and lack of nausea or vomiting, this makes Campylobacter infection less likely. B Coeliac disease Coeliac disease may present with diarrhoea and evidence of malabsorption. However, the key to diagnosis here is the patient’s profession where the patient may have picked up the infection from a carrier dog’s faeces. Coeliac disease would result in negative stool cultures; however, anaemia due to iron or vitamin B12 deﬁciency would be expected on her blood tests. D Irritable bowel syndrome Irritable bowel syndrome is the main differential here due to the nature of the patient’s symptoms and the normal ﬁndings on examination and investigation. However, the patient’s profession and a relatively short course of symptoms make Giardia infection the more likely diagnosis in this case.

stem: A 42-year-old aid worker who has been teaching English in the Vietnamese jungle presents to the Emergency Department for review. He has been feeling increasingly unwell over the past 3 months with abdominal pain, bloating, heartburn and intermittent diarrhoea. He also has a dry cough and shortness of breath, and a recurrent rash affecting his thighs and buttocks. The local medical practitioner gave him a salbutamol inhaler, but this had little effect on his symptoms. On examination his BP is 110/80 mmHg; pulse is 70/min and regular. He has scattered wheeze on auscultation of the chest and heart sounds are normal. His abdomen is soft and non- tender, although it is mildly distended. There is an erythematous rash over his buttocks. Investigations; Hb 109 g/l WCC 10.1 x109/l Eosinophils 2.4 x109/l PLT 203 x109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 100 micromol/l CXR Patchy pulmonary inﬁltrates Stool sample No signiﬁcant abnormality identiﬁed Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
E Strongyloides serology The answer is Strongyloides serology -

Despite the fact that the initial stool sample was negative, given the symptoms, ﬁndings on clinical examination, eosinophilia, and patchy pulmonary inﬁltrates on CXR, strongyloides remains the most likely diagnosis. As well as checking the serology, repeat testing of stool samples is advised. Ivermectin given as a 2 day course of therapy has an effectiveness approaching 97%. Albendazole is an alternative, but a one week longer course is required. C CT thorax CT thorax, is incorrect, it is useful to conﬁrm pulmonary inﬁltration, although it does not provide a bacteriological diagnosis. A Anti-TTG antibody testing Anti-TTG antibody testing, is incorrect because whilst there are some features of malabsorption, the raised eosinophil count is against coeliac being the underlying diagnosis. B Aspergillus precipitins Aspergillus precipitins, is incorrect, ABPA is a possible cause of patchy pulmonary inﬁltration, although it is not associated with the GI symptoms seen here. D Endoscopy and small bowel biopsy Endoscopy and small bowel biopsy, is incorrect, it is more useful for conﬁrmation of villous atrophy. Duodenal ﬂuid is potentially useful to conﬁrm the presence of larvae, collected via upper GI endoscopy.

stem: A 31-year-old female is seen in Neurology Outpatients with a 4month history of poor concentration, memory loss and increasing clumsiness. Her partner tells you she has fallen three times in the last few weeks and that she now needs help doing up her laces. She has been incontinent of urine over the last 2 weeks. She is originally from Somalia and came to the UK 5 years ago. On examination, she is cachectic and appears agitated. She has an ataxic gait. She has generalised motor weakness, hyper-reﬂexia and has upgoing plantars bilaterally. There appear to be a number of small skin lesions shown below. She is JC antibody negative. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) results reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Protein 0.35 g/l < 0.45 g/l WCC 1/mm3 < 5/mm3 Red blood count (RBC) 0/mm3 < 5/mm3 Glucose 5.3 mmol/l 2.5–3.9 mmol/l Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain shows cerebral atrophy with wide sulci. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows gross white matter abnormalities, particularly in the periventricular area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B HIV encephalopathy This lady, who has come from Somalia, is likely to have undiagnosed AIDS. HIV encephalopathy (also called AIDS–dementia complex) comes on over a period of months with cognitive dysfunction and behavioural and motor abnormalities. Typically the presentation is of diffuse subcortical dementia, and poor balance, poor coordination, an ataxic gait and generalised motor weakness, and diffuse hyper-reﬂexia are often found. Patients become incontinent and develop seizures. HIV encephalopathy can be prevented by successful highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The skin lesions are characteristic of Kaposi’s sarcoma. Once the encephalopathy occurs, however, reversibility with HAART is variable. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus occurs almost exclusively in elderly patients; in addition, the clinical course is very slowly progressive over many months and years. It would therefore be highly unlikely here. C West Nile encephalitis West Nile encephalitis is caused by the West Nile virus (WNV), which is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Birds are the natural host. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic (most common) to a severe meningoencephalitis. CSF ﬁndings would typically show a raised protein and moderate lymphocytosis. WNV has not been reported in patients who have not travelled outside the UK. A Herpes simplex encephalitis Herpes simplex encephalitis is a viral infection of the brain parenchyma, typically caused by HSV-1 (but less commonly by HSV-2). Patients present with an acute history of fever and clouding of consciousness, with or without meningism. Typical CSF ﬁndings are of a lymphocytosis. D Progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy

Presentation typically includes a much more focal neurological presentation (e.g. hemiparesis, aphasia or ataxia), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows multiple non-enhancing white matter lesions, typically at the grey–white matter interface, without mass effect. The JC virus can usually be isolated on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) in PML, and antibodies to JC virus may also be demonstrated, this being another means of distinguishing between HIV encephalopathy and PML. E Normal-pressure hydrocephalus This classically presents with a triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and impaired cognition. MRI ﬁndings in normalpressure hydrocephalus are of ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement, which was not the case in the described patient.

stem: A 19-year-old student is admitted to the Emergency Department by ambulance. She has recently returned from a holiday to Northern Territory and Queensland in Australia two days ago. She has a severe fever, headache, and vomiting, and feels like her bones are going to break. She has also developed an extensive maculopapular rash. Her temperature is 39.5 oC, her blood pressure (BP) is 110/75 mmHg, and her pulse is 100 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. She has a conjunctival injection. There is generalised muscle ache, and she reluctant to move on the bed. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 148 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 123 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
options: Reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RTPCR) for Chikungunya
Thick and thin ﬁlm for malaria
explanation:
D RT-PCR for Dengue Dengue is an RNA virus which presents with severe fever, headache, and “bone-breaking” joint and muscle pains. Cases are frequently described in Queensland Australia but have not been described in the Northern Territory for a number of years. Early in the illness (≤5 days after symptom onset), laboratory conﬁrmation can be made from a single acute-phase serum specimen by detecting

dengue virus genomic sequences with RT- PCR or DENV nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) antigen via immunoassay. Later in the illness (patient presenting one week after onset of fever) , IgM antiDENV can be detected with ELISA. Treatment is supportive, with ﬂuid replacement and antiﬁbrotics commonly used. C Reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for Chikungunya Dengue is more likely to be found in Queensland than the Chikungunya virus. RT-PCR is the correct screening test at this point for Chikungunya however, as infection is early. It is an RNA virus transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, like Dengue. A Immunoglobulin M (IgM) serology for Chikungunya Although the presentation of Chikungunya fever is similar to that for Dengue, the epidemiology is slightly different, with outbreaks of Chikungunya more common in the Asia-Paciﬁc region outside Australia. It is also too early for IgM serology; antibodies to Chikungunya appear from around the ﬁfth day after infection with the virus. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies appear around 2 weeks after infection and persist for years. B IgM serology for Dengue Although given the clinical presentation of severe fever, bone and muscle pains, headache and macular rash typical of Dengue, it is potentially too early to test for IgM serology. Like Chikungunya, IgM antibodies become positive only around the 5th day post infection. IgG antibodies to Dengue are detectable from around day 7 of the infection. E Thick and thin ﬁlm for malaria Although this presentation creates diagnostic confusion and may be similar to that seen for malaria, malaria is not seen in Australia, while Dengue fever is. It is not impossible that the patient has acquired malaria from somewhere else, but it is extremely unlikely. Hence, a thick and thin ﬁlm is unlikely to be of value.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to Accident and Emergency. He is complaining of worsening breathlessness. It has been progressive for the last month and he is also experiencing a persistent dry cough. His only past medical history is of infective endocarditis 7 years ago which developed as a consequence of injecting drugs intravenously. He admits that he last injected heroin ‘the day before yesterday’ but is unsure how much. He is on no medication and has no drug allergies. He has been staying at a homeless persons’ hostel. On examination, he has a temperature of 39 °C. pulse 120 bpm, BP 140/70 mmHg. Oxygen saturations 93% RA (on room air); RR 26/min. On exertion, he desaturates to 82% breathing room air. He has 2 × 2 cm lymph nodes in his right groin but otherwise no lymphadenopathy. Chest is clear with no evidence of consolidation. He has 2 cm hepatomegaly and a spleen tip is palpable. Cardiovascular examination reveals a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge.
explanation: B IV co-trimoxazole Pneumocystis jirovecii, previously known as Pneumocystis carinii, is the organism responsible for Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP); the most common opportunistic infection in HIV-infected patients. A bronchoscopy will help conﬁrm whether this is Pneumocystis jirovecii or TB, although at the moment the clinical suggestion is more likely Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. E Nebulised salbutamol This would be the treatment for acute obstructive airway disease such as exacerbation of asthma or COPD. The lack of wheeze on auscultation make these unlikely diagnoses. A IV naloxone There is no evidence of opiate toxicity as he is tachypnoeic, not showing respiratory depression, and there is no mention of pin-point pupils. C IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin This could be a considered management plan if the primary diagnosis was infective endocarditis. However, the murmur is most likely to be chronic following the ﬁrst episode of endocarditis and there are several features, such as the severe hypoxia and lung shadowing that infective endocarditis cannot explain. D Isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide This would be the treatment for TB. TB is less likely than PCP because of the diffuse shadowing on the chest X- ray, severe hypoxia worsening on exertion and acute onset of illness

stem: You are asked to review a 35-year-old man with a history of HIV who has been admitted to the Cardiology Ward after myocardial infarction. He has not brought his anti-viral medications into the hospital with him as he collapsed at a restaurant. On examination, he has a peripheral fat loss and increased abdominal obesity. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 114 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 204 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Triglcerides 3.1 mmol/l < 1.5 mmol/l HDL 0.7 mmol/l > 1.0 mmol/l LDL 3.4 mmol/l < 3.5 mmol/l Glucose 8.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/ Which of the following HIV medications is most likely to be associated with the above blood picture?
explanation:
B Zidovudine Zidovudine is a nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor and was the ﬁrst medication developed against HIV. Zidovudine is associated with fat redistribution and biochemical changes consistent with the insulin resistant phenotype seen here; this HIV lipodystrophy picture tends to be worse with zidovudine compared with newer agents. Fosamprenavir, indinavir and abacavir are also associated with insulin resistance but to a lesser extent. A Fosamprenavir Fosamprenavir is a protease inhibitor most commonly used in combination with ritonavir (boosted fosamprenavir). Previously used as a third agent in HAART the British HIV Association (BHIVA) no longer recommends it due to side effects. Though its use is associated with insulin resistance, an alternative option is more likely to have caused the fat lipoatrophy described. C Indinavir Indinavir is a protease inhibitor which is no longer recommended for routine use by the British HIV Association (BHIVA) and has been associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Although indinavir is associated with insulin resistance, an alternative drug is more likely to have caused the described lipoatrophy. D Maraviroc Maraviroc is a CCR5 inhibitor (entry inhibitor). It is only effective in people infected with CCR5 trophic HIV (ie not CXCR4) and therefore testing is required prior to its use. Insulin resistance and

lipoatrophy are not commonly associated with maraviroc use. E Abacavir Abacavir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI). It is recommended by the British HIV Association (BHIVA) in association with lamivudine as an alternative to Truvada as part of a HAART regime. Abacavir cannot be used in patients who are HLAB5701 positive due to a high risk of hypersensitivity. Abacavir may be associated with insulin resistance and lipodystrophy, but to a lesser extent that zidovudine.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is admitted to the Respiratory Ward with a 4day history of shortness of breath and a cough productive of yellow sputum. She also complains of extreme fatigue and multiple episodes of vomiting and diarrhoea. Her appetite is reduced and she feels dehydrated and dizzy. She has a background of psoriasis, which is well controlled with topical steroid cream. There is no other past medical history of note and she reports to have previously been ﬁt and well after returning from a business trip one week ago. On examination, she has a temperature of 38.5 °C. She is tachypnoe- ic with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min and saturations of 97% on 4 litres of oxygen via nasal cannulae. She has a loud chesty cough and bilateral crackles at the lung bases. Her heart rate is 119 bpm and regular, and her blood pressure is 99/65 mmHg. Her heart sounds are normal. She has generalised abdominal tenderness but no focal guarding or palpable masses. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 132 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 12.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 11.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.9 × 109/l 0.8–5.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 304 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 126 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.3 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 125 µm/l 50–120 µm/l EGFR 60+ Bilirubin 20 µmol/l 1–22 µmol/l ALT 35 U/l 7–55 U/l ALP 85 U/l 30–150 U/l Albumin 40 g/l 35–55 g/l CRP 185 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most appropriate initial investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
options: Throat swab for viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
explanation:
D Urinary antigen This patient has legionnaires’ disease, a bacterial pneumonia caused by the bacterium Legionella pneumophila. It presents with symptoms of community-acquired pneumonia. However, additional symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea are commonly seen and blood tests often show hyponatraemia and deranged liver function tests. It is commonly spread in contaminated water supply and a careful travel history is needed as it can spread via air conditioning in hotels. In this case, the patient has returned from a business trip one week ago prior to the onset of her symptoms. The diagnosis of legionnaires’ disease is made by urinary antigen testing. B Acid-fast bacillus (AFB) stain An AFB stain is used in the diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. At least three consecutive positive sputum samples are needed to make a diagnosis. However, they do not play a role in the diagnosis of legionnaires’ disease. A Blood culture

This patient has legionnaire’s disease. A blood culture is a useful investigation in a febrile patient and forms part of the Sepsis Six protocol. However, it is not the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis in this patient as it is conﬁrmed on urinary antigen testing. C Mycoplasma serology This patient has an atypical pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is another bacterium that causes atypical pneumonia. However, the symptoms vary slightly and patients with Mycoplasma pneumonia often have a preceding phase of ﬂu-like symptoms, along with extrapulmonary manifestations, including erythema multiforme or haemolytic anaemia. E Throat swab for viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) A throat swab for viral PCR would not diagnose a bacterial pneumonia such as legionnaires’ disease.

stem: A 24-year-old man from central Africa presents to his brother’s general practitioner while visiting from overseas. He complains of painful groin lymphadenopathy and has a large hydrocoele. In addition, there are changes consistent with severe chronic lymphoedema affecting both lower limbs. Past medical history of note includes epilepsy, for which he takes carbamazepine. He also suffers from indigestion. Elephantiasis is suspected as the underlying reason for his leg swelling. You commence albendazole. Which of the following other interventions is most appropriate in this case?
options: Substitute carbamazepine with another anti-epileptic medication
Immobilise the worst affected limb where possible
explanation:
C Substitute carbamazepine with another anti-epileptic medication This man has lymphatic ﬁlariasis. Filariae resulting in lymphatic obstruction include Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori. Obstruction of lymphatic drainage is caused by the presence of adult worms. One treatment of choice includes albendazole, a broad-spectrum anthelminthic agent, which decreases the availability of ATP as the energy source for the worms, and results eventually in their immobilisation and death. Carbamazepine reduces the efﬁcacy of albendazole and, if possible, should be substituted by another anti- epileptic. Dexamethasone,

praziquantel and cimetidine are recognised to increase the risk of albendazole toxicity. E Immobilise the worst affected limb where possible Immobilisation is likely to make symptoms worse, as lymphatics would collect in the limb and accumulate to cause greater swelling. A Sodium stibogluconate intramuscular (IM) Sodium stibogluconate is used as treatment for leishmaniasis and is of therefore little use in this case. Leishmania are protozoa spread by sandﬂies in Africa, Asia, India, the Middle East, the Mediterranean and Latin America, causing granulomata. Cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions develop at the site of the bite, starting as an itchy papule which crusts to form an ulcer healing over 2-15 months. Visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, has an incubation period of months to years. It spreads to the lymphatic system and multiplies in macrophages, presenting with dry, warty, hyper-pigmented lesions whilst the patient complains of fever, burning feet, arthralgia, cough and epistaxis. Splenomegaly occurs in 96% and hepatomegaly in 63%. Diagnosis is with microscopy of lymph nodes, spleen or bone marrow, or antibody detection. Treatment is with amphotericin, but sodium stibogluconate can also be used. B Paromomycin IM Paromomycin is an antibiotic used to amoebiasis, giardiasis, leishmaniasis and tapeworm infections. D Surgical drainage of lymph nodes The swelling is likely to respond to medical management as the treatment is effective, and therefore there is no need for surgery.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a painless ulcer affecting his glans penis. He admits to unprotected sexual intercourse with a man some two weeks earlier. There is no other past medical history of note. Examination reveals a single oval, painless ulcer, surrounded by a bright erythematous margin. The base is clean and it is discharging clear serum. Dark ﬁeld microscopy of ulcer ﬂuid demonstrates spirochaetes. He is penicillin-allergic. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
explanation:
D Doxycycline

Doxycycline can be given for syphilis as a 14-day twice-daily course. Compliance may be an issue, but recent data suggest it is superior to the use of macrolides because of emergent resistance to azithromycin in particular. A Erythromycin Erythromycin is not a preferred option for the treatment of syphilis. Azithromycin as a single dose was preferred, but this has now begun to fall out of favour because of emergent azithromycin resistance. B Ceftriaxone Given there is up to 20% crossover with penicillin allergy and cephalosporins, and azithromycin is a suitable treatment option, ceftriaxone monotherapy is not recommended here. C Ciproﬂoxacin Quinolones were formerly used in the treatment of gonorrhoea, but signiﬁcant resistance now means that they are no longer a ﬁrst-line option. They may be considered where sensitivity testing conﬁrms ciproﬂoxacin is appropriate. E Trimethoprim Trimethoprim is an appropriate option for urinary tract infection but has no role in the treatment of syphilis.

stem: A 26-year-old woman attends the Sexually Transmitted Disease Clinic. She has noticed postcoital pain on a few occasions and some left-sided pelvic pain. There is a history of unprotected sexual intercourse with three different partners in the last 6 months. Pelvic examination reveals adnexal tenderness. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 134 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 301 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Chlamydia serology Positive Select the most appropriate therapy from those given below?
explanation: D Doxycycline Doxycycline given at a dose of 100 mg bd is an appropriate therapy for chlamydia infection. An alternative is azithromycin, which is an attractive alternative as it can be given as a single dose. Sexual contacts should also be traced and treated if possible. A signiﬁcant number of female patients infected with chlamydia may go on to develop pelvic inﬂammatory disease. One case series unfortunately estimated that the diagnosis is missed in nearly 50% of Emergency Room attendees. E Clarithromycin It binds to 50S rRNA in the bacterial ribosome preventing translation of peptides and is used for the treatment of streptococcal throat infection, lower respiratory tract infection, Helicobacter pylori infection and Lyme disease. A Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a second-generation ﬂuoroquinolone which selectively inhibit type II topoisomerases, causing DNA unwinding in bacterial cells. It can be used for respiratory tract infections, cellulitis, prostatitis, endocarditis, gastroenteritis and otitis externa. However current advice is to avoid use unless other alternative antibiotics are unavailable; this is due to risk of long term or permanent debilitating side effects such as tendonitis. B Penicillin V Penicillin V, or phenoyxymethylpenicillin, is a β-lactam bactericidal antibiotic indicated in streptococcal throat infections, otitis media and cellulitis and can be used prophylactically following splenectomy. C Amoxicillin It is a β-lactam antibiotic used for the treatment of streptococcal throat infections, lower respiratory tract infections, cellulitis and urinary tract infections.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a fever, shortness of breath, muscle aches, and vague right upper quadrant tenderness. He just returned from a family holiday to a farm in Switzerland. He is normally well and takes no regular medications. His temperature is 39.6 oC, his blood pressure (BP) is 118/80 mmHg, and his pulse is 106 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is occasional wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 149 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 14.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 243 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 145 mg/l < 10 mg/l ALT 1231 u/l 29 - 33 u/l You suspect he might have Q fever. Which of the following best describes the likely causative organism?
explanation:
A Gram-negative intracellular coccobacilli Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii (C burnetii). C burnetii is a strictly intracellular, gram-negative coccobacilli. Many species of mammals, birds, and ticks are reservoirs of C. burnetii, and as a consequence outbreaks are seen on farms and areas where animals are processed. A most recent outbreak was seen on farms in Switzerland and France. Outbreaks in Europe often manifest with symptoms of hepatitis, which ﬁts with the marked elevation in transaminases seen here. Doxycycline is the initial intervention of choice.

D Gram-positive extracellular coccus Streptococci and staphylococci are examples of gram-positive extracellular cocci. The clinical picture seen here with signs and symptoms of infective hepatitis in a person who has visited a farm is much more consistent with an atypical infection such as Q fever. B Gram-negative extracellular rod Escherichia coli (E coli) are an example of gram-negative extracellular rod-shaped bacteria which are a cause of gastroenteritis, particularly traveller’s diarrhoea, and a common cause of urinary tract infection. A Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus Neisseria is an example of gram-negative intracellular diplococci. There are a number of pathogenic Neisseria including gonorrhoea, which is responsible for gonorrhoea infection, and meningitis which is responsible for meningitis/Neisseria related septicaemia. E Gram-positive extracellular rod The Bacillus species are a good example of gram-positive extracellular rod-shaped bacteria. Examples include Bacillus cereus (B cereus) which causes food poisoning, particularly with respect to re-heated rice, and Bacillus anthracis, the cause of anthrax. B cereus requires supportive therapy only, with symptoms usually settling within 24 hours.

stem: A 63-year-old woman is admitted with breathlessness. She has a background of diabetes.
explanation: C Sulphadiazine Nocardia asteroides is an actinomycete infection responsible for pneumonia and cerebral abscess formation in the immunocompromised. Sulphonamides are the intervention of choice, with both sulphadiazine and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole potential options. These antibiotics act as inhibitors of bacterial dihydropteroate synthetase. Alternative antimicrobial agents with activity against Nocardia include amikacin, imipenem, meropenem, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, minocycline, linezolid, tigecycline, and amoxicillinclavulanic acid. E Gentamicin Nocardia asteroides tends to be resistant to gentamicin, preventing it from being a treatment option here. A Trimethoprim Although trimethoprim is a component of co-trimoxazole, used as the ﬁrst line therapy for Nocardia in the US, the beneﬁt of the trimethoprim component of the drug is unclear. B Ciproﬂoxacin Next generation quinolones such as levoﬂoxacin and moxiﬂoxacin are preferred to ciproﬂoxacin for the treatment of Nocardia infection. However, a 2019 Ut government drug safety update advises that ﬂuoroquinolones should now be avoided in non-severe or self-limiting infections and in mild to moderate infections unless other commonly recommended antibiotics are not suitable. This is due to rare reports of long lasting or potentially irreversible side effects such as tendinitis and peripheral neuropathy. Fluoroquinolones should be used with special caution in patients older than 60 years or those with renal impairment. Treatment with quinolones should be discontinued promptly at ﬁst signs of serious adverse reactions. D Chloramphenicol Chloramphenicol was a preferred agent for treating Nocardia until the 1990’s, but is now considered when resistance to other options is identiﬁed

stem: A 19-year-old woman returns home with diarrhoea, having worked on a gap year project in Africa. She also complains of abdominal bloating, that her stools are difﬁcult to ﬂush away and of excessive ﬂatulence. She has lost her appetite over the past couple of weeks and has lost 3 kg in weight. On examination, she has mild pyrexia (37.6 °C) and looks bloated. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 260 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 39 g/l 35–55 g/l Stool sample No cysts or ovae seen Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her?
explanation: D Metronidazole The history and exposure described are typical for giardiasis, infection with the protozoan parasite Giardia. First- line treatment of choice is with metronidazole or tinidazole. C Albendazole Albendazole is a parasitic drug with activity against a range of helminths and some protozoa. It is used second line to treat Giardia refractory to metronidazole. A Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotic with activity against many Gram negative, and some Gram-positive, bacteria. It is sometimes used to treat traveller’s diarrhoea, although recent recommendation is to avoid the use of quinolones wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating side effects. In this case the history and exposure are typical for Giardia and therefore ciproﬂoxacin would not be appropriate treatment. B Doxycycline Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity. It is used to treat Gram-positive and atypical bacterial infections, as well as malaria. In this case the history and exposure are typical for Giardia, and therefore doxycycline would not be appropriate treatment. E Artemesin Artemisinins are a group of drugs with activity against all species of malarial parasites. Artemisinin-based drugs are now ﬁrst line for the treatment of severe and complicated falciparum malaria and non-falciparum disease. The case described is typical of giardiasis, and artemisinin would not be the treatment of choice. 21022

stem: A 35-year-old African gynaecologist attends his pre-employment check for a 1-year fellowship in the United Kingdom. He has no past medical history of note. Clinical examination is entirely normal. Routine blood workup is normal, apart from his hepatitis serology, which is described below. Investigation Result HBsAg Negative HBeAg Negative Anti-HBc Negative Anti-HBs Positive Anti-HCV Positive HCV RNA Negative What is the correct interpretation of the above results?
options: Hepatitis B carrier, hepatitis C infection
Hepatitis B immunisation, hepatitis C immunisation
Hepatitis B positive, hepatitis C carrier
Hepatitis B immunisation, previous hepatitis C infection
Previous hepatitis B, previous hepatitis C infection
explanation: D Hepatitis B immunisation, previous hepatitis C infection The presence of anti-HBs alone suggests immunisation to hepatitis B, while negative HCV RNA and positive anti-HCV conﬁrms recovery from previous hepatitis C infection. E Previous hepatitis B, previous hepatitis C infection Although this patient has previously had hepatitis C, previous hepatitis B infection would appear as anti-HBc positive and HBsAg negative. A Hepatitis B carrier, hepatitis C infection The presence of anti-HBs alone suggests immunisation to hepatitis B, while negative HCV RNA and positive anti-HCV conﬁrm recovery from previous hepatitis C infection. A hepatitis B carrier would be anti-HBc positive and anti-HBs positive. B Hepatitis B immunisation, hepatitis C immunisation Although this patient has been vaccinated against hepatitis B, there is no vaccination against hepatitis C. C Hepatitis B positive, hepatitis C carrier A hepatitis B positive result would appear as HBsAg with or without HBeAg.

stem: A 31-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department, having awoken with neck spasms and rigidity. He suffered a ‘dirty’ wound three days earlier after falling from a ladder into a patch of soil. On examination, his BP is 145/82 mmHg and his heart rate is 85 bpm and regular. He has neck and jaw spasms, and his abdominal wall muscles appear rigid. There is markedly increased tone in all four limbs, coupled with intermittent spasms. A wound on his left calf is surrounded by erythema and appears to be oozing pus. Which of the following is the most important next step?
explanation: B Human tetanus immunoglobulin This patient has an infected wound and presents with tetanus signs and symptoms. Human tetanus immunoglobulin acts as an antitoxin to neutralise unbound toxin. As the toxin binds irreversibly and debridement may cause the release of further tetanus toxin into the circulation, debridement should therefore be avoided until the patient has had human tetanus immunoglobulin administered (a delay of a few hours is necessary). Without administering this, there is a risk that neurological symptoms could signiﬁcantly worsen during the course of wound debridement. E Drantolene Drantolene is a skeletal muscle relaxant which is effective in treating patients with severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). Here, the absence of a described fever, altered mental status, autonomic stability and the presence of a medication, like antipsychotics and antiemetics, which can cause NMS count against this as a differential. A Debridement of the wound Although the wound will contain a signiﬁcant amount of unbound tetanus toxin, there is a risk that debridement may result in further toxin release. Immunoglobulin must be administered ﬁrst. C IV benzylpenicillin Although benzylpenicillin is effective in clearing Clostridium tetani infection, immunoglobulin is a more important initial step. Penicillins may also worsen the neurological effects of tetanus infection, compared to metronidazole, because of blockade of the gamma-aminobutyric acid pathway. D Benztropine Drug-induced dystonia, such as an oculogyric crisis caused by metoclopramide, responds to benztropine. Here the lack of eye deviation and constant tonic contraction hint more towards tetanus as the underlying cause. Benztropine has no role in tetanus treatment.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with some crusted vesicles on the back of his left hand and enlarged lymph nodes in the left axilla. He says he has had a fever and felt off-colour over the past few days. A cat scratched his hand the weekend prior. What is the most likely causative agent responsible for his symptoms?
explanation:
A Bartonella henselae (B henselae) This patient has cat scratch fever. Lesions occur 3-12 days after an initial scratch from a cat (often one infested with ﬂeas or a kitten) and are accompanied by a non-speciﬁc illness and axillary lymphadenopathy. B henselae is an intracellular bacterium that infects red blood cells and is the cause of cat scratch fever. No treatment is usually required, although azithromycin can be used for patients with marked lymphadenopathy. E Streptococcus gallolyticus (S gallolyticus) S gallolyticus (formerly known as Streptococcus bovis) is a cause of bacterial endocarditis and is often associated with either a colonic malignancy or with abnormalities of the biliary tree. When it is identiﬁed as a cause of endocarditis it should prompt imaging of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract to rule out malignancy. B Clostridium perfringens (C perfringens) C perfringens is the cause of gas gangrene, where bacterial infection leads to subcutaneous emphysema and rapidly spreading infection. It is a surgical emergency which requires debridement of necrotic tissue as well as antibiotic therapy. Clindamycin, metronidazole, and rifampicin are potential interventions. C Pasteurella multocida (P multocida)

P multocida is a cause of cellulitis at the sites of injury in patients with both dog and cat bites. It contrasts to the picture here, where there are very limited local lesions and distant lymphadenopathy. Animal bites are usually managed with co-amoxiclav speciﬁcally to cover against Pasteurella infection. A Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus) Staphylococcal infection is associated with marked local cellulitis in contrast to the relatively minor local symptoms seen here. Flucloxacillin is the intervention of choice for staphylococcal cellulitis, with a macrolide such as clarithromycin the alternative option in patients with penicillin allergy.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of productive cough, weight loss and night sweats. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is on long-term corticosteroid therapy for autoimmune disease. On examination, he is febrile and has coarse crackles in the right upper lung ﬁeld. A CXR reveals a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. Sputum Gram staining shows ﬁlamentous, branching and Gram-positive rods. What is the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis of nocardiosis?
options: Sputum culture on standard bacterial media
Blood culture for aerobic and anaerobic organisms
Biopsy of the affected lung tissue
explanation:
A Acid-fast staining of sputum samples Nocardia species are partially acid-fast due to the mycolic acids in their cell walls. Acid-fast staining (using a modiﬁed Ziehl– Neelsen method) is a critical diagnostic test. Positive results, along with branching Gram- positive rods on Gram staining, strongly suggest Nocardia infection. D Biopsy of the affected lung tissue Lung biopsy may be considered in cases where sputum samples fail to provide a diagnosis. However, it is invasive and not the ﬁrst-line investigation when sputum samples can provide the necessary information. B Sputum culture on standard bacterial media While Nocardia can grow on standard bacterial media, prolonged incubation (up to two weeks) is required for colonies to become visible. Culture is an important diagnostic tool, but acid-fast staining provides more rapid results. C Blood culture for aerobic and anaerobic organ-

isms Blood cultures are less sensitive for diagnosing nocardiosis, as it is primarily a localised infection in the lungs, brain or skin, with haematogenous spread occurring only in severe cases. E Fungal culture of sputum samples Fungal culture is not appropriate for diagnosing Nocardia, which is a bacterial organism. Fungal cultures target organisms such as Aspergillus or Histoplasma, and would not detect Nocardia.

stem: A 35-year-old man returns from a signiﬁcant period abroad working abroad for a bank in Barbados. He complains of chronic diarrhoea over the past few months with associated weight loss, fatigue, and now lower limb oedema. Examination reveals pallor, stomatitis and glossitis. His BMI is only 20 and he admits to having lost 6 kg in weight in 2 months. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal values Blood count and ﬁlm Megaloblastic anaemia Albumin 24 g/l 35 - 55 g/l D-xylose malabsorption test Positive Faecal fat excretion 8.5 g / 24 h < 7 g / 24h Anti-endomysial antibodies Negative Which diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
C Tropical sprue First described by William Hillary in an account of medical observations of Barbados, this disease is most common in the Caribbean and the Far East. It is characterised by a picture of small intestinal malabsorption and the cause is thought to be infectious in origin. Jejunal biopsy reveals mild villous atrophy, increased villous crypts and mononuclear cellular inﬁltrates, enlarged epithelial cells, and large nuclei caused by folate and/or vitamin B12 deﬁciency. Tetracyclines or ampicillin are treatments of choice; prolonged therapy for 6 months or more may be required. Folate and B12 deﬁciencies should also be corrected: folic acid with oral replacement and B12 with

intramuscular injection. Complete recovery is possible with appropriate therapy. C Giardiasis Giardiasis can result in a malabsorption type picture, but the symptom picture is similar to intermittent irritable bowel syndrome after an acute diarrhoeal illness, rather than the marked faecal fat loss seen here. A Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is the alternative possible diagnosis, although negative anti-endomysial antibodies are possible in coeliac patients with selective IgA deﬁciency, given the history of travel to Barbados, tropical sprue is more likely. B Helicobacter pylori infection Helicobacter pylori infection is a cause of peptic ulcer disease rather than small bowel malabsorption syndromes. D HIV enteropathy HIV enteropathy may present with the symptoms of malabsorption seen here and could be considered a differential, although we are not provided with any pointers in the scenario towards possible HIV infection.

stem: A 17-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 3-week history of malaise, fever, abdominal pain and reduced appetite, with associated weight loss. She also reported nausea and vomiting. Although she suffered from diarrhoea at the beginning of the illness, this seems to have settled now. She did not have any respiratory symptoms. One month previously, she had noticed a rash on the front of her shins associated with lumps in her groin area, which had settled but which had been followed by the onset of her current symptoms. She took a picture of her shin at the time, which is shown below. On examination, her temperature was 37.1 °C. Her abdomen was generally tender, especially in the right lower quadrant. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. There were several small ulcers on her pharynx. There were no rashes, and she had a BCG scar on her upper arm. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 202 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bilirubin 9.0 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 19 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 61 IU/l 30–130 IU/l CXR Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Yersinia enterocolitica infection The patient has mesenteric adenitis, characterised by fever, abdominal pain and tenderness of the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. In association, the patient may also experience nausea, vomiting and aphthous ulcers of the mouth, all of which are present in this case. The symptoms may be preceded by the appearance of erythema nodosum – painful, raised red/purple lesion on the front of the shin – which is the ﬂeeting rash described by the patient in this case. Yersinia enterocolitica can also cause a reactive asymmetrical polyarthritis, enteritis, uveitis, appendicitis, and glomerulonephritis amongst other complications. C Salmonella infection This patient does not have diarrhoea, which would be unusual in Salmonella infection; furthermore, she has had symptoms for several weeks, whereas Salmonella typically causes acute symptoms. This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with mesenteric adenitis, and also erythema nodosum and mouth ulcers. This history would be consistent with Yersinia enterocolitica infection, which can also cause polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications. A Campylobacter infection Campylobacter typically causes a bloody diarrhoea; it would be unusual to have an infection without diarrhoea. It is also usually an acute illness, whereas this patient has three weeks of symptoms. This patient’s fever, abdominal pain (particularly in the right lower quadrant) and lack of diarrhoea, combined with the preceding rash of erythema nodosum, and then mouth ulcers, are suggestive of Yersinia enterocolitica infection. It causes a mesenteric adenitis, which accounts for her abdominal symptoms, and can also cause mouth ulcers, polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications.

B Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection This patient has had BCG vaccination (which does not rule out tuberculosis, but does reduce her risk). She also has a normal chest X-ray, which would be unusual in the context of tuberculosis. She does have a history and signs consistent with mesenteric adenitis and erythema nodosum (both of which can be caused by tuberculosis) – the right lower quadrant tenderness, vague history of malaise, abdominal pain and nausea without diarrhoea – and she also has mouth ulcers. This history would ﬁt with Yersinia enterocolitica infection, which can also cause polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications. C Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis does cause erythema nodosum, as described here. However, typically sarcoidosis would cause breathless and a dry cough, with an abnormal chest X-ray, but this patient has no respiratory symptoms or signs. In addition, she has a history and examination consistent with mesenteric adenitis; sarcoidosis would be very unlikely to cause this. A more likely diagnosis would be Yersinia enterocolitica infection, which would explain the mesenteric adenitis, the mouth ulcers and the erythema nodosum; it can also cause polyarthritis, uveitis, glomerulonephritis and other complications.

stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea since returning from a holiday to India one week ago. He reports > 10 bowel motions a day. Before this, he has been well, with no past medical history. On examination, he is afebrile. His eyes are sunken and he has reduced skin turgor. He has a heart rate of 130 bpm and blood pressure of 98/52 mmHg. On auscultation, his chest is clear and his heart sounds are normal. He is saturating well on room air. There is generalised discomfort on palpation of his abdomen, but no guarding or masses. Which of the following is the most common complication, given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Acute tubular necrosis

This patient has a history of profuse diarrhoea following a trip to India. Clinical examination ﬁndings indicate severe dehydration with sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor and hypotension. The history and examination together suggest a diagnosis of cholera caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Cholera is associated with poor sanitation and drinking contaminated water. The mainstay of treatment is aggressive ﬂuid resuscitation to prevent circulatory collapse, along with antibiotic treatment. Tetracyclines, such as doxycycline and ciproﬂoxacin, are both antibiotics of choice. There are a number of complications of the disease, including circulatory collapse, acute renal failure, sepsis, severe hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Acute tubular necrosis due to V. cholerae infection leads to acute renal failure and may require treatment with dialysis, although this frequently occurs where facilities are not available. A Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is a complication of Campylobacter jejuni infection, which leads to ascending paralysis that often requires Intensive Care support. Campylobacter infection is the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the United Kingdom. For V. cholerae infection, GBS is not a common complication. B Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a complication associated with Escherichia coli infection. It consists of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and kidney failure. It is usually associated with infection with the E. coli strain O157:H7. Given this man’s presentation with profuse watery diarrhoea following a holiday in India, the most likely diagnosis here is V. cholerae infection, the most common complication of which is acute renal failure. D Small bowel perforation Small bowel perforation is a complication of V. cholerae infection. However, this is less common than acute renal failure due to acute tubular necrosis. E Toxic megacolon Toxic megacolon is a complication associated with diarrhoeal diseases such as Clostridium difﬁcile infection and amoebiasis. Although bowel complications can rarely arise due to V. cholerae infection, it is more likely to cause small bowel obstruction, ileus or perforation, rather than toxic megacolon.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who received a cadaveric renal transplant two years ago comes to the Emergency Department complaining of watery diarrhoea that began three days ago. She has just returned from a holiday to Tunisia. Medication includes immunosuppression and ramipril for control of blood pressure. On examination, her temperature is 38.4 °C, her BP is 120/68 mmHg with a 20 mmHg postural drop and her heart rate is 92 bpm and regular. She looks dehydrated and has a soft, diffusely tender abdomen. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 185 μmol/l(142 μmol/l at the last clinic visit) 50–120 µmol/l Stool sample Oocysts (4-6 µm) identified, stained Red with modified ZN stain Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts only
explanation:
D Supportive therapy and oral nitazoxanide This woman almost certainly has Cryptosporidium acquired through the water supply at her Tunisian hotel. Given that she is signiﬁcantly dehydrated, as evidenced by her postural drop and elevated creatinine, it is appropriate to treat her with anti-microbial therapy. Patients with immunocompromising conditions other than HIV (eg, those who have undergone solid organ transplant) have also been reported to have refractory cryptosporidiosis. For such patients, the dose of immunosuppressive therapy should be reduced, if possible, and antimicrobial therapy should be started. Nitazoxanide (500 to1000 mg twice daily) interferes with the ability of the parasite to generate energy, by blocking the pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase reaction. Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts is of course also an essential part of therapy. C Supportive therapy and oral loperamide Given that this patient has signiﬁcant dehydration associated with diarrhoea, supportive therapy is an important aspect of treatment. However, the history is suggestive of an underlying infectious aetiology and in this context loperamide would be contraindicated. A Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts

only This patient’s clinical presentation and stool microscopy results are highly suggestive of Cryptosporidium. Supportive therapy with oral rehydration salts is an important part of her treatment; however, in the context of immunosuppression and signiﬁcant dehydration, antimicrobial treatment would also be indicated. B Supportive therapy and oral ciproﬂoxacin This patient’s presentation is suggestive of Cryptosporidium diarrhoea. Supportive therapy is important, but ciproﬂoxacin is not a recognised treatment. Furthermore quinolone use should be avoided wherever an effective alternative is available due to risk of debilitating side effects. E Supportive therapy and oral metronidazole This patient’s presentation is suggestive of Cryptosporidium diarrhoea. Supportive therapy is important, but metronidazole is not an effective treatment.

stem: A 31-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe, unremitting headache and muscle aches after recently returning from a business trip to the northern Philippines. He has been suffering from drenching fevers and sweats for ﬁve days since returning and tells you a rash started around two days into his illness. On examination, there is a maculopapular rash, conjunctival and pharyngeal injection, as well as lymphadenopathy affecting the neck lymph nodes. He has a fever of 39.5 °C. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
E Paracetamol The most likely diagnosis is dengue fever, which is endemic throughout the Philippines. Dengue fever is caused by infection with one of four subtypes of the dengue virus and was ﬁrst described in Chinese writings as early as AD 265. It typically produces severe fever, headache, rash and arthralgia, and in many cases, it is a self- limiting illness that lasts 5–7 days. The fever may only disappear for one day and then reappear, the so-called ‘saddleback’ pattern. A more severe form – dengue haemorrhagic fever – occasionally presents and requires more intensive supportive therapy, including correction of clotting abnormalities. As in this case, uncomplicated dengue should be managed with IV ﬂuid rehydration and paracetamol for pain relief and as an antipyretic.

D Oral quinine Oral quinine is a treatment option for malaria. The risk of malaria, except on Palawan and Mindanao Islands, is low and almost nonexistent in urban areas. The description of a maculopapular rash in the setting of muscle aches is more in keeping with dengue, which is endemic in the Philippines, rather than malaria. A A thick and thin ﬁlm The risk of malaria, except on Palawan and Mindanao Islands, is low and almost non-existent in urban areas. The description of a maculopapular rash in the setting of muscle aches is more in keeping with dengue, which is endemic in the Philippines, rather than malaria. Thick and thin ﬁlms, the standard investigation that can help identify malaria and the species involved, are therefore not required. B IV broad-spectrum antibiotics Although this patient has a fever, there is no evidence of a source of a bacterial infection. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are therefore not indicated. C IV quinine IV quinine can be used as a ‘loading dose’ in severe malaria. Severe malaria is characterised by the presence of Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia, impaired consciousness, generalised weakness, seizures, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia and acute renal failure. As these features are not present, IV quinine is, therefore, not indicated.

stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) comes to the Emergency Department for review. He felt something ‘go’ at the base of his left ankle, and he is now unable to weight bear or to move his foot up and down. He is currently suffering from an exacerbation of his COPD and has been prescribed prednisolone and oﬂoxacin by an Emergency General Practitioner (EGP). His other medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, and ramipril for hypertension and ischaemic cardiovascular disease. Examination of his left lower limb reveals a ruptured Achilles tendon. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his ruptured Achilles tendon?
explanation:
C Oﬂoxacin

Oﬂoxacin has been recognised in rare cases to cause tendon rupture, and the case rate may be further increased when prednisolone is also prescribed. Other problems with quinolone use can include arthralgia, pain in the extremities, gait disturbance, neuropathies associated with paraesthesia, depression, fatigue, memory impairment, sleep disorders, and impaired hearing, vision, taste, and smell. For these reasons, routine use of the class is no longer recommended, and the Common Safety Method (CSM) issued a warning to this effect in 2019. D Prednisolone Prednisolone use doesn’t lead to tendon rupture per se and is an essential component of the armamentarium to manage acute exacerbation of COPD. It is associated with increased insulin resistance, which may precipitate worsening of glycaemic control in patients who take it. In patients taking quinolones, it may further increase the risk of tendon rupture. A Aspirin Aspirin may increase the chance of traumatic bruising, but it is not associated with an increased risk of tendon rupture. Speciﬁcally, quinolones are not advised to be used in the management of bacterial infections unless no other options are available. B Atorvastatin Atorvastatin is associated with myositis, rather than with tendon rupture. Myositis is more likely to occur with drug-drug interactions which increase systemic exposure to statins. As atorvastatin is metabolised by the Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) system, potent inhibitors of 3A4 such as macrolide antibiotics may drive accumulation of statins. In patients taking these in combination with a background of atorvastatin or simvastatin, the dose of statin should be temporarily reduced or stopped. E Ramipril The major concerns associated with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor use are signiﬁcant worsening of renal function in patients who have a background of renovascular disease and angioedema. It is important to note that episodes of angioedema related to ACE inhibitor use may be seen many months after starting therapy, and do not necessarily need to be seen close to therapy initiation.

stem: A 45-year-old Eastern European man is identiﬁed at an asylum assessment centre as suffering from persistent cough. On questioning, he admits to fever, night sweats and weight loss which have continued for nearly a year. Occasionally, his sputum has been blood-stained. Past medical history includes smoking unﬁltered cigarettes for the past 20 years. On examination, his body mass index is noted to be 17; he is pyrexial at 37.9°C. On examination, there is non-speciﬁc wheeze and occasional crackles. Which of the following would be the most appropriate initial investigation in this case?
explanation: A Chest X-ray This history is highly suspicious for either pulmonary tuberculosis or underlying bronchial carcinoma. The most appropriate initial investigation therefore would be a chest X-ray to look for calciﬁed nodules or hilar lymph node calciﬁcation in primary infection, or ﬁbrosis and cavitation in the case of reactivation of the tubercle. E Mycobacterium serology Mycobacterium serology is not suggested as ﬁrst-line investigation. T-spot testing can be used to help aid diagnosis. A Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax Chest X-ray should be able to demonstrate pathological apical ﬁndings and a CT is seldom necessary. However, if a chest X-ray is normal then a CT can be helpful in ﬁnding further lesions. B Bronchoscopy with induced sputum First attempts should be to use sputum samples to test for acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, with conﬁrmation by growth. If no sputum can be obtained by coughing, then sputum should be induced. D HIV testing Clearly HIV positivity may increase the risk of tuberculosis, and testing should be considered later.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presented with a history of an abrupt onset of high fever, headache, cough and abdominal pain. About 2 days later, she developed a maculopapular rash that began on the extremities and there was associated swelling of the hands and feet. She works as a kindergarten teacher. She has no past medical history that she is aware of, but is unsure of her vaccination history as her parents divorced when she was young and there may have been missed vaccinations during the divorce proceedings. She denies any IV drug use and does not take any regular tablets. She a tattoo on her right ankle that she had done 3 months ago while on holiday in the USA. Apart from that trip, during which she was camping with friends, she has not had any other journeys outside of the UK. On examination, there is a rash as described affecting the hands and feet, but no other lesions. Her chest is clear on auscultation and she has no meningisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Atypical measles syndrome Atypical measles syndrome (AMS) occurs in persons who were incompletely immunised against measles. This may occur either because they were given the old killed-virus measles vaccine (no longer available) or they were given the attenuated (weakened) live measles vaccine which had been inactivated due to improper storage. The latter does not prevent measles but causes an alteration in its expression, resulting in AMS. The presentation of the patient above is typical of AMS: fever, headache, cough, headache and abdominal pain followed by a rash with oedema of hands and feet 1–2 days afterwards. Key to the diagnosis is also an immunisation history suggestive of incomplete immunity and contact with children, who are more likely to have measles. Virus isolation, serological studies, or both, may be necessary to conﬁrm the diagnosis. D Leptospirosis Leptospirosis is caused by Leptospira interrogans and is spread via rat urine. Contact can occur with activities associated with exposure to water, such as canoeing, cycling through puddles or swimming outdoors. Following an incubation period of 20 days there is fever, myalgia, chest pain and there can be haemoptysis. There is no clear exposure within the range of the incubation period and this would not explain her rash, abdominal pain or oedema. A Rocky Mountain spotted fever This condition is caused by infection with Rickettsiae rickettsii, a tick-borne pathogen endemic to the Rocky Mountains and the south-eastern USA, after an incubation period of days to up to 2 weeks. There is typically headache, high fever and muscle ache with abdominal ache and vomiting. This is followed by a macular rash of the hands and feet 2–5 days later which can then spread and become haemorrhagic. While the clinical description is similar, the fact that the trip was 3 months ago to a possible endemic area makes this diagnosis very unlikely. C Atypical pneumonia While she has a cough, fever and systemic symptoms, her hand and foot oedema, clear chest and abdominal pain make this a less likely diagnosis. Rashes with atypical pneumonia can occur, such as erythema multiforme. E Meningococcal meningitis While the patient does have a headache, fever and rash, it is not in keeping with a description of meningism such as neck stiffness and

photophobia and the rash is not petechial or non-blanching. Being in contact with children would increase the risk of meningitis.

stem: A 25-year-old man who has recently returned from a trip to Africa attends the clinic because he is feeling unwell. You understand that he had been swimming in a local river each day, while helping out on a school building project. After swimming, he noticed an itchy rash on his skin. Around a week later, he returned to the UK. Another 4 weeks passed, and symptoms of a viral illness have now developed including fever, myalgia, headache and lethargy. He is pyrexial 38.5 °C. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.0 × 10 /l(Increased eosinophil count) 4.0–11.0 x 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 290 × 10 /l 150–400 x 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 62 IU/l 5–30 IU/l CXR
explanation:
C Praziquantel This man has Katayama fever, which has developed some 4-6 weeks after infection with Schistosomes. It is usually caused by either schistosoma japonicum or mansonii infection. The high egg and worm antigen load is thought to lead to a serum sickness type syndrome. Management involves treatment with Praziquantel, an anti-heminthic agent which leads to a cure in around 85% of patients. In those who are not cured, the egg load is normally markedly reduced. A Quinine sulphate This would be a possible treatment for malaria. Malaria might have been suggested as a possible diagnosis by travelling to Africa and returning with a fever and malaise, but the history of an itchy rash

following swimming makes this a less likely diagnosis. Also, the absence of jaundice makes this a less likely diagnosis. B Paracetamol This would be part of supportive management if a diagnosis such as dengue fever was suspected. Whilst dengue could explain the myalgia, headache and fever, the incubation period is too long. D Primaquine This is a treatment option for malaria making it an incorrect choice. E Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin could be used as treatment for various bacterial infections but is no longer recommended as ﬁrst line if other options are available due to a small but signiﬁcant risk of permanent or long lasting debilitating side effects. The history of fever in the returning traveller is unlikely to warrant ciproﬂoxacin as treatment.

stem: A 32-year-old man was admitted after a motorcycle accident in which he suffered extensive soft tissue injury to his right lower leg. Prior to the accident, he had been ﬁt and well. He was reviewed on the ward 5 days later and was complaining of thoracic back pain. On examination, his temperature was 37.8 °C. He was tender over the T8 vertebra. Investigations: X-ray whole spine Normal MRI whole spine (T2) High signal in disc space; high signal in adjacent endplates, signifying bone marrow oedema: likely discitis Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible for his back pain?
explanation:
C Staphylococcus aureus This patient has symptoms and signs of discitis, which is conﬁrmed on MRI. It is common for X-rays to appear normal in the early stages of disease. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of discitis in immunocompetent patients and patients who do not use intravenous drugs. Given this patient’s extensive soft tissue injury, it is especially likely that Staph. aureus was able to enter his bloodstream and cause his discitis. He should have multiple sets of

blood cultures to conﬁrm the organism and its sensitivities. Sometimes needle aspiration of the disc space under imaging guidance is required for identiﬁcation. Once the organism and sensitivities are conﬁrmed, he should be treated with 6–8 weeks of intravenous antibiotics. D Staphylococcus epidermidis This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with infective discitis. It is common for X-rays to appear normal in the early stages of the disease. Staph. epidermidis is a common skin commensal and can be a cause of infective discitis, especially in a trauma setting, as seen here. However, it is not the most common cause, and therefore is not the most likely. Staphylococcus aureus would be a much more common cause of infective discitis in an immunocompetent individual, especially given the patient’s extensive soft tissue injury. A Clostridium perfringens Cl. perfringens causes gastroenteritis and gas gangrene, but would be a very uncommon cause of discitis. This patient has thoracic back pain and MRI ﬁndings consistent with infective discitis. It is common for the X-ray to appear normal in the early stages. The most likely causative organism, given his extensive soft tissue injury, is Staphylococcus aureus. This is the most common cause of discitis in the immunocompetent. B Mycobacterium tuberculosis This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with infective discitis. It is common for the X-ray to appear normal in the early stages of infection. Tuberculosis is an important cause of discitis and spinal abscesses (also known as Pott’s disease), but this patient was well before his accident with no symptoms of tuberculosis. He is not immunocompromised. The most common causative organism in discitis is Staphylococcus aureus: given his extensive soft tissue injury, this is particularly likely to be the causative organism in this case. E Viridans streptococci This patient has symptoms and signs of infective discitis, which is conﬁrmed on MRI: it is common for X-rays to appear normal in the early stages of the disease. Viridans streptococci are a relatively common cause of infective discitis in intravenous drug users or the immunocompromised: however, this patient is neither. The most common cause of infective discitis in the immunocompetent is Staphylococcus aureus, and this is made more likely by the patient’s extensive soft tissue injury.

stem: You are examining the peak and trough concentrations of gentamicin from a 32-year-old man who is treated with a once-a-day dosing regimen. You wish to minimise the nephrotoxicity from the antibiotic. Where is the most likely site of renal damage due to gentamicin?
explanation: D Proximal tubule Aminoglycoside related renal damage occurs predominantly in the proximal tubule. Aminoglycoside molecules bind to anion phospholipids within the plasma membrane of proximal tubular cells. They are taken up and transported by lysosomes to the Golgi body where they effectively act as a mitochondrial poison.
