E Vascular endothelium Vascular endothelial cells are not subject to damage by gentamicin. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) are renoprotective because they inhibit efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Other agents such as Sodiumglucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors are also thought to be renoprotective because they improve microvascular function. A Collecting duct Aminoglycosides are not taken up in collecting duct cells. Absorption of water in the collecting duct is governed by aquaporin2 expression, which is partially under the control of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH). Other biologically active agents which inﬂuence aquaporin-2 expression include bile salts. In patients with chronic liver disease, accumulation of bile acids may reduce water excretion and increase the risks of acute kidney injury. B Distal tubule Gentamicin impacts on cells in the proximal tubule. Cisplatin is an example of an agent that is toxic for distal tubular epithelial cells. Effects on renal function are generally dose-related, and both aminoaciduria and proteinuria are seen. C Loop of Henle The loop of Henle is not the primary site of toxicity for aminoglycosides. The function of the descending loop of Henle is to allow for reabsorption of water. The ascending loop of Henle is where sodium, potassium, and chloride ions are reabsorbed via the Na-KCl cotransporter.

stem: An 18-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and vomiting. She had returned from a holiday in Morocco 1 week ago. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history and she was well while on holiday. On examination, she is unwell and slightly jaundiced. There is no lymphadenopathy and abdominal examination was normal. Her temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure was 98/56 mmHg, pulse of 110 beats/min and Glasgow Coma score of 15/15. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 69 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 15.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 22 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 86 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Reticulocyte count 160 × 109/l 25–100 × 109/l Blood ﬁlm Multiple fragmented red cells Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 21.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 350 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 58 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l LDH 300 IU/l 100–190 IU/l AST 38 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALT 36 IU/l 5–30 IU/l What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
D Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS) Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome is characterised by widespread deposition of loose strands of ﬁbrin in multiple small blood vessels, which damage platelets and red blood cells (RBCs), resulting in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombocytopenia. The signs of the disease are: thrombocytopenia, fragmented RBCs on blood ﬁlm (acanthocytes, shistocytes, burr cells, helmet cell, etc.), fever, kidney disease, central nervous system (CNS) manifestations (confusion, coma) and jaundice (elevated direct and indirect bilirubin). HUS often follows gastroenteritis associated with Shiga-toxin-producing bacteria such as enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7. B Leptospirosis Leptospirosis is caused by a thin, spiral-shaped Leptospira bacterium, especially Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae. There may be liver abnormalities with jaundice. Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia is not a usual feature. A Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura (TTP) TTP and HUS are part of the same spectrum of microangiopathic disease. Similar to HUS, TTP is characterised by widespread deposition of loose strands of ﬁbrin in multiple small blood vessels, which damage platelets and red blood cells (RBCs), resulting in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, disseminated intravascular

coagulation and thrombocytopenia. In TTP, manifestation of ischaemic organ damage such as neurological disturbance (confusion and coma) and myocardial damage are characteristically found. TTP is differentiated from HUS by the following points: Children account for 90% of the cases of HUS, while adults are more frequently affected with TTP. Kidney disease and fever predominates in HUS, while in TTP neurological symptoms are more common. The prognosis is worse in TTP compared with HUS. Treatment is supportive with plasma exchange until the activity of the disease has subsided. Steroids are also beneﬁcial. C Familial Mediterranean fever Familial Mediterranean fever is an inherited condition with episodes of inﬂammation such as peritonitis, pleurisy and arthritis. E Acute hepatitis B infection Although acute hepatitis B infection cause acute hepatitis, it doesn’t lead to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. It wouldn’t also account for the acute GI upset and renal impairment seen here.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to hospital after being found by his home help in a confused state. He is usually able to care for himself, with help for cooking and cleaning, but on this occasion she found him slumped in a chair complaining of pain in his right knee, and shouting at her to get help. He has a history of gout and drinks four pints of beer per day. It is unclear whether he is compliant with medication for blood pressure. On examination, he is pyrexial (39.1 °C), his blood pressure (BP) is 95/70 mmHg and his pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. The right knee is swollen and erythematous, and he cannot ﬂex it more than 30 degrees. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 130 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 16.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 189 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 225 mg/l < 10 mg/l Urate 8.74 mg/dl 3.4 - 7.0 mg/dl (male) Knee joint asperate -ve birefringent crystals, 350 × 109 neutrophils/ml Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: C Flucloxacillin Given signiﬁcant evidence of sepsis, with relative hypotension, tachycardia and marked pyrexia, antibiotic intervention is essential until blood culture results are known. The neutrophil count is outside the normal range and may represent septic arthritis. Although urate crystals are seen in the joint, it is possible for sepsis and gout to co-exist. D Naproxen In this situation with a moderate elevation in creatinine, colchicine is potentially preferred as an anti- inﬂammatory. A Allopurinol Even in proven acute gout, allopurinol can worsen symptoms initially and therefore should be avoided during the initial period of therapy. B Colchicine This is a ﬁrst-line option for the treatment of gout, but given the degree of systemic symptoms, sepsis should be ruled out/treated ﬁrst. It is associated with symptoms of diarrhoea, which means it be poorly tolerated in some patients. E Prednisolone This is an option for acute gout, but there are signiﬁcant signs of sepsis and this should be the assumed initial diagnosis.

stem: A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of swelling and pain affecting his lower limbs, worse on the right than on the left. He also felt generally unwell and had had intermittent fevers. He had returned from Sri Lanka 2 days previously, where he had been working as an aid worker in rural areas surrounded by paddy ﬁelds. On examination, both legs were swollen with non-pitting oedema to the knee, unchanged by elevation of the legs. There was painful bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 10 /l 4–11 × 10 /l Eosinophils 1.2 × 10 /l 0.04–0.4 × 10 /l Chest X-ray Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates Ultrasound of the groin Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with lymphatic obstruction What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?
explanation:
A Ivermectin This patient has ﬁliariasis. He has travelled to an endemic area, surrounded by paddy ﬁelds which provide the perfect breeding ground for the parasitic vector (mosquitoes). The parasitic worms block the lymphatics, leading to limb swelling and lymphadenopathy. Filiariasis also explains his general malaise and intermittent fevers, and the marked eosinophilia and bilateral pulmonary inﬁltrates. First-line treatment is with diethylcarbamazine (DEC), but if there is any suggestion of a high parasitic load or concomitant onchocerciasis, ivermectin is an appropriate second-line treatment. D Itraconazole This patient has ﬁliariasis: this explains his intermittent fevers, leg swelling, painful lymphadenopathy and the ﬁndings on chest X-ray and ultrasound. The marked eosinophilia is highly suggestive of a parasitic infection. Filiariasis is caused by tiny parasitic worms which are contracted through vector transmission, by infected mosquitoes; paddy ﬁelds provide perfect breeding grounds for mosquitoes. The nematodes block the lymphatics, which leads to limb swelling and lymphadenopathy. Itraconazole is an antifungal medication, and therefore would not be appropriate to treat this patient. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) would be ﬁrst line, but should not be used if there is any suggestion of high parasite load or concomitant onchocerciasis. The most appropriate treatment for this patient would be ivermectin. B Chloroquine This patient has ﬁliariasis: this is infection with microscopic worms, causing blockage of lymphatics and hence lymphadenopathy and limb swelling. It is contracted through bites from mosquitoes carrying the parasite. This patient has been working near paddy ﬁelds: these watery environments provide perfect breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Filiariasis would explain his limb swelling and painful lymphadenopathy; the nematodes can also migrate to the lungs causing bilateral pulmonary inﬁltrates. Finally this patient has a signiﬁcant eosinophilia – an eosinophilia of this level is most likely to be caused by a signiﬁcant parasitic infection. Filiariasis can be treated with diethylcarbamazine (DEC), albendazole or ivermectin. Ivermectin is the most appropriate choice if there is any risk of concomitant onchocerciasis. Chloroquine would not be appropriate as it is an antimalarial agent; this patient’s symptoms and signs are not consistent with malaria. C Ciproﬂoxacin This patient’s leg swelling, intermittent fevers, bilateral pulmonary inﬁltrates and signiﬁcant eosinophilia would be best explained by ﬁliariasis. This is a parasitic worm infection contracted after being

bitten by an infected mosquito; rural paddy ﬁelds are typical breeding grounds for mosquitos. The ﬁlarial nematodes cause blockage of lymphatics, leading to lymphadenopathy and limb swelling. Ciproﬂoxacin is an antibiotic and will not treat this patient’s parasitic infection. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is ﬁrst line but should not be used if there is suggestion of a high ﬁlarial load or concomitant onchocerciasis. The most appropriate treatment for this patient would be ivermectin. E Metronidazole The intermittent fevers, malaise, limb swelling, lymphadenopathy and marked eosinophilia, against the background of this patient’s travel history, suggest ﬁliariasis. This is a parasitic worm transmitted through mosquitoes (for which rural paddy ﬁelds provide the perfect breeding ground). The worms block the lymphatics, leading to limb swelling and lymphadenopathy. They can also cause bilateral pulmonary inﬁltrates. As metronidazole is an antiprotozoal and antibacterial, it is not effective against a parasite such as ﬁlarial worms. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is ﬁrst-line treatment, but should not be used if there is suggestion of a high parasite load or concomitant onchocerciasis: the second-line option of ivermectin would be most appropriate in this case.

stem: A 46-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 2week history of a new rash. The rash ﬁrst appeared on his trunk and then spread to his arms and face. There is no history of itch or bleeding. He denies any recent coryzal symptoms but says he has been feeling generally more fatigued recently. His past medical history includes pneumonia, but he has otherwise been well, with no regular medications or allergies. His vaccination record is up-todate. On examination, he is afebrile. His heart rate is 89 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 112/65 mmHg. Chest sounds are clear, with saturations of 93% on air and heart sounds are normal. There is a widespread pale pink papular rash over his torso, with papules as shown below. The rash extends to his upper limbs and face where there are more small papules. The papules have a waxy appearance and an umbilicated centre. The surrounding skin is dry and erythematous. What is the next most appropriate investigation to reach a diagnosis?
explanation:
D Human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) antigen test This patient has a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum, a viral rash that is characterised by small pale pink waxy papules with an umbilicated centre which cluster. It usually presents in young children, and a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum in an adult raises suspicion of an underlying immunodeﬁciency, including HIV. HIV antigen testing, along with a CD4 count, should be measured in affected adults. C Viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) In rashes that produce vesicles, such as the herpes simplex virus, a viral PCR of vesicular ﬂuid can be sent for diagnosis. Although molluscum contagiosum is a viral rash caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, viral PCR does not play a role in diagnosis. A Full blood count

This patient has a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum, a viral rash that is often diagnosed clinically. The diagnosis is made based on the appearance of the rash characterised by clusters of small waxy papules with an umbilicated centre. While a full blood count is useful to investigate his fatigue and the extent of infection, it is not needed to make a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum and is not the next most appropriate test to request. B Skin biopsy Skin biopsies are also useful if a diagnosis is not certain and other differentials need to be excluded. However, molluscum contagiosum is usually a clinical diagnosis. In some circumstances, a skin biopsy can be taken for histopathology, but it is not normally required. E Herpes zoster virus (HZV) serology Herpes zoster virus (HZV) is responsible for shingles, a dermatomal painful vesicular rash that is caused by reactivation of the varicellazoster virus. While it mostly has a dermatomal distribution, in immunocompromised individuals, the rash may be bilateral or diffuse. However, this question describes a patient with a nonpainful, umbilicated papular rash. Furthermore, in contrast to HZV, the contents of the papules contain a thicker white material rather than clear vesicular ﬂuid. This makes a diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum more likely, making HZV serology incorrect.

stem: You are the medical senior house ofﬁcer (SHO) on call. A 40-yearold man has presented to the Emergency Department with jaundice. He gives a week-long history of worsening jaundice with associated nausea and malaise. He has had mild diarrhoea, although there is no history of abdominal pain. He has felt unwell for the past 3 weeks but initially his symptoms were more ‘ﬂu-like’ with muscle aches and fever. He reports multiple sexual partners in the past 3 months. He often has unprotected anal intercourse. He uses ecstasy and cocaine as recreational drugs. He used to occasionally inject drugs but has not done so for over 10 years. He regularly attends the Genitourinary Clinic for sexual health screens and his last HIV test was negative 6 months ago. On examination, he is afebrile, pulse 95 bpm. He is deeply jaundiced and his abdomen is soft with very mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. There is no organomegaly. The Emergency Department SHO performed some blood tests, which reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 132 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 360 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Bilirubin 154 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 872 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 300 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 30 g/l 35–55 g/l Hepatitis
explanation:
B Anti-hepatitis A Ab This patient has symptoms suggestive of hepatitis A infection, a ﬂulike prodromal illness followed by an icteric illness. He is at risk as he has had unprotected anal sex with many partners; anal intercourse is a likely route for enteral transmission. Parenteral transmission can also occur. A Liver ultrasound A liver ultrasound may be useful if, for example, the patient does have chronic hepatitis C and has now developed a hepatoma. However, in this case, the symptoms are highly suggestive of an acute viral infection. C Anti-hepatitis C Ab It would be correct when hepatitis C is the most likely diagnosis. Hepatitis C is almost always asymptomatic during the acute infection; furthermore he has not been at high risk of contracting hepatitis C virus (HCV) for over 10 years – sexual transmission is rare compared with blood transmission. Chronic HCV would present as chronic liver disease which does not ﬁt with this clinical picture. D Anti-hepatitis D Ab It would be correct when hepatitis D is the most likely diagnosis. Hepatitis D only causes this picture when superinfection occurs in patients who are already hepatitis B positive. His results show that he

has already been vaccinated against hepatitis B, or that he has had a previous (now inactive) infection. If HBsAg was positive then it might raise suspicion of hepatitis D infection. E HIV antibody test The patient may well be HIV positive but the HIV antibody titre will not give you the diagnosis on this occasion.

stem: A 32-year-old homeless man presents to the Emergency Department with severe headaches, behavioural changes and pyrexia. He has been admitted to the unit on two previous occasions with heroin overdoses. On examination, he is emaciated and has a number of needle marks consistent with drug abuse, his temperature is 38.6 °C. You also notice that he has ﬁnger clubbing and nail bed haemorrhages. There is an ejection systolic murmur. Neurological examination reveals evidence of mild papilloedema. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 101 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 11.2 x 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 120 x 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l ESR 87 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 155 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CT head Frontal lobe abscess He is to be urgently reviewed by the neurosurgical team. Which of the following would be the most appropriate initial antibiotic choice pending culture results?
explanation:
E IV linezolid In intravenous drug abusers (IVDAs), a methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) is the causative organism in about 60-70% of cases with haematogenous spread of the bacteria resulting in the frontal lobe abscess seen here. Linezolid is the initial empiric therapy of choice because it covers against MRSA infection and achieves good brain penetration. In the event that a sensitive staphylococcus is isolated, ﬂucloxacillin can be substituted. Trans-oesophageal echocardiography is the investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis of bacterial endocarditis B IV cefotaxime

This is the treatment for meningitis rather than cerebral abscess. If the picture was of a meningism and no evidence of raised intracranial pressure and a normal CT scan this would be a better treatment option. A IV penicillin This could be the treatment for a streptococcal cause of infection but this organism is unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s abscess. C IV co-amoxiclav This could be a useful broad-spectrum treatment if the patient was not known to be a IVDA. D Oral doxycycline Doxycycline is a potential oral option for community-acquired infection. Given the severity of infection here, it is unlikely to be sufﬁcient to clear the underlying staphylococcal infection.

stem: A 45-year-old farmer presents to the hospital with a 2-week history of fever, chills, headache and muscle aches. He reports exposure to cattle and sheep on his farm. Physical examination reveals a temperature of 38.5 °C and there is mild hepatomegaly without jaundice. Laboratory tests show mildly elevated liver enzyme levels and leukocytosis. Chest X-ray reveals mild inﬁltrates. Serology conﬁrms a diagnosis of Q fever caused by Coxiella burnetii. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 17.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
explanation:
B PO doxycycline for 14 days Doxycycline is the ﬁrst-line treatment for acute Q fever, administered over a 14-day course. It is highly effective against C. burnetii and helps to prevent chronic complications. In cases of acute Q fever, early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to reduce the risk of progression to chronic Q fever. E PO metronidazole for seven days Metronidazole is ineffective against C. burnetii and is not used in the treatment of Q fever, as it primarily targets anaerobic organisms. A PO azithromycin for ﬁve days

Azithromycin is not the ﬁrst-line treatment for Q fever. While macrolides are sometimes used in cases of severe allergy to tetracyclines, doxycycline remains the preferred choice due to higher efﬁcacy against C. burnetii. C IV amoxicillin IV amoxicillin is not effective for Q fever, as C. burnetii is resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. These are not used in the management of Q fever. D PO ciproﬂoxacin for 14 days Ciproﬂoxacin is not the ﬁrst-line treatment for Q fever and is generally less effective than doxycycline for this infection. Tetracyclines remain the preferred class of antibiotics.

stem: A 40-year-old farmer is admitted to the Cardiology Ward with a 2-month history of general malaise and weight loss. His symptoms were preceded by a ﬂu-like illness and intermittent fevers. There is no signiﬁcant past medical history, and he is normally ﬁt and well. His temperature is 38.7 °C, heart rate 105 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. On examination, there are vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. There is a loud pansystolic murmur radiating towards the apex. His jugular venous pressure (JVP) is not elevated and there are no signs of peripheral oedema. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 100 g/l 120–160 g/l WCC 15.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 350 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l ESR 70 mm/hour < 15 mm/hour ECHO Evidence of mitral regurgitation with visible vegetations on valve leaflets Blood cultures Negative × 3 sets What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
C Doxycycline This patient has infective endocarditis. The history of general

malaise and ﬂu-like symptoms, together with fever and a new murmur, is highly suggestive of the diagnosis. This patient’s pansystolic murmur and ECHO ﬁndings are indicative of mitral regurgitation, with the mitral valve being the most commonly affected valve in infective endocarditis. Blood cultures form part of the modiﬁed Duke criteria needed to conﬁrm the diagnosis. Coxiella burnetii causes blood culture-negative endocarditis. It is a zoonotic disease and individuals at higher risk of infection include those who work with animals such as farmers and veterinarians. Treatment is with a prolonged course of doxycycline. B Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin are used for cases of infective endocarditis caused by streptococcal species. It seems less likely to be the cause of this patient’s presentation, making benzylpenicillin an unlikely antibiotic of choice. A Amoxicillin and gentamicin Amoxicillin and gentamicin are usually given in the ﬁrst instance for infective endocarditis when a patient has native valves and an unclear causative organism. However, this patient is a farmer with negative blood culture results, making the probability of a zoonotic infection (eg C. burnetii) more likely. D Flucloxacillin Flucloxacillin is indicated for patients who are likely to be infected with Staphylococcus aureus (eg IV drug users). Given the negative blood culture results, this is very unlikely to be the causative organism in this patient, making ﬂucloxacillin an unlikely antibiotic of choice. Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin are combined as blind antibiotic therapy for patients with a prosthetic heart valve or those with S. aureus infection who are allergic to penicillin. There is no past medical history to suggest that this patient has had a heart valve replacement or that he is penicillin-allergic.

stem: A 49-year-old veterinarian is brought into the Emergency Department with a 7-day history of headache, deteriorating cognition and worsening confusion. His partner reports an obvious change in behaviour and no longer responds to simple questions appropriately. He has a past medical history of human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) infection and reports to be incompliant with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). On examination, he has a low-grade temperature of 37.9 °C. His heart rate is 90 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 122/82 mmHg. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen, with no palpable organomegaly. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 14 (E4 V4 M6) and he is clearly disorientated to time, place and person. There is mild left-sided hemiparesis, with 4/5 power on myotome testing of his left upper and lower limbs. CD4 count: 100 cells/µl Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scan: multiple ringenhancing lesions. What is the most likely causative organism for this presentation?
explanation:
E Toxoplasma gondii This patient has neurotoxoplasmosis, an opportunistic infection caused by the parasite T. gondii. It is the most common cause of neurological brain abscesses in patients with HIV. Domestic cats are a common source of transmission. This patient is a veterinarian, making his chances of contracting toxoplasmosis much more likely. Symptoms include headache, fever and neurological changes, including seizures, hemiplegia, cerebellar signs or an acute confusional state. Toxoplasmosis can be diagnosed with a combination of clinical history, serology testing and imaging. Classically, the disease can be seen on an MRI brain scan as multiple ring-enhancing lesions. D Streptococcus pneumoniae S. pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common causes of a bacterial brain abscess. Bacterial intracranial abscesses commonly arise from infections in adjacent structures, including otitis media, sinusitis or mastoiditis. Other sources of infection include bloodborne spread, such as from endocarditis. A swinging fever is common, along with headache and neurological symptoms. Cerebral abscesses appear as a radiolucent space- occupying lesion with ring enhancement. However, unlike toxoplasmosis, a double rim sign is common, secondary to a hypodense outer rim and a hyperdense inner rim. A Cryptococcus neoformans C. neoformans causes an opportunistic fungal infection of the central nervous system (CNS) called cryptococcosis. The disease presents similarly to meningitis with headache, fevers, confusion, altered mental state and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Imaging studies, including computed tomography (CT) and MRI, show leptomeningeal enhancement, cryptococcomas, hydrocephalus or dilated perivascular spaces. It usually occurs when the CD4 count drops below 100 cells/µl and it does not cause ring-enhancing lesions, making it incorrect here. B Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a viral infection which commonly causes illness in patients with HIV, particularly in those with a CD4 count < 50 cells/µl. The most common form of CMV is CMV retinitis and the presentation is variable due to involvement of the brain, meninges, spinal cord, retina and peripheral nerve roots.

However, cognitive decline is frequently seen. On imaging, meningoencephalitis and ventriculitis are most often present. C Mycobacterium tuberculosis M. tuberculosis can cause central neurological involvement from direct extension into the central nervous system (CNS) or via haematogenous spread. CNS involvement with M. tuberculosis can take various forms, most commonly tuberculous meningitis and tuberculomas. Tuberculosis is particularly more common in individuals with HIV and symptoms are usually similar to those of bacterial meningitis (eg fever, headache, meningism). Tuberculous meningitis can be seen on imaging as leptomeningitis from the presence of thick exudative material in the subarachnoid space, whereas tuberculomas present as ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding vasogenic oedema. In areas of the world where tuberculosis is endemic, tuberculous meningitis and tuberculomas are much more common. However, in this patient, the clinical history of working as a veterinarian and the presence of multiple ring-enhancing lesions make the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis more likely.

stem: A 21-year-old hill walker presents to the Emergency Department with severe fever, left-sided lower abdominal pain and diarrhoea with blood and mucus over the past 48 hours. He has no signiﬁcant past medical history and takes no regular medication. He has been staying in hikers’ huts over the past few days where cooking and toilet facilities are shared. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, with a postural drop of 30 mmHg on standing, and his pulse is 85 bpm. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 139 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 204 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 12.2 mmol/l 2.5–7.8 mmol/l CRP 152 mg/l < 5 mg/l Stool screen: Positive for Shigella. He is given oral rehydration sachets and wants to continue with his holiday. Which other intervention is most appropriate?
explanation: A Oral azithromycin Although quinolones were the default ﬁrst-line option for the treatment of symptomatic Shigella infection, their use is now discouraged because of the risk for seizures and tendon rupture associated with this drug class. A Cochrane meta-analysis showed that a range of antibiotics had similar efﬁcacy, including azithromycin, which drives this as the treatment of choice for Shigella infection here. C Oral Metronidazole Oral metronidazole is the intervention of choice for giardiasis, which is suggested by symptoms similar to irritable bowel syndrome with intermittent diarrhoea and constipation, and infection is usually acquired because of exposure to contaminated food or water. Infection is not usually seen in the United Kingdom. B Oral Ciproﬂoxacin Oral quinolones are now reserved for serious or life-threatening illness when other options for treatment are unavailable. This is because of a Committee on Safety of Medicines (CSM) warning detailing signiﬁcant adverse effects associated with their use, including seizures in patients with no known epilepsy and tendon ruptures. D Single-dose intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone IV ceftriaxone is the preferred option for patients who are severely unwell because of Shigella infection. Although this patient does have a postural drop in his blood pressure, oral azithromycin would be considered adequate to treat his infection. E No other intervention required Given this patient has severe dehydration and ongoing diarrhoea and is on an activity holiday, antibiotic intervention is warranted to relieve his symptoms here.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of profuse diarrhoea. She passed watery stool ﬂecked with blood up to 10 times per day. She also complained of cramping abdominal pain, a lowgrade fever and increased lethargy. She had recently completed a course of clindamycin for a dental abscess. On examination, her temperature was 37.8 °C. Her abdomen was soft but the lower portion was generally tender. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 18.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Urea 13.4 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 165 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Rigid sigmoidoscopy Raised, yellowish white plaques throughout sigmoid Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
D Oral vancomycin This patient has Clostridium difﬁcile infection, as evidenced by her profuse, offensive diarrhoea, pseudomembranous colitis on rigid sigmoidoscopy and high white cell count. This was probably caused by taking clindamycin, which increases the risk of C. difﬁcile infection. Oral vancomycin is the ﬁrst-line treatment for C. difﬁcile; other options include oral metronidazole and oral and intravenous ﬁdaxomycin. C Oral ciproﬂoxacin This patient’s profuse diarrhoea, pseudomembranous colitis on rigid sigmoidoscopy and high white cell count point towards Clostridium difﬁcile infection, probably precipitated by the clindamycin she was prescribed for her dental infection. Both clindamycin and ciproﬂoxacin are strongly associated with increased risk of C. difﬁcile infection; consequently ciproﬂoxacin would not be a good choice of antibiotic for treatment of this patient. First- line treatments would be oral vancomycin or oral metronidazole; secondline therapies include oral ﬁdaxomycin. A Intravenous ciproﬂoxacin This patient has developed pseudomembranous colitis on sigmoidoscopy, and her symptoms and high white cell count are consistent with C. difﬁcile infection. Clindamycin, which this patient had received for a dental infection, is known to be associated with C. difﬁcile infection. Unfortunately ciproﬂoxacin is also associated with the development of C. difﬁcile infection, and therefore would not be an appropriate choice of treatment. Also, please note that bioavailability for intravenous and oral ciproﬂoxacin is virtually identical, therefore treating with intravenous ciproﬂoxacin provides no advantage unless the patient is unable to take oral ciproﬂoxacin. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. First-line treatment of C. difﬁcile is usually oral vancomycin or oral metronidazole, but sometimes oral ﬁdaxomycin is used. B Intravenous vancomycin This patient has Clostridium difﬁcile infection, as evidenced by the profuse diarrhoea, pseudomembranous colitis on sigmoidoscopy and high white cell count. Clindamycin, which this patient has recently taken, is known to be associated with C. difﬁcile infection.

Whilst vancomycin is an appropriate choice of antibiotic, it should be given orally, not intravenously, otherwise it will not reach sufﬁcient therapeutic levels in the gut. Other antibiotic options include metronidazole and ﬁdaxomycin. D Rectal budesonide Budesonide is a steroid, and rectal budesonide is used in the treatment of inﬂammatory bowel disease and gut graft-versus-host disease in order to tackle inﬂammation. However, this patient has Clostridium difﬁcile infection, as evidence by her profuse, offensive diarrhoea and high white cell count after taking a course of clindamycin, an antibiotic known to be associated with C. difﬁcile. The rigid sigmoidoscopy conﬁrms a pseudomembranous colitis. Treating this with steroids would be highly inappropriate; she requires antibiotic therapy with oral vancomycin. Other appropriate options would be oral metronidazole or ﬁdaxomycin.

stem: A 31-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with right upper quadrant tenderness and bloody diarrhoea. He has been unwell since returning from a period supervising a 1-year Operation Raleigh expedition to Brazil. This was one of a number of trips to South America. While there, he took part in watersports and went fresh-water swimming. He visited the jungles and was bitten by the occasional insect. He was always careful however with what he ate and drank. He had night sweats and fever for 1 week, with headache, a non- productive cough and arthralgia. He smokes 40 cigarettes/day and drinks heavily on the weekend. He admitted to having casual unprotected sex with some of the local women. On examination, his temperature is 38.1 °C and his pulse 110 bpm. He has cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. His chest is clear but he has a large liver, which measures 10 cm below the right costal margin, and a spleen which is 8 cm below the left costal margin. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value WCC 15.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 9.3 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 3.2 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l Eosinophils 2.1 × 109/l 0.0–0.4 × 109/l Hb 101 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 84 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Platelets (PLT) 140 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ALT 36 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 134 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT) 157 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 21 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 34 g/l 35–55 g/l CXR Normal Abdominal ultrasound scan shows an enlarged liver 15 cm, enlarged spleen 10 cm, kidneys and pancreas normal, two gallstones in the gallbladder, no common bile duct (CBD) dilatation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Schistosomiasis This patient has an exposure to fresh-water immersion and jungle activity in a country where schistosomiasis is endemic. The key ﬁndings from his history and investigation are fever, hepatosplenomegaly and bloody diarrhoea in the returning traveller. The disease is caused by one of several species of parasitic trematodes of the genus Schistosoma. Schistosomes infect particular species of susceptible freshwater snails, which release cercariae, which are fork-tailed 1-mm-long free-swimming larvae. These survive in freshwater for up to 48 hours, during which time they must attach to human skin/susceptible host mammal or die. Once attached, they migrate through intact skin to dermal veins and, over the next several days, to the pulmonary vasculature. The worms then migrate through the pulmonary capillaries to the systemic circulation, which carries them to the portal veins where they mature. In the portal circulation the males and females pair off and produce eggs. Diagnosis is based on a good travel history with the risk of exposure clariﬁed. Patients in the acute stage can present with an urticarial illness as they react to the antigenic eggs produced. Symptoms are those of serum sickness and hepatosplenomegaly is often present. Diagnosis can be made by observing eggs in the stool or urine depending on which species of Schistosoma has caused infection. Treatment is primarily with praziquantel and supportive therapy. C Giardiasis It would not explain the bloody diarrhoea or hepatosplenomegaly. The patient could be exposed to Giardia lamblia, the causative pathogen, through unprotected sex or swimming and it would cause diarrhoea, but the additional features of the history and examination makes it less likely. Giardiasis typically presents as explosive diarrhoea and malabsorption. A HIV It does not explain the bloody diarrhoea or hepatosplenomegaly. Acute HIV seroconversion is more likely to present with fever and general malaise. However, it would be worthwhile to test for HIV due to the potential exposure history. B Crohn’s disease It cannot account for the hepatosplenomegaly and does not explain the lymphoadenopathy. It would ﬁt with the fevers, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, and could also explain the arthralgia as an extra-intestinal symptom, but the cough is difﬁcult to explain.

D Leishmaniasis Visceral leishmaniasis is a cause of fevers, night sweats and hepatosplenomegaly but would not present with bloody diarrhoea and does not cause arthralgia. Leishmaniasis is endemic to east Africa and India and more commonly presents in a cutaneous form, but visceral leishmaniasis is an important cause of hepatosplenomegaly as untreated it is often fatal.

stem: A 37-year-old woman attended clinic with a 6-month history of breathlessness, wheeze and general fatigue. She had returned to the United Kingdom 2 weeks previously after an 8-month mission in Zanzibar, mainly spent in rural areas. She swam in the lakes and walked around barefoot. She had been well during her trip, apart from a 2-month period during which she experienced vague abdominal discomfort, which disappeared after taking a tablet prescribed by her doctor. On examination, her pulse was 80 bpm and respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min at rest, increasing to 28 breaths/min on walking 40 m. Her body mass index (BMI) was 24, and she appeared pale. Auscultation of the chest demonstrated scattered wheeze. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 88 g/l 115 - 165 g/l MCV 72.1 ﬂ 80 - 96 ﬂ WCC 8.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 460 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Bilirubin 21 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l ALT 45 u/l 5 - 35 u/l ALP 84 u/l 45 - 105 u/l Albumin 32 g/l 37 - 49 g/l Chest X-ray Normal Urine Blood negative, protein negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Hookworm infection The patient mentions that she has been walking around barefoot, a classic risk factor for infection by hookworm. In the early stages of the infection, the hookworms are found in the small intestine (explaining her non-speciﬁc abdominal pain). They then migrate to the lungs and can cause wheeze and a dry cough and breathlessness. This can lead to poor exercise tolerance, as demonstrated in this case. Typically, patients present with iron deﬁciency anaemia from

ongoing gastrointestinal blood loss, as seen here. C Left ventricular failure Left ventricular failure would explain her progressive breathlessness. However, there is no underlying pathology to explain the development of heart failure in this patient. She does have anaemia; however, it is unlikely that this level of anaemia could have caused left ventricular failure. It also does not explain her vague abdominal pain. Left ventricular failure does not explain why she has developed anaemia. This patient’s presentation could be better explained by hookworm infection. A Duodenal ulcer A duodenal ulcer would cause central abdominal pain, worse at night and relieved by eating. A duodenal ulcer could explain her abdominal pain. However, the duodenal ulcer cannot explain her wheeze or breathlessness (if a duodenal ulcer was causing her to be anaemic, you would not expect the symptoms to have resolved after receiving a medication from her doctor). These symptoms could be better explained by hookworm infection. D Pulmonary embolism The time course is too long for an acute pulmonary embolism, and you would expect pleuritic chest pain accompanying sudden-onset breathlessness. Chronic pulmonary thromboembolic disease can cause breathlessness, but this patient is young and of normal weight; there are no identiﬁed risk factors for venous thromboembolism. It is unlikely that she would have chronic thromboembolic disease, and it does not explain the anaemia or the history of vague abdominal pain. This patient’s presentation could be better explained by hookworm infection. Treatment is highly successful with albendazole or mebendazole. B Schistosomiasis Schistosomiasis typically causes urinary pathology (such as haematuria and later urinary tract malignancies) or intestinal pathology (such as abdominal pain, diarrhoea and later hepatosplenomegaly), depending on the species. Schistosomiasis can cause katayama fever which can cause pulmonary symptoms and an acute illness. However, this patient's presentation could be better explained by hookworm infection due to the more chronic exercise tolerance and microscopic anaemia.

stem: A 35-year-old man attends the Dermatology Clinic with a growing lesion on the back of his arm. He initially noticed it two weeks ago when it appeared as a small red raised spot. The lesion is not painful or itchy, and he is otherwise well. He has just completed a tour in Iraq in the military. On examination, his chest is clear and his heart sounds are normal. He has a soft abdomen and no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. There is a 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm round lesion on the extensor surface of his arm, as shown below. His mucous membranes are spared and there are no further lesions on his body. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Leishmaniasis The lesion with an ulcerated centre and superﬁcial crusting is consistent with leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease spread by sandﬂies. Different species of Leishmania are responsible for different manifestations of the disease, with cutaneous leishmaniasis being the most common. Initially, a small red papule appears at the site of the sandﬂy bite, which gradually enlarges to up to 2 cm in diameter. It later ulcerates in the centre before spontaneously resolving. The time to resolution varies between two months and one year. This patient is a soldier, and countries in the Middle East, North Africa and Asia are more common areas for contracting the disease. E Yaws Yaws is a chronic skin infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum pertenue. It usually occurs in tropical parts of the world, including Africa, South East Asia and South America. It is spread through direct contact of infectious ulcers and the bacterium enters the skin through superﬁcial wounds and skin trauma. Similar to syphilis, yaws has several stages of illness. Initially, a papule appears at the site of infection, which enlarges and ulcerates. In secondary yaws, more widespread papules appear over the rest of the body, after which the bacterium enters either a silent latent period or a tertiary stage which begins to affect the bones. A Anthrax Anthrax is a bacterial disease caused by Bacillus anthracis. Infection is associated with exposure to infected carcasses and the introduction of the organism into the body through a superﬁcial wound. An initial pustule appears at the site of infection, which

progresses to a black eschar (a necrotic-looking ulcer with a black scab). The infection usually resolves spontaneously, but in some, it can lead to death. The lesion described and shown in this question is not that of a black eschar but rather that of a crusted ulcer from a sandﬂy bite. This makes leishmaniasis the most likely diagnosis. B Leprosy Leprosy is a granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, which affects the peripheral nerves and skin. Initial symptoms include numbness, typically with loss of temperature followed by light touch and pain, and ﬁnally deep pressure. Cutaneous lesions follow later in the disease and appear as hypopigmented patches of skin, with associated sensory loss. This patient has a painless, crusted ulcer, with no other lesions or neurological features, making leprosy an unlikely diagnosis. D Melioidosis Melioidosis is a bacterial illness caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. It is a tropical disease seen in South East Asia, as well as in Africa, the Middle East and the South Paciﬁc. In many, exposure to the bacterium causes asymptomatic seroconversion. In others, it can cause localised infection, with the appearance of a nodule or ulcer at the site of entry via the skin. In severe cases, it can progress to septicaemia and abscess formation. Localised infection is associated with fever and pain, which are not seen in this patient’s presentation, making melioidosis unlikely here.

stem: A 42-year-old man attends the clinic complaining of diarrhoea, fatigue, fevers and right upper quadrant pain. He admits to recreational use of crystal metamphetamine. On examination, he looks very thin and has tender hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. He attends with his partner who is very concerned about him. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.9 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 90 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 184 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 282 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Computed tomography (CT) abdomen Retroperitoneal, para-aortic lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly Small bowel biopsy Acid-fast bacteria (AFB) seen, MTB PCR negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Mycobacterium avium This patient is anaemic, with low platelets and a low white cell count giving evidence of infection, evidence of lymphadenopathy on CT scan, and non-TB AFBs identiﬁed on biopsy. The additional abnormalities seen in LFTs point towards the possibility of Mycobacterium avium as being the most likely cause of this presentation. This patient has a history of crystal metamphetamine use, raising the possibility of HIV infection, and subsequent immunocompromise. Triple antibiotic therapy is usually required in HIV-infected patients; one possible combination suggested is clarithromycin, ethambutol and rifabutin. C Myocbacterium tuberculosis Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic bacterial infection caused by M. tuberculosis. Primary TB most commonly affects the lungs, however almost all organ systems may be infected. A similar syndrome to that described may be present in patients with GI or miliary (disseminated TB); however we are told in the vignette that the MTB PCR is negative, this makes Mycobacterium TB infection much less likely. A Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection Primary CMV infection causes a glandular fever syndrome typiﬁed by fever, lethargy and lymphadenopathy. Although CMV reactivation in the immunocompromised host can present with colitis, the small bowel biopsy results point to an alternative diagnosis. B Cryptosporidium Cryptosporidium parvum is a protozoan which causes a self-

limiting diarrhoeal illness. In the context of immunosuppression it may cause a severe diarrhoeal illness or disseminated infection affecting multiple organ systems which may prove fatal. Treatment is primarily supportive in the immunocompetent host while treatment of the underlying immunosuppression (eg HAART in HIV-positive patients) is key in the immunocompromised. Here the small bowel biopsy results point to an alternative diagnosis. D Tropical sprue Tropoical sprue is a gastrointestinal condition in which inﬂammation and subsequent ﬂattening of small bowel villi leads to malabsorption. The underlying aetiology is not well understood but there may be an infectious cause. The presentation is with signs and symptoms associated with malabsorption (particularly of vitamin B12 and folic acid).

stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has begun HAART for the treatment of HIV a few months earlier and has recently returned from a holiday to Pakistan. Whilse there, she visited her uncle who has just been diagnosed with tuberculosis. She has a positive quantiferon gamma test. She did not receive the BCG vaccination as a child. Her chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: D Isoniazid / Rifampicin for 3 months With no symptoms of TB, a normal CXR and a positive quantiferon test, this patient ﬁts the criteria for diagnosis of latent TB. As such, the BHIVA guidelines recommend either 6 months’ treatment with Isoniazid or 3 months’ combination therapy. For non-CNS TB, BHIVA guidelines recommend treatment with 4 drugs for 2 months, then 2 drugs for a further 4 months. Where there is CNS TB, a 9-month treatment period is recommended. A Four-drug anti-TB therapy for 6 months This duration is for drugs in total. Four drugs are needed for two months, and then a further four months of two drugs. B Four-drug anti-TB therapy for 12 months Again, this duration is not usually needed for four-drug TB therapy. C BCG vaccination BCG is a live vaccination and, as such, it may be potentially harmful in this situation and is therefore not recommended. E Observe The positive quantiferon test means that latent TB is likely to be present, despite the absence of clinical evidence and X-ray ﬁndings. Patients with HIV have a much greater risk of progression to active TB from the latent state; for this reason, observation only is not appropriate.

stem: A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman presents to clinic complaining of shortness of breath. She has a CD4 count of 120 × 106/l and has recently been started on antiretroviral therapy (ART). She admits that she quite often forgets to take her medication, including her prophylactic co-trimoxazole. She describes a 1-week history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and of retrosternal chest pain. She has a dry cough and has not produced any sputum. On examination, she is febrile at 38.5 °C, respiratory rate is 28/min, O2 saturations 97% on air, pulse 100 beats/min. The chest is clear on auscultation, cardiovascular examination is normal. Her chest Xray is shown below. Which investigation is the most useful pointer to the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
C Exercise oximetry The chest x-ray shows reticular interstitial changes in all lung ﬁelds.The most likely diagnosis is obviously Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) Exercise oximetry is an extremely useful test in this setting, as patients who are oxygenated well at rest may desaturate dramatically on exercise. An arterial blood gas is also important as it will inﬂuence the treatment given. If p(O2) <9.3 kPa, then high-dose methylprednisolone should also be prescribed in addition to IV co-trimoxazole. The main differential here is of pulmonary embolus. Being HIVpositive is an independent risk factor for thromboembolic disease. However, the history is inconsistent, with a progressive course and a dry cough and a very immunocompromised patient. Retrosternal chest pain is commonly seen in PCP. The next investigation would probably be an electrocardiogram (ECG), but exercise oximetry and an arterial blood gas are even more pressing.

A Electrocardiogram (ECG) Whilst an ECG should deﬁnitively be done for this patient, the question asked is what investigation would most likely lead to a diagnosis. As the clinical history is suggestive of PCP, an ECG is unlikely to guide to that diagnosis and is therefore not the correct option. B Lateral chest ﬁlm A lateral X-ray would give a good view of the retrosternal space and would also help demonstrate a subtle pneumothorax, but would not help diagnose PCP. D Bedside spirometry Bedside spirometry is helpful in the diagnosis of obstructive airway illness, such as asthma and COPD, as well as restrictive airway disease such as idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis, but is unlikely to be useful in this patient. Had there been a history or examination ﬁndings of wheeze, diurnal variation or heavy smoking history this would have been more relevant. D D-dimer D-dimer is a biochemical test which can help exclude pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis and is very unlikely to lead to diagnosis even under those circumstances, due to low speciﬁcity. It should be requested in the case of a moderate suspicion of DVT or PE as determined by Wells score.

stem: A 44-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of painless lesions on his oral mucosa and sides of the tongue, as shown below. These lesions tended to change in appearance over the course of a few days. He travelled extensively in East Asia for work. He had no other medical conditions. On examination, he appeared underweight. He had painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, and the lesions on his tongue were as described. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 115 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.9 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 167 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Oral hairy leukoplakia The rough, white, painless patches on the oral mucosa is classic for this condition. The disease is caused by reactivation of Epstein– Barr virus, which occurs in patients who are immunosuppressed. This patient has weight loss and widespread lymphadenopathy, on a background of travel in East Asia: the implication is that he may have undiagnosed HIV. In most cases, the diagnosis of oral hairy leukoplakia is clinical, but EBV can be demonstrated in epithelial cells with immunohistochemical staining. Speciﬁc treatment for this condition is not usually required, but he should be encouraged to have HIV testing and be managed with appropriate anti- retroviral therapy. D Oral candidiasis You may have correctly surmised that this patient has signs and symptoms consistent with an undiagnosed HIV infection – speciﬁcally, widespread lymphadenopathy and weight loss, on a background of travel to East Asia. Oral candidiasis is a common complication of immunosuppression, and is seen in undiagnosed HIV relatively often. However, oral candidiasis causes smooth white patches and soreness of the oral mucosa – it is not painless, and the lesions are not rough. This description is more consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia, a dermatological manifestation of Epstein–Barr virus reactivation, which can happen as a consequence of immunosuppression (as seen in undiagnosed HIV infection). A Geographic tongue Geographic tongue is in fact caused by the loss of areas of papillae on the tongue; hence it is characterised by smooth, red areas interspersed with normal, paler areas with papillae present. These are seen on the dorsal surface of the tongue. It does not cause rough white patches on the sides of the tongue, as described here. This description is consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia, a condition caused by Epstein–Barr virus reactivation in immunosuppressed individuals. This patient has concerning signs – in particular, widespread lymphadenopathy and weight loss on a background of travel in East Asia – and he should be tested for HIV. B Herpes simplex infection Herpes simplex would cause mucosal ulceration, which can include the sides of the tongue, but does not cause rough, white patches as described here. This presentation is more consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia, caused by reactivation of Epstein–Barr virus. This reactivation tends to occur in individuals who are immunosup-

pressed. In this case, the patient has symptoms and signs that could be compatible with undiagnosed HIV: he has a background of travel in East Asia, and has weight loss and widespread lymphadenopathy with oral hairy leukoplakia. He should be HIV tested. C Lichen planus Lichen planus is a dermatological condition which has several oral manifestations, including painful mucosal ulceration and Wickham’s striae. Wickham’s striae appear as a white, lacy network on the buccal mucosa; this is not raised or rough (as described in this patient), and the appearance does not change over a period of days. This patient has mouth signs consistent with oral hairy leukoplakia. This is caused by a reactivation of Epstein– Barr virus, which most often occurs in immunosuppressed individuals. Given his weight loss, travel background and widespread lymphadenopathy, he should be tested for HIV.

stem: You see a patient in the HIV Outpatients Clinic. He was diagnosed HIV-positive 6 weeks ago and was found to have a CD4 count of 12 × 106/l. He was commenced on prophylactic co-trimoxazole, but developed a rash and derangement of his liver function tests and it was stopped. He feels well now. He is planning to go mountain trekking in the Himalayas for the next three weeks. You try and dissuade him on the basis that he needs to be more immunocompetent before he goes but he will not be moved, as the trip was organised months ago and is for charity. The patient wants to reduce his risk of catching a range of infections and would like some information about vaccinations. He wants to know what vaccinations he should have, both routine and for travelling purposes. Which of the following groups of vaccines would you recommend as being safe in HIV-positive patients?
options: Hep A, Hep B, BCG, ﬂu jab
Hep A, Hep B, ﬂu jab, pneumococcal vaccine
Flu jab, pneumococcal vaccine, typhoid 21a, Hep B
explanation:
C Hep A, Hep B, ﬂu jab, pneumococcal vaccine In general, non-replicating vaccines, including whole inactivated, polysaccharide, conjugated and subunit vaccines, can be safely used in HIV infected people. Live replicating vacines have traditionally been seen as contraindicated, but with immunorestoration following antiretroviral therapy some vaccines are recommended including MMR, varicella-zoster virus and yellow fever. For the latter three, a

CD4 count >200 is advised. Most clinics will routinely vaccinate all HIV-positive patients against hepatitis A and B. Every traveller with HIV should be sure they are vaccinated against hepatitis A and B. Pneumovax and ﬂu vaccine are recommended. Countries have different vaccination requirements for entry. If polio vaccine is required, it should be the inactivated version, not the live oral version. E Flu jab, pneumococcal vaccine, typhoid 21a, Hep B Typhoid is a live vaccine and is therefore contraindicated. A Hep A, Hep B, mumps Mumps is part of the MMR vaccine and is a live attenuated vaccine. As the patient is immunocompromised with a low CD4 count this is not recommended. B Hep A, Hep B, BCG, ﬂu jab BCG is a live vaccine and is therefore contraindicated. D BCG, Ty21a typhoid, pneumococcal vaccine BCG is a live vaccine and is therefore contraindicated.

stem: A 33-year-old Botswana woman with a 2-week history of confusion was brought to the Emergency Department by her husband. Over the preceding year, she had lost weight and had had intermittent fevers and night sweats and recurrent chest infections. In the 3 months before her presentation, she became withdrawn and irritable, then unsteady on her feet, before becoming confused and requiring help with daily activities. She had lived in the United Kingdom for 6 months. On examination, her temperature was 36.6 °C. There was widespread lymphadenopathy and mild hepatosplenomegaly. There was no neck stiffness or photophobia. She had dysarthria and an ataxic gait. There was left-sided hypertonia and mild weakness. Investigations and cerebrospinal ﬂuid investigation reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Blood glucose 7.8 mmol/l 5.0–10.0 mmol/l Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) Appearance of CSF Clear Opening pressure 18 mmH2O 12–25 mmH2O Glucose 4.1 mmol/l 3.3–4.4 mmol/l Protein 0.7 g/l 0.15–0.45 g/l WCC 4.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Computed tomography (CT) head with contrast Multifocal hypodense non-enhancing periventricular lesions Her chest X-ray is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy This is a progressive demyelinating condition caused by the JC virus. It is very rare in immunocompetent individuals. However, this patient has a year’s history of weight loss, fever and night sweats; combined with lymphadenopathy and recent emigration from an area of high prevalence, it is possible that she has human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV). The indolent history of personality change, confusion and ataxia are typical for PML. The CSF is usually unremarkable, besides a raised protein level, as in this case. CT ﬁndings of hypodense periventricular lesions are typical. This patient’s need for HIV treatment needs to be addressed rapidly, as, without it, the mean survival of a patient with PML due to untreated HIV is < 3 months. B Cryptococcal meningitis Cryptococcal meningitis would present acutely, not indolently as in this case. You would expect the patient to be febrile and have meningism (neck stiffness or photophobia). The CSF typically demonstrates a very low glucose level (normal in this case) and a raised WCC with predominantly lymphocytes (again, the WCC is normal in this case). The subacute course, personality changes, ataxia and CT ﬁndings in this case are typical of PML.

A Bacterial meningitis Bacterial meningitis would not present with such an indolent course of confusion and personality change and would not explain her constitutional symptoms. You would also expect fever, neck stiffness or photophobia, which are not present in this case. Lumbar puncture would show a high WCC (polymorphs) and low glucose level, but in this case, there is a normal WCC and glucose level in the CSF. The subacute course, personality changes, ataxia and CT ﬁndings here are typical of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). D Multiple sclerosis There are some features of this patient’s presentation that would ﬁt with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, namely: dissociated focal neurological signs, the CSF ﬁndings and the CT imaging (though patchy widespread lesions are more common). Personality change is sometimes seen but is a less common presenting feature of multiple sclerosis. However, multiple sclerosis could not explain her constitutional symptoms of weight loss, night sweats and fevers, or the lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Combined with her recent emigration from an area of high prevalence, it is more likely that these symptoms and signs are due to untreated HIV infection, and consequent PML. E Tuberculosis Tuberculous meningitis can present with an insidious course of personality change, cranial nerve signs and confusion, as seen here. It is also far more common in ﬁrst-generation immigrants from countries with a high tuberculosis rate, like Botswana. However, it would be very unusual for a patient to have a normal chest X-ray in the context of tuberculosis meningitis – you would expect to see apical abnormalities consistent with active or previous infection. If this were tuberculous meningitis, you would also expect the patient to have meningism, but there is no photophobia or neck stiffness here. Typically, a lumbar puncture in tuberculous meningitis reveals CSF with a spidery blood clot (here it is clear) and a low glucose level (normal in this case). Finally, CT imaging would show tuberculomas (which do enhance on CT imaging), whereas in this case there are multiple non-enhancing periventricular lesions, typical of PML.

stem: A 19-year-old student is brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance after his ﬂat-mates called 999. They had been back at university for approximately 10 days since the summer break. He complained initially of ﬂu like symptoms, but over the past 24 h has taken to his bed complaining of a severe headache and neck stiffness. He is now drowsy and confused. On examination, he is pyrexial (38.9 °C), his BP is 95/50 mmHg and pulse is 95/min and regular. He has cold peripheries and a purpuric rash which appears to be extending even as you examine him. By the time you ﬁnish examining him he is unresponsive to commands. The paramedics have started a normal saline IV which is running through stat. An intubation tray is prepared. Which of the following is the most important next step?
explanation: C IV ceftriaxone Early antibiotic therapy is crucial with respect to successful management of meningococcal meningitis. As such, IV ceftriaxone is the most important next step. Ceftriaxone covers meningococci, pneumococci, H. inﬂuenzae type B and streptococci, and is therefore a very prudent empirical choice. In the community, IM or IV benzylpenicillin should be given. D IV FFP DIC is a potential complication that can be noted on the coagulation screen, but treating the underlying cause is more appropriate. A Further IV ﬂuid loading Although this patient may require further circulatory support / ﬂuid loading, at this stage time to antibiotics is the most important factor in his survival. A IV hydrocortisone IV steroids may reduce neurological sequelae, and as such are an important addition to therapy, although not initially. C IV benzylpenicillin IV benzylpenicillin is not recommended because of the possibility of resistant meningococci.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of fever and malaise. She has a mild cough but denies shortness of breath or chest pain. She has noticed the onset of a new rash over her face that is spreading to her arms and chest. Her past medical history includes hypothyroidism and congenital kidney disease for which she received a renal transplant from her younger sister ten years ago. Her regular medications include levothyroxine, tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. She has no allergies. Until three days ago, she has been ﬁt and well and working as a nursery school teacher. On examination, she has a temperature of 40.1 °C. Chest sounds are clear, with saturations of 97% on air. Her heart rate is 140 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 125/76 mmHg. She has normal heart sounds and capillary reﬁll time is < 2 seconds. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender and a palpable mass is felt in the left iliac fossa. She has a widespread morbilliform macular rash over her torso, upper arms and face as shown below on her arm. Her conjunctivae are red and she has dry mucous membranes. What is the most appropriate initial investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
A Nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA) This patient is on immunosuppressive medication following a renal transplant. Immunocompromised patients are susceptible to an increased number of infections, including common childhood infections against which most are normally immunised. The history of coryza and a maculopapular rash over the face and torso, along with conjunctivitis, is suggestive of measles. Her occupation as a nursery schoolteacher further increases this risk. The investigation of choice for diagnosing acute measles is an NPA or a throat swab for viral PCR. This is particularly true in the immunocompromised, where a decreased immune response may reduce the sensitivity of serological evidence. D Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common cause of illness in the immunocompromised, particularly post-solid organ transplant. The virus can present itself in various ways, including a mononucleosislike syndrome similar to Epstein–Barr virus pneumonia, colitis and retinitis. While it is an important differential to consider, the presence of a morbilliform rash and conjunctivitis is more suggestive of infection with the measles virus. B Blood culture While a blood culture is a good investigation to rule out alternative diagnoses, it is not needed to diagnose measles. C Measles immunoglobulin M (IgM) serology

IgM antibodies are raised in the acute phase of measles and, therefore, can be sent for to test for the disease. However, in immunocompromised patients, there may be a reduced immune response, making it a less sensitive diagnostic test. E Monospot test A Monospot test is used to diagnose glandular fever. The disease can present similarly with a sore throat and high fever. Other distinguishing clinical features include swollen and tender lymph nodes, along with lymphocytosis and deranged liver transaminases on blood testing. However, it has no role in diagnosing measles.

stem: A 28-year-old man is admitted after collapsing with a severe headache at the airport. He has a 3-day history of fever and ﬂu-like symptoms. He has returned from Kenya the previous day after a 3week visit, including time spent visiting the national parks. He was prescribed doxycycline before his trip but admits that he has been poorly compliant. On examination, his temperature is 38.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 105 bpm and regular and ﬁngertip glucose level 4.5 mmol/l. The cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable. His abdomen is soft, with palpable splenomegaly. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 114 g/l 130 - 180 g/l WCC 15.6 × 10 /l 4.0 - 11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 44 × 10 /l 150 - 400 × 10 /l Blood gases Result Normal values pH 7.21 7.35 - 7.45 p(O ) 12.4 kPa 11.3 - 12.6 kPa p(CO ) 2.4 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa HCO 14 mmol/l 21 - 29 mmol/l Given the likely diagnosis, what clinical feature is most indicative of severe disease?
explanation:
B Metabolic acidosis According to the World Health Organization, the presence of severe metabolic acidosis (base deﬁcit > 8 mmol/l, HCO3- level < 15 mmol/l or plasma lactate level > 5 mmol/l) qualiﬁes as severe malaria. As this patient has a HCO3- level of 14 mmol/l, he has severe metabolic acidosis.

A Glucose 4.5 mmol/l Hypoglycaemia is a criterion for the diagnosis of severe falciparum malaria (as per the World Health Organization’s guidelines); however, this patient is not hypoglycaemic. A glucose level of < 2.2 mmol/l would qualify as hypoglycaemia and lead to a diagnosis of severe falciparum malaria. C Platelet count of 44 × 109/l Thrombocytopenia is almost invariable in signiﬁcant malarial infection and, in itself, is not sufﬁcient for a diagnosis of severe malaria. D Splenomegaly Splenomegaly is a clinical feature seen in patients with malaria. However, it is not an indicator of severe disease. E Temperature of 38.8 °C It is common for patients with malaria to have a high fever, regardless of whether they have severe falciparum malaria or not. A fever > 39 °C is signiﬁcant for severe disease.

stem: A 19-year-old man is referred to the Infectious Diseases Clinic for review. His problems began around six weeks ago, when he suffered cold symptoms for a period of approximately ten days. These symptoms resolved, but he is now left with paroxysms of rapid coughing after which he sometimes vomits. He tells you these leave him exhausted. He has normal breath sounds on auscultation of the chest. He did not receive vaccinations as a child. Investigations reveal the following: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 141 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 9.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 281 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 28 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
A Gram-negative coccobacillus This patient’s symptoms, with an initial cold-like illness followed by recovery and then paroxysms of coughing, in a patient who has not

received childhood vaccinations, are typical of Bordetella pertussis (B pertussis), or whooping cough. Symptoms are usually much less severe in adults, and, as a consequence, most patients present later to medical services. Although macrolides are effective in shortening the period of illness and symptoms, they only impact if used in the ﬁrst 3 weeks. E Gram-positive coccus Staphylococcus aureus is a typical gram-positive coccus which leads to human infection. It can cause pneumonia following an inﬂuenzae illness. It is not, however, a cause of the symptoms here, where ‘paroxysms of coughing’ are consistent with B pertussis infection leading to Whooping Cough. B Gram-positive coccobacillus Listeria is a bacterium characterised by small gram-positive coccobacilli. It is a cause of gastroenteritis, and may cause meningitis, particularly in very old or pregnant patients. Amoxicillin is the intervention of choice. C Gram-negative bacillus Gram-negative bacilli are a prominent cause of bacteraemia necessitating hospital admission. Risks of gram- negative bacteraemia are signiﬁcantly increased in patients with comorbidities, with the urinary tract a common source of infection. In approximately one-ﬁfth of cases, Escherichia coli (E coli) is identiﬁed as the cause of sepsis. Where pseudomonas is not suspected to be the cause, ceftriaxone and piperacillin-tazobactam are typical empirical agents used in monotherapy for treating gramnegative sepsis. Where severe pseudomonas infection is suspected, then an aminoglycoside is used in combination. A Gram-positive bacillus Bacillus cereus (B cereus) and Bacillus anthracis (B anthracis) are examples of gram-positive bacteria. B cereus is a cause of gastroenteritis related to reheated rice, while B anthracis leads to the development of anthrax, which is usually fatal if the spores are inhaled.

stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has recently returned from a diving training trip to the Caribbean and complains of severe cellulitis and irritation affecting his right ear. He has been diving both in the sea and in a large heated training pool. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication. Examination reveals an erythematous right external auditory meatus with obvious discharging pus, which has a very strong odour. The right eardrum appears not to have perforated. There is no signiﬁcant pain on palpation of the skull around the ear. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: A Gentamicin drops The most likely diagnosis is otitis externa, commonly caused by pseudomonas otitis externa. Pseudomonas infections are sensitive to local therapy with gentamicin drops. This can be combined with local corticosteroids to reduce local inﬂammation and pain due to swelling. Where the eardrum has perforated, local preparations that do not contain gentamicin are preferred to reduce the risks of ototoxicity. Should systemic therapy be indicated, such as if cellulitis spreads beyond the ear canal or has systemic signs of infection, then a 7-day course of ﬂucloxacillin or, in the case of penicillin allergy, clarithromycin is indicated. E Oral erythromycin This patient does not have features of systemic illness or cellulitis extending beyond the ear canal. As such, local therapy is indicated. Should systemic therapy be indicated, then a 7-day course of ﬂucloxacillin or, in the case of penicillin allergy, clarithromycin should be used. B Intravenous (IV) ciproﬂoxacin IV antibiotics are reserved for systemic infection and extensive local infection only. While quinolones +/- aminoglycosides are suitable IV options in severe disease, should there be an absence of suitable alternatives, quinolone use should be avoided due to orthopaedic and neurologic complications. C Oral ciproﬂoxacin The most likely diagnosis is otitis externa, commonly caused by pseudomonas otitis externa. The patient’s presentation indicates local infection and treatment should be guided based on this. Should IV treatment be required, due to severe or refractory disease, then ﬂuoroquinolones should only be used if there are no suitable alternatives due to orthopaedic and neurological complications associated with the class of antibiotics. D Oral co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav’s spectrum of antibiotic activity doesn’t covers pseudomonas. the ﬁrst treatment of choice in systemically well patients is gentamicin drops. Should systemic therapy be indicated, then a 7-day course of ﬂucloxacillin or, in the case of penicillin allergy, clarithromycin is indicated.

stem: A 33-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of frontal headache, nausea and vomiting. Eleven months ago, he had had a left cerebellopontine angle tumour removed, and 1 week before this presentation, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt had been inserted for hydrocephalus. On examination, the temperature is 37.9 °C. Pupils are reactive and equal to light, and fundoscopy is normal. There is a left facial nerve palsy, without sparing of the upper face. Kernig’s sign is positive.
