Initial investigations are as follows: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 310 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l C-reactive protein 180 mg/l < 10 mg/l Serum glucose 5.1 mmol 3.9–7.1 mmol/l ESR 35 mm/ﬁrst hour 1–10 mm/ﬁrst hour Cerebrospinal ﬂuid Glucose 2.7 mmol 3.3–4.4 mmol WCC 1400 /μl < 5/μl Protein 0.68 g/l 0.15–0.45 g/l Culture No growth after 48 h Which is the most likely causative organism to be found in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid?
explanation:
D Staphylococcus epidermidis

This is a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species and it is the most common cause of meningitis after neurosurgical procedures; this patient has just had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed. Therefore, it is the most likely culprit in this case. The consideration of coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species is important, and these organisms are typically penicillin-resistant. Treatment would need to be given in line with local guidelines but is likely to include vancomycin. C Neisseria meningitidis N. meningitidis is one of the most common causes of meningitis in the United Kingdom. However, this patient has had a neurosurgical procedure; meningitis in these patients is caused by a different group of organisms. The most common cause of post-procedure meningitis is S. epidermidis, a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species, and this is the answer in this case. A Escherichia coli Although E. coli is one of the causes of meningitis in patients following neurosurgical procedures (such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion), it is not the most common. The most common organism implicated in these infections is the coagulase-negative Staphylococcus epidermidis, which is the correct answer in this case. A Haemophilus inﬂuenzae type B Before routine vaccination against Haemophilus, this was a common cause of meningitis in ‘normal’ patients. However, a different group of organisms are implicated in post-surgical meningitis, the most common of which is the coagulase-negative S. epidermidis (which is the correct answer in this case). D Streptococcus pneumoniae This is one of the most common causes of meningitis in adults in the UK; however, this patient has recently had a neurosurgical procedure which has a different epidemiology. The most common cause of meningitis post- procedure is coagulase-negative S. epidermidis, and therefore this is the correct answer.

stem: A 32-year-old man is admitted unconscious to the Emergency Department, brought in by his partner. His partner states he has has been complaining of increasingly severe headaches over the past few days and collapsed that morning, having suffered a tonic–clonic seizure. The patient has lost approximately six kg in weight over the past ﬁve months and has been suffering from multiple chest infections. On examination, he is pyrexial at 38.1 °C. His BP is 155/90 mmHg and his heart rate 90 bpm and regular. He has a GCS score of 10. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema and his pupils are poorly reactive. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l CD4 lymphocyte count 82 cells/mm3 430–1690 cells/mm3 Platelets (PLT) 171 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 130 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 102 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l On the CT head, there are multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Toxoplasmosis This patient has a likely diagnosis of toxoplasmosis, given the presentation with fever, headaches, altered mental status, reduced GCS score and ring-enhancing lesions on CT, imaging. In association with a history of weight loss, recurrent infections and a low CD4 count (particularly under 200 cells/mm3), toxoplasmosis should be considered as the likely diagnosis. The CT ﬁndings typically include multiple ring-enhancing lesions of variable sizes. B Cryptococcal meningitis Cryptococcal meningitis is a fungal infection secondary to Cryptococcus neoformans and presents similarly to bacterial meningitis with fever, headache, altered mental status and seizures. However, CT imaging does not demonstrate ring-enhancing lesions. Rather, CT imaging shows leptomeningeal enhancement, cryptococcomas and hydrocephalus. A Cerebral lymphoma Cerebral lymphoma is a reasonable differential diagnosis, given the presence of ring-enhancing lesions in a patient with a likely underlying diagnosis of HIV with a CD4 count of under 200 cells/mm3. On the CT, a single ring-enhancing lesion may be seen. However, given the presence of fever and multiple ring-enhancing lesions, an alternative diagnosis, such as toxoplasmosis, must be considered. C Tuberculous meningitis Although immunosuppression would put this patient at risk of tuberculous meningitis, CT imaging is similar to cryptococcosis, with leptomeningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus in the later stages. E Subarachnoid haemorrhage Subarachnoid haemorrhage classically presents with the suddenonset occipital headache associated with nausea, vomiting,

photophobia, neck stiffness and reduced GCS score. This presentation is more gradual in onset and would not explain the CT ﬁndings.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Genitourinary Clinic for review. She complains of a 5-day history of mucopurulent vaginal discharge and dysuria. She conﬁrms that she has had three regular sexual partners and uses the intrauterine system as contraception. She has no past medical history of note and no allergies. On examination, she has a temperature of 36.7 °C. Her blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg and her heart rate is 88 bpm. There is lower abdominal tenderness on palpation. Endocervical swab – nucleic acid ampliﬁcation test (NAAT): Gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline and oral metronidazole
explanation:
A Intramuscular ceftriaxone This patient has a likely diagnosis of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, given the positive endocervical swab for Gram-negative diplococci. The most recent guidelines from the British Association of Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) advise giving a one-off dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone for the treatment of gonorrhoea. E Oral doxycycline Oral Doxycycline is not indicated for gonorrhoea. Rather, it is used in the treatment of chlamydia. B Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin This used to be the recommended treatment for gonorrhoea, particularly if there were concerns regarding additional infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. However, this is no longer recommended by BASHH. C Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline and oral metronidazole This is used in the treatment of pelvic inﬂammatory disease. Although Neisseria gonorrhoeae is capable of causing pelvic inﬂammatory disease, additional features that this patient would be expected to present with would be signs of systemic upset such as fever and tachycardia. D Oral ciproﬂoxacin Traditionally, this was the treatment of choice for gonorrhoea.

However, it is no longer the ﬁrst-line treatment of choice because of the widespread resistance of Gonococcus to quinolones.

stem: A 31-year-old man presents with his partner for review. For the past few days he has had worsening diarrhoea with voluminous ﬂuid loss. On further questioning, he admits to weight loss over the past 6 months. Modiﬁed acid-fast staining of stool culture reveals redstained round oocysts against a blue–green background. Investigations reveal a reduced CD4/CD8 ratio. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial step in this case?
explanation:
D HIV testing This patient has diarrhoea with a stool sample that suggests oocysts consistent with Cryptosporidium infection. The reduced CD4/CD8 ratio raises the possibility of HIV infection, and screening for HIV is clearly required. In patients with a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm3 blood, chronic diarrhoea is common once Cryptosporidium infection is established. Antibiotic trials for Cryptosporidium have been disappointing, and at present there is not enough evidence to recommend any particular regime, but some patients do appear to respond to nitzoxanide. In patients who are HIV-negative, the infection tends to be self-limiting and patients recover after only a few days. C IV cefotaxime Cefotaxime provides good broad-spectrum cover and is useful in meningitis and pneumonia rather than for gastrointestinal infections. A Oral ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin may be considered as a treatment option for gastrointestinal infection with Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter. The abnormal staining of acid-fast pathogens makes this unlikely. In addition, the partner is not unwell and there is no history of ingestion of contaminated food. B Oral metronidazole Metronidazole would be a good antibiotic choice if anaerobes such as Gardnerella, Entamoeba, Giardia or Clostridium were suspected. This might be suspected with bloody diarrhoea or, for C. difﬁcile, recent antibiotic use. E Oral co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav provides far better cover for respiratory and urinary infections and would be of little use for this patient.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with fever 1 week after returning from India. Her fevers followed a speciﬁc pattern, rising over the course of the day and then dropping by the next morning. She also had non-speciﬁc abdominal pain, malaise and a dry cough. She had noticed a rash on her trunk. On examination, her temperature was 38.1 °C and she appeared dehydrated. She had diffuse abdominal tenderness and a pink maculopapular rash over her trunk. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLatelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Stool culture Isolates of Salmonella paratyphi The patient is keen not to be admitted to hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
D Azithromycin This patient has typhoid fever, which can be caused by Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi subtypes. Her presentation with high intermittent fever, dry cough, malaise and abdominal pain is typical. Patients classically have constipation rather than diarrhoea. Typhoid fever can be treated with ﬂuoroquinolones; however, given that this patient has contracted typhoid fever after travelling to India, there is a high chance that the organism is ﬂuoroquinolone resistant, and azithromycin would be a safer choice of treatment. B Doxycycline This patient has typhoid fever, caused by S. paratyphi and indicated by her intermittent high fevers, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and non-speciﬁc abdominal pain, in combination with the ﬁndings on stool culture. Although doxycyline provides some coverage of Salmonella, there is widespread resistance amongst typhi and paratyphi species. A better and safer choice of antibiotic in this case would be azithromycin. A Ciproﬂoxacin

This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with typhoid fever: the high intermittent fever, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and non-speciﬁc abdominal pain, and stool culture has conﬁrmed the presence of S. paratyphi. Typhoid fever can be treated with ﬂuoroquinolones such as ciproﬂoxacin; however, there is widespread resistance amongst typhoid organisms to ﬂuoroquinolones, especially in India. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. Consequently, azithromycin would be a safer choice of treatment for this patient. C Erythromycin This patient has typhoid fever – hence the intermittent high fever, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and non-speciﬁc abdominal pain – conﬁrmed by the ﬁnding of S. paratyphi in the stool culture. Salmonella paratyphi is a Gram- negative rod: erythromycin has poor Gram-negative coverage and is used for Gram-positive infections. Consequently it would be a poor choice of antibiotic to treat this patient: a better choice would be azithromycin. Ciproﬂoxacin can also be used to treat typhoid fever, but resistance to ﬂuoroquinolones is rife, especially in India, and therefore azithromycin is the best choice in this case. E Flucloxacillin This patient’s intermittent high fever, dry cough, lack of diarrhoea and diffuse abdominal pain is consistent with typhoid fever, given her travel history. This is conﬁrmed with the ﬁnding of S. paratyphi in her stool. Salmonella paratyphi is a Gram-negative rod: ﬂucloxacillin is typically used for Gram-positive infections and has poor activity against Salmonella. Ciproﬂoxacin or azithromycin would be better choices of antibiotic for this patient. Due to the prevalence of ﬂuoroquinolone resistance, especially in India, azithromycin would be the best choice in this case.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department, having returned 24 hours earlier from a holiday to Thailand. He has been living in the remote north of the country and been eating mainly local food. He admits to a diarrhoeal illness a few days earlier but now feels constipated and is complaining of increasing abdominal pain and distension. He also has a severe headache that is non-responsive to paracetamol. On examination, his temperature is 38.9 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg and pulse 85 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination reveals mild hepatosplenomegaly with tenderness. Bowel sounds appear sluggish but normal, and the rectum is empty on rectal examination. You notice a rash with sparse pink papules over the upper body. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 189 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 189 mg/l < 5 mg/l Glucose 7.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: B Ceftriaxone The history here ﬁts with possible typhoid fever, given the likelihood of exposure during his holiday to Thailand and typical features, including abdominal pain and a typhoid fever-associated skin rash. In this case, with signiﬁcant fever and abdominal pain, ceftriaxone is the most appropriate intervention. Use of quinolones (an alternative here) is discouraged because of adverse events associated with the class. A Chloramphenicol Chloramphenicol is an option for treating typhoid fever where there is evidence of multidrug resistance. We have no evidence here that treatment with ceftriaxone will be unsuccessful. C Metronidazole Metronidazole is the intervention of choice for giardiasis, which does not ﬁt with the symptom picture here. Giardiasis is associated with symptoms typical of irritable bowel syndrome. D Oral rehydration salts Oral rehydration salts are most important in the management of severe diarrhoea where pre-renal failure may ensue. Examples where they are of value is in norovirus infection in vulnerable patients and in patients with cholera. E Senna Prokinetic agents, such as senna, are not advised in the treatment of typhoid fever. Bowel function recovers slowly once the underlying infection is treated.

stem: A 62-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of fever, shortness of breath and a cough with haemoptysis. He had returned from Mississippi 3 weeks previously, where he was studying bats. He had no other medical conditions. On examination, his temperature was 37.6 °C, and oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. He appeared well and comfortable at rest. There was bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 112 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 120 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 35 mm/1st hr 0–10 mm in the 1st hour Sputum culture Yeast forms His chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
A Itraconazole This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with a diagnosis of histoplasmosis. This would also ﬁt with his travel history as it is endemic to areas with large bat and bird populations, such as Mississippi, Ohio and Missouri. In this relatively mild case, a prolonged course of itraconazole would be most appropriate. C Doxycycline Doxycycline is an antibiotic used in the management of communi-

ty-acquired pneumonia in patients with pre- existing respiratory conditions, and in the management of rickettsial illness (e.g. Rocky Mountain spotted fever). It would not be appropriate for the treatment of a fungal or yeast infection, as seen here. It has no role in histoplasmosis. B Amphotericin This patient has symptoms, signs and investigations consistent with histoplasmosis where amphotericin would be the correct treatment in severe disease, but here in relatively mild disease, a prolonged course of itraconazole would be more appropriate. D Ganciclovir Ganciclovir is an antiviral therapy, which would not be appropriate for the treatment of this patient’s yeast infection. E Prednisolone Occasionally steroids such as methylprednisolone may be used in conjunction with antifungals in the treatment of severe disease, or complications of histoplasmosis (such as pericarditis); however, prednisolone has no role in treating mild disease.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a febrile illness one day after commencing oral doxycycline prescribed by the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic the previous day. He has a temperature of 38.0 °C; his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. There is a generalised maculopapular rash. His cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable and his neurological examination is entirely normal. Investigation results from Genitourinary Medicine Clinic are shown below: Investigation Result Treponemal enzyme immunoassay (EIA) Positive Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) serology Positive Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
E Paracetamol This patient has a diagnosis of syphilis, given the positive

treponemal enzyme immunoassay and venereal disease research laboratory serology tests. He almost certainly is experiencing a Jarisch–Herxheimer (JH) reaction, which is thought to be related to the sudden release of large amounts of endotoxin due to the death of spirochaetes after initially commencing antibiotics. In the majority of patients, it carries a benign course and no intervention is required. Initial therapy is with paracetamol. Steroids and non-steroidal antiinﬂammatory drugs can be considered for patients with severe symptoms, although they are not thought to inﬂuence outcomes. D Prednisolone Corticosteroids are usually only prescribed for patients with a severe JH reaction whose symptoms are not responsive to paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs. They do not have an impact on the clearance of syphilis infection. A Aspirin Given the Jarisch–Herxheimer (JH) reaction is driven by endotoxin release, aspirin does not have a role in its management. Paracetamol is the initial therapy of choice, and a conventional non-steroidal antiinﬂammatory drug, such as ibuprofen, could be added in the event that symptoms are not controlled. B Chlorpheniramine Although chlorphenamine is not a routine component of treatment for the JH reaction, it is recommended as part of European guidelines on syphilis as pre-treatment to prevent it from occurring. C Diazepam Sedatives are not usually considered in the management of the JH reaction. In cases where sedation is required, a sedating antihistamine, such as chlorphenamine, is more commonly prescribed.

stem: A 50-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 2week history of malaise, headaches and reduced oral intake. He also has a history of dry cough for the last week and sharp right-sided chest pain on deep inspiration. His observations show a temperature of 38.3 °C, a heart rate of 108 bpm and regular and a blood pressure of 142/91 mmHg. On examination, he has coarse crackles at the right base but no audible wheeze. His respiratory rate is 23 breaths per minute, with oxygen saturations of 90% on room air. He has dry mucous membranes with mild stomatitis.
explanation:
D Mycoplasma pneumoniae This patient has an atypical pneumonia that is most likely secondary to the bacterium M. pneumoniae. Common presenting features include a preceding phase of ﬂu-like symptoms before the onset of respiratory symptoms, including shortness of breath and productive cough. Extrapulmonary symptoms are also seen. This patient has erythema multiforme, as shown by the target lesion rash, and the low haemoglobin and raised bilirubin levels suggest a haemolytic process. It is likely that this patient would have a positive Coombs’ test.

C Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is a common cause of pneumonia in patients following an infection with the inﬂuenza virus. Although this patient does give a history of ﬂu-like symptoms, staphylococcal pneumonia would not cause all of this patient’s presenting symptoms. A Mycobacterium tuberculosis M. tuberculosis is the organism responsible for the respiratory illness tuberculosis. Symptoms of tuberculosis have a more insidious onset, with constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fever and night sweats also common. This is not seen in the patient, making it unlikely here. B Streptococcus pneumoniae S. pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of communityacquired pneumonia. However, it does not explain the erythema multiforme. These additional symptoms suggest an atypical pneumonia, with Mycoplasma pneumonia being the most likely diagnosis. E Legionella pneumophila Legionnaire’s disease is a bacterial pneumonia caused by the bacterium L. pneumophila. It presents with symptoms of community-acquired pneumonia. However, additional symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea are commonly seen and blood tests often show hyponatraemia and deranged liver function tests. It is commonly spread in contaminated water supply, and a careful travel history is needed as it can spread via air conditioning in hotels. It does not explain all of the ﬁndings in this patient, making M. pneumoniae more likely here.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the Sexual Health Clinic with painful lesions on his penis that have progressively worsened over the past four weeks. He reports having unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. The lesion began as small, red and raised and slowly progressed to intensely painful ulcers. On examination, he was found to have multiple painful penile ulcers, with the largest measuring 2.5 cm. A tender, soft, ﬂuctuant swelling is present in the right inguinal region. Gram staining from the base of the largest penile ulcer revealed Gram-negative rods arranged in a chain-like fashion. Which of the following is the best line of treatment in this patient?
explanation: D Single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone This person is suffering from chancroid due to infection with Haemophilus ducreyi. Gram staining shows the presence of a school of ﬁsh appearance. Single-dose therapy with intramuscular ceftriaxone is recommended as the ﬁrst line of management. Oral azithromycin has also been found to be equally effective. In addition, ﬂuctuant lymphadenitis (as present in this patient) should be drained by needle aspiration. E Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole is not the ﬁrst line of management for chancroid. It has been used as an alternative to azithromycin in the management of granuloma inguinale caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. A Intramuscular benzathine penicillin Intramuscular benzathine penicillin has been used for the treatment of syphilis, which usually presents with a painless ulcer and nonﬂuctuant, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. B Oral aciclovir Genital herpes usually presents with multiple painful ulcers that start as vesicles and Gram staining is usually negative. Treatment for genital herpes is oral aciclovir. C Oral doxycycline Oral doxycycline is the treatment of choice for lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. LGV presents with a small, painless ulcer, which usually disappears by the time the inguinal buboes appear.

stem: A 63-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with a 2week history of increasing fatigue, fever and rigors. The fever appears to come on every few days. He has recently come back from Long Island, where he stayed with family. He remembers being bitten by a tick, which he subsequently removed. He has a history of hypertension and he had his spleen removed following a road trafﬁc accident 12 years ago. He is taking aspirin, an angiotensinconverting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and penicillin V. He is a nonsmoker. On examination, he is jaundiced, looks unwell, is slightly confused and has a temperature of 38.7 °C. He has no lymphadenopathy. His pulse is 120 bpm and regular and blood pressure 95/60 mmHg. His chest is clear and his abdomen is soft but non-speciﬁcally tender. He has no neurological abnormality. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 71 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 97 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 189 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l MCV 80.2 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ CRP 213 µg/l < 10 mg/l Serum electrophoresis Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia CXR Clear Urinalysis Haemoglobinuria What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Babesiosis This is a tick-borne malaria-like illness caused by species of the intra-erythrocytic protozoan Babesia. Patients present with similar symptoms to malaria, i.e. fever, chills and rigors. The intraerythrocytic Babesia destroy the red blood cells, causing haemolytic anaemia and haemoglobinuria. Symptoms are greater with a higher percentage of parasitism. A B-lymphocyte response is elicited with a secondary reactive polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia Babesiosis is frequent in endemic areas of the USA, particularly Long Island, New York and Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts. Patients without a spleen have a more fulminant and prolonged clinical course and may have an overwhelming infection and a fatal outcome. Babesiosis is often a clinical diagnosis, and the history of a recent trip to Long Island and being bitten should differentiate this from malaria. In addition, patients with malaria often have a more pronounced headache. Lyme disease does not cause haemolytic anaemia, and nocardiosis is only fulminant in the immunocompromised. For immunocompetent individuals with mild to moderate Babesia microti infection, treatment with oral azithromycin plus oral atovaquone is needed. For immunocompetent individuals with severe B. microti infection, treatment with intravenous (IV) azithromycin plus oral atovaquone; IV clindamycin is an alternative regimen. Patients with severe B. microti infection may warrant exchange transfusion. Exchange transfusion is recommended for patients with high-grade parasitemia (>10%), severe hemolysis (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), or organ (pulmonary, renal, or liver) impairment. For immunocompromised patients with severe B. microti infection, initial treatment with IV azithromycin plus oral atovaquone is recommended. The usual duration of treatment is 7-10 days. In immunocompromised with high risk of relapse up to 6 weeks of treatment may be required.

C Lyme Disease Lyme disease is an infectious illness caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi. It is transmitted through tick bites. It initially presents with a slowly expanding skin lesion around the tick bite, erythema migrans, malaise and joint aches. If not treated, neurological, cardiac and joint involvement can occur. The patient described here is profoundly unwell and does not have erythema migrans; this would not be typical of acute Lyme disease. B Perforated duodenal ulcer The history presented here is not consistent with a perforated duodenal ulcer, you would not expect a 2-week history of fatigue and rigors. In addition, examination would more usually reveal abdominal guarding with tenderness localising to the epigastrium. Jaundice and thrombocytopenia would also not be present. D Malaria Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by several different species of the genus Plasmodium. It is transmitted by the female anopheles mosquito. Malaria is endemic neither in the United States nor the United Kingdom, and therefore could not be the diagnosis in this patient. E Nocardiosis Nocardiosis is an uncommon infection caused by Gram-positive bacteria of the genus Nocardia. It may present as a localised (most commonly pulmonary or central nervous system) or systemic infection. The majority of patients affected have underlying immunodeﬁciency (HIV, immunosuppressive therapy, malignancy), which makes nocardiosis unlikely in our patient.

stem: A 33-year-old pregnant woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 6-day history of worsening shortness of breath. Since the breathlessness has worsened, she has developed pleuritic chest pain and a cough productive of purulent green sputum. She has been feeling very lethargic with generalised body aches and occasional episodes of diarrhoea. Her past medical history includes iron deﬁciency anaemia, for which she takes ferrous sulfate 200 mg three times a day. She has no known drug allergies. On examination, she is tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 29 breaths/min and her saturations are 89% on room air. She has audible crackles at the base of her right lung. Her heart rate is 100 bpm and regular and her blood pressure is 110/69 mmHg; her heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is soft, with a palpable uterus consistent with 20-week gestation. She has a temperature of 38.1 °C. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: C Intravenous amoxicillin This question describes a pregnant woman who has presented with symptoms of pneumonia. She is lethargic with ﬂu-like symptoms and is systemically unwell on examination with tachycardia, tachypnoea and hypoxia. A presentation similar to this in a pregnant woman should raise suspicion of listeriosis. Patients who are immunocompromised and pregnant women are more susceptible to listeriosis and it can lead to miscarriage or premature delivery, making prompt treatment vital. Treatment of listeriosis is with amoxicillin or ampicillin. D Intravenous ceftriaxone This patient has listeriosis. Listeria has shown resistance to cephalosporins, making ceftriaxone a less appropriate choice. A Intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin This patient has listeriosis, the treatment of which is intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin. While intravenous co- amoxiclav would be appropriate, clarithromycin is teratogenic and studies have shown higher rates of spontaneous abortion in those treated with clarithromycin in the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, clarithromycin should be avoided. B Oral doxycycline Doxycycline is not used in the treatment of listeriosis and is contraindicated in pregnant women due to the risk of teratogenic side effects, including enamel hypoplasia and teeth discolouration and should be avoided when possible. E Oral ciproﬂoxacin This patient has listeriosis, the treatment of which is intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin. Ciproﬂoxacin has no role in treating listeriosis. Animal studies have shown an increased risk of arthropathy during pregnancy and for that reason, ciproﬂoxacin is contraindicated in pregnant women.

stem: A 27-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of ﬂu-like symptoms and fatigue. Six weeks previously he had had unprotected receptive anal sexual intercourse. On examination, he had low-volume cervical lymphadenopathy; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal Values WCC 5.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 3.9 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.9 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) Hepatitis B surface antigen 40 × 109/l - 150 - 400 × 109/l Hepatitis B core antibody + HIV antibody - Epstein–Barr virus IgM - Epstein–Barr virus IgG + Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
D HIV This would explain the patient’s ﬂu-like illness and lymphadenopathy, and the timing would ﬁt with his exposure through unprotected sexual intercourse: seroconversion is typically at 6 weeks after exposure. The lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia are common features of seroconversion. It is quite common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion: a p24 antigen test should also be carried out, and testing should be repeated as suspicion is high. If investigations conﬁrm the diagnosis, guidance suggests that the patient should be started on antiretroviral therapy straight away. E Inﬂuenza Inﬂuenza would explain his symptoms, and the lymphopenia (commonly seen in viral infections). However, lymphadenopathy is less typical of inﬂuenza and he does not complain of any coryzal symptoms. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion; he has had a potential exposure 6 weeks previously, which would ﬁt with the timing of his illness. HIV seroconversion would also explain his thrombocytopenia and lymphadenopathy. It is common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion. A Early Epstein–Barr virus This patient has serology consistent with a previous, but not a recent, infection. After Epstein–Barr infection, IgG remains positive at a variable titre for life; IgM is only positive 4–8 weeks after an acute infection, and remains positive for up to a year. This patient has a positive IgG, indicating previous infection, but with a negative IgM it is unlikely that this is acute Epstein–Barr virus infection. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion – HIV antibody can be negative before seroconversion is complete. This would explain the ﬂu- like illness and lymphadenopathy; the timing would also ﬁt with a possible exposure through unprotected sexual intercourse. B Hepatitis B This patient has serology consistent with past infection with hepatitis B virus (i.e. he is core antibody positive), but there is no evidence that he is a carrier as he is surface antigen negative.

Hepatitis B surface antigen would be positive within the ﬁrst 3–5 weeks of infection. Instead, this patient has symptoms and signs consistent with acute HIV infection and seroconversion: he has a ﬂu-like illness, lymphadenopathy and he has had unprotected sex 6 weeks previously. It is common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion. C Herpes Patients who contract genital herpes can have a prodromal ﬂu-like illness and lymphadenopathy, but this would typically occur earlier than 6 weeks after exposure. There are no genital ulcers on examination, though these can occur after the ﬂu-like illness has subsided. Instead, this patient is more likely to be in HIV seroconversion: this would explain his ﬂu-like illness and lymphadenopathy, and the timing would ﬁt with his exposure through unprotected sexual intercourse. It is quite common for HIV antibodies to be negative during seroconversion.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with type I diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with severe earache and discharge. She has recently returned from a holiday in the Dominican Republic where she regularly swam in the hotel pool. She saw her GP one week early and was prescribed co-amoxiclav, but her partner thinks that the problem is getting worse and they can now see the infection around her ear. Her ear is shown below. Which of the following represents the most likely infectious agent?
explanation: C Pseudomonas aeruginosa The image shows severe otitis externa with surrounding erythema and tissue destruction. This woman has presented with so called “Swimmer’s Ear” due to pseudomonas infection which may have occurred via the swimming pool at the hotel where she was staying Pseudomonas is the cause of swimmer’s ear and is not responsive to co-amoxiclav therapy. Severe spreading infections occur more commonly in patients who also suffer from diabetes mellitus, as in this case. Therapy may involve a combination of systemic and locally delivered antibiotic therapy, and in this case an ENT surgical opinion should sought. C Streptococcus pneumoniae Streptococci are gram-positive diplococci, of which S. pneumoniae cases pneumonia, meningitis and otitis media. The clinical ﬁnding of otitis externa makes this a less likely pathogen. A Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is a gram-positive commensal pathogen which can cause infection of skin, eyelids and wounds. In severe infections can cause pneumonia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis and septic arthritis. The toxins can cause food poisoning and toxic shock syndrome. S. aureus is unlikely to cause infection, and unlikely to be acquired by swimming in a swimming pool. B Staphylococcus epidermidis S. epidermidis is a coagulase negative species of Staphylococcus. These species are only pathogenic if associated with immunosuppression or insertion of foreign objects such as following hip replacements. These bacteria are likely to cause otitis externa in an immunosuppressed individual. D Streptococcus pyogenes S. pyogenes is s group A Streptococcus, referring to the Lanceﬁeld classiﬁcation by degree of heamolysis. These species cause wound and skin infections, including impetigo and erysipelas, and are also associated with tonsillitis, scarlet fever and rheumatic fever.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. Her bowel movements were normal. On examination, her temperature was 37.9oC and her blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg. Her abdomen was soft but tender in both iliac fossae. There was anterior tenderness on digital rectal examination. On speculum examination there was profuse white–yellow vaginal discharge and tenderness. A urine pregnancy test was negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Acute salpingitis Most cases are associated with sexually transmitted infection. Patients present with lower abdominal pain, a fever and vaginal discharge. The Fitz–Hughes–Curtis syndrome associated with Chlamydia infection is caused by infection tracking up the right paracolic gutter to cause a peri-hepatitis. These patients may also have right hypochondrial pain, fever and mild elevations in liver biochemistry. D Ectopic pregnancy This patient has a negative pregnancy test, which would make an ectopic pregnancy very unlikely. Ectopic pregnancies typically cause a unilateral lower abdominal pain, and may be accompanied by vaginal bleeding. It would not cause vaginal discharge of the type seen here. This constellation of abdominal pain, fever and vaginal discharge is more suggestive of acute salpingitis. A Acute appendicitis Acute appendicitis is an important differential diagnosis in any patient presenting with right iliac fossa pain; however, this patient is opening her bowels normally, does not have any signs of peritonism and has vaginal discharge. Acute salpingitis would be a better explanation of her presentation. C Bacterial vaginosis Bacterial vaginosis does cause vaginal discharge, but does not cause abdominal pain or fever. It is most commonly caused by Gardnerella vaginalis. This patient’s abdominal pain, fever and vaginal discharge are suggestive of acute salpingitis, which is typically caused by a sexually transmitted infection such as Chlamydia. Gardnerella is not a sexually transmitted infection. E Ruptured ovarian cyst A ruptured ovarian cyst can cause abdominal pain, but it could not explain the vaginal discharge seen here. The patient may have a low-grade fever. Instead, this patient’s symptoms of abdominal pain, fever and vaginal discharge are consistent with acute salpingitis.

stem: A 47-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with foul-smelling diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and excessive burping since returning from his annual summer holiday to Thailand. Examination reveals a BP of 122/72 mmHg, and his heart rate is 70 bpm and regular. He is apyrexial. His abdomen is mildly distended, but soft and non-tender. There are active bowel sounds. Flagellate protozoa are identiﬁed in the stool sample. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: D Metronidazole The symptoms here ﬁt with giardiasis, and the presence of protozoa in the stool sample conﬁrms the underlying diagnosis. Potential interventions include metronidazole and tinidazole. Some activity of mebendazole is noted against Giardia, although it is not a ﬁrst-line therapeutic option. Long-term complications of giardiasis are rare. Lactose intolerance is the most commonly reported long-term consequence of infection. Very rare sequelae include cholecystitis and reactive arthritis. A Azithromycin Azithromycin can be used in the treatment of traveller’s diarrhoea caused by Escherichia coli, although it does not have a role in the treatment of giardiasis. B Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a potential intervention for Salmonella or Campylobacter infection. These are both associated with acute presentations with gastroenteritis rather than with the chronic symptoms of Giardia colonisation seen here. C Nitazoxanide Cryptosporidium is a reasonable differential for giardiasis. It results in a diarrhoeal illness with lethargy, nausea, abdominal cramps and fever. It typically occurs in patients who are immunocompromised, such as patients with untreated HIV. It can be distinguished from giardiasis via stool antigen testing or microscopy, where the oocysts can be seen, unlike in the stool sample here. Where a patient has untreated HIV, the initial management is supportive and with the initiation of anti-retroviral therapy. Where symptoms are persistent, but not severe, nitazoxanide can be considered. E Praziquantel Praziquantel is an anthelmintic used to treat ﬂukes and schistosomiasis. While it does have some efﬁcacy in treating giardiasis, it is not used as it is not as effective as metronidazole or tinidazole.

stem: A 76-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department some 8–12 h after eating a ready-made chicken meal. She complains of fever, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. She has recently been taking co-amoxiclav for a respiratory tract infection, but nothing else of note. Her blood pressure (BP) is 122/72 mmHg, with a post-drop of 20 mmHg on standing with corresponding increase in pulse rate. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 129 g/l 135 - 175 g/l Platelets (PLT) 560 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l WCC 4.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 148 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 18.4 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 195 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: E Salmonella This patient has acute bacterial gastroenteritis. She is likely to have acquired this from the ready-made chicken meal eaten some hours previously. Given this food history and the evidence of severe dehydration due to the infection, the most likely candidates are Salmonella or Campylobacter infection. The incubation period of Campylobacter infection can sometimes be much longer, up to 7 days, but can be as short as 24 h, as is the case here. The incubation period of Salmonella gastroenteritis is 6–72 h, making it the more likely diagnosis in this case. Uncomplicated infections with these agents do not require treatment, but where there is signiﬁcant dehydration as in this case, oral or intravenous rehydration therapy ± quinolone antibiotics could be considered. D Giardiasis It is caused by Giardia lamblia, a ﬂagellated protozoon, which infects the jejenum and deuodenum following faecal–oral spread. Causes explosive diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and malabsorption. Diagnosis is with stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites or PCR. Treatment is with tindazole 2 g stat, with high levels of hygiene. May cause lactose intolerance as well. A Norovirus Norovirus causes symptoms 12–48 h after exposure. It is spread via droplets and is highly infectious. It causes outbreaks of ‘winter vomiting illness’, with projectile vomiting, diarrhoea and fever and settles quickly. Treatment is supportive but patients will need to be strictly isolated. B Rotavirus Rotavirus is a cause of viral gastroenteritis up to the age of ﬁve. Following 1–5 days of incubation there is malaise, diarrhoea, vomiting and fever. C Amoebiasis Ameobiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoon. Spread is via the faecal–oral route. Presentation is usually with gastrointestinal symptoms but in 1% there can be invasive liver disease. Subtle amoebic dysentery presents slowly but can lead to bloody diarrhoea and fever. Diagnosis is with stool microscopy demonstrating trophozoites, bleed and pus cells.

stem: A 53-year-old woman presented to clinic with concerns about her exposure to chickenpox. She had a background of systemic lupus erythematosus and was taking high-dose prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine. She had no personal history of chickenpox. The patient had been exposed to chickenpox 2 days ago whilst looking after her 4-year-old granddaughter, who had become symptomatic with chickenpox. The patient is tested for IgG varicella antibody, which is found to be positive. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
C Reassurance This patient is IgG positive for varicella, and therefore she has previously had chickenpox and is immune to her granddaughter’s infection. She may have been so young, or had sufﬁciently mild symptoms, that she has no memory of the original infection. There is no need for any treatment and the patient can be reassured. E Varicella zoster immunoglobulin This would be the correct treatment if this patient had never had chickenpox and had been exposed, given her background of immunosuppression. However, this patient is in fact immune to chickenpox: she is varicella IgG antibody positive. She may have had the infection at such a young age that she has no memory of it, or she may have been minimally symptomatic and therefore failed to realise that she had contracted the disease. As she is immune, she does not require any speciﬁc treatment and can be reassured. A Aciclovir This patient is IgG antibody positive, which suggests that she has had a previous chickenpox infection and therefore will be immune to reinfection. Even if this patient were not immune, aciclovir would not be appropriate: instead the patient should be given varicella immunoglobulin within 4 days of exposure. In this case, as the patient is already immune to chickenpox, no treatment is necessary and she can be reassured. B Ganciclovir As this patient is IgG antibody positive for varicella, she has previously had chickenpox. Sometimes patients are almost completely asymptomatic with only a few lesions, and she may have contracted the disease at a young age and had no memory of it. As such, she is immune and therefore reassurance is the only management necessary. If she had not been immune, varicella immunoglobulin would have been the most appropriate treatment. D Varicella immunisation Varicella is a live vaccine and therefore should not be given to immunosuppressed patients. In fact, this patient is already immune to varicella (as she is IgG positive). She may have had the disease at a very young age and forgotten, or had minimal symptoms. As such, she does not require any treatment and can be reassured. If she were

not immune, varicella immunoglobulin would be the appropriate treatment.

stem: A 56-year-old woman returns from a trip to America in May. During her stay, she became unwell with a high fever, headache and muscle pains. She consulted a local doctor who noticed a rash on the palms of her hands and soles of her feet. She was admitted to hospital where a diagnosis was made and she was commenced on antibiotics. The patient improved and was discharged and allowed to ﬂy home with a course of oral antibiotics. She recalls the doctors in America telling her that the infection had been transmitted by a tick bite. She currently takes medication for diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease and atrial ﬁbrillation. What medication would you stop till the antibiotic course is ﬁnished?
explanation:
B Aluminium hydroxide The patient is most likely to be taking a tetracycline antibiotic for a rickettsial infection. The diagnosis in this patient is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. It is caused by a tick bite that results in the above symptoms. The classic rash is described as occurring on the palms and soles. Treatment of choice is doxycyline, which is a tetracycline and acts on 30S ribosomes to prevent protein synthesis in the infecting organism. Aluminium hydroxide can complex with this antibiotic in the gastrointestinal tract, preventing absorption. Dairy products ingested at the same time can also cause this. Side effects of tetracyclines include discoloration of teeth in children, hepatoxicity and photosensitivity. D Aspirin The main concerns with respect to aspirin are pharmacodynamic ones with anti-coagulants or other anti- platelet agents. A Metformin There are few signiﬁcant drug interaction concerns for metformin. One of the main problems is bile salt malabsorption leading to diarrhoea, which can be worsened if the dose is increased too quickly in the early stages of therapy. C Gliclazide Concurrent use of gliclazide and doxycycline may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia and the patient should have been warned about this at the time of commencing antibiotic therapy, although there is

no need to discontinue treatment. E Atorvastatin The main concern with respect to atorvastatin prescription is use with CYP3A4 inhibitors, which may lead to an increase in atorvastatin exposure.

stem: A 37-year-old Ghanaian woman was referred with fatigue. She has been followed for the past year with bizarre behaviour and psychotic symptoms and is treated with amisulpiride. She was diagnosed ﬁve years ago with HIV-1 infection but was lost to follow-up. The physical examination was unremarkable. CD4 count was 16 × 106/l and HIV viral load > 500 000 copies/ml. Treatment with antiretroviral medications was commenced and the patient was discharged. One month later the patient presents to you with confusion. She is afebrile on admission. She is disorientated in time and place but not in person. On this occasion, the CD4 count is 44 × 106/l and HIV viral load 503 copies/ml. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 100 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.5 × 10 /l 4.0 - 11.0 × 10 /l Neutrophils 72% Lymphocytes 18% Platelets (PLT) 435 × 10 /l 150 - 400 × 10 /l C-reactive protein (CRP) 8 mg/l < 10 mg/l Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain reveals multiple lowdensity lesions in the left hemisphere Investigation Result Normal values Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) WCC 120/ml < 5 /ml CSF glucose 3.4 mmol/l 3.3 - 4.4 mmol/l CSF protein 0.56 mg/dl 0.15 - 0.45 mg/dl CSF culture No growth in 48 h CSF cryptococcal antigen Negative CSF toxoplasmosis PCR Negative India ink stain Negative Four days later, in hospital, she develops right-sided weakness. Magnetic resonance of the brain with contrast diffusely enhances the lesions. Which one of the following diagnoses is most likely?
explanation: B Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy The history and investigations are consistent with cerebral lymphoma or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). PML is characterised by hemiparesis, disturbances of speech and vision and progressive dementia. The lesions in the brain comprise multiple areas of demyelination, abnormal oligodendrocytes and later pronounced astrocytosis. Lesions may enhance with gadolinium contrast. However, they do not usually have the characteristic ring-enhancing appearance seen in the cerebral lesions of toxoplasmosis. PML is associated with the ‘JC’ virus named after the patient in whom the polyoma virus was ﬁrst isolated. A Toxoplasmosis Typically, presentation can occur with neurological signs developing over days to weeks and then can cause seizures. In addition, raised intracranial pressure can cause headaches and vomiting. Some present with diffuse encephalitis causing confusion, seizures and reduced consciousness. Normally toxoplasmosis would show ring- enhancing lesions on a CT scan. Also, the negative PCR makes this unlikely. B Cryptococcal meningitis Crytococcal infection is a common cause of meningitis and meningoencephalitis in HIV-infected patients. It can present with headache, confusion, altered mental status, seizures and can have focal neurological signs present. The absence of antigens makes this less likely. B Cytomegalovirus encephalitis CMV establishes latent infection which reactivates as immunosuppression in HIV progresses. CMV can affect the central nervous system, retina, GI tract, lungs and biliary tract. In CNS infection there is usually progressive disorientation, withdrawal and apathy. On examination cranial nerve palsies and nystagmus are typical signs. Typically ring-enhancing lesions are seen on CT, but MRI is the best mode of imaging and diagnosis is conﬁrmed on CSF PCR and treatment is with ganciclovir. The imaging ﬁndings in this patient makes CMV an unlikely but ideally should be excluded on PCR. B Tuberculous meningitis With this condition there would likely be meningeal enhancement on imaging studies, detectable AFB in the CSF and low glucose in the CSF as well.

stem: A 41-year-old Ugandan woman is seen in the HIV Clinic. She has a CD4 count of 140 × 106/L and was started on prophylactic cotrimoxazole 2 weeks previously. Unfortunately, this resulted in a severe rash and deranged liver function tests and was discontinued. She has glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deﬁciency and is a type 2 diabetic. Her only current medication is metformin 500 mg bd. What is the most appropriate Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) prophylaxis?
explanation: E Pentamidine nebuliser This is a patient with a low CD4 count. If a patient has a CD4 count below 200 × 106/l then they should be offered prophylaxis against PCP. First-line treatment is oral co-trimoxazole. If this cannot be tolerated then the second-line treatment is oral dapsone. However, this is inappropriate in a patient with G6PD deﬁciency. Third- line prophylaxis is with nebulsed pentamidine. D Oral clindamycin Clindamycin can be used in the treatment of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) but not the prophylaxis. A Co-trimoxazole nebuliser The drug cannot be administered by nebuliser and may also be associated with haemolysis in patients with G6PD deﬁciency. B Oral dapsone It can cause haemolysis in patients with G6PD deﬁciency. Other drugs that have a deﬁnite risk include primaquine, methylthioninium chloride, nitrofurantoin, quinolones (including ciproﬂoxacin, moxiﬂoxacin, nalidixic acid, norﬂoxacin and oﬂoxacin) and sulfonamides. C Oral pentamidine Pentamidine is only effective in nebulised form or delivered IV.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has been referred to the General Medical Clinic with persisting dysuria. Since returning from a long trip around Africa, she has continued pain on passing urine and has recently noticed haematuria towards the end of micturition. She otherwise feels well. The general practitioner (GP) has tried a couple of antibiotics with no improvement in her symptoms. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 134 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 7 × 109/l 2.5–7.8 × 109/l Lymphocytes 3.1 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l Eosinophils 1.3 × 109/l 0.04–0.4 × 109/l Basophils 0.1 × 109/l 0.0–0.1 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 252 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Urine sample microscopy Schistosome eggs What is the appropriate treatment?
explanation: C Praziquantel The patient has urinary schistosomiasis, most likely caused by Schistosoma haematobium. Diagnosis is made with the raised eosinophils and the schistosome eggs in the urine. Other forms of schistosomiasis (Schistosoma mansoni, Schistosoma japonicum) affect the portal venous system, the lung and the central nervous system. It is a disease of the tropics and treated with praziquantel. With urinary schistosomiasis there is an increased risk of bladder cancer. B Mebendazole This is used to treat the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides; this remains asymptomatic in many cases. A Metronidazole It will treat amoebic dysentery and amoebic liver abscesses (Entamoeba histolytica) and is also used in the treatment of giardiasis. D Nifurtimox Nitrofurimox is used to treat Trypanosoma cruzi, the organism responsible for causing Chagas disease. E Niclosamide Niclosamide is used to treat tapeworm infections, which may be asymptomatic or present with iron deﬁciency anaemia ± GI disturbance.

stem: A 26-year-old woman was brought to the Emergency Department by ambulance with a 2-day history of headache and nausea, and a 6 h history of increasing drowsiness and confusion. She has no past medical history. On examination, her temperature was 37.9 °C. She was drowsy and confused. There was no nuchal rigidity or photophobia. Investigations reveal the following: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Opening pressure 160 mm H O (50–180)Protein 0.33 g/l (0.15– 0.45)Glucose 3.7 mmol/lWCC16/ml (lymphocytes) (< 3) Serum glucose 4.9 mmol/l CXR Normal Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) head Shown below What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Herpes simplex encephalitis This short history of increasing confusion and drowsiness is typical, and she has the characteristic MRI ﬁndings of signal increase in the temporal lobes. Seizures and a prodrome of headache and nausea are common. Treatment with intravenous aciclovir should be started. A Cerebral lymphoma This is highly unlikely given the acute nature of the patient’s

presentation and her fever. Cerebral lymphoma would typically present insidiously as confusion or focal neurological signs, or it could present suddenly with a stroke-like picture. Instead, this short history of fever, confusion and drowsiness is more typical of herpes simplex encephalitis. B Cryptococcal meningitis Cryptococcal meningitis would be extremely unlikely in an immunocompetent patient. This presentation, with a short history of increasing confusion, drowsiness and mild fever, would be more consistent with herpes simplex encephalitis. D Pneumococcal meningitis This presentation does not ﬁt with bacterial meningitis – she has a low-grade fever and there are no signs of meningism. The MRI ﬁndings are typical for herpes simplex encephalitis, which would also explain her presentation. E Tuberculous meningitis Tuberculous meningitis typically has an insidious onset; this patient has become unwell acutely. TB meningitis can cause confusion but may also cause cranial neuropathies, as it can affect the basal skull. It would be unusual to have TB meningitis with a normal chest X-ray. This patient is more likely to have herpes simplex encephalitis; this would ﬁt with her presentation and would also explain the MRI ﬁndings.

stem: A 24-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with what they describe as “the worst headache he has ever had”, coupled with a severe fever with a temperature of 39.4 oC. He also has muscle and joint pains which he describes as like someone has broken his bones. He has also vomited three times. He returned from a holiday to the Queensland (Australia) rainforest some 24 hours earlier. His blood pressure is 95/70 mmHg, and his pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm). He has an extensive macular rash. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 140 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 119 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 141 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l AST 421 iu/l 0 - 37 iu/l Which of the following insect types is most likely have transmitted his infection?
explanation:
A Aedes mosquito Possible differentials for this patient’s presentation include both Dengue fever and malaria. Given Queensland is malaria-free, this means Dengue fever is the most likely diagnosis and is consistent with the symptoms of severe fever, a macular rash, and “bone-

breaking” muscle and joint pains. Dengue is spread via the Aedes aegypti mosquito. Most patients recover following the febrile phase - which this patient is currently in - although some may progress to developing Dengue related coagulopathy. 90% of severe Dengue cases occur in children. D Tokunagayusurika midge Tokunagayusurika midges are lake ﬂies, which were ﬁrst identiﬁed in Japan. They are not associated with signiﬁcant human disease apart from frequent allergic reactions to midge bites. B Anopheles mosquito The Anopheles mosquito is responsible for the transmission of malaria. Although there may be cross-over between symptoms of malaria and those of Dengue, malaria is not present in Australia. This makes Dengue, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, much more likely to be the diagnosis here. C Ixodes tick The Ixodes tick is carried on deer, and is responsible for the carriage of Borrelia, which is the causative organism responsible of Lyme disease. (In many areas of the world tick-borne encephalitis). Erythema chronicum migrans is the most prominent initial feature of Lyme disease and is often what prompts initial presentation to medical services. E Xenopsylla ﬂea The Xenopsylla ﬂea is a cause of ﬂea-borne typhus, which is caused by the bacterium Rickettsia typhi. Signs are similar to those of Dengue and include headache, fever, muscle pains, joint pains, nausea, and vomiting. A rash is seen later, where 40–50% of patients will develop a discrete rash six days after the onset of other signs. Doxycycline is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 4-day history of general malaise and loss of appetite. Her past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis, for which she takes methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. Her childhood vaccinations were administered appropriately, as far as she is aware. Her temperature is 39.2 °C and her BP is 125/82 mmHg. She has bilateral conjunctivitis, as well as a rash which covers her face, upper arms and trunk. The patient's rash is shown below: What is the most likely complication of this diagnosis?
explanation: C Otitis media This patient has a diagnosis of measles. Clinical symptoms and signs leading to the diagnosis include a history of coryzal symptoms followed by a maculopapular rash, as shown here, spreading from the face to the torso. Conjunctivitis and Koplik spots are also common features. This patient is taking immunosuppressant medication, making it more likely for her to develop measles, even if she was vaccinated as a child. The most common complication of measles is otitis media, affecting approximately 1 in 10 people. E Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is an extremely rare complication of the measles virus, characterised by progressive neurological decline, including memory loss, behavioural changes and seizures. It often develops within 2–10 years after initial infection with the measles virus and affects 1 in 25 000 patients. A Encephalitis Encephalitis is a rare complication of measles, affecting 1 in 1000, and results in permanent neurological sequelae in 25% of those affected, with a fatality rate of 15% of cases. B Glomerulonephritis Glomerulonephritis can be seen in patients diagnosed with group A Streptococcus infection. However, it is not a common side-effect seen secondary to the measles virus. D Pneumonia Pneumonia is the most common cause of death secondary to measles. However, it is not the most common complication. It affects 1 in 20 people.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the Immunology Clinic for review. He has a history of multiple infections including two episodes of otitis media, three episodes of pneumonia, and one episode of Campylobacter infection over the course of the past year. He admits to unprotected sexual intercourse with other men on two occasions in the past two years. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 122/82 mmHg; pulse is 70/min and regular. There is no lymphadenopathy and his BMI is 23. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 12 mg/l 0–10 mg/l ESR 14 mm/1st hour 0–10 mm in the 1st hour IgG 4.0 g/l (low) 5–16 g/l IgA 0.5 g/l (low) 1.0–4.0 g/l ALT 23 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline phosphatase 85 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 10 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 35 g/l 35–55 g/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Common variable immunodeﬁciency The answer is Common variable immunodeﬁciency (CVI) - Both the IgA and IgG are low, coupled with the range of infections this patient has suffered from, raises the possibility of CVI. It is a rare defect of B cell maturation (1 in 25,000 incidence), which produces reduced immunoglobulin production. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy reduces the risk of infection and is the primary intervention of choice. C Protein losing enteropathy Protein losing enteropathy is incorrect, it is ruled out by the normal albumin of 35 g/l. B HIV infection

HIV infection is incorrect, it is less likely here given he has suffered primarily from opportunistic bacterial infections, and two episodes of unprotected intercourse represents relatively limited potential exposure to HIV. D Selective IgA deﬁciency Selective IgA deﬁciency is incorrect, it is ruled out by the fact that IgG deﬁciency is also reduced. E Severe combined immunodeﬁciency Severe combined immunodeﬁciency is incorrect, it presents in early childhood with massive infection.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought by her partner to the Emergency Department. She has been complaining of worsening headache and neck stiffness over the past few days and is now drowsy and disorientated. On examination, she has signs of meningism, a pyrexia 39 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and pulse 105 bpm. There is a purpuric rash. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 15.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Lumbar puncture Decreased CSF glucose, increased protein, neutrophils, gram-negative diplococci You commence IV benzylpenicillin and there is initial improvement. 72 h later, however, she spikes a new fever of 39 °C, with increased eosinophil count in the peripheral blood. What is the most important management step?
options: Stop penicillin and substitute an alternative antibiotic
explanation: A Stop penicillin and substitute an alternative antibiotic Penicillin is one of a number of agents which may cause an eosinophilic drug reaction. Other causes include meloxicam, ltryptophan, dantrolene and ethambutol. Clearly this woman does have meningococcal meningitis given that she presented with fever and menigisms and found to have diplococci in her CSF. As such it is important to continue antibiotic therapy. Alternatives to penicillin include cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime at high dose. Indeed, most centres use a cephalosporin as ﬁrst line therapy because of the small risk of meningococcal resistance to penicillin. D Commence amphotericin Amphotericin is a potent antifungal medication which can be used against systemic aspergillus which can be a cause of eosinophilia. However, there is very strong evidence for bacterial, not fungal, infection, and this is a very unlikely diagnosis given the original presentation of meningism, purpuric rash and fever. B Commence prednisolone This is a very tempting option as the patient likely has suffered a drug reaction. However, removing the offending drug is a far more sensible option than using prednisolone to mitigate the drug reaction. C Commence aciclovir This would be the correct treatment option for viral meningitis but the presence of diplococci in the blood ﬁlm and purpuric rash on presentation makes this an unlikely diagnosis and therefore makes acyclovir an inappropriate treatment option. E Commence chlorpheniramine Chlorphenamine is an antipruritic medication which would only provide symptomatic relief against itch and therefore not address the underlying problem. Given that there is a fever and haematological evidence of eosinophilia an underlying cause should be saught and addressed.

stem: A 28-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of severe headache and neck stiffness. He also had a 4-day history of nonbloody diarrhoea. On examination, his temperature was 37.9 °C, blood pressure was 128/72 mmHg and pulse rate was 88 beats/min. He had meningism and mild photophobia. There were no neurological signs. Investigation Result Normal Values Random plasma glucose 6.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l CT head Normal Lumbar puncture: Investigation Result Normal Values Opening pressure 22 cmHg 10 - 20 cmHg Appearance Clear ﬂuid Appearance No organisms seen Cell count cells/mm3 (lymphocytes) Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) protein 0.8 g/dl 0.15 g/dl Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) glucose 4.2 mmol/l 3.3 - 4.4 mmol/l What is the most important next investigation?
explanation:
C CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with meningitis (headache, fever, meningism). Investigations are suggestive of a viral cause (lymphocytic CSF, normal glucose, no organisms on CSF microscopy). It is likely that this patient’s meningitis was caused by an enterovirus, given his preceding diarrhoea. However, it is important to rule out herpes simplex meningoencephalitis, as this would require speciﬁc treatment with aciclovir. If this is simply enterovirus, he can be treated with supportive therapy only. D CSF spectrophotometry This is a useful investigation where subarachnoid haemorrhage is suspected and CT head is normal: spectrophotometry can identify xanthochromia, caused by blood breakdown products in the CSF.

However, the CSF was not bloody and this patient does not describe a sudden-onset headache. This patient’s fever, headache and meningism are more suggestive of an infective meningitis: this is most likely viral given the CSF lymphocytosis and lack of organisms on microscopy. Herpes simplex meningoencephalitis should be ruled out with CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR). A Blood cultures This patient has symptoms and signs consistent with meningitis (fever, headache, meningism) and the investigations are suggestive of a viral meningitis (lymphocytosis in CSF, normal glucose, no organisms seen). The most important investigation is CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to identify whether this is herpes simplex meningoencephalitis. Given this patient’s preceding diarrhoea, however, it is likely that this meningitis has been caused by an enterovirus. Blood cultures should be taken in addition to other investigations, as he is febrile, but it is not the most important investigation. B CSF culture Fluid should be sent for culture to rule out a bacterial cause for this patient’s meningitis, but investigations suggest that this is a viral meningitis (lymphocytic CSF, normal glucose, no visible organisms). Fluid culture results will take some time, and therefore are not going to be immediately useful in the management of this patient. CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR), however, would be helpful, as this could rule out herpes simplex meningoencephalitis, which would require speciﬁc treatment. If this is negative, the patient can be treated with supportive care only. E MRI head This patient likely has viral meningitis: he has a fever, headache and meningism, and investigations demonstrate a clear, lymphocytic CSF with no visible organisms. His preceding diarrhoea suggests enterovirus as a cause. CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) should be carried out to rule out herpes simplex meningoencephalitis: this can produce suggestive features on MRI, but MRI is not the diagnostic tool of choice.

stem: A general practitioner (GP) refers a 21-year-old man, who had been previously ﬁt and well, for a second opinion. He had presented with a 6-week history of ﬂitting arthralgia and myalgia. Prior to the onset of this problem, he had been on holiday in the Far East where he had unprotected sexual intercourse on one occasion only. On general examination, there was no evidence of arthritis but it was noted that the patient had bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Investigations showed a white cell count at the lower end of normal, mild anaemia, normal urea and electrolytes, and abnormal liver function tests with all the liver enzymes elevated. Urethral swabs for chlamydia and gonococcus were negative. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Acute HIV infection Acute HIV infection can affect any number of organ systems, including the lymphatics, skin, gastrointestinal system, genitourinary system, bone marrow and nervous system, with the clinical ﬁndings being related to the organ system affected. These signs include persistent generalised lymphadenopathy, oral thrush, oral hairy leukoplakia, shingles (especially in a patient under the age of 40), anaemia, thrombocytopenia and secondary opportunistic infections, eg Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The work-up of the patient varies depending on the initial presenting complaint but it is important to exclude all other treatable causes. Acute infection may be detected by the presence of P24 antigen or HIV RNA, both of which precede the development of IgM or IgG antibodies. E Relapsing polychondritis The clinical picture does not match relapsing polychondritis, which is characterised by nasal and auricular chondritis and usual onset is between 40 and 50 years. It can have greater systemic involvement and can even be fatal with airway involvement. It would explain the arthralgia but little else in the history. B Brucellosis The lack of direct exposure and travel to an endemic area makes it a less likely diagnosis. It is a zoonosis endemic in the Middle and Far East, as well as Bosnia, which is spread via the contact with animals, their exhalations or some animal products, such as unpasteurised goat’s milk. It is therefore common in veterinarians and farmers. Presentation of brucellosis is highly varied, but generally includes fever and malaise. A Reactive arthritis It is a triad urethritis, conjunctivitis and seronegative arthritis secondary to infection in another part of the boy. There is not enough evidence to make this diagnosis likely, and there is also no evidence of a sexually transmitted infection, the most likely cause. In addition, this diagnosis would not explain the abnormalities in the blood tests. B Adult-onset Still’s disease The presentation makes it unlikely. Adult-onset Still’s disease is characterised by a triad of persistent and high fevers, arthralgia and a salmon-coloured rash. There is no evidence of a rash and hence still’s disease is unlikely.

stem: A 58-year-old man presented to clinic with a 10-day history of malaise, headache, fever, night sweats, back pain and myalgia. He was a sheep farmer, and had no other medical conditions. On examination, he appeared unwell. His temperature was 37.9ºC, and there was widespread lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. There was mild tenderness on palpation of the sacroiliac joints. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 138 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6.4 × 109/l 4.0 – 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 3.4 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Basophils 0.08 × 109/l < 0.1 × 109/l Eosinophils 0.1 × 109/l 0.04 - 0.4 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 100 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Bilirubin 35 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l ALT 102 u/l 7 - 55 u/l AST 51 u/l 10 - 40 u/l Blood film Leukoerythroblastic X-ray lumbar spine Lumbar degenerative changes with osteophyte formation What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Brucellosis It is caused by a Gram-negative bacterium that is transmitted by contact with infected livestock. The typical incubation period is 1–3 weeks with an insidious onset. This patient’s symptoms of malaise, fever, back pain and night sweats are typical. Back pain is common, occurring in around 50% of patients. The ﬁndings of a leucoerythroblastic blood ﬁlm and raised transaminases ﬁt with the diagnosis. Diagnosis is via bone marrow culture or serum agglutination testing. E Organophosphate poisoning Organophosphate poisoning leads to an over-abundance of acetylcholine, and therefore causes pinpoint pupils, excess salivation and seizures. It does not cause a subacute malaise, fever and back pain as seen here. This picture, combined with the transaminitis and history of sheep farming, would ﬁt with brucellosis. A Acute myeloid leukaemia Typically a patient with acute myeloid leukaemia would either have a very high white cell count or very low, but it would be unusual to have a normal white cell count. Furthermore, you might expect bone marrow failure, with bleeding and bruising, and pancytopenia. Lymphadenopathy is possible but not common. Instead, this patient’s symptoms, signs and investigations would be consistent with brucellosis through exposure to sheep.

C Chronic myeloid leukaemia You would expect a patient with chronic myeloid leukaemia to have a raised basophil and eosinophil count, but these are normal here. You might also expect a leucocytosis and teardrop poikilocytes on the blood ﬁlm. This patient’s signs and symptoms are more consistent with brucellosis through exposure to infected sheep. D Hydatid disease Hydatid disease can be caught from sheep. In 90% of cases it causes liver dysfunction. However, that is characteristically obstructive in nature, whereas this patient’s investigations ﬁt with a hepatitic cause. This patient’s symptoms and signs are more consistent with brucellosis.

stem: A 43-year-old HIV-positive man is on day seven of his inpatient treatment for tuberculosis (TB) on the Infectious Diseases Ward with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He has a CD4 count of 91 × 106/l, and the plan is to start him on antiretroviral therapy as an inpatient. On the ward, he has a 30-second seizure, which self-terminated. Neurological examination reveals right-sided weakness affecting the arm and leg. Urgent CT of the head is requested and performed, which reveals a solitary focal lesion in the left internal capsule, with some surrounding oedema and mild effacement of the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle. What is the most urgent next step?
options: Add in an additional antituberculous drug
explanation:
D Commence sulphadiazine and pyrimethamine Possible causes for a solitary focal lesion in a HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count include cerebral toxoplasmosis, lymphoma and tuberculoma (although solitary lesions are only seen in about 15% of toxoplasmosis cases).
