This leads to the appearance of pale plaques on the tongue, when in fact the abnormality is the smooth, erythematous regions inbetween (the pale plaques are islands of normal papillated tongue). This patient has mouth signs consistent with oral candidiasis: mucosal soreness with non-adherent white plaques. On a background of lymphadenopathy, weight loss, travel to South East Asia and intravenous drug use, this is suggestive of underlying immunosuppression due to HIV infection. The patient should be tested for HIV. B Herpes simplex Herpes simplex causes cold sores and mucosal ulceration. While mucosal ulceration could explain his generalised mouth soreness, no ulcers were seen on examination, and herpes simplex could not explain his non-adherent white patches. This patient has signs consistent with oral candidiasis, and underlying HIV infection (lymphadenopathy, weight loss and a background of intravenous drug use and travel to South East Asia). He should be tested for HIV. C Herpes zoster Herpes zoster causes shingles, a blistering skin rash that normally manifests in a dermatomal distribution. This patient has white, sore patches in the mouth that would be more consistent with oral candidiasis. On a background of lymphadenopathy, weight loss, intravenous drug use and travel to South East Asia, this is suggestive of an undiagnosed HIV infection, for which he should be tested.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a dry cough over the past two days and a slight fever. He says the cough is keeping him awake at night. He smokes ﬁve cigarettes per day, drinks occasional alcohol, and works in a warehouse. His blood pressure is 112/82 mmHg, and his pulse is 78 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. He is apyrexial. His chest is clear. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 139 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 209 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 103 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
explanation:
A Reassurance This patient has a viral upper respiratory tract infection with no evidence of signiﬁcant smoking-related lung disease. As such, there is no indication for antibiotic therapy or even for temporary use of a salbutamol inhaler. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest that a no antibiotic or delayed antibiotic prescribing policy should be agreed for patients presenting with any of the following: • acute otitis media • acute sore throat/acute pharyngitis/acute tonsillitis • common cold • acute rhinosinusitis • acute cough/acute bronchitis. B Salbutamol Temporary use of a salbutamol inhaler might be considered for patients with viral hyper-reactivity and wheeze associated with an acute viral upper respiratory tract infection. Although this patient has a cough, there is no evidence that this is related to signiﬁcant bronchospasm. Reassurance is, therefore, the most appropriate next step. A Amoxicillin Amoxicillin would only be considered where there is deﬁnitive evidence of a bacterial respiratory tract infection. Given that this patient’s cough is non-productive, there are no chest sounds, and his white cell count is normal, this is unlikely. Reassurance is the most

appropriate option. B Clarithromycin Clarithromycin might be considered as monotherapy for a respiratory tract infection where there is evidence of bacterial infection, and the patient is penicillin allergic. Given the normal chest signs and white cell count, bacterial infection is extremely unlikely, and there is no evidence that the patient is allergic to penicillin. Therefore, reassurance is the more appropriate next step. C Doxycycline Doxycycline is considered a potential ﬁrst-line option for patients with chronic chest disease who acquire a bacterial respiratory tract infection. Although this patient is a modest smoker, he has no evidence of chronic chest disease, and it seems this acute episode is viral in aetiology. For this reason, doxycycline is not required, and he can be reassured.

stem: A 22-year-old American man presents to the Genitourinary Medicine Clinic. He is a man who has sex with men and feels that he needs a full sexual health screen. He has had six partners in his life and has had unprotected anal sex with three of them in the space of one year. Currently, he has no symptoms and feels well. He agrees to an HIV test and tests for Chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Upon enquiry, he is unsure if he received the hepatitis vaccinations. He thinks he may have been vaccinated against something whilst in America but knows no details.
explanation:
A Offer no vaccination or treatment This question is about interpreting hepatitis serology. Hepatitis A IgG is detectable for life and is no marker of acute infection. HBsAg is present for 1-6 months in acute infection. HBeAg persists

for up to three months and signiﬁes highly infectious patients. Antibodies against HBcAg coupled with the negative antigen results imply past infection, whilst antibodies against HBsAg only implies vaccination. The presence of Hep B core ab implies previous infection and immunity and therefore no vaccination should be offered. A Offer hepatitis B vaccination The patient is immune as he has been previously infected with hepatitis B and has already established immunity. B Offer hepatitis A vaccination The presence of Hep A IgG without acute hepatitis implies previous infection and established immunity and therefore vaccination is not necessary. C Start antiviral treatment There is no evidence of acute infection and the patient is well. No active treatment is needed. E Repeat tests in six weeks The serology is unlikely to change and therefore would not need retesting unless the patient became unwell with hepatitis.

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has felt increasingly unwell over the past two months with weight loss, fatigue, poor dietary intake, and night sweats. He spent three months abroad at his uncle’s dairy and sheep farm in France before returning to the United Kingdom (UK) some ten weeks ago. He tells you that he had a heart murmur noted some ten years ago but was told by his General Practitioner (GP) not to worry about it. His blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, and his pulse is 78 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. He has an ejection systolic murmur loudest in the aortic area. His chest is clear. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 149 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 223 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 123 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 95 mg/l < 10 mg/l ALT 824 u/l 29 - 33 u/l ECHO Blood culture Aortic valve thickening -ve Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Coxiella endocarditis The clue here is the patient has spent time on a farm in France, has had a subacute illness afterwards, and has both cardiac features (the murmur), and evidence of hepatitis (the raised ALT). Taking these factors together, Q fever caused by Coxiella burnetii a possible diagnosis. Over recent years, outbreaks on farms in both France and Italy have been reported. Combination therapy with hydroxychloroquine and doxycycline is recommended. C Klebsiella endocarditis Endocarditis related to Klebsiella is rare, accounting for less than 1% of cases of endocarditis. It is seen in complex hospital patients with multiple comorbidities and in other patients with immunosuppression, such as those with chronic alcoholism. Infection is usually identiﬁed on blood culture. Klebsiella is sensitive to aminoglycosides and to quinolones. A Bartonella endocarditis Bartonella henselae, the cause of cat scratch fever, and Quintana, the cause of trench fever, are both recognised as causes of Bartonella endocarditis. Like Coxiella, (the cause of this patient’s symptoms), it is a cause of culture-negative endocarditis. We are given no indication of exposure to Bartonella. Aminoglycosides are the intervention of choice for Bartonella endocarditis, with more than 14 days therapy recommended. D Streptococcal endocarditis Streptococcal endocarditis is more likely to be culture-negative when patients have been partially treated with antibiotics, and we are given no evidence of that scenario here. Given no obvious risk factors for streptococcal endocarditis, the negative cultures, and the extended farm stay, Coxiella is much more likely to be the cause of the symptoms seen here. E Tropheryma endocarditis Tropheryma whipplei is the cause of Whipple’s disease. Evidence of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbance and arthropathy would be expected in a patient with Whipple’s, and neither are features of the scenario described here. Whipple’s is a cause of culture-negative arthritis and is usually treated initially with intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone.

stem: A 14-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of fever, abdominal pain and diarrhoea for the past two days. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg and her heart rate is 104 bpm. Her temperature is 38.2 °C. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the right iliac fossa. The patient is taken up for an appendectomy. Intraoperatively, the appendix is noted to be normal and the area surrounding the appendix, including the terminal ileum and mesenteric nodes, is found to be inﬂamed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: E Yersinia enterocolitica infection This patient has clinical features and intraoperative ﬁndings classical of Y. enterocolitica infection. It causes pseudoappendicitis, which may resemble appendicitis. However, the symptoms are due to ileocolitis and mesenteric adenitis. Mild cases require only symptomatic management and are usually self-resolving. In more severe, complicated infections, antibiotics such as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole or tetracyclines may be used. A Acute appendicitis There are no intraoperative ﬁndings to suggest that this patient has acute appendicitis. A Crohn’s disease Crohn’s disease can commonly involve the terminal ileum and caecum. However, the duration of this patient’s illness is too short for Crohn’s disease to be considered. In addition, Crohn’s disease usually causes multiple strictures which are not seen in this patient. B Ileocaecal tuberculosis Ileocaecal tuberculosis occurs in immunosuppressed individuals and presents with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, rather than with the acute presentation seen in this patient. C Meckel’s diverticulitis Meckel’s diverticulum is the most common congenital abnormality of the small intestine. However, the intraoperative ﬁndings in this patient do not suggest the presence of a Meckel’s diverticulum.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a spreading rash affecting his lower face. He feels unwell and his mother tells you that he has been irritable over the last few days, with reduced appetite. He has no previous history of skin disease. He takes no regular medications. On examination, he has crusting lesions over his chin and left cheek. There is no oral involvement. General examination reveals no abnormalities. What is the most likely microbial cause?
explanation:
D Staphylococcus aureus The diagnosis here is impetigo, a superﬁcial infection of the epidermis due to Staphylococcus aureus, group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus or a mixture of both. Children are mainly affected. It is very contagious. Typically it starts as macules, vesicles or pustules. These evolve into superﬁcial erosions which then form honeycoloured crusts. The bullous variant presents with ﬂaccid bullae and erosions. Alongside cleansing the affected areas and removing the crusts, topical antibiotics (eg 1% hydrogen peroxide, fusidic acid or mupirocin) may be sufﬁcient for localised disease, whereas systemic treatment is generally used for more widespread involvement. This should cover both staphylococci and streptococci, so ﬂucloxacillin or a macrolide would be appropriate. B Herpes simplex The somewhat punctate crusts in this example of impetigo might be mistaken for eczema herpeticum. There is, however, no history of eczema. A Haemophilus inﬂuenzae This does not produce impetigo, though sometimes causes cellulitis in babies, particularly affecting the head and neck.

C Pseudomonas aeruginosa P aeruginosa is a common coloniser of ulcers, but is not associated with impetigo. E Viridans streptococci This includes several species of commensal bacteria mostly found in the mouth, though skin colonisation can also occur. They can cause a variety of infections in the context of impaired host defence mechanisms, but are not implicated in impetigo in an otherwise healthy child.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department for review. She has returned from her honeymoon in Sri Lanka a week earlier and is concerned as she seems to be suffering from abdominal bloating, diarrhoea and extremely offensive ﬂatulence. She mentions eating local street food with her husband, and he is apparently suffering from similar symptoms. Her abdomen is mildly distended, with active bowel sounds, on clinical examination. Investigations reveal a slightly elevated WCC and a CRP level of 82 mg/l. Which of the following is likely to be the most effective intervention?
explanation:
E Metronidazole The symptom pattern here ﬁts with giardiasis, which is spread via the faeco-oral route and results in symptoms similar to irritable bowel syndrome. Both tinidazole, delivered as a single dose, and metronidazole, delivered as a one-week course of therapy, are effective in eradicating the parasites. Prognosis is excellent, although some patients may suffer residual lactose intolerance and reinfection may also occur. A Azithromycin Azithromycin is effective in controlling giardiasis but would be considered a second-line option in patients for whom metronidazole or tinidazole are unsuitable or contraindicated. B Cephalexin Third-generation cephalosporins are considered as treatment options for Salmonella infection, which does not ﬁt with the clinical picture described here where acute gastroenteritis would be expected. C Ciproﬂoxacin

Quinolones can be used for the treatment of Salmonella infection, although signiﬁcant antibiotic resistance exists. Their use is also discouraged because of neurological side-effects and tendon rupture associated with the class. Colpermin Colpermin is an anti-spasmodic agent used in the management of non-infective irritable bowel syndrome. It does not have a role in the management of this patient with giardiasis.

stem: A 24-year-old man known to be HIV positive presents with a 3-day history of worsening shortness of breath, fevers and a cough productive of green sputum. His last CD4 count 2 months ago was 220 × 106/l and he is on no treatment, despite it having been strongly recommended on several appointments. On examination, O2 saturation is 91% on breathing room air, temperature 38.8°C, pulse 120 beats/min, crackles are heard in both midzones. Chest X-ray shows diffuse interstitial shadowing bilaterally. Arterial blood gas (on air) p(O2) 10.5 kPa, p(CO2) 3.7 kPa, bicarbonate 22 mmol/l, O2 saturation 90%. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
B Amoxicillin and clarithromycin The history is classical of a community-acquired pneumonia and does not suggest Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), which generally has a more subacute time course with a dry cough. The Xray would support a diagnosis of an atypical pneumonia. As well as opportunistic infections, HIV-positive patients are also more susceptible to common bacterial infections than nonimmunocompromised patients. The treatment for communityacquired pneumonia is amoxicillin plus a macrolide, according NICE guidelines. E Metronidazole It would be the treatment for an intra-abdominal cause of infection rather than respiratory infection. Voriconazole can be used for invasive aspergillosis. A Intravenous (IV) co-trimoxazole This would be the ﬁrst-line treatment for PCP, which is not the most likely diagnosis. PCP is characterised by a more indulent course of a dry cough, commonly a normal chest X-ray and severe hypoxia. It is also associated with pneumothorax. The clinical picture is more in keeping with an atypical chest infection rather than PCP.

C Clindamycin and primaquine This is the second-line treatment for PCP. If the patient could not tolerate co-trimoxazole and the diagnosis was PCP then this would be an appropriate choice. D Liposomal amphotericin This is the treatment for severe fungal infection or leishmaniasis. Since the patient has a low CD4 count he is at risk of fungal infections, especially invasive aspergillosis, but this is an unlikely diagnosis given the duration of illness and the bilateral signs.

stem: A 29-year-old woman was admitted with a 3-week history of oedema and intermittent paraesthesiae of her left leg. Two months earlier, she had had painful muscle cramps, ﬁrst in her legs and later in her abdomen, and she had noticed her left leg was swelling and was intermittently numb and tingling. While working in Gabon 9 months previously, she had had extensive exposure to fresh water. On examination, she had 3-cm, non-tender hepatomegaly, without splenomegaly. Papular erythematous lesions were present on both legs, with pitting oedema of her left lower leg. Sensation to light touch over the left lower leg was reduced. Investigation Result Normal values WCC 16.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 4.9 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 5.9 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Eosinophils 5.4 × 109/l 0.04 - 0.4 × 109/l Hb 134 g/l 115 - 160 g/l Platelets (PLT) 364 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Loiasis Loa loa is a nematode causing ﬁlariasis. Classically it causes Calabar swellings – these are a transient subcutaneous swelling marking the migratory course through the tissues of the adult worm visible

across the patient’s legs. . Several months after the infection, it can cause temporary swelling of a limb due to blockage of lymphatic drainage. There can be numbness in the affected limb, as seen here. The hypereosinophilia found in this patient (> 1 × 109/l would be a signiﬁcant eosinophilia) strongly suggests parasitic, and particularly ﬁlarial, infection. E Trichinella spiralis It is a nematode acquired by eating poorly cooked pork products. You would see eosinophilia, as found here, but clinically signiﬁcant trichinellosis causes vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, then subsequently facial and peri-orbital oedema, malaise and fever. You would not expect it to cause leg swelling. These symptoms, signs and investigations could be better explained by loiasis. B Malaria Malaria does not cause unilateral leg swelling. A rash may be visible if there is disseminated intravascular coagulation in severe malaria, but it does not cause a maculopapular rash. You would not expect such a chronic, indolent course of illness if this were malaria, and these symptoms are not typical of a malarial infection. Eosinophilia is uncommon in malaria. These symptoms, signs and investigations could be better explained by loiasis, which causes leg swelling due to blockage of lymphatic drainage. C Schistosomiasis Schistosomiasis is predominantly a urinary (manifesting as haematuria and later urinary tract malignancies) or intestinal (manifesting as abdominal pain, diarrhoea and hepatosplenomegaly) syndrome. Although at the point of infection, Schistosoma spp. can cause a rash (‘swimmer’s itch’), you would not expect it to cause leg oedema and a widespread papular rash over the lower limbs, as seen here. These symptoms, signs and investigations could be better explained by loiasis. D Taenia solium T. solium, also known as tapeworm, is usually transmitted through eating poorly cooked pork. Infection may be symptomatic or may cause diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Occasionally, it can lead to cysticercosis where larvae travel to the brain, lung or eyes and can lead to neurological problems or sight impairment. However, it does not cause rashes or leg swelling; loiasis could explain this patient’s symptoms and signs.

stem: An 18-year-old man returns from a trip helping a school project in the remote Thai jungle. Soon after returning home he began suffering from a severe fever accompanied by facial ﬂushing and a severe headache with retro- orbital pain. There is also myalgia and joint pains; most recently he has noticed bleeding from around his gums. On examination, he is pyrexic - his temperature is 41 °C. His blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg, while his pulse is 100 beats per minute. There is a maculopapular rash, and you also notice some petechiae and bleeding from the site where you took blood. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 105 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.8 × 109/l (relative lymphocytosis) 4.0–11.0 x 109/l Platelets (PLT) 40 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 209 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Prothrombin time (PTT) 25.2 s 10.6–14.9 s Thick and thin ﬁlm Negative Choose the most appropriate diagnosis from those given above?
explanation:
B Dengue fever Dengue fever is endemic in tropical South-East Asia, and outbreaks have also occurred in the tropical regions of Australia. The illness is a haemorrhagic fever, carried by the Aedes mosquito and is caused by the dengue virus. It is characterised by fever, severe headache and facial ﬂushing. In the early stages there is a lymphocytosis, with later lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and bleeding. Treatment is supportive. D Weil's disease Weil’s disease is a severe form of leptospirosis. The organisms are spirochaetes which are spread from rat urine into aquatic areas and then contact with abraded skin or mucosa leads to infection. Water activities increase risk. Following an incubation of 1–3 weeks, there is an abrupt onset of fever, headache, myalgia, dry cough and lethargy. This phase may resolve without treatment but can lead to an immune phase with jaundice, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, rash, meningitis and organ failure including renal impairment. This would be the main differential diagnosis here. In the UK sporadic cases are seen usually associates with at risk occupations such as farmers / abbatoir and sewage workers. Worldwide outbreaks are typically associated with over-crowded areas with poor contaminated water supplies such as refugee camps. A Typhoid fever Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella subspecies, typically 10–20 days following exposure. It causes a high fever, dry cough, malaise, abdominal pain following by green diarrhoea and hepatosplenomegaly and in the ﬁnal stages it can cause complications in multiple organs. There can be associated bradycardia as well.

Diagnosis is by culture, and treatment is usually with azithromycin, but if severe then IV ceftriaxone is used. This patient’s tachycardia, renal injury and thrombocytopenia make this a less likely diagnosis. C Malaria Malaria is a protozoal disease caused by species of the Plasmodium genus. It can occur following mosquito bites in the tropics. It is associated with fever, headache, cough, myalgia, gastrointestinal upset, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and jaundice. In severe disease bleeding, renal injury and hypoglycaemia can occur. Diagnosis is by thick and thin blood smears stained with Giemsa stain. Thrombocytopenia and anaemia are common, as are abnormal LFTs, but the absence of jaundice and the rapid progression make this a less likely diagnosis. However, two additional thick and thin ﬁlms should be taken to exclude malaria. E Japanese encephalitis This infection is caused by a mosquito-borne ﬂavivirus endemic across Asia. It presents after 5–15 days with fever, headache, diarrhoea and myalgia leading to neurological disease ranging from confusion to coma and commonly seizures. It is associated with leukocytosis and neuroimaging can show bilateral thalamic lesions with haemorrhage. The abnormal liver, renal and haemaglobin tests and severe fever make this an unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 31-year-old hiker presents with ﬂu-like symptoms and a left Bell’s palsy. She is seen by her general practitioner and treated with oral corticosteroids. She has just returned from a three-week trip to Southern Germany. A few days later, she returns, complaining that the facial weakness is becoming bilateral and she feels that she has begun to develop weakness below her knee on the left. Examination reveals a temperature of 37.6 °C and a blood pressure of 110/60 mmHg. Her chest is clear, and there are no murmurs. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. She has a marked left facial palsy and there is minor facial weakness affecting the right- hand side of the face. There is a left common peroneal nerve palsy. Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Perform MRI brain and spinal cord
explanation:
C Perform Lyme serology

The presentation here is with mononeuritis multiplex caused by Lyme disease. The major clues here to the underlying diagnosis include the fact this patient is a hiker, she has travelled to Southern Germany (a high-risk area for Lyme disease) and has evidence of bilateral facial nerve palsies, coupled with peripheral nerve involvement. As there is no history of a tick bite, Lyme serology is the logical next step. Lyme serology takes three to four days to return. Therefore, doxycycline should be commenced once the condition is suspected. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting the results. D Perform MRI brain and spinal cord The presentation is likely due to a peripheral nerve lesion. An MRI scan of the brain and spine cord would investigate for potential central nervous system lesions, which are not the cause of this patient’s facial nerve palsy. Should the Lyme serology be negative, then alternative causes of bilateral facial nerve palsy should be sought. These include Guillain–Barré syndrome, neurosarcoidosis, tuberculosis and human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV). A Continue corticosteroids Corticosteroids should be stopped in Lyme disease, as there is no evidence behind their use. There is some research to suggest that continuing them potentially risks worsening/widening the neurological deﬁcit seen, although data are lacking. B Give intravenous (IV) immunoglobulin IV immunoglobulin is not classically used in the management of multiple sclerosis. It is more commonly used in cases of Guillain– Barré syndrome. E Give Penicillin V The treatment of choice for Lyme disease is doxycycline, not penicillin V.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department. He has come straight from the airport on returning from his holiday to the Democratic Republic of Congo. He was bitten by a stray dog four weeks ago and while he washed the bite immediately, he is concerned about the risk of rabies. He had all recommended vaccinations before travelling, including the rabies vaccine. His bite has remained clean and the skin was punctured, but not deeply. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, all of his observations are normal and the wound has completely healed. What is the most appropriate way to manage this patient’s risk of rabies?
options: Vaccination today and on day three
Vaccination today and on days three, seven, 14 and 30
Vaccination today and on days three, seven, 14 and 30, and also give immediate RIG
explanation:
C Vaccination today and on day three This is a patient who has been previously vaccinated against rabies presenting with a potentially dangerous bite. Rabies is a rhabdovirus that is spread by infected mammals, with an incubation period of nine–90 days. It can present with a prodrome of malaise, agitation and pruritus surrounding the bite, leading to infection, as well as headaches, before proceeding to spasms and hydrophobia. Since this patient has presented with a bite that may be at risk, he should be treated. Since he had a previous vaccination, he will only need vaccination today and in three days to establish immunity. E Vaccination today and on days three, seven, 14 and 30, and also give immediate RIG This would be the full treatment if the patient had not had any vaccination for rabies before and presented within a week. Typically, IV immunoglobulins are not thought to be effective if given after one week, as by that time, the patient should have established their own antibody response. A No further action needed This patient is at risk of infection, as he has had a skin-penetrating mammal bite in a region in which rabies is endemic. B Intravenous (IV) rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) For patients who have not been previously vaccinated, postexposure prophylaxis should include passive (immunoglobulin), as well as active, immunisation (vaccination). D Vaccination today and on days three, seven, 14 and

This vaccination schedule would be an appropriate option if this patient had never been vaccinated before and if it was used in conjunction with intravenous (IV) immunoglobulins.

stem: A 21-year-old student presented with a 2-day history of progressive severe retro-orbital headache, myalgia, nausea and vomiting. She had returned from Northern Queensland 1 day previously. On examination, her temperature was 39.5 °C, and blood pressure was 125/70 mmHg lying and 105/65 mmHg standing. She appeared dehydrated and had a petechial rash over her trunk and limbs. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 149 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 95 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 15.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 187 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 280 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Blood ﬁlm (thick & thin) Negative for malarial parasites What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
C Paracetamol and rehydration This patient has dengue fever: she has travelled to an at risk area and has developed a fever with thrombocytopenia and a petechial rash, in conjunction with the classical retro-orbital headache and ﬂu-like symptoms. No speciﬁc treatment is required: supportive therapy with paracetamol and rehydration is adequate. Occasionally in severe cases, clotting factors may be required. Diagnosis is via serology; however, due to the specialist nature of these serological tests often results will not be available for 1–2 weeks and patients must be treated according to clinical suspicion. E Ibuprofen This patient has dengue fever; she has returned from an at risk area, has a petechial rash, thrombocytopenia, deranged liver function tests and a severe retro-orbital headache with ﬂu-like symptoms. Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral haemorrhagic fever: due to the risk of bleeding and relative thrombocytopenia, ibuprofen and other NSAIDs should be avoided, due to their effects on platelet function. No speciﬁc treatment is required for this patient; she should be supported with ﬂuid replacement and paracetamol. Occasionally, in severe cases, clotting factors may be required. A Aciclovir Aciclovir is an appropriate treatment for suspected encephalitis, which may present with severe headache. However, this patient’s symptoms and signs are more suggestive of dengue fever: she has travelled to an endemic area, and retro-orbital headache, ﬂu-like illness, fever, and thrombocytopenia with deranged liver function tests are typical. Dengue fever is caused by a mosquito-borne virus. Treatment is supportive; it is a haemorrhagic fever and in severe cases support with clotting factors may be required, but otherwise paracetamol and rehydration are the only treatments required. B Benzylpenicillin Intramuscular benzylpenicillin is an appropriate primary care treatment for suspected meningococcal meningitis; as this patient

has a rash, fever and severe headache, this is an understandable differential diagnosis. However, given her travel history, the retroorbital nature of the headache and her thrombocytopenia and deranged liver function tests, dengue fever is the likely diagnosis here. This is a virus carried by mosquitoes, and does not require treatment with antibiotics. In fact the most appropriate treatment is supportive, with paracetamol and ﬂuids. It is a haemorrhagic fever and, in severe cases, patients may require clotting factor replacement. D Ceftriaxone Ceftriaxone would be an appropriate treatment for meningococcal meningitis; however, this patient has symptoms and signs that suggest dengue fever, rather than meningitis. A severe, retro-orbital headache is a classic symptom of dengue fever, and she has travelled from an area where dengue is endemic. Her thrombocytopenia, petechial rash and deranged liver function tests are also suggestive of dengue fever. The most appropriate treatment for this viral haemorrhagic fever is supportive, with paracetamol and ﬂuids. Rarely, in severe cases, patients may require clotting factors.

stem: A 24-year-old single woman presents with a second episode of left iliac fossa pain in the past four months. Additionally, she has noticed inter-menstrual bleeding and has suffered an intermittent mucopurulent cervical discharge, although there are no external lesions. On examination, she has lower abdominal pain, worse on the left-hand side. The abdomen is soft and there is no rebound tenderness. Urine testing is negative, pregnancy test is negative. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate next step in this case?
options: Sexually transmitted disease screening including chlamydial nucleic acid ampliﬁcation testing
explanation:
A Sexually transmitted disease screening including chlamydial nucleic acid ampliﬁcation testing This patient’s history is suggestive of Chlamydia infection, and therefore the most appropriate initial intervention is chlamydial nucleic acid ampliﬁcation testing followed by a 1-week course of doxycycline. Alternative antibiotics include macrolides, quinolones or amoxicillin. Patients should refrain from intercourse for a period of seven days, and contact notiﬁcation should be encouraged

where possible. Long-term complications in women include the possibility of pelvic inﬂammatory disease, infertility and transfer to the newborn infant during childbirth. E Arrange abdominal ultrasound An abdominal ultrasound would be of minimal diagnostic value in this patient as it would be suited to evaluation of renal pathology. A transvaginal ultrasound can be considered for adnexal infection and gynaecological abscesses, but with a negative pregnancy test and a soft abdomen it is likely to be of any help. B Penicillin V 500 mg po qds This would be the correct treatment for tonsillitis, otitis media, erysipelas, cellulitis, group A streptococcal infection, rheumatic fever and pneumococcal infection prophylaxis. Benzathine penicillin can be used to treat syphilis. C Aciclovir po Aciclovir is the treatment for herpes simplex. Herpes causes painful genital ulceration without discharge. Whilst diagnosis can be conﬁrmed by PCR viral swabs, it is generally considered a clinical diagnosis. The absence of painful ulcers and presence of discharge and abdominal pain makes this a very unlikely diagnosis and therefore makes this option incorrect. D Admit for surgical observation This is a patient with a soft abdomen with no signs of peritonism. She is unlikely to require acute surgical intervention and therefore surgical observation would not be necessary.

stem: A 33-year-old pregnant woman presents to her General Practitioner with concerns about her exposure to chickenpox while at a birthday party two days ago. She denies previous exposure to chickenpox and is worried about the effects that it may have on her baby. Currently, she feels well and has no symptoms of note. On examination, her observations are within normal limits. Her chest sounds are clear and her heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is soft, with a palpable uterus, in keeping with 19 weeks’ gestation. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
B Varicella antibody testing

Exposure to the varicella-zoster virus increases the risk of fetal varicella syndrome, which may cause skin scarring, microcephaly and learning disabilities. Rapid antibody testing determines whether or not treatment with varicella-zoster immunoglobulin is indicated. E Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin This would be the correct treatment if this patient has a negative varicella antibody result. However, as this patient has not yet been tested for varicella-zoster, giving immunoglobulin would be inappropriate. A Aciclovir prophylaxis Exposure to varicella-zoster infection in pregnancy is potentially very serious for mother and baby. Prompt identiﬁcation of immunity is required to establish whether or not treatment should be initiated. Aciclovir would be given as prophylaxis to patients of > 20 weeks’ gestation. Alternatively, it would be administered as treatment for acute infection. It is not the most appropriate management option for this patient. C Neonatal varicella immunoglobulin Neonatal varicella immunoglobulin is indicated for neonates if mothers develop chickenpox seven days before to seven days after delivery. This is not the case for this patient. D Varicella immunisation Varicella is a live vaccine and should be used with extreme caution in pregnant women. However, in the acute setting, the vaccine would be unable to provide adequate protection. Therefore, varicella antibody testing and/or immunoglobulin administration is preferable.

stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. He is HIV positive and continues to have unprotected sexual intercourse with males, despite having been warned not to, usually in relation to use of crystal methamphetamine. On examination he has a large painless ulcer with rolled edges on the glans penis, and there is associated minor enlargement of inguinal lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Syphilis The answer is Syphilis - The presentation here is typical of primary syphilis. EIA IgM is the usual investigation of choice for primary syphilis, with possible

treatment options including a single IM dose of Benzylpenicillin, a 2-week course of Doxycycline, and a single oral dose of Azithromycin. The course of the disease is similar in patients with early HIV compared to those who are HIV negative. E Trichomoniasis Trichomoniasis is incorrect, it is associated with vaginitis in women and is usually asymptomatic in men. A Chlamydia trachomatis Chlamydia trachomatis is incorrect, chlamydia trachomatis is associated with urethritis rather than painless ulcer formation. B Herpes simplex Herpes simplex in incorrect, it is associated with formation of multiple painful ulcers. C Lymphogranuloma venereum Lymphogranuloma venereum is incorrect, is associated with signiﬁcant inguinal lymph node enlargement, to the point where discharging lymph nodes are actually seen.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a rash on her inner thighs and lower abdomen. She is concerned that it is unsightly, and about passing the rash on to her boyfriend. A picture is shown below: Which of the following is the most effective intervention for the rash?
explanation: C Cryotherapy The rash shown here is molluscum contagiosum with umbilicated papules. In adults, the infection, usually caused by molluscum contagiosum virus 1 (MCV1), is transmitted sexually or by sharing items of clothing or towels. It improves spontaneously with resolution, taking up to 18 months in some patients. A Cochrane meta- analysis concluded that there is limited evidence to support the range of interventions currently used for molluscum contagiosum. However, it appears cryotherapy is the most effective of a number of therapies trialed over the years. E Olive oil Olive oil has been shown in clinical trials to be inferior to other options for the treatment of Molluscum. It is, therefore, not recommended as a therapy option. A Aciclovir Acyclovir and famciclovir are potential interventions in the treatment of genital herpes. Genital herpes is characterised by multiple small erosions which are extremely painful. Often, the lesions are so painful that they can precipitate urinary retention in women. Use of an antiviral agent such as acyclovir is proven to shorten the duration of an acute episode and improve symptoms. B Benzoyl peroxide Although benzoyl peroxide is effective in the treatment of mild to moderate acne vulgaris, it has been proven across a range of small clinical trials to be ineffective in treating Molluscum contagiosum. Other options such as cryotherapy are preferred. D Imiquimod The Cochrane meta-analysis on interventions for Molluscum did not reveal convincing evidence of any beneﬁt for Imiquimod 5% topical therapy with respect to resolution of lesions, and in fact use was associated with a worse adverse event proﬁle than other treatments with respect to inﬂammatory skin reactions.

stem: You are a senior house ofﬁcer in The Genitourinary Medicine Clinic.
options: Further three doses of benzathine penicillin
Further one dose of benzathine penicillin
explanation: C No further treatment required This patient has been adequately treated for early latent syphilis and her RPR is stable, but remaining positive. She is serofast and you would only be concerned at the possibility of reinfection if the RPR increased by twofold or more. In fact, it has decreased slightly since her last blood test, so there is no cause for concern. The titre of TPHA is meaningless and should not be done. TPHA will remain positive all her life and simply indicates previous syphilis infection, giving no information about treatment. Treatment for syphilis is generally with benzathine penicillin IM with dose and need for repeat of treatment dependent on the stage of syphilis and if the patient is pregnant. For early syphilis, including primary, secondary and early latent, a single dose of 2.4 MU is needed. For latent, cardiovascular and gummatous syphilis three doses over 3 weeks are needed. Note that for cardiovascular syphilis, steroids should be given as well, starting the day before antibiotics. For neurosyphilis, procaine penicillin and probenecid is needed for 2 weeks. In pregnancy, treatment for early syphilis is one dose up to 27 weeks of pregnancy and two doses from week 28 to term. E 2 weeks of doxycycline In pregnancy, procaine penicillin is an alternative to benzathine penicillin as doxycycline is not appropriate in pregnancy. In patients who are not pregnant, doxycycline can be used as an alternative treatment. A Further three doses of benzathine penicillin There is no further need for treatment as RPR is not changing. This management is not generally recommended. B Further one dose of benzathine penicillin There is no further need for treatment as RPR is not changing. If a patient is treated in the third trimester then a further dose is needed and she is in week 15 of pregnancy. D 3-monthly monitoring of RPR during pregnancy RPR monitoring is not needed.

stem: A 26-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of severe and worsening headache. He also complained of nausea, worse in the morning. He did not have photophobia. He was born in Nigeria but had moved to the UK 1 year previously. On examination, his temperature was 38°C, pulse rate was 110 beats/min and blood pressure was 130/70 mmHg. His oral mucosa and tongue were coated with white patches which scraped away to reveal erythematous and sore mucosa. He had cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy and appeared thin. There was no meningism, but there was a right-sided weakness with associated brisk reﬂexes. There was a right homonymous hemianopia. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 118 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 2.8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.8 × 109/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 270 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Cerebral toxoplasmosis There are symptoms and signs suggestive of HIV in this patient: he appears to have lost weight, has widespread lymphadenopathy, has oral candidiasis and a marked lymphopenia. This immunocompromise would render him vulnerable to infections such as toxoplasmosis. Headache with vomiting, no meningism and focal neurological signs is suggestive of raised intracranial pressure, and on a background of potential HIV cerebral toxoplasmosis should be the top differential. The patient should have an MRI head which will show ring-enhancing lesions. Treatment requires combination therapy with septrin or pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine and folinic acid. He should also be tested for HIV and started on retroviral therapy if he is found to be positive. D Meningococcal meningitis This patient does not have meningism: there is no neck stiffness and no photophobia. This would be unusual in meningococcal meningitis. Instead, he has focal neurology with headache and vomiting: this is suggestive of a mass effect from focal lesions causing raised intracranial pressure. He also has weight loss, lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis and a marked lymphopenia: this is suggestive of undiagnosed HIV. Putting this presentation together, the most likely diagnosis is cerebral toxoplasmosis, to which he is vulnerable as a result of undiagnosed HIV. B Cryptococcal meningitis Indeed, this patient appears to have signs and symptoms suggestive of undiagnosed HIV – weight loss, widespread lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis and a marked lymphopenia – but you would expect

cryptococcal meningitis to cause meningism and photophobia. Although focal neurology can be seen with cryptococcal meningitis, the combination of headache with vomiting and focal neurology is suggestive of a mass lesion causing raised intracranial pressure: this patient is more likely to have cerebral toxoplasmosis. C Lyme disease This patient has weight loss, widespread lymphadenopathy, oral candidiasis and a marked lymphopenia: this is suggestive of undiagnosed HIV. The most common neurological manifestation of Lyme disease is unilateral or bilateral facial palsies; it may also cause meningitis (but this patient, although he has a headache and fever, does not have meningism). It would be unusual for Lyme disease to present with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting) and cortical focal neurology. This patient’s neurological signs are more likely to be explained by cerebral toxoplasmosis, to which he will be vulnerable if he does have undiagnosed HIV. E Middle cerebral artery thrombosis Although this patient has focal neurology consistent with an MCA territory stroke, he also has a headache and vomiting, which are more suggestive of raised intracranial pressure and therefore of a mass lesion in this area of the cortex. He also appears to have lost weight, has lymphadenopathy and oral candidiasis, and a marked lymphopenia. This is suggestive of undiagnosed HIV infection, rendering him vulnerable to opportunistic infections such as cerebral toxoplasmosis.

stem: A 28-year-old patient currently on FLAG-IDA chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) presents with fever. Bloods on admission show that he is ﬂat neutropenic and he is therefore started on pipercillin/tazobactam (tazocin) and gentamicin for febrile neutropenia. His fevers continue, and on day 3 his antibiotics are changed to meropenem and vancomycin. Unfortunately, his fevers persist and no clear source of infection has been identiﬁed. As part of a full work-up, you repeat all cultures and arrange a high-resolution CT chest, which is reported as consistent with invasive aspergillosis. Which of the following would be an appropriate treatment choice?
explanation:
C Voriconazole Voriconazole is an antifungal drug with a broad spectrum of activity against both yeasts and moulds. In this patient, with

neutropenia and CT ﬁndings suggestive of invasive aspergillosis, voriconazole would be an appropriate addition to his antimicrobial therapy. Compared to amphotericin B, it is associated with a reduced incidence of renal impairment and decreased morbidity. E Gentamicin Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic with activity against resistant Gram-negative organisms, including extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producers and Pseudomonas. However, it is unlikely to add any additional cover for our patient, who is already receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics. A Co-amoxiclav Co-amoxiclav is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid; it has a broad spectrum of activity against both Gram-positive and negative bacteria. However, it adds no additional cover for our patient, who is already receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics. B Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin is a ﬂuoroquinolone antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity against Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria. However, it adds no additional cover for our patient, who is already receiving broad- spectrum antibiotics. Furthermore, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever there is an effective alternative available due to the risk of debilitating adverse effects. D Fluconazole Fluconazole is a triazole antifungal with activity against many yeasts, but no activity against moulds such as Aspergillus, which is the concern in this patient.

stem: A 73-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with an 8-day history of intermittent fevers, dry cough and progressive shortness of breath. His wife is concerned as this morning he appeared acutely confused and could not recognise his whereabouts. His past medical history includes ischaemic heart disease and gastritis, for which he takes aspirin, bisoprolol, atorvastatin and lansoprazole daily. He is otherwise well in himself and returned from a convention at a Spanish seaside hotel a few days earlier. Examination reveals a temperature of 39 °C, a BP of 100/80 mmHg and a heart rate of 98 bpm and regular. There are coarse crackles at the right lung base and he appears tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. His oxygen saturations are 94% on air. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 137 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 15.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 199 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 128 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l His CXR is shown below: Which of the following is the most appropriate choice of antibiotic for this patient?
explanation:
A Azithromycin This patient has Legionnaires’ disease with a typical history of fever with a dry cough and shortness of breath, coupled with hyponatraemia and an increased white cell count. The CXR shows right middle lobe consolidation. Macrolides and ﬂuoroquinolones are the recommended ﬁrst-line options for the treatment of legionella. Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic and is, therefore, the preferred option. Other macrolides commonly used include clarithromycin or erythromycin. D Doxycycline Although tetracyclines can be used for the treatment of Legionnaires’ disease, they are recommended as second-line antibiotics of choice due to potential resistance. B Benzylpenicillin Benzylpenicillin is commonly used in the treatment of pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. However, given this patient’s clinical presentation and laboratory ﬁndings, Legionnaires’ disease is much more likely, making a macrolide antibiotic appropriate. C Co-amoxiclav Legionella is not sensitive to penicillin, ruling out co-amoxiclav as a treatment option here. Co-amoxiclav is, of course, used empirically in the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, usually in combination with a macrolide such as clarithromycin.

E Gentamicin Gentamicin is a ﬁrst-line treatment for Gram-negative sepsis where dosing is tailored according to renal function. It does not have a role in the treatment of Legionnaires’ disease.

JAM Amoebiasis Amoebiasis is a term used to describe a spectrum of diseases caused by entamoeba histolytica.  Overview Key Facts  Amoebiasis is a term used to describe a spectrum of diseases caused by entamoeba histolytica.  Entamoeba histolytica is found worldwide, particularly in areas of poor sanitation:  transmitted by ingestion of food or water contaminated with amoebic cysts secreted in the faeces of asymptomatic individuals  highly variable incubation period ranging from a few days to several months.  The most common manifestation of amoebiasis is amoebic dysentery:  clinical features include fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhoea  differential diagnosis should include typhoid, shigella, and salmonella  investigation of choice is microscopy of stool samples for ova, cysts, and parasites.  Another important manifestation is amoebic liver abscesses:  patients typically present with right upper quadrant pain, referred right shoulder tip pain and fevers - hepatomegaly may be seen on examination  differential diagnosis for amoebic liver abscess includes pyogenic abscess, primary and secondary liver cancers, and disseminated tuberculosis  investigation of choice is microscopy of aspirated samples  cross-sectional computed tomography (CT) imaging is helpful in characterising abscess size and location.  Treatment of choice for both forms of amoebiasis is metronidazole (which kills active parasites) and diloxanide furoate (which kills cysts to prevent recrudescent infection):  large liver abscesses may require repeated therapeutic aspiration. Amoebiasis life cycle:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Animals As A Vector Of Disease  Overview Key Facts  The World Health Organization (WHO) defines a vector as a ‘living organism that can transmit infectious pathogens between humans, or from animals to humans.  Seventeen per cent of all infectious diseases are carried by vectors.

DR. JAM  Vector-borne diseases account for more than 700 000 deaths each year.  Examples of Vectors Aedes Mosquito (‘Yellow Fever Mosquito’)  Chikungunya:  caused by the chikungunya virus (CHIKV)  most prevalent in the Indian subcontinent, Africa and Asia  main symptoms include fever and severe joint pain  treatment revolves around the relief of symptoms and there is no vaccine  the disease is rarely fatal.  Dengue fever:  caused by the dengue virus (DENV)  dengue is endemic in Africa, South-East Asia, the Western Pacific, the Americas and the Eastern Mediterranean  symptoms include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pains, nausea and vomiting, swollen glands and rash  ‘severe dengue’ may develop after 3–7 days and may cause severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, haematemesis, tachypnoea, bleeding gums fatigue or restlessness  treatment is symptomatic  a vaccine called CYD-TDV or Dengvaxia® is now available for use in several countries, but should only be used in people previously infected with dengue, as it can increase the risk of severe dengue in people who are infected for the first time after the vaccination.  Lymphatic filariasis:  also known as ‘elephantiasis’ due to the severe lymphoedema that can be caused by the disease  caused by infection with roundworms, most commonly Wuchereria bancrofti  the roundworms nest in the lymphatic system, disrupting lymphatic flow and causing lymphoedema, most commonly of the limbs or scrotum  some infected people remain asymptomatic  preventive chemotherapy is given annually in high-risk areas to reduce transmission of infection.  Rift Valley fever:  a viral zoonosis transmitted via infected mosquitoes or contact with the blood or organs of infected animals (most common)  mainly affects sub-Saharan Africa  most infections cause mild symptoms but can progress to ocular disease (leading to blindness), meningoencephalitis causing a permanent neurological deficit, or haemorrhagic fever (which has a mortality rate of 50%)

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  treatment is supportive only.  Yellow fever:  caused by the yellow fever virus (a Flavivirus)  endemic in Africa, Central and South America  symptoms are non-specific and include muscle pain, vomiting, lethargy, fever and headache  a minority of patients develop severe disease which can be fatal  treatment is supportive  there is an effective vaccine.  Zika virus  most people infected with the virus are asymptomatic  symptoms may include headache, lethargy, rash, fever, conjunctivitis and muscle and joint pain  infection in pregnancy classically causes microcephaly in infants  the virus can be transmitted via sexual intercourse  infection can lead to neurological complications such as Guillain–Barré syndrome and myelitis  treatment is symptomatic  very rarely fatal, but can cause a high level of morbidity if there are neurological complications or in cases of vertical transmission. Anopheles Mosquito  Lymphatic filariasis:  see Aedes Mosquito.  Malaria:  caused by Plasmodium spp. parasites carried by infected female mosquitoes  children under 5 years are at the highest risk of mortality  most deaths are in sub-Saharan Africa, but malaria is also present in South-East Asia, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Western Pacific and the Americas  parasites grow and multiply within red blood cells  the most common causative parasite is Plasmodium falciparum and this is also the most commonly fatal  treatment for P. falciparum malaria is with artemisinin-based combination therapy. Culex Mosquito  Japanese encephalitis:  caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) (a Flavivirus)  affects countries in South-East Asia and the Western Pacific  most infections cause mild symptoms, but approximately 1 in 250 can develop encephalitis and neurological symptoms and the fatality rate can be as high as 30% in these patients

DR. JAM  some people may suffer permanent psychiatric or neurological symptoms  treatment is supportive  a vaccine is available.  West Nile fever:  transmitted through bites of infected mosquitoes  found in Africa, Europe, the Middle East, Asia and North America  eighty per cent of people infected are asymptomatic  if symptomatic, people can suffer from a flu-like illness; severe disease can cause neurological problems such as paralysis and it can be fatal  treatment is supportive. Aquatic Snails  Schistosomiasis:  a parasitic disease caused by trematode worms carried by aquatic snails  people become infected through contact with infested water and larval forms of the parasite penetrate the skin  water becomes infested when it is contaminated by faeces containing parasite eggs  symptoms include abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea and haematuria and may cause bladder and kidney damage  increases the risk of bladder cancer and may cause infertility  treatment is with praziquantel. Blackflies  Onchocerciasis (river blindness):  caused by the parasitic worm Onchocerca volvulus and transmitted by infected blackflies  most common in Africa  causes severe itching and eye lesions, which can lead to blindness  treated with ivermectin. Lice  Typhus:  caused by infection with the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii carried by infected lice  now relatively rare  presents with non-specific flu-like symptoms  treatment is with doxycycline. Sandflies  Leishmaniasis:  caused by Leishmania spp. parasites carried by sandflies

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  three distinct forms of the disease are recognised: visceral, cutaneous and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis  treatment is complex and depends on the type of disease and the individual patient  no vaccine is available. Ticks  Lyme disease:  caused by bites from ticks infected by the spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi  the disease is present in Asia, Europe and the USA  initially presents with flu-like symptoms and often a classic erythema migrans rash  later symptoms include central nervous system involvement (eg meningitis) and facial palsy  treatment is usually with doxycycline. Triatome Bugs  Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis):  the triatomine bug transmits the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi  most common in Latin America  can also be transmitted vertically, via blood or blood products or orally (food-borne)  initial presentation can be non-specific, but up to 30% of people suffer cardiac complications that can lead to sudden death  treatment is with benznidazole and nifurtimox and is more effective if taken as soon as possible after infection. Tsetse Flies  Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis):  endemic in sub-Saharan Africa  invariably fatal in non-treated cases  the parasite Trypanosoma brucei gambiense is responsible for >98% of cases  the remaining 2% caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense  patients can be asymptomatic for months or years, but when symptoms do appear, they usually represent damage to the central nervous system (parasites are able to cross the blood-brain barrier)  patients may also have a disrupted sleep cycle, hence the name  six different drugs are used for treatment and treatment depends on the stage of infection  early disease is treated with IV pentamidine or suramin.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  resistance to specific antibiotic classes may be intrinsic (eg P. aeruginosa resistance to penicillins) or acquired  antibiotic therapy imposes strong selective pressure for resistant strains  resistance can be acquired by de novo mutations or transfer of genetic material in bacterial plasmids (within and between species)  mechanisms of resistance include decreased cell permeability, active antibiotic efflux, altered target site, and antibiotic inactivation.  Always consider allergies and drug interactions (eg clarithromycin and statin; erythromycin and warfarin) when prescribing antibiotics.  Side effects are common and include gastrointestinal upset and rashes:  anaphylaxis is a rare side effect but a very important consideration in antibiotic prescribing. Epidemiology  Bacterial infections are common worldwide with highest mortality in infants, elderly patients and immunocompromised.  Antibiotics are regulated in the UK (prescribed by doctors) whereas they are widely available in other countries which greatly contributes to resistance. Aetiology  Antibiotics exploit physiological differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells to inhibit bacterial growth (bacteriostatic) or directly kill bacteria (bacteriocidal):  disruption of bacterial cell wall synthesis or integrity:  beta lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems)  polymixins (colistin)  glycopeptides (vancomycin and teicoplanin).  disruption of bacterial ribosome function:  30S subunit – tetracyclines, aminoglycosides (eg gentamicin, amikacin)  50S subunit – macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), clindamycin, linezolid and chloramphenicol.  disruption of nucleic acid synthesis:  folate synthesis (folate is an essential substrate for DNA backbone synthesis) – sulphonamides (sulfomethoxazole) and trimethoprim  DNA gyrase – quinolones (eg ciprofloxacin)  RNA polymerase – rifampicin. cs table: action Indication Side effects bition of nding ssary for all crossStaphylococcal and Streptococcal infections Anaphylaxis Interstitial nephritis (rare) Encephalopathy (rare)
