JAM replication transcription, in cell death a preventing replication Bactericidal ant Nitroimidazole Metronidazole Production of radicals in ana micro-organi Bactericidal ant Aspergillosis Aspergillosis is a fungal infection caused by the Aspergillus species that primarily affects the lungs and can lead to a range of respiratory symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Aspergillosis is an infection caused by the inhalation of spores from Aspergillus species, which are filamentous fungi.  It is very rare in immunocompetent hosts.  It encompasses a spectrum of disease including isolated infections of individual areas, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and invasive aspergillosis.  Diagnosis is made via a computed tomography (CT) scan and serum aspergillus galactomannan antigen detection.  Treatment is with antifungal agents such as voriconazole.  Prognosis depends upon the disease pattern. Epidemiology  Aspergillosis is seen in all regions because the fungus is ubiquitous in soil throughout the world.  It mostly occurs in immunocompromised hosts, such as recipients of stem cell or solid organ transplants, those with haematological malignancy or acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy.  Only 2% of invasive aspergillosis occurs in non-compromised hosts.  Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis occurs on a background of other pulmonary diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), tuberculosis and sarcoidosis. Aetiology  Aspergillus spp. are ubiquitous fungi that grow in soil.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI and nducing and cell n. tibiotics Pseudomonas (ciprofloxacin is the only oral preparation available) Bacterial gastroenteritis f free aerobic sms . tibiotics Anaerobic gastrointestinal infections – C. difficile, amoebiasis, giardiasis Avoid with alcohol – severe vomiting and disulfiram-like reaction Cytopenias  The fungus grows as a filament and produces aerial stalks. Spores (conidia) are produced at the tips of the stalks.  The spores become aerosolised and are inhaled by humans or they settle on surfaces.  Spores are usually eliminated from the respiratory tract; however, in immunocompromised hosts, there may be colonisation and infection.  There are over 200 species of Aspergillus, but Aspergillus fumigatus is responsible for up to 70% of cases of aspergillosis.  Some other species that cause disease in humans include Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus terreus; A. terreus is resistant to amphotericin B and therefore has a poor prognosis. Pathophysiology  There are four types of disease pattern. 1. Invasive aspergillosis (IA)  Following inhalation of spores, immunocompetent hosts are able to clear the organism via ciliary clearance and pulmonary macrophages.  However, in immunocompromised hosts, the spores germinate and form hyphae, which invade the pulmonary parenchyma.  There is an interaction between aspergillus ligands and Toll-like receptors on macrophages that leads to the production of proinflammatory cytokines.  Hyphae locally disseminate via the pulmonary vasculature, causing inflammation, thrombosis and tissue infarction.  This is followed by haematogenous dissemination into the brain, skin, eyes, heart, kidney, liver, spleen, bone and gastrointestinal tract. There may also be a direct invasion from the paranasal sinus into the orbit and brain parenchyma. 2. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)  A hypersensitivity reaction, usually to antigens from Aspergillus fumigatus.

DR. JAM  Typically affects patients with cystic fibrosis or asthma due to increased mucous secretion and impaired mucociliary clearance which results in reduced clearance of spores.  The allergens induce type I and type III hypersensitivity reactions.  The proximal bronchi become dilated and filled with mucous leading to bronchiectasis and airway obstruction. 3. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA)  An indolent, destructive infection of the lung which results in fibrosis and gradual loss of lung tissue.  Describes several types of disease pattern, including:  aspergilloma – a fungal ball consisting of fungal proteins, mucus, tissue debris, inflammatory cells and fibrin that forms in pre-existing cavities, commonly resulting from tuberculosis  aspergillus nodule – a small mass of infection that can be single or multiple and may cause cavitation  chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) – formation of one or more pulmonary cavities, usually occurring in immunocompetent hosts  chronic necrotising pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA) – similar to chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, but progresses more quickly and is associated with COPD and excess alcohol use. 4. Isolated infection  Can infect several isolated areas, such as the nails, eyes, skin, sinuses and ear canals.  Endocarditis can occur from direct invasion during cardiac surgery.  Endophthalmitis can occur following trauma or surgery to the eye.  Clinical Presentation Disease entity Signs and symptoms Invasive aspergillosis (IA) Lung manifestations: pleuritic chest pain non-productive cough haemoptysis pleural rub dyspnoea Other manifestations: fever weight loss night sweats

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI fatigue nasal ulcer intracranial – headache, seizure, cranial nerve palsy, altered mental status skin – ecthyma gangrenosum (erythematous, tender, lesions with a necrotic or ulcerated centre) sinuses – facial pain, headache, congestion or sinus tenderness orbits/eyes – endophthalmitis, chemosis, reduced visual acuity, photosensitivity heart – endocarditis GI tract – appendicitis, abdominal pain, ulcers, bleeding Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) Asthma-type symptoms, eg wheezing, dyspnoea Haemoptysis or cough productive of brown mucous Pleuritic chest pain Fever Finger clubbing Weight loss Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) Nodules – mostly asymptomatic, but rarely cough, pneumonia or exacerbations of existing lung disease Aspergilloma – mostly asymptomatic, but may cause symptoms described below Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) and chronic necrotising pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA) present similarly with cough, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, weight loss, fever, fatigue and night sweats  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  other pulmonary fungal infections, eg histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, candidiasis, pneumocystis  mycobacterial infection  pulmonary embolism  malignancy  COVID-19.  Diagnosis/Investigation Laboratory  IA:

DR. JAM  positive serum aspergillus galactomannan by enzyme immunoassay; galactomannan is a component of the cell wall; this test has high sensitivity and specificity when performed serially  serum (1-3)-β-D-glucan – not specific for aspergillus as β-glucan is found in other fungal infections  PCR detection of ribosomal DNA – may allow early detection when combined with the tests described above.  ABPA:  elevated serum total IgE antibodies and aspergillusspecific IgE  elevated aspergillus-specific IgG  positive weal and flare reaction on skin test  a full blood count will show eosinophilia.  CPA:  elevated serum IgG antibodies. Imaging  IA:  chest X-ray may be normal; other findings include nodules, consolidation, pulmonary infiltrates and cavities  high-resolution chest CT scan – multiple nodules, halo sign (ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule), aircrescent sign (crescent of air surrounding a fungal colony), infiltrates and pleural effusions  high-resolution sinuses CT scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sinuses – mass within the sinus cavity and local bone erosion  high-resolution brain CT scan and MRI brain – focal lesions, space-occupying lesions, abscesses and hemorrhagic areas.  ABPA:  chest X-ray – infiltrates (commonly middle-upper lobe), bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction  high-resolution chest CT scan – mucoid plugging and impaction, bronchiectasis and pulmonary infiltrates.  CPA:  chest X-ray and high-resolution chest CT scan – upper lobe mobile mass with an air-crescent (aspergilloma), multiple nodules and cavities (often associated with pleural thickening). Culture/histopathology  IA and CPA:  sputum culture – sputum yield is usually low but may grow Aspergillus spp.  sputum smear – to identify hyphal elements  bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for galactomannan antigen enzyme immunoassay, fungal culture or fungal stain  tissue biopsy – the most definitive method of diagnosis; samples are sent for culture and pathology; they may be

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI obtained via CT-guided needle aspiration for peripheral lesions, video-assisted thoracoscopy surgery (VATS) biopsy or open lung biopsy; aspergillus stains with Gomori’s methenamine silver (GMS) stain.  ABPA:  sputum culture and microscopy – mucous plugs, fungal elements and eosinophils.  Management IA  Suspected – since the diagnosis is difficult to confirm, high-risk patients should be treated empirically with amphotericin B or an echinocandin (such as caspofungin).  Confirmed – there are two steps of treatment:  reversal of the underlying immune deficiency – colonystimulating factors may be considered and steroids may be given in reduced doses  antifungal therapy – isavuconazole and voriconazole are the first-line options; if there are signs of improvement, therapy should be continued for at least three months; if there is clinical deterioration, voriconazole can be switched to amphotericin B or an echinocandin, or an echinocandin can be given in combination with voriconazole.  Antifungal prophylaxis with posaconazole may be considered in high-risk patients.  Surgical intervention – may be considered if lesions are continuous with the great vessels or pericardium and in severe haemoptysis from a single cavity. ABPA  The mainstay of treatment is systemic corticosteroids to treat acute symptoms.  Once in remission, treatment is aimed at improving the management of underlying asthma or cystic fibrosis.  Courses of systemic corticosteroids can be repeated during exacerbations of symptoms.  Antifungal therapy is an adjunct rather than primary therapy; considered when systemic corticosteroids are having to be used on an ongoing basis. itraconazole is used most commonly. CPA  Treatment depends on the subtype of CPA.  Stable and asymptomatic aspergillomas can be monitored. There is insufficient evidence that aspergilloma responds to antifungal agents.  Antifungals are used as a curative therapy in aspergillus nodules and to improve symptoms in CCPA and CNPA.  Similarly to IA, isavuconazole and voriconazole are the firstline options. If there is clinical deterioration, voriconazole can be switched to amphotericin B or an echinocandin or an echinocandin can be given in combination with voriconazole.  Surgery is a potentially curative option in aspergillus nodules and simple aspergilloma. Lobectomy is the most common procedure.

DR. JAM  Bronchial artery embolisation is a minimally invasive procedure used to control massive haemoptysis.  Prognosis  Prognosis is very poor for IA, with a 1-year survival of 59% in solid organ transplant recipients. Complications include lifethreatening haemoptysis, dissemination, severe hypoxia, obstructive pneumonia and adverse effects of antifungal therapy (such as adrenal suppression and hepatotoxicity).  Prognosis is good for ABPA with prompt diagnosis and treatment. Complications include bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis and adverse effects of corticosteroids and antifungal therapy.  There are limited data for CPA given the spectrum of disease. Simple aspergilloma has a good overall prognosis, but there is significant mortality if associated with massive haemoptysis. Severe disease has a 15–30% mortality in the first six months and mortality is primarily from pneumonia and massive haemoptysis. Bacterial Meningitis Meningitis is an acute infection caused by inflammation of the meninges – that is the outer membranous lining covering of the brain and the spinal cord.  Overview Key Facts  Meningitis is an acute infection caused by inflammation of the meninges – that is the outer membranous lining covering of the brain and the spinal cord.  Meningitis can be caused by either bacterial, viral or fungal infections or non-infective causes like tumours, autoimmune disorders, trauma, and certain drugs.  Bacterial meningitis affects all ages – most commonly seen in children. It is a life-threatening condition.  Route of transmission is close contact (droplets or secretions from the upper respiratory tract).  The cardinal symptoms of meningitis include headache, fever, photophobia, vomiting and neck stiffness.  Diagnosis is made with blood tests, computed tomography (CT) scan and lumbar puncture.  Intravenous (IV) Ceftriaxone is the treatment of choice for bacterial meningitis. Epidemiology  Developed countries – 2 to 5 cases per 100 000 annually.  Meningococcal infection (mostly caused by Men B subtype) is more common compared to pneumococcal infection.  Neisseria Meningitidis is the causative organism of recurring epidemics of meningitis every 8–12 years.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Most cases are sporadic, outbreaks occur especially in adolescents.  Influenza A, asplenia and complement deficiencies predispose to infection. Aetiology  In the United Kingdom (UK), the most common causative organisms of acute bacterial meningitis in children > 3 months and adults include:  Neisseria meningitidis (Meningococcal infection)  Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcal infection)  Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).  Most common causative organisms in neonates < 1 month of age:  Streptococcus agalactiae  Escherichia coli  S. pneumoniae  Listeria monocytogenes (also a concern in the elderly). Pathophysiology Bacteria initially colonise in the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells ⇢ transported across the cells to intravascular space by creating separations in the apical tight junctions of columnar epithelial cells ⇢ bloodborne bacteria reach intraventricular choroid plexus ⇢ directly infect choroid plexus epithelial cells and gain access to the CSF ⇢ bacteria adhere to cerebral capillary endothelial cells and migrate through the cells to reach the CSF ⇢ rapid multiplication of bacteria within CSF due to absence of effective host immune defence system ⇢ elevated consequence of elevated levels of CSF cytokines and chemokines ⇢ clinical signs and symptoms.  Clinical Presentation  Triad of fever, headache, nuchal rigidity (pathognomonic sign of meningeal irritation).  Level of consciousness decreased – ranging from lethargy to coma.  Diffuse erythematous non-blanching maculopapular rash.  Photophobia.  Capillary refill time > 2 seconds.  Kernig's and Brudzinski's sign positive – signs of meningeal irritation.  Kernig's sign -pain and resistance on passive knee extension with hips fully flexed.  Brudzinski's sign - hips flex on bending the head forward.  Focal seizures due to focal arterial ischaemia or infarction or focal oedema.  Cushing's reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration, cerebral herniation).

DR. JAM  Non-specific signs like fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, decreased appetite, chills.  Differential Diagnosis  Fungal meningitis  Viral encephalitis  Central nervous system malignancy  Brain or spinal epidural abscess  Para meningeal infection  Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever  Non-infective causes like SLE, Beçhet’s syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full Blood Count  Polymerase chain reaction  CT or magnetic resonance imaging  Lumbar puncture – CSF abnormalities in bacterial meningitis:  opening pressure > 180 mmH2O  white blood cells 10 microL to 10,000 microL : neutrophils predominate  CSF glucose – < 0.4  glucose < 2.2 mmol/l  protein > 0.45 g/l.  Glass test for rashes.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Adequate rest  Adequate hydration and nutrition. Pharmacological Suspected Meningococcal infection with a nonblanching rash:  hospital admission  single dose of Benzylpenicillin at the earliest in the outpatient set up:  dose:  child < 1 year – 300 mg  child 1 – 9 years – 600 mg  adults and child 10 years and above 1200 mg. Suspected Meningococcal infection without non- blanching rash:  hospital admission

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  empirical antibiotics – either Benzylpenicillin, Cefotaxime, Chloramphenicol  vancomycin is added if the patient has a history of travel outside the UK. Chemoprophylaxis for post-exposure or close contacts:  given to all individuals who were in close contact with the patient for seven days prior to the onset of the illness  medical professionals involved in the care of the patient  ciprofloxacin is preferred antibiotic over rifampicin. Ciprofloxacin is preferred as a STAT dose  dexamethasone is added to reduce the risk of complications.  Prognosis  The mortality rate ranges between 3%–7%  Risk of death increases with various factors including low level of consciousness, children, decreased CSF glucose.  Complications of meningitis include the following:  hearing loss  memory Impairment  seizures  gait disturbances  motor deficits  hydrocephalus  visual disturbances. Bacterial Vaginosis Bacterial vaginosis occurs when there is an overgrowth of nonlactobacilli anaerobic bacteria in the vagina.  Overview Key Facts  Bacterial vaginosis (BV) occurs when there is an overgrowth of non-lactobacilli anaerobic bacteria in the vagina.  BV is not a sexually transmitted infection (STI) but is associated with sexual activity and concurrent STI presence.  In BV, vaginal conditions become more alkaline and the healthy high levels of lactobacilli are replaced by other anaerobic bacteria.  BV is linked to an increased risk of other conditions and/or complications.  Antibiotic treatment is normally only for symptomatic BV (about 50% are asymptomatic).

DR. JAM  Treatment needs to be combined with patient education and avoidance of contributing factors.  Prognosis with appropriate treatment and adherence is good; however, recurrence is common (up to 70%). Epidemiology  It is the most common cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women.  Prevalence varies among different groups:  approximately 1 in 20 asymptomatic students  approximately ≤ one-third of pregnant women. Aetiology  Risk factors: ‘douching’, use of ‘specialised vaginal toiletries’ such as soaps and deodorants, smoking, sexual activity, semen in the vagina (as it is high pH), presence of an STI, recent new sexual partner, Afro-Caribbean, receptive oral sex, copper intrauterine devices.  Risk is reduced by condom usage, hormonal contraception (oestrogen favours the growth of lactobacilli) and having a circumcised sexual partner. Pathophysiology  In BV there is an overgrowth of non-lactobacilli anaerobic bacteria in the vagina. Without BV With BV Normal vaginal pH is below 4.5 pH is high: 4.5–6.0 Anaerobic bacteria levels are raised (> 1000 × normal amounts) Normal vaginal flora is mainly lactobacilli Reduction in lactobacilli Common present microorganisms: Gardnerella vaginalis Atopobium vaginalae Prevotella spp. Mycoplasma hominis Mobiluncus spp.  Clinical Presentation  Around 50% of those with BV are asymptomatic.  Be aware that BV is more common in those with other STIs, so symptoms may be mixed.  Symptom recognition may be elicited at other gynaecological consultations or antenatal clinics.  Symptoms include:  ‘fishy’ or ‘offensive’ discharge.  soreness  itching  irritation.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis The differentials for BV can be split into infective causes and ‘other’:  Infective:  candidiasis  trichomoniasis  chlamydia  gonorrhoea  genital herpes  mixed infection of BV + above.  Other:  normal physiological discharge  discharge in ‘vaginal atrophy’  gynaecological cancers  foreign body  allergy, eg to latex.  Diagnosis/Investigation On examination  White, thin, homogenous vaginal discharge.  ‘Fishy’ odour.  Lack of inflammation.  Include:  pH assessment via swab  high-vaginal (or ‘self’ low-vaginal) swab to assess organisms present if there is: recurrence, recent gynae procedure or clinical suspicion of other cause.  Diagnosis may be made on clinical history alone.  Otherwise, pelvic examination, including with speculum, is necessary.  BV presentation is a good opportunity for STI screening, eg chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomoniasis and consideration for GUM referral.  Management  Start empirical treatment based on patient history alone if:  low STI risk  not pregnant  not pre- or post-gynaecological procedure  first episode  previous BV with the same clinical history and examination performed previously  not post-natal or post-miscarriage  no other symptoms.  Treatment involves assessment for associated STIs and aetiological factors and antibiotics:  normally only symptomatic patients are treated

DR. JAM  patient education: BV may recur, avoid ‘douching’ and other unnecessary vaginal hygiene practices, and sexual health and contraceptive advice  empirical treatment may be started without examination in some groups (see table below)  there is no ‘gold standard’ for treatment in recurrence and aside from first-line metronidazole, there is insufficient evidence to suggest one treatment or dosing regimen is better than another. Antibiotics for BV Not Pregnant Pregnant First-line Oral metronidazole ✓ ✓ Others Metronidazole gel ✓ ✓ Clindamycin cream ✓ ✓ Less preferred Oral clindamycin ✓ ✓ Oral tinidazole ✓ ✗  In recurrence, assess:  previous treatment appropriateness and compliance  other possible diagnoses  repeated contributing factors.  Prognosis  Prognosis with appropriate treatment and adherence is good; however, recurrence is common (up to 70%) and further assessment may be necessary. Associations with BV  There is a slight link in pregnant women between BV and a higher risk of contracting HIV.  Treatment of BV may reduce chlamydia acquisition.  BV is seen in many with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).  It is associated with gynaecological surgery complication risks, eg post-termination of pregnancy endometritis or PID, and posttransvaginal hysterectomy vaginal cellulitis and abscess formation.  Obstetric complications: prematurity, late miscarriage, prelabour rupture of membranes, postpartum endometritis, low birthweight.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Brucellosis Brucellosis is a bacterial infection transmitted from animals to humans, causing flu-like symptoms and long-term complications if left untreated.  Overview Key Facts  Brucellosis is a notifiable disease caused by Brucella species.  Many Brucella species exist, of which all are Gramnegative intracellular bacteria.  Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease. Transmission is from infected animals or more rarely via human-to-human contact.  Clinical features include acute fever, malaise and possible organ involvement.  Serious complications include pneumonia, infective endocarditis and central nervous system (CNS) infection.  Treatment involves antibiotic dual/triple therapy under guidance from microbiology.  Prevention – many countries have good surveillance programmes and livestock vaccination.  Most patients recover fully, especially if compliant with the antibiotic regimen. Mortality is low, but there is a higher mortality risk if brucella infective endocarditis occurs. Epidemiology  Rare in the United Kingdom (UK) (incidence approximately 0.3 in 1 million per annum).  Endemic in countries with lower socio-economic status (where incidence is approximately more than 1 in 1000 per annum in some).  Higher risk areas include the Middle East, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Turkey, North Africa, Central Asia and Central/South America.  Mainly an occupational or travel-related disease in countries where good control measures are in place (disease surveillance/vaccination of livestock). Aetiology  Many Brucella species exist, of which all are Gramnegative intracellular bacteria.  Most common species causing human illness:  Brucella melitensis  Brucella abortus  Brucella suis  Brucella canis.  Bacterial reservoir – animals, mostly cattle (eg sheep, goats, cows, pigs).  Most common transmission is via infected unpasteurised milk.

DR. JAM  Other forms of transmission from infected animals:  ingesting raw/undercooked meat  direct contact via broken skin/mucous membranes or inhalation of bodily fluids (mostly occurs from inhalation of contaminated faeces).  Human-to-human transmission, possible but rare, via:  infected blood products/breast milk/bone marrow  sexual contact  perinatal/transplacental exposure.  From time to time outbreaks do occur, even in well-controlled areas and often can be isolated to individual dairies. Pathophysiology  Following inoculation, Brucella invades nearby mucosa.  The bacteria then spread via the lymphatic system to the lymph nodes followed by haematogenous spread to the reticuloendothelial system.  The immune response alone is not able to combat Brucella infection for many reasons, eg the organism is able to multiply fast in phagocytes and nonphagocytic cells and doesn’t produce a macrophage response, thus reducing T-cell response.  Immunity following infection is not adequate and people can be re-infected.  Incubation period varies from days to months.  Clinical Presentation  Note, some patients are asymptomatic.  Variable onset of illness (1–2 or > 7 days).  The symptoms can be acute, chronic or even relapsing following treatment.  The infection can also be localised or systemic.  Pyrexia is common.  Non-specific flu-like symptoms including sweating, tiredness, myalgia.  Joint involvement – arthritis/arthralgia, common.  Possible lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.  Epididymo-orchitis or urinary symptoms possible.  Rarer:  pneumonia  cardiac involvement (eg endocarditis)  central or peripheral nervous system involvement  jaundice  skin rashes  septic arthritis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  other causes of pyrexia of unknown origin, eg tuberculosis, malaria, lymphoma, human immunodeficiency virus  other causes acute arthritis, eg rheumatoid, septic joint, gout  infective endocarditis  septic arthritis, with another causative agent  pneumonia  CNS infection, with another causative agent  lymphoma  other causes of epididymo-orchitis, eg mumps.  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis  Diagnosis is based on the history of risk factors and laboratory confirmation.  Travel and/or occupational history is especially pertinent.  It is also important to ensure close contacts are not infected. Investigation  Laboratory confirmation:  Brucella detected in blood cultures or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample, or antibody testing  note – antibody testing is often used in areas with fewer resources.  Bloods – variable pattern of white cell count (WCC) abnormalities; liver function tests– mild elevation of transaminases indicating an inflammatory response.  Chest X-ray showing pneumonia.  X-ray of affected joints – may show inflammatory destruction.  Lumbar puncture might be needed if signs of CNS infection.  Joint aspirate or further bone imaging might be used to exclude other causes of septic arthritis.  A liver biopsy may be needed to exclude other causes of hepatomegaly.  Bone marrow biopsy often used when uncertain of diagnosis (ie when investigating pyrexia of unknown origin).  Management  A long course of dual or triple antibiotic therapy is required.  Disease notification to Public Health England.  Regular monitoring – to ensure medication compliance, symptom resolution, assess for complications.  Specialist involvement if in pregnancy and in those < 8 years old; no gold standard of treatment exists.  Specialist involvement if specific systems involved, eg cardiology if causing endocarditis.

DR. JAM Non-pharmacological Prevention  Animal control – disease surveillance, vaccination.  Avoiding unpasteurised milk and its products.  Travelling – avoid contact with farm and wild animals in endemic areas.  Avoid raw and undercooked meat.  Animal workers – wear protective clothing and cover open skin.  Possible for secondary prevention with antibiotics for postexposure prophylaxis. Pharmacological  Choice of therapy to be discussed with microbiology consultant. Antibiotic choice Notes PO doxycycline 6 weeks + IM streptomycin 2–3 weeks Most effective therapy, but more costly and difficult for compliance as IM Or PO quinolone (eg ofloxacin 6 weeks) + PO rifampicin 6 weeks Quinolone combination with rifampicin better tolerated in patients Or PO doxycycline 6 weeks + PO rifampicin 6 weeks  Prognosis  Most patients recover fully, especially if compliant with antibiotic regimen.  Mortality is low; higher risk if brucella infective endocarditis.  Risks in pregnancy – spontaneous abortion, intrauterine fetal death, prematurity and congenital infection.  Other  Note that Brucella spp. have been previously used in bioterrorism.  Interesting resource – Public Health England. Brucellosis: factsheet for veterinary exposure. 2017. Available  In the UK, infection in animals is legally required to be reported to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.  Symptoms of Brucella infection in livestock

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Cattle Abortions Premature calf birth Sheep and goats Abortions Swollen udders Swollen testicles ‘Nervousness’ Fever C.Difficile And Pseudomembranous Colitis Pseudomembranous colitis is an acute exudative colitis that is most commonly associated with toxins produced by the overgrowth of Clostridium difficile.  Overview Key Facts  Pseudomembranous colitis is an acute exudative colitis that is most commonly associated with toxins produced by the overgrowth of Clostridium difficile (C.difficile).  The condition is precipitated by broad spectrum antibiotic use disrupting normal gut flora, and is more common in elderly or chronically ill patients in hospital.  The condition is a major healthcare problem and accounts for up to 25% of all hospital acquired diarrhoea cases associated with antibiotic use.  The most common causative agents include:  ampicillin  cephalosporins  clindamycin  carbapenems  fluroquinolones.  Patient-to-patient spread in hospital is common through the faecal-oral route.  Signs and symptoms of C.difficile infection vary depending on severity, ranging from asymptomatic carrier status to severe pseudomembranous colitis which may be associated with severe and copious diarrhoea which may be bloody, with associated fever and abdominal pain.  Treatment depends on severity of C.difficile infection and may include rehydration and replacement of electrolytes, removal or change of antibiotics, oral vancomycin or metronidazole, and in severe cases may require surgical intervention.  Pseudomembranous colitis is associated with significant morbidity and mortality levels; appropriate and limited

DR. JAM antibiotic prescribing as well as rapid detection and management of the condition as it develops plays a significant role in reducing this. Epidemiology  The condition is a major healthcare problem and accounts for up to 25% of all hospital acquired diarrhoea cases associated with antibiotic use.  The mortality rate of C.difficile infection in the elderly is up to 25%. Aetiology  Overgrowth of Clostridium difficile, which is precipitated by broad spectrum antibiotics.  Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the normal bowel flora.  Most common causative agents are:  ampicillin  cephalosporins  clindamycin  carbapenems  fluroquinolones.  Patient-to-patient spread in hospital is common through the faecal-oral route  Risk factors for developing the condition include:  increasing age  long duration of hospital care/long-term care facilities  immunocompromise  prolong antibiotic courses  presence of co-morbidities. Pathophysiology  Clostridium difficile is a gram-positive, anaerobic, sporeforming rod that produces toxin A and B.  Toxin A and B cause an inflammatory response in the large intestine leading to vascular permeability and pseudomembrane formation.  The incubation period is 2-3 days.  Spores are implicated in infection spread and may persist for months.  Spread is via the faeco-oral route.  Clinical Presentation  Watery diarrhoea (may be bloody), which may be severe and debilitating.  Abdominal pain.  Fever.  Abdominal tenderness.  Note mild C.difficile infection may be self-limiting with mild symptoms, in some cases the patient may be an asymptomatic carrier.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Other infective causes of diarrhoea (gastroenteritis, salmonellia, cholera, etc).  Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).  Ulcerative colitis.  Crohn’s disease.  Diverticular disease.  Acute abdomen.  Diagnosis/Investigation  History and examination.  FBC (elevated WCC) and U&E.  Stool guaiac (faecal occult blood test).  Stool PCR, stool immunoassay for glutamate dehydrogenase.  Stool immunoassay for toxins A and B.  Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy – characteristic plaques are evident in around 50% of patients.  Imaging such as abdominal films or CT may be used to detect complications (ie toxic megacolon or perforation). Colonoscopy image of colon with PMC due to Clostridium difficile infection:  Management Assess the severity of infection (defined as per Public health England 2013):

DR. JAM  Mild  no increase in white cell count (WCC)  typically associated with less than three episodes of loose stools (defined as loose enough to take the shape of the container used to sample it) per day.  Moderate  increased WCC (but less than 15 × 109/l)  typically associated with 3–5 loose stools per day.  Severe  WCC greater than 15 × 109/l  an acutely increased serum creatinine concentration (greater than 50% increase above baseline)  a temperature higher than 38.5°C  evidence of severe colitis (abdominal or radiological signs).  Life-threatening  hypotension  partial or complete ileus  toxic megacolon  computerised tomography (CT) evidence of severe disease  Note that C.difficile is only treated when it causes diarrhoea.  Patients with severe or life-threatening infection require admission (if not already in hospital).  Discontinue antibiotics or change to an antibiotic that is less likely to cause the condition.  Adopt infection control.  Oral or IV fluid as required and address any electrolyte imbalance.  Oral vancomycin or metronidazole is first line pharmacological therapy, or fidaxomicin (associated with lower rates of recurrence) for 10-14 days.  Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), which contains C.difficile antitoxin is recommended as an appropriate adjunct to antibiotics in relapsing and severe C.difficile colitis.  Faecal microbiota transplantation may be a treatment option.  Surgery may be required for cases of acute severe colitis.  Close monitoring of FBC, CRP, albumin and electrolytes is required.  C.diffile infection is a notifiable disease and should be reported to Public Health as per local protocols.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  The condition is associated with prolonged hospital stays and can cause severe debility.  Complications include:  dehydration  electrolyte imbalance  low albumin levels  acute kidney injury  toxic megacolon  perforation  hypotension  sepsis  in hospitalised patients, the condition is also a significant cause of mortality, especially in frailer patients or those with significant co-morbidities.  In patients who are relatively healthy, there is often a good response to treatment, especially when management is initiated early. Cellulitis Skin infections can be superficial (erysipelas), spread to subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis) or infect deep subcutaneous tissue and fascia (necrotising fasciitis).  Overview Key Facts  Skin infections can be superficial (erysipelas), spread to subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis) or infect deep subcutaneous tissue and fascia (necrotising fasciitis).  Cellulitis is an acute skin infection affecting both the dermis and the subcutaneous tissue, caused by microorganisms such as Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus gaining entry due to breaks in the skin barrier.  The area affected is usually warm, erythematous, swollen and painful and may blister or have fluid-filled bullae.  Erysipelas can be differentiated from cellulitis by an elevated and sharp border.  The infection can affect any area of skin but commonly affects the legs.  Patients may become systemically unwell, with pyrexia, rigours, nausea and vomiting.  Risk factors for developing cellulitis include skin trauma (cuts/bites/burns), ulceration, previous history of cellulitis, lymphoedema and obesity.  Diagnosis is usually clinical, but swab cultures may be taken to confirm diagnosis and guide management.

DR. JAM  Management depends on the severity and may require admission for intravenous (IV) antibiotics; oral antibiotics (usually flucloxacillin) may be used if the patient is systemically well.  Most episodes of cellulitis respond well to antibiotic treatment.  Complications of cellulitis are rare but can include necrotising fasciitis, sepsis and persistent leg ulceration. Epidemiology  Cellulitis incidence rates range from 0.2 to 24.6 per 1000 population.  An episode of cellulitis significantly increases the risk of recurrence. Aetiology  Risk factors include:  previous cellulitis infection  skin trauma (burns, bites, cuts)  lymphoedema  venous insufficiency  previous vein surgery  ulceration  pregnancy  obesity. Pathophysiology  Cellulitis is an acute skin infection affecting both the dermis and the subcutaneous tissue.  The condition is most often caused by micro-organisms such as Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus gaining entry due to breaks in the skin barrier.  Less commonly, the infection may be caused by:  Pseudomonas aeruginosa:  hot tubs  sponges  nail puncture.  Vibrio vulnificus:  saltwater.  Aeromonas hydrophila:  freshwater.  Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae:  butchers  vets  fish handlers.  Mycobacterium marinum:  aquarium handlers.  Pasteurella multocida:
