JAM Carbuncle Large, red and painful lumps Pus Non-infective causes to consider:  deep vein thrombosis  septic arthritis  acute gout  thrombophlebitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis can often be confirmed with history and examination.  Other tests may include:  swab for culture  skin biopsy  white cell count (WCC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP)  ultrasound to detect potential underlying abscess.  The Eron classification can be used to grade severity. The Eron classification for cellulitis: Class I No systemic symptoms and no comorbidities Class II Systemically unwell or comorbidity Class III Severe systemic symptoms (tachycardia/hypotension) or unstable comorbidities Class IV Severe infection, eg necrotising fasciitis

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Carbuncle:  Management  The Eron classification can be used to guide management.  Admit to hospital if systemic symptoms or severe infection (usually class II or above).  Also consider specialist referral or admission if:  infection is close to the eyes or nose  could be caused by uncommon organisms (ie exposure to waterborne organisms or infection caught outside the UK)  the patient is not responding to oral treatment or has lymphangitis  cannot tolerate oral antibiotics  if there could be associated complications such as septic arthritis or osteomyelitis.  All other class I cases in adults can be managed in primary care with:  analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen)  antibiotics (as per the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommendations):  flucloxacillin 500–1000 mg four times daily for 5–7 days  if flucloxacillin is unsuitable or the patient is allergic to penicillin, prescribe:  clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 5–7 days or  doxycycline 200 mg on the first day then 100 mg once daily, for a total of 5–7 days or  erythromycin (in pregnancy) 500 mg four times daily for 5–7 days  co-amoxiclav, or clarithromycin plus metronidazole, is used if the infection is near the eyes and the patient does not require admission

DR. JAM  amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily is used instead if the patient has associated lymphoedema  leg elevation (if the leg is affected)  advice regarding adequate fluid intake  advice to return if the infection is not responding to treatment or spreading  review in 2–3 days.  Class II/III/IV:  requires hospital admission  intravenous (IV) antibiotics (usually flucloxacillin, or clindamycin if allergic to penicillin)  fluids (IV if oral fluid intake is not tolerated)  analgesia and elevation of the affected area  demarcate area.  General measures also include addressing/managing risk factors and underlying causes.  Prognosis  Most episodes of cellulitis respond well to antibiotic treatment without complications.  Complications of cellulitis are rare but can include necrotising fasciitis, sepsis and persistent leg ulceration.  Cellulitis is more likely to recur in patients who have had a previous episode, with each recurrent episode increasing the risk of further recurrence.  Recurrent episodes are associated with longer hospital admissions. Chlamydia Genital chlamydia infection is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the United Kingdom, predominantly affecting those under 25.  Overview Key Facts  Genital chlamydia infection is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) in the United Kingdom (UK), predominantly affecting those under 25.  It is caused by the bacteria chlamydia trachomatis.  Infection can be classed as uncomplicated (lower genital tract only) or complicated (ascending infection causing epididymoorchitis or pelvic inflammatory disease).  70% of women and 50% of men are asymptomatic.  Signs and symptoms if symptomatic include:  dysuria

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  abnormal/purulent discharge  pelvic pain  dyspareunia.  Diagnosis is via endocervical/vulvovaginal swab in women or first-pass urine in men.  Patients should be referred to genito-urinary medicine (GUM) clinic for education, testing for other STIs and partner notification.  First line therapy is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days – azithromycin/erythromycin are alternatives.  Patients should be advised to avoid sexual contact until they/their partners have completed their course of treatment (and for 7 days after if taking azithromycin).  Patients should be re-tested 3-6 months after the course of treatment is complete to check for re-infection.  Possible complications of untreated chlamydia include:  pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)  epididymo-orchitis  sub/infertility  reactive arthritis  conjunctivitis  complications in pregnancy/neonates. Epidemiology  Genital chlamydia infection is the most common bacterial STI in the UK.  Young adults < 25 years account for around 70% of cases.  Studies have estimated infection rates of 1.5-10% in people aged 15-24.  The National Chlamydia Screening Programme recommends annual screening for all sexually active people < 25 years old (or more frequently if they change their partner).  Risk factors for chlamydia infection:  age < 25 years  new sexual partner  more than one sexual partner in the last year  lack of consistent condom use  social deprivation. Aetiology  Caused by the obligate intracellular bacteria, Chlamydia trachomatis.  Infection is primarily due to penetrative sex but can occur via autoinoculation or splash from genital fluids. Pathophysiology  In men, it infects the urethra. In women, it infects the endocervix/urethra.  It can also affect: conjunctiva, rectum and nasopharynx.  It is an uncomplicated infection if it has not ascended to the upper genital tract.

DR. JAM  A chlamydial infection is termed complicated when the infection has spread to the upper genital tract causing PID in women or epididymo-orchitis in men.  Clinical Presentation  At least 70% of women and 50% of men with a chlamydia infection are asymptomatic.  Symptoms/signs for women when symptomatic include:  post-coital/inter-menstrual bleeding  purulent vaginal discharge  mucopurulent cervical discharge  deep dyspareunia  pelvic pain/tenderness  inflamed or friable cervix  dysuria  cervical motion tenderness.  Symptoms/signs for men when symptomatic include:  dysuria  urethral discharge  urethral discomfort  epididymo-orchitis  reactive arthritis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis includes:  gonorrhoea  urinary tract infection  candida albicans  bacterial vaginosis  trichomonas vaginalis  endometriosis  pregnancy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Samples are taken for testing differently in men and women:  women - endocervical or vulvovaginal swab (speculum exam) or first-void urine sample  men - first-void urine sample or urethral swab.  Asymptomatic people who should be tested for chlamydia include:  sexual partners of those who have tested positive for chlamydia  all sexually active people < 25 years annually  all people with concerns about sexual exposure – if exposure < 2 weeks ago, test and then re-test in 2 weeks’ time  < 25 years and completed treatment for chlamydia in last 3 months

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  people with 2 or more sexual partners in the last 12 months  all women seeking termination of pregnancy  all men and women attending GUM clinics.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Contact tracing – encouraging people who test positive to get in touch with any partners themselves or provide details to healthcare providers to enable contact tracing.  Treatment should be initiated promptly after a positive test for chlamydia or patients have symptoms strongly suggestive of chlamydia.  Ideally the person should be referred to a GUM clinic for treatment and screening of other STIs – this also allows partner notification.  Patients should be educated and given written information about:  what chlamydia is/how it is transmitted  the importance of assessing and treating their sexual contacts  that sexual intercourse (including: genital, oral and anal sex – even with a condom) should be avoided until both them and their sexual contacts have completed their course of treatment.  if azithromycin has been taken, advise additional sexual abstinence for 7 days after treatment (or until sexual contacts have completed their treatment).  Repeat testing should be offered to all people < 25 years, 3-6 months after treatment is complete to check for re-infection.  Repeat testing should also be considered for people > 25 years who are at high risk of re-infection. Pharmacological  1st line = Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days:  or if contra-indicated, azithromycin (1 g OD followed by 500 mg OD for 2 days) or erythromycin (500 mg BD for 10-14 days).  In women who are pregnant/breastfeeding, one of:  Azithromycin 1 g one-off dose + 500 mg OD for 2 days  Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 7 days  Erythromycin 500 mg QDS for 7 days.  A test of cure (TOC) not usually necessary unless patient is pregnant – test 3 weeks after treatment completed.  Prognosis  Untreated infection may persist or spontaneously resolve – clearance more likely with a longer duration of untreated infection (< 50% of infections resolve within 12 months).  PID (including endometritis and salpingitis) occurs in up to 16% of women with untreated chlamydia infections.  PID increases the risk of:

DR. JAM  pubal infertility – risk 1-20% after PID  prolonged exposure by persistent infection or frequent re-infection are major risk factors for tubal tissue damage  ectopic pregnancy  chronic pelvic pain.  Chlamydia in pregnancy associated with:  increased risk of premature rupture of membranes, preterm delivery and low birth weight  intra-partum pyrexia and late post-partum endometritis  neonatal infection: eyes, lungs, nasopharynx and genitals.  Other  Other complications of chlamydia infection include:  epididymo-orchitis - pain, swelling or inflammation of the epididymis and/or testicles – can result from untreated chlamydia infection in men  adult conjunctivitis - can occur via auto-inoculation or splash from genital fluids  sexually acquired reactive arthritis – more common in men. Clostridium Botulinum Clostridium botulinum is a Gram-positive, anaerobic bacillus.  Overview Key Facts  Clostridium botulinum is a Gram-positive, anaerobic bacillus.  It produces a neurotoxin responsible for botulism – a neuroparalysis characterised by cranial nerve palsies, oculobulbar weakness and symmetrical flaccid paralysis.  Diagnosed by detection of the toxin in bodily fluids.  Treatment consists of supportive care and administration of antitoxin. Patients should have their vital capacity, oxygen saturation and inspiratory force monitored in an intensive care setting.  Long-term complications include fatigue, weakness and dyspnoea on exertion.  Respiratory dysfunction is a potential complication and may occur due to upper airway obstruction or diaphragmatic muscle weakness.  The mortality rate is 3–5% overall and < 1% in infant botulism. Epidemiology  Spores are ubiquitous in the soil worldwide and are found in agricultural products and the intestinal tract of animals, including fish.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Extremely rare in the United Kingdom (UK), more common in the United States of America (USA).  Men and women affected equally.  Wound botulism is the most common form in the UK, whereas infant botulism is the most common in the USA.  Food-borne botulism is most commonly seen in outbreaks.  Intravenous (IV) drug users are at particular risk of wound botulism. Aetiology  Clostridium botulinum exists as a spore until environmental conditions are optimal to allow germination.  There are three naturally occurring forms of botulism:  food-borne botulism – ingestion of preformed toxin in contaminated foods, most commonly home-canned fruits and vegetables and smoked or preserved meats and fish.  wound botulism – spores germinate within contaminated wounds.  infant botulism – ingestion of spores (commonly from honey or soil) which germinate in the intestinal tract and release neurotoxin.  Inhalation botulism is another form, but does not occur naturally and is caused by the release of the toxin in aerosol, such as bioterrorism.  There are seven distinct neurotoxins produced by the organism and human disease is caused by toxins A, B and E. Pathophysiology  Botulism occurs from entry of the toxin into the systemic circulation via the mucosa or a break in the skin.  Once in the circulation, the toxin is transported to the presynaptic nerve terminal of peripheral and cranial nerves.  The toxin is a metalloproteinase that cleaves SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction.  This prevents the fusion of transmitter-containing vesicles with the presynaptic membrane and therefore inhibits the release of acetylcholine.  This results in paralysis or autonomic dysfunction.  Clinical Presentation  All three types of botulism present with neuroparalysis, including:  blurred vision, diplopia and ptosis secondary to cranial nerve lll, lV and Vl palsies  dysarthria and dysphagia secondary to oculobulbar weakness or cranial nerve lX, X and Xll palsies  oculobulbar weakness can also contribute to blurred vision and diplopia  symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes  in infants, there may be hypotonia, feeding difficulties and weakened cry

DR. JAM  urinary retention, constipation, postural hypotension and dry mouth secondary to autonomic dysfunction.  Food-borne and infantile botulism are associated with GI symptoms, such as cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.  Fever is characteristically absent.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  Guillain–Barré syndrome  myasthenia gravis  Lambert–Eaton syndrome  toxicity, eg magnesium, shellfish.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bioassay for botulinum toxin in samples from serum, vomit, gastric secretions, stool or foods.  Culture of samples may be performed in food-borne or infantile botulism.  Electromyography (EMG) testing may be considered and is useful for investigating other differentials such as Lambert– Eaton syndrome. In botulism, sensory nerve studies are normal, but muscle action potentials are significantly reduced.  Management  Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment and patients should have their vital capacity, oxygen saturation and inspiratory force monitored in an intensive care setting.  Mechanical ventilation is appropriate in any patient with upper airway compromise.  Rapid administration of the antitoxin is essential, of which there are several types:  intravenous (IV) human botulism immunoglobulin is preferred in infants  horse-derived heptavalent botulism antitoxin is preferred in adults.  Gastric lavage may be attempted in adults with food-borne botulism if exposure was recent.  Surgical debridement is performed in wound botulism.  Prognosis  Respiratory dysfunction is a potential complication and may occur due to upper airway obstruction or diaphragmatic muscle weakness.  Mortality rate is 3–5% overall and < 1% in infant botulism.  Full recovery takes weeks to months.  Long-term complications include fatigue, weakness and dyspnoea on exertion.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Cryptosporidiosis Cryptosporidiosis is a zoonotic parasitic infection caused by Cryptosporidium spp.  Overview Key Facts  Cryptosporidiosis is a zoonotic parasitic infection caused by Cryptosporidium spp.  It is a common cause of gastroenteritis and the most common cause of infective diarrhoea in those with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).  Cryptosporidiosis is contracted from drinking contaminated water or food.  The immunocompetent develop self-limiting gastroenteritis and treatment is usually supportive. No curative agent exists.  In the immunocompromised, it is more likely to cause severe illness with accompanying mortality risk.  Preventative measures are important in reducing transmission. Epidemiology  Cryptosporidiosis occurs worldwide.  In developed countries Cryptosporidium spp. cause occasional outbreaks.  Cryptosporidium spp. are widespread in developing countries.  Common in those with HIV or after travel.  The most common age group affected are children < 5 years age.  Difficult to present epidemiological figures because of the range of symptoms and low presenting numbers. Aetiology  Cryptosporidiosis is a parasitic infection resulting from infection by any member of the Cryptosporidium genus. C. hominis and C. parvum are the most common identified pathogens.  Transmission is from ingesting water, eating food or oral contact with objects contaminated with the parasitic oocysts. This can happen from contaminated drinking water supplies and in other sites, such as swimming pools.  Less than or equal to a third of those infected are asymptomatic, but still, excrete cysts in bowel movements. Pathophysiology  Following ingestion, the parasite enters cells of the small intestine and releases oocytes as part of its life cycle which are then excreted allowing further transmission.  It is unknown as to what exact mechanism causes diarrhoea.  Oocytes shed for a mean period of seven days.

DR. JAM  Chronic infection occurs in the immunocompromised as the immune system cannot combat the parasite.  Low infective doses (via ingestion) are needed to cause illness.  Cryptosporidium spp. are resistant to usual water-treatment strategies, eg chlorination.  Clinical Presentation  Duration of illness is 1–2 weeks, typically (can last months in the immunocompromised).  Symptoms:  diarrhoea (likely loose, watery)  abdominal pain  pyrexia (low grade)  anorexia  nausea and vomiting.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include other causes infective gastroenteritis, eg E. coli, Shigella spp., viral.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis based on clinical history, the presence of risk factors and laboratory confirmation. Laboratory confirmation  Stool microscopy detecting Cryptosporidium oocytes.  Stool presence of Cryptosporidium antigens.  Stool/other tissue specimens detecting Cryptosporidium DNA via PCR.  Management  Treatment aims to reduce diarrhoea duration, avoid the development of complications and remove the parasite.  No agent is fully effective against the parasite; thus, prevention is the most important measure.  In those with HIV, effective antiretroviral treatment reduces symptom severity. Non-pharmacological  Supportive, eg fluids, analgesia. As per usual diarrhoeal illness.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pharmacological  No agent is fully effective in removing the parasite.  Nitazoxanide reduces parasitic load and can be used.  Prognosis  In most, cryptosporidiosis self-limiting illness.  Can lead to mortality in infants and the immunocompromised.  Possible complications:  reactive arthritis  long-lasting symptoms  post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome  death possibly secondary to diarrhoea, especially in children  spread in chronic cryptosporidiosis – gastric epithelium, biliary tract, the liver, pancreas and respiratory system.  Prevention:  good hand hygiene  boiling drinking water >1 minute or using a personal drinking filter  children with cryptosporidiosis should not go to school/nursery  food handlers and those working with risk groups need to abstain from work until 2 days post-diarrhoea  not to use swimming pools until 2 weeks after diarrhoea ends. Cytomegalovirus Cytomegalovirus is a common worldwide infection with high levels of seropositivity.  Overview Key Facts  Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common worldwide infection with high levels of seropositivity.  It causes severe illness in the immunocompromised and neonates, but mostly asymptomatic or mild ‘infectious mononucleosis’ type illness in the immunocompetent.  May lead to severe illness in most bodily systems.  Congenital infection risks hearing, neurological and cognitive function.  In the immunocompromised, it may lead to morbidity and mortality.  Treatment and prevention are possible with antivirals. Antivirals needed for all those with immunocompromise or severe congenital infection.  CMV infection is self-limiting and mild in the immunocompetent.

DR. JAM  Congenital infection can cause sensorineural deafness, learning disability, sight problems and developmental delay. Epidemiology  High rates of seropositivity worldwide.  The most common cause of non-genetic sensorineural hearing loss in children.  Seropositivity common, studies quote 30–98% positive in the worldwide population, with the higher rates in developing countries (eg high figures in Brazil, lower in Germany).  Two peaks of primary infection – under age 3 and in adolescents (the latter peak thought to be due to sexual activity).  Approximately 1% of all neonates in developed countries have CMV infection, with approximately 5–10% of these being symptomatic.  In developing countries, the occurrence of CMV in live births is approximately 6%. Aetiology  Transmission, via body fluids/tissues:  blood, blood product transfusion  transplantation from CMV-positive to CMV-seronegative recipient  sexual contact  saliva  transplacental (vertical transmission following maternal latent reactivation or primary infection; congenital infection more likely in primary infection).  Vulnerable groups for severe infection – neonates and the immunocompromised.  Transplant recipients are especially at risk as they may contract CMV from the received material and develop a severe infection due to the immunosuppressants needed to counteract rejection.  Those with HIV are most at risk if CD4+ count is less than 50. Pathophysiology  Human CMV is a β-herpes virus (human β-herpes virus type 5).  Following primary infection, the virus develops latency.  Latency sites – endothelial cells of arterial walls, T cells.  Reactivation in the immunocompetent is normally asymptomatic with active viral shedding at this point.  In the immunocompromised, primary infection or reactivation may cause disseminated and thus severe infection.  Due to the variety of CMV strains that exist, someone can be reinfected, producing a secondary primary infection, but these tend to be milder.  Severe infection is mostly associated with immunocompromised states impacting on CD4 count (eg transplant recipients, HIV, older age).

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation In the immunocompetent  Majority asymptomatic:  possible, ‘infectious-mononucleosis type syndrome’ with – tiredness, pyrexia, lymphadenopathy, mild hepatitis, non-typical lymphocytosis  associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome. In the immunocompromised  Many possible presentations and complications:  hepatitis  GI involvement – mainly gastritis, oesophagitis and/or ulceration  renal – cause of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or cystitis  pancreatitis  chest – pneumonia, pneumonitis  ocular– uveitis/retinitis  CNS – encephalitis, abscess  primary adrenal insufficiency, due to adrenitis and/or adrenal necrosis  cutaneous – pustles/necrotic ulcers.  Note:  might be referred to as an ‘AIDs- defining illness’  onset post-transplant normally weeks–months. Associated symptoms  Symptoms include:  tiredness  fever  loose stools  nausea, vomiting, reflux, dysphagia  eye – floaters, reduced acuity  skin lesions  swelling  jaundice. Severe complications  Neurological – Guillain–Barré syndrome, meningoencephalitis.  Cardiac – pericarditis.  Haem – haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia.  GI ulceration. Congenital infection in neonates

DR. JAM  Symptoms:  lethargy  microcephaly  hearing loss  abnormal head lag  poor muscular tone  abnormal motor function  hepatosplenomegaly  skin – petechiae, purpura.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  infective hepatitides, other causes, eg Epstein–Barr virus  infective oesophagitis, other causes, eg herpes simplex virus  other infectious lymphadenopathy, eg toxoplasmosis  infectious mononucleosis  HIV seroconversion illness  other viral illnesses.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis tends to be due to clinical suspicion and CMV detection. Investigative confirmation  CMV DNA isolation from PCR assay of tissue samples (eg possible from blood, serum, plasma, urine, saliva, amniotic fluid).  CMV antibodies – IgM (indicating primary infection), IgG (latent immunity).  Culture – possible from tissue swabs of patients with active infection. Investigation  First-line: Full blood count In the immunocompetent – raised WCC with abnormal differential In the immunocompromised – low Hb, low WCC, low platelets In neonates – low platelets Urea and electrolytes Not typically abnormal, unless causing renal damage Liver function tests Raised transferases

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Bone profile If GI involvement may cause raised ALP  Further investigation may be based on system-specific enquiries: Chest X-ray Pneumonia Gastroscopy or colonoscopy Inflammation Ulceration CMV isolated from biopsy CT chest If causing pneumonitis: Nodules Alveoli involvement  Serum viral load measurement – used to monitor treatment effectiveness.  Management  In the immunocompetent antivirals are not needed  Antiviral drug resistance does occur and this needs to be monitored for. Non-pharmacological  Supportive in mild infection in the immunocompetent, eg analgesia, adequate hydration.  When hospitalised, isolation needed from other patients with infection control measures utilised.  In neonates, antiviral therapy tends to be used in severe cases only. Prevention  CMV-status assessment in all transplant donors and recipients.  Only giving CMV-negative material to CMV-negative recipients.  Prophylaxis with antivirals if a CMV-positive transplant is given to a CMV-negative recipient.  Barrier contraception.  Handwashing, especially before and after eating and toileting.  Stringent hygiene in the pregnant.  In HIV patients – regular monitoring of immune status (aiming CD4+ > 100), medication selection and adherence. Occasionally antivirals are given to those with CD4+ < 50 to prevent CMV infection.

DR. JAM Pharmacological  Antivirals needed for all those with immunocompromise or severe congenital infection.  Antivirals are the standard treatment of choice; this can reduce infection severity, further deterioration of affected sites and viral load.  Common antivirals of choice are valganciclovir PO or ganciclovir IV; these are given for approximately 1 month.  Route of delivery (PO or IV) dependent on clinical status.  Retinitis – intravitreal antivirals if sight-threatening.  In AIDs – maintenance antiviral therapy may be needed.  Immunoglobulins may be used in combination with antivirals.  Prognosis  Infection self-limiting and mild in the immunocompetent.  CMV-induced hepatitis is normally mild with most recovering fully.  Severe infection may lead to mortality; most deaths from CMV pneumonia.  Congenital infection has the possibility of sensorineural deafness, learning disability, sight problems and developmental delay.  Side-effects of long-term antivirals may contribute to morbidity (eg ganciclovir/valganciclovir can cause bone marrow suppression). Dengue Fever Dengue fever is caused by a virus transmitted by female mosquitoes.  Overview Key Facts  Dengue fever is caused by a virus transmitted by female mosquitoes, most commonly of the species, Aedes aegypti and less commonly by the species Aedes albopictus.  Dengue is endemic in Africa, South-East Asia, the Western Pacific, the Americas and the Eastern Mediterranean.  There has been a significant increase in dengue over the last few decades.  Mosquitoes become infected with dengue when they feed on the blood of an infected person. They are then infected for life and transmit the virus to other humans during subsequent blood meals.  Symptoms include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pains, nausea and vomiting, swollen glands and rash.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  ‘Severe dengue’ may develop after 3–7 days and may cause severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, haematemesis, tachypnoea, bleeding gums fatigue or restlessness.  May be misdiagnosed in up to 50% of cases as symptoms are relatively non-specific and common to most bacterial and viral infections.  Diagnosis is made from blood tests which can be sent for RTPCR (reverse transcriptase PCR), NS1 (a viral protein) and ELISA (detection of IgG and IgM).  IgM is detectable after about 1 week and up until about 12 weeks, and IgG is indicative of past infection and can remain in the blood for many years.  Treatment is symptomatic. Paracetamol can be taken to reduce fever and muscle pains but nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) should be avoided (due to bleeding risk if severe dengue develops).  A vaccine called CYD-TDV or Dengvaxia® is now available for use in several countries but should only be used in people previously infected with dengue, as it can increase the risk of severe dengue in people who are infected for the first time after the vaccination.  There are ongoing efforts to control mosquito populations in affected countries to reduce the transmission of dengue. Epidemiology  There are an estimated 100–400 million cases of dengue each year, which represents a significant increase over the past few decades.  Dengue is endemic in Africa, South-East Asia, the Western Pacific, the Americas and the Eastern Mediterranean.  Asia represents approximately 70% of the global cases.  Dengue is not endemic in the United Kingdom (UK), but 347 cases of dengue were diagnosed in the UK in 2014 in travellers returning from affected countries. Aetiology  The virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family and is transmitted by female mosquitoes, usually of the species Aedes aegypti and less commonly by the species Aedes albopictus.  These mosquitoes also carry chikungunya, Zika virus and yellow fever.  There are four serotypes of the virus, known as DENV-1, -2, -3 and -4; infection confers life-long protection against that serotype, but it does not protect against other serotypes in the long term.  Some regions have all four serotypes. Pathophysiology  Mosquitoes become infected with dengue when they feed on the blood of an infected person.  Humans can transmit dengue to mosquitoes around 2 days before symptoms develop until approximately 2 days after the fever resolves.  The virus replicates in the gut of the mosquito and disseminates to the salivary glands.

DR. JAM  The mosquito is then a vector for the disease and remains infectious for life, infecting humans during subsequent blood meals.  There is a very small rate of vertical transmission.  Dengue in pregnancy can lead to premature birth, a low birth weight infant and fetal distress.  Clinical Presentation  The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests that dengue should be suspected when a fever of > 40°C is accompanied by two of the following:  headache  pain behind the eyes  muscle or joint pains  nausea  vomiting  swollen glands  rash.  ‘Severe dengue’ can occur 3–7 days after the onset of the illness and is a potentially fatal complication leading to multiple organ failure.  Signs of severe dengue include:  severe abdominal pain  persistent vomiting  haematemesis  tachypnoea  bleeding gums  fatigue  restlessness.  Differential Diagnosis  Dengue is often misdiagnosed, possibly in as many as 50% of cases, due to the fact that the symptoms are common to most viral illnesses and infections.  It may be commonly mistaken for other diseases, including (but not limited to):  other mosquito-borne diseases such as chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika virus  malaria  influenza  meningitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is made from blood tests:  RT-PCR (reverse transcriptase PCR)  NS1 (a protein produced by the virus)  ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) detection of IgM and IgG anti-dengue antibodies:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  IgM is detectable after about 1 week and up until about 12 weeks  IgG is indicative of past infection and can remain in the blood for years.  Management  There is no specific treatment and management remains symptomatic.  Paracetamol can be used to reduce fever but NSAIDs should be avoided due to the risk of haemorrhage if severe dengue develops.  Prognosis  A vaccine for dengue fever known as CYD-TDV or Dengvaxia® is now approved for use in several countries. It is efficacious in people who have previously been infected with dengue but may cause severe dengue if a patient becomes infected with dengue for the first time after vaccination.  The WHO recommends pre-vaccination screening for antibodies and vaccination of people who have had a previous infection only.  Other  The key to reducing dengue infections and other mosquitoborne diseases is to attempt to control the mosquito population in affected countries.  This includes:  reducing mosquito breeding  increasing the use of personal protection such as clothing that covers more exposed skin and the use of repellents  community education  reacting to outbreaks by using insecticides  monitoring of mosquito populations  ongoing research. E. Coli Infection E. coli infection is caused by the bacterium Escherichia coli, resulting in symptoms like diarrhoea, abdominal pain and sometimes severe complications.  Overview Key Facts  Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium.  E. coli is a commensal organism that colonises the gastrointestinal tract.

DR. JAM  Virulence factors include lipopolysaccharide, K1-capsular polysaccharide, shiga-like toxin, heat-stable or -labile enterotoxins and P fimbriae.  There are five common strains of E. coli that cause most of the clinical presentations:  enteroinvasive (EIEC)  enteroaggregative (EAEC)  enterotoxigenic (ETEC)  enteropathogenic (EPEC)  enterohaemorrhagic (EHEC).  Most cases of E. coli infection are foodborne.  It is the most common cause of urinary tract infection in women.  Diagnosis can be made from analysing stool culture.  Treatment is supportive. It involves rehydration and correction of electrolyte imbalance. Antibiotics are mainly used to treat traveller’s diarrhoea, which is commonly caused by ETEC. Epidemiology  Immunocompromised, infants, older people and alcohol users are at increased risk of infection.  Commonly found in developing regions of the world with poor sanitation.  Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) is a frequent cause of infant diarrhoeal infections. It commonly affects children aged below 2 years.  Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is a common cause of community-acquired and traveller’s diarrhoea:  approximately 380 000 deaths occur annually in children in developing countries and 210 million cases.  Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) is a less common cause of diarrhoeal illness compared with other pathological forms of E. coli:  most outbreaks are due to the consumption of undercooked meat or raw leafy vegetables. Aetiology  E. coli is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium.  Indole positive, and ferments glucose, lactose and sorbitol.  This bacterium is a commensal organism that normally exists in the intestine.  Within a few hours of birth, this commensal organism colonises the gastrointestinal tract.  Infection by E. coli occurs through ingestion, usually via contaminated food or water. Most cases are therefore foodborne.  The most common cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in women.  E. coli is the most common cause of traveller’s diarrhoea. Hence a travel history should be taken.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Outbreaks in the past have been due to:  contaminated meat, eg ground beef, spinach or other green leafy vegetables  unpasteurised milk  contaminated food workers, which then spread to others via the faecal–oral route. Pathophysiology Mechanism of virulence factors Presentation Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) Macrophage activation ⇢ widespread release of IL-1, IL-6 and TNFα Bacteraemia ⇢ septic shock K1 capsular polysaccharide Prevents phagocytosis and complement-mediated lysis Neonatal meningitis Pneumonia Verotoxin (shiga-like toxin) Inactivates 60S ribosomal component ⇢ halting protein synthesis ⇢ cell death Phage encoded ⇢ production ⇡ by iron deficiency Bloody gastroenteritis HUS Heat-stable or heat-labile enterotoxins Promotes fluid and electrolyte secretion from intestinal epithelium Watery gastroenteritis P fimbriae Allows adhesion to uroepithelium UTI Each E. coli subtype exerts a different pathological response: Toxin and mechanism Clinical features Enteroinvasive (EIEC) Invades intestinal mucosa ⇢ necrosis and inflammation Dysentery D/D ⇢ shigella Enterotoxigenic (ETEC) Adheres to epithelial cells via pili ⇢ plasmid-encoded heatlabile and heat-stable toxins ⇢ no inflammation or invasion Traveller’s diarrhoea ⇢ watery N/V, abdominal pain, fever Developing regions, poor sanitation Enteropathogenic (EPEC) No toxin produced Adheres to apical surface ⇢ flattens villi ⇢ prevents absorption Diarrhoea, usually in children Enterohaemorrhagic (EHEC)

DR. JAM O157:H7 ⇢ MC serotype in the USA Undercooked meat, raw leafy vegetables Shiga-like toxin ⇢ microthrombi on damaged endothelium ⇢ mechanical haemolysis ⇢ haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) ⇢ triad: anaemia thrombocytopenia AKI Dysentery ⇢ toxin alone causes necrosis and inflammation Haemorrhagic, Hamburger's, haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) Peripheral smear ⇢ schistocytes MCC of acute renal failure in children Low ID50 ⇢ 10–100 organisms needed for clinical manifestations Enteroaggregative (EAEC) Adhere to the intestinal mucosa in an aggregative or ‘stackedbrick’ pattern ⇢ do not invade Persistent diarrhoea in infants of developing world and immunosuppressed  Clinical Presentation  Diarrhoea:  most pathogenic subtypes of E. coli cause watery diarrhoea  EHEC infections cause bloody diarrhoea.  Abdominal pain/discomfort.  Volume depletion, eg dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension.  Uncommon symptoms – fever, nausea/vomiting, anorexia, lethargy:  fever lasting beyond 2–3 days is rare  persistent high fever is indicative of potential bacteraemia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  viral gastroenteritis  amoebiasis  non-infectious food poisoning  ulcerative colitis  Crohn’s disease  non-infectious gastrointestinal pathologies.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Stool cultures:  should be sent from patients with:  persistent gastroenteritis-like symptoms  presence of fever or dehydration  bloody diarrhoea.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  positive for pathogenic E. coli species, eg E. coli O157:H7.  FBC/blood film:  E. coli O157:H7 is associated with haemolytic uraemic syndrome (manifests as anaemia and thrombocytopenia, along with schistocytes on blood smear)  anaemia may be due to gastrointestinal blood loss  FBC may show raised WCC and may show low haemoglobin and/or platelets.  Renal function and electrolytes:  raised urea and creatinine  hypokalaemia.  Stool polymerase chain reaction:  EHEC strain may be identified.  Blood cultures:  may be positive if there is E. coli bacteraemia.  Inflammatory markers (CRP and/or erythrocyte sedimentation rate):  may be raised.  Abdominal X-ray:  exclude toxic dilatation  consider it if there is a presence of severe toxicity, ie tachycardia, hypotension, fever ≥ 38°C.  Endoscopy:  exclude other causes of diarrhoea.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Oral rehydration therapy, eg glucose-containing fluids.  Intravenous rehydration therapy in patients who cannot tolerate oral fluids/who have worsening volume depletion/escalating sepsis.  Avoid milk sugars in severe gastroenteritis, due to transient lactose intolerance.  Caffeine should be avoided.  Measures to prevent spread of infection.  E. coli infections generally respond to supportive therapy.  EHEC infection is a notifiable disease. The local health department should be informed. Pharmacological  Bismuth (bismuth subsalicylate).  Antibiotic therapy, eg ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin/norfloxacin/rifaximin/azithromycin:  patients with severe ETEC infection (traveller’s diarrhoea) should be offered antibiotics.  Antimotility agents, eg loperamide, codeine phosphate:

DR. JAM  antimotility agents should not generally be used due to an increased risk of toxic dilatation; self-limiting diarrhoea may eliminate the pathogen effectively.  Prognosis  Most E. coli infections are asymptomatic or mild and selflimiting.  Most patients respond to supportive therapy and recover within 2–5 days.  The majority of deaths are due to volume depletion.  Other  Risk factors of E. coli infection are:  contaminated food products  travel  poor hygiene  contact history (due to faecal–oral contamination).  Complications of E. coli infection:  haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)  bacteraemia  irritable bowel syndrome. Encephalitis Encephalitis is defined as an inflammation of the brain, most commonly caused by viral infection, but can also be due to other pathogens or a primary autoimmune process.  Overview Key Facts  Encephalitis is defined as an inflammation of the brain, most commonly caused by viral infection, but can also be due to other pathogens or a primary autoimmune process.  The condition is relatively uncommon but cases can be severe and even fatal, especially in extremes of age.  The most common organism causing encephalitis in the United Kingdom (UK) is Herpes simplex virus type I, which can be severe in the elderly and particularly in neonates.  Altered behaviour along with features of an acute febrile illness is commonly found.  These symptoms can deteriorate into altered consciousness, seizures and coma.  Diagnosis is often based on clinical and is confirmed with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis along with laboratory testing and neuroimaging.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Acyclovir is commenced for presumed viral encephalitis in the first instance - before plymerase chain reaction (PCR) diagnosis of herpes infection is confirmed. Benzylpenicillin is also often given to cover the possibility of meningitis. Epidemiology  The prevalence of Encephalitis in the UK ranges between 5-8 / 100 000 per year.  Most cases are seen in the extremes of age, ie in children and the elderly population. Aetiology Viral  Herpes Simplex – most common.  Varicella Zoster.  Enterovirus.  Adenovirus.  Parechovirus.  HIV. Bacterial  Mycobacterium Tuberculosis.  Listeria.  Streptococcus Pneumonia.  Neisseria Meningitidis.  Syphilis. Other infective causes  Cryptococcus Neoformans.  Toxoplasma.  Rickettsial.  Fungal. Antibody associated encephalitis  Paraneoplastic.  Non paraneoplastic.  Hashimotos encephalitis.  Steroid responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis.  Clinical Presentation  Patients may initially have flu like symptoms.

DR. JAM  The classical presentation is a triad of fever, headache and altered behaviour/mental status.  Other signs and symptoms incude:  meningeal signs - neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting  aphasia  ataxia  tremors  cranial nerve deficits  focal or generalised seizures  coma.  Neonatal herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) usually presents within 4-11 days after birth. Clinically the symptoms and signs include:  lethargy  poor feeding  irritability  bulging fontanelle  shock  jaundice  purpuric/vesicular rash.  Management  Patients with suspected encephalitis require urgent admission with antibiotic cover (IV/IM benzylpenicillin) given in case of meningitis, as well as IV acyclovir. This should not be delayed by waiting for confirmation of diagnosis.  Broad spectrum antibiotic cover is also added where bacterial infection is suspected.  Other therapy is mainly supportive and may include fluids, antiemetics, sedation and analgesia as required.  Prognosis  Encephalitis is a serious condition with around 70% mortality rate if untreated.  Extremes of age (neonates and the elderly) and immunocompromised are associated with a worse prognosis.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Meningitis.  Lyme Disease.  Whipple’s Disease.  Stroke transient ischaemic attack (TIA).  Cerebral Malaria.  Behçet’s disease.  Syphilis.  Haematological malignancies.  Diagnosis/Investigation Full blood count and blood fill, blood cultures, urea and electrolytes (U&E), LFT, glucose, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and c-reactive protein (CRP).  Computed tomography (CT) to rule out other causes of symptoms and check for raise intracranial pressure which warrants delay of lumbar puncture.  Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis including CSF virology PCR.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan provides detailed imaging for evidence of demyelination.  Electroencephalogram (EEG) is often abnormal. n central nervous system infections: Viral Tuberculous Fungal ormal High/very high Very high –1000 5–500 0–1000 (lymphocytes) 0.5–1.0 (lymphocytes) 1.0–5.0 (lymphocytes) 0.5–2.0 0–66

Filariasis Filariasis is a mosquito-borne tropical disease, causing infection with filarial parasites, which damage the lymphatic system and can cause debilitating lymphoedema.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Filariasis is a mosquito-borne tropical disease, causing infection with filarial parasites, which damage the lymphatic system and can cause debilitating lymphoedema.  It affects countries in Asia, Africa, the Western Pacific, South America and parts of the Caribbean.  Infection is usually acquired in childhood and lymphoedema, elephantiasis and scrotal swelling may not appear until later in life.  Wuchereria bancrofti causes 90% of cases.  It is transmitted by the anopheles or culex mosquito.  Infected mosquitoes transfer filarial larvae to humans when they take a blood meal. Larvae mature and inhabit the lymphatic system; once adult they release microfilariae into the human bloodstream which are then ingested by mosquitoes when they take another blood meal. Microfilariae mature into larvae inside the mosquito and the cycle begins again.  Symptoms include fever, lymphoedema (usually affecting the legs), scrotal hydrocele, lymphadenopathy, adenolymphangitis (ADL), hardening of the skin (‘elephantiasis’) and secondary bacterial skin infections.  Lymphoedema due to lymphatic filariasis should be differentiated from other causes of lymphoedema, such as cardiac failure.  Diagnosis is from blood film, where microfilariae can be seen and bloods can also be tested for anti-filarial IgG4.  The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends preventative chemotherapy or mass drug administration (MDA) programmes to entire populations who are at risk; drugs usually consist of a combination of albendazole and/or ivermectin or diethylcarbamazine citrate (DEC).  The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) recommends DEC as the drug of choice for lymphatic filariasis infection; it is both microfilaricidal and active against the adult worm.  Lymphatic filariasis is rarely fatal but causes high levels of morbidity. Aetiology  Wuchereria bancrofti causes 90% of cases.  Brugia malayi and Brugia timori (in Asia).  The highest risk of infection is to people who have had many mosquito bites over a period of many years. Risk is low to short-term travellers. Pathophysiology  Infected mosquitoes (anopheles or culex) deposit filarial larvae when they take a blood meal from a human.  The larvae reside in the human lymphatic system and develop into adults.  Adult worms may measure up to 10 cm in length.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Adult worms produce ‘microfilariae’ (an early larval form) which are consumed by mosquitoes during a blood meal from an infected host.  Microfilariae develop into larvae inside the mosquito vector and the larvae then infect another human when a blood meal is taken.  Clinical Presentation  Infection may be asymptomatic, although the infection can still be passed on. People infected in childhood may develop lymphoedema later in life.  Symptoms include:  fever  lymphoedema:  usually affects the limbs  may be severe and debilitating  swelling may also affect the arms, breasts and genitals  scrotal hydrocele is seen in some men.  lymphadenopathy  adenolymphangitis (ADL) – lymphangitis and painful lymphadenopathy, often accompanied by fever; may resemble cellulitis or erysipelas  hardening and thickening of the skin (‘elephantiasis’)  secondary bacterial skin infections. ‘Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is a severe complication associated with W. bancrofti and B. malayi infections, typically seen in Asia. It involves pulmonary infiltration with eosinophils, wheezing, hypereosinophilia, splenomegaly and bloody sputum.  Differential Diagnosis  Lymphoedema of lymphatic filariasis should be differentiated from:  primary lymphoedema  cardiac failure  malnutrition  deep vein thrombosis  podoconiosis (non-filarial elephantiasis)  pelvic malignancy.  Other differentials may include:  scrotal hydrocele  inguinal hernia  cellulitis/erysipelas.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood film to identify microfilariae:

DR. JAM  blood should be taken at night when the concentration of microfilariae in the blood is highest.  Bloods for anti-filarial IgG4.  Lymphoedema may develop years after infection, in which case lab tests may be negative.  Management  The CDC recommends DEC as the drug of choice for lymphatic filariasis infection. It is both microfilaricidal and active against the adult worm. DEC is contraindicated in people who have onchocerciasis.  The WHO recommends preventative chemotherapy or mass drug administration (MDA) programmes to entire populations who are at risk, to reduce microfilariae in the bloodstream and prevent the spread of infection.  Effective MDA regimes depend upon which other diseases are endemic in an area and vary widely by country, but generally consist of:  albendazole  ivermectin or DEC.  Symptomatic management includes:  management and monitoring of lymphoedema and associated complications (eg secondary bacterial infections):  decongestive physiotherapy, exercise and elevation.  surgery for hydrocele  management of acute adenolymphangitis (ADL).  Prognosis  Although lymphatic filariasis is rarely fatal, it causes significant morbidity due to debilitating lymphoedema, which may cause psychosocial and financial issues resulting in poverty.  Other  Despite the advent of mass drug administration, vector control is still a key part of reducing the transmission of lymphatic filariasis. Measures such as insecticide-treated nets, spraying and personal protective measures may all help to reduce the spread of infection. Fungal Infections Fungal infections are very common and usually associated with low morbidity and mortality.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Fungal infections are very common and usually associated with low morbidity and mortality:  onychomycosis – fungal nail infections with thickening and discolouration  candidiasis – oral, oesophageal and vaginal manifestations  ringworm – tinea infection affecting groins, scalp and other skin sites  histoplasmosis – caused by the fungus histoplasma.  Fungi are important commensals on the skin and within the gastrointestinal tract; immunocompetent hosts are rarely susceptible to severe infection.  Invasive fungal infection is an important problem in immunocompromised patients:  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) co-infection  following chemotherapy or bone marrow transplantation.  Aspergillosis is an important disorder in patients with asthma.  Suspect diabetes mellitus in patients with recurrent presentations with fungal illness.  Organisms causing endemic fungal infections include cryptococcus and histoplasma. Epidemiology  Annual global incidence of fungal infection is estimated at > 1 billion cases.  However, deaths from fungal infection are rare – estimated at < 1.5 million per year with the key risk factor for invasive fungal infection being immunosuppression.  Key risk factor for histoplasmosis is caving (transmitted from bat droppings). Aetiology  Important fungal pathogens include candida albicans, tinea spp, aspergillus spp, cryptococcus neoformans, histoplasma spp and pneumocystis jirovecii. Dermatophytes Trichophyton rubrum T. interdigitale Epidermophyton floccosum (tinea pedis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea unguium) Yeasts Candida spp. (intertrigo, oral, genital or systemic) Pityrosporum orbiculare; pityriasis versicolor Pathophysiology  Unlike bacterial infection, the pathophysiology of fungal infections is still poorly understood. Several mechanisms are likely to contribute to virulence in humans.

DR. JAM  Fungi have dual morphology – yeast form and filament-like hyphae form.  Either or both may be involved in pathogenesis of certain infections.  Invasive forms of aspergillosis show evidence of disseminated hyphae within tissues.  Clinical Presentation  The presentation of candidiasis depends on the site affected:  oral candidiasis – white plaques within the oral cavity overlaying raw red mucosa  oesophageal candidiasis – odynophagia  vaginal candidiasis – ‘cottage-cheese’ white discharge.  Tinea infection presents with annular, erythematous skin lesions:  tinea capitis – non-scarring alopecia and overlying scaly changes.  Aspergillosis has a wide range of clinical manifestations, reflecting variation in the host immune status and responses. There are four major sub-types of aspergillosis:  aspergilloma – usually asymptomatic, sometimes mild haemoptysis  invasive aspergillosis – fever, cough with copious sputum production, and pleuritic chest pain  allergic pulmonary aspergillosis – productive cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath  chronic pulmonary aspergillosis – chronic productive cough and shortness of breath.  Cryptococcus infection is usually seen in immunocompromised host:  presents with a subacute history (1–2 weeks) of headache, fevers and confusion  rarer forms of cryptococcosis include wound infection and pulmonary involvement (dry cough, fever, and fatigue).  Typical features of histoplasmosis include:  dry cough and shortness of breath  fever  headache  malaise, fatigue, and arthralgia.  Differential Diagnosis  Oral candidiasis – oral hairy leukoplakia, lichen planus, and malignancy.  Ringworm – psoriasis, alopecia areata, pityriasis versicolor, and vitiligo.  Aspergilloma (haemoptysis) – malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism (PE), and pulmonary-renal syndrome.  Aspergillosis (wheeze and chronic cough) – Churg-Strauss disease and tuberculosis.  Cryptococcal meningitis (headache and fever) – bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, and viral encephalitis.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Histoplasmosis – community-acquired pneumonia, pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), and malignancy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Most simple fungal infections do not require further investigation unless there is significant diagnostic doubt and can usually proceed with trial of treatment:  tinea infections – consider skin scrapings with potassium hydroxide microscopy  oral candidiasis – consider taking sample beneath white plaque for microscopy.  In patients with recurrent infections, measure fasting glucose to in case of diabetes.  In patients with invasive fungal disease, always perform HIV testing.  Aspergillosis:  imaging:  chest X-ray may demonstrate cavitation, nonspecific consolidation  high resolution computed tomography (CT) is the most sensitive test – pulmonary infiltrates with characteristic ‘halo sign’  serology – aspergillus RAST, IgE, beta-glucan, and galactomannan  BAL (invasive aspergillosis) – fungal hyphae and fungal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of aspirates.  Histoplasmosis:  chest X-ray – may show diffuse reticulonodular changes but no change in 40–50%.  sputum culture  blood tests for histoplasma antigen.  Cryptococcal meningitis:  lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) staining with India ink.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Patients with invasive fungal disease are often severely unwell and required good quality supportive care in an High Dependency Unit (HDU) and/or Intensive Care Unit (ITU) setting. Pharmacological  Oral candidiasis is usually managed with miconazole oral gel or nystatin mouthwash; oral fluconazole may be required for severe or persistent infection.  Oesophageal candidiasis requires a more prolonged course of ‘azole’ drug.  Vaginal candidiasis can be managed using an antifungal pessary or ointment (eg clotrimazole) or short courses of oral fluconazole.

DR. JAM  Tinea infection is usually managed with topical antifungals (eg terbinafine) extensive involvement may require oral antifungal treatment.  Invasive aspergillosis is treated aggressively with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B.  Drug treatment for aspergilloma is usually reserved for patients with recurrent haemoptysis, systemic symptoms or with evidence of local fungal invasion:  intracavitatory instillation of amphotericin paste  oral voriconazole.  Acute and chronic severe forms of pulmonary histoplasmosis are managed with intravenous azole drugs (eg voriconazole).  The treatment of choice for cryptococcal meningitis is liposomal amphotericin B.  Surgical  Patients with aspergilloma who present with massive haemoptysis may require bronchial artery embolisation.  Large aspergillomas can also be excised surgically.  Prognosis  Severe fungal infection is rare in immunocompetent individuals.  However untreated infection such as candida can persist for months or years.  Fungal infection of the skin may often relapse following treatment.  Conditions may become chronic in susceptible people.  Despite good supportive care, the prognosis for patients with severe invasive fungal disease is poor.  Other Tinea corporis – note annular erythematous lesion with overlying scaling:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Oral candidiasis – loosely adherent white plaques over patient’s tongue: Gastrointestinal Disease In Advanced HIV Gastrointestinal disorders are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced HIV disease and fall into four major categories based on clinical presentation.  Overview Key Facts  Gastrointestinal disorders are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced HIV disease and fall into four major categories based on clinical presentation:  oral/oesophageal disease – candidiasis, periodontal disease (gingivitis), oral herpes simplex, Kaposi’s sarcoma, aphthous ulcers, and oral hairy leukoplakia  diarrhoea – opportunistic infection with atypical Mycobacteria, Cryptosporidium and Microsporid ia; CMV colitis; Giardia lamblia infection; and bacterial dysentery  biliary and pancreatic disease – cholangiopathy and pancreatitis  anorectal diseases (proctitis and anal warts) – HSV, CMV, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia proctitis and HPV.  Chronic diarrhoea in advanced HIV is associated with HAART treatment failure, and may lead to severe malnutrition, further impairment of immunity, and resultant cyclical infection.

DR. JAM  Diarrhoea is also a side effect of protease inhibitors, especially lopinavir. Epidemiology  Up to 90% of untreated HIV positive patients in Africa will develop chronic diarrhoea. Aetiology  Bacterial infections such as non-typhi Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter and E. coli account for 20% cases of diarrhoea in advanced HIV.  Mycobacterial infection – notably atypical Mycobacteria – account for 10-15% cases.  40% of cases are due to protozoal infection e.g. Cryptosporidiosis and Microsporidiosis.  Viruses such as CMV account for 20% of cases of diarrhoea in advanced HIV. Pathophysiology  The low CD4 count in advanced/untreated HIV places patients at high risk of infection by ‘professional’ and ‘opportunistic’ pathogens.  Clinical Presentation  Dysphagia and odynophagia are commonly caused by oesophageal candidiasis.  Discrete mouth lesions:  painful ulceration is seen with aphthous ulcers and HSV infection  adherent white plaques are seen in oral hairy leukoplakia and oral candidiasis. The former is unaffected by toothbrushing, whereas the white surface material rubs away in Candida to leave a raw bleeding surface beneath.  Diarrhoea may be watery (cryptosporidium, microsporidia) or bloody (salmonella, CMV).  Biliary disease presents with jaundice, steatorrhoea, and dark urine; patients may also develop pancreatitis which manifests as severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting.  Anorectal disorders typically present with anal discharge (often purulent), tenesmus (feeling of incomplete emptying), perianal itch, bleeding, and diarrhoea.  Differential Diagnosis  Oral/oesophageal disorders:  discrete lesions within the mouth – aphthous ulcers, oral hairy leukoplakia, oral candidiasis, Kaposi’s sarcoma  HSV – perioral cold sores.  Diarrhoea:  ‘professional’ pathogens – Salmonella, Shigella, Giardia, CMV  opportunistic infections – MAI complex, Isospora, Cryptosporidium, Microsporidia

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Anorectal disorders:  anal warts and ulceration – HPV (common warts), HSV, anal cancer  proctitis – rectal gonorrhoea, Chlamydia, lymphogranuloma venereum, syphilis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Oral disorders are often diagnosed clinically. However, useful investigations include:  viral and fungal swabs for suspected HSV or Candida infection  biopsy and microscopy of suspected oral hairy leukoplakia.  Diarrhoea requires extensive investigation:  full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E), liver function tests (LFTs), c-reative protein (CRP) – look for signs of dehydration from severe diarrhoea  blood cultures (salmonellosis)  stool culture – microscopy, culture and sensitivity and ova, cysts and parasites  sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with tissue biopsy:  CMV colitis – ‘owl’s eye’ sign due to inclusion bodies in colonic mucosa.  BMI should be calculated (measure arm circumference in children) to gauge a patient’s nutritional status.  Anorectal disorders:  rectal swabs (nucleic acid amplification tests for gonorrhoea and Chlamydia)  biopsy warts and ulcers suspicious for malignancy.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Diarrhoea:  refer to nutritionist to optimise dietary intake  monitor ongoing GI losses and input to gauge fluid balance status. Pharmacological  Oral and oesophageal candidiasis – fluconazole 100-200 mg OD for 14 day course.  Diarrhoea:  CMV colitis – ganciclovir  microsporidium – albendazole  MAI infection – prolonged course (> 12 months) of antituberculous therapy  cyclospora or Isospora – co-trimoxazole  salmonella or Shigella dysentery – azithromycin  side effect of HAART (diagnosis of exclusion) – loperamide, withdraw if severe

Giardiasis Giardiasis is caused by the protozoon Giardia lamblia.  Overview Key Facts  Giardiasis is an important cause of traveller’s diarrhoea.  It is characterised by severe diarrhoea, bloating, cramping, abdominal pain, flatulence and significant weight loss.  Caused by the protozoon Giardia lamblia.  Transmitted by ingestion of cysts from faecal-contaminated water, and occasionally person-to-person.  Has an incubation period of 3-20 days with symptoms often persistent.  Investigation of choice is stool microscopy to identify cysts.  Treatment of choice is a single dose of oral tinidazole or a short course of metronidazole; alongside rehydration and maintaining good hygiene. Herpes Simplex Virus Herpes simplex virus is a common virus that causes cold sores or genital herpes, with recurrent outbreaks triggered by stress or illness.  Overview Key Facts  Three main infection sites of herpes simplex virus (HSV) – oral, genital and ocular.  The majority of oral infection (herpes labialis) is due to HSV-1 and genital by either HSV-1 or HSV-2.  Primary infection can lead to ganglia dormancy or recurrent reactivation.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Both genital and oral have similar sensory pre-infection symptoms, but genital may have this alone without ulcer development.  Ocular HSV, a leading cause of blindness, can exist alone or due to autoinoculation from another site.  Complications of infection are more likely in immunocompromised patients, pregnant women and infants. Epidemiology  Approximately a third of people have HSV labialis during their lifetime  Oral HSV-1 first infection normally occurs in those < 5 years old.  Recurrent HSV labialis – seen more in healthy people, with reductions in episodes over 35 years of age.  Recurrent HSV gingivostomatitis – seen more in the immunocompromised.  Worldwide estimates – 90% by age 40 are HSV-1 seropositive, with 40% of these having recurrent infections.  Genital herpes simplex is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI), and ≤ ¼ of UK/US adults have HSV2 antibodies. Aetiology  Risk factors for seropositivity include female sex, black race, increasing age and not using condoms.  Risk factor for ‘clinical presentation’ of reactivation – human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), other causes of immunosuppression, high-risk sexual behaviour.  Risk factors for severe, possibly life-threatening infection – infanthood, pregnancy, immunocompromise.  HSV-2 infection is usually spread via sexual contact but infection from the mother might be transferred to neonates via vaginal birth.  Reactivation triggers include sunlight, trauma, stress, another infection-causing pyrexia, tight clothing/underwear, alcohol, smoking. Pathophysiology  Oral HSV – 90% cases due to HSV-1; HSV-2 mainly presents orally through orogenital sex transmission.  Genital HSV – both HSV-1 and HSV-2 accountable through sexual contact.  The first infection with herpes is often caused by direct skin or mucosal contact from people who have active vesicles/clinical symptoms, or from people who are viral shedding without symptoms. The incubation period ranges between 2 and 26 days.  The most contagious period is from lesion rupture until scab formation.  Following primary infection, the virus moves to the local sensory ganglia and may remain dormant. HSV-1 often moves to the trigeminal ganglia and HSV-2 to the sacral ganglia. If reactivated they can cause a clinically active infection or asymptomatic viral shedding.

It also has the highes risk of recurrence increasing w 2 years versus 70% by 7 years Recurrence rates and complic immunocompromised Herpes Zoster Herpes zoster, also called shingles, is the reactivation of varicellazoster virus (VZV) in a sensory nerve and its associated dermatome.  Overview Key Facts  Herpes zoster, also called shingles, is the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in a sensory nerve and its associated dermatome.  The incidence increases with age and with immunosuppression.  Presentation is commonly severe pain followed by a vesicular eruption in a unilateral dermatomal distribution.  May permanently affect hearing and/or vision if there is reactivation at these sites (Ramsay Hunt syndrome and ophthalmic shingles).  Management – most cases are self-limiting, but prompt antivirals (and/or steroids) may reduce illness severity and/or length and are especially important in risk groups.  Common complications – secondary skin infection, postherpetic neuralgia.  Less common complications – neurological/CNS/respiratory infection, systemic dissemination.  In most patients, shingles are self-limiting and recurrent herpes zoster is rare. Aetiology  Shingles or herpes zoster is the disease resulting from reactivation of the latent VZV.  Possible reactivation triggers include sunlight, trauma, stress, infection, alcohol, spinal surgery and radiotherapy at the level of the affected nerve root.  Reactivation is more likely with age, immunocompromise and pregnancy. Pathophysiology  Reactivation of latent VZV. Following primary infection, it lies latent in sensory dorsal root/cranial nerve ganglia.  It is unknown why the reactivation occurs, but there are some possible triggers and it is seen more in the immunocompromised, where the disease can be much more severe due to viral dissemination.  It is more frequent in older people due to a natural reduction in cell-mediated immune function with age.  The skin eruption is unilateral and ‘dermatomal’ because it is restricted to the sensory nerve where it was reactivated.  Ramsay Hunt syndrome is due to VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of cranial nerve VII, the facial nerve.  Ophthalmic herpes is due to reactivation in cranial nerve V1 (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve).  The vesicles contain active replicating VZV and can cause primary varicella zoster (chickenpox) infection following skin contact in VZV-naïve people. But it is less infectious than primary infection.

JAM Histoplasmosis Histoplasmosis is a fungal disease caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.  Overview Key Facts  Histoplasmosis is a fungal disease caused by Histoplasma capsulatum.  Histoplasma spores are commonly found in soil that contains bird or bat droppings.  Infection occurs following inhalation of the microscopic fungal spores.  It is not contagious between people or from animals.  Histoplasmosis commonly affects the lungs but may disseminate and can be fatal if untreated.  Treatment is not usually required unless patients are immunocompromised.  Disseminated histoplasmosis (commonly found in immunocompromised patients) has a high mortality rate. Epidemiology  Histoplasmosis is common in temperate regions of the world, such as around the river valleys of the USA, other parts of Central and South America, and Africa.  It is less common in Europe and usually picked up during travel.  About 1% of affected individuals are symptomatic.  Severe disease is more common in immunocompromised patients and histoplasmosis is an opportunistic pathogen in patients with AIDS. Aetiology  Histoplasma capsulatum is a fungus that exists as a yeast at body temperature.  It leads to infection when it is inhaled by a patient.  The manifestation of the disease is dependent on the background of the patient:  patients with underlying chronic lung disease will likely develop chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis.  Types of histoplasmosis:  latent asymptomatic  acute pulmonary histoplasmosis  chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis  disseminated histoplasmosis. Pathophysiology  Histoplasma capsulatum grows in material that is contaminated by bird or bat droppings and is released into the air and inhaled by the patient.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The spores enter the lungs and change into yeast cells at a person’s body temperature:  macrophages ingest microconidia in the alveoli  microconidia are transformed into yeasts  yeasts grow and multiply in phagosomes.  The yeast travels to lymph nodes and other organs.  Immune system of the patient: TNF-alpha, interferon-gamma and IL-12 stimulate macrophages to fight off the fungus.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following symptoms:  asymptomatic  flu-like symptoms develop between 3 and 17 days after exposure:  fever  cough  fatigue  headache  myalgia.  Symptoms tend to resolve in a few weeks to months.  Chest X-ray appears normal in 40–70% of patients.  Histoplasmosis can cause complications such as:  mediastinitis  hepatosplenomegaly  lymphadenopathy  pneumonia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  tuberculosis  community-acquired pneumonia  sarcoidosis  cryptococcus  blastomycosis  coxsackievirus  herpes virus infection.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Histoplasmosis is diagnosed via numerous tests, as listed below.  Chest X-ray:  performed in all patients to determine the extent of involvement  calcified granulomas.  Urine test:  antigen detection via enzyme immunoassay  PCR to detect Histoplasma capsulatum.
