JAM  Blood test:  antibody testing:  2–6 weeks before antibodies develop  immunodiffusion  complement fixation.  cultures  full blood count (FBC), liver function tests (LFTs).  Sputum secretion cultures.  Microscopy.  Computed tomography (CT) chest:  if indicated in immunocompromised patients.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Awareness and prevention:  surveillance  avoiding areas and activities where Histoplasma capsulatum is prevalent:  caves  old buildings  cleaning chicken coops  material (soil, wood) that contains bird or bat droppings. Pharmacological  Patients often do not need pharmacological treatment unless immunocompromised.  Antifungal medication (first line):  amphotericin B:  binds with ergosterol  forms pores on the fungal cell membranes to cause ions to leak and fungal cell death  should be monitored for renal function.  other azole antifungals  itraconazole  inhibits synthesis of ergosterol.  Surgical • Surgical treatment is not indicated.  Prognosis  Approximately 90% of patients who do not have an immunocompromised system do not need any treatment. Disseminated histoplasmosis may be fatal if untreated.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI HIV And AIDS Human immunodeficiency virus is a term that refers to HIV-1 and HIV-2 retroviruses.  Overview Key Facts  Human immunodeficiency virus is a term that refers to HIV-1 and HIV-2 retroviruses:  HIV-1 is common worldwide  HIV-2 is endemic to West Africa.  HIV infection causes progressive loss of CD4 T lymphocytes.  After a period of several years, untreated or undertreated patients go on to develop acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), characterised by multiple, recurrent, and often fatal opportunistic infections.  Many doctors and patients now use the term ‘advanced HIV’ rather than AIDS due to the negative connotations associated with AIDS campaigns in the 1980s and 1990s.  HIV is now a highly treatable infection; for most patients, good compliance with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) normalises life expectancy.  Patients with an undetectable viral load cannot transmit the virus to their partners via unprotected sex (undetectable = untransmittable, U=U). Epidemiology  Over 36 million people are living with HIV worldwide, with over two thirds in sub-Saharan Africa and an emerging epidemic in Eastern Europe and Russia.  In the United Kingdom (UK), around half of all patients newly diagnosed with HIV present late (CD4 count < 350) and 25% present with advanced disease (AIDS, CD4 < 200).  During the initial outbreak in California, homosexual men were disproportionately affected. The demographics have since changed and > 90% of HIV positive people identify as heterosexual.  In many countries, the prevalence of HIV remains high in certain sub-groups – sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), and intravenous drug users.  Factors that increase the risk of sexual transmission include: concurrent sexually transmitted infections (particularly HSV-1 and other ulcerative infections); hepatitis C co-infection; high viral load; and advancing stage of disease. Aetiology  HIV is a viral infection which can be spread by exposure to bodily fluids:  sexual intercourse – oral, vaginal and anal sex (in order of increasing risk)  exposure to contaminated blood – therapeutic blood transfusions (in areas with poor screening programmes); needle sharing in intravenous drug use; needle-stick injuries in healthcare workers

DR. JAM  vertical transmission from untreated mother to child:  prevention of transmission at birth – antiretroviral therapy (reduces transmission to 0.5% if started before third trimester); C-section at 36/40  HIV can be transmitted via breast milk – mothers are encouraged to bottle feed. Pathophysiology  HIV retroviruses have a tropism for CD4 positive immune cells – T-helper (CD4) lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and CNS cells:  the retrovirus enters cells via the CD4 receptor and CXCR4 or CCR5 co-receptors  the virus then integrates itself into the host cell genome – infection is irreversible.  Clinical latency period - after patients seroconvert (develop persistent detectable antibody response to HIV), they enter a prolonged period of clinical latency, lasting 5-10 years. During this period, we see a progressive fall in CD4 count and rise in viral load.  Early and late AIDS – after reaching a tipping point, patients begin to develop opportunistic infections due to defective cellmediated immunity.  CD4 count and viral load are important laboratory markers of infection that can be used to determine the need for opportunistic infection prophylaxis and monitor treatment response.  Clinical Presentation  Many patients who contract HIV infection show no symptoms until they develop AIDS.  However, 40-90% patients will develop an acute seroconversion illness, 2-4 weeks after infection. This is a viral infection similar to glandular fever:  fever, myalgia, pharyngitis +/- tender cervical lymphadenopathy  erythematous maculopapular rash.  Most patients remain asymptomatic during a prolonged latent period, when CD4 count falls slowly but remains above the threshold required to effectively fight infection.  There are a wide range of AIDS-related illness which present in advanced HIV infection, including skin disorders and malignancy; respiratory disease; gastrointestinal disease; and neurological and ophthalmic disorders in advanced HIV.  Differential Diagnosis  HIV-1 seroconversion illness:  glandular fever  streptococcal pharyngitis  influenza  acute viral hepatitis  simple viral upper respiratory tract infection.  Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome:  haematological malignancies eg multiple myeloma

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  drug-induced eg patients on long-term immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and corticosteroids  severe malnutrition  primary immunodeficiencies eg combined variable immunodeficiency.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The investigation of choice for suspected HIV infection is serology for HIV antibody:  there is a three-month window period between inoculation and the serological test becoming positive - routine testing may therefore give false negative result  in the window period, test for HIV RNA (viral load) and p24 antigen.  Markers of infection activity are viral load (HIV RNA) and CD4 count.  Hepatitis B and C serology – co-infection increases risk of transmission.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Counselling, patient education and patient support groups.  Contact tracing. Pharmacological  Antiretroviral therapy is usually given as combination therapy with the following aims:  suppression of viral replication to undetectable levels  reducing the risk of viral resistance emerging with three or more drugs  improving patient immunity with reduction of morbidity and mortality.  Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) involves combinations of at least three drugs:  reverse transcriptase inhibitors either competitively or non-competitively inhibit the enzyme responsible for synthesising the DNA construct from the retrovirus which is integrated into the host cell genome.  nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors – zidovudine, lamivudine  non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors – efavirenz, nevirapine.  protease inhibitors disturb the function of an enzyme needed to make the virus viable outside the cell; these include ritonavir, darunavir, and saquinavir  integrase inhibitors prevent viral DNA from being incorporated into the host cell genome; these include raltegravir and elvitegravir  emerging drugs which do not make up part of most firstline regimens include Maraviroc (CCR5 inhibitors which inhibit viral entry).

DR. JAM  These drugs are generally well tolerated but are associated with some unpleasant side effects:  up to a quarter of ward admissions in HIV positive patients are due to drug toxicity  patients on HAART require regular treatment to monitor for response, adherence and adverse effects  follow-up should include:  clinical examination to monitor oral cavity (oral candida, oral hairy leukoplakia, ulcers), skin (opportunistic infections and drug rashes), lymph nodes and chest (TB and lymphoma), and weight (good marker of response to treatment)  blood tests – U&E, LFTs, CD4 count, viral load, lipids, blood glucose.  Treatment failure is suggested by 2× raised sequential viral load tests in adherent patient.  this should prompt further testing for viral resistance.  Post-exposure prophylaxis is recommended for people who have had an occupational or known or suspected sexual exposure to HIV:  occupational exposures eg needle-stick injuries in healthcare workers should be risk assessed using official guidelines  post-exposure prophylaxis is routinely given to victims of sexual assault.  Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a novel strategy to reduce transmission:  HIV negative patients in at-risk groups eg MSM take regular combination treatment with tenofovir/emtricitabine – reduces risk of contracting infection by > 99%.  Other  Two cases (Berlin and London patients) have been reported of HIV-1 positive patients being cured of the condition through bone marrow allografts:  the Berlin patient was treated for a haematological malignancy and his bone marrow was therefore ablated prior to transplant. He received a transplant from a CCR5 negative donor (rare mutation), which prevents the retrovirus from infecting his new T cell population  due to the high cost associated with this technique, and the very high risk of immunosuppression in patients who undergo chemotherapy to destroy their native immune system before bone marrow transplant, this is not a tractable strategy for others with HIV.  Prognosis  HIV is now considered as a treatable chronic illness, not a fatal disease.  If left untreated patients will almost always progress to advanced HIV with low CD4 count and opportunistic infections 3-20 years after onset of HIV infection (median 8-10 years).  If infection is identified early (with CD4 count > 350), and with good compliance to HAART, patients living with HIV have a normal life expectancy.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  If started before the third trimester of pregnancy, HAART reduces the risk of vertical HIV transmission from 25% to < 1%. Hookworm A parasite is an organism that lives on or in a host and causes harm to a different host organism.  Overview Key Facts  A parasite is an organism that lives on or in a host and causes harm to a different host organism.  Parasites commonly cause disease in humans.  Many parasites such as hookworm are types of helminth worms which:  can be grouped based on morphological characteristics  are rarely fatal  can be associated with significant morbidity and disability, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.  Hookworm infection (common pathogens include Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) is endemic in the Americas, South-East Asia, India and Africa.  The worm initially infects humans as larvae via skin-contacting sandy soil contaminated with infected faecal matter (often by walking barefoot)  The initial infection can cause intense local itching, with a typical serpiginous rash termed cutaneous larva migrans.  The larvae then migrate to the lungs and are swallowed, infecting the gut.  During passage through the lungs, they can cause allergy-like respiratory symptoms.  Once in the gut, the larvae mature into worms and can lead to microscopic blood loss and an iron deficiency anaemia.  With heavy infection, the patient may have abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea and anorexia.  Hookworms cause anaemia by attachment to the upper gastrointestinal mucosa leading to chronic bleeding and iron deficiency:  they are the most common cause of iron deficiency anaemia worldwide.  Diagnosis is via the identification of ova in a stool sample.  Blood tests may reveal eosinophilia, which is typical of helminth infection.  Treatment is commonly with albendazole or a similar agent, based on availability.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Hookworm infection affects 25% of the global population and is endemic in areas such as South America, South-East Asia and Africa.  It is the most common cause of iron deficiency anaemia worldwide. Aetiology  Hookworm is a parasitic nematode worm (helminth).  The organism lives in the small intestine of the infected host.  The two species that commonly infect humans are Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. Pathophysiology  The worm initially infects the human host in its larval form via skin-contacting sandy soil contaminated with infected faecal matter.  The initial infection can cause intense local itching with a typical rash termed cutaneous larva migrans.  The larvae then migrate to the lungs via the bloodstream, where they ascend the bronchial tree and are swallowed, setting up infection in the gut.  Here, the larvae mature to adult worms and produce more ova, which are then released in the stool.  Clinical Presentation  Many patients with infection are asymptomatic.  The most common signs and symptoms when they occur are the typical serpiginous rash named cutaneous larvae migrans and associated intense itching.  Patients may also present with gastrointestinal symptoms such as:  abdominal pain  nausea  vomiting  diarrhoea.  Iron deficiency anaemia is a very common complication due to occult GI bleeding:  patients may also present with signs and symptoms related to this, which may include:  lethargy  breathlessness  tachycardia  reduced exercise tolerance  pallor.  Large volumes of protein loss may lead to hypoproteinaemia and its consequences.  Lung infection can also lead to breathlessness and may be associated with wheeze.  Cutaneous larvae migrans on the foot:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  ascariasis  schistosomiasis  strongyloidiasis  bacterial/viral gastroenteritis  asthma  pneumonia  contact dermatitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  After 8–12 weeks following initial infection, hookworm ova will be produced by adult worms in the GI tract, and will be present in the faeces; the isolation of these is the investigation of choice.  Serology will also show marked eosinophilia, although this is typical for all helminth infections.  Chest X-ray may show alveolar infiltrates in patients with severe lung involvement.  Management  In many mild cases, infection may be self-limiting and clear without treatment.  Pharmacological treatment is anthelmintic drugs; those effective against hookworms include albendazole, mebendazole and thiabendazole, as well as ivermectin.

DR. JAM  Iron, B12 or folate treatment may be necessary to replenish lost red blood cells.  In severe or persistent infection, surgical removal of parasites may be required.  Prognosis  Although the infection can be treated effectively with oral treatment, rapid reinfection commonly occurs in areas where the condition is endemic.  The condition is a leading cause of iron deficiency globally and also contributes significantly to childhood developmental delay, malnourishment and reduced growth in endemic areas.  The condition is also associated with low birth weight in newborns of infected mothers. Human Papillomavirus Human papillomavirus is a double-stranded DNA virus responsible for epithelial lesions (skin/anogenital warts, oral warts) and cancers (cervical and oral cancer).  Overview Key Facts  Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a double-stranded DNA virus responsible for epithelial lesions (skin/anogenital warts, oral warts) and cancers (cervical and oral cancer).  Most HPV infections are asymptomatic or have minor features that do not present clinically.  Infection with some types of HPV dramatically increases the risk of cervical and some oral cancers.  Prevention is available through a national immunisation schedule.  Treatment is not always necessary and side-effects (eg scarring) often outweigh the benefit in simple cutaneous cases.  Treatment mainly involves lesion removal and topical products.  Cutaneous wart treatment is possible in the community.  Anogenital warts may require secondary-care involvement.  Recurrence of warts following treatment is common. Treatment may result in long-term side effects including scarring or hypo/hyperpigmentation. Epidemiology  Direct epidemiological surveillance of HPV is difficult because there is a high proportion of infected individuals that are asymptomatic and a potentially long incubation period:  anogenital warts are one of the commonest sexually transmitted infections (STIs), affecting approximately 10% of the sexually active population in their lifetime

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  as with all STIs, the presence of one increases the likelihood of co-infection with another (with HPV, approximately one-third have co-infection)  HPV is detected in 99% of cervical cancers  increasing age is seen to increase HPV infection contraction rates  non-smokers have an improved treatment response  cutaneous warts are uncommon in infants. Aetiology  There are > 100 HPV types:  types 6 and 11 are commonest for anogenital warts  types 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 27 and 57 are the commonest for cutaneous warts  types 16 and 18 are most commonly associated with cervical cancer  type 16 is the most common in oropharyngeal cancer:  all oral carcinomas are tested for HPV.  Neonatal infection is transmitted from the birth canal in mothers with HPV but does not occur in all cases.  Most warts in the anogenital and oropharyngeal region are benign.  Nail biting, and the trauma from it, is a risk factor for cutaneous warts. Genital HPV infection  Factors for increased risk – unprotected sexual intercourse (no barrier method), multiple sexual partners, immunosuppression, presence/history of other STIs.  Risk reduction – caesarean delivery, vaccination, condom usage. HPV and cervical cancer  HPV 16 and 18 are most commonly implicated in cervical cancer.  The NHS cervical screening programme uses the presence of HPV as the primary screening method and only goes on to assess for dyskaryosis if the smear is found to be HPV positive.  In England, women are invited into the screening programme from ages 25 to 49 (3-yearly) and thereafter 5-yearly until age 64.  Women with HIV require yearly smears due to increased risk. Pathophysiology  HPV is transmitted to a ‘HPV naïve’ person by direct skin contact with those that have active warts or asymptomatic infection.  It can also occur from environmental contamination, eg surfaces.

DR. JAM  It infects squamous epithelia in the skin plus anogenital/upper airway mucosa.  Most people are asymptomatic, others develop warts and the associated cancer risk implications; this is not fully understood why.  In cutaneous warts, it causes hyperkeratinisation and epidermal thickening; this produces the typical raised, coarse-skin appearance of the lesions.  It is possible for autoinoculation due to shaving or picking at skin lesions.  The incubation period is approximately two weeks to eight months (but can be much longer).  HPV infection can worsen in immunosuppression/pregnancy.  It is thought that ‘self-resolution’ is due to cell-mediated immune response.  HPV is not detected in most (approximately 95%) two years following anogenital wart appearance, whether due to treatment or self-resolution.  Clinical Presentation  Most HPV infections are asymptomatic or have minor features that do not present clinically.  Warts are possible on the skin, anogenital and oropharyngeal regions; they appear more commonly at ‘trauma sites’.  Skin (cutaneous) warts:  appearance – papular lesions that have a rough superficial texture, often have ‘black dots’ (bleeding sites) within  most commonly on the hands and feet  mostly seen in children and adolescents  ‘common warts’ normally on fingers  plantar – aka ‘verrucae’ are on the feet, often flat, may be tender, ‘dots’ more likely to be seen if ‘pared down’  plane – small, ‘skin’-coloured or pigmented with a ‘flat’ top and no surface coarseness or ‘dots’; normally appear in multiples on the face/backs of hands  facial – often have an elongated (‘filiform’) appearance.  Genital warts:  may have a ’stalk’  may be painful (due to local trauma; however the warts themselves are not painful)  may be itchy  may bleed  different locations between genders, but tend to appear in areas of skin-to-skin contact during intercourse:  women – any site in the external genitalia; in the vagina or cervix, there may be flat warts, only seen by internal examination  men – commonest sites are the penile shaft and suprapubic area but can exist in the urethra or the perianal region/rectum.  Relapse or failure is common with treatment.  Clinical presentation worsens (ie the warts may increase in size or spread) in immunosuppression or pregnancy.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses are listed below.  Anogenital:  secondary syphilis  folliculitis  primary cancer.  Other skin infections, eg molluscum contagiosum.  Hand/feet corns or callouses.  Dermatological:  seborrhoeic keratitis  lichen planus  cutaneous horn  actinic keratosis  malignant melanoma  basal cell carcinoma  skin tags.  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis  Diagnosis based on clinical examination, history and risk factor assessment.  Examination in women should include internal with a speculum.  In both genders, proctoscopy may be appropriate.  HPV may be detected in the cervical cancer screening programme which alters the cervical risk management/monitoring pathways in that individual. Investigation  Full assessment for other STIs, including of their partners.  Biopsy + viral typing (rarely performed) if there are atypical lesions, diagnostic doubt or high malignancy suspicion.  ‘Safeguarding’ – anogenital warts in children can be an indicator of sexual abuse and need a full assessment.  Management  Treatment not always required; sometimes the warts stay the same, increase in size or spontaneously resolve.  The mainstay of treatment is to evoke an immune response to the virus in order to eradicate it.  Treatment depends on the severity and location of lesions, as well as if they are recurrent.  With cutaneous warts, the problems from treatment might outweigh the benefit; it is more likely to be beneficial if the warts cause pain or cosmetic concerns.  Treatment failure and relapse is common; smoking is a major risk factor for treatment failure and recurrence.  Patient education is important, especially to prevent autoinoculation, secondary infection of lesions or transmission to others.

DR. JAM Referral  Anogenital warts:  GUM clinic referral needed for further STI testing  cervical warts may benefit from colposcopy referral  internal anal warts may need general surgical referral.  Cutaneous warts:  dermatology referral is needed if: there is diagnostic uncertainty, persistence despite treatment, in the immunocompromised, facial location or severe spread.  Prevention:  barrier contraception  national vaccination, currently of girls and boys aged 12– 13 years, reduces the risk of cervical cancer and anogenital warts by targeting HPV types 6, 11,16 and 18; previous vaccination (approximately 2008–2012) was mainly aimed at cervical cancer prevention (only given to girls and targeting types 16 and 18)  NHS also offers vaccination to men who have sex with men and ≤ 45 years. Non-Pharmacological  Full STI screening needed and prevention of autoinoculation.  A woman with anogenital warts, unless told otherwise, should continue with standard cervical screening recall. Pharmacological  Cutaneous warts:  in the community (simple, on hands or feet)  weekly paring (eg with emery board) + topical treatment with salicylic acid  this combination can increase resolution speed  liquid nitrogen ‘cryotherapy’ and/or topical salicylic acid.  Note, it is possible to get cutaneous wart treatment ‘over the counter’. Secondary care  Physical removal – excision, laser or photodynamic treatment.  Antimitotic agents, eg topical podophyllotoxin (cream/solution), topical/oral retinoids or intralesional bleomycin application.  Immunomodulators, eg topical imiquimod 5% or intralesional interferon.  Immune ‘sensitisers’, eg squaric acid dibutylester.  Virucides, eg formaldehyde or glutaraldehyde.  Blistering agent cantharidin.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Anogenital warts  If possible, all patients with anogenital warts should be managed in sexual health services:  options for treatment include ablation (using cryotherapy), excision or topical therapies  common topical therapies include topical podophyllotoxin or imiquimod 5% cream  treatment depends on whether the warts are keratinised (cryotherapy is preferred for keratinised lesions).  In pregnancy – anogenital warts are often treated with cryotherapy alone and may, but not always, be an indication for caesarean section.  Surgical  Excision might be suitable for wart removal, more likely if they are small and not clustered. Immunodeficiency Immunodeficiency can be classified as either primary or secondary, by the faulty component, or according to individual clinical syndromes. It results in partial or full impairment of the immune system leading to a suboptimal response to infection.  Overview Key Facts  Immunodeficiency can be classified as either primary or secondary, by the faulty component, or according to individual clinical syndromes.  it results in partial or full impairment of the immune system leading to a suboptimal response to infection.  Primary immunodeficiency is inherited and arises from genetic defects in B and T cells, these patients usually present at birth or early childhood.  Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired and a result of disease or environmental factors and includes HIV/AIDS, malnutrition or medical treatment (eg chemotherapy).  There are over 300 types of immunodeficiency.  Both forms of immunodeficiency result in recurrent infections.  Investigations in primary care include full blood count and antibody levels and become more specialised in secondary care.  Management includes prophylactic antibiotics, immunoglobin replacement or bone marrow transplant in primary immunodeficiency whereas treatment for secondary immunodeficiency focuses on the underlying disorder causing immune suppression, eg HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy) for HIV/AIDS.

DR. JAM Primary immunodeficiency (PID):  Rare and usually the diagnostic remit of paediatricians.  Mostly inherited single gene disorders that present in infancy or early childhood, however common variable immunodeficiency is the exception and usually presents in adulthood.  B-cell defects account for 50% of primary immunodeficiency, T-cell defects account for 30%, phagocytic deficiencies 18%, and complement deficiencies 2%. Secondary immunodeficiency (SID):  Due to disease or medication is common and is encountered by adult physicians on a daily basis in routine practice.  Common in people hospitalised for:  malignancy  HIV  malnutrition  metabolic disorders  renal disease requiring dialysis  protein loss (eg nephrotic syndrome). Epidemiology Primary:  six million people live with PID worldwide but 70-79% undiagnosed with 5000 of these individuals in the United Kingdom (UK)  there are 39,000 PID related hospital admissions in 2014-2015 in the UK. Secondary:  it is more common than primary immunodeficiency disorders which are relatively rare  more common in developing world where people are more likely to suffer from malnutrition and/or HIV/AIDS  there are 100,000 patients with HIV in the UK and 600 HIVrelated deaths in the UK in 2015  15000 HIV related hospital admissions in 2014–2015 in the UK. Pathophysiology Patterns of immunodeficiency  Neutrophil defects:  result in recurrent bacterial or fungal skin infections (cellulitis/abscesses)  eg primary: chronic granulomatous disease; secondary: diabetes mellitus.  Complement deficiency:  can be uncovered incidentally as it is not always symptomatic – many are undiagnosed

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  most important clinical associations with complement deficiency include hereditary angioedema and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  when infections occur it usually implies a final common pathway defect manifesting with recurrent and/or invasive Neisseria spp. infections  eg primary: inherited final common pathway deficiencies, secondary: eculizumab (C5 inhibitor used for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria).  B cell/antibody deficiency:  results in sinopulmonary infections/bronchiectasis  eg primary: common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, Bruton’s hypogammaglobulinaemia; secondary: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, rituximab, gold, and phenytoin.  T cell deficiency:  infections are opportunistic eg Pneumocystis jirovecii, invasive viral infections (cytomegalovirus), intracellular bacterial infections (eg salmonellae and mycobacterial infections)  eg primary: DiGeorge syndrome, severe combined immune deficiency (SCID), ataxia telangiectasia, secondary: HIV infection, ciclosporin and anti-CD3 therapy.  Clinical Presentation  Immunodeficiency disorders characterised by:  recurrent, persistent and complicated infections (often bacterial) affecting:  respiratory tract (eg pneumonia, bronchitis and sinusitis)  mouth (eg thrush and gingivitis)  ears (eg otitis)  skin (eg pyoderma and warts).  general symptoms:  fevers/chills  loss of appetite/weight loss  abdominal pain – due to hepatomegaly/splenomegaly  chronic diarrhoea – causing failure to thrive in infants/children  poor growth and weight loss.  Diagnosis/Investigation Primary and secondary immunodeficiency:  Initial tests in primary care:  full blood count (FBC), IgG, IgM and IgA  microbiological swabs  chest X-ray.

DR. JAM  Specialist tests:  lymphocyte response assays  antibody response to immunisation of diphtheria, tetanus and pneumococcal polysaccharides  phagocytosis assay  flow cytometry.  Management Primary and secondary immunodeficiency: Non-Pharmacological  Healthy lifestyle and protection from infection (eg regular dental checks).  Chest infections – physiotherapy and lung exercises. Pharmacological  Prophylactic antibiotics (eg for those who have undergone splenectomy).  Antivirals (eg amantadine).  Intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous (SC) immunoglobulin replacement.  Surgical  Bone marrow transplant – definitive treatment for T-cell deficiency conditions and those with bone marrow destruction following chemotherapy treatment. Primary immunodeficiency specifically:  Other experimental treatment:  cytokines  thymic transplants  gene therapy  stem cell transplantation.  Prognosis  Primary immunodeficiency is most commonly genetic and has lifelong implications.  Better prognosis if the condition is diagnosed early and infections treated regularly.  Worse outlook for patients with severe combined immunodeficiency where patients tend to have chronic illness and require intensive treatment.  Secondary – tend to resolve when underlying pathology is treated.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Infective Endocarditis Infective endocarditis is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart.  Overview Key Facts  Infective endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart.  IE is most commonly caused by bacterial infection affecting damaged or prosthetic heart valves.  IE can lead to valve insufficiency, heart failure, pericarditis and myocardial infarction.  Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci are noted to be the most common causes.  The most common location is the mitral valve.  Symptoms can be non-specific including malaise and tiredness. Fever and a new murmur should be investigated for IE.  Diagnosis is made using an echocardiogram.  Length of treatment is usually 4–6 weeks of antibiotics.  Empirical treatment for native valve endocarditis, unless staphylococcal infection is suspected, is intravenous amoxicillin (2 g every four hours) with gentamicin (1 mg/kg twice daily).  For prosthetic valve endocarditis, vancomycin and gentamicin plus rifampicin (300–600 mg every 12 hours) are currently recommended.  The condition is usually fatal if not diagnosed and managed rapidly.  The mortality rate is 30% with IE caused by staphylococci and 6% by sensitive streptococci. Epidemiology Incidence is 1.7–6.2 cases per 100 000 patient-years. Aetiology  IE is most commonly caused by bacterial infection affecting damaged or prosthetic heart valves.  Organisms may originate from dental disease, intravenous lines, surgical intervention and intravenous drug use.  Almost any pathogenic organism may be implicated, particularly in immunocompromised patients.  Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause off endocarditis overall (both acute and sub-acute).  Other common causes include Streptococci (particularly, viridans-type streptococci, the most common cause of subacute endocarditis) , followed by coagulase negative Streptococci such as S.epidermidis and S.lugdenesis  Streptococcal endocarditis presents more indolently than staphylococcal endocarditis.  Right-sided staphylococcal endocarditis often occurs in intravenous drug users.

DR. JAM  Endocarditis is less commonly caused by the HACEK group of organisms (around 5% of all cases):  Haemophilus aphrophilus and H. paraphrophilus  Actinobacillus hominis  Cardiobacterium hominis  Eikenella corrodens  Kingella kingae and K. denitricans.  Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections requires surgical intervention  Enterococci are less commonly implicated.  The following organisms are associated with culture negative endocarditis  Brucella  Bartonella  Coxiella burnetti (Q fever)  Chlamydia  Legionella  Mycoplasma  Whipples disease (Trophyerma whipplei  Fungal organisms can also cause an infective endocarditis (subacute).  Marantic (metastatic-related) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)-related (Libman–Sacks) endocarditis are causes of noninfective endocarditis. The following conditions are associated with an increased risk of endocarditis:  acquired valvular heart disease with stenosis or regurgitation  valve replacement  structural congenital heart disease, including surgically corrected or palliated structural conditions, but excluding an isolated atrial septal defect (ASD), fully repaired ventricular septal defect (VSD) or fully repaired patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and closure devices that are judged to be endothelialised  previous infective endocarditis  hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). Pathophysiology The usual location of infection is a mitral valve. Typically, the invading organism adheres to the valve and causes invasion of the leaflets. Groups affected by endocarditis Percentage of all cases Chronic rheumatic disease

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI No previous valve disease

Intravenous drug abuse

Congenital defects

Prosthetic

 Clinical Presentation The patient may present with non-specific symptoms of malaise, tiredness and infective-type symptoms. IE should be considered in patients fulfilling the following criteria:  fever and a murmur of new valvular regurgitation  fever, a pre-existing at-risk cardiac lesion and no other apparent source of infection  fever and:  predisposition and recent intervention with associated bacteraemia  evidence of congestive cardiac failure  vascular or immunological phenomena: embolic events, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes  a new stroke  peripheral abscesses (renal, splenic, cerebral, vertebral) of unknown cause.  a protracted history of sweats, weight loss, anorexia or malaise, and an at-risk cardiac lesion  any new, unexpected embolic events  unexplained, persistently positive, blood cultures  intravascular, catheter-related, bloodstream infection with persistently positive blood cultures 72 hours after catheter removal. Janeway lesions:  Differential Diagnosis  Polymyalgia rheumatica  SLE

DR. JAM  Antiphospholipid syndrome  Reactive arthritis  Collagen vascular disease  Myocarditis  Rheumatic fever.  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis is based on the Duke’s criteria Cases are ‘definite’ if they fulfil: two major, one major and three minor, or five minor Duke’s criteria; Cases are ‘possible’ if they fulfil: one major and one minor or three minor Duke’s criteria. Two sets of blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics are initiated. Major Duke’s criteria Microbiological: typical infective endocarditis organism from two separate blood cultures (viridans-type streptococci, Streptococcus bovis, HACEK group, Staphylococcus aureus, community- acquired enterococcal bacteraemia without obvious source) or organism consistent with infective endocarditis from persistently positive blood cultures or single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or serology positive for C. burnetii. Cardiological: new valvular regurgitation or positive echocardiogram. Minor Duke’s criteria predisposition to infective endocarditis (intravenous drug use,cardiac abnormality) fever vascular phenomena immunological phenomena positive blood cultures not meeting major criteria.  A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) is the initial imaging of choice and will allow visualisation of vegetations (bacterial growth) on the valves of the heart. JAM Influenza Influenza is a highly infectious, acute respiratory tract infection caused by influenza virus A and B.  Overview Key Facts  Influenza is a highly infectious, acute respiratory tract infection caused by influenza virus A and B.  Characterised by upper and lower respiratory tract symptoms, such as fever, chills, myalgia, rhinorrhoea and cough.  Typically occurs during the winter months.  Transmitted via inhalation of respiratory droplets (from sneezing or coughing).  Diagnosis is usually clinical, but a viral culture may allow detection of viral antigen.  Management is usually supportive.  Vaccination is widely available. Epidemiology  Estimated to affect 20% of children and 5% of adults worldwide each year.  Most infections occur during the winter because the virus can tolerate cold, dry climates.  There have been four influenza pandemics since 1918.  The most recent was swine flu (H1N1) in 2009. Aetiology  There are three types of influenza virus based on antigenic differences – A, B and C:  influenza A causes frequent outbreaks and is more associated with severe and complicated infections  influenza B typically has a milder course but still has the potential to cause outbreaks  influenza C is not associated with outbreaks and causes a mild or asymptomatic disease.  These are single-stranded RNA viruses of the orthomyxovirus family.  The RNA codes for five structural proteins and three nonstuctural proteins.  Protein M and nucleoprotein NP are used to differentiate influenza into A, B and C.  Haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) are two glycoprotein antigens found in the plasma membrane.  H antigen binds the virus to sialic acid on the surface of cells, allowing viral entry. N antigen allows viral escape from the cell by cleaving host neuraminic acid.  Influenza A and B are divided into several subtypes that are defined by the H and N antigens.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  There are three subtypes of H antigen (H1, H2 and H3) and two subtypes of N antigen (N1 and N2).  Antigenic drift describes the process by which influenza viruses constantly change due to small point mutations in H and N antigens:  this usually produces viruses that are closely related to one another and the immune system will therefore recognise and respond to them (cross-protection)  however, these small changes can accumulate over time and produce viruses that are antigenically different  this means hosts can have the infection multiple times and new vaccines are required each influenza season.  Antigenic shift is a significant change in one or both surface antigens, usually due to reassortment of genetic segments between two subtypes of viruses:  this tends to occur when human and animal viruses undergo reassortment  this process creates new subtypes which may result in pandemics. Pathophysiology  Transmitted via infected respiratory droplets produced by coughing, sneezing or talking.  May also spread via contact with contaminated surfaces.  Incubation is 1–3 days.  The virus binds to and enters the tracheobronchial epithelium via the H antigen.  The virus then replicates in the nucleus of the cell.  New virions migrate to the cell membrane and the N antigen allows viral particles to exit the cell.  This is followed by the death of the host cell, triggering an immune response.  Peak viral shedding occurs in the first 2–3 days of exposure.  Clinical Presentation  Asymptomatic or mild in 75% of cases.  Common symptoms include:  fever with chills  sore throat  nasal congestion  dry cough  headache  arthralgia  myalgia  fatigue.  Some patients may experience diarrhoea, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting.  Symptoms typically last 5–7 days.  If there is a cough productive of purulent sputum and dyspnoea, a secondary bacterial pneumonia should be suspected.

JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  bacterial pneumonia  COVID-19  parainfluenza virus infection  respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations are only required if the results are likely to affect the diagnosis or treatment.  Investigations to consider:  full blood count – elevated WCC and lymphocytosis  C-reactive protein – elevated  chest X-ray – normal in uncomplicated cases, but may show lobar consolidation or interstitial infiltrates in secondary bacterial infection  viral culture – detection of influenza virus or viral antigen from a nasopharyngeal swab, nasal wash, bronchial wash, nasal aspirate or sputum; not often used for clinical management as results take up to 72 hours  direct immunofluorescent antibody staining or reverse transcriptase PCR – allows detection of influenza virus from a nasopharyngeal swab, nasal wash, bronchial wash, nasal aspirate or sputum; generates a result within 2–4 hours  enzyme immunoassay – allows detection of influenza virus from a nasopharyngeal swab, throat swab, nasal wash or bronchial wash; generates a result within 2 hours.  Management  Treatment depends on whether the infection is uncomplicated or complicated.  Complicated infection is defined as requiring hospitalisation, having features of a lower respiratory tract infection, CNS involvement or exacerbation of an underlying condition. Complicated infection is associated more with influenza A infection.  Uncomplicated infection:  usually self-limiting and treatment is supportive, such as antipyretics, analgesics and increased fluid intake  patients are usually managed in the community  patients who are otherwise healthy (excluding pregnant women) do not require antiviral treatment  patients at high risk of developing complications should be offered oseltamivir.  Complicated infection:  treatment is more aggressive supportive care, often requiring hospitalisation, antibiotics and/or antivirals  antibiotics should be considered for certain complications, such as bacterial pneumonia, sinusitis and otitis media

Kaposi Sarcoma Kaposi sarcoma is classically found as an indolent tumour, arising in older men living around the Mediterranean.  Overview Key Facts  Kaposi sarcoma is classically found as an indolent tumour, arising in older men living around the Mediterranean.  In these classic cases, the disease was associated with diabetes and not human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).  HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma is the most common malignancy found in patients with HIV.  Iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma can be caused by immunosuppressive drug therapy (this is particularly an issue in patients who have had organ transplants).  Despite its name, the condition is no longer classified as a sarcoma; it is derived from the vascular and lymphatic endothelial cells.  Kaposi sarcoma may involve the skin and viscera:  skin – purple plaques and violaceous nodules  pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma should be suspected when lesions are noted within the oral cavity; this usually presents with cough and shortness of breath  gastrointestinal Kaposi sarcoma can present with diarrhoea, abdominal pain and PR bleeding.  Cancers are common in advanced HIV and result from dysregulated immune function.  10–15% of patients with AIDS will have Kaposi sarcoma at first presentation.  The disease is caused by Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV), which is most commonly transmitted by sexual contact.  Decreasing CD4 cell count is strongly associated with AIDSassociated and classic Kaposi sarcoma.  Generally, the lower the CD4 count, the more extensive and aggressive the condition.  Almost all cases of Kaposi sarcoma regress within months of initiation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART):  alternatives for patients with awkward lesions or poor response include local treatments, interferon and chemotherapy.

Legionella Legionnaires' disease is caused by the bacterium Legionella pneumophila.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Legionnaires' disease is caused by the bacterium Legionella pneumophila.  The condition presents with a pneumonia and often extrapulmonary manifestations, including confusion, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal and liver involvement and hyponatraemia.  Legionnaires' disease most commonly affects middle-aged and older patients, often with underlying lung disease.  It is commonly associated with travel to Mediterranean countries; due to its ability to colonise water tanks, it can lead to clusters of cases related to infected water systems or airconditioning units.  First choice of diagnostic test is a urinary antigen test, which has good sensitivity and specificity, and can be performed rapidly.  Overall mortality is 10–15%, but can be up to 80% if untreated in an immunocompromised or older patient.  Treatment is with intravenous macrolide, fluoroquinolone or tetracycline antibiotics for up to 3 weeks.  L. pneumophila also causes a less common non-pneumonic infection known as Pontiac fever, which is generally selflimiting. Epidemiology  Legionnaires’ disease usually affects middle-aged and older patients, often with underlying lung disease  Men are affected more than women (3:1).  It is commonly associated with travel to Mediterranean countries and, owing to its ability to colonise water tanks, can lead to clusters of cases related to infected water systems or airconditioning units. Aetiology  The organism breeds in water, multiplying within amoebae and other single-celled protozoa, which provide nutrients and protect it from adverse conditions.  Disease is caused when bacteria are aerosolised, allowing for inhalation.  Outbreaks typically occur around cooling towers, misting machines and poorly maintained air-conditioning units; personto-person spread is extremely rare. Pathophysiology  Aerosol inhalation leads to multiplication of the organism in alveloar macrophages, leading to targeted destructive alveolar inflammation.  Clinical Presentation  Pulmonary signs and symptoms may include:  cough  breathlessness

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Leprosy Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) is an infectious disease that causes severe, disfiguring skin lesions or sores and nerve damage in the arms, legs and skin areas of any of the part of the body.  Overview Key Facts  Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) is an infectious disease that causes severe, disfiguring skin lesions or sores and nerve damage in the arms, legs and skin areas of any of the part of the body.  It is caused by Mycobacterium leprae (M. leprae), an acidfast rod-shaped bacillus bacterium.  Leprosy is contagious but cannot be transmitted by casual touch. It can be transmitted only if the person comes into close and repeated contact with the patient with leprosy. It is transmitted via nose and mouth droplets of untreated or undertreatment patients.  M. leprae may take 3–5 years or more to cause the disease effects or symptoms after entering the human body.  Treatment is possible but the disfiguring skin sores which involve arms and hands can be limited if the treatment is delivered timely.  Treatment is with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin and clofazimine), which is funded by the World Health Organization (WHO).  Prognosis is good if treatment is delivered on time; however delayed treatment can result in complications. Epidemiology  There were approximately 200 000 cases of leprosy in 2018 according to the WHO.  Most of the cases are in Africa and Asia.  India is the most affected country with the largest number of patients.  Statistically males are more affected than females.  In UK, 396 people were affected between 1982 and 2012. Leprosy is a notifiable disease in the UK. Aetiology  Causative organism is M. leprae.  Route of transmission is respiratory droplets.  May transmitted via skin and nasal mucosa.  Entry route is not definitely known. Pathophysiology  M. leprae infection initiates an extensive range of cellular immune responses.  Permanent peripheral neuropathy occurs as a result of the immunological host response to the organism.  M. leprae grows at 27–30°C, therefore skin, being suitable for its growth, is most affected.

Pharmacological  Long-term antibiotics (multidrug therapy, MDT) is the mainstay of pharmacological treatment.  Treatment depends on the type of leprosy.  Paucibacillary – two antibiotics: dapsone (also known as diaminodiphenyl sulfone) once daily and rifampicin monthly.  Multibacillary – clofazimine and dapsone once daily, besides monthly rifampicin.  Prednisolone or other steroids are also used to control nerve pain and muscle pain.  NSAIDs for anti-inflammatory effect.  Analgesics for pain.  Thalidomide – to suppress the immune system. It is well known for causing birth defects. Therefore contraindicated in pregnant mothers.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Surgical  Decompressive surgery is used for treating nerve damage.  Remedy motor paralysis due to primary nerve impairment.  Claw fingers and Z-thumbs caused by ulnar nerve paralysis are among the most common deformities.  Prognosis  Prognosis is good if treatment is delivered on time.  Delayed treatment can result in many complications.  Complications of leprosy can include:  blindness  glaucoma  uveitis  alopecia  impotence  disfiguration of the face (including permanent swelling, bumps and lumps)  erectile dysfunction  renal failure  muscle weakness and paralysis  disfiguring of the skin of hand leading to claw-like fingers  permanent necrosis of nasal mucosa, leading to repeated nasal bleedings  permanent peripheral neuropathic damage of affected skin patches.  Other  The WHO provides free treatment for all people with leprosy.  In the last two decades, 16 million people with leprosy have been cured.  M. leprae was discovered in 1873 by scientist Gerhard Henrik Armauer Hansen, a Norwegian physician. 95% of people have natural innate immunity to leprosy. Leptospirosis  Overview Key Facts  Leptospirosis is a zoonotic spirochaete infection transmitted by substances contaminated with the urine of infected mammals (dogs, rats) through broken skin.  Transmission is usually via contaminated water, but can also occur via infected soil and via contact with infected urine/animal tissue.

DR. JAM  There is often a history of occupational (sewage or agricultural workers) or recreational (ﬁshing, water sports) exposure.  Leptospira species including interrogans is responsible for disease.  The incubation period is usually 7–12 days.  Clinical manifestation can vary from asymptomatic, to a shortlived febrile illness, or severe illness including Weil's disease and multi organ failure.  The majority of leptospiral infections are self-limiting and may require no treatment,  Severe cases may need antibiotic therapy and hospital admission for supportive care.  With severe cases that progress to Weil's disease, the mortality rates are approximately 20% in developing countries and around 5% in the United Kingdom.  Clinical Presentation  In some cases there may be minimal to no symptoms at all.  In symptomatic cases, there is usually a combination of:  headache  fever  myalgia  rigors  neck stiffness,  Initial symptoms often last for 4–5 days due to leptospiraemia.  Some recover after this phase, but for others, as the organism localises a more severe disease and causes:  vasculitis and capillary injury  further fever  suffused conjunctivae  aseptic meningitis  jaundice, renal impairment and proteinuria (Weil's dease)  In this severe form, known as Weil's disease, there is often multiple organ failure.  The liver, heart, brain and lungs may also be affected.  Differential Diagnosis  Meningitis  Influenza  Malaria  Typhoid fever  Toxic Shock Syndrome  Yellow fever  Dengue fever  Scrub typhus  Legionnaires' disease

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  On blood testing, there is typically a neutrophilia, raised creatine kinase (CK) and lymphocytic CSF.  Diagnosis can be confirmed by the culture of blood/CSF/urine, which is often difficult and may take time to achieve a positive result.  Serology for antibodies can aid diagnosis after 10 days of infection.  PCR assay can rapidly diagnose the condition in early stages of infection.  Management  Many cases of infection are self-limiting and do not require intervention.  Severe cases require hospitalisation and IV antibiotics (often penicillin G) or a third generation cephalosporin, along with supportive measures,  The first-choice of antibiotic in adults who are not critically ill is usually oral doxycycline or azithromycin, starting within 48 hours of illness.  In mild infection, the role of antibiotics is unclear,  Prognosis  The majority of leptospiral infections are self-limiting. With severe cases that progress to Weil's disease, the mortality rates are approximately 20% in developing countries and around 5% in the United Kingdom. Listeria Listeria is an infection caused by Gram-positive bacteria transmitted via contaminated food.  Overview Key Facts  Listeria is an infection caused by Gram-positive bacteria transmitted via contaminated food.  Tends to be asymptomatic or cause febrile gastroenteritis in immunocompetent hosts.  Has the potential to cause sepsis, meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess and endocarditis in immunocompromised hosts.  Pregnant women usually have a mild clinical picture, but the effects of congenital listeriosis can be devastating.

DR. JAM  Diagnosis is via blood cultures.  Treatment for systemic listeriosis is ampicillin.  Complications of listeriosis include cardiac valve insufficiency and residual neurological damage from meningitis. Gastroenteritis alone tends to be self-limiting.  Approximately one-fifth of fetal listeriosis results in septic abortion or stillbirth. Epidemiology  The third leading cause of death from foodborne illness in the USA.  Has a predilection for pregnant women, neonates, adults over the age of 65 and immunocompromised hosts.  Most cases are sporadic, occurring in high-income countries.  Listeria spp. can be found in the stool of 5% of healthy adults. Aetiology  Listeriosis is caused by a motile, Gram-positive, anaerobic bacillus.  There are six species of Listeria, but only Listeria monocytogenes is able to infect humans.  Listeria is widespread in nature and transmission is usually through ingestion of contaminated food, such as unpasteurised milk products, raw vegetables, soft cheeses and raw meat and fish.  Rarely it is transmitted vertically, either transplacentally or through a contaminated birth canal. Pathophysiology  The severity of the disease depends on the immunological function of the host.  Immunocompromised patients, older adults, pregnant women and neonates are at particular risk due to impaired cellular immunity.  Incubation time is 10–70 days.  The listeria organism is an intracellular pathogen that uses host cell nutrients for proliferation.  It has mechanisms that allow a degree of immune escape:  actin rocket tails allow movement intracellularly and from cell to cell  listeriolysin produced by the pathogen mediates escape from the phagosome into the cytoplasm and inactivation of T-cell receptors.  It is able to invade the intestinal epithelium and enter the bloodstream. It can invade every organ but tends to migrate to the central nervous system and placenta.  It requires iron for metabolism and division. Iron overload is therefore a risk factor for listeriosis.  Clinical Presentation  In immunocompetent hosts the infection is usually asymptomatic but may cause febrile gastroenteritis, presenting with fever, diarrhoea and abdominal pain.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Listeriosis in pregnancy:  pregnant women tend to develop a mild flu-like illness with fever, arthralgia, headache, fatigue, diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain  it may be asymptomatic in some women  however, listeriosis can cause fetal loss, premature delivery and neonatal bacteraemia and meningitis.  Listeriosis in neonates:  unlike maternal illness, neonatal listeriosis is serious  early onset:  symptoms occur in the first 7 days of life  the mother is likely to have had a flu-like illness described above  neonates are frequently born pre-term and associated with chorioamnionitis  the fetus presents with features of septicaemia, meningitis or pneumonia, such as fever, lethargy, irritability, diarrhoea, poor feeding, vomiting and respiratory distress  granulomatosis infantiseptica is the most severe form, presenting with disseminated abscesses and granulomas in multiple organs, including the liver, spleen, lungs and intestines.  late-onset:  more often associated with meningitis  fetuses tend to be born to asymptomatic mothers.  Listeriosis in immunocompromised hosts:  features of CNS involvement (meningitis, encephalitis and brain abscess) include fever, headache, drowsiness, cranial nerve deficits, cerebellar signs, seizures and focal neurological signs  less commonly it can cause endocarditis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, peritonitis and endophthalmitis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  viral gastroenteritis, eg rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus  bacterial gastroenteritis, eg Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., Shigell a spp.  other causes of meningitis, eg Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae  other causes of encephalitis, eg varicella-zoster virus, HIV, echovirus, coxsackievirus.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bedside:  urine pregnancy test.  Laboratory:  full blood count – leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia

DR. JAM  blood cultures  lumbar puncture and CSF analysis – elevated protein, decreased glucose, positive Gram stain and culture  listeria serology, food analysis and stool cultures – may be performed in outbreaks or severe infections  placenta and amniotic fluid culture – when neonatal infection is suspected; may be combined with cervical swab culture to aid diagnosis  meconium culture – may help to diagnose neonatal listeriosis.  Imaging:  head computed tomography or magnetic resonance imagining – when CNS infection is suspected  echocardiography – when endocarditis is suspected.  Management  Listeria gastroenteritis is usually self-limiting, requiring supportive treatment only, such as fluid hydration.  Antibiotic treatment is required in patients with febrile gastroenteritis who are immunocompromised, over the age of 60 years or pregnant. Amoxicillin or co-trimoxazole for 3–5 days is first-line.  In patients with systemic infection or meningitis/meningoencephalitis, ampicillin is the first-line agent and may be combined with gentamicin.  Patients with bacteraemia generally receive 14 days of antibiotics, whereas meningitis/meningoencephalitis receive 21 days and endocarditis and brain abscess require up to 6 weeks of therapy.  Prognosis  Approximately one-fifth of fetal listeriosis results in septic abortion or stillbirth.  Complications of listeriosis include cardiac valve insufficiency and residual neurological damage from meningitis.  Gastroenteritis is usually self-limiting. In immunocompromised patients, meningitis is particularly dangerous, with a mortality rate of up to 55%. Lyme Disease Lyme disease is a bacterial infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected blacklegged ticks, leading to symptoms such as fever, fatigue, joint pain and a characteristic "bull's-eye" rash, if left untreated, it can cause more severe complications affecting the heart, joints, and nervous system.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Infection with the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi (or other species of the genus Borrelia), with ixodid ticks as the vector.  It is an endemic disease in many areas of the northern hemisphere.  There are three main stages of infection, usually starting with the pathognomonic feature of erythema migrans and later the development of arthritis.  Lyme disease can often be missed or misdiagnosed; it is often detected following serology testing for medically unexplained symptoms.  First-line treatment is oral antibiotics (doxycycline or amoxicillin) for three weeks.  Lyme disease can be self-limiting without treatment; patients treated early with antibiotics have a reduced illness duration.  Approximately 5–10% develop chronic complications (eg Lyme arthritis), despite antibiotic treatment. Epidemiology  It is the most common vector-borne illness in the northern hemisphere.  Seen in the United States (US), Europe, Russia, East Asia and South-east Asia.  Responsible for approximately one-quarter of cases of facial palsy in endemic areas.  Annual incidence is approximately 2000–3000 cases in England and Wales.  Approximately 2% of people in Europe/US develop Lyme disease following a tick bite.  Location differences with the most common causative species:  North America – Borrelia burgdorferi  Europe’s most common – Borrelia garinii and Borrelia afzelii. Aetiology  Caused by an infection with a bacterium within the Borrelia genus; the species group from this genus that causes Lyme disease can be named as a group ‘Borreliella’.  Deer are the main carrier of the bacteria and the ticks (ixodid species) become infected from feeding on them.  The ticks are normally active in rural woodlands in spring and early summer, and occasionally in early autumn.  Transmission occurs via the ticks biting humans (often lower limbs from grass) and, as a result, staying attached.  Infection risk is reduced greatly if the tick can be detected and removed within 48 hours.  Prevention of the initial tick bite is the main disease-reducing factor (eg in endemic areas – insect repellent and keeping lower-limb skin well covered).  No vaccine is currently available.

DR. JAM  Chronic complications have been linked to an extended period in the 'active infection’ stage; however, the development of complications despite treatment is not fully understood. Pathophysiology  The initial infection (stage 1) develops due to ticks carrying the bacteria infecting the patient. This normally leads to a localised inflammatory and infective response. This stage often does not progress further with adequate antibiotic treatment.  Bacterial dissemination leads to the development of features beyond the localised skin response (ie stages 2 and 3 of the disease).  It is not known why chronic complications, or dissemination, may occur despite antibiotic treatment showing infection resolution. Some thoughts are that it might be due to an abnormal immune response or re-infection.  Clinical Presentation  A positive history of tick bite or outdoor activity in endemic areas is common.  There are three clinical stages of the infection if insufficiently or untreated: Stage Features Time

Localised infection  Erythema migrans at the bite site  Features include:  red/purple/pink colour  round or oval  mostly flat, some have raised rash border  5% have central vesicle/pustule  ‘central sparing’ or typical ‘target-like’ appearance in 65–80% of European cases and only 20–35% of US cases  Regional lymphadenopathy  Fever  Headache Approximately 1–4 weeks post tick bite

Rash and complications  Further rash distribution in some (eg many < 5 cm areas of erythema migrans)  Others develop myalgia  Approximate complication rates:  25% arthritis  15% neurological (eg meningitis, cranial/peripheral neuritis) Weeks– months post stage 1

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI commonly presenting with facial palsy  5% cardiac involvement (eg heart block, pericarditis)

Chronic complications  Chronic oligoarthritis in 10% affected (knees most common site)  Chronic neurological disease  Acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (widespread dermal atrophy, peripheral nerve involvement + possible dermal sclerosis) Months–years later  A rarer manifestation of the disease might be eye symptoms, eg uveitis or keratitis.  Example of erythema migrans: An example of erythema migrans.https://phil.cdc.gov/Details.aspx?pid=9874 License: public domain  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  simple hypersensitivity reaction to a tick bite  insect-bite hypersensitivity  spider bites  chronic fatigue syndrome  other infections, eg cellulitis, fungal  other dermatological, eg erythema multiforme, urticaria, granuloma annulare  other inflammatory arthritis, eg rheumatoid, reactive.

DR. JAM  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis of Lyme disease is normally based on clinical history (eg of tick bite/outdoor activity in endemic areas), supported by examination and investigation findings.  Erythema migrans is a pathognomonic feature of Lyme and diagnosis can be made on its presence alone.  Lyme disease can often be missed or misdiagnosed. It is often detected following serology testing for medically unexplained symptoms.  First-line investigations – routine bloods and blood cultures, lesion skin swabs for microbiology, culture and sensitivity (MC&S), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) antibody testing (request ‘Lyme-specific’ IgG/IgM), ECG and exclude differentials (eg urinalysis).  Second-line investigations may be needed for diagnostic confirmation, eg CSF analysis, imaging, immunoblot antibody testing. Results indicating Lyme disease  Microbiological detection of the Borreliella spp. in the skin, blood or CSF.  In blood:  IgM (detected within the first month postinfection) and IgG against Borrelia spp. (positive ELISA results confirmed with immunoblotting)  markers of inflammation and/or infection eg raised white cell count, raised C-reactive protein, raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (in stages 2 and 3 biochemical markers of active infection are absent). Limitations of antibody serology  Clinical features might precede antibody formation.  May show previous, not current, infection.  Cannot be used to determine antibiotic efficacy.  Approximately 3–5% are seropositive without any clinical manifestation.  If the ELISA test is negative and performed:  > 4 weeks and Lyme is still suspected, the ELISA needs repeating  > 12 weeks and Lyme is still suspected, immunoblot is needed.  For diagnostic confirmation, immunoblot testing is always performed after a positive ELISA, but, even if immunoblotting is negative and Lyme is still suspected, then specialty referral is needed.  Management  Early antibiotic treatment is important, without waiting for test results or further referral.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Community management can occur if erythema migrans is the isolated feature.  Referral (eg to neurology, dermatology, cardiology, rheumatology) is needed if:  the patient has more features than erythema migrans  there is diagnostic uncertainty  there is primary treatment failure.  Response to treatment is based on clinical assessment of signs/symptoms, not typically bloodwork.  With poor treatment response – diagnosis should be reconsidered, compliance assessed, risk of re-infection assessed or whether chronic complications have developed despite antibiotics. Non-pharmacological  Patient education, including:  prevention of re-infection  that ongoing symptoms do not often represent active infection – and resolution might take months or years, or the symptoms represent a permanent/chronic complication.  Support for clinical features, eg physiotherapy for arthritis.  Referral to a specialist often is needed.  Inform patients that there is a risk of a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction with antibiotic treatment and that this should not be mistaken for allergy or impair treatment compliance.  Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction:  self-limiting reaction to antibiotics in Lyme thought to be secondary to bacterial death  onset – hours first  few days following  start of antibiotics  symptoms:  worsening fever  myalgia and headache  duration 3–48 hours  post-onset  management:  symptom support. Pharmacological  Early stages – oral antibiotics for three weeks, eg typically amoxicillin or doxycycline; if treatment has failed – trial of alterative oral antibiotic.  Late disease – intravenous antibiotics, eg ceftriaxone is a typical choice.  A third antibiotic is not normally considered unless the case is discussed with a national reference laboratory or further specialist input.  Prophylaxis of Lyme disease with antibiotics, following tick bite and removal, is not usually recommended.

DR. JAM  Prognosis  Lyme can be self-limiting without treatment.  Patients treated early with antibiotics have a reduced illness duration.  Approximately 5–10% develop chronic complications, despite following antibiotic treatment. Chronic complications of Lyme disease include arthritis and neurological and dermatological illnesses. Malaria Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by five different Plasmodium species spread by a common vector – the female Anopheles mosquito.  Overview Key Facts  Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by five different Plasmodium species spread by a common vector – the female Anopheles mosquito.  It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, South East Asia and parts of South America.  It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide with over 200 million cases each year.  The most severe form of disease is caused by Plasmodium falciparum.  Important signs of severe malaria include reduced level of consciousness, seizures, hypoglycaemia, oliguria, raised lactate and acidosis.  The key diagnostic test is serial thick and thin malaria blood films.  Treatment depends on severity, organism and local resistance profiles.  Simple measures taken to prevent malaria include use of mosquito nets and repellent sprays, and taking chemoprophylaxis before travelling to affected areas. Epidemiology  Over 200 million cases are reported each year, causing approximately 600 000 deaths.  Most deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, and the highest mortality is seen amongst children < 5 years.  Worldwide, mortality is highest in sub-Saharan Africa, but it occurs throughout the tropics. Aetiology  Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by five different Plasmodium species:  P. falciparum

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  P. vivax  P. ovale  P. malariae  P. knowlesi.  P. falciparum most commonly causes severe disease and accounts for most deaths due to malaria.  All malaria parasites are transmitted by a common vector – female Anopheles mosquitoes – which require blood for the development of their eggs.  Parasites can also be transmitted by blood transfusion.  Different species show distinct incubation periods – P. falciuparum is usually 7-14 days, but may be longer. Incubation periods are longer for other species. Pathophysiology  Female Anopheles mosquitoes inoculate human hosts with sporozoites when feeding.  Sporozites travel to liver cells where they replicate (schizont).  The schizont ruptures, leading to the release of merozoites which infected red blood cells:  merozoites induce periodic haemolysis, which gives rise to the anaemia, jaundice (high circulating unconjugated bilirubin) and swinging fevers seen in malaria.  Red blood cell (RBC) lysis leads to further release of merozoites and cyclical infection.  P. vivax and P. ovale have an additional ‘hypnozoite’ stage in which parasites remain dormant within the liver, which can cause relapse months or even years after the primary infection. Life cycle of malaria parasite:

DR. JAM Source: https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/about/biology/  Clinical Presentation  Major clinical features include:  fever  headache  rigors  myalgia  diarrhoea  jaundice – mostly pre-hepatic, due to haemolysis (often leads to initial misdiagnosis as acute hepatitis).  Key complications of malaria include:  cerebral malaria – reduced level of consciousness, seizures and focal neurological disorders with no meningism  renal failure – ‘Blackwater fever’ (dark urine due to high volume of haemoglobin within urine) – may necessitate urgent haemofiltration  severe anaemia – haemolysis and bone marrow suppression  hypoglycaemia  algid malaria – malaria complicated by sepsis caused by Gram negative organisms  thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy  hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly (‘tropical splenomegaly syndrome’) – massive splenomegaly, which may resolve with continuing antimalarial therapy.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis include:  dengue fever  acute viral hepatitis  haemolytic anaemia.  Differential diagnosis of cerebral malaria (reduced level of consciousness, seizures and fevers):  viral encephalitis  bacterial meningoencephalitis  trypanosomiasis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The investigation of choice is a malaria blood film:  gold standard = 3× thick and thin blood films over 24-48 h  thick blood film is used to check for parasites and load (this test is more sensitive than thin films)  thin blood films then identify the species of the parasite.  Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are also useful in reaching a diagnosis of malaria:  they do not provide information about species or parasite load.  Other important tests to assess the severity of the infection include:  bloods – full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E), liver function tests (LFTs) and C-reactive protein (CRP):  FBC – anaemia, thrombocytopenia and raised white cell count (WCC)  LFTs – raised bilirubin, alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and often normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  U&E – to exclude acute kidney injury (AKI) in context of severe algid malaria  venous blood gas (VBG) – acidosis, lactate and glucose  chest X-ray – exclude pulmonary oedema.  Features of severe malaria:  laboratory features:  anaemia heamoglobin (Hb) < 50 g/dL  hypoglycaemia < 2.2 mmol/l  metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.30  lactataemia with lactate > 5  clinical features – impaired consciousness or seizures (cerebral malaria), oliguria, shock (blood pressure [BP] < 90/60) and haemoglobinuria (Blackwater fever).

DR. JAM  Management Non-Pharmacological  Malaria is a notifiable disease and Public Health England must be informed if a case is diagnosed.  Basic preventive measures – mosquito nets and repellent sprays. Pharmacological  Malaria chemoprophylaxis can significantly reduce the risk of infection:  usually taken by travellers in endemic areas; local populations have a degree of immunity and therefore rarely take medications to prevent infection  agents either prevent formation of schizonts within the liver or kill merozoite parasites that have replicated within infected red blood cells  recommended prophylactic drugs include doxycycline, atovaquone-proquanil (Malarone) and primaquine. Use varies based on local resistance patterns.  Malaria treatment depends on the causative organism and severity of the infection:  uncomplicated Falciparum malaria – artemesinin combination therapy taken as tablets for at least three days  severe Falciparum malaria – IV artesunate  second line treatment is five-day course of IV quinine followed by a second agent (eg doxycycline) for seven days.  Prognosis  Untreated severe malaria is nearly always fatal.  Disease severity may progress rapidly over hours.  Of the > 200 million cases of malaria diagnosed worldwide each year, more than 500 000 are fatal.  Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria carries the highest mortality. P. vivax infection is also associated with severe anaemia, acute kidney injury and splenic rupture. Measles Measles is a preventable and potentially fatal infective disease caused by the RNA morbillivirus.  Overview Key Facts  Measles is a preventable and potentially fatal infective disease caused by the RNA morbillivirus.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Most patients recover; however, it may cause respiratory or neurological complications. This is most likely in high-risk groups.  Clinical features include generalised signs and/or symptoms of viral infection, a rash and the pathognomonic Koplik’s spots.  Immunisation in the United Kingdom (UK) occurs via the MMR vaccine at 12 and 40 months.  Measles is a notifiable disease and should be reported to Public Health England who will assist with testing and controlling the spread.  In most people, measles is a self-limiting illness and supportive treatment only is required.  Complications can be neurological (seizures, encephalitis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis) and/or secondary bacterial infection (otitis media, pneumonia). Fatality ratios range widely from approximately 0.01% to 5%. Epidemiology  It was previously endemic in the UK.  It is relatively rare following the MMR vaccine introduction in 1988 (< 1000 cases in 2019 vs up to 100 000 cases per annum in the 1980s).  Complication rates in developed countries are between 10% and 20%, but much higher in the developing world.  In 2016 there were around 90 000 deaths worldwide. Aetiology  In a susceptible population (those without full vaccination or previous immunity) one infectious person will infect 15–20 individuals.  Infection usually emerges from foreign travel or in clusters of those who have not had the MMR vaccine. Pathophysiology  Measles is caused by a morbillivirus (RNA virus) which is airborne and very contagious.  Spread is airborne via droplets (sneezing, coughing, close contact) and by direct contact with respiratory tract secretions.  Infections originate in the respiratory tract, where secondary infections often occur.  Once infected, a person has life-long immunity.
