JAM  the not fully immunised  pregnant women.  In the majority, measles is self-limiting within a week.  Supportive management is sufficient for most (good hydration, rest, paracetamol and/or ibuprofen).  Assess a patient’s vaccination status and enquire about contact with those with measles.  Admission needed if there is associated pneumonia or neurological complications.  Reducing spread is important. Patients should avoid contact with high-risk groups and stay at home from work or school for at least four days from the start of rash development. Susceptible health workers need urgent assessment and isolation as they may cause transmission. Notification  Measles is a Notifiable Disease and the local health protection team (HPT) should be informed if suspected.  The HPT will assist with managing measles in the pregnant, the immunocompromised and infants.  Once recovered, encourage any outstanding vaccinations in the patient.  Those who have been in contact with the patient may require a ‘post-exposure’ vaccination. This is ideally done within 72 hours of exposure. Pregnant women may benefit from IM immunoglobulin.  Prognosis  Most people recover well at home combined with supportive treatment.  Measles in pregnancy leads to a higher risk of miscarriage, prematurity, intrauterine death and stillbirth. Fatality ratios range widely from approximately 0.01% to 5%. Molluscum Contagiosum Molluscum contagiosum is a skin infection that is caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, a type of poxvirus.  Overview Key Facts  Molluscum contagiosum is a skin infection that is caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, a type of poxvirus.  It is spread by direct contact (skin to skin, including sexual contact), but can also be spread by contact with contaminated surfaces, and via auto-inoculation.  The condition is common in children and immunocompromised individuals.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Lesions are clustered, pearly papules with a central umbilicus and numbers can range from a few to hundreds.  The condition is usually self-resolving (often by 18 months) and no treatment is required in immunocompetent people.  Patients should be given information regarding hygiene measures to prevent the spread of infection.  A referral is indicated if there is diagnostic uncertainty, history of immunocompromise or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, anogenital involvement, or extensive pain or persistent disease.  Rarely, there may be complications such as scarring, superimposed bacterial infection, or conjunctivitis or keratitis. Epidemiology  The exact prevalence is unknown, as most people with the condition do not seek medical intervention.  Incidence seems to be highest in pre-school age children. Aetiology  Risk factors include:  close contact with an affected individuals  immunocompromise, such as HIV infection  tropical climates  atopic eczema. Pathophysiology  Molluscum contagiosum is caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, a type of poxvirus.  Clinical Presentation  Molluscum contagiosum presents as:  clusters of small round papules  range in size from 1 to 6 mm  colour can vary from shades of white, pink or brown  often look shiny or waxy  there is a central pit (umbilicus)  numbers can range from a few to hundreds (larger numbers and larger atypical lesions are more common in immunocompromised).  It is often found in areas that are warm and moist, such as creases and armpits.  In adults, sexual contact can cause lesions on the genitalia, pubis, thighs and lower abdomen.  Lesions are usually asymptomatic unless they become inflamed or develop an eczematous-type reaction.  Molluscum contagiosum on child’s armpit:

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  bacterial skin infection  eczema  milia  warts.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is predominantly clinical; the classic appearance usually excludes other conditions.  Diagnostic investigations are not usually necessary.  Dermatologist input may be required if there is diagnostic uncertainty.  Management  In most cases, no treatment is required.  Immunocompetent patients should be advised that most cases spontaneously resolve over a number of months to a year; in some cases, they may persist for longer periods.  Patients should be advised regarding hand hygiene and to not share towels, clothing and other personal items.  In immunocompromised patients, the infection may be very persistent.  Dermatology referral is indicated for patients who are severely immunocompromised, have extensive or painful disease, or if there is diagnostic uncertainty.  Sexual health referral may be indicated for persons with anogenital involvement.  HIV specialist referral may be required in patients with molluscum who have HIV.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Treatment, if indicated, can include either pharmacological treatments or surgical intervention. Pharmacological management  Antiseptics, eg hydrogen peroxide cream or povidoneiodine solution.  Podophyllotoxin cream.  Topical salicylic acid preparations.  Cantharidin solution.  Surgical management  Surgical (physical) treatments include:  curettage  laser  cryotherapy.  Note, these interventions can cause scarring.  Prognosis  Most cases resolve over time without medical intervention; most cases resolve in 18 months but some may persist for over 2 years.  The condition may cause distress to the patient regarding its appearance.  Complications are uncommon; they include:  bacterial infection  dermatitis  scarring  eye infection – conjunctivitis/keratitis. In people who are immunocompromised, lesions can persist for over 5 years. Mycoplasma Pneumonia Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an organism that causes respiratory illness, which can vary from mild respiratory symptoms to pneumonia.  Overview Key Facts  Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an organism that causes respiratory illness, which can vary from mild respiratory symptoms to pneumonia.  It is the most common cause of atypical pneumonia (5–15% of all pneumonia cases).  Mycoplasma pneumoniae tends to affect children and young adults; it occurs in epidemics every 3–4 years.

DR. JAM  There is typically a longer prodrome, usually greater than two weeks.  Signs and symptoms include:  cough  breathlessness  wheeze  pleuritic pain  fever (less common in the elderly)  increased work of breathing.  Extrapulmonary complications include:  pericarditis/myocarditis  erythema multiforme  erythema nodosum  Stevens–Johnson syndrome  haemolytic anaemia  disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  thrombocytopenia  meningoencephalitis  cranial and peripheral neuropathies  bullous myringitis  hepatitis  pancreatitis.  Severity can be graded using the CURB-65 score, which is also a prognostic indicator.  Treatment depends on the severity of the condition; this determines the route and type of antibiotic needed as well as the need for admission (up to 40% of cases).  Most cases resolve without treatment; in a small number of cases there may be complications and rarely the condition can be fatal. Epidemiology  Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes up to 15% of all cases of pneumonia and is the most common atypical organism cause of pneumonia. Aetiology  Mycoplasma pneumonia is caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae bacteria, which lack a cell wall and have an affinity for respiratory epithelial cells in humans. Pathophysiology  Mycoplasma pneumoniae is mainly a mucosal pathogen, but during disease it may have a systemic spread.  The pathogenicity of the organism may be due to the activation of cytokines and other inflammatory mediators.  Clinical Presentation  Mycoplasma pneumoniae tends to affect young adults; it occurs in epidemics every 3–4 years. There is typically a longer prodrome, usually of > two weeks.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Signs and symptoms include:  cough  breathlessness  wheeze  pleuritic pain  fever (less common in older patients)  increased work of breathing  extrapulmonary complications include:  pericarditis/myocarditis  erythema multiforme  erythema nodosum  Stevens–Johnson syndrome  haemolytic anaemia  disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  thrombocytopenia  meningoencephalitis  cranial and peripheral neuropathies  bullous myringitis  hepatitis  pancreatitis.  Differential Diagnosis Other causes of pneumonia include:  Streptococcus pneumoniae (60–70% of all cases of pneumonia).  Haemophilus influenzae.  Staphylococcus aureus.  Gram-negative organisms.  Other atypical organisms:  Legionella pneumophila  Chlamydia psittaci  Chlamydia pneumoniae  Coxiella burnetii (Q fever).  Viral causes:  influenza  varicella-zoster  cytomegalovirus (CMV).  Other differentials:  asthma  acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)  pulmonary embolism (PE)  tuberculosis (TB)  whooping cough  post-natal drip

DR. JAM  gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Clinical judgement should be used to diagnose the condition alongside history and examination.  If the patient has signs and symptoms of community-acquired pneumonia, assess for severity using the CRB-65 score:  confusion (< 8/10 score on the abbreviated mental test (AMT))  respiratory rate > 30 breaths/min  blood pressure (BP) < 90 mmHg and/or diastolic <60 mmHg  age > 65 years.  Investigations in primary care include:  pulse oximetry (urgent admission for saturations less than 90%)  chest X-ray if there is suspected underlying lung pathology, or if the diagnosis is uncertain (not usually initially required in the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia)  sputum culture – in moderate severity, cases managed in the community.  All patients who are admitted to hospital with suspected severe pneumonia should have the following tests performed on admission as per British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines:  oxygenation saturations  arterial blood gases if necessary – may show type I respiratory failure  chest X-ray to allow accurate diagnosis  bloods:  C-reactive protein (CRP) to aid diagnosis and as a baseline measure  full blood count (FBC) – white cell count is often normal in Mycoplasma pneumoniae  cold agglutinins occur in 50% of cases  liver function tests (LFTs) which may demonstrate transient hepatitis  urea and electrolyte tests (U&Es) to inform severity assessment. Specific tests for Mycoplasma pneumoniae  Where available, PCR of sputum should be the method of choice for confirming the diagnosis of mycoplasma pneumonia.  In the absence of a sputum or lower respiratory tract sample, if mycoplasma pneumonia is suspected, a throat swab for Mycoplasma pneumoniae PCR is recommended.  Serology with the complement fixation test and a range of other assays may also be available.  Mycoplasma pneumonia chest X-ray (child):

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Two chest x-rays in the case of a child with a case of mycoplasma pneumonia.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Smoking cessation should be advised in the long term for patients with pneumonia.  Patients with a score of 3 or above using the CURB-65 score require urgent hospital admission.  Admission should be considered with a score of 1 or 2.  Home treatment should be considered in patients with a score of 0 (take into account comorbidities, general frailty, pulse oximetry values and if the patient is pregnant).  If hospital admission is not required, advise rest, hydration and the use of simple analgesia for symptom relief (alongside antibiotic treatment). Pharmacological  If pneumonia is classed as low severity (based on CURB-65 score of 0 and clinical judgement) with atypical organisms suspected, the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends:  oral doxycycline 200 mg on the first day then 100 mg once a day for four days (total course of five days), or  oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice a day for five days, or  oral erythromycin (in pregnancy) 500 mg four times a day for five days.  If moderate severity (based on clinical judgement and a CURB 65 of 1 or 2) and it is appropriate for the adult patient to be managed in the community:  oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for five days and oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice a day for five days, or  oral erythromycin (in pregnancy) 500 mg four times a day for five days

DR. JAM  if penicillin-allergic, use oral doxycycline 200 mg on the first day then 100 mg once a day for four days (total course of 5 days), or oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice a day for five days.  In children with suspected atypical infection:  oral clarithromycin 250–500 mg twice a day for five days, or  oral erythromycin (in pregnancy) 250–500 mg four times a day for five days, or  oral doxycycline 200 mg on the first day, then 100 mg once a day for four days (total course of five days).  In hospital:  non-severe cases – oral amoxicillin and a macrolide (eg clarithromycin)  severe – intravenous (IV) broad-spectrum, beta-lactamase, stable antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav and a macrolide in severe cases  newer fluoroquinolones (eg moxifloxacin) provide an alternative for patients who are allergic to penicillin or macrolides  IV treatment should be stepped down to oral treatment after 48 hours provided that the patient is improving  if a specific organism is isolated, the appropriate antibiotic is given  treatment should continue for 7–10 days depending on response  up to 21 days of treatment is recommended for legionella pneumonia.  Prognosis  Markers of increased pneumonia severity (and therefore poorer prognosis) include:  hypoxaemia (PO2 8 kPa despite oxygen therapy)  multilobar involvement  white cell count < 4.3 x 109/l or > 20.3 x 109/l  hypoalbuminaemia  positive blood cultures. All though the prognosis is generally good with treatment, some patients may go on to develop severe pneumonia, which can lead to complications such as deterioration of renal function, aplastic anaemia, Stevens–Johnson syndrome and, very rarely, encephalitis. Necrotising Fasciitis Skin infections can be superficial (erysipelas), spread to subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis) or infect deep subcutaneous tissue and fascia (necrotising fasciitis).

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Skin infections can be superficial (erysipelas), spread to subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis) or infect deep subcutaneous tissue and fascia (necrotising fasciitis).  Necrotising fasciitis is an uncommon but acute and threatening medical emergency, caused by infection spreading to deep subcutaneous tissue and fascia.  Occasionally the infection can also spread to the muscles.  It is associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality, even with treatment.  Toxins released by the causative organism result in ischaemia, thrombosis and tissue destruction which is rapidly progressive.  The common causes of necrotising fasciitis are Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus spp. and Clostridium perfringens.  The condition can be divided into four types depending on the causative organism:  type I – polymicrobial infection (anaerobic and aerobic bacteria)  type II – group A streptococci (GAS)  type III – marine organisms  type IV – fungal infection.  Infections occur when the skin barriers are compromised, which could be through trauma, ulcers or skin disorders.  This can occur in healthy individuals, but risk factors include immunocompromise, chronic liver or renal disease, diabetes, malignancy and substance abuse.  The condition can affect any part of the body but usually involves the extremities, perineum or trunk.  Signs and symptoms develop over a few days but can progress much more rapidly in some cases, such as infection caused by marine organisms and fungi.  The presenting signs are usually non-specific skin changes (redness, swelling) and accompanied by pyrexia.  The person is usually systemically very unwell and may appear to have disproportionate pain before skin changes progress.  Necrosis and gangrene of the skin occurs as the infection progresses.  Clostridium perfringens causes gas production that can produce a crepitus below the skin.  The diagnosis is predominantly clinical; there should be a strong index of suspicion in patients presenting with severe pain.  Patients with the condition require management in an intensive care setting.  Necrotising fasciitis requires urgent and early surgical debridement to prevent spread and complications.  Patients may require amputation to prevent spread, or surgical reconstruction to affected areas due to large areas of tissue loss.  Necrotising fasciitis is associated with a high rate of complications and mortality, which may be due to renal failure and sepsis.

DR. JAM  Death may occur in up to 40% even with surgical intervention; prognosis is worse in patients with delayed diagnosis and in those with diabetes. Epidemiology The condition is relatively rare, with an incidence of approximately 500 cases per annum in the United Kingdom (UK). Aetiology  The common causes of necrotising fasciitis are:  Staphylococcus aureus  Streptococcus spp.  Clostridium perfringens.  Necrotising fasciitis can be divided into four types, depending on the causative organism.  Each type has its own risk factors for infection.  Type I:  polymicrobial infection with aerobic and anaerobic bacteria  usually in patients with immunocompromise or chronic disease.  Type II:  group A streptococci (GAS)  occurs in any age group and in otherwise healthy people  occasionally accompanied by staphylococcal infection.  Type III:  Gram-negative monomicrobial infection  includes marine organisms such as Vibrio spp. and Aeromonas hydrophila  occurs following sea-water contamination of wounds, fish fin or sting trauma, or raw seafood consumption – particularly in patients with chronic liver disease.  Type IV:  fungal infection  zygomycetes following traumatic wounds or burns  candida infection in the immunocompromised. Pathophysiology  Infection occurs when the skin barriers are compromised, which could be through trauma, ulcers or skin disorders.  Toxins released by the causative organism result in ischaemia, thrombosis and tissue destruction.  Clinical Presentation  Presenting features may include both skin signs and systemic features such as hypotension and fever.  The condition can affect any part of the body but usually involves the extremities, perineum or trunk.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The presenting signs are usually non-specific skin changes (redness/purple rash, blistering or swelling) accompanied by pyrexia.  The person is usually systemically very unwell and may appear to have disproportionate pain around the affected site before skin changes progress.  Necrosis and gangrene of the skin occurs as the infection progresses.  Clostridium perfringens causes gas production that can produce a crepitus below the skin on palpation.  The presence of skin bullae is usually diagnostic.  Fournier's gangrene is a specific form of the condition that affects the perineum or genitalia:  it is rapidly progressive and causes thrombosis of the small subcutaneous vessels and necrosis of the overlying skin.  Early necrotising fasciitis of the leg:  Progressed necrotising fasciitis of the leg:

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  cellulitis  deep vein thrombosis  septic arthritis  acute gout  thrombophlebitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is predominantly clinical; there is no particular diagnostic test and there should be a high index of suspicion.  The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis (LRINEC) parameters can guide diagnosis:  raised C-reactive protein (CRP), white blood cells (WBCs), creatinine and glucose  low haemoglobin and sodium.  Other tests to confirm diagnosis and extent include X-rays which may show gas in the soft tissues and MRI to show the extent of spread.  However, diagnosis can only be confirmed by exploratory surgery, which should be used to confirm or exclude the condition.  Testing should not lead to a delay in surgical exploration if there is strong clinical suspicion.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Admission to the Intensive Care Unit.  Oxygen.  Fluids.  Maintain blood pressure.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pharmacological  Intravenous (IV) antibiotics (broad-spectrum antibiotics such as benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin) and adjust after sensitivities.  If group A streptococci (GAS) organisms are the cause, consider antibiotic prophylaxis for contacts.  Surgical  Surgical debridement to remove all tissue affected is the mainstay of treatment.  This should be carried out without delay if there is strong clinical suspicion of the condition, to avoid further spread of infection and associated complications.  Amputation may be required to contain infection and prevent spread.  Patients may also require plastic surgery to replace lost tissue.  Prognosis  The condition is rapidly progressive and is associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality.  Necrotising fasciitis can have detrimental complications, such as:  tissue necrosis  rhabdomyolysis  nerve damage  renal failure  sepsis  death – in up to 40% of cases even with surgical intervention.  Prognosis is worse when there is delayed diagnosis, poor surgical debridement or co-exisiting diabetes. Necrotising fasciitis caused by marine organisms and fungal infection can be particularly virulent and can cause death within 48 hours. Neurological And Ophthalmic Disease In Advanced HIV Neurological disease can be the first presentation of AIDS in 10% of patients with the condition and is associated with significant disability and mortality.  Overview Key Facts  Neurological disease can be the first presentation of AIDS in 10% of patients with the condition and is associated with significant disability and mortality.

DR. JAM  Important presentations include hemiparesis and seizures (focal disorders) and confusion and drowsiness (generalised disorders).  Sub-clinical opportunistic CNS infection can also be unmasked after starting treatment with highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) due to immune reconstitution syndrome (IRIS).  Prolonged HIV infection also has direct neurotropic effects, notably HIV dementia.  Focal neurological disease in advanced HIV caused by toxoplasmosis and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (meningitis and abscesses) and carries a high mortality.  Reduced level of consciousness is seen in cryptococcal meningitis, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis.  AIDS may also affect any layer of the eye:  the most clinically significant causes of retinitis in patients with AIDS are CMV infection and toxoplasmosis. Epidemiology  HAART has significantly reduced the global incidence of opportunistic CNS infections over the last 10-20 years.  The most common CNS infections in advanced HIV are:  toxoplasmosis – accounts for 90% focal lesions in HIV and occurs in 10% AIDS patients. Key risk factor is exposure to infected cat faeces  cryptococcal meningitis – cause a subacute meningitic illness in 5-10% AIDS patients  PML  CMV encephalitis  aggressive and atypical neurosyphilis.  CMV retinitis occurs in up to a quarter of untreated patients with AIDS. Aetiology Focal neurological disease in AIDS:  toxoplasmosis  TB meningitis. Generalised neurological disease in AIDS:  cryptococcal meningitis  PML – JC virus  CMV encephalitis. Pathophysiology  Low CD4 count causes defective T cell and humoral responses, and increases susceptibility to opportunistic infection.  HIV retrovirus also has direct effects on cognition and can cause progressive dementia.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Fever, headache, neck stiffness and reduced level of consciousness (meningitis) are seen in cryptococcal, bacterial, viral and tuberculous meningitis. Distinguishing features include:  cryptococcal meningitis – subacute presentation over 1-2 weeks, often combined with encephalitic features of disorientation and confusion  tuberculous meningitis – subacute presentation over several weeks, with associated constitutional symptoms of weight loss, night sweats and fever.  Cognitive impairment may manifest as mild impairment of social functioning through to incapacitation.  Focal neurological disease commonly presents with dysphasia, hemiparesis and seizures.  fever is non-specific additional symptom  other constitutional symptoms eg weight loss/night sweats could point to tuberculous meningitis and primary CNS lymphoma.  Important ocular symptoms include progressive visual blurring and floaters:  CMV retinitis typically presents subacutely over 1-2 weeks  characteristic findings on ophthalmoscopy are ‘creamycoloured’ retinal discoloration and overlying haemorrhages – ‘pizza-pie’ appearance  retinal toxoplasmosis produces a similar picture.  Patients with neurosyphilis can develop a highly aggressive and atypical form of disease characterised by myelopathy, retinitis and meningitis.

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Reduced level of consciousness:  cryptococcal meningitis  CMV encephalitis  PML.  Cognitive impairment:  AIDS dementia  vascular dementia  alzheimer’s dementia  PML.  Focal neurology:  TB meningitis  cerebral toxoplasmosis  primary CNS lymphoma  stroke.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Useful investigations include:  full blood count (FBC) and CRP (acute inflammatory response)  renal and liver function tests prior to initiating treatment  viral load and CD4 count  lumbar puncture for CSF microscopy, serology, and viral PCR.  In high resource settings, CT and MRI imaging are also useful:  cerebral toxoplasmosis manifests as solitary or multiple ring-enhancing lesions  MR imaging is more consistent than CT in PML, and typically shows consistent widespread small white matter lesions.  Cryptococcal meningitis can be confirmed by:  CSF staining with India ink - visualises yeast cells in 6080% patients  serology – serum cryptococcal antigen (CRAG) has a specificity and sensitivity > 99% in patients with HIV.  Besides neuroimaging, the investigation of choice for suspected toxoplasmosis infection is toxoplasma serology (positive in > 90% cases).  A typical CSF picture for tuberculous meningitis is low cell count (100-500) with lymphocytosis, low CSF glucose, and very high CSF protein:  AFB positive in around 70% of patients.  A definitive diagnosis of PML is made by brain biopsy, but this is rarely performed premortem. The investigations of choice are neuroimaging and CSF for JC virus DNA.  Investigations in patients with ophthalmic disease include:  CMV and toxoplasma IgG  CMV viral load.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The investigation of choice in patients with suspected neurosyphilis is serological testing (treponemal and nontreponemal tests).  Management Non-Pharmacological  All patients with suspected opportunistic eye infection require same-day referral to an ophthalmologist for further assessment. Pharmacological  It is always important to consider the underlying diagnosis of advanced HIV and institute HAART at the earliest opportunity (while remembering the risk of IRIS).  The treatment of choice for toxoplasmosis is pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine:  co-prescribe folinic acid to prevent bone marrow suppression.  Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV+ patients is usually managed with combination antifungal therapy – amphotericin B, flucytosine and fluconazole.  TB meningitis is managed with:  prolonged (6-12 month) combination therapy – isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, with pyridoxine prophylaxis for peripheral neuropathy  a weaning dose of steroids to mitigate the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome.  Neurosyphilis is managed with a 17 day course of IM penicillin and oral probenecid.  PML has no specific treatment – early introduction of HAART helps to reverse infection.  Patients with severe sight-threatening CMV retinitis require intravitreal AND oral antiviral therapy with intravitreal ganciclovir and intravenous valganciclovir.  Surgical  Patients with severe cerebral toxoplasmosis may develop secondary complications including CSF obstruction and hydrocephalus necessitating neurosurgical involvement.  This should be guided by neuroimaging.  Prognosis  HAART has significantly reduced the global incidence of opportunistic CNS infections over the last 10-20 years.  Focal neurological disease in advanced HIV caused by toxoplasmosis and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (meningitis and abscesses) and carries a high mortality.  10% of patients with cerebral toxoplasmosis will die. 25% will sustain enduring disability.

DR. JAM Parasitic Infections A parasite is an organism that lives on, or in, a host, and causes harm to a different host organism.  Overview Key Facts  A parasite is an organism that lives on, or in, a host, and causes harm to a different host organism.  Parasites commonly cause disease in humans.  Many parasites are types of helminth worms which:  can be grouped based on morphological characteristics  are rarely fatal  can be associated with significant morbidity and disability, particularly in low and middle income countries.  Patients may be asymptomatic with disease only detected after further investigation after a finding of isolated eosinophilia. This is seen in schistosomiasis, strongyloides and filariasis. Epidemiology  Global prevalence of helminth infection is estimated at 1.5 billion.  Morbidity correlates with the burden of disease – highest in hyperendemic regions.  Important consequences in children include:  poor nutrition and anaemia  direct disease complications such as intestinal obstruction  poor school performance.  Neurocysticercosis is thought to be the major cause of epilepsy worldwide.  Schistosomiasis is an important cause of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa (notably around Lake Malawi), South America and South East Asia.  S. mansoni; endemic in South America and Africa – associated with liver/GI disease  S. haematobium; endemic in sub-Saharan Africa – chronic infection associated with bladder cancer.  Lymphatic filariasis is a mosquito-borne parasitic infection common throughout the tropics.  Roundworm (ascaris lumriocoides) is one of the most common intestinal worm infections worldwide.  The most common parasitic worm infection in the UK is threadworms (enterobius vermicularis) which infests the gut. Aetiology  Most helminth infections are transmitted via faecal-oral route or direct inoculation of skin through the soil.  Important examples of parasitic worm infections include:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  threadworm (enterobius vemicularis)  tapeworms – cysticercosis, hydatid disease (echinococcus)  roundworms (nematodes) – lymphatic filariasis, loiasis, onchocerciasis and ascariasis  flatworms – schistosomiasis and liver fluke.  Several parasitic worm diseases are ‘zoonoses’ – they can be transmitted to humans from animals, such as:  hydatid (sheep and goats)  cysticercosis (pigs)  schistosomiasis (freshwater snails). Pathophysiology  Clinical disease can result from several different mechanisms:  direct impact of adult worm within tissues (eg ‘worm bolus’) causing intestinal obstruction in ascariasis.  deposition of immature parasite ‘daughter cells’ within tissues (eg onchocerciasis)  dissemination of disease through generation of cystic structures (eg neurocysticercosis and hydatid disease).  Stronglyoides infection is unusual in that the parasite can complete the full life cycle within the human host – illness can persist for many years after initial infection.  Hydatid is an unusual disease caused by propagating cysts formed by echinococcus granulosis. Cysts can develop within the liver and rarely in the lungs.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation varies with parasite type and with route of transmission.  Threadworm presents with intense perianal itching which is worse at night.  Hookworm commonly presents with symptomatic anaemia – reduced exercise tolerance, shortness of breath and fatigue.  Onchocerciasis presents with skin lesions and progressive eye disease with eventual blindness.  Neurocysticercosis presents with new onset epilepsy – frequently in teenagers.  Lymphatic filariasis presents with profound (often unilateral) lower limb swelling.  Strongyloides infection usually presents with diarrhoea and associated skin changes (larva currens rash) although hyperinfection (disseminated strongyloidiasis) in immunosuppressed presents as a Gram negative sepsis and organ failure.  Schistosomiasis can present with wide variety of symptoms at different time points:  acute cercarial dermatitis (‘swimmer’s itch’) - selflimiting, intensely pruritic erythematous papular rash within 24 hours of freshwater exposure  katayama fever (acute schistosomiasis) – fever, urticaria, diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly, wheeze and cough at 4-8 weeks post-infection  chronic disease manifestations vary with site of high worm burden:

DR. JAM  urinary tract – terminal haematuria, fibrosis and calcification  bowel and liver – bloody diarrhoea, splenomegaly, ascites and GI bleeding (due to periportal fibrosis and resultant portal hypertension).  Hydatid disease has a range of clinical presentations, depending on the site of hydatid cysts:  liver cysts – abdominal pain and distension  breathlessness – lung and cardiac involvement  early morning headaches, nausea and focal neurology – brain involvement  anaphylactoid-reaction due to rupture of abdominal or lung cysts. This is seen in around 2% of patients who experience cyst rupture.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis varies with region and clinical presentation.  Diarrhoea – strongyloides, hookworm, ascariasis and inflammatory bowel disease.  Liver lesion – hydatid disease, amoebic liver abscess, bacterial liver abscess, haematoma, simple cyst and malignancy.  Multiple brain lesions – neurocysticercosis, hydatid disease, toxoplasmosis and malignancy.  Asymptomatic eosinophilia – any parasitic infection, ChurgStrauss and drug reaction.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  full blood count (FBC) for eosinophilia  liver function and renal function.  Stool for multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS) and OCP (ova, cysts and parasites) – particularly useful in suspected strongyloides and hookworm infection.  Terminal urine (sample taken at end of urination) for OCP for suspected schistosomiasi  Specific investigations vary with suspected disease:  onchocerciasis – skin snips to detect microfilariae  neurocysticercosis – serology, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning  hydatid disease - echinococcus serology, ultrasound imaging  lymphatic filariasis – night-time blood for microscopy and serology.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Patients with neurocysticercosis are at significant risk of further seizures and require standard epilepsy advice – avoid driving, safety measures at home and around water.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pharmacological  Isolated hydatid cysts are often managed with prolonged (several weeks or months) courses of albendazole or praziquantel.  Lympatic filariasis – diethylcarbamazine (DEC).  Onchocerciasis – single dose ivermectin.  Hookworm – mebendazole.  Strongyloides – ivermectin or albendazole.  Schistosomiasis – praziquantel.  Threadworm – mebendazole.  Roundworm – mebendazole.  Surgical  Some hydatid cysts are managed using the PAIR (percutaneous aspiration, injection and reaspiration) procedure with appropriate steroid and antihelminth cover. Cysts are aspirated and injected with hypertonic saline to kill the daughter cysts within.  Extensive abdominal hydatid disease and any hydatid pulmonary or cardiac involvement usually require surgical removal – must be performed by expert surgeon to minimize risk of spilling cyst contents within abdominal cavity and further seeding.  Lymphatic filariasis involving the scrotum and causing severe hydrocoele may require surgical repair.  Prognosis  Prognosis varies with parasite sub-type and access to treatment. Despite antibiotic treatment, many patients with lymphatic filariasis will have residual deformity and oedema requiring surgical management. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Pelvic inflammatory disease is a general term for infection of the upper genital tract.  Overview Key Facts  Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is a general term for infection of the upper genital tract.  Infection spreads superiorly from the endocervix into the uterus, where it continues to the fallopian tubes and ovaries.  PID is almost always due to a sexually transmitted infection (STI).  Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common causative organism.

DR. JAM  Complications of PID include tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain.  Symptoms of PID include:  pelvic or lower abdominal pain (usually bilateral)  deep dyspareunia  abnormal vaginal bleeding (intermenstrual, postcoital, or 'breakthrough')  abnormal vaginal or cervical discharge  right upper quadrant pain  secondary dysmenorrhoea.  Signs of PID include:  lower abdominal tenderness (usually bilateral)  adnexal tenderness (with or without a palpable mass)  cervical motion tenderness  uterine tenderness (on bimanual vaginal examination)  abnormal cervical or vaginal mucopurulent discharge (on speculum examination)  fever (temperature is more often normal).  Women with suspected PID should ideally be managed in a genito-urinary medicine (GUM) clinic or other local specialist sexual health service.  Empirical broad spectrum antibiotics should be started as soon as possible if the condition is suspected to avoid risk of longterm complications.  Sexual contacts should be also be traced and managed appropriately.  Sexual abstinence (or a barrier method of contraception) is recommended until both the patient and her current partner (if applicable) have completed treatment. Epidemiology  According to a Public Health England (PHE) report on Rates of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) in England (2000–2013):  in 2011 in GP settings: the overall rate of definite/probable PID diagnoses among women aged 15– 44 years was 176 diagnoses per 100 000 person.  rates of PID diagnoses were highest among woman aged 20–24 years. Aetiology  Risk factors for developing PID include:  early age of first coitus  multiple sexual partners  tecent new partner (within the previous 3 months)  history of STI in the woman or her partner  unprotected intercourse.  Recent instrumentation of the uterus or interruption of the cervical barrier, such as due to:  termination of pregnancy

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Insertion of an intrauterine device (within the past 4–6 weeks, especially in women with preexisting gonorrhoea or C. trachomatis infection)  Hysterosalpingography  In vitro fertilization and intrauterine insemination. Pathophysiology  Pelvic inflammatory disease is a general term for infection of the upper genital tract.  Infection spreads upwards from the endocervix causing one or more of the following:  endometritis  salpingitis  parametritis  oophoritis  tubo-ovarian abscess  pelvic peritonitis. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is almost due to a sexually transmitted infection (STI):  Chlamydia trachomatis (14–35% of cases).  Neisseria gonorrhoeae (2–3% of cases).  Mycoplasma genitalium has been associated with upper genital tract infection in women and is a common cause of PID.  Organisms in normal vaginal flora (such as anaerobes, Gardnerella vaginalis, Haemophilus influenzae, enteric Gram-negative rods, and Streptococcus agalactiae) have also been implicated.  Pathogen-negative PID is common.  N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are detected less commonly in older women with PID.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms associated with PID include:  pelvic or lower abdominal pain (usually bilateral but can be unilateral)  deep dyspareunia particularly of recent onset  abnormal vaginal bleeding (intermenstrual, postcoital, or 'breakthrough') which may be secondary to associated cervicitis and endometritis  abnormal vaginal or cervical discharge as a result of associated cervicitis, endometritis, or bacterial vaginosis  this is often very slight and may be transient, especially with chlamydial infection  right upper quadrant pain due to peri-hepatitis (Fitz– Hugh–Curtis syndrome)  secondary dysmenorrhoea.  Signs associated with PID include:  lower abdominal tenderness (usually bilateral)

DR. JAM  adnexal tenderness (with or without a palpable mass), cervical motion tenderness, or uterine tenderness (on bimanual vaginal examination)  abnormal cervical or vaginal mucopurulent discharge (on speculum examination)  pyrexia, although the temperature is often normal.  Differential Diagnosis  Ectopic pregnancy.  Threatened abortion.  Ruptured corpus luteal cyst.  Acute appendicitis:  nausea and vomiting occur in most women with appendicitis, but in only 50% of women with PID.  cervical motion pain occurs in about 25% of women with acute appendicitis.  Endometriosis: the relationship between symptoms and the menstrual cycle may be helpful in establishing a diagnosis.  Gastrointestinal disorders, including irritable bowel syndrome, acute bowel infection, or diverticular disease.  Complications of an ovarian cyst, such as rupture, torsion, or haemorrhage; symptoms are often of sudden onset.  Urinary tract infection, often associated with dysuria and/or urinary frequency.  Functional pain (unknown physical origin).  Diagnosis/Investigation  A diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) should be made on clinical grounds.  Diagnosis and initiating treatment should not be delayed whilst waiting for the results of laboratory tests.  Negative swab results do not rule out a diagnosis of PID. Tests include:  High vaginal swab to rule out bacterial vaginosis & candidiasis.  Test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.  Bloods to check for elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), c-reactive protein (CRP), and leucocyte count supports the diagnosis of PID but is non-specific.  Management  There should be a low threshold for initiating empirical broad spectrum antibiotic treatment to prevent long term complications of PID Non-Pharmacological:  Management should take place in a sexual healthcare setting.  Sexual contacts should be traced and managed appropriately.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Sexual abstinence (or a barrier method of contraception) is recommended until both the patient and her current partner (if applicable) have completed treatment. Pharmacological: As per NICE recommendations:  If the risk of gonococcal infection is low, prescribe either:  ceftriaxone 1 g as a single intramuscular (IM) dose, followed by oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, plus oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days  oral ofloxacin 400 mg twice daily, plus oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days  levofloxacin (500 mg once daily for 14 days) may be used as a more convenient alternative to ofloxacin  oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily for 14 days.  If none of the first-line regimens are suitable, consider:  ceftriaxone 1 g as a single IM dose, followed by oral azithromycin 1 g per week for 2 weeks.  If the risk of gonococcal infection is high (for example the woman's partner has gonorrhoea, her symptoms and signs are clinically severe, or she has had sexual contact whilst abroad):  prescribe ceftriaxone 1 g as a single IM dose, followed by oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days.  For women infected with HIV:  offer the same treatment as women who are not infected with HIV  PID should be managed in conjunction with their HIV physician.  Treating pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)  Surgical:  Drainage of tub-ovarian abscesses can be undertaken should women present with sepsis or recurrent flare ups.  Prognosis  Prompt detection and early treatment reduces the risk of long term complications.  Severe and repeated episodes of PID are associated with a greater risk of these complications.  Complications of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) include:  infertility  ectopic pregnancy  chronic pelvic pain  tubo-ovarian abscess Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (rare complication of upper quadrant pain associated with peri-hepatitis especially when PID is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis infection).

DR. JAM Prescribing Safely (Breastfeeding And Pregnancy) A fetus or breastfed baby may be exposed to drugs due to a lack of maternal understanding and access to ante/postnatal care, additionally, maternal substance abuse can lead to exposure of drugs.  Overview Key Facts  Pregnancy  A fetus or breastfed baby may be exposed to drugs due to a lack of maternal understanding and access to ante/postnatal care, additionally, maternal substance abuse can lead to exposure of drugs.  There is a risk of women of childbearing age taking medications and then becoming pregnant during this period, leaving the growing fetus vulnerable to potentially harmful drug exposure, particularly if the mother has a history of chronic conditions.  There is little drug testing on pregnant and breastfeeding women for ethical reasons but this makes it difficult to advance in terms of effective prescribing for these patients.  In pregnancy, drugs with a molecular weight of < 100 Da can cross the placenta.  Healthcare professionals have a duty to discuss any risks and medication side effects in women of childbearing age who take medications that may be harmful in pregnancy and during lactation.  If a woman of childbearing age is taking a teratogenic drug such as lithium, she must be on an effective long-acting reversible contraception to avoid pregnancy.  Drugs that should be avoided in pregnancy include:  excessive caffeine  excessive alcohol  cocaine  marijuana  topiramate  ACE inhibitors  acebutolol  fluoxetine  sulphonamides  iodine  warfarin  isotretinoin  androgens and diethystilbestrol  lithium  methotrexate  thalidomidpenicillamine  anticonvulsants:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  phenytoin  sodium valproate  carbamazepine  trimethadione/paramethadione.  Breastfeeding  Almost all drugs, to some extent, pass into breast milk, but generally, this is less than 1% of a drug.  Clinicians should only prescribe medications while a patient is breastfeeding when absolutely indicated.  Although most drugs are safe to continue taking during lactation, they are often unlicensed for use during this period.  In general, it may be appropriate to prescribe a drug if the maternal risk is greater than the fetal risk.  mothers should be made aware of any negative impacts from not breastfeeding and that stopping breastfeeding abruptly can be difficult and hard to restart.  Before prescribing for a breastfeeding mother these factors should be considered:  mother’s need for the drug  age and maturity of the baby  breast milk volume consumed daily by the baby  any available information on drug safety.  Drugs that are considered safer to prescribe when breastfeeding include those that are or have:  highly protein-bound drugs which are less able to enter the milk  low plasma : milk ratio  shorter half-life as less able to accumulate  drugs known to be safe in pregnancy through experience and/or common use and reports, rather than new drugs  drugs that are available in a children’s formulae are mostly safe for breastfeeding women  topical or inhaled drugs, which usually do not reach significant serum levels eg nasal Loratadine for hay fever.  Safe drugs:  poor bioavailability drugs are considered low risk, eg heparin, insulin, gentamicin, third-generation cephalosporins, omeprazole/lansoprazole, inhaled steroids and beta-agonists.  ibuprofen and similar NSAIDs are considered safe  warfarin and heparin are highly protein-bound and thus considered safe  emergency contraception – Levonelle is safe to use when breastfeeding but progesterone may decrease the milk supply momentarily.  Contraindicated drugs while breastfeeding include:  amiodarone  anti-neoplastics  chloramphenicol  ergotamine

DR. JAM  iodides  methotrexate  lithium  tetracyclines  cabergoline  pseudoephedrine.  All recreational drugs should be avoided.  cocaine is extremely toxic and after use, breastfeeding should be avoided for 48 hours minimum  methadone that is prescribed and taken correctly is reported as safe.  Some common drugs that can be used while breastfeeding:  paracetamol: often the first-line drug of choice for analgesia, however, caution is recommended in pre-term, low-birth-weight infants  flucloxacillin: found only in trace amounts in breast milk  erythromycin/clarithromycin: only trace amounts found in breast milk, manufacturers advise clarithromycin should be used in breastfeeding women only if the benefits outweigh the risks  fluconazole: only small amounts identified and believed to be too small to be of risk Managing common minor Ailment Conservative advice Nausea and vomiting Reassurance that this is normal and often stops by 16 weeks Foods/ drinks containing ginger t a k s s Constipation Fibre and fluid intake Regular light exercise. Vaginal discharge Reassure that an increase in the volume of this is normal. I u d s

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  domperidone and metoclopramide can be prescribed to improve milk supply by increasing the level of prolactin. Pathophysiology  Organogenesis takes place between weeks three and eight post gestation and hence the fetus is most vulnerable to maternal medications taken during this period which may lead to congenital malformation  such drugs are known as teratogenic.  Exposure to drugs during the second and third trimesters is more likely to negatively impact growth or functional development  fetotoxicity is the term used to describe functional changes that can occur to the fetus as a consequence of medication in the latter two trimesters.  Negative impacts suffered by the baby may be noticeable while still in-utero through monitoring, seen at birth or early on, or may not be apparent until much later. Later manifestations include those associated with brain development eg social interactions, IQ level, and functioning.  Management r ailments in pregnancy Drug advice Escalation Oral promethazine or oral cyclizine then reassess 24 hrs later – all antiemetics are unlicensed in pregnancy then continue the drug or switch to another if not rehydrated and no ketonuria. 24hr review then 1 week stop the drug when can specialist advice if second-line fails Dehydration of ketonuria ⇢ IV rehydration Reassess and stop when possible First-line is a bulk-forming laxative Second-line lactulose or macrogol or if stools are soft but difficult to pass or poor emptying then bisacodyl or senna short course. Antacids (aluminium and mg) or alginates. Calcium products should only be used for the short term. If severe or persisting symptoms, then need acid suppression. Omeprazole is licensed, but ranitidine isn’t despite its common use Investigate and treat for an underlying cause if the increase in discharge is associated with odour, soreness/pain, itching, dysuria. Suspected STI – GP, GUM clinic or community sexual and reproductive health services.
