Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Possibilities are BV, trichomoniasis, Candida. Topical haemorrhoid treatment is usually short term. The haemorrhoids usually develop later than when organogenesis occurs (1st trimester).

DR. JAM Prescribing for psychiatric conditions in pregnancy:  Lithium is associated with teratogenicity – heart defects, Ebstein’s anomaly, neonatal thyroid problems, floppy baby syndrome:  only prescribe to childbearing age women if alternatives ineffective and have been risk counselled: offer specialist fetal echo and monitor drug levels four weekly to 36 weeks, then weekly  do not change brands, as bioavailability varies  stop lithium during labour  check a 12-hour post-dose level and restart based on this  women with bipolar disorder are at high risk of postpartum relapse  contraindicated when breastfeeding.  Anti-psychotics: fetal abnormalities are increased in those with schizophrenia, even in those taking no drugs. This may be associate with raised prolactin levels with amisulpride, sulpiride, risperidone:  women taking antipsychotics associated with weight gain should have an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)  clozapine – do not BF ⇢ fetal agranulocytosis  avoid depot medication in women of childbearing age.  Benzodiazepines – linked to cleft lip, palate, so should be avoided:  diazepam during delivery as neonatal withdrawal can occur. Prescribing in epilepsy during pregnancy:  Aim to optimise treatment before conception: try to be on the lowest dose of the drug and avoid polypharmacy to minimise the risk of congenital malformation.  Consider stopping if seizure-free for > 2 years. Most women have no change in seizure frequency, but those who have poorly controlled epilepsy are most likely to experience the deterioration:  do not prescribe valproate and carbamazepine  valproate 10% NTF, craniofacial abnormalities, neurodevelopmental problems – if this is given high dose folic acid is also recommended  lamotrigine has a 2% malformation rate  avoid all in breastfeeding.  Consultant led care should be provided.  If epilepsy is well controlled, the patient should stay on the antiepileptic, the dose may need adjusting or medications may need to be restarted if there is a risk of recurrence.  Vitamin K in the last four weeks of pregnancy if on hepatic inducing anti-epileptics.  After delivery, the anti-epileptic can be reduced gradually back to pre-pregnancy levels.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Sleep deprivation, reduced drug absorption, hyperventilation ⇢ make seizures more common intrapartum and postpartum. Iron therapy prescribing  Pregnancy increases iron needs by 700–1400 mg throughout and can lead to deficiency, increasing plasma volumes may also contribute to dilutional anaemia.  Iron and folate supplements are recommended in many countries and also helps in the prevention of hookworm and malaria in developing countries.  Oral iron is often given as ferrous sulphate 200 mg BD PO.  Parenteral iron may be given as iron dextran or iron sucrose - beware anaphylaxis – use only if cardiopulmonary resus facilities to hand.  Haemoglobin (Hb) rises by 8 g/l per week over six wks so late severe anaemia < 90 may need a blood transfusion. One unit of blood increases Hb by ~7 g/l. Q Fever Q fever is a zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Coxiella burnetti.  Overview Key Facts  Q fever is a zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Coxiella burnetti.  Q fever is spread via close contact with infected animals (wild or domesticated). Farm and abattoir workers are at high risk.  It is usually asymptomatic and harmless but can lead to complications in certain populations, such as pregnant women, immunocompromised patients and people with valvular heart disease.  Clinical features include fever and onset of a flu-like illness (myalgia, malaise, headache and fatigue). Hepatitis can occur with acute infection.  Diagnosis is by serology and treated with antibiotics (doxycycline is first-line).  There is currently no vaccine for Q fever.  Q fever is usually self-limiting and if diagnosed and treated promptly has a good prognosis. The mortality rate is < 1%. Epidemiology  Coxiella burnetti is found globally but tends to affect males more than females due to the employment rates in professions that involve farm animals.  It is more common in people who work in at-risk occupations that work with animals (eg farm workers).

DR. JAM  50–100 human cases in the United Kingdom (UK) every year.  About 50% of people infected by C. burnetti will develop symptoms. Aetiology  Spread to humans via close contact with infected farm animals:  placenta  blood  urine  faeces  fur and wool.  Bacteria can be inhaled or transmitted from unpasteurised milk.  Most commonly sporadic cause. Pathophysiology  The pathophysiology is not fully understood.  C. burnetti is a Gram-negative coccobacillus:  with an incubation time of 9–40 days  attaches to host macrophages and then becomes internalised  multiplies and eventually ruptures out of host cell to spread within the body  leads to antibody formation as part of the immune response.  Transmitted to humans by:  placenta of animals  hides and furs  unpasteurised milk and goat cheese  transfusion of blood products  vertical transmission  tick bites.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following symptoms:  can be asymptomatic  flu-like symptoms from 2–3 weeks of being infected and can last up to two weeks:  fever  myalgia  fatigue  sore throat  nausea  vomiting  diarrhoea.  can lead to complications such as:  atypical pneumonia  hepatitis  endocarditis

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  pregnancy-related complications:  abortion  premature birth  low birth weight.  chronic Q fever:  in < 5% of infected patients  when symptoms last for more than a few weeks and up to months  can lead to endocarditis and need longer treatment.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  legionella infection  rickettsial infections  dengue fever  Epstein–Barr virus  mycoplasma pneumonia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Q fever is diagnosed by patient history, clinical evidence and antibody testing. It should be a clinical diagnosis and there should be no delay in treatment if suspected of having Q fever.  Patient history:  contact with animals  high-risk occupations.  Clinical evidence:  blood results:  raised inflammatory markers  low platelet count  normal leukocytes  elevated LFTs.  Antibody testing.  PCR testing of C. burnetti DNA.  Q Fever management algorithm: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/Q_fever_man agement_algorithm.gif  Management Non-Pharmacological Prevention and education is important  At-risk groups should avoid animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, cats:  pregnant women:

DR. JAM  should particularly avoid sheep and lambs during January to April  animals usually are asymptomatic so precaution is important.  immunocompromised people  people with heart valve disease or grafts.  There is currently no vaccine. Pharmacological  Acute Q fever:  antibiotics most effective if started within three days of symptoms:  doxycycline (first line)  tetracycline  chloramphenicol  ciprofloxacin

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  hydroxychloroquine.  Chronic Q fever:  may need prolonged antibiotics  commonly doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine.  Q fever in pregnancy:  five weeks of co-trimoxazole.  Surgical  Surgical treatment is indicated for associated problems, eg endocarditis/valve defects.  Prognosis  Q fever is usually self-limiting and if diagnosed and treated promptly has a good prognosis. The mortality rate is < 1%. With appropriate treatment, the mortality rate of chronic Q fever is reduced to 10%.

DR. JAM Respiratory Disease In HIV And AIDS Advanced HIV infection is associated with various respiratory disorders.  Overview Key Facts  Advanced HIV infection is associated with various respiratory disorders.  The most important are bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, and pneumocystic jirovecii (PJP/PCP) pneumonia.  Tuberculosis is very common in endemic settings:  notably sub-Saharan Africa and Eastern Europe  extra-pulmonary and multi-drug resistant forms of TB more common in this group.  Maintain a high index of suspicion for viral, fungal, and protozoal infections.  Useful investigations include induced sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage, X-ray, and CT imaging. Epidemiology  Pneumonia is the commonest opportunistic infection and clinical presentation of AIDS.  PCP pneumonia accounts for 40% of all AIDS-defining illness worldwide. Aetiology  Bacterial infection – Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and atypical Mycobacterial infection.  Fungal infection – invasive Aspergillosis, Candida, Histoplasmosis, Cryptoco ccus, Nocardia.  Viral infection – CMV pneumonitis.  Malignancy – Kaposi’s sarcoma and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma:  the presence of mucosal Kaposi’s sarcoma within the mouth is an important clinical sign which signals very high likelihood of lung involvement. Pathophysiology  The low CD4 count characteristic of AIDS leads to defective T cell responses and broader immune dysregulation. This places patients at risk of opportunistic infection.  Clinical Presentation  Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is characterised by sub-acute (1-2 weeks) fever, malaise, dry cough, and dyspnoea.  Focal signs are often absent on chest examination.  Tuberculosis infection is more likely to present in an atypical fashion and can occur in patients with any CD4 count:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  extra-pulmonary involvement:  TB lymphadenitis – painless lymph node swelling, usually cervical chains  TB spondylitis – back pain and distal focal neurology  TB meningitis – subacute presentation with headache, fevers, vomiting.  fevers, night sweats, and cavitation are less common in people living with HIV.  Acute bacterial pneumonia usually presents with rapid onset (13 days) of fever, cough productive of mucopurulent sputum, chest pain, and malaise.  Differential Diagnosis  Cavitating lung lesions – Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cavitation is seen less frequently in HIV positive patients – other presentations include miliary TB, effusions, consolidation), Nocardia, Staphylococcus aureus.  Consolidation – Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Toxoplasma.  Pleural effusions - Tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Useful tests in all HIV+ patients presenting with respiratory disease include:  pulse oximetry  chest X-ray  sputum culture, or where appropriate, bronchoalveolar lavage  CD4 count and viral load.  Pneumocystis pneumonia:  pulse oximetry – hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) is commonly seen in patients with moderate-tosevere disease. However, in those with normal oxygen saturations, an exercise-induced reduction of 5% or absolute fall to < 90% are suggestive of PCP  chest X-ray – bilateral interstitial shadowing in mid and low zones is typical. Atypical changes – such as cavitation, upper load opacification and pneumothorax – are seen in 10% patients. X-ray can also be normal in PCP  induced sputum or BAL for PCP cysts – useful test, particularly in the ITU setting.  Tuberculosis:  chest X-ray – cavitation is less common (due to inadequate immune response); may be normal or show miliary picture, consolidation, or effusions  induced sputum/BAL for acid-and-alcohol fast bacillin on ZN stain. Typical appearance of PCP on X-ray with bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates:

DR. JAM  Management Pharmacological  The treatment of choice for PCP pneumonia is co-trimoxazole (high dose, 14 days):  side effects of co-trimoxazole are common and often debilitating – these include nausea, vomiting, rash, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia and bleeding  steroids are indicated in severe hypoxia (PaO2 < 9.3 kPa (or 70 mmHg) or SpO2 < 92%)  alternative treatments (second-line or useful in patients with co-trimoxazole intolerance or allergy) include IV pentamidine, clindamycin/primaquine and dapsone/trimethoprim.  Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is indicated in patients who have previously required treatment and in patients with no history of infection with a CD4 count < 200.  Prophylaxis should be continued until CD4 count has increased above 200 with HAART.  Pulmonary tuberculosis treatment does not differ significantly from that in HIV negative patients – combination therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for patients with drug-sensitive TB.  Prognosis  Poor prognostic indicators for PCP infection include:  co-infection  pneumothorax  poor response to treatment  the need for mechanical ventilation. Recurrent PCP infection is common – 50% of patients will experience a second episode within the next 12 months.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Rickettsial Infections Rickettsial infections are caused by bacteria transmitted by ticks, fleas, or mites, leading to symptoms such as fever, rash and headache.  Overview Key Facts  Rickettsial infection is common worldwide and spread by various different disease vectors:  all rickettsial infections are characterised by febrile illness with rash, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.  Rickettsial infections include Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Mediterranean spotted fever, scrub typhus and African tick-bite fever.  African tick-bite fever typhus (Rickettsia africae) is an important rickettsial infection to consider in returning travellers, particularly from Africa.  Travel to game parks in southern Africa is a particular risk factor for R. africae.  Rocky mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is spread by ticks and commonly seen in the USA in forested areas:  it is caused by the organism Rickettsia rickettsii.  The time from infection to symptomatology is between five and 14 days.  Symptoms are non-speciﬁc and may include fever, headache and myalgia.  The maculopapular rash of RMSF usually appears 2–6 days after the onset of fever and progresses through stages and distribution that are never pathognomonic.  The rash begins as a maculopapular eruption on the wrists and ankles and spreads centripetally to involve the trunk and extremities.  The rash involves the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.  Later in the illness, the rash becomes petechial in 50% of patients.  An eschar may be present at the site of a tick bite, with local lymphadenopathy and conjunctival infection.  RMSF can be lethal and physicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for RMSF in patients who are febrile, as it is essentially a clinical diagnosis.  Diagnosis can be confirmed by serology.  Treatment is doxycycline.  Clinical Presentation  Time from infection to the beginning of symptomatology is usually between 5 and 14 days.  Symptoms are non-speciﬁc and may include fever, headache and myalgia.  The maculopapular rash of RMSF usually appears 2–6 days after the onset of fever and progresses through stages and distribution that are never pathognomonic.

DR. JAM  The rash begins as a maculopapular eruption on the wrists and ankles and spreads centripetally to involve the trunk and extremities.  The rash involves the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.  Later in the illness, the rash becomes petechial in 50% of patients.  Differential Diagnosis  Fever in the returning traveller:  Asia – malaria, Dengue fever, malaria, scrub typhus and leishmaniasis  sub-Saharan Africa – falciparum malaria, HIV infection, viral haemorrhagic fever (VHF) and rickettsial infection.  Diarrhoeal illness in the returning traveller:  watery – traveller’s diarrhoea, cholera, giardia and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)  bloody – amoebic dysentery, VHF and IBD.  Rashes in the returning traveller:  bites and stings – look for black eschars on the skin (scrub typhus)  maculopapular rash – Dengue fever, HIV seroconversion, Chikungunya and Zika  urticarial rash – acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) and Strongyloides.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is predominantly clinical and there should be a high suspicion in patients who have recently been in endemic areas presenting with fever and rash.  Diagnosis can be confirmed by serology.  Management  Treatment is with antibiotic therapy, first-line is doxycycline in adults.  Chloramphenicol may be used as an alternative.  Prognosis  Early antibiotic therapy is key to reducing mortality from 20% to approximately 5% in RMSF. Other complications of the condition include end-organ damage, peripheral gangrene or secondary infections. Scabies Scabies infestation is due to the parasite sarcoptes scabei and causes intense itching.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Skin infections can be divided into bacterial, fungal and viral infections and infestations.  Infestations include sarcoptes scabiei (scabies mite) infestation and lice (pediculosis) infestation.  Scabies infestation is due to the parasite sarcoptes scabei and causes intense itching.  Scabies is endemic in some populations and can occur at any age; however, it is more common in women and between the ages of 10–19.  Scabies is spread by close or direct contact with an infected individual.  Clinical signs include excoriated erythematous papules, burrows where grey, thread-like tracks appear on the skin, and patients may also present with violet nodules.  Diagnosis can be confirmed from scrapings, but a history and examination may be sufficient.  Scabies is treated using topical insecticide and is usually successful in irradiation (after two treatments) symptoms resolve around two weeks after successful treatment.  Treatment of close contacts is also required.  Crusted scabies is a severe infestation of thousands of mites causing widespread skin scaling and exfoliation.  This occurs in the immunocompromised and elderly.  This condition needs specialist input and requires more intensive treatment. Epidemiology  There is increased prevalence of scabies in those aged between 10–19 years.  Scabies is more common in women.  There are 300 000 000 cases worldwide and scabies is endemic in some populations.  There is increased prevalence in areas with high levels of social deprivation and in developing countries.  There are epidemic cycles in the United Kingdom with a length of around 15 years. Aetiology  Scabies occurs due to the human parasite, sarcoptes scabei.  This is easily transmitted by close contact, eg skin-to-skin.  Transmission can often occur after sexual intercourse and can also occur via clothing, towels and bed sheets.  Risk factors include crowded living conditions and institutionalisation.  Crusted scabies can occur in the immunocompromised and elderly. Pathophysiology  A delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the mite saliva and their faeces or eggs occurs 3–6 weeks after infection.

DR. JAM  The average number of mites in a person with initial infection is up to 15.  Crusted scabies is a hyperinfestation due to poor immune response; for instance, in those who are immunosuppressed.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for scabies include:  intense pruritus, often worse at night  tracks of burrowing mites may be visible; tiny, grey, irregular, thread-like elevations of superficial epidermis, often between fingers and on wrists, axillae, buttocks, penis and heels  erythematous papules are often found in web spaces, sides of fingers, wrists, elbows, umbilicus, axilla, penis and scrotum in men and areola in women  palms and sole involvement is seen in children and the elderly  violet nodules, common on the penis, scrotum, axilla, buttocks and groin  crusted scabies presents with thick, erythematous scaling. Skin may be fissured and this can affect any part of the body. Pruritus may be absent in these cases. Scabies infestation of the hand:  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for scabies include:  lice  insect bites  acropustulosis  atopic eczema  folliculitis  impetigo

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  lichen planus  psoriasis (crusted).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnoses and investigation for scabies would include the following:  history and examination including close contact history  take skin scrapings to remove mites from burrow and identify under microscopy  ink applied and removed with alcohol to define burrows.  Management  History and examination including close contact history.  Take skin scrapings to remove mites from burrow and identify under microscopy.  Ink applied and removed with alcohol to define burrows.  Management (relate to guidelines wherever possible). Non-Pharmacological  Identify close contacts and provide treatment.  Avoid close contact with others.  Wash bedding, towels and clothing at high temperature.  Emollients for dry skin. Pharmacological  Topical insecticide is applied to the entire body and is then repeated one week later.  First line = permethrin cream.  Second line = malathion lotion.  Topical crotamiton may relieve itching.  Secondary infection should be treated as appropriate.  Crusted scabies warrants dermatological advice as topical insecticide and oral ivermectin are likely requirements.  Persistent nodular scabies – requires Dermatology referral as intralesional/oral steroids may be required.  Prognosis  Most infestations can be resolved with two courses of permethrin; longer and more intensive regimes are required for crusted scabies.  If scabies is untreated, secondary bacterial infection may occur due to streptococcus or staphylococcus groups.  Untreated secondary infection can lead to renal failure, rheumatic heart disease or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (this occurs in developing countries).  Prolonged immune response to scabies can cause the development of nodular scabies, which can persist for months. Crusted scabies can lead to sepsis.

DR. JAM Salmonella Salmonella is a bacteria that can cause food poisoning with symptoms like diarrhoea, fever and abdominal cramps.  Overview Key Facts  Salmonella spp. are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacilli.  They can be loosely divided into non-typhoidal and typhoidal salmonella.  Non-typhoidal salmonella causes self-limiting gastroenteritis, whereas typhoidal salmonella causes enteric fever.  Most cases of non-typhoidal salmonellosis are mild, but it can rarely be life-threatening depending on the serotype.  Outbreaks tend to be due to poultry, dairy and undercooked eggs.  Diagnosis is via stool cultures.  Treatment is mainly supportive and antibiotics are reserved for severe cases.  Immunosuppressed and older patients are at increased risk of invasive bacteraemia and infants are at particular risk of severe dehydration.  The vast majority of cases resolve without any treatment in 3–7 days. The overall mortality is < 5% in the West.  The highest mortality rate is in older patients and in those with underlying medical conditions. Epidemiology  One of the most common causes of food-borne illnesses in the West.  1.2 million cases each year in the USA and accounts for 30% of all deaths associated with food-borne disease.  Infants, young children and older people are at the highest risk.  Also common in the developing countries in Asia, Africa and South America. Children in these countries are at particular risk of invasive bloodstream salmonellosis due to an increased incidence of malaria and malnutrition. Aetiology  There are two species of Salmonella – Salmonella enterica and Salmonella bongori.  Salmonella enterica has over 2500 serotypes. These can be divided into non-typhoidal (such as S. enteritidis and S. typhimurium) and typhoidal (S. typhi and S. paratyphi).  Non-typhoidal salmonellosis is therefore defined as an infection with S. enterica other than S. typhi or S. paratyphi.  S. enteritidis and S. typhimurium are the two most important serotypes transmitted from animals to humans in most parts of the world.  Salmonella is often found in domestic and wild animals, including poultry, pigs, cattle, dogs, cats, birds and reptiles.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Salmonella infections occur via ingestion of contaminated food, usually meat, eggs and dairy. It can also be transmitted via contact with infected animals and between humans via the faecal–oral route. Pathophysiology  The onset of symptoms is 12–36 hours following ingestion.  Gastric acid is an important barrier to salmonella infection.  However, salmonella has evolved a degree of tolerance from acidity and, after passing through the stomach, is able to invade the mucosa of the distal ileum and proximal colon.  The host response consists of neutrophil infiltration, followed by lymphocytes and macrophages. This is responsible for the gastroenteritis symptoms, such as diarrhoea and abdominal cramps.  Patients with a low gastric pH (eg those taking antacids) are at particular risk of infection.  The higher the ingested dose of salmonella, the shorter the incubation period and the more severe the disease.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms are usually relatively mild and include nausea and vomiting, non-bloody diarrhoea, fever, myalgia and headache.  Examination may reveal diffuse, mild abdominal tenderness, signs of dehydration and increased bowel sounds.  The illness lasts 2–7 days.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  shigellosis  Campylobacter spp.  Escherichia coli  listeriosis  viral gastroenteritis, eg norovirus  parasitic gastroenteritis, eg cryptosporidium.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Stool studies – either by culturing the organism or detection of specific DNA via multiplex PCR.  A low-selective media (eg MacConkey agar) or a more selective media (eg Hektoen agar) can be used.  Stool studies should be performed in patients with moderate-tosevere disease with symptoms > 7 days, or diarrhoea with fever, bloody or mucoid stools, severe abdominal pain or signs of sepsis.  Stool testing should also be performed in symptomatic patients with a clear source of salmonella infection, eg outbreaks in hotels, cruise ships, etc.  Blood cultures should be considered in certain patient groups – < 3 months of age, if signs of septicaemia, the immunocompromised, those with high-risk conditions and those who have travelled to fever-endemic areas.

DR. JAM  Imaging may be considered if endovascular infections or localised complications are suspected, such as aortitis, mycotic aneurysms, peritonitis and toxic megacolon.  Management  Salmonella is usually self-limiting and most cases do not require antibiotics.  The mainstay of management is supportive treatment, including:  fluid replacement:  in most cases, adequate fluid hydration can be maintained with increased oral intake  oral rehydration solution (ORS) is recommended for mild-moderate dehydration associated with vomiting or severe diarrhoea  ORS is given until the patient is rehydrated and can be continued to replace ongoing losses  nasogastric administration may be considered when oral intake is not tolerated  intravenous (IV) fluids should be given in cases of severe dehydration, shock, reduced GCS or failure of ORS therapy; the fluid of choice is normal saline or Ringer’s lactate.  adjuncts:  anti-diarrhoeal and anti-emetic agents can be used once hydration is adequate; loperamide can be given to immunocompetent adults with acute diarrhoea, but should be avoided in toxic megacolon; ondansetron can increase tolerance of oral rehydration in children > 4 years of age  probiotics may reduce the severity and duration of symptoms in immunocompetent patients  zinc may be given to reduce the duration of diarrhoea in children who have signs of malnutrition or who are at risk of zinc deficiency.  antibiotics:  a short course of antibiotics may be considered in patients with severe illness, extraintestinal disease or who are at increased risk of severe disease, such as in infants < 3 months of age or adults > 50 years, HIV-infected patients, immunocompromised patients and patients with vascular abnormalities or prosthetic joints  the antibiotic of choice is ciprofloxacin or azithromycin, depending on local guidelines  foreign travel is associated with ciprofloxacinresistant strains and an alternative antibiotic may have to be considered, such as a third-general cephalosporin.  chronic carriage occurs in 0.5% of cases and is defined as a positive stool culture 12 months after the acute infection; this requires long-term antibiotics with amoxicillin, co-trimoxazole or ciprofloxacin; cholecystectomy is recommended if concurrent gallstones and there is failure to respond to antibiotic therapy.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Complications:  reactive arthritis usually involving the lower limbs can be a short-term or chronic complication  immunosuppressed and older patients are at increased risk of invasive bacteraemia and infants are at particular risk of severe dehydration  endovascular or localised infections can occur if salmonella spreads beyond the gastrointestinal tract and are more common in patients with underlying medication conditions such as immune deficiencies; examples of extraintestinal disease include aortitis, mycotic aneurysms, meningitis, osteomyelitis and septic arthritis  salmonella meningitis tends to occur in children and salmonella osteomyelitis is particularly prevalent in children with sickle cell disease  toxic megacolon and peritonitis are very rare complications.  The vast majority of cases resolve without any treatment in 3–7 days; the overall mortality is < 5% in the West.  The highest mortality rate is in older patients and in those with underlying medical conditions. Salmonella CNS infections have a mortality rate of 50%. Schistosomiasis Schistosomiasis is a tropical disease caused by a group of parasites called schistosomes.  Overview Key Facts  Schistosomiasis is a tropical disease caused by a group of parasites called schistosomes.  These worms are also called blood flukes, which belong to the trematode family.  Five main types of schistosomes are responsible for most human disease.  The disease is prevalent in developing tropical or subtropical countries where clean water is scarce.  The condition mainly affects the liver, urinary bladder and intestine.  It can also affect the lungs and brain, initially entering the human via the skin.  The parasite can live for many years in the affected organ.  Genital schistosomiasis can be transmitted sexually like any other STDs.  Treatment of infection is with praziquantel (PZQ); surgery may be required in some cases to remove tumour masses.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Over 200 million people around the world are infected by these parasites.  They cause around 200 000 deaths in sub-Saharan Africa every year.  They affect some of the poorest countries in the world.  The mortality rate is 1 in 1000 infected persons. Aetiology Type of schistosome Disease Found in Schistosoma haematobium Urinary and genital disease Africa and MiddleEast S. mansoni Bowel and liver Africa, South America and the Caribbean S. japonicum Bowel and liver China and SouthEast Asia S. mekongi Bowel and liver Cambodia and Laos S. guineensis Bowel and liver Central Africa Pathophysiology  Schistosomes have a very complex life cycle involving:  humans  snails  freshwaters like ponds, lakes and reservoirs. Life cycle  Infected humans pass schistosomes through their faeces or urine into freshwater.  These eggs then hatch into larvae and infect certain species of snails present in the freshwater.  After a period of development in the snail, the schistosomes are released back into the water in a form called cercariae.  Cercariae can swim and can penetrate the skin.  They enter the human body through the skin and travel to the liver where they grow into adult worms.  They migrate to blood vessels surrounding organs, where they can live for many years.  Some species live around the bowel and some species will live around the bladder.  Adult worms can lay thousands of eggs a day, some of which find their way back to water by urine or faeces and restart the lifecycle.  Clinical manifestations of schistosomiasis occur as a result of immunological reactions to Schistosoma eggs confined in organ tissues.  Antigens are released from the egg and stimulate a granulomatous reaction involving T lymphocytes, macrophages

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI and eosinophils that results in the long-term manifestation of the disease.  These eggs can cause hardening of the bladder walls, obstruction and can even result in bladder cancer.  They can cause both long-term (such as bladder obstruction, bladder cancer and fibrotic liver disease) and short-term symptoms (fever and skin rash).  The penetration of cercariae in the skin can cause an itchy rash called fisherman’s rash. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:03_Hegasy_Schistosomias is_Wiki_EN_CCBYSA.png  Clinical Presentation  Skin rash (fisherman’s rash).  Fever, diarrhoea, rash and respiratory symptoms in katayama fever, also known as acute schistosomiasis; occurs after four weeks of exposure to the parasite.  Katayama fever is usually self-limiting.  Urinary obstruction and haematuria (bladder schistosomiasis).  Abdominal pain, diarrhoea and blood in the stool (intestinal schistosomiasis).  Enlargement of liver, obstruction of bile, and jaundice due to scarring of the liver (liver schistosomiasis).  Anaemia due to chronic infection especially in children.  Bleeding varices.  Other organs such as genitals, lungs and brain can also be infected.

DR. JAM  Headache and seizures if the brain is infected.  Coughing, wheezing and shortness of breath in case of infected lungs.  Generalised symptoms include fever, chills, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and blood in the urine.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  filariasis  food poisoning  gastroenteritis  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)  salmonellosis  urinary tract infection (UTI)  viral hepatitis A  viral hepatitis B  viral hepatitis C.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urine and stool microscopy.  Biopsy of tissues (liver, intestine and urinary bladder).  Antibodies for schistosomiasis are detected in blood and urine.  Ultrasound to rule out other causes of abdominal pain such as cholelithiasis.  Management  Recovery of the affected organ depends on the type of organism and the extent of the damage. Non-Pharmacological  The mainstay of management is the prevention of disease.  People in areas with a high incidence of disease can be scheduled for mass drug administration.  Large-scale drug administration has been an effective option for the prevention of schistosomiasis.  Reduction in contamination of water; this involves educating people on proper sanitation and providing necessary facilities such as toilets.  Some countries have tried the elimination of snails by various chemicals. The effectiveness of this step is variable.  Reduction of human contact with contaminated water.  Tourist guidelines should be provided, ie not to swim in areas where the disease is prevalent.  Provision of clean water for drinking, cooking and washing clothes.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pharmacological  Drug of choice for schistosomiasis is praziquantel (PZQ).  PZQ is an anthelmintic and is effective against all major types of schistosomes:  PZQ is more effective against the mature or adult parasite than the juvenile parasite.  PZQl 20 mg/kg, followed by 20 mg/kg after 4–6 hours for S. haematobium and S. mansoni.  PZQ 20 mg/kg three times a day for one day for S. japonicum.  Sometimes the dose is repeated a few weeks later.  Methylprednisolone or other steroid medications are used sometimes to relieve the symptoms of acute schistosomiasis.  Lung and brain symptoms caused by schistosomiasis can also be treated by steroids.  The application of insect repellents can reduce penetration of the skin.  Surgical  Surgical removal of the tumour masses, eg bladder tumour.  Ligation of oesophageal varices.  Large granulomatous tissues can also be removed surgically in the urinary bladder or lungs.  Prognosis  A single dose of praziquantel (PZQ) is up to 90% effective in killing schistosomes. Delayed administration can lead to permanent organ damage. Sepsis Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening end organ dysfunction secondary to a dysregulated response to infection.  Overview Key Facts  Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening end organ dysfunction secondary to a dysregulated response to infection.  The condition is common worldwide and overall associated with 10% mortality.  Septic shock is sepsis where particular profound circulatory, cellular and metabolic abnormalities substantially increase mortality (> 40%).  Most cases of sepsis are caused by bacterial infection.

DR. JAM  When assessing a patient with sepsis, it is crucial to identify the source of infection to initiate appropriate treatment – commonly urinary tract infection (UTI) and chest infection.  Other important sources are skin and/or soft tissues, the biliary tract and perianal abscesses.  The ‘Sepsis Six’ reflects key investigations and management priorities in patients with sepsis.  To optimise survival, these tasks should all be completed within one hour of diagnosis:  do three things; blood cultures, venous blood gas (VBG)/arterial blood gas (ABG) (lactate) and measure urine output  give three things; oxygen, IV fluids and IV antibiotics. Epidemiology  Sepsis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide – especially in immunocompromised patients and at extremes of age.  Sepsis accounts for > 50 000 deaths each year in the United Kingdom. Aetiology  Gram-positive pathogens associated with sepsis include S. aureus, Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), enterococcus and S. pneumoniae.  Gram-negative pathogens associated with sepsis include E. coli, Pseudomonas spp, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae.  In immunocompromised patients, sepsis can be caused by invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis. Pathophysiology  Sepsis results from a systemic, deleterious immune response to infection:  a cascade of inflammatory mediators – notably tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 causing increased capillary permeability and end organ dysfunction.  Gram-negative sepsis (eg in meningococcal disease) is associated with widespread intravascular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) polysaccharide deposition.  Clinical Presentation  Important clinical features of sepsis include:  fever > 38 °C (or less commonly hypothermic)  tachycardia; age-dependent, in adults > 90 bpm  tachypnoea; age-dependent.  Signs may also include  flushing and/or warm skin  bounding pulse.  Symptoms specific to site of infection:  urinary – burning or stinging, increased frequency, suprapubic pain etc  GI – nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, abdominal pain

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  respiratory – productive cough, shortness of breath etc.  Differential Diagnosis  Sepsis is characterised by a systemic inflammatory response (SIRS).  SIRS can also be seen in several other disorders.  The differential diagnoses for sepsis is vast and includes:  pancreatitis (non-infectious inflammation of the pancreas)  toxic shock syndrome (TSS)  alcohol withdrawal  Addisonian crisis  pulmonary embolism  thyrotoxic storm  haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The most widely used diagnostic aid is quick sequential organ failure assessment (qSOFA). This can help to identify adults requiring Intensive Care Unit treatment for suspected sepsis:  low blood pressure < 100 systolic  high respiratory rate > 22 breaths per minute  acutely altered mental state – Glasgow Coma Scale score < 15.  The investigation of choice in suspected sepsis is blood cultures (aerobic/anaerobic) along with targeted further cultures (such as pus from abscesses, urine, throat, skin swabs etc).  Positive blood cultures confirm bloodstream infection and provides information about the organism and sensitivity.  Other investigations mandated by the ‘Sepsis Six’ include VBG for lactate urine output monitoring. Further investigations should look to identify the source and prognosticate.  Important blood tests include a full blood count to identify:  raised white cell count, suggestive of infection  low platelets in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), an important complication of sepsis  C-reactive protein – raised inflammatory markers also point to infection  VBG/ABG for lactate (> 2 mmol/l suggests end organ impairment) and acidosis  urea and electrolytes – evidence of acute renal failure (raised creatinine and urea)  liver function tests – evidence of biliary source for infection  clotting (low fibrinogen in patients with DIC).  Other tests to help to confirm the source of infection include:  chest X-ray and respiratory swabs or deep samples  urine dipstick/multiple chemical sensitivity  if suspected wound infection or abscess/collection – wound swab or aspirate

DR. JAM  if suspected line sepsis – culture from central/peripheral lines +/- removal of lines  consider targeted cross-sectional imaging if no clear source of sepsis identified.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Communication between clinical teams is crucial in managing patients with suspected sepsis.  Ensure that key investigations and treatments are instituted promptly and patients are referred appropriately to Intensive Care.  Patients with evidence of septic shock should be managed in a high dependency or Intensive Care Unit setting as they are likely to require inotropes and close monitoring.  Besides antibiotics, the mainstay of sepsis management is good supportive care:  high-flow oxygen  regular urine output monitoring – oliguria is a sensitive marker for sepsis.  Patients with neutropenic sepsis should be managed in a positive pressure side room to prevent super-added infection by organisms in the environment. Pharmacological  Prompt fluid resuscitation with intravenous crystalloid.  poor haemodynamic response to 2 L crystalloid suggests septic shock and should prompt senior review and/or Intensive Care Unit referral.  Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics as guided by local protocols and suspected source of infection:  patients with neutropenic sepsis (suspect in setting of recent chemotherapy) often require more comprehensive antibiotic regimen, eg piperacillin-tazobactam and aminoglycoside.  Surgical  Certain sources of sepsis, eg deep abscesses and soft tissue infections (necrotising fasciitis), may require surgical involvement to achieve adequate source control.  Prognosis  Sepsis is a leading cause of mortally in infection, and also causes significant morbidity (organ failure, malnutrition, coagulopathy).  Prognosis depends on the age of patients, existing comorbidity, speed of diagnosis and monument, and level of resultant organ dysfunction.  If the ‘Sepsis Six’ are completed within the ‘Golden Hour’, ie the first hour after diagnosis, prognosis improves significantly.  Mortality is estimated at 10% in sepsis and 40% in septic shock.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Case fatality seems to be improving – this may be due to increases in awareness and reporting of cases, faster diagnosis and improved management protocols. Shigella Shigella is a rod-shaped, non-motile, Gram-negative bacterium that belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family.  Overview Key Facts  Shigella is a rod-shaped, non-motile, Gram-negative bacterium that belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family.  It is a facultative anaerobe – it can survive with or without oxygen.  There are four species of Shigella, each species has its own serotypes:  the most serious infective serotype is Shigella dysenteriae serotype 1.  In humans, all of the species can cause shigellosis.  It causes a contagious infection of the intestines, particularly of the colon.  Shigella can survive the acidic pH of the stomach making it extremely virulent.  Outbreaks of Shigella are more common in prisons, military barracks and child care centres.  Shigellosis can progress to dysentery, which means the inflammation of the colon resulting in severe abdominal pain and diarrhoea.  The route of transmission is the faecal–oral route.  The organism enters the body through contaminated food or water, particularly when food is eaten or prepared by unwashed hands.  It can also be transmitted through sexual contact.  Shigellosis is the most common type of dysentery in the United Kingdom (UK).  The severity of infection can vary, it may not require treatment at all or may result in renal failure or colonic perforation. Epidemiology  Shigella is endemic in underdeveloped countries where sanitary conditions are poor.  50% of diarrhoea in young children is due to Shigella.  Worldwide it known to cause 80–165 million cases with 600 000 thousand deaths annually; the majority are in young children.  Shigella flexneri is endemic in UK. Aetiology  There are four species of Shigella:

DR. JAM 1. Shigella dysenteriae 2. S. flexneri 3. S. boydii 4. S. sonnei. Pathophysiology  Ingested Shigella multiplies in the small intestine and then passes into the colon.  In the colon, it targets the epithelial layer of the mucosal lining or microfold cells.  The mucosal cells phagocytose the bacterium and release the bacterium into the mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue.  The mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue immune cells, such as macrophages, engulf the bacteria and apoptosis of the bacteria occurs.  As a result of the death of macrophages, a variety of cytokines are released such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) which activates an intense inflammatory process that recruits additional immune cells, resulting in the death of epithelial cells and damage to the colon leading to the formation of colonic ulcerations and abscesses.  Shigella dysenteriae serotype 1 produces Shiga toxin which has two subunits (A and B):  the two subunits are joined by a disulfide bond; the B subunit helps in binding the toxin to the host cell membrane and the A subunit targets the ribosomes of the host cell and cleaves the 28S rRNA protein, ending in the arrest of protein synthesis followed by cell death.  When Shiga toxin breaches into the bloodstream it causes haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) by entering into the kidneys.  In the kidneys, the toxin binds to the endothelial cells lining the glomerulus making them die by apoptosis.  Consequently, a dead endothelial cell leaves a gap in the capillary wall resulting in leaking of the protein molecules, hence causing proteinuria.  Platelets clot the gap in the endothelial lining resulting in thrombocytopenia in the blood.  Microangiopathic haemolysis can also occur due to the toxic effect of Shiga toxin in kidneys, resulting in anaemia.  The clots can result in overall low blood flow to the kidneys resulting in ischaemic death and subsequent uraemia.  Clinical Presentation  Dysentery can last for seven days.  Symptoms of dysentery include:  abdominal and rectal cramping  abdominal and body pains  fever  vomiting  loss of appetite  faecal incontinence

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  watery/mucosal flaked diarrhoea (blood/pus).  In extreme cases, particularly in children, tonic-clonic seizures may happen and loss of consciousness may occur.  Reactive arthritis may occur in the weeks following the infection; this usually affects the knee joint causing pain and swelling.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  E. coli infection  Campylobacter spp. infection  salmonellosis  bacterial gastroenteritis  amoebiasis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Shigella does not produce hydrogen sulfide gas; hence special culture mediums like MacConkey agar can be used for its identification.  A faecal sample is cultured on MacConkey agar for definitive diagnosis, on which non-lactose fermenting and non-hydrogen sulfide producing colonies of Shigella are formed.  Stool sample stained with methylene blue also shows polymorphonuclear leukocytes.  A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can directly identify Shigella DNA.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Practising good hygiene and sanitation, particularly handwashing with soap.  The condition is usually self-limiting and resolves in 3–7 days.  Patients should be advised to drink plenty of fluids during the course of the disease.  Infected patients should avoid cooking after 48 hours of the last episode of diarrhoea.  Patients should be advised to stay at home for 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea to reduce the risk of transmitting infection. Pharmacological  Fluid and electrolyte replenishment intravenously in cases of dehydration.  Antibiotics such as beta-lactams (penicillin and cephalosporin), macrolides and quinolones are used to treat more severe cases.  Antibiotics are not indicated for mild infection which is usually self-limiting.

DR. JAM  Painkillers and antipyretic drugs (paracetamol) are indicated for pain and fever.  Antidiarrhoeal agents such as loperamide should be avoided.  Surgical  Surgical repair may be required in colonic perforations (in very severe cases).  Prognosis  Usually, the infection is mild and gets better on its own after 3– 7 days without the use of antibiotics.  Sever shigellosis will take 3–6 weeks to recover completely.  It may take several months before bowel habits become entirely normal in severe cases. An infected person can be a carrier for up to four weeks after the onset of symptoms, even with treatment. Staphylococcus Aureus Staphylococcus aureus is a common bacteria that can cause various infections in humans.  Overview Key Facts  Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci that are typically seen as ‘clusters’.  Staphylococci can be further subdivided based on the coagulase test:  coagulase-negative staphylococci include Staphylococcus epidermidis:  this is usually a harmless skin commensal (and often a blood culture contaminant) but can form biofilms to cause long-term catheter-associated and periprosthetic infections.  coagulase-positive Staphylococcus aureus is an important human pathogen.  Infections caused by S. aureus include:  skin and soft tissue – carbuncles, impetigo, cellulitis, erysipelas, necrotising fasciitis  bone – a common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis  necrotising cavitating pneumonia – associated with Panton-Valentine leukocidin  food poisoning – toxin-mediated rapid-onset gastroenteritis with prominent vomiting, usually within six hours of eating contaminated food

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  toxic shock syndrome – a super-antigen-mediated disorder characterised by sepsis and associated with retained tampons in young women  infective endocarditis – the most common cause of infective endocarditis (IE), notably in intravenous (IV) drug users.  Treatment of choice varies with the site of infection: however, S. aureus remains largely susceptible to penicillins. Strongyloidiasis Strongyloidiasis is a common infection that occurs in the tropics, subtropics and Far East, caused by the parasitic roundworm Strongyloides stercoralis.  Overview Key Facts  Strongyloidiasis is a common infection that occurs in the tropics, subtropics and Far East, caused by the parasitic roundworm Strongyloides stercoralis.  It is caught by contact between bare skin and soil contaminated with larvae (ie walking barefoot in endemic areas).  Strongyloidiasis can present acutely with diarrhoea and associated migrating pruritic skin changes (larva currens rash).  Chronic infection frequently occurs and may be asymptomatic:  however, it can also cause abdominal pains, intermittent diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss  patients may also present with signs and symptoms of Löffler syndrome, which is a type of pneumonitis that can be caused by the migration of the larvae to the lungs.  Patients may less commonly present with hyperinfection (disseminated strongyloidiasis) which can affect multiple organ systems, especially if immunosuppressed – and can present as a Gram-negative sepsis and organ failure.  Strongyloides infection commonly causes a marked eosinophilia on blood testing.  Diagnosis can be confirmed identification of larvae in the stool or duodenal fluid; serum antibodies may be demonstrated in chronic infection if microscopic evidence is not found but infection is suspected.  All patients with infection should be treated regardless of symptomatology to avoid the risk of hyperinfection syndrome.  Ivermectin is the appropriate treatment and albendazole can be used as a second-line agent.  Treatment is usually curative, although re-infection is common in endemic areas.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Infection in endemic areas is extremely common and may affect up to 50% of people in areas where there are inadequate disposal methods of human waste products. Aetiology  Infection and symptomatology are caused by the parasitic roundworm Strongyloides stercoralis.  Infection is acquired by skin contact with infected soil in areas where the infection is endemic.  Severe infection is more likely in patients with immunocompromise (consider screening for HIV). Pathophysiology  Larvae enter the body via the skin on direct contact with infected soil and initiate the parasitic cycle.  Filariform larvae travel via the bloodstream to the lungs and then migrate to the pharynx.  The larvae are swallowed and reach the gastrointestinal tract.  In the small intestine, the female filariform larvae moult twice and become adult worms, which then produce rhabditiform larvae, which can either be passed in the stool or can cause autoinfection.  In autoinfection, the larvae become infective filariform larvae, which can penetrate either the intestinal mucosa or the skin of the perianal area and then travel back to the lungs via the bloodstream, re-initiating the cycle.  They may also disseminate to other parts of the body.  Clinical Presentation  The condition may cause ‘larva currens’, a linear, pruritic rash that is caused by larvae migrating under the skin, which advances as the parasites move under the skin and may be found on the legs, buttock or trunk.  Chronic infection frequently occurs and may be asymptomatic:  however, it can also cause abdominal pains, intermittent diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss.  Pulmonary migration of the larvae can lead to pneumonitis (Loeffler syndrome), which may present with cough, bronchospasm and shortness of breath, with pulmonary haemorrhage in some cases.  Patients may less commonly present with hyperinfection (disseminated strongyloidiasis) which can affect multiple organ systems, especially if immunosuppressed – and can present as a Gram-negative sepsis and organ failure.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  diarrhoea – hookworm, ascariasis and inflammatory bowel disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  full blood count (FBC) for eosinophilia  liver function and renal function.  Stool for microbiology, culture and sensitivity (MCS) and OCP (ova, cysts and parasites) – particularly useful in suspected Strongyloides  Marked eosinophilia and elevated CRP, coupled with infiltrates on the chest X-ray, are consistent with a heavy Strongyloides infection and pulmonary larval migration.  Chest X-ray in cases of pneumonitis may show patchy pulmonary infiltrates.  Management  Albendazole and ivermectin are treatments of choice for Strongyloides infection.  Albendazole is given at a dose of 400 mg BD for three days, repeated after three weeks if required.  Antihistamines may be used for itching in the case of significant skin involvement.  Prognosis  Treatment usually results in clearance of worms, although reinfection in endemic areas is very common. The prognosis is much worse if the patient develops hyperinfection, with considerable associated mortality. Syphilis Syphilis infection is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.  Overview Key Facts  Syphilis infection is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.  Prevalence is increasing in the United Kingdom (UK).  Transmission is usually through direct contact with an active lesion.  Untreated syphilis can remain for many years and progress through several stages:  early syphilis (< 2 years post-infection) - primary, secondary and early latent  late syphilis (> 2 years post-infection) - late-latent and tertiary.  Syphilis must be treated early to prevent progression to later stages of which symptoms may be irreversible.  Signs and symptoms depend on stage of the disease and may include a painless ulcer (chancre), maculopapular rash on palms/soles, condylomata lata (moist, wart-like lesions), snail-

DR. JAM tract ulcers (oral mucosa) and unexplained neurological/ophthalmic symptoms.  Diagnosis should ideally take place in a genito-urinary medicine (GUM) clinic and will involve detailed history and examination, serology testing and dark-field microscopy tests of swabs taken from a suspected chancre.  All patients with suspected syphilis should be advised to avoid sexual contact/exposing others to active lesions until diagnosis excluded/fully treated.  Antibiotic therapy is primarily procaine penicillin (10 days if primary/secondary or 17 days in tertiary infection).  If left untreated, syphilis can cause several complications including:  neurological syphilis  cardiovascular complications  Gummatous disease  adverse outcomes in pregnancy  facilitation of other infections, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Epidemiology  Transmission rates of syphilis through sexual contact range from 10-60% - highest in primary and secondary syphilis.  Prevalence of syphilis in the UK greater than doubled from 2013-2018 to 7541 cases in 2018.  Most new diagnoses (75%) in men who have sex with men (MSM).  Risk factors for the condition include:  unprotected sex  multiple/anonymous sexual partners  transactional sex  substance use before sex  other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) previously/currently  social vulnerability (poverty, homelessness, migrant/refugee status)  needle-sharing contact with a known syphilis case. Aetiology  Syphilis is an infectious disease caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.  Incubation period is around 21 days but can range from 9-90 days and is dependent on the infectious dose.  Most cases are sexually transmitted via direct contact with an infectious lesion.  Transmission may also occur via:  vertical transmission from mother to child in pregnancy  sharing needles in intravenous drug users (IVDUs)  blood products/organ transplants (screened for in UK).

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Untreated syphilis can persist for years and progress through several stages:  early syphilis (< 2 years of infection) = primary syphilis, secondary syphilis and early latent syphilis  late syphilis (> 2 years since infection) = late latent syphilis and tertiary syphilis.  Early syphilis:  primary syphilis is defined as a painless ulcer (chancre) at the site of infection + local lymphadenopathy  secondary syphilis is systemic involvement which may include: maculopapular rash (palms/soles), condylomata lata, patchy alopecia, snail-tract lesions (oral mucosa), generalised lymphadenopathy, low-grade fever, headache and malaise.  early latent - confirmed infection in absence of any current clinical features.  Late syphilis:  late latent is defined as confirmed infection in absence of current clinical features (infection > 2 years ago)  tertiary syphilis is rare, and may present with: cardiac disease, gummatous lesions or neurological disease.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms and signs can be varied and may include:  genital lesions – characteristic lesion of primary syphilis is a single, painless, indurated genital ulcer (also known as a chancre)  non-pruritic maculopapular rash (typically affecting palms and soles)  moist wart-like lesions (condylomata lata)  patchy lesions of the oral mucosa (snail-track ulcers)  generalised lymphadenopathy  unexplained neurological/ophthalmological symptoms.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis include:  genital herpes  balanitis  Behçet's syndrome  genital cancer  cervical erosion  chancroid lesions (haemophilus ducreyi).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full history – including symptoms of syphilis, risk factors (full sexual history) and past medical history (including treatment for previous STIs).  Examination – genital area, skin, eye, neurological and cardiovascular.

JAM  Referral to GUM clinic for full sexual health screen and diagnosis:  serology (usually positive from around 4 weeks but can take up to 3 months)  non-specific tests include venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) + rapid plasma reagin (RPR) (useful serial titres but high false + rate)  specific tests include treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA) and treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA)  dark-field microscopy – demonstrates T. Pallidum from swabs taken from primary lesion (high specificity but low sensitivity) – negative result doesn’t exclude syphilis.  All positive screening tests must be confirmed with a different serological test.  Negative serology tests should be repeated at 6 and 12 weeks post-infection or 2 weeks after possible chancre.  Management Non-Pharmacological  All patients with suspected syphilis should be referred to genitourinary medicine (GUM) clinic for general advice, management and contact tracing.  Patients should receive advice regarding avoidance of any form of sexual contact and avoidance of exposing others to the active lesion until the diagnosis excluded or successful treatment completed.  Explain the condition, risk factors and potential complications.  Look-back periods for contact tracing will vary but as an idea:  primary syphilis - approximately 3 months  secondary syphilis - approximately 2 years  tertiary syphilis - more than 2 years (back to the estimated time of infection).  People with suspected syphilis or a diagnosis of syphilis who decline testing/treatment should be advised that if they are found to have infected others with syphilis after knowing of their own infection, they may be subject to prosecution. Pharmacological Early syphilis  Procaine penicillin 750 mg IM OD for 10 days.  Or benzathine penicillin 2.4 mg IM for 1-2 doses, 1 week apart.  If penicillin allergic, doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days should be the preferred alternative. Late syphilis  Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mg IM for 3 doses, 1 week apart.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Or amoxicillin 2g PO TDS plus probenecid 500 mg QDS for 28 days.  If penicillin allergic, doxycycline 200 mg PO BD for 28 days.  Prognosis  If left untreated, around 1/3 of cases will progress to later stages of the disease and can lead to severe (and sometimes irreversible) complications including:  neuro-syphilis – neurological involvement which can occur at any stage of infection. Can affect: meninges, arteries, cranial nerves, eyes, brain and spinal cord  cardiovascular syphilis – aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, angina and heart failure  gummatous syphilis – granulomatous lesions with a necrotic centre, most commonly affects the skin and bones  adverse outcomes in pregnancy facilitation of HIV transmission. Tetanus Tetanus is an acute neurological condition characterised by skeletal muscle spasm and autonomic nervous system dysfunction/disturbance.  Overview Key Facts  Tetanus is an acute neurological condition characterised by skeletal muscle spasm and autonomic nervous system dysfunction/disturbance.  It is caused by a powerful neurotoxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium tetani (C. tetani).  C. tetani is an anaerobic bacterium found in the environment, especially in soil. It enters the body through a wound, commonly a penetrating injury.  It is preventable by vaccination and immunisation.  Tetanus commonly occurs where vaccination coverage is low, ie in third-world countries.  Vaccination is almost 100% effective.  Tetanus vaccine is also recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) worldwide during each pregnancy and is given between 27 and 36 weeks of gestation, along with the vaccine for diphtheria and pertussis (Tdap). This is to protect the fetus from tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis.  Established tetanus is a very severe disease associated with a very high mortality rate. Death occurs due to respiratory failure or cardiac arrest. Epidemiology  It is a rare disease in developed countries.  Persons > 60 years of age are at greater risk.

DR. JAM  Injection drug abusers are also at greater risk of contracting this disease.  In 2019 there were only four cases of tetanus reported in England. Aetiology  C. tetani is the causative organism and the toxin produced by this organism is responsible for the skeletal muscle spasms. Pathophysiology  C. tetani spores are introduced into a wound through contamination of the wound with soil, dirt, etc.  In anaerobic conditions (eg in a deep puncture wound), the spores germinate and start producing the neurotoxin (tetanus toxin).  The toxin enters motor neurones and travels up the neurones through the axon to the spinal cord.  Tetanus toxin arriving in the motor neurone cell body interferes with the action of inhibitory neurones responsible for the relaxation of skeletal muscles by releasing inhibitory neurotransmitters.  The tetanus toxin prevents the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters by inhibitory neurones at the synapse resulting in the constant firing of motor neurones.  This leads to repeated muscular contractions leading to total spasm of the body.  Clinical Presentation  There are usually no immediate symptoms of tetanus; it can take up to three weeks for symptoms to appear.  Symptoms include:  jerking or seizures of the body  difficulty in swallowing  stiffness of the lower limbs  contraction of neck and spine resulting in an arch-shaped body  extremely painful spams can also cause bone fractures  the most common symptom is the locked jaw which may be very severe and can lead to suffocation  respiratory distress  fever.  Neonatal tetanus is an illness occurring in a neonate who has the normal ability to suck and cry in the first two days of life but loses this ability between days three and eight of life and becomes rigid and has spasms:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Neonatal_tetanus_6374.jpg  Maternal tetanus occurs during pregnancy or within six weeks after the conclusion of pregnancy (whether with birth, miscarriage or abortion).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  drug-induced dystonia  neuroleptic syndrome  strychnine poisoning  Moersch–Woltman syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Tetanus is diagnosed on the basis of immunisation history and signs and symptoms and physical examination.  Laboratory or radiological investigations are not helpful in diagnosing this condition.  Management Non-Pharmacological  There is currently no known cure if the disease has manifested its effects.  The only way when the disease has occurred is to treat the symptoms until the disease naturally resolves itself.  Tetanus vaccination is the only way to prevent this disease.  Hygienic delivery conditions for babies.

DR. JAM  100% prevention can be achieved by vaccination.  Booster shots after every 10 years.  Efficient immunisation programme. Pharmacological  Antibiotics such as penicillin, metronidazole and doxycycline are administered for the prevention of local infiltration of C. tetani.  Surgical  In severe cases, surgery or mechanical respirators can be used until full recovery.  Surgical debridement of the wound.  Prognosis  Prognosis is excellent for immunised individuals.  The mortality rate in mild-to-moderate cases of tetanus is up to 10%.  In severe cases, the mortality rate can be as high as 60–70%.  Other  The risk of death is high if the patient is diabetic.  C. tetani is found in dirt, dust and on the surface of iron objects.  Tetanus can also reoccur.  It can be spread by animal bites including those of pet animals, eg dogs. One can also be infected from different surgical procedures if not immunised. Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxic shock syndrome is an acute, severe, multisystem inflammatory response secondary to streptococcal and staphylococcal bacterial toxin release.  Overview Key Facts  Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is an acute, severe, multisystem inflammatory response secondary to streptococcal and staphylococcal bacterial toxin release.  The most common pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus (Staph A) and Streptococcus pyogenes (Strep P).

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Presentation – ‘viral-type’ symptoms, pyrexia, shock (hypotension), a rash with potential future desquamation, circulatory collapse and the potential for organ failure.  Treatment involves support, assessment and management of shock, identification and possible removal of the cause, alongside antibiotics.  Mortality is high, roughly between 5% and 10%. Epidemiology  Difficult to determine accurate epidemiology in the United Kingdom (UK). In the USA it is a notifiable disease in many states.  USA numbers reach a rough maximum of 0.05 cases per 100 000 population; it is thought that UK numbers are similar.  Previously there were higher numbers, with most cases linked to tampon usage. However, since 1980s and 1990s, improved tampon production methods and user information have reduced the number of cases.  Now about one-third of TSS cases are in children. Aetiology  Aetiology based on method of introduction streptococci or staphylococci into the system.  Risk increased by:  wound packing (including that for nose bleeds)  wounds, eg boils, cuts, burns, surgical  sinusitis  immune deficiency, eg HIV, malignancy  intravenous (IV) drug use  preceding staphylococcal/streptococcal infection, eg strep throat, cellulitis or impetigo  female specific – tampon usage (especially incorrect use), female barrier contraception, childbirth, presence of vaginal Group A strep infection. Pathophysiology  The most common bacteria implicated in TSS are Staphylococcus aureus (Staph A) and Streptococcus pyogenes (Strep P).  Staphylococci exist in healthy skin flora.  Staph A is often harmless and found in around ¼ of people.  However, Strep P is not normally on the skin and it often leads to disease.  Strep P is often known as Group A Strep, but this is an inaccurate name, as other streptococci can also display the Group A antigen in lab testing.  Infections resulting in TSS normally occur due to the breakdown in the skin, the first layer of defence.  In an infection, the bacteria in TSS release exotoxins that can cause a large immune response. These exotoxins stimulate a very pronounced response; as a result, they are called ‘superantigens’.  The resulting massive immune response (aka ‘cytokine storm’) involves the overactivation of the complement cascade, eg
