JAM increase in bradykinin will reduce blood pressure and factor XII will cause coagulation.  The overall effect will be of fever, vasodilatation, capillary leakage, altered metabolism, tissue damage and potential disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).  The exotoxin most responsible is produced by Staph A and is known as TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome toxin-1).  Clinical Presentation Symptoms  Fever.  Headache, chills, muscle ache, cough, sore throat.  Nausea and vomiting.  Diarrhoea.  Rash.  Peeling of hand/feet skin.  Dizziness/fainting.  SOB.  Confusion, drowsiness.  Potential wound on the skin. Signs  Pyrexia > 39 °C.  Rash – diffuse, erythematous, papular; said to resemble ‘sandpaper’; may desquamate 7–14 days after onset.  Hypotension.  Bright red appearance of palms, soles, tongue and mucous membranes.  Confusion (caused by potential encephalopathy).  GI symptoms.  Myalgia, muscle weakness.  Any skin lesion, eg from an insect bite, may or may not show local signs of infection.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  other causes of septic shock  meningitis  cellulitis  viral infection with accompanying exanthem  drug reactions, eg erythema multiforme.  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis is made through clinical history and physical examination, including assessment for the source of the investigation.  Physical examination should include the ABCDE approach, with the circulatory and respiratory systems requiring careful assessment.  Examination may include a gynaecological examination to assess the presence of a tampon or retained contraceptives.  Skin examination of the rash should be done alongside, looking for potential infection entry sites. Investigation  Bloods:  routine bloods (typical picture is ↑leukocytes, ↓platelets, ↓Ca2+, electrolyte abnormalities, ↑urea, ↑creatinine, ↑LFTs, ↑CK)  blood cultures (positive in approximately 50%)  arterial blood gases (ABGs).  Others:  urinalysis – potential microscopic haematuria or myoglobulin presence  swabs of any wounds for MC&S, potential throat swab for streptococci  if respiratory concerns, consider chest X-ray  imaging of previous surgical sites or abscess, eg via MRI/CT.  Ruling out other causes:  lumbar puncture might be needed.  Monitoring:  important to monitor patient response to intervention via clinical observations/bloods for resolving respiratory/haemodynamic compromise and infection improvement.  Management  The first step may include the urgent management of Shock.  otherwise, early treatment is important to prevent further immunological upregulation.  Admission is necessary for monitoring and treatment.  Intensive Care Unit intervention may be required.  IV fluids and catheterisation are needed in most patients.  Analgesia might be needed for the skin manifestations of the ‘flu-like symptoms’.

DR. JAM Non-Pharmacological  Important to remove any precipitating infection site, eg vaginal foreign body, wound ‘packing’. Pharmacological  IV antibiotics for treatment of the infectious source is important. Normally MRSA cover is included until full MC&S results have returned.  Common antibiotic regimen:  IV clindamycin + IV flucloxacillin/vancomycin  most localities have their own prescribing practices.  IV antibiotics duration might be needed ≥ 2 weeks.  Surgical  Surgical intervention might be needed for wound debridement, site exploration, wound package or abscess drainage.  Prognosis  Mortality approximately 5–10%.  Prevention – hygiene/correct usage of tampons and female barrier contraceptives, rapid first-aid of wounds. The public should be aware of signs of wound infections. Recurrence prevention – avoiding the female barrier contraception/tampons. Toxoplasmosis An intracellular obligate parasite Toxoplasma gondii causes toxoplasmosis.  Overview Key Facts  An intracellular obligate parasite Toxoplasma gondii (T. gondii) causes toxoplasmosis.  Rate of incidence is very high, yet many people remain asymptomatic (almost 90%).  Immunocompromised patients such as patients with HIV/AIDS suffer from the symptoms of toxoplasmosis.  Can also affect people on cancer chemotherapy or those on immunosuppressive drug treatment.  T. gondii can be found in the intestines of cats, which is the ultimate host of this parasite.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The symptoms are more like flu symptoms with fatigue, tiredness, fever and body aches. Symptoms can be from mild to severe depending upon the strength of the immune system of the affected person.  T. gondii can create cysts in the brain, muscles and heart.  The infection may pass from pregnant mothers to the fetus through the placenta and can cause a scale of complications ranging from mild eye infections to severe infections, causing serious eye disorders, seizures, mental disability, hearing loss or stillbirth.  The source of infection is raw uncooked or improperly cooked meat or cysts found in cat faeces or in goat's milk. Epidemiology  Prevalence is at its highest in tropical areas of the world such as South America, India and Malaysia, with a prevalence of around 60%. This is followed by southern European countries where there is a prevalence of around 54%.  Incidence in the United Kingdom (UK) is around 25%.  There are thee main strains of T. gondii.  T. gondii in Europe and North America – type I is the most virulent and type III the least; type II is the most common strain found in humans in Europe and North America. Aetiology  Pathogen – T. gondii, which is an obligate intracellular parasite.  Route of transmission is via oral or placental, or by blood transfusion or organ transplantation.  The cysts of T. gondii present in cat faeces are eaten by other animals such as goats or cows and enter the meat (either raw or improperly cooked), or they can gain entry to the human body by drinking unpasteurised goat's milk.  Most commonly acquired through undercooked meat (most commonly pork or lamb) which contain tissue cysts. It can also be acquired through drinking contaminated water.  Risk factors identified are eating raw minced beef, raw oysters, clams, mussels, drinking unpasteurised goat’s milk and having three or more kittens. Pathophysiology  After the ingestion of T. gondii cysts, viable organisms are released which enter epithelial cells of the small gut where they multiply through asexual or sexual cell cycles and form oocysts (containing zygotes), which are released and then tachyzoite attach to the cell membrane of the host cell.  The attachment is augmented by the host cell’s protein.  After utilising the cellular matrix for its growth, the organism is then released into the blood circulation.  The response to the gut epithelial entry of the tachyzoite is the release of chemokines which bring macrophages and neutrophils to the site of damage.  An autoimmune pathway is then activated to recruit interleukin-12 (IL-12). This then stimulates interferongamma (IFN-gamma) synthesis by T lymphocytes and NK (natural killer) cells. (This is the most important step in controlling the infection of T. gondii.)

DR. JAM  In immunocompromised patients these autoimmune pathways are not regulated which allows T. gondii to replicate unopposed and damage the epithelial cells, as well as cause cerebral toxoplasmosis.  The incubation period is 1–2 weeks.  It is transported to the gut via lymphatics and to the rest of the body via blood circulation.  Clinical Presentation  90% of patients are asymptomatic.  In immunocompromised patients, the symptoms are more like flu symptoms, including fever, body aches, chills, sore throat or pharyngitis, or maybe hepatosplenomegaly.  The level of suspicion should be high in patients with HIV/AIDS or patients who have undergone organ transplantation or multiple blood transfusions.  Neurological symptoms are evident in cerebral toxoplasmosis, including fever, seizures, confusion and severe headache with focal neurological deficit.  It can also cause chorioretinitis or pneumonitis in which the patient will present with vision disturbance or ocular pain, or breathing difficulty or cough, respectively.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  HIV infection  AIDS infection  CNS lymphoma or brain tumour  cerebral tuberculomas  progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy  herpes viral encephalitis  human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5) or cytomegalovirus  brain abscess (bacterial or fungal).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Serological investigation by identifying IgM and IgG antibodies.  Detection of T. gondii by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).  Biopsy for definitive diagnosis is not routinely performed in toxoplasmosis; it is only indicated for patients who fail to respond to treatment to rule out differential diagnosis.  Radiological investigations:  CT scan of the brain for cerebral toxoplasmosis  MRI for differentiating brain lesions and cerebral tuberculosis (the preferred choice of investigation)  PET (positron emission tomography) scan has the highest specificity.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management Non-Pharmacological  Avoid uncooked/raw or improperly cooked food.  Keep the pets, especially cats, healthy.  Always drink pasteurised milk.  Thorough washing of fruits and vegetables.  Avoidance of stray cats. Pharmacological  Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine given for several weeks in combination is the first choice of treatment if the infection is not self-limiting.  Folinic acid (reduced folic acid) supplementation and weekly blood cell counts are required with the above treatment to avoid complications.  Alternative combinations can be considered as follows:  pyrimethamine – clindamycin  pyrimethamine – clarithromycin  pyrimethamine – azithromycin.  In immunocompromised symptomatic patients, long-term prophylaxis is also required with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole until the patient gains his/her immunity.  Spiramycin to avoid vertical transmission.  Surgical  Only attempted for ocular toxoplasmosis.  Antibiotic treatment is the mainstay of the treatment.  Prognosis  It is self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals.  Prognosis is good without any long-term side effects of the infection.  Timely diagnosis and detection and commencement of antibiotic treatment and antiviral treatment in patients with AIDS, improve the outcome many folds.  Other  Although the primary infection is self-limiting, the risk of latent reactivation is increased to 60% in immunocompromised patients.  Patient education is the key to its prevention, especially for patients with immunocompromised states.  The parasite T. gondii may change its behaviour, varying from host to host.

Travel-Related Medicine Common clinical presentations in returning travellers include fever, diarrhoea, and rash.  Overview Key Facts  Common clinical presentations in returning travellers include fever, diarrhoea, and rash.  The commonest causes of fever in the returning traveller are those causing fever in the non-traveller, ie simple lower respiratory tract/urinary infections.  The priorities when assessing a returning traveller are identification and treatment of life-threatening infection and controlling the spread of infection.  Key differential diagnoses include malaria, viral haemorrhagic fever, rickettsial infections (Lyme disease), HIV, typhoid, and Dengue fever.  Important investigations include thick and thin films for malaria parasites; HIV testing; and serological studies.  Important factors to elucidate in the history include:  dates of travel, destinations  purpose of visit (business trip vs. holiday)  activities and exposures (bites, environmental factors, food and drink)  sexual history.  Many risks can be mitigated in travellers by seeking appropriate specialist input in advance:  advice (eg avoiding unprotected sex, food, and drink hygiene)  vaccines and chemoprophylaxis. Epidemiology  Approximately 25% of people travelling to any destination worldwide will experience ill health abroad or on returning home.  The group at highest risk of tropical illness is immigrants returning to their country of origin to visit friends and relatives (VFR) after many years abroad. Aetiology  Pathogens vary with location; elucidate the dates of travel in the history as this will alter differential diagnosis based on incubation periods.  Important pathogens in travellers returning from sub-Saharan Africa include:  Plasmodium falciparum

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  HIV (acute seroconversion and AIDS-defining illnesses)  Rickettsia spp  Ebola.  Important pathogens in travellers returning from South Asia include:  P. falciparum and P. vivax/ovale  Dengue virus  Salmonella typhi/paratyphi  HIV.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical features are often non-specific – fever, diarrhoea and vomiting, shortness of breath/cough, urinary symptoms, and rashes.  Viral haemorrhagic fever (VHF), eg Ebola, Lassa fever and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever:  shock – tachycardia, tachypnoea, and hypotension  spontaneous haemorrhage ranging from petechiae to lifethreatening bleeding - Epistaxis, subconjunctival haemorrhage, and bloody diarrhoea are common features  confusion.  Dengue fever classically presents with a ‘saddleback’ (biphasic) recrudescent (repeated episodes) of fever, chills, a retro-orbital headache, and a widespread maculopapular rash:  dengue haemorrhagic fever is an important lifethreatening complication which results from subsequent infection by a separate viral serotype. Clinical presentation is similar to VHF with evidence of shock and spontaneous haemorrhage.  Typhoid (enteric fever) is a non-specific febrile illness characterised by chills, myalgia, dry cough, abdominal pain, and frequently constipation (sometimes diarrhoea):  symptoms are usually mild with most patients presenting in the second or third week of illness due to persistent fevers  ‘Rose spots’ are small, pink blanching macules on the trunk – rare diagnostic finding  a ‘relative bradycardia’, ie heart rate not as high as might be expected in setting of high fevers is seen in around 50% of patients with confirmed enteric fever  persistent illness lasting > 3 weeks may be complicated by sepsis or intestinal perforation, which carry a mortality of 15% if untreated.  Rickettsial infection is common worldwide and spread by various different disease vectors:  all rickettsial infections are characterised by febrile illness with rash, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly  Rocky mountain spotted fever is spread by ticks and commonly seen in the USA in forested areas. Rocky mountain spotted fever rash:

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  Fever in the returning traveller:  Asia – malaria, Dengue fever, malaria, scrub typhus and leishmaniasis  Sub-Saharan Africa – falciparum malaria, HIV infection, VHF, and Rickettsial infection.  Diarrhoeal illness in the returning traveller:  Watery – traveller’s diarrhoea, cholera, Giardia, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)  Bloody – amoebic dysentery, viral haemorrhagic fever, and IBD.  Rashes in the returning traveller:  Bites and stings – look for black eschars on the skin (scrub typhus)  Maculopapular rash – Dengue fever, HIV seroconversion, Chikungunya, and Zika  Urticarial rash – acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) and strongyloides.  Diagnosis/Investigation Investigations depend on clinical symptoms and where a patient has travelled.  Key initial investigations for patients presenting with fever include:  Thick and thin blood films for malaria parasites +/- rapid diagnostic test  Blood cultures – diagnostic for typhoid  Blood tests – full blood count (FBC) (thrombocytopenia in Dengue); C-reactive protein (CRP), urea and electrolytes (U&E), liver function tests (LFTs), and VBG for lactate

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Serological tests for specific suspected illnesses, eg HIV/Dengue/Zika  Adjunctive tests include urine dipstick and chest X-ray.  Management Non-Pharmacological  Patients with evidence of sepsis or symptoms in presence of significant comorbidities may require hospitalisation with good supportive care:  for example, Dengue fever has no effective treatment; supportive care only.  Patients with potentially communicable diseases (eg Ebola) infection require careful barrier nursing to minimise the risk of disease transmission as well as specialist ID team input. Pharmacological  Patients with severe malaria should be treated with IV artesunate (see malaria for full summary).  Typhoid – azithromycin generally first line but consult local guidelines due to resistance.  Rickettsial infection – doxycycline.  Prognosis  Prognosis ultimately depends on the causative pathogen and prompt treatment where available.  Dengue fever is generally mild and self-limiting but haemorrhagic and shock complications are associated with significant mortality > 5%. Prompt antibiotic treatment reduces the risk of mortality in patients with complications of typhoid fever (perforation or sepsis) from 15% to 1-3%. Trypanosomiasis Trypanosomiasis is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, with a distinct form (Chagas disease) seen in South America. Each have different vectors and clinical manifestations.  Overview Key Facts  Trypanosomiasis is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, with a distinct form (Chagas disease) seen in South America. Each have different vectors and clinical manifestations. African trypanosomiasis:

DR. JAM  African trypanosomiasis is caused by protozoa transmitted by the tsetse fly. There are two major parasite species with distinct geographical distributions:  trypanosoma brucei gambiense predominates in West Africa  trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense predominates in East Africa.  In the first stage of infection, trypanosomes multiply in the blood and lymphatic tissues. Early clinical features include fever, headaches, arthralgia, and pruritus.  In the later stage of infection – which may occur many months or even years after the first – trypanosomes invade the central nervous system and cause of meningoencephalitis. Signs and symptoms include personality change, agitation and severely disordered sleep:  the term ‘sleeping sickness’ reflects the progressive somnolence displayed by patients during this phase of the disease.  Although rare in the UK, suspect African trypanosomiasis in travellers returning from Safari in West and East Africa.  The investigations of choice are thick and thin blood films, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) microscopy and serology.  Treatment depends on the stage of the disease and organism type:  first stage:  West African – pentamidine  East African – suramin.  central nervous system (CNS) stage:  West African – nifurtimox and eflornithine  East African – melarsoprol. South American trypanosomiasis:  South American trypanosomiasis is caused by trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by reduviid bugs. It can also be transmitted via blood transfusion.  Acute infection is non-specific. Patients typically develop chronic Chagas disease 10-20 years after initial infection. There are three classic manifestations to be aware of:  cardiomyopathy and cardiac arrhythmias (typically complete heart block)  mega-oesophagus and megacolon. Both result from destruction of the parasympathetic nerves supplying these structures. Patients may present with recurrent aspiration, bloating, or severe constipation.  Diagnosis is based on serology and identification of trypanosomes in acute illness.  Treatment is with benznidazole or nifurtimox. Patients with megacolon or megaoesophagus may require surgery.  Chagas disease is associated with around 20 000 deaths annually, most of these cases occurring in in central and south America.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI African trypanosomiasis life cycle: Tuberculosis Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that can affect any part of the body but usually affects the lungs.  Overview Key Facts  Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that can affect any part of the body but usually affects the lungs.  The number of new cases of tuberculosis (TB) declined in the UK throughout the twentieth century, mainly due to the improvement in living standards.  Three main categories are:  primary TB  post-primary TB  miliary TB.  The most commonly involved site is the lung – but TB also affect lymph nodes, bones, the renal tract, and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.  Tuberculous meningitis is the most serious complication.

DR. JAM  Treatment combination of antibiotic therapy: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol. Epidemiology Groups most at risk include:  Those on low incomes.  Homeless people.  People with alcohol problems.  HIV-positive individuals.  Immigrants from countries with a high incidence of TB.  Patients with diabetes. Aetiology  Primary TB: primary infection occurs in those without immunity.  Post-primary TB: organisms disseminated by the blood at the time of primary infection may reactivate many years later.  Miliary TB: widespread dissemination of infection via the bloodstream.  Commonest causative organism is mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology Primary TB:  A small lung lesion known as the Ghon focus develops in the mid or lower zones of the lung, and is composed of tubercleladen macrophages.  Bacilli are transported through the lymphatics to the draining lymph nodes, which enlarge considerably and undergo caseation.  Infection is often arrested at this stage and the bacteria may remain dormant for many years.  The peripheral lung lesion and the nodes heal and may calcify. The entire process is often asymptomatic. However, specific immunity begins to develop and tuberculin skin tests become positive. Post-primary TB:  The most common site is the lungs, with bone and lymph node sites being less common.  Reactivation may be precipitated by a waning of host immunity, eg due to malignancy, or immunosuppressive drugs (including steroids).

DR. JAM Milliary TB:  The infection is spread via the bloodstream.  Clinical Presentation  Primary infection is often asymptomatic, but may cause mild cough and wheeze or erythema nodosum.  Features of reactivation/reinfection:  persistent cough  haemoptysis  pneumonia  weight loss  night sweats  lymphadenopathy  meningitis  ‘cold’ abscess – anterior triangle, tense, not hot erythematous, slow growing.  In miliary TB, hepatosplenomegaly eventually develops and choroidal tubercles may be visible on fundoscopy.  Children can present with non-specific symptoms and signs such as fatigue, poor weight gain, and persistently raised temperature.  Differential Diagnosis  Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI).  Asthma.  Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI).  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Pulmonary fibrosis.  Lung cancer.  Lymphoma.  Opportunistic mycobacterial infections.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Chest X-ray (CXR):  patchy shadowing in the upper zones  volume loss and cavitation, and ultimately fibrosis  Miliary TB: multiple rounded shadows a few millimetres in diameter. CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI CT scan shows a cavitating lesion in the left lung: Three respiratory samples (confirms diagnosis).  Sputum collections: at least three, including one early morning sample:  for acid- and alcohol-fast bacilli (AAFB) using Ziehl– Neelsen or auramine stain and smear

DR. JAM  Then cultured on Lo¨wenstein–Jensen medium for at least 6 weeks (organism is slow growing)  polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for tuberculous DNA can be used to provide a rapid diagnosis, whilst awaiting a culture result – allows for earlier initiation of antituberculous chemotherapy in acutely unwell patients with smear-negative samples, particularly if immunocompromised  allows for early differentiation from non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection (important to know before embarking on an extensive screening programme of contacts). Can also be used to detect multidrug-resistant disease.  Bronchoscopy and lavage: used for those unable to expectorate; transbronchial biopsy if miliary disease is present is a possibility.  Additional test if extrapulmonary TB suspected. Depending on site:  X-rays: Joint and spinal  ultrasound scan: abdominal/renal tract/lymph node  urine sample: dipstick, microscopy and culture  echocardiogram  CT: chest, CNS, bones/joints.  Aspiration  pleural effusion  bone marrow.  Biopsy  liver  lymph nodes. The images are of the same patient. The thickening of the terminal wall was eventually suspected to be due to TB and the CXR performed revealed right upper lobe consolidation due to TB.  Usually, small bowel or colonic TB is due to the patients’ digestion of sputum that has been produced by the affected lung.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI http://www.svuhradiology.ie/case-study/tb-terminal-ileitis/ Screening People who are eligible for screening include:  those who are/have been in contact with active laryngeal/pulmonary TB need to be screened for latent TB  people who are immunocompromised  new entrants to the UK from high-risk countries who have not had pre-entry screening  new NHS employees working with patients or clinical specimens  people who have not completed treatment with evidence of TB scarring or untreated fibrotic changes on chest x-ray. Screening tests  Mantoux testing (first line) involves injecting tuberculin intradermally and inspecting the skin for signs of a local skin reaction (induration) after 2–3 days, test is considered positive at an induration of 5 mm or more, regardless of previous BCG vaccination history:  May be offered to children and young people aged 2–17 years who have been in close contact with people with pulmonary or laryngeal TB; and to new entrants to the UK from high TB prevalence countries.  Interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) is a blood test that detects the response of white blood cells to TB antigens.  Both a Mantoux test and IGRA may be offered to people who are severely immunocompromised at risk of TB:  People younger than 65 years of age from under-served groups (such as the homeless or substance misusers) may be offered a single IGRA test.

DR. JAM  The use of anti-tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) therapy can be associated with reactivation of latent TB. Patients due to start such treatment should be screened for active/latent/past TB. Those who have had adequately treated past TB should be monitored closely. Where past TB has not been treated fully or latent TB is identified, a course of chemoprophylaxis is given.  Management Non-Pharmacological:  Physiotherapy may be of benefit when there is joint involvement. Pharmacological:  Management of active TB is delivered in a combination of four drugs:  Rifampicin  Isoniazid  Pyrazinamide  Ethambutol.  Short courses of treatment for 6 months are now standard. All drugs are given for 2 months, and isoniazid and rifampicin are continued for a further 4 months.  For patient with active TB of the CNS, continue isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin for a further 10 months.  Steroids are also indicated in meningeal TB for at least 3 weeks before being weaned down gradually.  All four drugs are continued until sensitivities are known.  If pyrazinamide has to be discontinued due to side-effects, a 9month regimen is necessary.  Second-line agents (eg ethionamide, propionamide, streptomycin, cycloserine) may be needed.  Compliance can pose major problems and directly observed therapy (D.OT – larger doses of drugs administered three times per week) is used when poor compliance is anticipated.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Ongoing investigations and results:  Once 2 weeks of anti-tuberculous chemotherapy has been completed, a smear-positive patient is considered to be noninfectious.  Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) signifies resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, and currently accounts for 1.8% of tuberculous infections.  Extremely drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) signifies resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid, a quinolone, and a second-line injectable agent (eg amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin). There were 3 cases of XDR-TB in 2017. Side-effects from these drugs are common. They include:  Hepatitis due to rifampicin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide. There is an increased risk of hepatotoxicity from anti-tuberculous chemotherapy with age.  Optic neuritis: may be caused by ethambutol; visual acuity should be checked before treatment is initiated. May also cause yellowing of vision.  Peripheral neuropathy: may be due to isoniazid; 10 mg pyridoxine daily is given in those at particular risk of this complication (eg people with alcohol problems, diabetes, and patients with renal failure).  Urinary discolouration (red/orange colour) – Rifampicin. Bacile Calmette-Guerin (BCG) Vaccination:  The school BCG programme has now been withdrawn.  Neonatal BCG immunisation is recommended for babies at high risk of tuberculosis infection.  Unimmunised children between 4 weeks and 16 years of age with an increased risk should be offered BCG immunisation.  The efficacy of BCG varies in different communities but usually helps prevent severe, disseminated disease. If a latent TB infection test is positive, then an assessment for active TB should be performed. If there is no evidence of active infection on the basis of symptoms and chest Xray, the person should be treated for latent TB infection. Chemoprophylaxis is usually either:  three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin  six months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine).  Surgical:  In Pott’s disease (crush fracture of thoracic spine due to tuberculous osteomyelitis), surgery may be necessary to correct the deformity and prevent spinal complications. May require drainage of abscess and evacuation of infected material.  Prognosis  Milliary TB is universally fatal if left untreated.

DR. JAM  Other relevant information:  Tuberculosis (TB) is a notifiable disease. A clinician (usually a TB specialist) should notify a new culture-confirmed case of TB, or where TB is suspected and a decision has been made to treat the person, within 3 working days.  Opportunistic mycobacterial infections.  These account for 10% of all mycobacterial infections. Causative organisms include the following:  Mycobacterium kansasii (most common)  M. xenopi  M. malmoense  M. avium intracellulare.  These organisms cause disease that is clinically and radiologically identical to TB, and indistinguishable from TB on sputum smear.  pulmonary disease, lymphadenitis (in children), and disseminated infection are the most common clinical problems.  most patients are middle-aged/elderly with significant underlying COPD, bronchiectasis or previous TB.  a minimum of two positive cultures taken a week apart in a patient with an appropriate clinical picture is necessary to make the diagnosis.  The organisms are ubiquitous in the environment and are lowgrade pathogens. Opportunistic mycobacterial infections constitute a relatively higher proportion of mycobacterial infections in patients with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS).  The onset of symptoms is usually gradual.  Treatment programmes are generally longer than for TB, and are continued for at least 9 months and often for 2 years.  Rifampicin and ethambutol are the mainstay of treatment; clarithromycin or ciprofloxacin may be added.  Opportunistic infections do not need to be notified. Contact tracing is unnecessary as person-to-person infection is very rare. Typhoid Fever Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi, leading to symptoms like high fever, abdominal pain and weakness.  Overview Key Facts  Salmonella spp. are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacilli.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  They can be loosely divided into non-typhoidal and typhoidal salmonella.  Non-typhoidal salmonella causes self-limiting gastroenteritis, whereas typhoidal salmonella causes typhoid (enteric) fever, a systemic disease characterised by prolonged fever, abdominal pain and a rose spots rash.  Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi (S. typhi) and Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphi (S. paratyphi) are responsible for typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever, respectively.  Most typhoidal salmonella infections occur in developing countries with poor sanitary conditions and untreated water supplies.  Diagnosis is via blood culture.  Treatment is with antibiotics, usually fluoroquinolone.  There is an excellent prognosis and complications are rare when treated appropriately with antibiotics. Epidemiology  There are 11–21 million cases per year worldwide.  Highest incidence is in East and South-east Asia, Africa and Central and South America.  May occur in developed countries among travellers returning from endemic areas. Aetiology  There are two species of salmonella – Salmonella enterica and Salmonella bongori.  Salmonella enterica has over 2500 serotypes. These can be divided into non-typhoidal (such as S. enteritidis and S. typhimurium) and typhoidal.  Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi (S. typhi) and Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphi (S. paratyphi) are responsible for typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever, respectively.  S. typhi is responsible for 60–80% of cases.  S. paratyphi A, B and C differ in geographical distribution. For example, S. paratyphi A is most common in India, whereas S. paratyphi B is most common in South America and S. paratyphi C in Africa.  Humans are the only known reservoir.  Transmission is via the faecal–oral route. This can be either person-to-person or in contaminated food and water. Pathophysiology  The bacteria first have to adhere to and invade the gut wall.  They migrate into the Peyer's patches of the distal ileum and spread throughout the reticuloendothelial system to the liver, spleen and bone marrow. They are also able to enter the bloodstream, resulting in bacteraemia.  Incubation is typically 2–3 weeks.  Until bacteraemia is established the patient is usually asymptomatic.  Distribution throughout the reticuloendothelial system and bloodstream allows for loci of secondary metastatic infection,

DR. JAM such as splenic abscesses, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, arthritis and cholecystitis.  Clinical Presentation  There are three stages of symptoms, each lasting approximately 1 week.  Week 1:  high fever, occurring in a stepwise fashion of daily increments.  relative bradycardia (the heart may only be moderately increased in the presence of a high fever)  disturbance to bowel habit, constipation is more common than diarrhoea  prodromal symptoms, eg headache, malaise, cough  nausea and anorexia.  Week 2:  persistent fever  rose spots (erythematous maculopapular rash on the chest and abdomen)  ‘pea soup’ diarrhoea  abdominal pain  splenomegaly  neurological symptoms such as confusion, delirium and drowsiness.  Week 3:  if left untreated, complications may develop such as hepatomegaly, bowel perforation and gastrointestinal bleeding, meningitis, haemolytic anaemia, acute cholecystitis, renal failure and myocarditis.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  malaria  dengue fever  infectious mononucleosis  typhus.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Laboratory:  FBC – anaemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia  LFTs – transaminitis  blood cultures – can be detected from the first week of symptoms  stool cultures – ideally collected more than 1 week following the onset of fever  urine cultures.  Investigations to consider:  bone marrow culture  rose spot culture

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Widal’s agglutination test – demonstrates antibodies to antigens of S. typhi or S. paratyphi.  Management  Mainstay of management is antibiotic therapy and supportive care, such as antipyretics and intravenous fluids.  Suspected diagnosis:  antibiotic therapy – first-line choice is a third-generation cephalosporin (usually ceftriaxone or cefixime) alone or in combination with oral azithromycin  azithromycin is usually added if no clinical response after 4–5 days of antibiotic therapy.  Confirmed diagnosis:  the choice of antibiotic agent is adjusted according to the sensitivity assays  if sensitive to all antibiotics, ciprofloxacin should be used; if resistant to fluoroquinolones, a third-generation cephalosporin with or without azithromycin is appropriate  extensively drug-resistant strains may be treated with meropenem in combination with azithromycin.  Management of complications:  dexamethasone is used in patients with neurological complications  prolonged courses of antibiotics or surgery may be required in cases of loci of secondary infection.  Prevention:  strict hygiene rules, such as avoiding contaminated water  vaccination:  there are three types of vaccine (the live attenuated oral vaccine, the capsular polysaccharide vaccine and the conjugated vaccine)  these are recommended for travellers staying in endemic areas for more than 1 month or in locations where antibiotic-resistant strains are prevalent.  Prognosis  Excellent prognosis and complications are rare when treated appropriately with antibiotics.  Complications include:  multidrug-resistant strains of S. typhi and S. paratyphi are prevalent worldwide, particularly in India  typhoid hepatitis and splenic abscesses  intestinal perforation and gastrointestinal bleeding  acute cholecystitis and chronic biliary carriage  pneumonia  myocarditis, pericarditis and endocarditis  encephalitis and meningitis. Mortality rate is < 1%. Death is much more common in endemic areas (up to 30%).

DR. JAM Varicella Zoster Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus is also known as chickenpox.  Overview Key Facts  Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus is also known as chickenpox.  It is a common childhood infection presenting with a ‘contagious’ rash, sore throat and pyrexia.  In well children, chickenpox is normally self-limiting with good recovery.  Higher complication risk – older adults, pregnancy, immunocompromised states, neonates.  Complications in adults include varicella pneumonia, hepatitis and encephalitis.  Management of at-risk groups includes antivirals and/or varicella zoster immunoglobulin.  Complications are more likely with increased age, immunocompromise, pregnancy, comorbidities, neonatal or intrauterine infection.  80% of varicella zoster deaths occur in adults. Epidemiology  United Kingdom (UK) – most common in childhood; approximately 90% seropositive before adolescence.  Both sexes equally affected.  Endemic in most countries, usually epidemics in spring/winter.  Higher risk of contraction with certain jobs (eg healthcare, schools).  Illness severity and complication risk increase with age, pregnancy, smoking status and immunocompromise. Aetiology  Varicella zoster is a disease due to primary infection with varicella zoster virus (VZV), occasionally referred to as herpes virus 3. Pathophysiology  Transmission occurs in two ways:  airborne (to upper respiratory mucosa, eyes)  direct contact.  The incubation period is approximately 2–3 weeks (but can be as short as 9 days).  The infectious period is 2 days prior to rash onset until all lesions are crusted.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Possible to also contract from those with shingles (aka herpes zoster), but this would specifically require lesion contact.  VZV multiples at the transmission site and presents to the immune system.  It spreads via blood.  The blisters are intraepithelial and the vesicular fluid has high viral counts.  Direct spread from upper respiratory mucosa leads to lower respiratory complications such as viral pneumonia.  Viral dissemination can lead to multisystem spread and severe complications. This is normally in the immunocompromised.  Pregnancy also has the added risk of generating intrauterine infection.  After recovery from varicella zoster, the virus becomes latent in the cranial nerve and dorsal root ganglia.  Extremely rare to have varicella zoster a second time; reactivation causes the disease named herpes zoster or shingles.  Clinical Presentation  Prodrome:  fever  headache  malaise  abdominal (D&V, pain) lasting less than a few days.  Skin lesions rapid progress in few hours through these stages:  macules  papules (vesicles)  pustules  crusting (last less than a few weeks).  Typical prodrome:  possibly mild or absent in the young  more severe in older children and adults, pregnancy, the immunocompromised  symptoms improve at lesion onset.  Typical lesions:  common locations are head and trunk (limbs, genitals, soles of feet, palms of hands and oral mucosa less common)  are highly pruritic  can exist in all phases at the same time and in the same location  crust-over within 5 days of lesion onset  heal without scars.

DR. JAM  Differential Diagnosis  The differential diagnosis is based on the skin appearance and/or systemic features and can be categorised into simple dermatological condition and infections with skin lesions.  Simple dermatological:  eczema  contact dermatitis  insect bites  dermatitis herpetiformis.  Infections:  herpes simplex virus  impetigo  scabies  hand, foot and mouth disease (coxsackievirus).  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis  Diagnosis is made clinically (ie via clinical history and examination). Investigation  Possible for diagnostic confirmation:  VZV DNA detection from vesicular fluid sample skin swab (eg via PCR/ microscopy/immunofluorescence/culture)  serology for VZV antibodies, or in severe disease VZV in blood cultures.  For complications or differentials:  bloods  chest imaging, eg chest X-ray in VZV pneumonia – typically showing diffuse changes in both lungs  head imaging  CSF analysis.  Management  Mostly self-limiting; in healthy children, treatment is not usually given.  In higher-risk groups treatment should be given quickly from onset.  Immunoglobulins are also given prophylactically if the patient has been in contact with someone with active disease.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Referral  Urgent advice for the pregnant, breastfeeding, neonates and the immunocompromised.  Referral needed for varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZV-IG) treatment in these groups.  Hospitalisation for possible severe complications.  Severity also indicates whether oral or IV antivirals are needed. Non-pharmacological  Patient information (eg reducing transmission to others by staying at home until lesions are crusted over as well as avoiding high-risk groups; risk of secondary infection and avoiding scratching).  Emollients for lesions.  Trimming children’s fingernails (common introduction of secondary infection via scratching).  Supportive – rest, adequate fluid intake.  Breastfeeding considered safe if the mother has active VZV infection, unless lesions are on the nipples (but still, specialist advice is needed). Pharmacological  Analgesia/symptom control with paracetamol.  Antihistamines may reduce pruritis (eg oral chlorphenamine, but not in pregnancy).  Acyclovir is the usual first line treatment for severe infections and complications such as varicella pneumonia. Group Pharmacological treatment >14 years of age Antivirals (eg aciclovir 800mg PO 5×/day for 1 week) More effective in acute phase (1–3 days from onset) Immunocompromised VZV-IGs + antivirals Specialist advice needed, eg from infectious disease or OBGYN Pregnancy VZV-IGs + antivirals Note: no antiviral licensed for pregnancy Prevention

DR. JAM  Serology testing for VZV antibodies performed in healthcare workers and pregnancy (often at 12-week appointment).  Vaccination possible, especially during preconceptual planning if naïve (routine childhood VZV vaccination not in the UK, happens in the USA).  Vaccination is given to naïve healthcare workers.  Transmission reduction in active infection – avoidance of the immunocompromised/pregnant, staying home from school/work.  Post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis via VZV-IGs:  given to the immunocompromised  if VZV-naïve pregnant woman has contact with someone with chickenpox and < 20 weeks or ≥ 37weeks of gestation  neonates if the mother develops chickenpox about 1 week prior to delivery and within about 1 week from birth (though may be considered beyond this).  Prognosis  In younger, healthy people – normally good outcome, with resulting lifelong immunity (but not to shingles).  Poses mortality risk (80% of VZV deaths occur in adults).  Complications are more likely with increased age, immunocompromise, pregnancy, comorbidities, neonatal or intrauterine infection. Possible complications  Common – secondary skin infection.  Dehydration (usually in the prodrome phase).  Pneumonia (normally < 1 week following lesion onset).  Arthritis.  Orchitis.  Organ – glomerulonephritis, hepatitis, pancreatitis.  Ocular – optic neuritis, iritis, keratitis.  CNS – eg acute cerebellar ataxia, Reye syndrome, meningitis, encephalitis.  Blood – thrombocytopenia, disseminated intravascular coagulation.  CVS – myocarditis. Specific complications of maternal chickenpox  10% develop pneumonia (risk increases with length of gestation).  Miscarriage.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Prematurity.  Intrauterine infection.  Neonatal infection:  1–4weeks prior to delivery – approximately half of the neonates become infected  if the mother’s lesion onset is 1 week before or after delivery, there is a higher risk of severe neonatal infection  one-third of cases are fatal  neonates have a higher risk of dissemination or haemorrhagic consequences.  0–28 weeks' gestation – fetal varicella syndrome (incidence < 1% if ≤ 12 weeks, and approximately 2% in 13–20 weeks)  20–27 weeks' gestation – higher risk of shingles in infancy/early childhood.  Other Fetal varicella syndrome is the presence of ≥ 1 of these features:  dermatomal skin scarring  eye defects  limb hypoplasia neurological abnormalities. Viral Infections And Antivirals A virus is a small intracellular organism comprising nucleic acid and outer protein coat, they cause a wide spectrum of viral illness worldwide from common cold to HIV infection.  Overview Key Facts  A virus is a small intracellular organism comprising nucleic acid and outer protein coat:  they cause a wide spectrum of viral illness worldwide from common cold to HIV infection  viral infection can cause worldwide pandemics eg Spanish flu pandemic 1918, the current coronavirus pandemic (COVID-19).  Influenza is a very common viral disease worldwide, associated with significant mortality in young children, elderly patients, and the immunocompromised.  Viral haemorrhagic fever is a rare clinical presentation endemic in the tropics and associated with very high case fatality. Examples include Ebola; Lassa fever is a rare clinical presentation.  Many viral infections, including measles, mumps and rubella, are prevented by vaccination.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Horizontal transmission is very common, with various different routes eg body fluid exposure (HIV), blood-borne (Hepatitis B and C), aerosol-borne (influenza) and vector-borne eg Dengue fever.  Vertical transmission of infection is seen in some viral infections, notably HIV, Hepatitis B, Rubella and varicella zoster infection. Aetiology  Classification is based on the underlying genetic structure (RNA vs. DNA), viral structure, and replication cycle. Important groups of viruses include:  herpes viruses eg HSV-1, are associated with a wide range of clinical disease, including peri-oral and genital ulceration, infectious mononucleosis, and chickenpox  pox viruses – double stranded DNA viruses including smallpox virus  retroviruses eg HIV-1 and HTLV-1. These are single stranded RNA viruses which use a reverse transcriptase enzyme to form DNA that is integrated into the host genome  arboviruses (arthropod-borne viruses) are a group of heterogeneous viruses transmitted by animals, including Dengue virus (mosquito-borne). Pathophysiology  As intracellular pathogens, viruses usually cause disease by directly inducing cell death.  Certain viruses eg EBV, Hepatitis C, and HPV are oncogenic.  Clinical Presentation  There is a wide spectrum of clinical disease associated with different virus types.  Clinical features of influenza infection include:  rhinorrhoea  fever  rigors  malaise  myalgia  arthralgia  dry cough  shortness of breath  Viral hepatitis infection may be asymptomatic, or present acutely with fulminant liver failure, and present after slow insidious progression to chronic hepatitis:  acute – right upper quadrant pain, myalgia, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea. This is usually self-limiting, but a proportion of patients may develop fulminant liver failure with jaundice and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy).

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  chronic infection (hepatitis B and C) – several years after initial infection, patients develop signs of chronic liver disease eg itch, abdominal swelling, spider naevi.  Herpes viruses have several different clinical presentations:  herpes simplex virus-1 – perioral cold sores; confusion, disorientation and fever due to meningoencephalitis; progressive visual deterioration with ophthalmic HSV  herpes simplex virus-2 – painful genital ulceration; meningoencephalitis  varicella zoster virus – widespread erythematous vesicular rash (chickenpox – primary infection) and subsequent unidermatomal blistering rash (shingles)  cytomegalovirus (CMV) – bloody diarrhoea (colitis) and visual blurring (retinitis) in severely immunocompromised patients eg advanced HIV infection, colitis and retinitis in immunosuppressed patients  epstein-Barr virus (EBV) – primary infection in adolescence or adulthood manifests as fever, persistent pharyngitis, malaise, and myalgia (infectious mononucleosis)  human herpes virus-8 infection causes a mild viral illness in most patients. Reactivation in immunocompromised hosts is associated with Kaposi’s sarcoma.  Mumps is a highly contagious disease of childhood which presents with headache, fever, and bilateral parotitis. Important complications of mumps include orchitis (swollen, painful testicles with long-term sub-fertility) and an acute meningitis.  Measles is a highly infectious disease of childhood which presents with fever and a diffuse erythematous maculopapuilar rash. It is associated with rare but important complications:  pneumonia – cough and shortness of breath  encephalitis – drowsiness, weakness and seizures.  Rubella presents with fever, a diffuse erythematous macular rash, and post-auricular lymphadenopathy. It is usually selflimiting but causes serious complications in pregnancy, including miscarriage and congenital rubella (deafness and congenital cataract).  Differential Diagnosis  Influenza infection – infectious mononucleosis, upper respiratory tract infection, bacterial pneumonia, sepsis.  Acute viral hepatitis – hepatitis A, E, B or C infection, EBV infection, CMV infection, HIV infection, paracetamol overdose, drug toxicity.  Encephalitis – HSV-1 encephalitis, VZV encephalitis, enterovirus, autoimmune disease.  Fever and rash – roseola (self-limiting macular viral exanthem), Scarlet fever, measles, rubella, meningococcal sepsis, relapsing fever, typhus, Dengue fever.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Most viral infections can be diagnosed clinically but in cases of diagnostic doubt, viral PCR and serological testing for specific IgM antibodies (indicating acute infection) can be useful.  In unwell patients, blood tests can be performed to exclude organ damage:

DR. JAM  full blood count (FBC) – non-specific findings eg neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, lymphopenia  LFTs – transaminitis seen in acute/chronic Hepatitis and EBV infection.  Serological testing is important in patients presenting with acute or chronic liver disease as Hepatitis B and C can progress to chronic infection and cancer, and are widely treatable.  Chest radiograph is useful in breathless patients (typically see diffuse interstitial shadowing in contrast to focal consolidation with bacterial infection).  Management Non-Pharmacological  Many viral infections, including measles, mumps, rubella, Hepatitis A and E, EBV and Dengue fever are self-limiting and managed conservatively with good supportive care.  Non-immune pregnant women exposed to rubella infection should be referred urgently to an obstetrician and paediatric infectious diseases specialist. Unfortunately, IVIG is not widely effective in preventing congenital rubella and termination is often recommended. Pharmacological  Influenza infection - oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is recommended for ‘at risk’ patient groups – adults > 65 years, children under 6 months, pregnant women and patients with diabetes mellitus, chronic respiratory, heart, kidney and liver disease and severe immunosuppression:  shortens the duration of infection by one day (reducing duration of infectivity) and reduces mortality in critically ill patients  hospital in-patients exposed to influenza infection are generally treated with prophylactic oseltamivir.  Pharmacological treatment of Hepatitis B infection depends on clinical presentation:  fulminant liver failure – antiviral therapy with lamivudine or tenofovir  chronic liver failure – prolonged 6-12 month course of antiviral (entecavir or tenofovir) or pegylated interferon. These treatments are reserved for patients with active chronic disease with potential for high infectivity.  Pharmacological treatment of Hepatitis C infection is reserved for patients with chronic infection lasting > 6 months and is managed by specialists.  Surgical  Fulminant liver failure due to Hepatitis B, EBV, or CMV infection may necessitate emergency liver transplantation.  Prognosis  Risk factors for severe influenza include extremes of age, pregnancy, and comorbidities. Most viral infections are self-limiting with low morbidity and mortality.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Viral Hepatitis Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver that can be caused by a number of different aetiologies.  Overview Key Facts  Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver that can be caused by a number of different aetiologies, including:  viruses  autoimmunity  ischaemia  alcohol  genetics.  Some people have no symptoms, while others can develop:  jaundice  poor appetite  lethargy  abdominal pain  diarrhoea.  Viral hepatitis is the most common cause of hepatitis globally.  There are five major hepatitis viruses:  hepatitis A:  spread via the faecal–oral route  virus – ribonucleic acid (RNA)  no chronic state.  hepatitis B:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – DNA  can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  hepatitis C:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  can progress to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  hepatitis D:  spread – blood-borne (dependent on concurrent hepatitis B infection for replication)  virus – incomplete  chronicity – those with chronic hepatitis B have an increased incidence of cirrhosis.

DR. JAM  hepatitis E:  spread – faecal–oral, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  chronicity – only in those severely immunocompromised.  Hepatitis can be acute or chronic and rarely results in acute liver failure.  Management is often supportive and dependent on the type, which can be self-limiting.  Hepatitis B and C can progress to chronic hepatitis which can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer.  Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with end-stage liver disease/decompensated cirrhosis. Epidemiology  Viral hepatitis is the most common type of hepatitis globally.  Hepatitis A is endemic in Africa and South America.  Hepatitis B is endemic in the Far East, Africa and the Mediterranean.  Risk groups for hepatitis B:  people born or bought up in a country where the infection is common  intravenous (IV) drug users  health workers  commercial sex workers  men who have sex with men  people who have had multiple sexual partners. Aetiology  There are five major hepatitis viruses.  Hepatitis A:  spread via the faecal–oral route  virus – ribonucleic acid (RNA)  chronicity – no chronic state.  Hepatitis B:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – DNA  chronicity – can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  Hepatitis C:  spread – blood-borne, sexual transmission, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  chronicity – can progress to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.  Hepatitis D:  spread – blood-borne (dependent on concurrent hepatitis B infection for replication)  virus – incomplete

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  chronicity – those with chronic hepatitis B have increased incidence of cirrhosis.  Hepatitis E:  spread – faecal–oral, vertical transmission  virus – RNA  chronicity – only in those severely immunocompromised.  Other viral infections can cause hepatitis:  Epstein–Barr virus  yellow fever  cytomegalovirus  rubella  herpes simplex. Pathophysiology  Hepatitis virus replicates in hepatocytes, interfering with cell function and causing liver inflammation, injury and wound healing.  Over time (for some viruses) this process may lead to fibrosis.  Clinical Presentation  Viral hepatitis infection may be asymptomatic, present acutely with fulminant liver failure or present after slow insidious progression to chronic hepatitis:  acute:  right upper quadrant pain, myalgia, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea  usually self-limiting, but a proportion of patients may develop fulminant liver failure with jaundice and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy).  chronic infection (hepatitis B and C):  several years after initial infection, patients develop signs of chronic liver disease, eg itch, abdominal swelling, spider naevi.  Hepatitis A:  fever  malaise  anorexia  nausea  arthralgia  jaundice.  Hepatitis B:  most people are asymptomatic  some may present with complications, eg:  cirrhosis  hepatocellular carcinoma  liver failure.  often resembles hepatitis A, although arthralgia and urticaria are much more common (prodromal illness).  Hepatitis C:

DR. JAM  less severe than A or B  often asymptomatic  people who are chronically infected will experience nonspecific symptoms including malaise, weakness and anorexia.  Hepatitis E:  presentation similar to hepatitis A  self-limiting illness  however, acute hepatic failure is common in those who are pregnant. Yellow discolouration of the sclera in a jaundiced patient:  Differential Diagnosis  Hepatitis caused by a number of different aetiologies, including:  autoimmunity  ischaemia  alcohol  genetics  other infections:  viruses:  Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)  yellow fever  cytomegalovirus  rubella  herpes simplex.  malaria  toxoplasmosis  brucellosis  leptospirosis.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  In patients with suspected hepatitis, blood tests can be performed to exclude organ damage:  full blood count (FBC) – non-specific findings, eg neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, lymphopenia  LFTs – transaminitis seen in acute/chronic hepatitis and EBV infection  coagulation screen  serological testing is important in patients presenting with acute or chronic liver disease, as hepatitis B and C can progress to chronic infection and cancer and are widely treatable.  Further tests for individual diagnoses are listed below.  Hepatitis A:  hepatitis A serology:  checks for hepatitis A virus immunoglobulin M (HAV-IgM) and hepatitis A virus immunoglobulin G (HAV-IgG)  positive HAV-IgM and HAV-IgG means acute hepatitis A is likely  positive HAV-IgG and negative HAV-IgM indicates past hepatitis A or immunity from previous vaccination.  check liver function tests – alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) may be significantly increased (>1000 IU/l).  Hepatitis B:  hepatitis B serology:  hepatitis surface antigen (HBsAg) rises in current hepatitis B infection  after HBsAg is detected, hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) and hepatitis B virus DNA (HBV-DNA) are detectable around the same time.  presence of HBsAg, HBeAg and HBV-DNA indicates progression to chronic hepatitis B  IgM anti-HBc indicates infection within the last 6 months  IgG anti-HBc persists for life and indicates past infection  anti-HBs without anti-HBc is a marker of immunisation.  Hepatitis C:  anti-HCV antibodies confirm exposure  HCV-PCR confirms ongoing infection.  Management Pharmacological and conservative management  Hepatitis A:  symptomatic supportive care for nausea, pain or itch  rest  if pain relief required suggest paracetamol/ibuprofen/weak opioid, eg codeine if mild liver impairment

DR. JAM  nausea – metoclopramide or cyclizine  itch – maintain cool, well-ventilated environment, wear loose-clothing, avoid hot baths or showers or chlorphenamine  notify the Health Protection Unit for surveillance and contract tracing  avoid alcohol.  Hepatitis B:  symptomatic care as above  notify the Health Protection Unit  avoid alcohol  antivirals – pegylated interferon alpha-2a  or nucleotide analogues, eg tenofovir – not usually indicated for acute hepatitis B except in cases of fulminant hepatitis.  Hepatitis C:  notify Health Protection team  lifestyle advice:  stop alcohol consumption  stop smoking  maintain healthy body weight and diet.  acute hepatitis C  up to 45 percent of acute cases spontaneously clear without treatment within 6 months  if treatment is required, this should be the same regime as with chronic hepatitis C.  chronic hepatitis C:  antiviral therapy –direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are now considered first-line treatment  the type will depend on the genotype of the infection  usually a once daily, oral tablet regimen for either 8 or 12 weeks  The goal of treatment is to eradicate the virus, achieve a sustained virological response (SVR) and prevent disease progression.  SVR (undetectable HCV RNA in the blood 12 weeks after treatment completion) is considered to be equivalent to a cure.  Hepatitis E:  no specific treatment  self-limiting disease.  Surgical management  Hepatitis may progress to end-stage liver disease.  Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with end-stage liver disease/decompensated cirrhosis.  Prognosis  Hepatitis A is usually self-limiting:

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  chronicity does not occur and < 1% of patients develop fulminant hepatitis.  In hepatitis B, there is a risk of extra-hepatic manifestations, eg:  glomerulonephritis  vasculitis  polyarteritis.  15–20% of chronic hepatitis B patients will develop cirrhosis.  In hepatitis C, 20–50% will clear the virus spontaneously without treatment. 50–80% will develop chronic hepatitis C. Viral Meningitis Inflammation of the meninges can be caused by a variety of viruses.  Overview Key Facts  Inflammation of the meninges can be caused by a variety of viruses.  Viral meningitis is usually self-limiting with no serious complications. However, it may be clinically indistinguishable from acute bacterial meningitis.  Can become complicated in infants, immunocompromised patients and patients infected with herpes or arboviruses.  Management involves supportive care and antiviral treatment (for confirmed HSV, varicella zoster or CMV).  Good prognosis with viral meningitis, with neurological damage being very uncommon. Epidemiology  Common infection of the CNS.  Estimated incidence of 2.73 per 100 000 people.  Affects all ages but is most common in children.  No differences between ethnicities.  Boys more commonly affected compared with girls. Aetiology  Commonly caused by human enteroviruses.  Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV2) is the most common cause of viral meningitis in the West. Pathophysiology  Enteroviruses replicate in the muscle, liver and respiratory and GI tracts and then spread to the CNS through the blood.  The viruses then penetrate the blood–brain barrier by infecting endothelial cells or by use of migrating leukocytes.

DR. JAM  Viruses then spread through the subarachnoid space to cause meningitis.  The immune system responds to CNS infection by releasing inflammatory cytokines, eg IL-6, TNF and lymphocytes.  Clinical Presentation  Presentation:  headache  nausea and vomiting  photophobia  neck stiffness  fever  rash.  Differential Diagnosis  May be clinically indistinguishable from bacterial meningitis.  Other differential diagnoses:  encephalitis  drug-induced meningitis  tuberculous meningitis  cryptococcal meningitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  CSF microscopy – WCC > 5 cells/mm3 (adult) and > 20 cells/mm3 (newborn)  CSF Gram stain – negative.  CSF bacterial culture - negative.  CSF protein – normal or elevated.  CSF glucose – may be low.  CT/MRI head scan – unremarkable.  Management  Supportive care – hydration, anti-pyretics, anti-emetics and analgesia.  Antiviral therapy – IV aciclovir or valaciclovir (for confirmed HSV, varicella zoster or CMV).  Prognosis  Good prognosis with viral meningitis, with neurological damage being very uncommon.  Headache and malaise may persist for several weeks.  Can recur with different serotypes.  Other  Neurodevelopmental deficits in infants. Persistent headache and malaise.

Infections part 2 MIL ALRAJHI

stem: A 61-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with increasing shortness of breath over the past two months. He also complains of increased lethargy, night sweats and 3-kg weight loss. He has no past medical history of note and no allergies. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 134/72 mmHg and a heart rate of 84 bpm and regular. His temperature is 37.9 °C. There is a diastolic murmur in the aortic area on auscultation. His chest is clear and there are no signs of cardiac failure. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Value Hb 103 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 171 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 85 mm/ ﬁrst hour 0–10 mm/ﬁrst hour Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
explanation:
A Amoxicillin and gentamicin This patient has symptoms and signs of infective endocarditis. Management of native valve endocarditis in a patient with no drug allergies includes amoxicillin and gentamicin as the initial empirical approach. There is no evidence to suggest a route of entry for staphylococcal infection such as drug abuse, surgery or penetrating injury. C Flucloxacillin Flucloxacillin is usually used when Staphylococcus aureus is considered a risk such as in cases where patients who are injecting drug abusers present with endocarditis or where there is a history of recent orthopaedic surgery or injury. A Benzylpenicillin Benzylpenicillin is used in the management of infective endocarditis secondary to streptococci (eg Streptococcus viridans). It is not used as the initial antibiotic in the blind treatment of infective endocarditis. D Cefuroxime and gentamicin Cephalosporins are considered in the treatment of endocarditis related to HACEK organisms, HACEK being an acronym based on the ﬁrst letter of each organism: Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter (previously Actinobacillus), Cardiobacterium, Eikenella corrodens and Kingella. E Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin

This is a typical regimen considered for prosthetic valve endocarditis, ensuring robust antistaphylococcal coverage.

stem: A 59-year-old ﬁsherman has been referred to the Ophthalmology Department with a 6-month history of deteriorating vision. For a long time, he has been feeling generally more fatigued with myalgia and has lost approximately 6 kg in weight in the last two months since he moved from Nigeria to the United Kingdom. He has a background of type II diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, for which he takes metformin, aspirin, bisoprolol and atorvastatin. On examination, he has multiple excoriations over his entire body and there are some patches of skin depigmentation. Using a slit lamp, multiple corneal opacities and keratoconjunctival lesions are seen bilaterally. His visual acuity is 6/36 in both eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Onchocerciasis Onchocerciasis, otherwise known as African river blindness, is a ﬁlarial infection secondary to the nematode Onchocerca volvulus and is the second most common cause of infective blindness in the world. It is spread by the blackﬂy, which breeds in nearby fastﬂowing rivers and is endemic in East, West and Central Africa, along with South America and the Middle East. The disease can initially begin with dermatological signs, such as subcutaneous papules, lymphadenitis and skin depigmentation, before the onset of eye disease. O. volvulus will affect all ocular tissues, including the eyelid and conjunctiva and as the disease progresses, the cornea and sclera. Multiple ocular ﬁndings can be seen on examination, depending on the stage of disease, including chronic conjunctivitis, chemosis and corneal opacities. Occasionally, the nematode can be visualised in the anterior chamber using a slit lamp. Treatment is with ivermectin. E African trypanosomiasis African trypanosomiasis, otherwise known as African sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease caused by the parasite Trypanosoma brucei, which is transmitted to humans by bites of infected tsetse ﬂies. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa. Initial symptoms are nonspeciﬁc and include general malaise, fever, myalgia and occasionally pruritus. A painless chancre appears at the site of the bite. As the disease progresses into its later stages, the central nervous system

begins to become impaired with continuous headaches, daytime somnolence and behavioural changes before stupor and coma. B Blackwater fever Blackwater fever is the term given to intravascular haemolysis in a malarial infection causing symptoms, such as jaundice and acute kidney injury. It does not cause ocular symptoms as seen in this patient. C Schistosomiasis Schistosomiasis is a parasitic disease caused by ﬂukes. The disease is contracted when a host comes into contact with contaminated water and the larval form of the parasite infects the host through direct invasion of intact skin. The larvae are then able to mature inside the host and lay eggs. It is the host’s reaction to this process that causes the initial symptoms, including abdominal pain, diarrhoea and liver enlargement. In urogenital schistosomiasis, haematuria can be seen, followed by urogenital ﬁbrosis, with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. While it is a common disease, it does not cause blindness. D Mansonellosis Mansonellosis is a ﬁlarial disease that is commonly asymptomatic. The larvae are introduced into the host through different vectors, including an infected midge. They reside in the skin, subcutaneous tissues and body cavities, including the peritoneal and pleural cavities and occasionally the pericardium. If symptoms do appear, they are generally non-speciﬁc and include fever, fatigue and pruritus, although abdominal pain, pericarditis and pleuritis can occur. The microﬁlariae are capable of entering the eye and causing ocular symptoms. However, this is less common than onchocerciasis.
